papers.title: View, Review, Repeat: Towards Design Guidelines for 360° Virtual Experiences
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: 360° panoramic virtual experiences have become a widely adopted medium for enabling remote exploration of cultural heritage sites and tourist destinations. Compared to fully immersive virtual reality systems, these experiences provide accessible, cost-effective web-based environments that allow users to navigate panoramic scenes enriched with interactive and multimedia elements. Despite their growing use in museums, tourism, and heritage dissemination, the design characteristics of contemporary 360° virtual experiences remain insufficiently examined from a holistic perspective. This study investigates how such experiences are structured and designed in practice. We conducted a structured review of 29 publicly available 360° virtual experiences from cultural heritage and tourism contexts, examining technical implementation, navigation mechanics, information presentation, and content formats. In addition, a focus group with 6 experts in digital experience design and cultural heritage applications qualitatively evaluated a subset of 20 content-rich experiences, assessing aesthetic quality, usability, informational clarity, and structural coherence. Our findings reveal recurring design patterns as well as common limitations, including reliance on sequential navigation, inconsistent integration of interpretive content, and limited support for layered information exploration. By synthesizing quantitative structural analysis with qualitative expert insights, this work proposes a preliminary set of empirically grounded, expert-informed design hypotheses, paving the way towards supporting the development of more engaging 360° virtual experiences for cultural heritage and tourism applications.

papers.title: Assessing the role of spatial coordinates in K-means clustering for capturing geometric patterns in archaeological FDEM data
papers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Identifying archaeological features through geophysical data interpretation remains a key challenge in non-invasive prospection. Geophysical surveys are increasingly combined with unsupervised machine learning, particularly K-means clustering, to enhance the detection of buried remains. However, it operates only in attribute space, ignoring the spatial nature of archaeological structures. This study assesses whether adding spatial coordinates in K-means clustering of Frequency Domain ElectroMagnetic data improves the delineation of anthropogenic features. A 2D approach, based only on electromagnetic components, is compared with a 4D configuration including geographic coordinates. FDEM data from the Iron Age site of Torre Galli (Italy) show that adding spatial coordinates does not outperform the 2D approach. Instead, results become more sensitive to normalization and often reflect spatial proximity rather than geophysical contrasts, reducing interpretability. These findings indicate that incorporating spatial coordinates into a standard K-means framework does not systematically improve archaeological feature delineation and increases sensitivity to data preprocessing.

papers.title: Digital Reconstruction and Motion-Based Interactive Presentation of Qing Dynasty Court Opera Costumes
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Qing Dynasty court opera costumes are material cultural heritage objects whose meanings are closely tied to performance, movement, and symbolic visual systems. While static digitization can document costume forms and surface details, it often fails to convey how motifs, sleeve structures, and bodily motion shape the performative experience of court opera. To address this limitation, we present an interactive digital system for the reconstruction and motion-based presentation of Qing Dynasty court opera costumes. The system combines: (1) high-fidelity 3D reconstruction of 30 representative costumes; (2) a FLUX-based diffusion generation module with LoRA fine-tuning for user-driven pattern exploration within the visual vocabulary of court opera costumes; and (3) a markerless pose-estimation pipeline using a single monocular camera to drive real-time costume animation and self-implemented lightweight hybrid costume dynamics in Unity. A comparative user study ( \(N=22\) ) evaluated the system against a static 3D display condition. Results indicate that the interactive system maintained comparable perceived costume-feature reproduction while significantly improving system usability and immersion ( \(p=0.0067\) ) and perceived cultural dissemination value ( \(p=0.0224\) ). These findings suggest that digital reconstruction, generative pattern exploration, and motion-based interaction can extend static costume archives into more engaging visual heritage experiences for objects whose cultural meanings depend on both material appearance and performative use.

papers.title: A methodological protocol for the generation and evaluation of AI-generated cultural heritage content
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in cultural heritage dissemination has outpaced the development of rigorous procedures to ensure historical accuracy, formal coherence, and educational reliability. This article proposes a methodological protocol for the generation and evaluation of AI-generated cultural heritage content, with a particular focus on image-based representations. To establish the need for such a protocol, a bibliometric review of literature published between 2020 and 2025 in Web of Science and Scopus was conducted, confirming the absence of a comprehensive and replicable framework specifically designed to assess the historical veracity of AI-generated heritage imagery. The proposed protocol integrates four components: (1) a standardised image-generation procedure based on zero-shot prompting and first-output selection; (2) an interdisciplinary expert evaluation instrument comprising 12 items organised into five analytical dimensions; (3) an automated multimodal validation layer designed to contrast human and AI-based assessments; and (4) a predefined analytical plan encompassing internal consistency, inter-rater agreement, descriptive statistics, and qualitative thematic analysis. Rather than presenting empirical findings, the article offers a reproducible framework intended to support future comparative studies and professional applications in heritage communication, education, and digital dissemination. This article offers a reproducible framework intended to support future comparative studies and professional applications in heritage communication, education, and digital dissemination. The proposed protocol aims to reduce the risks of misinformation, enhance methodological transparency, and promote historically grounded uses of GenAI in cultural heritage contexts.

papers.title: Automated Indexing of Historical Postcards: An End-to-End Approach Combining Image and Text Analysis
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Historical postcards are of great interest to different researchers and especially historians. Preserving these documents for future generations is important. Indeed, they represent valuable cultural heritage documents combining visual imagery with textual information, but manual indexing of large digitized collections is prohibitively expensive in time and resources. This paper presents an end-to-end approach for automated historical postcard indexing that integrates computer vision and natural language processing techniques. Our modular pipeline employs fine-tuned YOLO models to detect text types and postal markings, EasyOCR for text transcription, CamemBERT for named entity recognition enabling automatic geolocation, and DINOv2 models for visual content classification across ten semantic topics. Support Vector Machines predict keywords for images lacking textual descriptions using DINOv2 image embeddings, while complex postal markings are segmented and transcribed. We demonstrate our approach on the recto (illustrated front side) of 4,293 digitized postcards from the Grand Est region of France (1899-1930). Our results show that, among the latest YOLO models, fine-tuned YOLOv12x achieves 0.83 weighted average precision for detection. Fine-tuned DINOv2 attains 0.91 weighted average precision for image classification, while CLIP and other classification models do not exceed 0.83. Finally, named entity recognition successfully geolocates 52% of postcards. In fully automatic operation, the complete pipeline assigns at least a coarse topic to almost every postcard and at least one richer field (a keyword, a geolocation, or a date) to about 80% of them, leaving fewer than 1% essentially un-indexed. Our work contributes to digital humanities by demonstrating effective integration of multiple AI techniques for automated heritage document analysis and provides a publicly available dataset for future research.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Information Guided Super-Resolution for Mural Hyperspectral Image
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Hyperspectral image (HSI) supports non-invasive pigment analysis and digital restoration of ancient murals, yet its spatial resolution is fundamentally constrained by acquisition hardware and fragile heritage environments. Existing hyperspectral super-resolution (SR) approaches are largely developed for remote sensing imagery and assume homogeneous textures, linear spectral mixtures, and large-scale training data. These assumptions do not hold for mural imagery, where fine brushstroke details coexist with smooth plaster substrates and mineral pigments exhibit nonlinear spectral mixing. Consequently, directly applying conventional HSI-SR models often leads to over-smoothed textures or spectral distortion. We propose FIGNet, a mural-oriented hyperspectral SR framework explicitly designed to address these domain mismatches. First, FIGNet introduces an adaptive gated spectral–spatial frequency decomposition to explicitly separate structural background and high-frequency cultural details, enabling differential processing aligned with mural texture characteristics. Second, FIGNet performs joint spectral–spatial contextual refinement to preserve pigment signatures during sub-pixel reconstruction. Finally, a hybrid optimization objective incorporating spectral–spatial variation regularization and adaptive frequency-domain supervision is designed to stabilize reconstruction under limited training data and reduce spectral inconsistency. Extensive experiments on two mural HSI datasets under multiple upscaling factors demonstrate that FIGNet achieves superior spatial detail recovery while maintaining spectral fidelity, validating the importance of frequency-aware and spectrally coupled modeling for cultural heritage HSI-SR.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of an AI-mediated Visual Co-Creation System for Participatory Cultural Heritage in Museums
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: In response to the limited participatory and experiential depth of traditional display-based museums, this study explores how AI can mediate more meaningful cultural engagement. It adopts a three-phase research pathway—CoDesign, CoCreation, and Evaluation—to reimagine how AI can support participatory cultural heritage experiences. Through CoDesign workshops with museum professionals, designers, and visitors, we iteratively developed an AI-mediated co-creative system integrating iPad sketching, gesture-based control, AI image generation, and a virtual exhibition environment. Based on 349 visitor responses, we applied PLS-SEM and fsQCA to examine how configurations of co-creative interaction design quality, embodied engagement, aesthetic experience, cultural participation, and cultural perception shape cultural identity. Findings show that AI-driven co-creative design significantly strengthens visitors’ cultural participation and cultural perception, while supporting immediate perceived cultural connection. These findings offer both a validated case of AI-enabled participatory heritage and transferable principles for museums transitioning toward co-creative, visitor-centered exhibition models.

papers.title: Preserving Intangible Cultural Heritage Through Augmented Reality and Machine Learning: A Case Study of the One-Bead Netting Stitch
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Bead weaving, as a form of Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH), embodies tacit procedural knowledge transmitted through high-dexterity, fine-motor practice. Existing digital preservation approaches predominantly emphasize artifact documentation, image archives, or stepwise visual overlays, offering limited capacity to capture and formalize the embodied micro-actions that constitute craft expertise. This paper presents a computational framework for modelling bead weaving gestures as structured, classifiable units using egocentric Augmented Reality (AR) sensing and sequential deep learning. Focusing on the One-Bead Netting stitch as a bounded and repeatable workflow, a gesture taxonomy was developed through craft analysis and expert consultation to operationalize core micro-actions for segmentation and supervised modelling. The system was deployed on Microsoft HoloLens 2 to capture lightweight three-dimensional hand skeletal data from two novice participants who completed structured training prior to data collection. Gesture data were recorded from an egocentric perspective, enabling non-invasive tracking of fine-motor weaving actions during natural weaving of the One-Bead Netting stitch. Following a supervised learning pipeline encompassing schema design, skeletal normalization, temporal segmentation, and model training, a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network and Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) architecture was trained to classify four compulsory bead weaving gestures, achieving 69.22% validation accuracy. A reduced two-class model focusing on the primary stitching gestures achieved 73% validation accuracy. Beyond classification performance, the study demonstrates a reproducible methodology for translating embodied craft practice into computationally interpretable representations. The proposed framework contributes to the development of gesture-level preservation strategies and lays the groundwork for AR-based instructional feedback systems that support the transmission of embodied cultural knowledge within Human-Computer Interaction contexts.

papers.title: Chinese Painting Semantic Resource for Resolution-Aware Digitisation and Structured Heritage Access
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Chinese painting digitisation poses a distinctive heritage-informatics challenge: culturally salient visual structures such as brushwork, intentional blank space, and text–image coexistence are difficult to document, access, and research with general-purpose collection and computational representations. We present the Chinese Painting Semantic Resource (CPSR), comprising 1,797 deduplicated painting-image records with a 12-column experiment-facing metadata release and a bilingual, 24-type lightweight semantic application profile. Using single-seed classification experiments across six architectures as diagnostic probes of resized derivative inputs, we find that 512 \(\times\) 512 gives the best primary-category result (96.7%) and broad gains over 224 \(\times\) 224, whereas the effect of 1024 \(\times\) 1024 on seven merged technique–subject classes is model-dependent: it gives the best individual result (81.7%) but a 0.9 percentage-point lower cross-model mean than 512 \(\times\) 512. Three post-hoc Grad-CAM case studies provide exploratory, correlational observations rather than quantitative localisation validation. By linking culturally grounded profile design to representative CIDOC-CRM, Getty AAT, IIIF, and W3C Web Annotation mappings, CPSR shows how local semantic distinctions can be retained while preparing for standards-aligned access; it does not claim complete per-record profile population or model-level semantic understanding.

papers.title: An Object Detection Benchmark of a Novel Byzantine Iconography Dataset
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: A novel dataset of Byzantine iconography, ByzArtX, is presented and benchmarked against several state of the art object detectors. The dataset contains images of religious significance from the Byzantine and Christian Art Museum in Athens and Mount Athos, Greece. The icon images have been manually annotated to contain 124 classes, which represent personas and objects of religious significance. The superior performance of attention-based DETR networks over YOLO-based detectors has been confirmed in our benchmark, consistently with available literature. To the best of the authors knowledge the present dataset is the first application of Computer Vision technology to Eastern Orthodox Christian iconography.

papers.title: Non-destructive wood species identification in cultural heritage artefacts: Multi-angle CT imaging combined with AI-enhanced recognition
papers.abstract: Non-destructive wood species identification is a critical requirement in cultural heritage conservation, yet traditional thin-section anatomical methods demand destructive sampling unacceptable for irreplaceable artefacts. This study presents a practical, open-source framework combining multi-angle X-ray micro-computed tomography (Micro-CT) with an enhanced YOLOv8 deep learning model for direct adoption by museum and conservation practitioners. CT images acquired from three orthogonal sections (transverse, radial, tangential) capture complementary anatomical features—vessel distribution, growth ring patterns, and density variations—enabling species discrimination in traditional furniture, carvings, and musical instruments without physical contact. A Multi-Scale Dynamic Weighting (MSDW) mechanism—the core architectural innovation of this work, inspired by dynamic convolution attention—adaptively extracts both large-scale structural patterns and fine-grained anatomical detail from CT images. Physics-informed feature analysis identifies mean density and vessel distribution as the primary discriminants for species classification, followed by growth ring contrast and anisotropy indices. The optimised V8NGB model achieves 97.0% mAP50 across 17 wood species central to Chinese cultural heritage—a 9.4% gain over baseline YOLOv8—at only 6.5 ms inference time, meeting the demands of real-time conservation workflows. All trained models and source code are openly available at https://github.com/liwei0214/wood-CT-heritage .

papers.title: Geometry-Constrained Bidirectional Point Cloud Registration for Thin, Sheet-Like Heritage Artifacts
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Non-contact three-dimensional reconstruction of thin, sheet-like heritage artifacts poses significant geometric and registration challenges. Due to their fragility, these artifacts cannot be suspended or equipped with artificial markers, necessitating independent acquisition of their front and back surfaces. Subsequent registration proves difficult due to the limited number of shared geometric features and the scarcity of explicit physical constraints, which may result in rotational ambiguity, instability, and structural collapse during iterative optimization. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry-constrained bidirectional point cloud registration method specifically tailored for thin, sheet-like heritage artifacts. The method integrates semantic-guided preprocessing, Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-based geometric normalization, and a thickness-aware registration strategy. The estimated physical thickness is incorporated as a geometric constraint to preserve structural integrity during registration. Rotational ambiguity is resolved by evaluating a finite set of global rotation hypotheses, each refined using the point-to-plane Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm, with the optimal transformation selected via a geometry-aware fitness criterion consistent with the thickness scale. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves competitive or improved performance in most cases, particularly in projected area consistency and physically plausible front–back alignment. In addition, the thickness-aware constraint and rotation hypothesis evaluation reduce the risk of degenerate configurations in which the two surfaces are incorrectly flipped while still yielding deceptively acceptable numerical scores, supporting reliable non-contact digitization of delicate and thin heritage artifacts. Implementation details are available at https://zyz-nwpu.github.io/GCBPCR/ .

papers.title: Advancing 3D Cultural Heritage Digitization between the 5D Culture Project, the 4CH Project, and the Twin it! Campaign
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: The integration of advanced digital technologies is reshaping cultural heritage (CH) documentation, enabling new approaches to conservation, analysis, and dissemination. This paper presents an integrated and open digital workflow for the survey, management, and reuse of complex architectural heritage, using Villa Aldrovandi-Mazzacorati as a case study. The approach combines fixed-station laser scanning, terrestrial and aerial photogrammetry, and mobile SLAM-based mapping to generate high-resolution, reality-based 3D datasets. The proposed multi-sensor acquisition framework is critically assessed in terms of completeness, geometric accuracy, efficiency, interoperability, and long-term reuse. Results demonstrate that the integrated approach delivers reliable and comprehensive metric documentation while significantly reducing acquisition time compared with single-sensor strategies. The resulting HBIM model and associated web-based platform support structured information management, conservation planning, multidisciplinary collaboration, and online dissemination. In parallel, reality-based 3D meshes are successfully repurposed for immersive virtual reality (VR) experiences, enhancing accessibility and public engagement. By adopting open and standardized data formats, the workflow promotes long-term sustainability and FAIR-compliant reuse of digital heritage assets, offering a scalable and transferable framework for future 3D heritage initiatives across architectural and territorial contexts. Overall, the approach supports both specialist conservation workflows and public-facing dissemination, bridging the gap between technical heritage documentation and cultural interpretation.

papers.title: Community-driven literary archives: Reddit book discussions across the COVID-19 pandemic
papers.abstract: Abstract Online communities increasingly function as informal collective memory archives, preserving and curating literary discussions outside traditional digital libraries. This paper investigates the evolution of book-related discourse within the Reddit community r/books across three periods surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic: pre-pandemic (2019), pandemic (2020–2021), and later period (2022). Leveraging a combination of text mining, named entity recognition, and keyword extraction, we examine changes in book mentions, co-occurrence patterns, dominant genres, and thematic emphases in user comments. Our findings indicate that discussions during the pandemic period largely intensified and diversified existing reading interests rather than introducing entirely new preferences. We observe temporal shifts in discussion topics, from narrative-focused critiques to broader social and political themes during the pandemic years, followed by increased attention to introspective and experimental topics in the later period. While these patterns coincide with the pandemic period, they should be interpreted alongside other social, political, and cultural developments that occurred during the same period and may also have influenced literary discussions. Overall, the study highlights the value of computational analysis of community-generated digital archives for documenting evolving literary practices and understanding how online reading communities reflect broader historical contexts.

papers.title: Machine Learning Techniques for Inter- and Intra-Site Analysis of Middle and Upper Paleolithic Stone Artifacts from the Mirak and Delazian Sites, Iran
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: The study of Paleolithic assemblages is fundamental to understanding early human technology and dispersals. However, traditional analysis relies on subjective methods that are challenging to scale. This study introduces a machine learning (ML) framework to bring quantitative approaches to the techno-typological analysis of lithic artifacts. We focus on datasets from two neighboring Paleolithic sites on the Iranian Plateau: Mirak and Delazian. The former comprises three archaeological deposits including an Upper Paleolithic deposit dating to approximately 21-28 ka, a Middle Paleolithic one around 43-55 ka, and an intermediate phase with mixed characteristics dated between 26 and 33 ka and the latter includes an Upper Paleolithic deposit with the estimated dating around 20-40 ka. We developed and evaluated six ML models, including a high-performing ensemble combining Random Forest and XGBoost. The ensemble achieved 97% accuracy in pairwise classification and 84% in multiclass scenarios, successfully distinguishing closely related archaeological and chronological artifacts based on techno-typological attributes. Leveraging this validated classification framework and evaluating the similarity of these assemblages, we propose a structured method for chronological refinement. By benchmarking the Delazian assemblage against the absolutely dated stratigraphic sequences at Mirak, we constrain its broad age estimate of early Upper Paleolithic (20–40 ka to a more specific timeframe of 21–33 ka). This data-driven methodology offers a robust and replicable tool for chronological assessment, especially in regions dominated by unstratified surface sites, and demonstrates the transformative potential of ML in archaeological research.

papers.title: Chatty art labels: Evaluation of a conversational museum guide
papers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: This study explores the potential of a large language model (LLM)-powered Conversational Agent (CA) as a virtual museum guide to enhance visitor experi-ences. A prototype was developed, enabling natural language interactions with an LLM-powered CA about augmented reality (AR) artwork viewed through a head-mounted device (HMD). An exploratory field study with 22 museum vis-itors found positive evaluations based on a multimedia guide assessment scale. Results showed that the most prevalent were fact-based questions, while qual-itative findings highlighted appreciation for personalized information, concerns over information gaps, challenges in formulating questions, and discomfort with public voice interactions. The study underscores the potential for LLM-powered guides for museum experiences, while identifying design challenges for future re-search and development.

papers.title: AltarData: A novel annotated dataset for object detection in the Brazilian heritage altars using deep learning
papers.abstract: The evolution of machine learning techniques has enabled significant advances in the field of object detection using computer vision applied to historical buildings. Indeed, studies in this area can contribute to applications ranging from automatic digital documentation to the technological enhancement of inspections in cultural heritage sites. However, a recurring challenge lies in the quality and public availability of image datasets that enable the application of deep learning models in the context of heritage churches, particularly those focused on the interior environments of these religious buildings. In this context, the objective of this paper is to present a novel annotated dataset for object detection in Brazilian heritage altars using deep learning. The proposed dataset, named AltarData, comprises 1278 high-quality images collected from 33 churches located in 12 historical cities in Brazil. Three of these urban ensembles are recognized as UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Historic Town of Ouro Preto, the Historic Centre of Salvador de Bahia, and the Historic Centre of the Town of Diamantina. The data were carefully annotated, resulting in 12,093 labeled instances across six categories frequently found in Baroque and Rococo heritage altars: altar table, column, crucifix, saint sculpture, tabernacle, and throne. In addition, a deep learning with hyperparameter tuning approach was proposed, enabling the optimization of object recognition in heritage altars, achieving validation accuracies of up to 92.0% (altar table), 87.1% (column), 72.2% (crucifix), 85.1% (saint sculpture), 97.3% (tabernacle), and 84.7% (throne). In the test experiments, an F1-score of 79% was achieved using the MobileNetV2 configuration with width multiplier 0.35 and learning rate 0.0100. Overall, this paper contributes to the research field of new datasets for deep learning in cultural heritage sites, fostering advances in multi-object recognition within the interior environments of historical churches.

papers.title: A deep learning-driven mobile application for monitoring of tile degradation in heritage buildings
papers.abstract: Heritage buildings are vulnerable to gradual deterioration, making continuous inspection and regular maintenance essential for preventive conservation. However, conventional inspection methods rely heavily on manual on-site fieldwork, specialized heritage knowledge, and skilled personnel. This study presents an artificial intelligence-powered mobile application for real-time, on-site monitoring of tile degradation in heritage buildings. The developed Android-based application integrates several workflows, including automated pixel-wise damage detection using the deep learning algorithm You Only Look Once (YOLOv11), panoramic façade damage analysis enhanced through close-up semantic segmentation, and a question-based module designed to assist inspectors in damage identification. The application was developed to detect tile defects (craters, glaze detachment, and cracks) in heritage buildings. A dataset of 4965 annotated images was used for model training and evaluation, achieving a mean average precision (mAP50) of 68.2% for bounding-box detection and 51.8% for semantic segmentation on the test dataset. The proposed framework provides an accessible tool for automated heritage tile inspection, and has been tested on several cultural heritage buildings in Portugal.

papers.title: Collective Memory and Narrative Cohesion: A Computational Study of Palestinian Refugee Oral Histories in Lebanon
papers.abstract: This study uses the Palestinian Oral History Archive (POHA) to investigate how Palestinian refugees in Lebanon sustain a cohesive collective memory of the Nakba through shared narratives.Grounded in Halbwachs theory of collective memory, we employ statistical analysis of narrative pairwise similarities, examining the influence of shared gender and geography.We use textual representations and semantic embeddings to represent the interviews.Our analysis yields robust findings.Shared origin emerges as the primary driver of narrative similarity across thematic, factual, and semantic measures.This foundational connection is significantly amplified by a shared residence in Lebanon, with refugees sharing both origin and residence, exhibiting the highest narrative cohesion.Additionally, women's narratives show greater thematic cohesion, particularly in recounting experiences of the British occupation, underscoring the gendered dimensions of memory formation.This research deepens understanding of collective memory in diasporic settings, emphasizing the critical role of oral histories in safeguarding Palestinian identity and resisting erasure. Plain Language SummaryFor over seventy-five years, Palestinian refugees in Lebanon have kept memories of 1948 alive through storytelling.These oral histories describe life before the Nakba, the trauma of displacement, and the hardships of exile.More than personal records, they sustain collective identity across generations.Our research asks: Do refugees from different villages and backgrounds tell similar stories?What shapes those patterns?Drawing on theories of collective memory to form two hypotheses.First, gender would shape storytelling, since men and women experienced the Nakba and exile differently.Second, geography would matter, particularly when refugees from the same village settled in the same Lebanese camp, reinforcing shared narratives through continued proximity.We tested these ideas using the Palestinian Oral History Archive (POHA), one of the largest collections of refugee testimonies, preserving hundreds of Arabic semi-structured interviews documenting displacement, survival, and community life.We analyzed the collection using two complementary computational approaches.First, we examined archival metadata cataloging the people, places, and events mentioned in each interview.Comparing these references reveals whether refugee groups consistently highlight the same historical figures, landmarks, or episodes.Second, we developed a method for comparing narrative themes.We segmented interviews into topic-specific passages (such as Nakba-era violence or camp life), used language models to generate concise summaries, and then converted those summaries into numerical representations called semantic embeddings.This allowed us to measure how similar or different stories are thematically.Together, these methods provide distinct perspectives on collective memory.Our findings strongly confirm that gender structures memory.Women's narratives consistently cluster with other women's accounts, while men's stories show greater similarity to other men's.We also found that geographic continuity (when people from the same village are exiled to the same Lebanese camp) increased narrative similarity.However, shared origin or shared residence alone produced mixed results.This research demonstrates both the endurance of Palestinian collective memory in exile and the potential of computational methods to illuminate patterns in oral history at scale.By combining archival metadata with semantic analysis, we show how digital humanities approaches reveal structure in large collections of testimonies while respecting their complexity and human significance.

papers.title: ALMA: Automated Alignment of Ancient Texts using Linguistic and Semantic Analysis
papers.abstract: Textual criticism, the task of reconstructing a text as close as possible to its original form based on multiple ancient copies, is a central concern of philologists studying ancient literature.After identifying and cataloging the available manuscripts, scholars align the texts to produce a list of variants, a process known as collation.Automating this task has been one of the earliest areas of interest for applying computational methods to the humanities.Most current approaches rely on sequence alignment algorithms, originally developed for bioinformatics.However, recent advances in mono and multilingual neural alignment, capable of modeling semantic, syntactic, and grammatical relationships, remain largely underutilized in this field.In this paper, we introduce ALMA (Alignment and Learning for Manuscript Analysis).This new pipeline integrates lexical, grammatical, and semantic analysis to perform automatic textual alignment.We evaluate ALMA against three established alignment methods, each representing a different paradigm, on four manuscripts of the Gospel of John, two in Latin and two in Greek.ALMA achieves mean alignment scores of 94.12% (Latin) and 95.77% (Greek), significantly outperforming all baseline methods: alignment scores are improved over a deep learning-only approach by 1.93% and 1.09%, over a grammar-based approach by 23.39% and 10.14%, and over a sequence alignment method by 38.57% and 13.39%, respectively, for Latin and Greek.Notably, in this study, ALMA is the only approach to achieve a perfect median of 100% success on both datasets.These results highlight ALMA's substantial potential for advancing computational approaches for textual collation and more generally for computational philology.

papers.title: Multilingualism in digital humanities scholarship: a bibliometric review
papers.abstract: Abstract This study addresses linguistic diversity in Digital Humanities (DH), specifically within its scientific publication. Its core objective is to contribute to the development of DH’s self-knowledge—particularly its multilingual nature—through the characterization of scientific publication in the field. A bibliometric analysis of DH scientific publication indexed in Web of Science and Scopus between 2012 and 2021 is conducted. The following parameters are examined: distribution by year of publication, by country of author(s), by journal (considering the language in which each journal is published), by document language, and by DH subfields (Web of Science Categories). Bibliometric network visualizations of country co-authorship and bibliographic source co-citation analyses are also conducted using the software VOSviewer. The number of multilingual publications has been increasing, with a total of 29 distinct languages identified. Setting aside the expected and pronounced supremacy of English, Spanish and German are the most prominent languages. Spain and Germany are the most productive countries, and Spain has collaborated most extensively in multilingual scientific publication. The hegemony of the West and of Western languages is conspicuous, hence the underrepresentation of languages using non-Latin scripts. Literature and History predominate in multilingual DH, whereas Philosophy, Religion, Classics, and the Arts lag behind. Whereas discussion of linguistic diversity in DH has remained largely theoretical, this research offers an empirical examination of DH’s multilingualism. The study’s main contribution lies in deepening DH’s self-knowledge as a discipline, with practical implications at the level of conferences, journals, and project funding.

papers.title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence Techniques in Oracle Bone Inscriptions
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Oracle Bone Inscriptions (OBIs), incised over 3,000 years ago, represent one of humanity’s earliest extensively attested writing systems and preserve invaluable records of early Chinese civilization. Despite their status as UNESCO Memory of the World Register, OBI research still faces severe challenges, including extreme data scarcity, pervasive physical degradation, and persistent semantic ambiguity because many characters remain undeciphered. This paper reviews recent artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for OBI studies across three domains: organization and digitization for authentication and periodization, character-level detection and retrieval, and higher-level paleographic analysis, including semantic interpretation and known-class recognition support. We review representative approaches and publicly available datasets, highlight key technical bottlenecks such as data scarcity, weak cross-domain generalization, and semantic gaps between visual matching and cultural interpretation, and outline future directions, including robust models for degraded materials, methods that generalize across diverse collections, and approaches that integrate computational efficiency with paleographic expertise. By integrating computational methods with traditional paleography, this review shows how AI can accelerate OBI curation and enable large-scale cultural heritage analysis.

papers.title: Distinct strategy using an integrated methodology of innovative and traditional techniques for discriminating superimposed historical inks in revised manuscripts
papers.abstract: This study concerns a non-invasive, multi-analytical methodology proposed to overcome legibility limitations in compromised handwritten parts of historical manuscripts. In such official documents, literary works, or personal letters, ink traces may be revised after the original draft through overwriting, crossing out, or erasure. The inks used for these later modifications often closely resemble those of the original text in both appearance and chemical composition, making them particularly challenging to distinguish. Over the centuries, a variety of black inks have been produced using similar ingredients, such as polyphenols derived from galls or logwood and metal salts involved in ink formation, resulting in comparable chemical and physical properties when analysed. The main aim was to characterise and discriminate overlapping inks to achieve effective separation and visualisation of superimposed writing layers through a systematic methodological approach. The methodology combines a multispectral imaging system, Hypercolorimetric Multispectral Imaging (HMI), with complementary spectroscopic techniques, including single-point and mapping X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and micro-Raman spectroscopies. The approach was first tested on laboratory specimens, simulating overwritten handwriting, prepared using inks produced according to historical recipes (carbon-based, iron-gall, and logwood inks), dating from the 15th to the 18th centuries. It was subsequently applied to a specific case selected (e.g., text with a stroke of later corrections) from the original manuscript Ms. Tic. 67 (late 18th–early 19th century), an important testimony to Pavia’s erudition and historiography, preserved at the University Library of Pavia (Pavia, Italy). HMI was applied to inks for the first time, providing high-resolution images with spectral reflectance and colourimetric coordinates for each pixel. Multispectral data processed with image processing tools enabled enhanced visualisation and contrast between underwritten text and cross-out marks, particularly when inks belonged to different classes, and in some cases even when compositions were similar. XRF and Raman spectroscopies provided complementary elemental and molecular characterisation. XRF proved effective in distinguishing metal-tannin inks with different metal contents, while Raman spectroscopy enabled identification of the characteristic bands of carbon-based inks and the metal–polyphenol complexes associated with iron-gall and logwood inks, as well as the detection of layered and mixed ink systems. Overall, the results demonstrate both the advantages and disadvantages of the proposed methodological approach, highlighting that each case represents a complex and unique paper–overlapping ink system in which imaging and analytical outcomes are influenced by ink composition, application technique and deposition ink amount.

papers.title: Annotation-guided multi-scale UAV spectral mapping of a ruined medieval hermitage: masonry and façade material discrimination using multispectral data
papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry and multispectral imaging are increasingly used in cultural heritage documentation, but the interpretation of spectral products remains challenging when no independent radiometric calibration or exhaustive field validation is available. This paper presents an annotation-guided, multi-scale UAV workflow for the spectral mapping and characterisation of the ruined Sant Miquel Hermitage in Corbera, Valencia, Spain. Red-Green-Blue (RGB) and four-band multispectral data acquired with a DJI Mavic 3M and processed in DJI Terra are used as scene-relative contrast layers. The workflow is applied at two complementary scales. At the landscape scale, manual annotations of visible masonry are used to generate reference masks for index ranking. The analysis therefore evaluates the ability to discriminate known visible fabric rather than the independent detection of previously unknown archaeological features. At the façade scale, seven annotated material and construction zones are analysed using RGB chromatic indices, multispectral indices, and Grey-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) texture features. The results show that composite indices combining brightness, vegetation absence, and microrelief provide the most robust discrimination of visible masonry. Among single spectral indices, vegetation-based contrasts remain highly effective, but new non-vegetation-based formulations based on visible/NIR balance provide an interpretable alternative linked to the spectral behaviour of exposed mineral surfaces. At the façade scale, RGB-derived brightness, greenness, redness, and colouration indices are more informative than multispectral vegetation indices for material discrimination, while GLCM texture adds an independent axis for distinguishing dressed stone, rammed earth, and weathered surfaces. The study demonstrates that commercial UAV datasets can support reproducible heritage interpretation when combined with explicit annotation, comparative index ranking, and careful treatment of uncertainty. Rather than claiming a detection capability equivalent to excavation, the workflow provides a transparent framework for mapping visible masonry, characterising façade materials, and identifying surface anomalies that merit targeted field verification.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Cultural Heritage Characterization: Towards Scalable and Sustainable Territorial Inventories
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: The depopulation of rural areas across Southern Europe has accelerated the deterioration and disappearance of cultural heritage assets, many of which remain undocumented, undervalued, or at risk. This paper presents a hybrid methodology that combines artificial intelligence (AI) techniques with expert knowledge to improve the identification, classification, and validation of cultural heritage in rural territories. The proposed system processes unstructured textual data to extract and categorize information on tangible and intangible heritage elements. A pilot case study was carried out in the Valle de Amblés and Sierra de Ávila (province of Ávila, Spain), a region characterized by severe demographic decline but high heritage potential. Four municipalities (Amavida, Cardeñosa, La Torre, and Solosancho) were selected for testing based on heritage diversity, available documentation, and accessibility. In each case, AI-generated outputs were compared with manually curated validation files to assess the detection performance and applicability of the system. Results show that while traditional fieldwork and historical interpretation remain essential, AI can significantly enhance the speed and scalability of heritage documentation, particularly in under-resourced areas. The methodology reinforces the value of interdisciplinary collaboration and supports the development of territorial heritage strategies for sustainable rural regeneration.

papers.title: Semantic takhrij for cross-collection Hadith retrieval: a leakage-controlled evaluation framework
papers.abstract: Abstract Hadith scholarship requires tracing semantically related reports across collections, variants, and transmission settings, yet existing computational work concentrates on lexical search, narrow question answering, or heterogeneous evaluation setups that limit scholarly usefulness and weaken cross-study comparability. This article specifies semantic takhrij as a distinct cross-collection retrieval task in which a query Hadith is used to recover canonically grounded, semantically related evidence across collections, and constructs a leakage-controlled evaluation framework suited to the structural properties of Hadith corpora. The framework defines the query unit, candidate evidence space, graded relevance schema, provenance-aware output record, annotation logic, family-aware split philosophy, stable canonical identifiers, transparent normalization rules, and documentation requirements needed for auditable and reproducible evaluation. A four-level relevance model treats exact matches, near-parallel reports, semantically supportive evidence, and nonrelevant results as distinct outcomes rather than collapsing them into a single similarity class, while a family-aware partitioning strategy prevents evaluation-breaking leakage inherent in cross-collection Hadith settings. This is the first work to formalize semantic takhrij as a provenance-aware, graded, and leakage-controlled retrieval task, integrating task definition, annotation logic, and split discipline as a single coherent methodological unit, thereby advancing digital humanities scholarship by providing operational design vocabulary for evidence-oriented retrieval in Arabic religious corpora and directly supporting reproducible and source-grounded computational study of Islamic textual traditions.

papers.title: From margins to models: addressing digital exclusion and reimagining inclusive language infrastructures
papers.abstract: Abstract This article examines the structural technological disadvantages faced by low-resource minority languages in India through a case study of Sindhi within contemporary Natural Language Processing and digital language infrastructures. While state-of-the-art language technologies depend on large standardized corpora, in post-Partition India, Sindhi’s territorial displacement, orthographic plurality, and declining formal language education have substantially impacted the development of digital corpus, annotation frameworks, and speech-resources suitable for the language. The study combines a dataset-level analysis of major Indian language technology initiatives with semi-structured interviews with Sindhi corpus practitioners to investigate how infrastructural design assumptions, such as script stability, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) compatibility, and broadcast-based speech pipelines, shape the language’s limited representation across digital platforms. The findings demonstrate that Sindhi’s marginal presence across digital language infrastructures reflects structural misalignment rather than simple data absence. In response, the article advances a community-integrated Digital Humanities framework that situates native linguistic expertise at the center of corpus creation. A collaborative Sindhi audio archival initiative is presented as a model for culturally grounded digitization that derives from the language’s historical and cultural context rather than adapting it to dominant technical standards. The article argues that minority language digitization must be understood as an infrastructural and cultural process, requiring language-specific strategies capable of sustaining both technological participation and long-term linguistic continuity.

papers.title: Connecting Contemporary Industry and Society with Cultural Heritage Through Semantic Tools for Searching and Visualizing the Content of an Archive that Preserves the Valencian Design Legacy
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Design has profoundly influenced our lives, yet design archives that capture these narratives remain largely neglected. Preserving and making these archives accessible can enhance visual literacy, creativity and innovation. The Arxiu Valencià del Disseny (AVD) aims to preserve and share the cultural heritage of Valencian designers with a collection of over 150,000 items reflecting the region’s design history. This article reviews the outcomes of the "Arxiu Valencià del Disseny: shaping the future, designing the present, rescuing the past" project, which includes digitising the collection, creating a Design Memory Archive, and launching a web app that enables advanced semantic searches. The app integrates data from various archives using the CIDOC-CRM model, showcasing documents, sketches, products, and designer information. It also features interactive 2D and 3D maps, virtual galleries, and a Product Map highlighting material use and morphology. Future efforts will substantially expand content depth by integrating uncatalogued archives and extracting complex relational data from video interviews via automatic semantic processing. This phase will apply advanced AI for image-based recommendations and leverage mixed reality techniques to enable immersive, intuitive interaction with the knowledge graph.

papers.title: Can automatic reading be close? On the implications of using a large language model to identify interactions between lighting and emotions in French literature, 1838–1928
papers.abstract: Abstract This article evaluates whether a generic large language model (LLM) can be used to support literary scholarship by (1) identifying relevant passages and (2) producing explanations for those selections in response to a research question. We designed a workflow that combined semantic retrieval, vector search, and GPT-4o-based evaluation, and applied it to ninety novels set in Paris between 1838 and 1928, including works by Flaubert, Zola, Colette, and Proust, as well as lesser-known authors. Asked to identify passages in which artificial light played a role in the depiction of romantic or loving feelings, the model was relatively successful. Although it recovered only about 16 per cent of examples already located through manual reading, 56 per cent of the 506 additional passages it suggested were judged potentially valid in a scholar-evaluated sample. However, the model failed to generate explanations that would be convincing close readings. Critiquing the notion of ‘automatic close reading’, we apply our own close reading to the model’s imitations of close reading, and identify four recurrent shortcomings: (1) the problem of contemporary semantics being applied to a historical corpus, (2) a possible sentimentalist bias, (3) difficulty in detecting irony, and (4) misattribution of causality. We conclude that, if LLMs were to be trained for literary research, a model would need ‘knowledge’ of the whole text, extensive cultural and historical awareness, and training in reasoning informed by literary scholarship.

papers.title: Bridging the gap between contemporary remote sensing and archaeology: The S.A.D.A. platform for accessible remote-sensing image analysis
papers.abstract: Remote sensing now supplies abundant, high-resolution imagery for archaeological prospection, yet many projects still underuse these data due to technical barriers. This paper presents S.A.D.A. (Smart Anomaly Detection Assistant), an open-source, GUI driven application that integrates common pre-processing (index calculation, histogram adjustment, PCA), multiple anomaly-detection families (Standard, RX, Isolation Forest, LOF, one-class SVM), unsupervised clustering (K-means, DBSCAN), and spatial autocorrelation tools (LISA) within a guided, human-in-the-loop workflow. We evaluate S.A.D.A. on three contrasting datasets—multispectral UAV imagery from Veio, a thermal UAV frame from Jesolo, and a pan-sharpened Pléiades-1A scene from Metaponto—illustrating how the platform can support iterative, method-agnostic exploration and export GIS-ready outputs. Results indicate that S.A.D.A. can lower the practical cost of applying established techniques across heterogeneous sensors and scales, while keeping interpretation with the analyst. The discussion considers usability (guardrails, contextual tooltips, explicit pipelines) and limits (no automatic site detection, the need for archaeological validation), and outlines development priorities, including multi-modal support and optional human-in-the-loop deep learning. We suggest that tools like S.A.D.A. may help normalize remote sensing as a routine—yet critically interpreted—component of archaeological practice, particularly where budgets and specialist capacity are limited.

papers.title: Application of generative AI to realistic image rendering in virtual reconstruction: the crypt of the Royal Monastery of Saint Engracia in Zaragoza
papers.abstract: This study proposes a methodology that combines traditional two-dimensional (2D) drawing and three-dimensional (3D) modelling methods with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for the virtual reconstruction of destroyed buildings. This methodology can reduce production and texturing times without compromising the historical accuracy or photorealistic quality of the final images. As a case study, we propose to reconstruct the crypt of the Royal Monastery of Saint Engracia in Zaragoza, Spain, a space of Early Christian origin dating from the fourth century AD that reached its greatest extent in the 17th century. The complex was destroyed in the 19th century during the French invasion of 1808-1814 and subsequent interventions removed the surviving architectural remains. Consequently, no physical remains are available as a basis for the reconstruction. The methodology is therefore based on the analysis of historical documentation and architectural analogues. An initial floor-plan hypothesis was developed using AutoCAD 2025, followed by the creation of a detailed 3D model in Rhinoceros 8. In the final stage, the model was rendered without materials or textures in D5 Render. The resulting images were then processed using Nano Banana Pro, Gemini's image-generator tool, to generate textures and wall paintings with GenAI. Although the results were satisfactory, GenAI was found to introduce arbitrary artefacts or random interpretations into textures and architectural elements. For this reason, the tool should not operate autonomously, as human supervision is required to filter and validate each action and ensure that automatic generation does not compromise technical and historical accuracy. In conclusion, integrating GenAI into virtual reconstruction not only accelerates the workflow, but can also allow us to overcome the technical obstacles that hinder the virtual reconstruction of lost buildings, provided that its use is guided by scientific criteria and human oversight.

papers.title: ¿Puede la IA generativa ser una herramienta de documentación geométrica del patrimonio desaparecido?
papers.abstract: El inesperado desembarco de la inteligencia artificial (IA) generativa en 2023 provocó un movimiento telúrico que ha afectado a todos los ámbitos científicos, docentes y laborales. Este trabajo pretende valorar las aportaciones más recientes de la modelización 3D a través de la IA generativa, sobre todo en un aspecto para el que puede tener un gran potencial, aquel patrimonio destruido del que solo se disponga de unas pocas fotos o ilustraciones. Es decir, un patrimonio perdido, por la incansable evolución-involución urbanística de cualquier ciudad o por la destrucción provocada por los conflictos bélicos, y que han dejado tan solo una escasa documentación gráfica. El artículo pretende evaluar si estamos ante las puertas de un nuevo paradigma en la documentación geométrica que supere en este aspecto los métodos “clásicos”. Un nuevo paradigma que sería aplicable a situaciones en las que no era posible la construcción “tradicional” de modelos 3D, reservada en primera instancia al tratamiento con escáner 3D o a los algoritmos de Structure From Motion (SfM)/Multi-View Stereo (MVS), y a las más recientes aportaciones de los Neural Radiance Fields (NERF). Para realizar la mencionada evaluación se han tomado algunos casos de estudio a los cuales se les han aplicado programas de IA generativa como Google Gemini 2.5 Flash Image y Nano Banana, combinado con Hitem3D, Archsynth, Meshy o Hexagen. El estudio ha incluido, aplicándolo al caso de un elemento patrimonial existente, un análisis de distancias entre superficies mediante funciones del programa CloudCompare, para determinar el nivel de precisión y fiabilidad que podrían proporcionar estos modelos. Asimismo, se propone una adaptación, a partir del uso de la IA generativa, de los procedimientos de documentación que permiten identificar los niveles de autenticidad del modelo 3D generado, en consonancia con los aspectos tratados respecto a esta cuestión en la Carta de Londres y los Principios de Sevilla.

papers.title: Parsing Middle High German: exploring cross-lingual NLP for treebank construction in low-resource historical languages
papers.abstract: Abstract Building syntactically annotated corpora, such as treebanks, for historical languages is a challenging yet vital task in digital humanities, as it underpins linguistic analysis and facilitates a range of interdisciplinary research. However, the scarcity of annotated data and the need for extensive expertise in historical linguistics make this process particularly demanding. In this study, we explore the potential of cross-lingual natural language processing (NLP) techniques as a semiautomatic solution for treebank construction in low-resource historical languages. We use Middle High German (MHG) as a case study. Leveraging the linguistic continuity and structural similarities between MHG and Modern German (MG), we effectively utilize the extensive MG treebank resources to develop a constituency parsing system tailored for MHG. Specifically, to design a semiautomatic system that integrates automatic annotation with manual validation, we explore two cross-lingual transfer techniques: zero-shot transfer and delexicalization; the latter removes lexical information to focus on syntactic structure. In our experiments, we first train parsers on MG treebanks, and then transfer them to MHG using the two cross-lingual transfer techniques. The delexicalization method achieves a parsing performance of 67.3 per cent in terms of F1-score. This performance significantly surpasses the zero-shot cross-lingual method by a margin of 28.6 percentage points. These investigations validate the effectiveness and feasibility of cross-lingual transfer techniques for historical language treebank construction. This study highlights the potential of NLP tools to streamline the semiautomatic annotation process, reducing the reliance on extensive linguistic expertise and manual effort, and paving the way for broader applications in digital humanities research.

papers.title: Digital Deconstruction and Inheritance of Intangible Cultural Heritage Costumes: An Innovative Workflow Integrating Generative AI and Physical Simulation
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: In the context of the digital economy era, the digital preservation and innovation of traditional apparel crafts face dual challenges in cultural dissemination and technological integration. This study proposed and validates an integrated digital workflow that incorporates generative AI and physical simulation integrating artificial intelligence and high-fidelity physical simulation to facilitate the contemporary transformation of traditional apparel culture. A technical framework of “intelligent pattern generation — parametric structural modeling — dynamic physical simulation — virtual-real integration” was constructed, with the costumes of the nationally recognized intangible cultural heritage, Nuo Opera, serving as an empirical case. By building a dedicated dataset and employing lightweight fine-tuning techniques, intelligent derivation and stylized control of Nuo mask patterns were achieved, alongside three-dimensional simulation of the structural characteristics and dynamic aesthetics of traditional costumes. Experimental results indicate that the patterns generated by this method exhibit significantly higher visual complexity compared to conventional design approaches, while the design process is effectively streamlined. The physical simulation demonstrated commendable performance in both garment form stability and color fidelity of cultural elements. This study demonstrated that the workflow can support cross-media dissemination and innovative application of ICH craftsmanship through digital twin systems, providing a reference solution with both theoretical and practical value for the intelligent upgrading of the apparel industry and cultural heritage preservation.

papers.title: Knowledge graph-based cultural heritage recommender systems with condition-aware similarity and zero-shot embedding
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Museums worldwide face a fundamental shift from preservation toward accessibility as digital collections grow. Traditional keyword-based search overwhelms users with thousands of results, while the curated flow of exploration that physical exhibitions provide is lost in digital environments. This paper presents a knowledge graph-based recommender system that leverages rich metadata rather than sparse user interaction data to address these challenges. Using a dataset of 12,972 Korean cultural heritage items provided by the National Museum of Korea, we construct a knowledge graph with 14,637 entities, 146,263 triples, and 18 relation types spanning contextual, taxonomic, physical, biographical, provenance, and administrative metadata. Building on RotatE embeddings, which model relations as rotations in complex space, we develop three key capabilities. First, condition-aware recommendation allows visitors to specify exploration directions by combining heritage embeddings with relation-induced condition targets. Second, a zero-shot embedding mechanism based on inverse rotational aggregation provides a closed-form way to integrate newly acquired heritage items without retraining. Third, KGC predicts missing metadata such as artist attribution, enriching data quality while supporting curatorial workflows. Experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the recommendation and metadata-completion components of our metadata-driven approach while also establishing a scalable framework for future zero-shot integration experiments in continuously growing museum collections.

papers.title: Digital cultural heritage in Cyprus: mapping museums, priorities, and challenges
papers.abstract: Abstract In the last decades, European policies have highlighted the need to digitize cultural heritage material to enable Member States to be active actors in the long-term preservation, accessibility, and usage of heritage. So far, many institutions have grappled with diverse technologies to expand their digital offer, enrich the promotion of their collections, and enhance visitors’ experiences. However, many others still fight to find their place in the digital space. In this article, I will discuss the level of digitization reached by museums in Cyprus. The work integrates traditional approaches with quantitative and qualitative methods to identify the needs and challenges organizations and professionals face in dealing with digitization. The results show that a variety of digitization projects are underway across several museums, yet the majority have not been completed due to financial, organizational, and technical constraints. Moreover, a set of needs such as digitizing the collection, investing in technology for collection management, and enhancing on-site visitor experiences has been identified as a priority by professionals. The comprehensive review of the results contributes to giving visibility to the recent achievements in the digitization of heritage in an underexplored context of the South-Eastern Mediterranean, while also highlighting areas for improvement that serve as a foundation for theoretical reflections and practical solutions about the museum digitization.

papers.title: Culture, politics and codes of ethics: A study on whether similarity between codes is predicted by socio-political factors
papers.abstract: Abstract The extent to which codes of ethics (and ethics more generally) are influenced by social, political and cultural factors have been discussed in the literature for some time. We can find several direct examples of this in codes themselves, with some explicit about the need to interpret their content in light of broader social and political forces. Despite these discussions however, we have not yet been able to quantify these differences or the factors that influence codes. Utilising natural language processing, this study sought to explore this, examining whether similarities between codes of ethics were related to a range of socio-political factors. Data for this study came from 202 medical and nursing codes of ethics from around the world. To explore associations, a number of common metrics were utilised, including macro-economic, political, cultural and healthcare related variables. To compare each document, cosine similarity was calculated (on the whole document text and TF-IDF) providing two measures of similarity between document pairs. The other variables included for modelling were also transformed into pairs, categorising them or calculating differences between scores. Generalised linear mixed models revealed that sharing a profession (medical or nursing) and language had the strongest associations with code similarity. Colonial history (i.e. countries with a coloniser-colonised relationship) and greater similarities between GDP and individualism/collectivism were also associated with greater similarity. The pattern when it came to political and healthcare system variables was less clear, showing no clear and consistent association across models. We discuss these findings in light of the broader literature and theoretical debates within bioethics.

papers.title: Leveraging Dual-Deep Learning and Grade-Shift Algorithm for Intelligent Coin Grading
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: The assessment and grading of coins based on preservation is a fundamental task in numismatics and automated museum technologies. Traditional grading relies on visual inspection, which is an inherently subjective measurement approach due to the dynamic and variable nature of coin conditions within the Sheldon scale. While prior research has explored automated grading, existing studies remain limited in functionality, often focusing on specific coin types or historical periods, which restricts their practical feasibility. To address these gaps, we propose a computer vision-based approach for automated coin grading, combining a dual deep-learning model with a grade-shift algorithm. The approach integrates modified ResNet-D and Normalized Free Residual Network (NFResNet) architectures to leverage their complementary strengths, overcoming the limitations of single-model approaches. The grade-shift algorithm determines the final grade by evaluating the probability distributions from both models, computing confidence distances, and incorporating the domain knowledge enabling robust classification even for diverse coin datasets. We evaluate the proposed solution on the dataset provided by a grading company. The dataset encompasses multiple U.S. coin types and Mint years across a broad historical period, introducing substantial intra-dataset diversity compared to prior efforts. Experiments demonstrate classification into three major grade categories: Circulated (CR), Almost Uncirculated (AU), and Mint State (MS) , achieving accuracy 0.894 and F1-score 0.851. Gradient Weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) visualizations validate that the model learns numismatically meaningful features, providing interpretable evidence for its decision-making process. This work advances automated grading by establishing a scalable and objective framework for heterogeneous coin collections, while laying a foundation for future research in coins pattern recognition for numismatics and museum technologies.

papers.title: UncCy: neural parsing of New Testament Greek manuscripts via collation-based annotation transfer
papers.abstract: Abstract Ancient Greek manuscripts present major challenges for computational analysis due to the lack of diacritics, orthographic variation, and scribal conventions. Consequently, current state-of-the-art parsers perform poorly at lemmatization and morphological analysis. In this paper, we address this challenge by developing a new method that automatically collates annotated printed editions and manuscript traditions to generate silver-annotated datasets, using New Testament uncial manuscripts written in Koine Greek as our use case. After training a neural parser on this dataset, called UncCy (Uncial-Spacy), we demonstrate on a manually annotated manuscript that our parser reaches 93.6% performance on lemmatization, 96.9% on morphology, and 98.8% on POS, which corresponds to a gain of +40 pp in lemmatization, +34 pp in morphology, and +8 pp in Part-of-Speech (POS) compared to the current state-of-the-art parsers. This study thus provides the first production-ready parser for the study of New Testament uncials, opening the perspective of studying hundreds of currently unexploited transcriptions. All the resources generated during this study are fully available as Open-Source software and datasets.

It confirms the positive impact of AI-assisted contextualization and multimodal narrative interaction on learning outcomes in cultural heritage contexts.

papers.title: WhiteTesseract: Reframing the Interpretation of Cultural Heritage through XR and Conversational AI
papers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Cultural heritage exhibitions often struggle to sustain attention and support reflective engagement. While physical exhibitions incorporate various interpretive aids, such as labels, audio guides, and tactile features, they often deliver fixed content that lacks adaptability to individual backgrounds or curiosity. Their effectiveness is highly dependent on a visitor's Personal Context, prior knowledge, cultural literacy, and interpretive confidence. Meanwhile, digital exhibitions often prioritize convenience and accessibility but risk weakening the Physical and Social Contexts that define embodied cultural experience. WhiteTesseract addresses this gap by enabling in-situ interpretation through high-resolution XR and conversational AI. The system integrates spatial intelligence via artwork recognition and perceptual modulation to allow visitors to selectively reduce environmental distractions (via diminished reality) and engage in context-aware dialogue (via large language models). The goal is to preserve the richness of the physical and social environment while providing a flexible space for personal reflection, enhancing Personal Context without compromising physical authenticity. We deployed the system in a Claude Monet exhibition and conducted a controlled user study with 27 recruited participants, among which 26 completed the entire experiment and were included in the analysis. Quantitative results showed that WhiteTesseract modulation significantly increased average viewing duration from 35.3 to 98.3 seconds ( p < 0.001). In parallel, analysis of 529 visitor–AI interactions revealed that 60% extended beyond factual queries to include analytical, emotional, and comparative inquiries. These findings demonstrate how XR and AI can enrich the physical exhibition experience by supporting deeper, more personalized engagement without displacing the embodied value of cultural heritage. We discuss technical and social constraints for real-world deployment and limitations of our controlled experimental setting.

papers.title: User eXperience research & design for heritage science: from personas to user interface development in Codex4D project
papers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: This paper presents a methodological framework for applying User eXperience Research (UXR) and User eXperience Design (UXD) in the context of Heritage Science, focusing on the case study of the Codex4D. The project explores the digitisation, visualisation, and interactive exploration of complex documentary heritage –ancient codices– through a user-centred design approach. The UXR phase utilised qualitative research methods like stakeholder interviews, field observations and participatory workshops to create user personas, task models and interaction scenarios. These insights directly informed the UXD process, which followed an iterative cycle of prototyping, co-design, and usability testing. The resulting user interface seamlessly integrates 2D and 3D representations of the codices, multispectral imagery and contextual metadata, offering users multiple levels of interaction and interpretation. Grounded in international standards and principles of Universal Design, this research demonstrates how UX methodologies can enhance the accessibility, engagement, and scientific value of digital heritage tools.

papers.title: Interpretive computing: designing for interactions between people, AI, and cultural heritage collections
papers.abstract: Abstract This article introduces interpretive computing, a humanistic design framework for artificial intelligence systems that support collaborative meaning-making, narrative construction, and cultural responsiveness in archival contexts. Moving beyond explainability and automation, interpretive computing positions AI as a scaffold for situated interpretation—one that centres context, dialogue, and plural epistemologies. We develop this concept through a case study involving the Smithsonian Institution and U.S. Library of Congress Civil Rights History Project—oral history collection, where large language models are used to generate thematic metadata, segment interviews, and construct dynamic, user-curated story paths. Our prototype interface features include editable metadata annotations and thematic playlists, allowing users—whether educators, students, or community members—to engage in co-authorship of historical understanding. Grounded in traditions from hermeneutics, narratology, and digital humanities, this work reimagines metadata and interface design as interpretive acts, offering a model for AI systems that support dialogic, reflexive, and culturally situated engagements with the past.
