emotionPapers.title: Machine Learning Applications in Use-Wear Analysis: A Critical Review
emotionPapers.journal: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology
emotionPapers.abstract: Use-wear analysis examines the macroscopic and microscopic patterns of traces left on tool surfaces as a result of use. Recently, machine learning (ML) has been employed as a promising method for automating and standardizing the identification of these traces. While the number of use-wear analysts using ML continues to grow, discussions regarding the effectiveness and appropriate implementation of these methods are ongoing. The main aim of this literature review is to provide recommendations for the more effective application of ML in use-wear analysis and archaeological research, by identifying trends, research gaps, and evaluating the quality of the models developed. There are three key challenges identified. Firstly, the limited adoption of open science practices restricts the creation of large datasets and hinders reproducibility and transparency. Secondly, research efforts are concentrated within limited institutions, focusing on certain research questions, algorithms, raw materials, and use-wear traces. Thirdly, the inadequate quality, quantity, and diversity of data affect the performance of the models being developed. To address these challenges, this paper advocates for the promotion of open science and the systematic gathering of experimental and analytical data. Involving a broader range of institutions can improve research quality and promote greater diversity of perspectives. Collaboration with computer scientists and computational archaeologists is essential to integrate the expertise necessary for designing and implementing effective ML methods. By addressing these factors, this paper facilitates the effective use of machine learning, enabling use-wear analysts and archaeologists to develop robust models that automate, accelerate, and improve their research.

emotionPapers.title: Exploring Emotional and Cognitive Engagement with Holographic Displays in Museums
emotionPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
emotionPapers.abstract: Emotional engagement with exhibits and artefacts enhances learning by anchoring memories more vividly and improving information retention. These interviews involved 16 professionals, including museum experts, designers and cultural heritage practitioners, to gain in-depth insights into their perspectives on holographic displays. The study uncovered various emotional responses, with ‘curiosity’ and ‘wonder’ emerging as predominant sentiments. This indicates that holographic displays have the capacity to significantly enhance visitors’ engagement and learning experiences. This research highlights the importance of understanding and catering to visitors’ emotional and experiential needs in the evolving landscape of museum exhibit design, and the long-term impact of these experiences, suggesting that the display of holograms can leave a lasting impression and foster sustained interest in museum visits.

emotionPapers.abstract: With the growth and popularization of social virtual reality (VR) in the heritage sector, particularly in multiuser environments like the metaverse, this study explores its potential as a platform for virtual heritage communication to support cultural learning. emotionPapers.title: Recolonization dynamics of lichens after biocidal treatments: A limitation in the spreading of water-based solutions beneath thalli as species-specific influencing factor
emotionPapers.abstract: Recolonisation by lichens of recently cleaned heritage surfaces is a major issue for conservation, but subtending processes were only partially unveiled, particularly with respect to species with a low potential of propagule dispersal, for which a rapid ingress from external sources is rather unlikely. In this work, recolonisation by lichen species of Megasporaceae and Verrucariaceae was investigated on the marble balustrades of two residences of the Royal House of Savoy (UNESCO-WHS 823bis; NW Italy), cleaned approx. 20 and 12 years ago, respectively. The work aimed to verify if (i) lichen recolonisation started immediately after the conservation interventions and if (ii) this may depend on a scarce effectiveness of devitalization treatments. With regard to this latter point, a possible specific resilience due to a high depth of hyphal penetration within the substrate and/or a limitation in the biocide spread and penetration beneath thalli -due to stone properties and/or a lichen-related effect- were experimentally evaluated. The calculation of growth rates and minimum age of thalli on the balustrades indicated that recolonisation started immediately after the conservation interventions. Blocks of marble from the ancient quarry sites were used to verify the spread and penetration of water-based solutions, mimicking those of quaternary ammonium salt biocides, in presence and absence of Megasporaceae and Verrucariaceae lichens. Lichen cover was shown to influence the capillary water absorption, but the depth reached by the water-based solution (visualised with fluorescein dye) was still higher than that of hyphal penetration structures. On the other hand, some hydrophobic volumes were detected just beneath/below lichen thalli. The applications of water-based biocides do not likely affect lichen structures observed in these rock volumes, which may thus act as viable remnants rapidly starting recolonisation process. Such scenario may thus account for the frequent occurrence of species of Megasporaceae and Verrucariaceae, having a low potential of propagule dispersal, on recently cleaned marble heritage surfaces.

emotionPapers.title: Impact of storage conditions on the preservation of taphonomically altered human skeletal remains: Insights from ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and DNA analysis
emotionPapers.abstract: • The effects of storage conditions on bone samples are substantial. • Changes in DNA at room temperature were linked to mineral and collagen alterations. • Changes in DNA in the freezer were associated with changes in mineral. • Freezer storage mitigates degradation by minimizing mineral and collagen loss. • Room-temperature accelerates changes, particularly in collagen quality and quantity. The preservation of skeletonised human remains is crucial for successful archaeological and forensic analyses, yet it is influenced by various intrinsic and extrinsic factors. While numerous studies have addressed preservation states and their implications, the effects of storage conditions on taphonomically altered remains have been largely overlooked. This study examines the impact of storage conditions—freezer and room temperature—on bone samples from 21 femur shafts excavated from a World War II mass grave over a period of 1, 2, and 3 years. Changes were analysed using ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and DNA analysis to explore correlations between molecular alterations and DNA preservation. Results demonstrate that storage conditions significantly affect bone preservation. Freezer storage showed minimal degradation, primarily characterised by changes in mineral crystallinity due to the loss of loosely bound ions, while collagen quality improved initially, likely due to molecular reordering. In contrast, room-temperature storage accelerated both mineral and collagen deterioration, with pronounced effects on collagen quantity and quality correlating with increased crystallinity and apatite domain proportions. DNA quality and quantity exhibited similar trends under both conditions, though correlations with mineral and collagen changes varied by storage environment. Over three years, freezer storage mitigated degradation by limiting mineral and collagen loss, whereas room-temperature storage accelerated changes, especially in collagen. These findings highlight the importance of controlled storage conditions, as significant molecular and structural alterations were observed within a relatively short period. This has important implications for the long-term preservation of forensic and archaeological samples, emphasising the need for appropriate storage strategies to ensure sample integrity for future analyses.

emotionPapers.title: Digitizing Guardianship Registers in Senegal (1895-1910): Naming as Evidence and Ethical Concern
emotionPapers.abstract: Drawing from research on liberated minors, formerly enslaved children whom the colonial state in Senegal entrusted to guardians following their emancipation, this article describes the process of building a database consisting of identifying information about formerly enslaved children in early colonial Senegal based on data originally collected in the early twentieth century, and it uses the database to ask both historical and ethical questions about naming practices and aliases, experiences of unfreedom, and the agency of marginalized African children. As such, scholars should include them in databases and other digital history projects, but only if ethical concerns can be addressed and resolved.

emotionPapers.title: Lexical richness viewed through lexical diversity, density, and sophistication
emotionPapers.abstract: Abstract Recognizing vocabulary as the essential language foundation and determining its richness continues to be a challenge in quantitative linguistics. This issue has also been widely applied in various practical contexts, including language acquisition, language change, psychology, and cognitive science. However, vocabulary is complex, and lexical richness has been typically measured using three distinct indicators: lexical diversity, density, and sophistication. Among them, lexical diversity has been widely studied, yet reliable metrics independent of text length remain lacking. The characteristics of lexical density and sophistication have not been dealt with in depth, and studies focusing on the Japanese language are limited. This study aimed to delineate the distinctive features of lexical diversity, density, and sophistication, and to explore their interrelationships within Japanese. A corpus of formal policy speeches delivered by Japanese prime ministers was utilized. Numerical experiments were conducted in two stages: first, lexical diversity, density, and sophistication were analyzed separately; subsequently, the impact of text length on these indicators was examined. The findings indicated that text length did not affect lexical density and sophistication, and no consistent relationship was observed among the three indicators.

emotionPapers.abstract: Abstract This article examines William Shakespeare’s sonnet form by using both qualitative and quantitative methods, particularly with the aid of digital technologies such as sentiment analysis. While most critics have analyzed the volta through a qualitative approach (i.e. a close reading of poems), I consider the volta as a statistical problem of identifying a turning point in a sequence of fourteen values—in this case, sentiment scores assigned to each line in a sonnet. Furthermore, this study enhances the results of quantitative and computational analysis with a qualitative analysis of the sonnets’ structure and emotions, incorporating the human-in-the-loop approach. By integrating digital methods with close reading practices, this article both confirms and complicates a standard view that the volta in Shakespeare’s sonnets tends to occur before the final couplet. In addition, this study offers new insights into the function of the Shakespearean volta, expanding the focus of formalist inquiry from where it occurs to how it works: the volta induces not so much a line-to-line transition as a section-to-section transition.

emotionPapers.title: Comprehension of the Shakespeare authorship question through deep impostors approach
emotionPapers.abstract: Abstract This article investigates the authorship question surrounding William Shakespeare’s works using a novel approach called the ‘Deep Impostor’ methodology. The approach uses a set of known impostor texts to analyze the origin of a target text collection. Both the target texts and impostors are divided into an equal number of word segments. A deep neural network, either a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) or a pre-trained BERT transformer, is then trained and fine-tuned to differentiate between impostor segments. Once assigned, each target text is transformed into a numerical signal by averaging its segment assignments. The Dynamic Time Warping distance is afterward evaluated between these signals to measure their similarity. The Isolation Forest algorithm identifies outliers within the target text collection for each impostor pair by assigning appropriate scores to each tested text. In the summarizing step, the tested creations are clustered into two groups. In the case of a CNN-based model, the first resulting cluster contains fifteen creations. General evaluations lead to the conclusion to suggest that these are not authored by Shakespeare. The remaining documents are classified as authentic Shakespearean works.

emotionPapers.title: A Deep Learning-Based Method of Investigating Rammed-Earth Wall Damage on the Ming Great Wall Military Defense System
emotionPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
emotionPapers.abstract: The collection, detection, and statistical analysis of massive damage information from large cultural heritage sites is an important issue that affects the progress, depth, and quality of cultural heritage protection efforts. The Ming Great Wall of China, known for its vast size, poses a significant challenge to protection efforts. Conventional methods for collecting and recognizing damage information from the wall are nearly impossible due to its scale. The limitation has significantly hindered efforts to safeguard the vulnerable rammed-earth walls of the Ming Great Wall. To address this issue, we developed new technical schemes that combine the efficiency of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) for low-altitude surveying and mapping with the accuracy of AI detection. This enables the efficient collection, detection, and statistical analysis of a massive amount of damage data from the Great Wall sites. The system achieved an average damage detection accuracy of 0.838, as measured by the average precision (AP). Additionally, the system’s average effective detection range exceeded 91.5%, while reducing manual labor time by about 95%. These results provide accurate, efficient, and timely data and technical support for efforts such as status investigation, condition evaluation, protection and maintenance, and budgeting for the Great Wall sites. Furthermore, this research proposes a potential approach for gathering and analyzing data from other large-scale cultural heritage sites.

emotionPapers.title: Crafting Digital Experiences: Embedding Human-Centred and Participatory Design into Archaeological Practice
emotionPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
emotionPapers.abstract: As digital archaeology has grown as a field of practice, so has the number of digital resources developed for specialists and nonspecialists alike. However, the creation of such outputs has not always been accompanied and informed by design theory and practices. Design—used in its broadest definition as a process of conceptual making—is an integral, if often implicit, part of archaeological practices and it is through design that we develop and share our work—from data collection and analysis to interpretation and dissemination—and engage with our stakeholders. Engaging with core design practices offers meaningful opportunities for generating new forms of archaeological knowledge production and sharing, as well as creating digitally mediated experiences that are not guided by our own assumptions about our stakeholders’ needs and can really affect people’s engagement with the past. In this article, I investigate the benefits of embedding Human-Centred and Participatory Design into the archaeology and heritage sectors to create more critically engaged digital encounters with the past.

emotionPapers.title: Identifying Cultural Perceptions by Nature Language Processing Method: Differences of Historical Gardens and Urban Parks in Suzhou, China
emotionPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
emotionPapers.abstract: Historical gardens, as important components of urban green spaces, have ecological, social, and significant historical heritage value. Urban residents develop close connections with nature, culture, and historical elements through landscape perception behavior in their daily activities, leading to different preferences and value judgments. However, it is still necessary to conduct in-depth research to explore whether there are differences in cultural perception and preferences between historical gardens and newly built parks during residents’ daily visits. To fill these gaps, this research utilized user-generated contents and natural language processing method focuses on a sample of 40 historical gardens and newly built parks in Suzhou, China, to address the following three research questions: (1) Which elements do park visitors perceive more strongly in historical gardens and new parks? (2) Is there a correlation between the cultural perception preferences and the attributes of the gardens and parks? (3) What are the sentimental preferences of visitors between historical gardens and new parks? The research findings reveal that cultural and aesthetic perception is more pronounced in historical gardens compared to newly built parks, while the latter places greater emphasis on the perception of natural features. Additionally, attribute features of parks, such as area, perimeter, and public transportation facilities, equally impact visitors’ landscape perception. This study distinguished the cultural perception and preference characteristics of urban residents in historical gardens and new parks, providing urban managers and urban green space planning and design professionals with more experience in areas such as the preservation and renovation of urban historical landscapes.

emotionPapers.title: "I Fregi del Ceppo”: when artificial intelligence and geomatics meet theatre
emotionPapers.abstract: Highlights: The reuse of 3D reality-based digital data in theatre productions supports the cross-valorisation of cultural activities. The frieze of the Ospedale del Ceppo: from digital documentation for preservation to scenic design and performance. The integration of digital technologies, avatars and artificial intelligence in contemporary theatre scenography. Abstract: The integration of three-dimensional (3D) digital technologies into cultural heritage and theatre is transforming how historical works are preserved and experienced. This paper focuses on the performance I Fregi del Ceppo, which exemplifies this trend by using 3D data to bring the Renaissance friezes of the Ospedale del Ceppo in Pistoia, Italy, to life. Originally digitised for conservation, the friezes served as the foundation for a theatrical production. The project used artificial intelligence (AI) tools to analyse and animate the frieze characters’ postures and relationships. The performance incorporated a 180º multi projection system that synchronised human actors with digital projections, merging live performance with digital heritage. This work highlights the broader trend of integrating AI and digital tools into theatre. Body scans, motion tracking, and emotion recognition enable new storytelling methods, while virtual characters and avatars allow performers to explore identity and interaction in novel ways. The fusion of AI with performance art is pushing the boundaries of creativity, generating dialogues, analysing performances, and enabling real-time interaction with human actors. I Fregi del Ceppo demonstrates how digital heritage can enhance theatre, extending the life of historical works and offering new cultural experiences. It also points to a future where AI and 3D technologies will play an increasingly central role in shaping the performing arts.

emotionPapers.title: Research on the Development of Crack Diseases at the Jiayuguan Rammed Earth Site in Multivariate Time Series Based on Deep Learning and Transfer Learning
emotionPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
emotionPapers.abstract: Jiayuguan, the first majestic pass at the western end of the Ming Dynasty’s Great Wall, is an important world cultural heritage site with high historical, scientific, social, and artistic value. It is primarily constructed of rammed earth and has existed in the form of earth relics for over 600 years. Due to prolonged exposure to natural environmental factors such as rainfall, wind-borne sand, and temperature variations, typical crack diseases have developed significantly, posing a threat to the overall stability of the earthen site. To ensure the long-term safety of rammed earth sites, we explore the primary environmental factors influencing the progression of damages in these sites using monitoring techniques. Additionally, employing data mining techniques to analyze the development trends of these damages for predictive warnings will prove to be a challenging task. In this context, this paper collects monitoring data on crack diseases and the occurrence environment of the Jiayuguan rammed earth site, and uses the wavelet correlation analysis method and Boruta feature screening to find the main environmental factors that affect the development of crack diseases. Then, combining with environmental factor variables, it uses deep learning LSTM, GRU, Transformer and transfer learning Transformer-LSTM, GRU-Transformer, and A-SBiLSTM to predict the development trend of crack diseases on the north wall and beacon tower respectively. It can be seen that (i) Transformer model RMSE = 0.0154, R 2 = 0.973; (ii) Transformer-LSTM model RMES = 0.0290, R 2 = 0.937; and (iii) Transformer model and Transformer-LSTM model are closer to the actual SD value than other models. The research results show that the Transformer and Transformer-LSTM models have high accuracy, good stability, and optimal prediction effects. They are suitable for predicting the development trend of crack diseases at the Jiayuguan rammed earth site. These models have application potential in related research fields and provide references for subsequent research.

emotionPapers.title: “Rhetoric behind the digital screen”: wayfinding across the splinternet of AI—a rhetorical quartet of an affective writer
emotionPapers.abstract: Abstract Drawing on and recontextualizing Elizabeth Forbes’ theory regarding the quartile facets of a developing writer—(1) maker, (2) artist, (3) creator, and (4) performer, and Karen Lunsford’s approach of wayfinding—(1) worlds apart, (2) literacy in the wild, (3) ecologies and networks, and (4) transfer in writing studies, this study, inspired by the notion of affective economy and splinternet, offers a rhetorical quartet pertaining to the literary career of China-related writers to argue that circulation naturalizes the rhetorical processes that govern meaning within the configuration of digital age. Moreover, this study examines the role of digital algorithms as accelerants, magnifying the dissemination of these narratives and marrying a mutual dance between text and reader. In our view, emergence of affect unsettles AI-dominant networks of literature, offering a middle ground to recalibrate the relationship between rhetorical circulation and splinternet transfiguration.

emotionPapers.title: From dictionaries to LLMs – an evaluation of sentiment analysis techniques for German language data
emotionPapers.abstract: Abstract In this study, we perform a comprehensive evaluation of sentiment classification for German language data using three different approaches: (1) dictionary-based methods, (2) fine-tuned transformer models such as BERT and XLM-T and (3) various large language models (LLMs) with zero-shot capabilities, including natural language inference models, Siamese models and dialog-based models. The evaluation considers a variety of German language datasets, including contemporary social media texts, product reviews and humanities datasets. Our results confirm that dictionary-based methods, while computationally efficient and interpretable, fall short in classification accuracy. Fine-tuned models offer strong performance, but require significant training data and computational resources. LLMs with zero-shot capabilities, particularly dialog-based models, demonstrate competitive performance, often rivaling fine-tuned models, while eliminating the need for task-specific training. However, challenges remain regarding non-determinism, prompt sensitivity and the high resource requirements of large LLMs. The results suggest that for sentiment analysis in the computational humanities, where non-English and historical language data are common, LLM-based zero-shot classification is a viable alternative to fine-tuned models and dictionaries. Nevertheless, model selection remains highly context-dependent, requiring careful consideration of trade-offs between accuracy, resource efficiency and transparency.

emotionPapers.title: Generative modelling of Monopteros and Tholos temples using existing data: The case study of Vesta temple in Tivoli
emotionPapers.abstract: • Generative programming enables the creation of digital representations of built cultural heritage. • The Vesta temple in Tivoli was chosen as a case study for this research. • Francesco Piranesi's 18th-century etchings informed the layout and modular design. • The workflow allows the generating of exportable files compatible with simulation software. • Parametric modelling provides high reusability and adaptability of algorithms. This paper presents a novel method for generating geometric models of architectural heritage in the absence of a digital survey. The method employs a Generative Programming (GP) algorithm for geometric model generation, with the Temple of Vesta in Tivoli chosen as a case study. Francesco Piranesi's 18th-century etchings are utilised as references to identify the architectural layout and modularity. The effectiveness of the proposed generative workflow is highlighted through its time efficiency and the reusability of the algorithm. The workflow includes the capability to generate an export file suitable for structural simulation software packages. The generated geometric model is then used to conduct nonlinear dynamic analysis using a concurrent continuous/block-based approach within a Finite Element environment. The simulations are performed with the structure in its current state and do not account for retrofitting interventions, i.e. anchorages and tie rods are not taken into account. The numerical model reveals how local failure mechanisms of columns and entablature affect the structural safety of the Vesta temple.

emotionPapers.title: Heritage Data Governance in Regeneration: Lessons from England’s High Street Heritage Action Zones
emotionPapers.journal: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology
emotionPapers.abstract: Heritage data management has become increasingly critical as regeneration initiatives generate vast quantities of digital information, yet systematic approaches to data governance remain inconsistent across the sector. This paper examines heritage data practices within England’s High Street Heritage Action Zone (High Street HAZ) programme, focusing on case studies from Northallerton, Kirkham, and Chester. Through semi-structured interviews, questionnaires, and data audits conducted between 2021–2024, this research investigates how heritage datasets are created, shared, and preserved within planning processes, community wellbeing initiatives, and heritage research projects. Key findings reveal widespread data reuse across all programme strands, alarmingly low awareness of Data Management Plans (DMPs), and fragmented approaches to data sharing and preservation. The study uncovers significant disparities between above-ground and below-ground archaeological data management, with the former lacking systematic archival requirements despite comparable heritage value. Commercial intellectual property practices often conflict with public access principles, whilst community-generated datasets face particular vulnerability without institutional support. The research demonstrates that easily accessible datasets are routinely reused whilst those requiring specialist access remain underutilised, highlighting the critical importance of data discoverability. The paper advocates for mandatory DMPs, hybrid governance models balancing local autonomy with national oversight, and clear intellectual property frameworks ensuring public benefit from publicly funded research. These findings contribute to emerging debates on digital heritage governance, offering evidence-based recommendations for improving data stewardship in heritage-led regeneration initiatives.

auditPapers.title: Designing an MR-Based Educational System for Open-Storage Art Museums: A Case Study of MMCA Cheongju
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Open storage museums offer a distinctive mode of exhibition by publicly displaying collections within storage environments. However, high-density displays without sufficient interpretive support often confine visitors to passive observation, giving rise to what has been described as the “open storage dilemma.” To address this limitation, this study proposes a mixed reality (MR)–based educational system developed for Apple Vision Pro. The system was designed based on the storage environment of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) Cheongju and provides a seated experience in which users interact through system-level spatial interaction and hand-based gestures. These findings indicate that MR-mediated spatial experience can visualize the invisible operational systems of storage-type museums and reconfigure observation-centered spaces into immersive, understanding-oriented educational environments.

auditPapers.title: ‘Un livre problématique’: Official History, Anglo-French Relations, and the Fallout from M. R. D. Foot’s SOE in France
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract As the first official history of a secret service, SOE in France (1966) by M. R. D. Foot represented a major departure from the long-standing culture of secrecy that surrounded Britain’s intelligence community. Following publication, the book was criticized in France for its treatment of the resistance and its leader, Charles de Gaulle. This reaction was so vituperative that fears surfaced in Whitehall that the government-sanctioned book would be weaponized by de Gaulle, now president of France, to block a second application by the United Kingdom to join the Common Market. This article examines the missteps that were made by officials in charge of the project that put the British government on a collision course with the French downstream. It is argued that, while officials should have concentrated on the book’s portrayal of the resistance, they were preoccupied with removing unflattering material about statesmen like Winston Churchill and Anthony Eden. The article examines how officials, to safeguard a second EEC bid, refused to acknowledge their own failings and instead painted Foot as a second-rate historian. It speaks to a fascinating conversation about the dangers of scholars working with the state, which is more powerful and has agendas at odds with academic historians.

auditPapers.title: Anglicization Of and Through Law: British North America, Ireland, and India Compared, 1540–1800
auditPapers.abstract: Historians of British North America, Ireland, and India write, each in their own ways, about the convergence of societies in the English empire toward metropolitan models, a process generally known as “anglicization.” Yet anglicization has never been studied as a feature connecting the global British Empire. Scholars typically consider a single region and seldom engage with others. We pursue a comparative approach, using law as our vantage point. Our goal is to explore anglicization of law and through law in British North America, Ireland, and India over the course of the long early modern period from the sixteenth through early nineteenth centuries. Our article begins with brief histories of anglicization in Ireland, America, and India that establish a foundation for comparison, for identifying commonalities and differences. We describe the “life cycle” or sequence of anglicization taking place upon different timelines in each of the three regions. Lest we overstate the extent of anglicization, we next consider difficulties that arise when deploying the concept. We conclude by suggesting how our project might stimulate comparative imperial history by developing categories that are portable, transferable across place and time, and useful in studying both British overseas expansion globally and in connecting the British experience to that of other empires. Toward this end, we apply our approach to a contrast case: the Spanish Empire’s fraught efforts to construct legal authority over Indigenous peoples in New Spain and Peru.

auditPapers.title: Italian Crimes and Austrian Punishment: Carbonari Trials and the Legacy of Austrian Law
auditPapers.abstract: This article presents a history of Italian (political) crimes and Austrian punishments in the post-1815 Austrian Empire from the standpoint of Austrian legal practices, in particular with regard to crimes against the state and political crimes. It brings together several distinct historiographies—of post-1815 European international security, Austrian law, the Italian Risorgimento—to examine the history of the Czech Spielberg fortress, a central political prison in the Empire. The trials and detainment of the most important Carbonari leaders at Spielberg can teach us a great deal about the Austrian legal practices consolidated between the late eighteenth and the early nineteenth centuries that affected law in much of Central Europe through 1918, as well as beyond the Empire’s collapse. The unique tradition of punishing political criminals by incarcerating them in one of the central prisons of the Empire, as opposed to exiling them to remote areas; the consistent publicity surrounding their trials and detention; the preferential treatment of state criminals compared to regular criminals; and strict adherence to the law—all became defining features of the Austrian legal system under the Empire. I explain this system of law through the prism of the Austrian trials of the Italian Carbonari and their detainment at Spielberg in the early nineteenth century, viewing them against the backdrop of Austrian legal history as well as Spielberg’s history across several centuries.

auditPapers.title: Internment Camps and the End of Empire: How Civilian Incarceration Helped Define Citizenship in Interwar Poland
auditPapers.abstract: This article explores the short life of post–World War I Polish internment camps as a prism for understanding the shift from empire to nation-state in Europe’s new democracies. It focuses on the chain of detention facilities scattered across Polish territory that incarcerated thousands of refugees, asylum seekers, former POWs, and potentially disloyal “foreign” residents. I argue that the differential treatment of the diverse population of internees was one manifestation of the increasingly ethnonationalizing Polish government agenda that sought to shape a hierarchy of citizenship and belonging. I demonstrate first that the varied approach to civilian internment among government officials and the porousness of the camp system itself exposes the heterogeneity of “the state” at its genesis. Second, I show how internees often fought back, challenging their characterization as national outsiders. Petitioners relied on imperial era tropes such as professional honor, military service, or regionalism to demonstrate their loyalty, especially in cases where they presented clear attachments to minority ethnic groups. The negotiation among internees, government authorities, and the communities in which they were embedded calls into question the top-down imposition of citizenship criteria in this period, suggesting that subjectivity in the Second Republic was shaped through a dynamic and constantly shifting tension between state actors and ordinary people. The text is based on documents in Polish state, police, and military archives, including records of camp interrogations, prisoner appeals, and reports of civic commissions monitoring the camps.

auditPapers.title: Habsburg Central Europe: Dynasty, Territoriality, and Governance, 1790–1867
auditPapers.abstract: As he lay on his deathbed in late January 1790, Joseph II wrote to his brother and successor, Leopold II, summing up his restless, striving life: “I am unfortunate in everything I undertake, the appalling ingratitudewithwhich my good arrangements are viewed and I am treated … all this fills me with doubt” (Derek Beales, Joseph II: Against the World, 1780–1790 [Cambridge, 2009], 628). Joseph’s reforming zeal and personalized rule left a difficult and ambiguous legacy. Formany, Joseph and his reign represented a model and template for progressive, interventionist government and the possibilities of public-spirited reform. Yet, upon Leopold’s ascension, there was widespread discontent at the rapid pace of Joseph’s drive for rationalization and improvement, including a military uprising in Austrian Netherlands (roughly present-day Belgium) and serious unrest in Hungary. Together with an expensive, interminable war against the Ottoman Empire (which posed the possibility of Prussian support against Austria) and ongoing financial problems, the monarchy was facing a moment of crisis. To some extent, Joseph’s rule had shown not only the possibilities but also the limitations of direct personal rule by fiat, however well-intentioned.
topics: Central European and Russian historical studies

auditPapers.title: 3D GPR assessment of the conservation state of a frescoed wall in the Monastery of St. John (Müstair, Switzerland)
auditPapers.abstract: The Monastery of St. John in Müstair (Switzerland), a UNESCO World Heritage Site, preserves an exceptional cycle of Carolingian and Romanesque frescoes. This study presents the results of a Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) investigation designed to assess the conservation state of a frescoed wall and to characterize the interaction between the mural surfaces and the underlying irregular masonry. Conducted within the MOLAB transnational access program, the survey employed complementary medium-frequency (900 MHz) and high-frequency (2 GHz) antennas to detect plaster stratigraphy, voids, detachments, and fractures. The results reveal a complex structural condition, including a dual-layer plaster system, localized voids and fractures, and areas of historic infill associated with past repair interventions. These findings are essential for planning targeted conservation measures and confirm the effectiveness of GPR as a non-invasive diagnostic tool in complex historical architectural contexts.

auditPapers.title: Inside and Outside the Archive: Tracing the Life and Career of a UNHCR Officer
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article traces the research itinerary of the authors, beginning in the archives of UNHCR, the United Nations refugee agency. Engagement with holdings that had until recently remained beyond historians’ reach redirected their inquiries to focus on a UNHCR officer, Candida Toscani. Her professional trajectory offers insights into the role and conduct of UNHCR personnel in the postwar international refugee regime. Drawing on official documents, personnel files, private memoirs, and information provided by Toscani’s daughter, the article examines what these materials disclose about an institution coming under closer historical scrutiny, while reflecting on the epistemological dilemmas that shape historical research.

auditPapers.title: Prompt-to-Structure: Knowledge-Grounded LLM-Assisted Procedural Modeling of Qing Dynasty Architecture
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for integrating natural-language interaction with procedural content generation (PCG). However, heritage architectural modeling requires more than syntactically valid parameter generation, as generated forms must comply with historically grounded construction rules, component dependencies, and executable asset constraints. This study takes Qing-dynasty official timber architecture as a case study and presents Prompt-to-Structure , a knowledge-grounded framework that translates natural-language generation intent into minimal, executable procedural specifications. The framework integrates a reference corpus derived from architectural treatises and scholarship, a domain knowledge graph encoding architectural rules and applicability constraints, and a metadata-indexed 3D component library. Given a user prompt, retrieval-augmented grounding supports specification generation, while deterministic validation and component resolution ensure that the resulting parameters can be instantiated procedurally in Blender. Experiments show that, compared with unguided LLM baselines, the complete pipeline improves rule compliance while maintaining semantic alignment and reliable procedural executability. These results demonstrate the potential of constrained LLM–PCG workflows for rule-consistent heritage architectural generation and hypothesis visualization under historically grounded constraints.

auditPapers.title: 17th-century copies of a 15th-century early Netherlandish painting uncovered through technical and art-historical research
auditPapers.abstract: Studies of Early Netherlandish panel paintings have long implemented techniques such as dendrochronology, pigment analysis and infrared reflectography. However, knowledge about the production of workshop replicas from fifteenth century paintings, and later copies, remains limited. As a result, the attribution of such paintings poses a challenge to art historians. Here, we present a multidisciplinary investigation into two copies of an Early Netherlandish panel painting attributed to the fifteenth-century Flemish painter Pieter Cristus (or Petrus Christus), active in Bruges (Belgium) between c. 1445 and 1460 CE. Earlier research dated these works to the late 15th century based on dendrochronology and pigment analysis, although alternative hypotheses suggested a 17th-century origin or even modern forgery. To resolve this debate, we applied dendrochronology, radiocarbon dating, MA-XRF, infrared reflectography, Raman spectroscopy, and stylistic analysis. The new dendrochronological results, supported by radiocarbon dating, proved key in refuting the hypothesis of the 15th-century date, revealing that the trees were cut around the mid-17th century. Furthermore, while the pigments identified were largely consistent with 15th-century painting practices, the stylistic characteristics and the presence of the inscription “I.P.C” ( invenit Petrus Cristi ) in one of the paintings supports a production in the mid-17th century or shortly afterwards. These findings challenge the reliability of earlier dendrochronological assessments and illustrate that pigment analysis alone cannot securely date paintings, as historical materials and techniques persisted over time. Overall, our research highlights the practice of copying Early Netherlandish paintings in the 17th-century and the importance of integrated technical and art-historical approaches for accurate attribution.

auditPapers.title: Applicability of automated sonic tomography inspection systems for the on-site structural assessment of the internal condition of historical stone masonry walls
auditPapers.abstract: Among common non-destructive testing techniques, sonic testing is frequently used for the qualitative assessment of historical masonry structures. The present study aims to improve the current capabilities of the sonic test method by exploring: (a) the advantages of automating the inspection; and (b) the use of advanced imaging methods to aid in the interpretation of the results for structural diagnosis. An automated sonic tomography inspection system previously developed by the research team was tested on-site in two remote heritage sites in Albania and Switzerland. The automation of the inspection allowed collecting the large amount of data required for 3D tomographic imaging the interior of different types of masonry walls, which can help detecting and estimating the extension of both poor and sound areas of masonry, as well as inner cracks. Results show the potential of the use of robotic systems for the structural diagnosis of heritage buildings, which can greatly enhance our capabilities of imaging the subsurface of masonry structures.

auditPapers.title: Circulating Subjects: Sex Work and Migration in Russia, 1885-1935
auditPapers.abstract: The author of this compelling book, Philippa Hetherington, died in November 2022, a scholar barely into mid-career but already established as a transformative historian of Russian and Soviet gender, sexuality, and migration. She left the substantially completed manuscript of this book, posthumously edited by colleagues Alessandro Iandolo and Gregory Afinogenov. The product of deep archival research and years of thinking about migration, sex work, and “liberal and illiberal internationalisms,” Hetherington’s study of how Russians responded to the perceived crisis of “trafficking in women” will be essential reading for historians of international law and gender, and scholars of sexualities and migration too. Circulating Subjects asks how Imperial and later Soviet Russia conceptualized and regulated cross-border migration for sex work, which in the late nineteenth century was dubbed “the traffic in women” or “white slavery.” After numerous non-governmental and diplomatic conferences, by 1910 an International Convention on the Suppression of the White Slave Traffic was signed by thirteen European countries including the Russian Empire; it became a foundational piece of international law “putting a gendered and sexualized understanding of international security at its core” (10). Hetherington argues that study of Russian engagement with this transnational issue offers fresh perspectives on Imperial and Soviet governmentality at home, and a particular challenge to historiographies of “trafficking” across borders, which tend to ignore Russia. She reads rich evidence from archives of the Russian Society for the Defense of Women (ROZZh) founded in 1899; Imperial government ministries; experts in medicine and law arguing for legal change; activist journalism; Soviet ideologists; and medical and legal experts at work under Lenin and Stalin.

auditPapers.title: Morphometric and experimental evidence for a cranial bandage hypothesis in the Sudarium of Oviedo
auditPapers.abstract: The Sudarium of Oviedo is a historical textile preserved in Oviedo, bearing blood stains and linear traces of uncertain origin. This study evaluates whether these features can be explained by the action of a cranial bandage applied during early post-mortem handling, within the broader context of ancient funerary wrapping practices in which cranial bandaging served stabilisation and containment functions. A three-stage analytical framework was developed. First, high-resolution raster scans were processed through a reproducible image-analysis pipeline including background correction, adaptive contrast enhancement, edge-preserving smoothing, percentile-based intensity mapping, and sub-pixel isoline extraction. These procedures enabled the identification of linear structures and local concentrations of intensity consistent with blood accumulation under external compression. Second, controlled laboratory experiments were carried out using a cranial model, linen textiles, and a warm blood simulant so as to replicate the sequence of postural changes and wrapping configurations derived from documented ancient funerary wrapping protocols. The image-based analysis revealed directionally coherent linear corridors across the frontal and occipital regions, with preserved orthogonality of the textile weave beneath the traces. Percentile isolines showed persistent clusters of high intensity that spatially correlate with anatomical prominences where compression would be expected. Experimental replication generated comparable linear flows, reorientation of fronts during positional changes, and compact accumulation points under light bandage pressure. Together, morphometric evidence and experimental outcomes indicate that the observed patterns are consistent with, but do not uniquely demonstrate, a compression-related wrapping mechanism. The framework provides a replicable method for evaluating compression-related traces in ancient textiles and informs broader archaeological interpretations.

auditPapers.title: Designing for Nature, Time and History: Novel Locative Technologies for Multilayered Heritage
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Natureculture heritage sites are dynamic spaces where ecological, cultural, and historical forces converge, often creating tensions between preservation, accessibility, and interpretation. This study explores how locative technologies can navigate these tensions by embedding digital interaction within the material and affective fabric of place, enabling context-sensitive storytelling and surfacing silenced narratives. We investigate visitor experiences at three contrasting sites — Madeira's Levadas (Portugal), the Avebury Landscape (UK), and the site of the Battle of the Boyne (Ireland) — to examine how visitors engage with more-than-human histories and temporalities, thus identifying six distinct design spaces within three overarching typologies of natureculture heritage: Ideal Nature , Ideal Time , and Ideal History . Based on how these novel typologies inform the operation of locative technologies as ethical mediators between human and nonhuman agencies, we subsequently present the design of seven bespoke locative experiences across the three sites, diversely exploring communication technologies in support of novel heritage encounters. This paper advances HCI debates on posthuman design for naturecultures by illustrating how locative media concepts can be informed by the particular context and challenges of the heritage site, and how its design can consider situated, relational, and ethically attentive engagement with multilayered heritage.

auditPapers.title: The Politics of Energy in Colonial Suriname
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In colonial Suriname, a society shaped by slavery and indenture, the infrastructure and technologies of energy arrived as extensions of a colonial order that had long concentrated resources among elites. Drawing on colonial and company archives, this article shows how working-class Surinamese women and men engaged with gas and electricity, destroying street lamps one day while demanding connection the next. During the tumultuous 1930s, these communities protested against unequal access to power, exploitative labour practices at energy plants, and the racialized logics of privatization. As a monopoly in a small colonial society eager to expand its customer base, the European energy utility was compelled to respond to these demands. Yet even as energy use crossed from public into private space, working-class households continued to thwart colonial expectations that it would appease them, instead adapting these technologies to the survival of their own social worlds. Whether on the street or in the home, working-class engagement with energy revealed an ambivalence towards colonial modernity that challenged the terms of its imposition. This examination of how energy became a site of conflict shaped by a Caribbean plantation context thus extends energy history beyond its usual focus of the Global North.
topics: Politics and Society in Latin America

auditPapers.title: Computational Strategies for Measuring and Visualizing Tonal Structures: Towards a Large-Scale Analysis of Wagner’s Ring Cycle
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Within Western classical music, Richard Wagner’s Der Ring des Nibelungen stands out as a monumental work, comprising nearly 22,000 measures and 15 hours of music with a continuous dramatic narrative. Structuring such a large-scale work comprises an enormous challenge, which particularly affects the work’s tonal organization. While other compositional techniques such as Wagner’s use of leitmotifs have been extensively studied, his approach to structuring the tonal framework of the Ring remains subject to musicological debate. In this paper, we present a computer-assisted approach for exploring the tonal organization of the Ring combining two traditional analytical perspectives based on sheet music with a novel computational strategy based on audio recordings. The first traditional perspective is the idealized tonal analysis by Alfred Lorenz from the 1920s, the second perspective examines key signature regions derived from Wagner’s original score. We complement and compare these two views with a third, computational perspective: an audio-based strategy for measuring diatonic scale content over time, which is based on deep-learning techniques introduced in our previous work. To integrate these three perspectives, we propose a visual overlay technique using a dedicated color scheme, which offers a comprehensive and comparative view of Wagner’s tonal conception. This integrated approach not only provides new insights into the Ring ’s large-scale tonal organization but also demonstrates the broader potential of computational methods for musicological research regarding their ability to address challenges such as scalability, reproducibility, and objectivity of analysis. Audio-based strategies, in particular, offer a promising alternative to using symbolic (machine-readable) scores, which are often unavailable for large-scale works and tedious to create. Overall, we demonstrate that by providing automated measurements of tonal structures, computational tools can significantly enhance and expedite the tonal analysis of large-scale musical compositions such as Wagner’s Ring .

auditPapers.title: Study of menthol sublimation kinetics to deliver essential oil for the disinfection of stone monuments
auditPapers.abstract: The biodeterioration of stone substrates represents a major issue in cultural heritage conservation, as microbial colonization – driven by environmental factors and stone bioreceptivity – can induce irreversible surface and structural damage over time. Chemical biocides remain widely used, but their environmental and toxicological drawbacks have prompted the search for sustainable and eco-compatible alternatives. Within this context, Essential Oils (EOs) are increasingly studied for their antimicrobial activity and low environmental impact, although their high volatility strongly limits persistence and long-term performance on stone surfaces. This study introduces an innovative approach based on the use of menthol as a film-forming, volatile binding medium for EOs, aimed at modulating its evaporation kinetics and enhancing coating stability. Oregano EO ( Origanum vulgare L.), one of the most frequently employed natural biocides against stone-colonizing microorganisms, was selected and combined with menthol at different ratios. The mixtures were characterized by ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, while sublimation kinetics were investigated on both non-porous glass slides and porous stone substrates (Carrara marble and Peperino). Gravimetric monitoring was performed under controlled conditions, and additional morphological and optical surface assessments were carried out using Optical Coherence Tomography and Fiber Optics Reflectance Spectroscopy. The results demonstrate that menthol affects the sublimation dynamics, film morphology, and evaporation rate of oregano EO. These findings highlight the potential of EO–menthol systems as sustainable and adaptable surface treatments. By addressing the intrinsic limitations of EO volatility, this work provides new insights into the design of next-generation, eco-compatible biocidal formulations specifically tailored to the preventive conservation of stone cultural heritage.

auditPapers.title: How narrative content supports reading immersion: an empirical analysis of digital reading traces of detective fiction
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Purpose: This study examines how narrative content in detective fiction is associated with indicators of reading immersion, using narrative transportation theory to connect textual topics with readers’ emotional and cognitive responses. Design/methodology/approach: The study analyses 27,999 reader-selected excerpts from 100 highly ranked detective novels on Douban, posted between February 2011 and January 2024. Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) was used to identify narrative topics, and a BERT classifier assigned excerpts to the resulting categories. Sentiment dictionaries and the Text Mind system generated emotional and cognitive indicators. Non-parametric tests examined temporal trends and differences across subtopics. Findings: The excerpts formed three narrative dimensions (plot, humanity, and society) and seven subtopics. Plot-related content received consistently high attention; attention to humanity-level content declined over time, whereas attention to society-level content increased. Positive and negative sentiment indicators both rose, and the seven subtopics showed distinct emotional and cognitive profiles. These patterns inform a three-stage interpretive model linking content accessibility, emotional and cognitive engagement, and intellectual extension. Originality: The study moves beyond reviews and self-reports by treating reader-selected excerpts as digital traces of textual salience and by integrating topic modelling, supervised classification, sentiment analysis, and cognitive-semantic analysis. Contribution to the field of digital humanities: It provides a content-sensitive framework and a reproducible computational workflow for investigating how literary form, reader selection, and interpretive response interact at scale.

auditPapers.title: Confocal and angular-resolved XRF: A comparative study of mobile techniques for the non-invasive analysis of layered structures in artworks
auditPapers.abstract: Cultural heritage artworks are complex heterogeneous objects, often with intricate stratigraphies. The study of such intricate strata traditionally relies on invasive cross-sectional analyses involving microsampling. These destructive approaches, nevertheless, raise conservation concerns and should be minimized. Nonetheless, and although a growing demand for mobile non-invasive methods exists in heritage science, few are able to directly and non-destructively analyze thin superimposed layers. Two X-ray Fluorescence (XRF) techniques may prove vital to solve this: Confocal XRF (CXRF), and Angle-Resolved XRF (AR-XRF). While CXRF has proven highly effective for the study of museum paintings and cave art, AR-XRF remains less explored in heritage studies. Here, we present a first comparative evaluation of both non-invasive approaches for cultural heritage using high-performance mobile instruments recently developed at the XRAYLab in Catania. The CXRF scanner provides vacuum-free, low-powered, fast 3D mapping capabilities (dwell times as low as 200 ms; 8.8 µm (FWHM) confocal depth resolution at Zr Kα), while also supporting 2D micro-XRF scanning. The compact AR-XRF vacuum-free instrument, equipped with a low-power monochromatic source, has been designed for portability and versatility (supports GI-XRF, AR-XRF, GE-XRF, and TXRF) and offers sub-ppm detection limits for surface elements. Both devices are compared here on thin-film metallic standards, paint-stratigraphy mock-ups, and real artwork stratigraphies, showcasing their complementarity, highlighting their respective capabilities, and demonstrating their power for future revolutionary heritage studies.

auditPapers.title: Decontamination of archival cultural heritage materials with gamma radiation: a non-destructive investigation of paper and parchment documents from Montecassino Abbey (Cassino, Italy)
auditPapers.abstract: The conservation of Cultural Heritage (CH) materials, particularly archival documents and manuscripts, faces ongoing challenges due to biological deterioration caused by mold, bacteria, and insects. Traditional conservation and restoration methods are often invasive, time-consuming, and may involve the use of hazardous chemicals. In this context, ionizing radiation emerged as an effective, non-invasive alternative for the stabilization of fragile historical materials. This study presents the results of an experimental treat- ment using gamma irradiation applied to selected parchment fragments and paper documents from the historic collection of the Archive of Montecassino Abbey (Italy). The treatment aimed to assess the com- patibility of gamma radiation for the conservation of both paper and parchment-based heritage objects. Pre- and post-irradiation analyses were conducted by coupling microbiological analyses with Raman, At- tenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR/ATR), UV–Vis spectroscopies and colorimetric measurements. The results confirm that gamma irradiation at the applied doses does not cause any sig- nificant structural or chromatic alterations to the treated materials, while ensuring a substantial decrease in fungal and bacterial microbial load. These findings support the suitability of gamma irradiation as a non-invasive and efficient approach for the decontamination of delicate CH objects, such as parchment and paper documents.

auditPapers.title: An empirical study on the complex network characteristics of the Japanese language
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This study selects eight registers of modern Japanese: interview, speech, official document, sci-tech text, political commentary, essay, poem, and novel, as corpora. Undirected and unweighted Japanese word co-occurrence networks are constructed using MeCab and Gephi. Based on complex network theory, this paper investigates the small-world and scale-free properties of Japanese linguistic networks. It applies quantitative tools: Erdős-Rényi random network benchmark, small-world index S, two-way analysis of variance, nonlinear fitting, piecewise regression, and Bootstrap resampling. Power-law tests follow the Clauset et al. method. Results indicate network size and register type exert significant main and interaction effects on small-world strength. The theoretically critical node number for small-world emergence is ninety-one, the empirical threshold eighty-nine, both falling within the 95 per cent confidence interval (81–146), confirming consistent theoretical and empirical findings. However, after removing high-frequency function words such as particles and auxiliary verbs, the network S-values are generally lower than 3, the threshold effect disappears, and the small-world property becomes unstable. The small-world property is neither an inherent attribute of the Japanese lexical system nor a direct outcome of the internal structure of word co-occurrence; instead, it heavily relies on the grammatical scaffolding constructed by high-frequency function words serving as hub nodes. Of the 119 sampled networks, 88 per cent pass power-law tests and show standard hierarchical scale-free features: core words form dense hubs, while peripheral words have sparse connections. There exists a moderately weak yet statistically significant correlation between the number of nodes and the power-law exponent. This research provides theoretical and methodological support for stylometry, Japanese structural linguistic analysis, and natural language processing.

auditPapers.title: “While We Have a Shared Past, We Do Not Have a Shared Memory”
auditPapers.abstract: In 2023, political leaders, museum curators, and documentary filmmakers marked the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement’s twenty-fifth anniversary. They hailed the Agreement as a historic watershed for peace in Northern Ireland but also diagnosed a faltering subsequent peace process. Their visions for reviving that process differed. Elite commemorations promoted an agreed memory of 1998 as a perennial testament to intercommunal compromise. By contrast, commemorative exhibitions and broadcast media deliberately amplified the conflict’s contested memory. This article analyzes how these contrasting commemorative practices proposed to reinvigorate Northern Ireland’s stalling peace process. First, it differentiates how elite politicians and public history practitioners marked the anniversary. The article proceeds to examine how curators and broadcasters amplified Northern Ireland’s disagreed past to reimagine its future democratic renewal.

auditPapers.title: “It Smelt Real”
auditPapers.abstract: Despite the emergence of sensory history and the increasing use of smell at museums and heritage sites, little attention has been paid to how smell experiences and public perceptions of the past mutually shape each other. Using newspapers, user-generated reviews, participant observation, and surveys, this article provides an analysis of smell’s use and reception at Jorvik Viking Centre, one of the first UK museums to use artificial ambient scents, from its opening in 1984 to the present. Both distributions of the sensible and longer histories of smell media have shaped the way academics, museums professionals, and visitors have responded to Jorvik’s smells. In contrast to existing work that has dismissed the use of smell in museums and heritage spaces as a curatorial trick that contrasts a foul-smelling past with contemporary odorlessness, this article argues that Jorvik’s scents offer an example of a “key smell” that allows for the exploration of multiple overlapping experiences of the past and that draws on an audience equation of realism and authenticity with the strength, emotional intensification, and distillatory quality of reconstructed smellscapes.

auditPapers.title: Miniature Material Worlds: Women and the Baby House in Eighteenth-Century England
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Unlike modern dolls’ houses, eighteenth-century baby houses were more than playthings meant only for children. For genteel women and girls alike, these small-scale spaces held positions of large significance. Taking a material culture approach that combines analysis of extant baby houses with an array of archival evidence, this article reconstructs their role as important affective agents within women’s lives. Expanding upon existing studies which illuminate the connection between the baby house and the full-scale domestic interior, it argues that these miniature material realms were also inherently entwined with the ever-growing world of goods around them. Rather than simply replicating this wider material world in miniature, the baby house represented a powerful and especially intimate medium through which the female user could contemplate and negotiate her place within it. Furthering a flourishing literature concerned with the analytical potential of smallness, the article demonstrates how a close focus upon these personal objects can shed new light on women’s emotional, sensory, and material experiences in this period. It thus advances recent efforts to rehabilitate the status of feminine toys and trinkets, doubly dismissed because of their size, and inherent association with women, as essential historical agents worthy of scholarly investigation.

auditPapers.title: Hugo Grotius’ Protestant Positive Law
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article reconsiders the novelty of Hugo Grotius by shifting attention from his idea of natural law to his reformulation of the idea of divine positive law. Modern scholarship has often questioned the novelty of Grotius’ natural law, emphasizing instead his dependence on earlier traditions, chiefly Catholic scholasticism. Against this view, the article argues that Grotius’ distinctive and influential interventions lay not in natural law as such but in his reconceptualization of divine positive law and its systematic separation from natural law. The term divine positive law first gained currency among Catholic theologians and was then employed specifically in defence of the sacerdotal authority of the Church. At the hand of Grotius, however, it was identified as the entirety of divine commands in Scripture, including the Decalogue and the Gospel. Through this transition, natural law became detached from Scripture, and its obligation unprecedently minimal and permissive. Situating these innovations within the developments of Remonstrant theology and Hebraic scholarship in the Protestant Dutch Republic, this article shows how Grotius’ idea of divine positive law gave rise to a new study of natural law as well as debates on the interpretation of the Old Testament and on the nature of Christian obligation.

auditPapers.title: Cultural and ethical dimensions of anthropomorphizing technology in Africa
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article examines how anthropomorphism, the attribution of human characteristics to non-human systems, acquires distinctive cultural, ethical, and technological significance in African societies, and develops a relational framework for understanding human–machine interaction that challenges prevailing Western narratives. The study adopts a critical interpretivist, narrative–synthesis approach, drawing on African philosophy, science and technology studies, artificial intelligence (AI) ethics, cultural anthropology, and posthumanism to construct an interpretive account of how technologies are domesticated, reinterpreted, and morally evaluated within African cosmologies. African anthropomorphism is rooted in traditions such as animism, totemism, oral storytelling, and communal ethics, and embodies a relational ontology in which personhood and agency are shared among human and non-human actors. Robots, AI systems, and Information and Communication Technologies are variously interpreted as moral subjects, children-in-training, or spiritually charged instruments, with notable regional variation across West, East, and Southern Africa. The article synthesizes a fragmented body of African scholarship on technology, animism, and relational ethics into a single, sustained framework for anthropomorphism, treating African cosmologies as a primary analytical lens rather than a comparative aside to Euro-American theory. The article contributes to a pluralistic understanding of technology ethics and offers a framework relevant to the design, governance, and study of AI and robotics in culturally diverse settings. This is done by foregrounding African relational epistemologies in debates on human–machine interaction.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

auditPapers.title: Bureaucratic Violence and the Home Office in the Long 1980s
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Drawing on Home Office records, anti-deportation campaign archives, memoirs, and interviews, this article examines the role of emotion and discretion in British deportation policy during the 1980s. It argues that deportation decisions were not simply the product of legislation or administrative procedure, but were shaped by the discretionary judgments of politicians and civil servants. Tracing the emotional dynamics between campaigners and state actors, the article reveals how deportation became normalized as an instrument of immigration control by the 1990s.

auditPapers.title: Mary McCarthy and the Watergate Crisis
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Watergate is conventionally understood through insider narratives about its complex daily churn as an unfolding political scandal. But the crisis also drove broader theoretical debates about democracy and the state in 1970s America. This article offers the first sustained account of Mary McCarthy’s Watergate writings. She theorized Watergate as a stark legitimacy crisis that revolved around the relationship between democracy and totalitarianism. Through dialogues with Hannah Arendt and others, McCarthy argued that Watergate turned politically on the public’s ability to unmask and contest the power of totalitarian state actors. By rejecting tragedy as a conceptual framework for Watergate, and by recentring the state in debates about US totalitarianism, McCarthy’s work shows how and why interactions between public opinion and state power could advance both democratic and anti-democratic politics.

auditPapers.title: “TO SEUNAGAN SEEKING HAS SPREAD”: THE TRANSMISSION OF ESOTERIC TRADITION AND HISTORY AS PROPHECY
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT In this essay, I explore accusations of heterodoxy, as well as rebuttals of these accusations, leveled at Sufi groups in late‐colonial and independent Aceh, the last region of what is today Indonesia to fall under Dutch colonial rule. What has been at stake in debates about the orthodoxy of such groups has not simply, or even primarily, been questions of proper belief or practice but concerns over historical and interpersonal relationships among participants in esoteric traditions. Following Nancy K. Florida's attentiveness to the ways in which “prophetic history” entails engagements with the past that entwine people across temporalities, I argue that accounts contesting the alleged heterodoxy of esoteric traditions in Aceh have been infused with an emphasis on seeking active and ongoing relationships across time and space, a mode that I identify as an intercessionary form of prophetic history. The proponents and detractors of any particular tradition make their claims not simply by referencing authoritative precedents but by cultivating relationships with those who populate the pasts that they invoke. This reframes orthodoxy as an ethical act of prophetic historiography.

auditPapers.title: Unsupervised rhyme recognition across multiple languages: training data size, human agreement, and linguistic differences
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Rhyme is deceptively intuitive: what is or is not a rhyme is constructed historically, scholars struggle with rhyme classification, and people disagree on whether two words are rhymed or not. This complicates automated rhymed recognition and evaluation, especially in cross-language research contexts. This article investigates how much training data are needed for reliable unsupervised rhyme recognition using RhymeTagger, a language-independent tool that identifies rhymes based on repeating patterns in poetry corpora. We evaluate its performance across seven languages (Czech, German, English, French, Italian, Russian, and Slovene), examining how training size and language differences affect accuracy. To set a realistic performance benchmark, we assess inter-annotator agreement on a manually annotated subset of poems and analyze factors contributing to disagreement in expert annotations: phonetic similarity between rhyming words and their distance from each other in a poem. We also compare RhymeTagger to three large language models (LLMs) using a one-shot learning strategy. Our findings show that, once provided with sufficient training data, RhymeTagger consistently outperforms human agreement, while LLMs lacking phonetic representation significantly struggle with the task.

auditPapers.title: Microhistory and Women’s Time Use
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Gender historians have pioneered attention to ‘doing words’ to identify otherwise invisible women’s work. Searches in court records for verbs with female subjects have documented women’s widespread participation in economic activity, often directing and managing, while playing down their unpaid care for family members. This article turns to a microhistorical source, diaries written by Peter Walkden, a farmer and Nonconformist minister living in eighteenth-century Lancashire. Walkden’s account of his farming routine and interactions with family and community incidentally describes the activities of his wife, Catherine. Evidence of her ‘doings’ identifies Catherine’s repertoire of tasks but is extended here to identify work and labour relations by the ownership of equipment, production for use or sale, and the need for occasional stand-ins when Catherine was indisposed or unavailable. Additional circumstantial evidence and other historical and modern sources enable the estimation of the frequency and duration of tasks, so providing the first breakdown of an early modern woman’s working day. Findings confirm the extent of women’s work but reinstate unpaid care as vital to the functioning of Walkden’s household, and by inference to social reproduction generally. Significantly, when Walkden himself had to provide care or pay for an understudy, it was understood as work and its value recognized.
