auditPapers.title: The importance of the optical properties of the materials involved in laser cleaning: the case of calcium oxalate and albumen patinas on oil paintings
auditPapers.abstract: The presence of calcium oxalate patinas on easel paintings is well documented in the literature, as they clearly affect the overall visual perception of an artwork due to their chalky appearance. Their formation mechanisms have been widely debated, with calcium oxalate believed to form either from constituent materials or due to previous conservation treatments. Traditional cleaning approaches involving mechanical methods, aqueous systems, solvents, chelating agents and enzymes can produce unsatisfactory results or be overly intrusive. Removing calcium oxalate films could damage the original paint layers, making this task challenging. This study investigates the effectiveness of different laser systems for thinning or removing calcium oxalate and albumen patinas from oil paintings. The initial case study focused on an 18th-century oil painting titled «Christ on the Cross», recently treated at the conservation laboratories of the Academy of Fine Arts in L’Aquila. A widespread patina of calcium oxalate and albumen was present on the artwork. This layer formation was ascribed to mineralisation of a white egg-based varnish applied during a previous restoration following a strong cleaning. The patina was partially thinned using a 2940 nm Er:YAG laser system, usually employed for calcium oxalate removal, followed by application of a new varnish layer to reduce the whitish visual effect of the residues and saturate the paint layer. Building on this case study findings, this research further investigated laser cleaning options by testing other laser ablation regimes applicability, such as ultraviolet light wavelengths. Mock-ups were created to simulate the painting stratigraphy, incorporating various paint layers (e.g. Cadmium Yellow, Raw Umber and Ultramarine Blue), that were then covered with an artificial calcium oxalate-albumen patina. The laser tests involved mock-ups irradiation with the fundamental beam (1064 nm), the second (532 nm) and third (355 nm) harmonics of a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser, along with a 248 nm beam emitted from a KrF excimer laser. Both systems emitted nanosecond-duration pulses, while a longer pulses regime was investigated using a Short Free Running (SFR) Nd:YAG system with pulses of up to 130 μs. Reflectance-derived absorbance spectroscopy identified the absorption characteristics of the undesired patina and optical microscopy (OM) was used to evaluate the laser cleaning tests and to analyse changes occurred to the surface after irradiation. Additionally, Attenuated Total Reflectance-Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) and Raman spectroscopies were employed to identify any remaining patina and investigate potential alterations to the paint. Irradiation at 1064 nm and 532 nm wavelengths was found to damage the paint layers, as was the 355 nm wavelength, despite its superior performance in patina ablation. Our research has identified the 248 nm KrF system, which has not been previously reported for this type of application, as a promising alternative for cleaning oxalate patinas when conventionally Er:YAG systems prove to be unsatisfactory. The proposed methodology combines controlled, laser-assisted patina reduction and traditional solvent application to effectively clean the surface while preserving the paint layer integrity, thereby advancing the current state of research.

auditPapers.title: Recurrence plots – a tool for exploring repetition in un(der)studied language data
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Repetition, with and without variation, pervades language use. We see it, for example, in spontaneous conversation, in memes on social media, in traditional rhetoric and, of course, in poetry and oral tradition. This paper presents recurrence plotting as a visualisation tool for the analysis of exact and inexact repetition in language. It is a particularly powerful tool for the exploration of un(der)studied data, such as those arising through language documentation work, as its reliance on the visual sense offers instant, holistic insights into the structures of large amounts of data. Recurrence plotting can be used with any type of connected source material, including audio (e.g., full-spectra, f0 contours, etc.) and written data (e.g., transcripts, glosses and translations). We illustrate in this paper the diverse potential of recurrence plotting with data from two oral traditions: the Old Indo-Aryan Rigveda, and the oral tradition Igu of the eastern Himalayan society of the Kera’a.

auditPapers.title: From emperor to god: applying statistical methods to the spread of the Roman imperial cult in the eastern Mediterranean (1st–3rd century CE)
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The imperial cult is generally seen as a main instrument used by Roman emperors to ensure their subjects’ fidelity and, at the same time, as a central aspect in the public life of Eastern cities of the Empire that changed dramatically over time. Building on Hellenistic ruler cults that already framed the relationship between rulers and ruled in the Greek-speaking world, Roman emperor worship in the East developed as a polycentric and locally negotiated phenomenon rather than as a top-down imposition by Rome. The aim of this paper is to analyze the relationship between the establishment of Roman rule and the development of the imperial cult in the Greek cities of the Eastern Mediterranean, from 27 BCE to 235 CE. We focus on the Eastern Mediterranean, with particular emphasis on Asia Minor, where evidence for the imperial cult is densest and inter-city competition for imperial honors is most clearly attested. Methodologically, the relationship between emperors, the Greek cities of the Eastern Mediterranean and the sites where emperors were worshiped can be seen as a complex network data structure, and, as such, this paper applies a multimode network approach to chart the evolution of the imperial cult. The methodology section includes accessible explanations of key network measures, including betweenness centrality—which identifies nodes that serve as bridges between different parts of the network—and community detection, which reveals clusters of closely connected entities. The final section is devoted to some general conclusions. auditPapers.title: Computed Tomography, an aid to study techniques of artisanal processing of bronze ornamental elements dating back to the Iron Age
auditPapers.abstract: X-ray imaging constitutes a fundamental non-invasive approach for investigating the internal, otherwise inaccessible features of artworks and archaeological objects. Conventional radiography often provides sufficient information to identify material distributions, manufacturing techniques, and indicators of conservation state. While particularly effective for paintings and other planar artefacts, radiography may prove insufficient for complex objects or when image superposition hampers interpretation. In such cases, computed tomography is required to obtain a complete three-dimensional visualization of the artefact or archaeological find. This study is dedicated to the characterization of the craftsmanship of small bronze ornaments from northern Italy, with the aim of reinterpreting and modelling cultural interactions in Europe during the Early Iron Age. The project is based on the analysis of approximately 1200 copper-alloy adornments originating from six settlements associated with three interacting cultural areas: the Golasecca culture (north-eastern Piedmont), the Ligurian communities (southern Piedmont), and the indigenous groups of the western Po Valley. The excellent state of preservation of the artefacts, housed in three museums in France and Italy, together with the high quality of the archaeological documentation, enables an innovative and comprehensive investigation of northern Italian metallurgical practices. This study spans multiple scales, from the micro-scale analysis of surfaces and technical features to the macro-scale examination of workshop organization and interregional interactions, particularly with the Celtic world. By integrating archaeology, archaeometry, statistical analysis and data modelling, the project seeks to identify regional metallurgical traditions in north-western Italy and to address issues of techno-cultural transmission. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of artisans in shaping technological choices, social identities and the emergence of cultural groups during the Iron Age. Within this framework, reconstructing the chaîne opératoire represents a key challenge for understanding production strategies, technical variability, and the balance between innovation and tradition. This paper presents the X-ray imaging investigations conducted to date, with a specific focus on radiographic and tomographic analyses of a selection of fibulae from the settlements of San Polo and Villa del Foro. Although typologically comparable, these objects originate from different contexts. The study aims to identify the modelling and decorative techniques employed in their manufacture, thereby providing new insights into the production systems underlying these ornaments. Furthermore, the results contribute to assessing the existence of local metallurgical traditions and their possible transmission, adaptation, or transformation across cultural contexts.

auditPapers.title: Black-on-Black Makeup and the History of Blackface
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article contributes to transnational perspectives on blackface by examining evidence of Black individuals and communities employing darkening make-up or black masks on both sides of the Atlantic. Cases from across the world reveal multiple meanings, ranging from resistance to stereotypes to the symbolic restoration of ancestral blackness and affirmation of racial pride. Taken together, the evidence makes plain the need to interpret black-on-black blackface within its specific historical and cultural contexts. Furthermore, it calls attention to the transnational circulation of Afro-Iberian traditions of racial impersonation, largely overlooked in scholarship, alongside the diffusion of US minstrelsy. By foregrounding these alternative genealogies, the article contributes to a more nuanced and globally informed understanding of blackface and ethnic impersonation in the Atlantic world.

auditPapers.title: Lower thematic concentration and diversified narratives: a comparative stylometric study of Southeast Asian Chinese new poetry versus Mainland Chinese counterparts
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Theme, as the core content of literary works, serves as a linguistic style marker, reflecting authorial characteristics. Thematic studies facilitate profound comprehension of literary texts. Thematic concentration, a quantitative linguistic measurement, indicates an author’s intentional emphasis on specific themes, while thematic diversity quantifies the lexical-semantic richness within literary expressions. As a significant branch of Sinophone diaspora literature, Southeast Asian Chinese-language literature constitutes modern Chinese “New Literature” with discernible Chinese cultural imprints. Scholarly investigations in this domain represent a crucial subset of Chinese literary studies. Current research exhibits a paucity of empirical comparative studies regarding stylometric similarities between Southeast Asian Chinese New Poetry and Mainland Chinese New Poetry. This study therefore employs computational stylometry through SPSS 27.0 and Python programming, implementing thematic concentration metrics for cross-regional poetic comparison. Through corpus-driven methodology, integrating high-frequency lexical analysis and Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modeling, we quantitatively assess thematic configurations. Findings reveal: (1) significantly lower thematic concentration in Southeast Asian works versus Mainland counterparts, indicating a stronger monothematic tendency in Mainland poetry versus polythematic expressions in diaspora creations; (2) divergent thematic salience patterns—Mainland poetry emphasizes quotidian narratives, whereas Southeast Asian works prioritize natural imagery; (3) the inclusion of prose as control texts further elucidates genre-specific thematic distributions between poetic and prose forms.

auditPapers.title: Convergence behaviour and computational efficiency of Gaussian Splatting in complex heritage environments
auditPapers.abstract: This study evaluates the performance of three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for the documentation and virtualisation of architectural cultural heritage. Six datasets acquired in different areas of the Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba were analysed, representing a variety of capture strategies and scene scales. The datasets were obtained using different acquisition devices, including a drone, a Digital Single-Lens Reflex (DSLR) camera, a mobile phone, and a 360° camera. The images were photogrammetrically orientated using a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) workflow in RealityScan, and the estimated camera intrinsics and poses were subsequently exported to COLMAP format. The datasets were processed using 3DGS, and the training behaviour was analysed across two hardware configurations (RTX3070Ti and RTX5070 GPUs). The study evaluated reconstruction quality and convergence behaviour using three complementary image quality metrics: Peak Signal-to-Noise-Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS). Additionally, training time and computational efficiency were analysed to determine how scene complexity and hardware configuration affect the optimisation process. The results show that most of the improvement in perceptual quality occurs during the early stages of training. In the majority of cases, 90–95% of the perceptual improvement is achieved between 10000 and 20000 iterations, while the remaining iterations contribute mainly to minor visual refinements. The analysis also demonstrates that the hardware configuration does not significantly influence the final reconstruction quality, although it strongly affects computational performance in large scenes due to the progressive densification of Gaussian primitives during training. Overall, the results suggest that the number of training iterations can be significantly reduced without substantial loss of perceptual quality. These findings highlight the potential of GS as an efficient methodology for the digital documentation and visualisation of architectural heritage, combining high visual fidelity, relatively short training times, and the capacity for interactive rendering for research, dissemination, and educational applications.

auditPapers.title: The VOC’s “Dirty Work”: sodomy prosecutions and the Dutch East India Company’s sexual–moral order from the Indies to the Dutch Republic, 1600–1730
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article examines sodomy prosecutions by the Dutch East India Company (VOC) during the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. It shows that long before the Dutch “gay panic” of 1730, colonial workers were actively (if selectively) prosecuted for sodomy by the VOC’s ship and fleet councils, as well as the corporate colonial courts in the Dutch East Indies. These prosecutions, this article argues, contributed to the construction of a Dutch sexual–moral order in the colonial encounter—within, and as a function of, European imperialist capitalism, and by extension, capitalist law. The overarching aim of the “VOC sexual-moral order” was VOC commercial hegemony in the Indies, and labor discipline, with “sexual enclosure” (following Christopher Chitty) delineating permitted and punishable practices. VOC leaders like J.P. Coen articulated an ideal Dutch identity, the “nation mirrored in the individual,” contrasting it with Asian (especially Muslim) societies. The contested VOC sexual–moral ordering “boomeranged” back to the Dutch Republic in the early eighteenth century. The story of one convicted sodomite, Leendert Hasenbosch, tracks this boomerang movement from the Dutch Indies back to the Dutch Republic, where, during the 1730s “gay panic,” the criminalization of sodomy served to strengthen and legitimize the nascent capitalist state apparatus. The case of the VOC shows that colonial history is part of Western history of sexuality, and illuminates how European, and eventually hegemonic, ideas about sexuality in fact developed in the colonial encounter. Conversely, it shows that sexuality, alongside race, forms a key part of the history of imperialism and European state-formation.

auditPapers.title: A new methodology based on a multiscale analysis of hammering indicators to further investigate the ancient manufacturing techniques of copper-based artefacts

Florida's account of Javanese “history‐as‐prophecy,” I demonstrate that al‐Saqqāf mobilized prophecy not as eschatological closure or antiquarian devotion but as a historiographic method that renders time morally legible and political generative. Through the concept of miṣdāq (extension), al‐Saqqāf aligned dispersed episodes of anticolonial resistance and Islamic revival with a prophetic ḥadīth about a continuously “victorious group,” thus reframing Indonesian history as an unfolding exegesis of Muḥammadan truth. I propose that history‐as‐extension‐of‐prophecy illuminates a distinctive temporal politics, one that carries inherited promises forward while activating unrealized possibilities in the present. It neither binds political life to a fixed past nor surrenders it to revolutionary novelty. Instead, it mediates continuity and interruption by treating disparate events as links in an open prophetic arc. The essay thus positions prophetic historiography as a critical resource for thinking moral legibility, historical responsibility, and alternative futurities beyond the tradition/revolution binary.

auditPapers.title: The proper use of t -tests in computational stylistics

auditPapers.title: Displaced women, law and competing patriarchies in late Ottoman Serbia

Their legal belonging remained tethered to household authority even as new centralizing political and legal orders took shape. In this unstable transitional period, patriarchy was distributed and enforced across competing scales and legal structures, including households, villages, Ottoman imperial institutions, and emerging Serbian state structures. The article contends that modern patriarchies emerged out of early modern household-based legal regimes and systems of village authority, and that modern forms of statelessness stem from problems that became legible during transitional periods and were never resolved.

auditPapers.title: Honour and Deceit in The Warres of Cyrus , Classical Persia, and Elizabethan Politics
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The role of drama in counselling the early modern monarch is well established, as is the centrality of classical Greek and Roman histories in early modern political culture. Through analysis of the Elizabethan play, The warres of Cyrus , this article argues that Achaemenid Persia should be placed alongside Greece and Rome as a key framework for early modern political discussion. The Achaemenid setting facilitated a vision of rule distinct from the usual classical models. In this Persian context, the virtuous prince was opportunistically ruthless, and unequivocally authoritarian. Performed by the children of the Chapel Royal in the 1570s, and published in the highly charged atmosphere of the 1590s, this drama casts light onto Elizabethan politics during times of marked political tension. Its emphasis on the disjuncture between appearance and reality evokes a political climate characterized by widespread fear of dissimulation. Elements at court, this article contends, met these fears with an emphasis on the stabilizing potential of a prince’s capacity for ‘policy’. At its first performance, The warres of Cyrus seems also to have sought to persuade Elizabeth to act leniently towards the captive Mary, Queen of Scots.

auditPapers.title: Institutionalization and Market Integration in the Archaic Greek Economy: Modelling Overseas Trade from the Distribution Pattern of Samian Transport Amphoras
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article advances the view that there was widespread institutionalization in the early Greek economy from the end of the eighth century bce. Challenging the widespread assumption that Mediterranean market integration crystallized much later and only by the end of the ‘archaic period’, agent-based modelling is used here alongside the archaeological distribution of Samian transport amphoras to demonstrate the coordination that must have existed between trade partners in shipping olive oil from one end of the Mediterranean to the other. ‘Brownian flow’ models of randomized drift fail to properly reproduce the amphora pattern, while a model based on a network of trade hubs stretching from the Black Sea to the shores of modern-day Spain provides a much more robust solution. These results shed light on the navigation of various environmental niches, on the lived experience of the sailors distributing products such as Samian olive oil, and most importantly suggest that the early Greek economy was more organized— and earlier, too —than we have previously suspected.

auditPapers.title: Deaf People, Language, and Emancipation in Modern France, 1789-1914. By Sabine Arnaud
auditPapers.abstract: In Deaf People, Language, and Emancipation in Modern France, 1789-1914, Sabine Arnaud explores a paradox in the history of deaf experience: how did the multiplicity of social exchanges between deaf and hearing people evident in 1800 lead to the segregation of these groups as “normal” versus “abnormal” a mere century later? In answering this question, Arnaud engages recurring themes from a small yet rich body of work by scholars such as Anne Quartararo, Harlan Lane, François Buton, Patrick Bourgalais, Jean-René Presneau, and Didier Séguillon—the contestation between the medical model of deafness as a disability versus the social and linguistic model of a minority community; the Foucauldian narrative of deaf education as one of institutional repression; and, most crucially, the resistance and agency of deaf people against the forces of normalization. In charting a history that seems to run contrary to the general expectation of gradually expanding disability rights over the modern era, this book celebrates the plurality of actors and ideas of an earlier time when alternative laws, norms, and systems could be imagined.

auditPapers.title: Food Security, Nitrates Capitalism, and the Haber–Bosch Revolution
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article reinterprets the early history of the Haber–Bosch process of ammonia synthesis through the transnational development of synthetic nitrogen production at Ludwigshafen am Rhein and Billingham-on-Tees, County Durham. It argues that the nitrates revolution in the early twentieth century was not simply a technological breakthrough but a contested project linking industrial strategy, state power, and food security. Tracing the British government’s wartime construction and subsequent privatization of the Billingham plant, it shows how economic orthodoxy constrained efforts to sustain state-led industrial co-ordination, even as private firms pursued cartelized forms of governance. It situates the British and German chemical industries within a shared political economy, and reframes fertilizer production as central to the emergence of modern food politics and the international political economy, anticipating later debates over sovereignty, inequality, and environmental limits. Recovering these histories reveals food security as a foundational problem of industrial modernity, with nitrates capitalism shaped by decisions about the governance of national resources, scientific expertise, and global markets.

auditPapers.title: THE PHILOLOGY OF RACE IN LATE QING CHINA
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article rethinks the problem of race from the late nineteenth century onward by examining how the concept of race configured an impasse in the relationship between history and nature in late Qing China. By analyzing the debate about race and history within late Qing philological discourse, it offers new readings of early foundational texts from China's long revolutionary twentieth century that address questions surrounding race, nation, and state. It takes late Qing intellectuals such as Zhang Taiyan, Liu Shipei, and Liang Qichao not as thinkers who were influenced by race but as thinkers of race—that is, individuals who scrutinized the coherence of a logic of race and its political possibilities. The fateful encounter between late Qing philology, the Kantian antinomy of race, and European comparative philology exposed the limits of a racial logic of reference by which the human was ordered on a global scale. This article locates within the reading and writing practices of late Qing philologists the demands on historical thought posed by a logic of race as well as its limits and contradictions. Thus, this article takes as its focus neither systems of racialization nor histories or genealogies of the concept of race. Rather, it scrutinizes the very use and coherence of race as a subject and/or object for historical thought. Through a critical appraisal of the late Qing philology of race, it seeks to delineate the pitfalls of the philological method while recovering the potential of its critical approach to history.

auditPapers.title: Unravelling the link between the simulacra of St Clemente of Palácio Nacional de Queluz and St Fortunato & St Semuc of Santa Casa da Misericórdia de Almada
auditPapers.abstract: This work presents a comparative osteological, material, and technical investigation of three 18th-century simulacra preserved in Portugal, aiming to clarify their origin, circulation, assembly, and shared workshop practices. Archival documentation and authentication seals confirmed their Roman origin and circulation during the 1770s. Radiocarbon dating places the skeletal remains between the 3rd and 5th centuries, spanning both periods of Christian persecution and subsequent imperial consolidation. Osteological, radiographic, and endoscopic analyses revealed differing anatomical configurations: St Semuc and St Fortunato incorporate remains from multiple non-adult individuals, assembled through deliberate substitution and consolidation practices, whereas St Clemente preserves a largely complete and anatomically coherent skeleton of a probable young adult male. Nevertheless, a similar assemblage for the body was uncovered for all simulacra . Facial modelling relied on silk gauze tiers, stiffened with various organic materials, alone or mixed, including proteinaceous and resin binders, such as collagen-based glues and conifer colophony-type. Imaging-based morphometric analysis was used to explore the weave type, and similar morphometric parameters were estimated, indicating a deliberate and coherent choice of gauze type. Ultimately, SEM-EDS showed that "false gold" strips (gilt-silvered-copper strips) were used in the simulacra's helmets. Overall, the interdisciplinary approach evidenced that simulacra were assembled as devotional reliquaries likely in Rome, and that they shared the same workshop or similar workshop practices.

auditPapers.title: Imaging (MSI, RTI) and spectroscopic (MFT, XRF) analyses of eighteenth-century gem drawings in the Princes Czartoryski Museum in Krakow
auditPapers.abstract: In the first half of the 18th century, Philipp von Stosch, in collaboration with several artists, created the most comprehensive and archaeologically advanced visual documentation of ancient engraved gems ever produced. Over time, however, his Paper Museum of Gems was dispersed and largely forgotten. This paper presents and discusses the results of X-ray fluorescence (XRF), reflectance transformation imaging (RTI), Multispectral imaging (MSI), and microfade testing (MFT) analyses conducted on selected gem drawings from the collection of the Princes Czartoryski Museum in Krakow, which comprises a substantial portion of the original archive. These investigations proved valuable on multiple levels. MSI enabled the reading of previously illegible texts, which in turn facilitated the identification of the original engraved gems depicted in the drawings and, in several cases, their dating. MSI also provided significant insights into the level of scholarship within Stosch’s circle. XRF and RTI yielded data supporting the attribution of groups of drawings to specific artists who worked for Stosch, particularly Girolamo Odam and Pier Leone Ghezzi. Finally, the combined use of MSI, XRF, and MFT helped to judge the condition of the drawings and allowed for the formulation of recommendations regarding the future conservation and handling of the drawings, including the implementation of protective measures due to the detection of toxic elements such as arsenic.

auditPapers.title: From Virile to Sterile: Science, Masculinity, and Modernity in Argentina, 1776-1852. By Adriana Novoa
auditPapers.abstract: Adriana Novoa’s new book is an intriguing deep dive into an important yet underappreciated dimension of late colonial and early national political culture in Argentina. Author of previous insightful studies of Darwinism and biological thought in nineteenth-century Argentine society, she has now turned to the contested and changing representations, understandings, and tensions around perceptions of gender in general, and masculinity in particular, during perhaps the most tumultuous period in Argentina’s political history. The last few decades of the eighteenth century and the first half of the nineteenth—that is, the beginning of the end of Spanish colonial rule and the first decades of the national period—were characterized by extreme political polarization, dramatic disagreement over national identity and the future of the nation, and horrible violence. Between 1810 and 1852, political struggle at the highest level broke down along lines of Federalists (aka the conservatives) and Unitarians (aka the liberals). Federalists represented traditional, Catholic, land-based interests; Unitarians were identified with “modernization” schemes, industry, and science, and looked to foreign sources for inspiration. There were also racial dimensions—real or imagined— to this divide, as conservatives were associated with the mixed-race, rural population, and liberals were unabashedly Eurocentric and sought to “whiten” the Argentine population through immigration. While at base much of their political conflict was rooted in competing views of the economic path of the new nation, not least control of valuable transportation routes and port city access to export goods from the interior, there were significant differences in their belief systems as well. Unitarians appear in hindsight to be part of post-Enlightenment liberal movements, that is, fostering democracy and political freedom, secularization, education, and science. Federalists were notorious for supporting authoritarian rulers like Juan Manuel de Rosas, suppressing free speech and press, and killing and torturing political enemies. Both groups, it should be pointed out, favored patriarchy of various flavors. There was little room for women’s voices or public roles; this was a man’s game.

auditPapers.title: Confusion of Places
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article explores the concept of “escape ecologies”—landscapes whose physical and institutional illegibility allows people to evade coercion—by linking the present-day Białowieża Forest to eighteenth-century Eastern Europe. Based on field observations made during the state of emergency on the Polish-Belarusian border in 2021, this essay shows that modernized environments, including abandoned drainage ditches, collapsed spruce monocultures, and dense undergrowth caused by forestry practices, grazing bans, and climate stress might serve as effective corridors and shelters for migrants, despite the presence of drones, patrols, and fences. Juxtaposing these observations with early modern maps and administrative records reveals analogous mechanisms in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. In this context, unregulated rivers, wetlands, riparian forests, and river islands allowed deserters, fugitives, dissenters (e.g., Old Believers), and commoners to move about, hide, negotiate, and resist. Such a perspective challenges power-centric historiography, which overinterprets textual archives produced by rulers while undervaluing environmental archives and vernacular practices. Thinking through escape ecologies makes it possible to see why the poorly governed marshes and forests of Eastern Europe attracted fugitives, dissenters, and migrants alike—and why, despite the radically different technological conditions, they continue to do so.
topics: Central European and Russian historical studies

auditPapers.title: Church of San Pietro Martire in Verona: A conservation-oriented approach between historical and structural interpretation
auditPapers.abstract: The study presents an integrated structural assessment and damage interpretation of the former Gothic church of San Pietro Martire in Verona (13th century) within a multidisciplinary, conservation-oriented framework. While recent studies on historic masonry churches increasingly integrate non-destructive diagnostics and modelling, a persistent gap remains in validating crack interpretations through combined historical, geometric and mechanical evidence, capable of distinguishing between long-term historic mechanisms and more later-stage damage phenomena. This research addresses this field by proposing and applying an integrated methodological workflow that combines historical–critical analysis, high-resolution geometric survey, vibration-based dynamic identification, microseismic testing and material investigations. Beyond documenting the building condition, the study develops a comparative and multi-criteria interpretation of the experimental data, aimed at the mechanical interpretation of the governing failure mechanisms. The results allow the differentiation between two structurally and chronologically distinct crack patterns: (i) a historic and currently active out-of-plane bending mechanism affecting the south façade, and (ii) a recent and presently inactive damage pattern associated with stiffness reconfiguration of the adjacent building aggregate. This distinction is supported by geometric displacement fields, modal shapes, experimentally derived stiffness parameters and first-level kinematic assessment. The novelty of the research lies in the cross-validated integration of historical, geometric, dynamic and local mechanical evidence to distinguish active and inactive crack mechanisms in historic masonry churches. This enables the definition of a transferable methodology in the framework of applied research, tested on complex and stratified cultural heritage sites within the operational and decision-making processes of the Superintendence, aimed at developing a global interpretation of structural behaviour that integrates the historical perspective of the research process with the current state of conservation of the building. The research is carried out within the framework of a collaborative process between the Cluster-Lab MATESCA of Università Iuav di Venezia and the Superintendence ABAP for the Provinces of Verona, Rovigo, and Vicenza (local office of the Italian Ministry of Culture), and the proposed methodology has constituted the knowledge base for the Ministry’s executive conservation design solutions.

auditPapers.title: Aluminum-copper alloy artifacts: A comparison between artificially-pitted mock-ups and aged aircraft materials
auditPapers.abstract: Collections of old aircraft stored outdoors in Air and Space museums often suffer from severe corrosion, highlighting the need for effective conservation protocols. This study examined the corrosion characteristics of two artifacts: a hatch from the Dassault Mirage IV-02 aircraft and an angle bracket from a Boeing 707 F-BHSL aircraft, known as “Château de Maintenon.” Even on painted surfaces, the long-term degradation of aluminum-copper alloys, such as the 2024 alloy, results in thick corrosion layers several hundred micrometers thick. This degradation often leaves highly corroded grain boundaries, which can lead to exfoliation and swelling of the metal. The goal of this study is to compare the heavily corroded states of these artifacts with those of 2024 alloy reference samples, which were later identified as effective mock-ups of old aircraft artifacts. This comparison aims to develop and eventually implement protective treatments for these mock-ups, since direct application to the original artifacts is not feasible. To achieve this goal, deep-pitted samples of two microstructurally distinct modern 2024 alloys have been artificially synthesized by straightforward electrochemical anodic polarization for several hours in a NaCl solution. Metallographic analysis using scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction reveals that the mock-ups and artifacts contain both aluminum hydroxide and pure copper nanoparticles among the corrosion products. For both the 2024 mock-up alloys and artifacts, the electrochemical behavior, as characterized by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, is very similar and can be easily interpreted in terms of active and passive electrochemical areas. The aircraft samples are somewhat less electroactive than the mock-ups, likely due to clusters of aluminum hydroxide on the surface and residues from surface treatments within the corrosion layer. Ultimately, both physicochemical and electrochemical characterizations indicate that these mock-ups closely mimic the two corroded aircraft artifacts, making them suitable for further development of conservation treatments.

auditPapers.title: Quantitative analysis of pigment mixtures on paper using fiber-optic reflectance spectroscopy and advanced optical modeling
auditPapers.abstract: Non-invasive methods are essential for studying materials in cultural heritage artworks. Among them, Fiber Optic Reflectance Spectroscopy (FORS) is widely employed for in situ analysis due to its portability and direct relationship with the optical properties governing color. However, FORS remains largely qualitative, as reflectance spectra of pigment mixtures show nonlinear behavior caused by complex absorption and scattering processes, especially on strongly scattering substrates such as paper. This work introduces the first quantitative application of the Yang–Miklavcic model to heritage pigments on paper. This model, an extension of the Kubelka–Munk theory, retrieves intrinsic absorption and scattering coefficients in inhomogeneous, highly scattering layers by accounting for the scattering-induced path variation of photons. Experimental tests were performed on mock-ups prepared on paper with single and binary mixtures of five pigments: ultramarine blue, chromium oxide green, burnt sienna, titanium white, and Naples yellow. Reflectance spectra were acquired with an integrating-sphere setup to measure diffuse reflectance. By using intrinsically derived optical coefficients, the method enables the separation of pigment scattering from that of the paper substrate, allowing accurate identification and quantitative estimation of the components in binary pigment mixtures on paper. The results demonstrate that FORS, when coupled with advanced optical modelling, provides reliable, non-invasive, and cost-effective quantitative compositional data for painted surfaces.

auditPapers.title: Multi-analytical assessment of dry plate negative cleaning using non-invasive optical methods
auditPapers.abstract: Cleaning has long been recognised as one of the most delicate operations in conservation, given its irreversible and potentially invasive nature. Despite its relevance to the conservation of photographic documents, the cleaning of mould-contaminated gelatine glass-plate negatives remains poorly documented. This study aims to assess the outcomes of cleaning treatments applied to mould-contaminated dry plate negatives using non-invasive and non-contact optical techniques. Both dry cleaning alone and combined with a hydroalcoholic solution were tested on fungal contamination. To assess cleaning efficacy, a novel acquisition setup for Reflectance Imaging Spectroscopy (RIS) was developed, enabling multispectral measurements on glass-plate negatives. These data were employed to calculate colour variation across the entire object surface. This approach combined with Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), optical microscopy-based profilometry, FTIR chemical imaging in reflectance mode, and stereomicroscopy, enabled systematic monitoring of the cleaning process. The results indicate only partial removal of mould from the emulsion layer, yielding important insights for conservators and highlighting the importance of preventive strategies against biological contamination. In addition, the conservation status of the negatives was investigated prior to cleaning using ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and OCT, providing additional information on the stratigraphy and degradation mechanisms of dry plate negatives and contributing to the advancement of knowledge of these still understudied cultural heritage objects.

auditPapers.title: Conservation of the painting “Genre scene in the countryside” by Włodzimierz Tetmajer (1861–1923) from the Silesian Museum in Katowice: application of nanocomposite organogel as novel system and emulsion removal
auditPapers.abstract: This study presents the first-ever application of a pNIPA-LAP nanocomposite organogel wax-resin removal system for the removal of emulsion mass during the conservation of a painting. The object of study – a 19th-century work by Włodzimierz Tetmajer from the Silesian Museum in Katowice, under conservation at the Jan Matejko Academy of Fine Arts in Kraków – was in a severely deteriorated condition, exhibiting extensive cupping of the paint layer and a thin emulsion mass of wax–resin and animal glue on the reverse of the canvas. Traditional conservation methods were deemed unsuitable due to the risk of further paint loss. The use of the pNIPA-LAP organogel, developed for controlled and minimally invasive cleaning, minimized the need for mechanical intervention on the reverse of the canvas. This article evaluates the performance of the pNIPA-LAP nanocomposite organogel and compares its effectiveness with that of two alternative materials traditionally used for wax–resin removal. The successful application of the organogel allowed the conservation of the painting to proceed to subsequent crucial stages. The comprehensive treatment included the removal of overpainting, consolidation of detached paint layers, extraction of wax and emulsion residues from the canvas, tear repair, relaxation of distortions, lining, filling of losses, and compositional reintegration – procedures consistent with the established conservation methodologies of the Faculty of Conservation and Restoration at the Academy of Fine Arts in Krakow.

auditPapers.title: Fragmented data, global bias: A synthesis of quantitative research on the illicit trade in cultural objects
auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Academic research into the illicit trade in cultural objects has grown substantially over the last 50 years. Yet our understanding remains dominated by fragmentary evidence, repetitive methodologies, and one-sided narratives that can enable epistemic blind spots and sensationalised claims. Without a comprehensive understanding of the trade, how it has been studied, and by whom, such blind spots will continue to limit the development of effective countermeasures. This review provides an initial synthesis of English-language quantitative research on the trafficking and trade in antiquities, examining how this research has been produced, by whom, where, and with what methods. Using systematic searches of academic databases and key outlets, we identified 168 English-language studies that used quantitative methods. Beginning with the first identified source from 1983, this constitutes a relatively limited body of work across more than four decades. Findings show a small and siloed subfield: nearly half of publications are solo authored and co-author clusters are weakly connected. Methodological approaches have become more interdisciplinary and diverse over time, yet explicit engagement with research ethics remains rare. Most notably, first authors are overwhelmingly based in the Global North while empirical focus falls disproportionately on Global South contexts, with limited collaboration involving scholars located in the regions under study. The article demonstrates that research into the illicit trade in cultural objects remains shaped by Anglo-American paradigms. By mapping existing evidence and its gaps, we hope to foster more diverse and effective evidence-based countermeasures.

auditPapers.title: TWO ACCOUNTS OF HISTORICAL KNOWLEDGE: HISTORIOGRAPHIC REASONING AND NARRATIVE ACCORDING TO AVIEZER TUCKER AND CHIEL VAN DEN AKKER1
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT This review essay examines a recurring distinction in the philosophy of history between the phase of establishing historical facts or knowledge claims and the phase of interpreting them. Focusing on two recent books by Aviezer Tucker and Chiel van den Akker, it analyzes how each author conceptualizes historical knowledge by emphasizing one of these phases. Tucker locates the core of historical practice in evidential reasoning and the production of knowledge claims about past events, which he regards as the basis for consensus among historians. In contrast, van den Akker concentrates on the construction and understanding of narrative theses and argues that historical narratives are not direct descriptions of evidence but unique interpretations. This review essay argues that, although the distinction between research and interpretation can be somewhat useful, an attempt to synthesize Tucker's and van den Akker's accounts into a single and more comprehensive theory of historical knowledge would be problematic. Since each framework highlights one phase and leaves the other underdeveloped, a meaningful theory of historical work must be developed internally within one conceptual framework rather than assembled from incompatible accounts with distinct priorities.

auditPapers.title: Making Marx More Readable: A Minimal Computing Approach to a Community-Driven Edition of Capital Vol. 1
auditPapers.abstract: The following article presents MARXdown, a minimal digital reading edition of Karl Marx’s Capital Vol. 1, as a retrospective case study in applying minimal computing principles to create accessible, community-driven digital humanities (DH) projects. Developed by graduate students at Carnegie Mellon University in 2019–20, MARXdown demonstrates how framing minimal computing as practical commitments can lower access barriers, demystify computing labor, and facilitate knowledge sharing. The project leveraged lightweight, open-source tools to create a collaborative reading environment that addressed specific community needs. This approach allowed for adaptability during the COVID-19 pandemic, transforming MARXdown into a vital support for collaboratively reading Marx under lockdown. The article argues that practical commitments to minimal computing can promote replicable models for building digital reading editions, useful for distributing marginalized or banned texts in underserved communities. By unpacking some of MARXdown's development process, this study offers insights into both the potential and limitations of minimal computing in academic and community-driven contexts, contributing to discussions about accessibility, sustainability, and ethics in DH.

auditPapers.title: American Philanthropy, European Pacifism, and the Parameters of the International Peace Movement before the First World War
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The establishment of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP) in 1910 was a transformative moment for the international peace movement, introducing significant financial resources and prioritizing an American-driven approach to global peace activism. Founded by Andrew Carnegie, the CEIP sought to eliminate war through rational, scientific, educational, and legalist efforts, promising a departure from the idealistic approaches considered typical of many European peace organizations. While Carnegie’s endowment provided much-needed support, it also exacerbated divisions (notably regarding how peace work should be done), and intensified personal animosities that already plagued the movement. Furthermore, European pacifists, particularly those associated with the International Peace Bureau (IPB), were wary of efforts to dominate and reshape the movement according to American priorities. The CEIP’s efforts to centralize control of the European movement antagonized existing organizations and anticipated the more interventionist aspects of American philanthropic endeavours in the interwar years and beyond. These divisions weakened the movement at a critical juncture. Despite its lofty ambitions, the CEIP’s European intervention in Europe highlighted the limitations of transnational peace activism.
topics: World Wars: History, Literature, and Impact

auditPapers.title: Bringing a new lens to vulnerable vernacular agricultural heritage: A novel classification of historical U.S. midwestern timber barns based on their fundamental structural system
auditPapers.abstract: The aim of this work is to develop a comprehensive structural typology for historical timber barns of the United States (U.S.) Midwest. These vernacular buildings provide significant cultural heritage value to communities both local and regional, while also figuring prominently in the broader American concept of the country’s agricultural roots. While they have garnered significant study from perspectives ranging from architectural, historical, and cultural geographical to structural and technological, no comprehensive classification exists for this population. Existing classifications are predominantly based on architectural, external, or functional features and thus do not adequately address structural forms. The few structural typologies that exist are limited to specific barns, such as Pennsylvania barns or New World Dutch Barns, or give a general and non-comprehensive overview of the population. Yet, structural forms and construction features of this vernacular population are intrinsically linked to the environmental, agricultural, social, and political dimensions of barns’ existence. The lack of a comprehensive classification and of clarity regarding form has multiple effects in the study and conservation of this population: it impedes systematic structural study of the population, hampers the consistency and quality of fieldwork and historical documentation, and limits the holistic and integrated study and characterization needed for such a multi-dimensional vernacular population. To fill this research gap, this work synthesizes a broad dataset of two hundred and forty-three barn structures from contemporary sources like agricultural periodicals and as-built records such as historical building records and regional inventories. The dataset encompasses all of the barn types addressed by the scholarly literature, and includes examples from every time period and region in the Midwest. The data is processed by first organizing it by chronology to allow comparison and synthesis of the forms, and then reorganizing by structural similarity. Then, after close examination of the structural forms, the structural feature of lateral stability mechanism is selected as the classifying characteristic to allow sufficient differentiation of forms in the dataset. This approach results in a structural typology with eight distinct fundamental types. These fundamental types can then be combined into hybrid types, also discussed, which together encompass the compiled dataset. Each type is presented through structural description, a structural diagram, and drawings showing examples of various possible realizations of the type. This new classification aims to overcome challenges of and complement existing classifications. A detailed and comprehensive structural typology will support more comprehensive and integrated study of this diverse vernacular population. It is intended to be used for easier and more systemized documentation and assessments. Additionally, it will allow population-scale structural study, including of structural vulnerability, a proposed future work.

auditPapers.title: Hydrophobic protection and consolidation of porous stone: Between multifunction and multilayer treatments
auditPapers.abstract: This study compares multifunction and multilayer conservation treatments designed to couple both hydrophobic and consolidation effects in porous stones, having in common ethyl-silicate based products. The practical difference lies in how the products are applied and where their effects concentrate. Multifunction treatments result from the application of products that co-deposit a consolidant and a hydrophobic agent in a single deep-penetrating step, whereas in multilayer treatments, a consolidant is first applied and then a hydrophobic product that acts mainly near the surface. Both strategies were investigated in two stones (limestone and sandstone) characterized by contrasting pore structures and mineralogy, using complementary assessments. The treatments met the primary objective of limiting liquid-water ingress while restoring cohesion, delivering comparable in-depth consolidation, more evident in silicate stone, and broadly similar changes in water-vapour permeability, which were governed by stones pore size. The colour change was associated with ethyl silicate, a component common to both systems. Multifunction treatments offered simplicity and stronger protection against capillary uptake, but the superficial hydrophobic effect diminished within months of outdoor exposure, and salts were retained in depth with potential for interfacial damage and stone collapse. Multilayer treatments allowed the choice of more stable hydrophobic agents, providing more durable superficial hydrophobic effect, and tended to favour salt crystallization nearer the surface, typically more visible yet easier to monitor and manage. Operationally, multilayer systems were more complex and included an interval between steps for consolidant curing; however, the lower need for re-treatments to restore the superficial hydrophobic effect may offset their apparent operational disadvantage. Overall, the results provide clear, actionable criteria for evidence-based, substrate-specific selection, allowing practitioners to balance operational constraints with technical performance.

auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article explores the management of correspondence between British MPs and the public, examining how citizens have used letter-writing as a tool to seek assistance, advocate for policies, and express support or dissent. It also considers the strategies employed by letter-writers to maximize their impact, from carefully crafted appeals to emotional rhetoric, frequently made in the knowledge that intermediaries would process their communications. The increasing volume of correspondence, facilitated partly by technological advances, reflects the enduring perception of letter-writing as an effective means of political engagement. While much scholarly work has focused either on a quantitative analysis of letter numbers and outcomes or a qualitative analysis of the substance of letters on controversial issues, this article shifts the focus to the broader processes of correspondence management and voter-politician interactions. auditPapers.title: Effectiveness and environmental performance of dry ice blasting for graffiti removal from outdoor metallic sculptures
auditPapers.abstract: CO₂-based cryogenic cleaning by dry ice blasting is increasingly regarded as a low-impact alternative for the removal of unwanted deposits from sensitive surfaces. The present study investigates the application of this method to the removal of unauthorised graffiti from contemporary outdoor metallic sculptures, focusing on steel and aluminium substrates protected with acrylic-urethane and acrylic-styrene clear coats. These protective coatings represent the original surfaces to be preserved, whereas the aerosol paint layers constitute the removable material. The experimental assessment evaluates removal efficiency, the persistence and morphology of residual paint deposits, and the energy demand and CO₂ consumption associated with the process. The characterisation of cleaning performance and residue distribution was achieved through the utilisation of high-speed imaging and optical and electron microscopy. The findings indicate that dry ice blasting enabled effective removal of a wide range of synthetic aerosol paints. No residual paint was detected on the acrylic-urethane coated steel substrate M; residual areas on substrate N remained below 0.023%, and most values on the acrylic-styrene coated aluminium substrate R were below 0.24%, except for the A94 aerosol, which reached 2.07%. Removal times for a fixed area of 4.34 cm² ranged from 0.46 to 4.35 s, while energy demand ranged from 0.41 to 2.28 kWh/m² depending on aerosol formulation and coating response. Overall, CO₂-based cryogenic cleaning can be considered a selective and controlled method for graffiti removal on synthetic clear coats commonly used in outdoor contemporary artworks, provided that CO₂ use, energy demand and repeated-treatment effects are transparently assessed.

auditPapers.title: Pre-revolution network connections of the 1989 Polish Round Table participants
auditPapers.abstract: Between the late 1940s and the collapse of Communism in 1989, the Polish United Workers Party (PZPR) controlled nearly all facets of political and social life in Poland. Communist rule was contested regularly, however, with a spontaneous worker uprising in Pozńan in 1956, a national student uprising in 1968, worker strikes in Gdańsk in 1970 and outside of Warsaw in 1976. These earlier uprisings were precursors to the strikes along the Baltic Coast that led to the creation of the independent, self-governing Trade Union "Solidarity" in August 1980. Solidarity was forced into the underground by a declaration of martial law in December 1981 but rebuilt itself as a broad-based social movement during the 1980s. When another round of strikes occurred in 1988, the Communist government turned to Solidarity to find a political solution to Poland’s endemic instability and the two groups joined Round Table meetings in early 1989. These negotiations resulted in a peaceful transition to a Democratic government later that year, the first revolution in a cascade of anti-Communist revolutions that swept the region in 1989/1990. Using a dataset of the institutional affiliations of the 567 Round Table participants, a purpose-built Shiny App for longitudinally analyzing the dataset, and a penalized logistic model, this paper shows that while the creation of the Solidarity Trade Union in August 1980 was the most transformational moment for the network structure that linked Round Table participants, events in 1968 were also highly predictive for whether an individual would end up on the Government or Opposition side of the Round Table. Beyond its specific argument, this paper documents the process of converting analog records in physical archives to fully digitized data science tools for quantitative study of longitudinal social connections, with three primary contributions: (1) we discuss and present a rich data package consisting of activities and organizational affiliations of 567 Round Table participants from 1945 to 1989; (2) we provide an overview of a purpose-built Shiny App for longitudinally analyzing the Round Table datasets, paying particular attention to the challenges of structuring data and analysis to reflect real-world conditions; (3) we fit and assess a penalized logistic model to provide insight into which activities and organizations are predictive of particular affiliations at the 1989 Round Table.

auditPapers.title: The Naxi Dongba MOOC: A Test Case for Digital Revitalisation of Endangered Writing Systems
auditPapers.abstract: From 2019 to 2023, three universities – the National Institute of Oriental Languages and Civilisations, the University of Geneva, and the Beijing Language and Culture University – collaborated to produce a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) entitled Initiation to the Dongba Script . The objective was to preserve and revitalise the Dongba script, an endangered writing system used by the Naxi people in southwestern China. The course aimed to engage learners around the world in learning the script and subsequently contributing to the preservation of this unique cultural heritage. Hosted by the French MOOC platform FUN, the MOOC ran for the first time from April to June 2023. Using a qualitatively led mixed research method integrating pre- and post-course questionnaire data, forum discussions, informal feedback, and fieldwork conducted in Lijiang in August 2023, this paper explores how participants experienced the MOOC as a learning and cultural engagement opportunity and which factors facilitated or constrained broader community participation, particularly from the Naxi community itself. The findings show that the MOOC successfully reached a highly educated, multilingual, international audience with strong intrinsic motivation. It achieved a completion rate more than double the global MOOC average, generating sustained post-course engagement across academic, creative and professional domains. The analysis reveals that, for many participants, the course functioned as a cultural threshold experience, repositioning the script from that of an unknown object to a personally meaningful one. Some learners went on to pursue academic research, creative applications, or further study of the Naxi language, suggesting the potential for longer-term engagement. These findings reveal a tension in MOOC-based heritage education: Open platforms can reach global audiences, yet local cultural transmission depends on sustained engagement with the living communities the heritage belongs to. They also offer valuable insights and lessons for digital heritage education initiatives in other endangered script contexts.

auditPapers.title: The British Government, Nuclear Testing, and the Arms Race, 1961–1962
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In 1961–2, when a three-year international moratorium on nuclear testing was broken by the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States agreed to resume testing in partnership: Britain would test underground at the American site in Nevada and the US would use the British site at Christmas Island for a new series of atmospheric tests. This article uses archival evidence to examine the British government’s position, showing that there was a great reluctance to resume testing and that, contrary to stereotypes, there was no strong lobbying for tests from the military or atomic scientists. While it was convenient to express the need for nuclear testing as a technical necessity, the requirement was fundamentally political: to support the United States. Meanwhile, Britain’s atomic scientists were working hard not only to test nuclear weapons but to ban testing, and the article also introduces the extensive scientific work done in support of nuclear test detection and arms-control verification. Although histories today emphasize the health and environmental impacts of nuclear testing, at the height of the Berlin crisis it was the nuclear arms race that worried politicians and scientists above all.

auditPapers.title: Unveiling the maniz. cod. 99: A microscopic and spectroscopic investigation of its writing inks
auditPapers.abstract: The Orthographia Pratica de Varias Letras is a unique 17th-century Portuguese codex, notable for its exceptional significance in the history of Latin calligraphy during the Modern period. Unfortunately, it faces complex conservation challenges due to the presence of iron gall ink (IGI). This work aimed to thoroughly characterise the inks and their impact on the manuscript using an integrated analytical approach. Extensive micro-XRF analysis revealed two distinct groups of IGIs based on their transition metal content. Zn-rich IGIs were found in half of the manuscript, suggesting the use of Zn-bearing green vitriol. In contrast, a more refined form of green vitriol was identified in the IGIs on the other half, suggesting that different types of vitriol were used. Variations in the binder-to-vitriol ratios were proposed, indicating distinct IGI formulations throughout the codex. The poor condition observed in some folios was primarily associated with greater ink coverage per surface area and lower binder content. FIB-SEM and PIXE analysis provided insights into the behaviour of Fe within the cellulose structure, including penetration and lateral migration. The IGI chromophore was further investigated by Mössbauer and XPS, which confirmed an Fe(III)-polyphenol mono-complex with a catecholate binding mode and Fe(III) in an octahedral arrangement.

auditPapers.title: Unruly Singing and Shouting: Listening to Labourers’ Work Songs in Modern Shanghai
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract As early as the third century bce, references to labourers’ work songs appeared in the Chinese court-sponsored compendium Lushi Chunqiu, and, for the 2,000 years that followed, labourers throughout China continued to sing these songs. During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, however, the sound of such songs became controversial among newly arrived Anglophone settlers as well as Chinese intellectuals in Shanghai, evoking emotions ranging from frustration, contempt, and desperation to compassion, admiration, and even inspiration. This article historicizes the contested interpretations of Chinese workers’ singing and shouting, exploring how different listeners’ anxieties and agendas shaped what they heard. At the same time, it juxtaposes these reactions with the labourers’ own justifications for the sounds they made, and their responses to the baffling modern cityscape they had to navigate. While reconstructing the histories of marginalized groups has long been hindered by the perception of archival silence, attending to sonic traces often dismissed as ‘mere noise’ can help to recover the vital sounds of those otherwise rendered voiceless by the historical record.

auditPapers.title: Evaluating Livestock Culling Practices Using Population Projection Models in Neolithic Dalmatia
auditPapers.journal: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology
auditPapers.abstract: Mortality profiles derived from age-at-death estimates of archaeological animal remains reveal the outcomes of prehistoric herders slaughtering decisions. Survivorship curves from these data are often interpreted as evidence for herd management strategies optimized for meat, milk, or wool production. Spatial and temporal comparisons can illuminate variation and development in agropastoral economies, but these profiles also carry assumptions. High juvenile mortality, for instance, may compromise long-term herd viability, while interpreting survivorship as a reflection of constant offtake rates across generations can oversimplify pastoral dynamics. This study addresses these issues by modeling sheep and goat herd demography with a stage-structured Lefkovitch projection model. Culling strategies derived from Neolithic Dalmatian sites, informed by caprine age-at-death data, serve as primary constraints on herd growth. By optimizing offtake rates, the simulations evaluate how herders might have adjusted their practices to maintain herd stability amid environmental and subsistence stresses. Results show that sheep herds were generally more sustainable than goat herds, highlighting the demographic impact of differing culling regimes. The findings underscore the adaptive nature of prehistoric herd management and the importance of flexible strategies for mitigating risk and ensuring long-term sustainability.

auditPapers.title: Unveiling ancient maritime secrets through X-ray computed tomography (CT): Iron-based finds from the archaic shipwreck of Giglio-Campese
auditPapers.abstract: In August 1961 the remains of a shipwreck, dating back to the early 6th century BCE, were located at the Island of Giglio in the Bay of Campese (Tuscany, Italy), announcing a major archaeological discovery. Owing to the extremely heterogeneous composition of the load of international scope, ranging from Etruscan to Greek productions, this finding reflects and testifies to the complexity of archaic trade networks across the Tyrrhenian Sea in the early 6th cent. BC. Within the framework of a broad multidisciplinary collaboration involving several institutions and experts, X-ray computed tomography (CT) was employed to investigate the hidden history of the ship and, by extension, aspects of our own cultural past. Among the numerous notable artifacts, the analysis concerned some heavily corroded and fragmented iron-based objects, whose original shape and function are no longer legible due to severe degradation and thick layers of concretions. To reconstruct their original morphology and thus identify the type of artifacts, two dedicated measurement campaigns were carried out in the X-ray imaging laboratory of the University of Bologna, Ravenna Campus (Emilia-Romagna, Italy), using a custom-designed CT system, equipped with a 200 kVp X-ray tube and a flat-panel detector with 127 µm pixel size. More than 20 tomographic scans were performed with a voxel size of about 100 µm, producing a substantial dataset for subsequent processing. The virtual removal of calcareous incrustations allowed us to formulate several hypotheses about the typology and function of the investigated artefacts. Preliminary interpretations have been proposed based on the observation of quadrangular cross-sectional profiles that originally contained metallic cores. These cores are now entirely or almost entirely consumed by corrosion, leaving only a layer of mineralized concretion with little to no metal preserved. Elemental composition was further assessed through complementary X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyses, performed on selected points of the finds, supporting our investigation. Although the objects recovered from the depths of the Tyrrhenian Sea survive only as “ghosts” of their originals, the integration of CT imaging, visual inspection and XRF results has contributed to shed light on the ship’s cargo composition of Greek and Etruscan provenance as well as on its route’s stages.

auditPapers.title: Searching for the Dutch Corner in the Republic of Letters: Network Science and Wittgenstein’s Family Resemblance
auditPapers.abstract: This article has a twofold contribution. First, it offers a new way to consider communities that are conceptually and analytically difficult to define. In a break from most existing applications of historical community detection, a different approach is used here, using a network object known as a multigraph, which allows characteristics to be viewed both as individual attributes and as parts of overlapping sets. Second, this article describes an application of this method to uncover a community that is often discussed but notoriously difficult to define and analyse: the Dutch ‘Republic of Letters’: this loose early modern sub-community included members from different denominations, professions, origins, and affiliations, but has been recognised qualitatively as a body of prolific and intellectually bonded individuals, with links within and beyond the United Provinces. In applying this method, we create a truer picture of how communities such as these operated and cohered, while avoiding reductive criteria for inclusion of such individuals. The uncovering of this particular Dutch community is a clear demonstration of the method in action and therefore offers a successful alternative to other community detection methods.

auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: The cave, called “Grotta delle Veneri” (Cave of the Venus), is located in the archaeological site of Parabita (Apulia, southern Italy). It is one of the most important archaeological constructions of the Salento peninsula since its discovery confirmed the presence of the Neanderthal man in the Mediterranean Basin. To highlight the presence of other cavities connected to the cave, a geophysical measurement campaign was undertaken. Given the site's geological and geomorphological conditions, the geophysical methodologies Ground Penetrating Radar and Electrical Resistivity Tomography were considered. The particular morphological condition of the ground surface linked to a series of differences in height and the presence of obstacles such as trees and bushes, 3D GPR data were acquired in limited areas. In these areas was possible to acquire the ERT 3d. The results are surprising and show different areas with the presence of cavities in the vicinity of the same cave. Results show a probable unexplored zone of the cave. The investigations revealed series of anomalies characterized by high resistivity and high amplitudes of electromagnetic wave reflection, interpreted as cavities. The geophysical data confirm that there are actually a series of cavities (not known until now) that could be connected to the main cave. The resulting model provides the necessary parameters (depth and volumes) for the design a series of direct investigations by archaeologists.

auditPapers.title: An integrated semantics–structure–strategy framework for analyzing discourse polarization: evidence from controversial issues on social media
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This study aims to systematically examine discourse polarization on Chinese social media through an integrated cognitive and computational lens. It proposes a three-dimensional semantic–structural–strategic framework to capture how linguistic meaning, network structure, and discursive strategy interact to produce polarization in digital discourse. Two highly contentious cases, the Delayed Retirement policy and Yang Li’s endorsement of JD.com, are analyzed across Weibo and Little Red Book. The study focuses on posts containing adversarial language, combining BERTopic clustering, semantic network construction, Louvain community detection, and critical discourse analysis. Structural indicators quantify polarization, while cohesion and fragmentation are assessed through community purity, intra-/inter-community similarity, and cross-community edges. Ten discourse strategies are coded, and sentiment analysis reveals affective feedback mechanisms. Results show that Weibo functions as a mass polarization accelerator, characterized by rapid isolate–integrate cycles and high emotional contagion, whereas Little Red Book exhibits low-intensity, niche polarization grounded in personal narratives. The findings demonstrate a feedback loop between extreme negative emotions and intra-community interaction, reinforcing group boundaries and antagonistic framing. This study develops a novel multidimensional framework that bridges micro-level discursive cognition and macro-level network structure, advancing the methodological integration of computational linguistics and cognitive discourse analysis. By operationalizing semantic, structural, and affective dimensions of online discourse, this research expands digital humanities approaches to include networked cognition and emotion-driven polarization. It provides empirical and conceptual tools for understanding collective meaning-making in digital environments and offers actionable insights for mitigating online hostility through platform-level discourse design.

auditPapers.title: Hydrophobic surface development on heritage stones through Paracoccus denitrificans biofilms
auditPapers.abstract: Water is a major factor in the deterioration of stone-built heritage. Although significant advances have been made in stone-protective treatments, persistent trade-offs remain between performance, compatibility, durability, and environmental impact. This study advances bio-based conservation by investigating whether Paracoccus denitrificans biofilms can be deliberately steered to modify stone surface properties in a controlled and sustainable manner. Two lithotypes: Bentheimer sandstone and Euville limestone, were treated under polysaccharide-rich and lipid-rich nutrient regimes promoting different extracellular polymeric substances (EPS). Surface chemistry, morphology and mechanics were evaluated through contact-angle measurements, FTIR spectroscopy, roughness (Sa, Sz, Sdr) and surface hardness testing. As a result, lipid-rich conditions enhanced hydrophobicity (contact angle ≥ 90°) and decreased water absorption rate between 50% and 85% for both stone types due to change in surface composition. On the other hand, certain polysaccharide-rich conditions shifted surfaces to a more hydrophobic character linked to reduced macro-roughness (Sa, Sz) and increased micro-complexity (Sdr increased moderately to 2–5%.), evidencing morphological control of wetting. Surface hardness changes were minor and substrate-dependent, with slight consolidation effect in Euville limestone (max 15%). Together, these results highlight P. denitrificans as a biological tool capable of tuning stone-water interactions via dual chemical and physical pathways. The work positions microbial surface steering as a promising addition to the field of biological conservation for cultural heritage materials.
