auditPapers.title: Introducing Authoritarian 101A Global History
auditPapers.abstract: Authoritarianism 101: A Global History is designed to offer teachers and students a broad perspective on the history of authoritarianism. This past summer, the AHR commissioned thirty historians working on authoritarian histories in Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, and North America to write teaching modules that explored a singular instance of an authoritarian past. Temporally, they range from the seventeenth to the early twenty first centuries, with the bulk of modules concentrating on the long twentieth century. Six of those modules are featured in this issue, and all of the modules will be available free to read on Authoritarianism 101’s dedicated website. The modules for Authoritarianism 101 have three basic components: a core question that goes to larger histories of authoritarianism; a single primary source to ground that big question in a particular time and place; and a short essay that offers context and ideas for teaching the source. The contributors have intentionally designed stand-alone modules. Everything you need to teach each module successfully in your classroom is bundled together. We imagine dropping individual modules into existing courses; combining several of them to do a deeper dive into particular aspects of authoritarian history over time and space; or using them to create a new course on histories of authoritarianism. We can also imagine using the modules in spaces adjacent to the classroom, such as discussion groups organized by high school history students, undergraduate history majors, or history graduate students, and in discussion forums, study groups, and perhaps even book clubs at public libraries and community centers. Many of the modules are concerned with the practices of authoritarianism and the tools of authoritarian control. They consider the political, economic, social, or cultural dimensions of a particular authoritarian turn; aspects of the daily workings of an authoritarian regime; the ways in which authoritarian states have sought to foster their legitimacy; authoritarian surveillance and censorship; authoritarianism and the judiciary; and how individuals and non-state actors have supported and collaborated with authoritarian rulers. Other modules concentrate on resistance to an authoritarian turn and explore the everyday histories of living under authoritarianism. Among the core questions that these modules collectively raise are: How do authoritarians use a sense of national crisis to justify their rule? How do ordinary people come to follow authoritarian leaders and regimes? What is the relationship between nationalism and authoritarianism? What role does visual culture play in maintaining authoritarian rule? How and why do authoritarian states repress dissent? How have authoritarian governments been challenged? What were the consequences of those contestations? Why do some business groups collaborate with authoritarian leaders? How do authoritarian regimes discipline the bodies of their people? The modules that make up Authoritarianism 101 explore these questions through a marvelously expansive range of primary sources from around the world. An interactive animated web documentary focused on the forced displacements of a young Polish man in the 1930s. US Senator Joseph McCarthy’s 1950 “The Enemy Within” speech. The 1943 Disney anti-Nazi propaganda film, Education for Death: The Making of the Nazi. Testimony in 1948 from Hindu nationalist leaders. A 1969 strip from the popular Argentinian comic Mafalda calling out state repression of freedom of expression. A 1980 letter from a prominent Turkish businessman offering support and advice to the country’s military dictator. Charlie Chaplin’s 1940 film The Great Dictator. Children’s board games designed to infuse authoritarian sensibilities in young people living in fascist Italy and the Soviet Union. Photos of potentially disenfranchised voters climbing ladders to evade the security police and enter polling places in the 2005 Egyptian election. A 1913 Quinault Indian Nation petition to US government agents they privately termed “little dictators.” Military regulations for proper student comportment in 1970s Congo. The “La Marseillaise” scene in the 1942 film Casablanca, among others. Figure 1: Some of the modules for Authoritarianism 101 use forms of visual culture as their primary source to explore dimensions of authoritarian history. Contributor Keith Rathbone centers his module on this Vichy era propaganda poster, “Le Sport cette chevalerie moderne,” to consider how authoritarian regimes promote control and legitimacy through physical culture and sports. Photo courtesy of La Contemporaine: Bibliothèque, Archives, Musée des Mondes Contemporains. Each module aims to provide the connective tissue that can take teachers and students from the granularity of these diverse primary sources to the big core question around the history of authoritarianism. In all of the modules, our contributors provide a brief context essay, based on the latest scholarship (including their own) to help a teacher understand the essential issues surrounding the selected primary source. We hope this will allow a busy teacher, perhaps with minimal background knowledge, to more easily put the source into its proper historical context. The context essay is concise but substantial, offering enough information to guide a teacher’s curricular decision-making on how to best plan the exploration of the core question and source. Each module also includes a short essay on teaching that suggests varied ideas on how to dissect the primary source. Here, we asked our contributors to speak from their teaching experience and offer creative approaches to help teachers and students find compelling human stories and complex dilemmas. The query-driven design of Authoritarianism 101 also helps remind students that although they sometimes think of history as an answer-based discipline—a regurgitation of “the facts”—history is fundamentally a question-based discipline. These modules foreground historical curiosity, even wonder, and the exploration of worlds local and distant, familiar and strange. We hope that high school social studies teachers see in the modules a way to study authoritarianism through the inquiry arc, and that college professors recognize the kinds of core questions that animate the research and teaching in their fields. And we hope, too, that potential users from the broader history-curious public will find this question-based method a satisfying way to approach the history of authoritarianism. Figure 2: Many of the modules for Authoritarianism 101 are designed to help students historicize the tools of authoritarian control. Contributor Lauren Stokes uses Adolf Hitler’s 1933 speech after the Reichstag fire, the home of the German parliament in Berlin, and his call to curtail basic domestic civil liberties to examine how authoritarian regimes manufacture crisis to consolidate their power. Photo by Pictorial Press/Alamy. Our peer review process for Authoritarianism 101 included classroom teachers at the high school level as well as college and university levels. We wanted to hear directly from them on how the modules might be taught in the classroom. This feedback allowed module contributors to further hone their teaching discussions. We are grateful to all our peer reviewers for their deep engagement with the project. Their feedback ultimately produced modules that combine the latest scholarship from experts in the field with best practices in teaching application and usage. In this issue of the AHR we feature just a sampling of the thirty modules that will make up Authoritarianism 101. Barbara Weinstein (New York University and former AHA president) looks at the authoritarian histories of Brazil through the lens of a striking 1970 photograph of then student activist and later Brazilian president Dilma Rousseff facing a military tribunal. Samuel Fury Childs Daly (University of Chicago) examines testimony at the state trial of Fela Kuti, a well-known Afro-beat musician and leading opponent of the 1970s military government in Nigeria, to ask whose side the rule of law is on in a dictatorship. Louise M. Young (University of Wisconsin-Madison) draws on an oral history with a Japanese woman living in Manchuria in the 1930s to explore why she came to support Japan’s military authoritarian government. Adrian Chastain Weimer (Providence College) unpacks a 1665 New England town petition to Charles II to consider how representative governments defended themselves against royal authoritarian practices. Lauren Stokes (Northwestern University) focuses on Adolf Hitler’s 1933 “Law to Remedy the Distress of the People and the Reich” speech to discuss the propensity of authoritarian regimes to manufacture crisis as justification for their policies. And finally, Mark Philip Bradley’s module goes to a deliberately provocative installation by a dissident artist in 1970s Indonesia (the cover of the March 2025 AHR features a detail of this work) to examine how the visual arts can reveal everyday histories of living under authoritarian rule. Figure 3: Another cluster of modules for Authoritarianism 101 focus on civil society challenges to authoritarianism. Contributor Samuel Fury Childs Day examines testimony at the state trial of Fela Kuti, a well-known Afro-beat musician and strong critic of the 1970s military government in Nigeria, to help students see the complexities of understanding whose side the rule of law is on in a dictatorship. Photo by Celluloid Records/Wikimedia Commons. The website for Authoritarianism 101 will house all of the project modules. It will also provide ideas for using them individually or in curated groups, including a series of video and podcast interviews with many of the project contributors who talk about how and why they created their modules and offer some additional teaching tips. The website also offers pathways to facilitate deeper dives into the histories of authoritarianism. The “Authoritarian 101 Reading List,” for example, provides an annotated list of the works our contributors believe are most important for understanding the histories of authoritarianism. Authoritarianism 101 is part of the AHR’s broader teaching initiative, the #AHRSyllabus project. We invite you to visit the website for Authoritarianism 101: A Global History, where all the modules and other content are free to access. Our hope is the collective work that informs this intentionally capacious project will allow you to deepen your understanding of the diverse and complex histories of authoritarianism and the challenges that have been mounted to it. auditPapers.title: Grasping the Pencil: Polish Memoirs of Childhood on the Eastern Front, 1914–1921
auditPapers.abstract: This article recovers the voices of civilian survivors of World War I in parts of today’s Ukraine, Lithuania, Belarus, and Poland. Drawing on a rare cache of retrospective accounts composed in 1930s Poland for memoir-writing competitions, it foregrounds the voices of peasants and poor people in villages and small towns at the front lines, particularly those who survived the war as children and young people. Surveying their narratives of violence, hunger, disease, and displacement, it asks how memoirists made sense of their wartime experience in an autobiographical context, considering the relationship between war, literacy, and knowledge, on the one hand, and trauma, “brutalization,” and resilience on the other. For all its horrors, the memoirs show that war could generate new mobilities, perspectives, and subjectivities; destruction and chaos could break open vistas of a wider world. The article concludes by considering how both nationalist frameworks and geospatial imaginaries have contributed to silencing this history of war from the margins. It argues that civilians’ experience on the Eastern Front should be centered not only in the history of World War I but also in the broader social history of twentieth-century warfare and state violence.

auditPapers.title: Communications
auditPapers.abstract: To the Editor: New Orleans, with its colonial roots in the Francophone Atlantic, its Latin European military and legal traditions, its complex religious culture, and its challenge to Anglo-America’s rigid color line, has long perplexed most United States historians. Andrew N. Wegmann proves this point in his review of my book, Creole New Orleans in the Revolutionary Atlantic, 1775-1877 (2023). Though the reviewer finds my use of the ethnic designation “Afro-Creole” a “potentially troubling term,” (American Historical Review 130, no. 2 [2025],956), it is widely used in academic discourse and in published works. In the essay, “Can the Church Evolve?” in the New York Review of Books (June 12, 2025:6), for instance, columnist Fintan O’Toole references Pope Leo XIV’s (Robert Francis Prevost) “Afro-Creole” roots in New Orleans as embodying the hybrid nature of the nation’s identity. My book, the reviewer also complains, “never productively defines the term and usage of ‘Creole,’” brushing aside or overlooking my discussion of its origins in Spanish America where colonial Black people coined the term “criollo” to apply to African-descended peoples born in the Americas (956). The Spaniards broadened the term’s usage to apply to all native-born colonists with the French, like the Spanish, applying “créole” to its colonial populations. With the arrival of Anglo-Americans in Louisiana, the designation came under increasing attack (Bell, 93).

auditPapers.title: On the Edge of Power: Peasants and Escape Ecologies in Eastern Europe, 1700–1850
auditPapers.abstract: The article explores the impact of inaccessible landscapes (such as forests, swamps, and wastelands) on the relationship between subjects and centers of power (such as the nobility and the state) in Eastern Europe during the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. This region’s situation was unique because successive disasters, including the Little Ice Age, eighty years of continuous warfare, epidemics, and economic collapse, resulted in significant depopulation and the re-wilding of vast areas of Poland, Lithuania, and Ukraine in the early eighteenth century. The dominant historical narrative portrays this period in an unequivocally negative light. This text aims to present a more nuanced perspective. While the disasters at the turn of the eighteenth century affected all social classes, the weakening of the repressive apparatus due to the crisis, coupled with the growth of forests, floodplains, and wastelands, caused the eighteenth-century Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth to become a destination for mass migration, particularly from neighboring enlightened monarchies. For many people in Central and Eastern Europe, migrating to a country offering ample hiding places, easy access to the commons, and significant privileges for folk colonizers was more appealing than living under the often repressive systems introduced by modern states, such as compulsory conscription, high taxes, and the elimination of cultural or religious autonomy.

auditPapers.title: Authoritarianism and the Rule of Law
auditPapers.abstract: Mr. Kayode-Idowu in the witness chair. Chairman examines Mr. Kayode-Idowu. Chairman: Where do you come from? Mr. Kayode-Idowu: I am a Yoruba. Q. What are you? A. A Freelance writer Q. Where do you live? A. 11 Issac Jones Street, Igbobi. Q. Tell us what you know about the incident. A. In the early part of January 1966, the Army came to power – Q. What are you saying? A. I am a member of the Young African pioneers. I want to brief you on some points. A. Did you see what happened on the 18th of February? A. Yes. Q. Why do you want to take me to 1966? Q. I will make my position clearer and you will see where I am coming from easily. Q. I cannot see where are coming from ten years ago (Laughter) A. The Army came into power and said they wanted to protect lives in this country. Q. I know that myself. What I do not know is what happened on the 18th of February, 1977. I am older than you are probably in a position better to know what you want to tell me. What I do not know is what happened on the 18th of February. If you do not want to talk about that, go and sit down but if you want, please go ahead. There must be a limit to all these jokes. Do you know what really happened on the 18th? A. Yes. For some time now in that area, we can see that members of the Armed Forces, especially the Army have us become “horrors”. For example, on Thursday 17th, February, I myself and my friend were looking for a taxi in front of the African Shrine. We saw a solider jumping in front of taxis trying to stop them. We too tried to stop the taxis but the solider said, “Who are you to stop the taxi I have stopped.” We told him that taxis cabs are public transport. My friend even went further to tell him that he was constituting a danger to us in the way he was behaving. The next thing he did was that he slapped my friend. I tried to ask him why he did this and he replied me with another slap. I then held on to that soldier. Luckily, the civilians and some members of the Young African Pioneers who were around came to my aid and this soldier had to run away. On the 18th, Sir, I was around Fela’s house around 10.30 a.m. because we have our Young African Pioneers’ office at the shrine. I happened to go to Fela’s house around 12.30 that day. I learnt that Fela was sleeping. I even met one Angus Okoli in the sitting room that day. Not quite ten minutes after I had gone back to the Shrine I heard people upstairs shouting “Soldiers have surrounded Fela’s house.” Knowing them before to have been coming to harass people like that, I ran along Kalakuta Close in order to call some of our members to see what help we could be. The next thing I saw was that solders started cordoning the whole area. We thought it as a joke. I had to leave my position because I saw that these people were really out for something because they were armed to the teeth, I went back to the Shrine. In the Shrine we have an open place where you can see everything that is happening within the distance of that area. The next thing I saw was a new consignment of soldiers coming and throwing stones and bottles at Fela’s house. They did this for about one hour or so. The whole area was filled up with solider. They stood across t roads driving all the civilians and even asking people to lock their doors. With the wave of violence, I did not know what to do. The situation was tense. Meanwhile they tried to enter the house but they could not because of the barbed wire fence. Some of them were shaking the fence while other threw stones inside the house. The next thing we saw was an Army vehicle, a Mercedes Benz 280S with Registration No. NA.56C parked in front of the Shrine. When this vehicle parked, an Amry officer came out—a short slimly built officer. I think he is a Colonel because he had a red band on his cap. He looked to me like Col. Tarfa. Ever since we released the YAP NEWS of November, second volume, and he wrote a letter to us, I have taken special note of Col. Tarfa and I can recognize him any where I see him. I think it was Major Daudu and some other officers who stood around the shrine while the boys carried on the operation after consultation with Col. Tarfa. Major Daudu, I am sure, gave the instruction by waving his hand. I was on the higher place and I could see them though I could not hear exactly want he said but I saw jerry cans and the boys went round the Ford that carried the generator and set it ablaze. They went on to the civilian bus, set it ablaze and then on to the Passat that was outside. At first Fela’s wagon was spared. That wagon looks like a bus it is a car and I saw Major Daudu pointing at it. The Army now have this type of bus and I am sure the way Major Daudu was pointing he seemed to be saying, Why did they leave that. The soldiers had left it originally while they sprayed the Ford, the Civilian bus and Beko’s Passat. I saw some soldier with some liquid, I did not know what it they were carrying. But it was this liquid that was used in spraying the car before it was set ablaze. The next thing they did was to cut the fence open and they went in and what followed had been described by people who have come before you, sir. Your Lordship, I must say that the action of the men in uniform that day debased us as Africans bearing in mind that they did not respect human beings. From their action on that day, one could see that they wanted to kill. Almost everybody that was brought out of Kalakuta Republic sustained injury on his or her head. These people, in fact, really mowed their victims because they did not spare them at all. They were taken away naked. After the incident, we stood and made sure we got down what happened. I took down some of the numbers of the cars that were around. There was a Landrover NA1563A, a Peugeot 504, NA AD.2499 and another 504 NA AD 2414 and another 504, NA 2312. These were cars belonging to the senior officers who were standing under the shrine that day. I was in a potion to see all what happened from where I was and I saw them as they parked their cars in front of the shrine watching their boys performing. What annoyed me most was that there was a top Army officer there. I saw him here yesterday. I do not know whether he is here today. He was standing there on the day and the way he stood I guessed he was coming out from the officers’ Mess. His belt was not properly on. He was standing in front of Lido Hotel. His “batsman”, I do not know what they are called in the Army, those who carry gun behind the officers, went into Fela’s house while the boys were looting the minerals in the kiosk that was inside the house. The batsman took three bottles of minerals one 7up and two bottles of Fanta. He opened one, gave a salute and gave it to his officer. The officer drank out of the looted property. I can identify this officer anywhere. I know him. A lot of them did the same thing. Your Lordship, as I was saying earlier on, the Army came to power with hope of protecting the lives of the citizens of this country. This was as a result of the political situation in this country then in 1966. Now, these people who are meant to protect lives of the citizens of this country are now destroying the lives of citizens. Now, how safe are we when members of the Armed Forces are looting and even robbing with arms, because they carried guns there and this portrayed them as armed robbers. There were Police men who could have arrested Fela if he had committed any offence. Your Lordship, the decision is yours, I hope the lives of innocent citizens of this country would be saved, because we hear of this attached everyday all over the place. Thank you. Mr. Kayode-Idowu in the witness chair. Chairman examines Mr. Kayode-Idowu. Chairman: How old are you? Kayode-Idowu: I am 21. Q. How old were you in 1966. A. I was about ten. Q. When did you become member of YAP? A. I am a foundation member. Q. What year did you start the YAP? A. Last year October. Q. What are the aims and objectives of the YAP? A. To spread economic and cultural awareness Q. Who is your president? A. Fela Anikulapo-Kuti. Q. Have you got a Vice President? A. We do not believe in Bureaucracy much. Q. You believe in the President but you – A. You see, Fela is a black President. Q. Who is your Secretary? A. We have a care-taker Committee. Q. Comprising how many people? A. Three members. Q. How often do you meet? A. Regularly. Q. How regularly? A. Everyday because we have an office at the shrine. Q. I understand your membership is at the moment about 25,000 strong? A. Yes, Sir. Q. From where do you draw your members? A. All over Africa. Q. In this party of yours – A. It is a movement and not a party. Q. All right, call it a movement, it teaches you to have courage. A. You do not fear anything. A. We learn how to defend our rights as citizens. Q. To muster all the courage you can? A. Yes, as far as you can sustain it. Q. On this day, you saw all these things happened, things that could disturb the conscience of everybody in your movement. You did not do anything, you stood with your arms folded. A. Like I said, I ran to Kalakuta Close. That was the first thing I did. Q. What positive action did you take, if any? A. The soldiers were too many for my members, at least, they were armed. Like it is said, once one section of the country is armed and the other section is not armed, the armed section constitutes a danger to the unarmed section. The soldiers who surrounded Fela’s house on that day had guns and dangerous weapons that could destroy human lives. Q. About how many of your members were present in the Kalakuta and around that day? A. We have YAP members who live – Q. About how many of you? A. I could not have estimated because there were over 50,000 Nigerians who saw what happened on that day. I could not say how many YAP members were there. The situation was so tense. I was trying to observe as much as possible and to survive so that I could testify against these people. Q. You said that about 50,000 Nigerians were around on the day? A. Yes, and they saw it as it happened on that day, Sir. Chairman: All right, thank you. Mr. Kayode-Idowu: Can I submit the car numbers? Chairman: They have been taken down by the Official Reporters. Testimony of Kayode Idowu, “Proceedings of the Administrative Board of Inquiry into the Disturbances at 14A Agege Motor Road, Idi-Oro, Held at Cinema Hall II, National Arts Theatre, Lagos, 16th March, 1977, Day 9.” Lagos State Research and Archives Board, LCE.A12C. In 1977, Nigeria’s military dictator tried to silence his most famous opponent. Since independence from Great Britain in 1960, Nigeria had gone through a brief period of democracy, a civil war, and a series of military coups. The latest of those coups had brought to power General Olusegun Obasanjo, an authoritarian who hoped military-style discipline would make the country more orderly and prosperous. His opponent was Fela Kuti, a famous Afrobeat musician with a silver tongue and a youth following that the military thought looked suspiciously like a militia (the “Young African Pioneers,” as they called themselves). He was popular, profane, and relentlessly critical of the army. He scorned both the military and the British colonizers who had come before them, and in one famous song, “Zombie,” he mocked soldiers for their blind obedience. He had many fans abroad, which made him especially threatening to Nigeria’s image-conscious dictatorship. The military wanted to silence Fela, but they knew that throwing him in jail might make him a martyr. Instead, they took an indirect approach—wearing him down through raids, investigations, and trials. In March 1977, the army burned down Fela’s house and nightclub during one of those raids. They then staged a “commission of inquiry” about the fire. Ostensibly its purpose was to determine how it had started, but really it was to drag Fela’s name through the mud. Like the United States, Nigeria has a common-law legal system where the judiciary’s role is not just to enforce the rules but to constrain what the other branches of government can do. Like many authoritarians, Nigeria’s military dictators thought that law was on their side, and they staged trials like this thinking that judges were their allies. But as they learned, what happens in a courtroom can be unpredictable. In this document, we see a young man who was part of Fela’s entourage using his day in court not to denounce Fela, but to go after the military. Ultimately, the inquiry did not come to much; Fela paid some fines, a few of his supporters went to jail, and the soldiers who burned his house down got off scot-free. So how meaningful was this young man’s testimony in court? It’s debatable. But the outcome of a case like this is less important than the questions it raises. On its own, this testimony is a good starting point for an in-class discussion about how dictators and their critics use law. The “rule of law” is an important but widely misunderstood concept, and you can use this source to invite students to start defining it. The rule of law is the principle that everyone, including the people in power, should be subject to clear, established laws that define what they can and cannot do. This trial illustrates what happens when that principle starts to fail. After giving some context, work through the document with your students. It is a transcript of one of Fela’s Young African Pioneers, Kayode Idowu, being questioned about the raid that burned down Fela’s nightclub (the African Shrine, also referred to as the Kalakuta Republic in the document). Idowu starts by trying to talk about the events that brought the military to power, which the judge impatiently shuts down. He then describes the raid, lingering on how the soldiers started the fire. He dwells on the image of some officers blithely drinking looted sodas while the nightclub burns. Then Idowu criticizes the military in general, which the judge now lets him do. They take a break, and when they reconvene the judge asks him about the Young African Pioneers. Idowu answers these questions tersely, and then he is dismissed. After figuring out what’s going on in the document, students can assess its values and limitations as a source. A transcript like this records what was said, but we shouldn’t necessarily trust that what was said in the courtroom was true. There are some clues that Idowu is exaggerating—did fifty thousand people really witness the blaze? A better way to think about the document is as a record of a power play. Who has the upper hand changes from one question to the next. The transcript alone doesn’t tell us everything. We don’t know the tone of the interrogation, for example, or its context in the trial transcript as a whole (which runs to several thousand pages). Nonetheless, you can interpret something about each party’s intent even in this little fragment. You might ask: What do you think Idowu is trying to do through his testimony? What about the judge? What rhetorical strategies does the judge use to discredit Idowu? Do they seem to work on him? Ultimately the judge lets Idowu speak his mind, which he does, seemingly without worrying that he might incriminate himself. Why would the judge let him? And why do you think Idowu chose to speak freely? Do you trust Idowu as a witness? After a close read of this testimony, and with a recommended group listening to some of Fela’s music–especially “Zombie”—students could engage in an inquiry discussion of the following questions: How can we tell when the rule of law has stopped working? Why do people make stands against a dictatorship in court, even if they’re unlikely to win? Even in a “show trial” with a predetermined outcome, legal proceduralism can end up giving people a soapbox to criticize those in power. Witnesses can speak their minds on the stand, and judges don’t always toe the political line. It’s easy to assume that “law and order” is naturally on the side of authoritarianism. Is it? Fela Anikulapo Kuti, “Zombie,” 1976, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qj5x6pbJMyU. Tejumola Olaniyan, Arrest the Music! Fela and His Rebel Art and Politics (Indiana University Press, 2004). This biography places Fela in the context of his times. Olaniyan describes the 1977 raid in detail, and his account is consistent with Idowu’s in some ways but not in others. This could be the basis for a debate about perspective: Whose version of events should we trust more, and why? Eboe Hutchful and Abdoulaye Bathily, editors, The Military and Militarism in Africa (CODESRIA, 1998). This collection of essays describes how Africa’s military dictatorships worked at a time when many of them were still in power. Depending on how you use it, it could be a primary source about how military regimes were viewed at the turn of the twenty-first century, or a secondary source about their structural characteristics in the decades prior. To hear Samuel Fury Childs Daly share more about the source and how to teach it, visit https://www.youtube.com/@AmericanHistoricalReview. Photo by Robert Salazar for Bob. Samuel Fury Childs Daly is an associate professor of history at the University of Chicago. He is the author of A History of the Republic of Biafra: Law, Crime, and the Nigerian Civil War (Cambridge University Press, 2020) and Soldier’s Paradise: Militarism in Africa After Empire (Duke University Press, 2024), which has a chapter about Fela Kuti and his legal troubles.

auditPapers.abstract: As lively as her sparkling white suit with pink polka dots and its matching pink hat, she alternately laughs and chokes with tears as she speaks in a rich Kanazawa dialect, with Russian, Chinese, and Manchurian words popping up to punctuate her points. She was one of more than eight hundred thousand Japanese colonists who moved to Manchuria after the region, as vast as the entire North-eastern United States, was severed from China by the Japanese army beginning on September 18, 1931, in what was called the Manchurian incident. “Ruled” by the newly installed Pu-Yi, the last Emperor of China, who had been toppled while still a child in 1911, the new state of Manchukuo was created in 1932. It attracted “pioneers”—bureaucrats, soldiers, farmers, shopkeepers, industrialists, thugs, and idealists-from all over Japan seeking to make new lives and to carve out an empire on the Continent. I wanted to be a pilot when I was in sixth grade. Whenever an airplane flew over, I’d rush out of class to look and was often scolded by my teacher. I was a “militaristic girl,” I guess. I thought I had to fly a plane or do something! I loved Joan of Arc and I wanted to be like her. I was so scatterbrained and bubbly. I don’t know why, but I thought I had to go to Manchuria. I had a strong sense of mission. I even got an award from the Hokkoku newspaper for selling flowers to raise money for our soldiers. My father was a retired navy man and ran a shipyard in the small town of Nanao in Ishikawa prefecture. I had eight brothers and sisters. My father urged us girls to become Red Cross nurses. “What soldiers appreciate most are good nurses,” he kept saying. Japan was a very militaristic state back then, so my five elder sisters became nurses. They didn’t have to pay for their training. In fact, they were actually paid for going to school. My dream was to be a kindergarten teacher. I studied one year at the Nursemaid Training School attached to the Metropolitan Education Association in Tokyo. My parents struggled to support me during my training. I returned to Nanao and wanted to pay them back for my education fees, but there was only one kindergarten in town and nobody would take me on. Still, that’s what I wanted to do, so I was ready when a schoolmate of mine told me of a chance she knew about. She was from Manchuria. “Furuko-san, you have to come,” she said warmly. “They’re building a kindergarten there.” I brushed aside my parents’ opposition and went to Fushun, Manchuria. I was so full of enthusiasm. I wanted to do everything. I believed “we have to take care of the children of Manchuria because Manchuria has been taking care of Japan.” I thought I might even marry someone in Manchuria. My mother was the daughter of a temple priest and married a military man. She hadn’t been able to do what she had dreamed of doing, but she supported me in going out on my own. I was nineteen. She gave me one hundred yen without letting my father know. It cost sixty or eighty yen for the boat and rail fare to Fushun. That was a lot of money. Mother told me, “However good a man or a woman may appear on the way, don’t be taken in by them. Go all the way to your destination at Fushun.” Beginning on the boat from Shimonoseki to Korea, I felt anxious. SoI was completely silent. I ignored everybody, all the way. On the boat and on the Chosen Railway and on the Manchurian Railway, you got your way by using Japanese. You always went unchallenged. At Fushun, the South Manchurian Railway Company had an open-pit mine outside the town that produced good quality coal. A large number of foreigners worked for the Fushun mine. The company had various businesses-mines, hotels, railways. The town was quite well developed. There were about a thousand women working there. That was still a time when married women stayed at home. Many were from the Homeland, including those who, like me, had jumped at the chance to come, and those who had come, relying on their relatives. The children in my care at the kindergarten were all from the Fushun office of the railway company. I loved them. After about a year I lost my voice and developed a slight fever. The head of the kindergarten and the head doctor of the children’s section of the Fushun South Manchurian Railway Company Hospital examined me and ordered me to be hospitalized immediately. I made no real progress, so they told me to return to Japan. There was nothing I could do about it, so I went back to my hometown. I was heartbroken. Back in Nanao, I was hospitalized in Kanazawa City and cured in two months. It was pleurisy resulting from the dryness. As soon as I was cured, I yearned to return. I was on leave of absence status from my job. Again I ignored what my parents said and I was soon on my way back to that kindergarten in Fushun. When you boarded a train and traveled across the wilderness of Manchuria, the red sorghum fields stretched on for an eternity and the evening sun set far, far away. It was so magnificent. I was seduced by that great expanse called Manchuria. December 8, 1941, came during my second stay in Manchuria. It was a bitterly cold morning. Everything was frozen. When the children came in and said good morning, one child-by coincidence her name was Tojo, Tojo Eiko-said “Japan and America have started a war.” I told her that couldn’t be, but she said she’d heard it on the radio. I was shocked. I knew America was large. I wondered why Japan would start a war against such a large country. But our lives were not much affected then. Miss Iwama, the head of the dorm where I lived, was such a warmhearted person. She loved the Manchus. She used to take me to Manchurian villages. “Let’s go and play, Yoshie,” she’d say, and we’d go to all kinds of filthy places. Whenever she found children, she’d pat their heads and play with them. She was good in their language. She took me to small local theaters and on the way home we’d eat melons and things. I really came to love Manchuria, but it didn’t seem to love me. Once more I came down with pleurisy and had to part from her and the children in sorrow. I had gone to Manchuria twice and now Manchuria seemed very close to me. But I realized that my physique was not really suited to it and I knew that each time I fell ill I caused many people much hardship. Again home in Nanao, the subject of marriage came up. The kimono-shop owner had a nephew who lived in Manchuria and wanted a bride from Japan. The only conditions he set were that she had to be physically healthy and capable of using the abacus. I loved the abacus. His nephew was really dear to him and the shop owner asked me to marry him. He showed me his picture. He looked like a nice person. The nephew was returning to Japan, and so a formal meeting was arranged in his uncle’s drawing room. We talked for two or three minutes, then I wanted to go to Manchuria so badly, I just told him, “I’ll go.” When I was about to be married, my mother’s elder sister came all the way to Nanao by boat and train to see me. “Yoshie,” she said, “are you really going to Manchuria? Do you know what’s happening to Japan now? It’s the middle of a war.” I just answered that Manchuria’s all right. It’s full of Japanese. The Soviets are good friends. Then she said gravely, “If Japan loses the war, you won’t be able to get back.” “Don’t say such things,” I told her, but she wouldn’t stop. “If you managed a temple as I do, it would be clear to you. The temple had to donate beautiful Buddhist altar fittings and temple bells to the country for metal. Recently, even the hangers for mosquito nets have had to be contributed. Everything’s vanished. I donated my own gold rings. Can such a country win? If Japan loses, Manchuria will be divided up. If we’re going to lose, it’s better to die together here.” At that time, deep inside me, I thought, what outrageous things this old aunt says! I told her Japan will not lose! My father said so. Anyway, the marriage was already arranged. Again I set out for Manchuria. It was 1943, in the middle of the Greater East Asia War. My husband had started his business in Tonei, in the northeastern province of Manchukuo, after being discharged from the army there. Tonei was the closest town to the Soviet Union, along the northeastern border of Manchuria. It was a special area, subject to special laws and controls. There were about three hundred thousand troops along that border. Maybe fifty thousand additional Japanese people, like rail-waymen, bankers, schoolteachers, and their families, were woven in among them. His store was well established. It had a signboard out front saying “Authorized Military Vendor.” I still remember the phone number-Tonei two-five-three. There weren’t many phones in those days. Here and there were empty houses. Those people must have gone home, thinking it would be dangerous. Maybe that means we were the only ones who didn’t know what was coming. The hamlets of the Manchurians were separated from us Japanese. We had four hired helpers in our store. One was Chō-san, who was fluent in Japanese. He had a long, oblong face. He was in charge of dispatching and supervising the shipping. Two youngsters-we called them Boy-san, twelve and thirteen-worked for us too. Sweet kids. We also had a girl who did laundry for me. “Taitai,” they’d call me, “Okusan” in Japanese. Up to that time I had always been the one who’d been used to do others’ work. Now I was Madame. On New Year’s Day we were invited to Clio’s house for a feast. He was the leader of his hamlet, but my husband bought many of the things they made there. He called my husband “Jiangui,” meaning “Leader.” My husband told me not to confide in Manchurians. Treat them kindly, warmly, he said, but in your heart, you cannot completely trust them. My husband said, “They’re likely to have vengeful feelings towards Japan.” Even the kids who worked for us would sometimes blurt out to me that Japan was bad for taking away their land. My husband bought a large dog from the army, a German Shepherd named Esu. It was a good dog and watched over me while my husband was away. My husband told me that they trained the dogs to bite only Manchurians. They’d dress someone in Manchu clothes and they trained the dog to attack when he came into a room, taking a big bite of his calf. The man’s life wouldn’t be endangered, but he couldn’t move. He could then be investigated to determine if he was a spy. Esu was brought up in that way. We told Cho-san never to wear Chinese clothes. My husband didn’t tell me everything, but there must have been many other things he knew, because he had twice been a soldier. We had a big house. Since we had many large rooms, my husband invited anyone he met from Ishikawa prefecture to come by for dinner. The principal of the school was the head of an Ishikawa Association and my husband served as its secretary. The head of the tax office was also from Ishikawa prefecture. People from Ishikawa stuck together. We had all the food we wanted-cans of bamboo shoots, dried tofu without limit, and shiitake and other mushrooms. Whenever people came, I fed them. It seemed my purpose in life and I enjoyed it. I soon became pregnant. I was ecstatic at that, too. In Japan there was so little already. Clothing was rationed and food had begun to disappear. Simply having so much food made Manchuria attractive. My husband would get purchase orders from the military for items specified and go on purchasing trips to places like Shanghai. If he thought those things would sell well, he’d buy large quantities and bring them back. He bought from Japanese trading companies and sometimes from the Manchurians. “Authorized military vendor” really meant “broker.” He made a great deal of money. I was amazed you could make so much money from the military. I was brought up in the family of a poor military man. When my father died from an accident at the shipyard, we got eight hundred yen in life insurance. My mother said that money came to us from our nation. It seemed a huge sum. I told my husband, “This must be a dream!” “Why?” he asked me, and I pointed to our bankbook entries showing deposits of three thousand yen, five thousand yen. My husband would order fish roe, yellowtail, or pickled radish from Mukden by the boxcar load and they’d ship it to us. I just couldn’t believe you could get money this way. I wondered if I might not be punished for eating things like pound cake. Soldiers came to relax at our place and I’d make simple country dishes that would delight them. One might ask me, “Okusan, what would you like to eat?” I’d say, “Pound cake!” “Great, I’ll get it!’ and he’d go to the commissary and buy butter, flour, sugar-the military had lots of everything, anything. If I said, “I’d like cream puffs,” someone might bring four or five. They took good care of me! The chance to eat Japanese food and talk to a Japanese woman was enough for them. There I was, a real country girl, without pretense, like their elder sister or somebody’s wife, really almost a high-school girl who chatted on about all kinds of simple things. They appreciated it. My husband’s business was booming and he delighted in making people happy. And I enjoyed it, too. I had no idea what lay ahead. Fukushima Yoshie, “Manchurian Days,” in Japan at War: An Oral History, ed. Haruko Taya Cook and Theodore F. Cook (The New Press, 1992), 56–60. During the early 1930s, the convergence of global and domestic crises drove a sharp shift to the right in Japan, triggering a decade of democratic slide that culminated in a de facto military dictatorship by 1940. The army gained popularity after its successful execution of the military occupation of Manchuria in 1931–33 and the establishment of Manchukuo—ostensibly independent of Republican China, but in fact run by the Japanese army. Military mobilization and the expanding investments in Manchuria together served to pull Japan out of a wrenching economic depression. When the League of Nations disputed the legality of the occupation, Japan withdrew from the League and declared a “Japanese Monroe Doctrine” for Asia. Both the occupation of Manchuria and the confrontation with the Western powers in the League were enormously popular. These events solidified public support for radical action advocated by the military both at home and abroad. To explore public attitudes, I have chosen an interview with a Japanese woman who was one of more than eight hundred thousand migrants to Manchuria (Northeast China) in the 1930s. Like many others, she moved into Japan’s expanding railroad towns and rural settlements and was part of the incorporation of Manchuria into Japan’s New Order in Asia. Manchukuo was presented as an independent state that embodied Pan-Asian ideals of racial harmony between Japanese, Chinese, Koreans, and others; it was heralded as a land of opportunity and endless growth. The interview with a settler captures the appeal of a life in Manchuria and the trust ordinary people placed in the military. Covering the period from the mid-1930s to the last years of the war, the interview highlights Fukushima’s residence in two sites of Japanese empire building: Fushun, a coal-mining town in South Manchuria that was run by the South Manchurian Railroad and that stood as the center of Japan’s colonial energy regime; and Tōnei, a strategic hamlet in North Manchuria, where Japanese settlers were located in military encampments to secure the border with the Soviet Union. auditPapers.title: Nations Behind Transnationalism: State Power and the Allegiances of Italian-Tunisians, 1920s–1940s
auditPapers.abstract: This article examines the intricate historical currents that shaped the conflicting allegiances of Italian-Tunisians during the interwar years. Marked by multilingualism and cultural hybridity, these communities expressed radical forms of nationalist identification with their country of origin. Through an exploration of the diverse sociocultural facets of the Italian-Tunisian communities and their intricate interplay with the Italian state’s involvements in Tunisia, the article analyzes the mechanisms underlying the paradoxical coexistence between nationalism and transnationalism. The article shows that these divergent traits had common roots in the sociopolitical position occupied by Italian-Tunisians in the context of interwar Tunisia. Consequently, these Italian-Tunisian communities emerge as the basis for a rich case study, shedding light on the possible alliances and mutual reinforcement that can occur between national political projects and migrant transnational social formations.

auditPapers.title: Andrew Lipman. Squanto: A Native Odyssey
auditPapers.abstract: In his Bancroft Prize–winning book, The Saltwater Frontier, Andrew Lipman presented a gripping account of the seventeenth-century American Northeast, centering maritime encounters and violence between the region’s Indigenous inhabitants and European arrivals. In that book, perhaps the most famous man from Patuxet makes a brief appearance. Named Squanto, or Tisquantum, Lipman explains that the man from Patuxet saved the Plymouth Colony through his role as translator in negotiations with neighboring Wampanoags and his willingness to teach the English colonists how to cultivate crops. Squanto’s appearance in the pages of The Saltwater Frontier was necessarily fleeting. Nor was Squanto an unknown figure in need of explaining when Lipman penned his first book—Squanto’s real-life efforts to ensure the survival of the English colony has earned him a larger-than-life place in the American imagination as the individual often credited with bringing about the first Thanksgiving. In his new book, Squanto: A Native Odyssey, Lipman turns back to the life and world of Tisquantum. As a contemporary and ally of the notoriously verbose Plymouth colonists, Squanto’s life was well documented and has been written about frequently by scholars ever since. Despite the attention paid to certain aspects of Squanto’s life, Lipman’s book represents the first stand-alone study of the Patuxet man. One reason for this lack of a detailed biography of Squanto is sources, which were predominantly penned by Englishmen who Lipman argues “were genuinely curious about Squanto and his people” but who wrote within a wider world in which “their motivation was to claim and rule Native land” (4). The documentary record has not allowed for a traditional biography of Squanto since basic biographical details, such as whether or not he ever married or had children, remain obscure. To counter the “blinkered perspectives” of colonial writers, Lipman draws from a multidisciplinary array of sources and methods to create a “mosaic of evidence” against which he critically and productively reads the colonial record (4, 5). The result is a compelling and important “new picture of a man too often rendered as a caricature” (6).

auditPapers.title: Ademide Adelusi-Adeluyi. Imagine Lagos: Mapping History, Place, and Politics in a Nineteenth-Century African City
auditPapers.abstract: As the digital humanities evolve to consider how marginalized histories can be produced using new technologies, it is still relatively rare to see Africa-focused scholarship represented in the historiography. Ademide Adelusi-Adeluyi’s monograph, Imagine Lagos is a strong contribution to the development of African digital humanities scholarship. Moreover, it is a major intervention in the fields of urban and social history. This monograph demonstrates the importance of interrogating the silences that exist within the archive, especially of Indigenous and other marginalized communities, and insisting on finding ways to recover their presence through innovative methodologies. Imagine Lagos builds a picture of life in Lagos as it underwent major transformations between 1845 and 1872, moving from being a major slave-trading port to a primary trading port for African commodities in the period of “legitimate” trade, and finally becoming a British colony (1861). The book tracks the political and social changes that unfolded during this critical period through the primary lens of space. It is a forensic reconstruction of the city, brilliantly executed using different kinds of spatial and documentary data. In the introduction, the author explains a unique methodology, performing a “walking cartography” of each main section of Old Lagos. This method entailed searching for clues of the city’s original contours and orientation by walking the city’s current main and side streets. Present-day streets hint at the original outline of long filled-in swamps and streams, and Indigenous street names have survived the continuous remaking of Lagos, pointing to a physical past that is barely perceptible. The maps she produced beautifully represent the hidden past of this now megacity.

auditPapers.title: Nicki Kindersley. New Sudans: Wartime Intellectual Histories in Khartoum
auditPapers.abstract: Nicki Kindersley’s book New Sudans: Wartime Intellectual Histories in Khartoum explores the intellectual, political, and educational lives of southern Sudanese displaced by the Second Sudanese Civil War (1983–2005) to the capital, Khartoum. One of the outcomes of the 2005 peace agreement that brought an end to the civil war was the independence referendum that brought about the secession of South Sudan in 2011, and thus the departure of many of those who had lived in Khartoum during the war years from the capital to join the new nation. Indeed, most of the research for this book was conducted in South Sudan in the years following secession. Yet the title speaks to alternative possibilities through its wink to the “New Sudan” vision most associated with John Garang, the leader of the Sudan People’s Liberation Army during the civil war. The New Sudan vision sought less to separate the south and more to emancipate all the marginalized populations in Sudan, who in the view of its advocates were being exploited by a hegemonic elite in Khartoum.

auditPapers.title: Multidisciplinary approaches and digital technologies in the study of Early Christian architecture: The Sacellum of SS. Teuteria and Tosca in Verona (mid 5th-early 6th century)
auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: This study presents a multidisciplinary investigation into the Sacellum of SS. Teuteria and Tosca in Verona, an early Christian chapel dated between the mid-5th and early 6th centuries. Conducted as part of the CaMeRoofs project under the HORIZON-MSCA framework (2024-2026), the research aims to reconstruct the architectural evolution and historical context of this unique monument through the integration of archaeological, architectural, and digital methodologies. The project builds upon a two-year preliminary study at the University of Florence (2021-2023) and employs state-of-the-art digital technologies to produce unprecedented documentation. Digital survey campaigns utilized Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS), UAV-based and ground-based photogrammetry (Structure from Motion), and 3D modeling, resulting in high-resolution point clouds and color-mapped models. These technologies enabled accurate geometric documentation and virtual navigation, as well as detailed stratigraphic, morphological, and material analyses. The integration of archival research and structural diagnostics supported a revised phasing of the monument, revealing both early Christian features – such as opus spicatum masonry, cruciform layout, and lantern vault – and Romanesque additions from the second half of the 12th century. Unpublished findings include a reevaluation of the Sacellum ’s original architecture, challenging prior assumptions by demonstrating its alignment with free Greek cross plans similar to the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia in Ravenna, rather than the inscribed Greek cross typology. This study underscores the critical value of digital survey tools for conservation and heritage enhancement and contributes new data to the fields of early Christian archaeology and architectural history. • 3D digital survey of Verona's sacellum using TLS, SfM, and UAV photogrammetry. • First stratigraphic analysis of masonry reveals new construction phasing. • Free Greek cross plan links sacellum to Ravenna's Galla Placidia model. • High-res 3D model supports conservation, analysis, and virtual navigation. • Unpublished data redefine early Christian architecture in northern Italy.

auditPapers.title: Bowl By Bowl: Black Women, Food Selling, and Survival in the Antebellum North
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article explores the lives of Black women, free and enslaved, who hawked prepared foods like pepper pot stew on the streets and in the markets of northern cities between the late-eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries. Though ubiquitous in their own time, evidence relating to female provisioners is scattered and thin. These women appear, fleetingly, in newspaper accounts, reminiscences, census records, legal documents, and visual culture. Stitching together these archival fragments reveals the importance of Black women to urban commerce. Food selling allowed them to evade the coercion associated with most kinds of work available to them but forced them into fraught negotiations in public space. Most Black women vendors earned meager incomes, but for a few of them, this selling offered relatively good compensation. By keeping a sharp focus on these petty entrepreneurs, this study offers a critical new perspective on northern urban life, labor, and racial hierarchies during the nineteenth century.

auditPapers.title: Open Tool Registries! Resolving the Directory Paradox with Wikidata
auditPapers.abstract: This paper introduces the conceptual framework for open and community-curated tool registries, posing that such registries provide fundamental value to any field of research by acting as curated knowledge bases about a community’s past and current methodological practices as well as authority files for individual tools. auditPapers.title: Striving towards automated writing – Views on authorship in story generation research
auditPapers.abstract: This article examines how authorship is approached in story generation research publications. Story generation research forms its own, distinctive context in which computer-generated literary texts are being produced. Through text analysis and comparisons to other forms of computer-generated literature, the article examines what kind of rhetoric is used when the authorship of computer-generated texts is described in this context, and how the roles of the programmers and the program are characterised. The findings suggest that the approach to authorship in story generation research is mainly technical, referring strictly to the production process of the text, and leaving out the meaning of authorship as responsibility and accountability of the work as an aesthetic whole. This technical view affects how human-computer relations are discussed in the research, as "human-generated" and "computer-generated" texts are contrasted with each other. Furthermore, this dichotomy of the human and the machine affects how the produced stories are evaluated.

auditPapers.title: Changing Movements in a Changing World: Modelling Early Pleistocene and Early Middle Pleistocene Climatic and Ecological Environments and Influences on Hominin Dispersal in Eurasia
auditPapers.journal: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology
auditPapers.abstract: In a world of drastic climatic and ecological changes, our knowledge of how the environment influenced hominin behaviour is of the utmost importance. Archaeology plays a key role in this domain, as it is the only discipline that studies empirical evidence of past societies’ responses to environmental change. Computational models generating predictions about past climatic and ecological conditions are vital for understanding the archaeological record and how these factors shaped the dispersal of hominins out of Africa and into Eurasia during the Early and early Middle Pleistocene. In this paper, various models for past reconstructions of climatic and ecological conditions and simulation techniques are presented to provide an overview of the diverse approaches, possibilities, advantages and constraints of using computational reconstructions in archaeological research. Focusing on studies of hominin dispersals out of Africa and into Eurasia during the Early and early Middle Pleistocene, this paper discusses the links between environmental factors and hominin dispersal behaviour. The use of simulation techniques to represent hominin populations, such as cellular automata or agent-based modelling, can contribute to connecting small-scale environment-induced influences on hominins to large-scale patterns, supported by ecological theories of species survival and spatial behaviour. Collectively, these approaches provide an elaborate foundation for understanding environmental influences on past hominin dispersals.

auditPapers.title: Reading John Selden’s Titles of honor (1614) as a Work of Polemic
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract First published in 1614, John Selden’s Titles of honor has long been ignored by historians of political thought. A large and compendious description of the various titles of Europe and the Near East; by its structure and tone, it resembles nothing more than a work of dusty antiquarianism. It attracted none of the controversy that would plague Selden’s Historie of tithes (1618); and it did not state its polemical purpose in such explicit terms as his Mare clausum (1635). If historians of political thought have remembered it at all, they have done so because Thomas Hobbes recommended the work in chapter 10 of Leviathan (1651). This article will treat Titles of honor as a work of political intention. Following Selden’s engagement with Roman Civil Law, it will argue that he composed the treatise to criticize sixteenth-century theories of resistance, and the medieval theories of divided sovereignty upon which they were founded. In short, this article will seek to reframe Titles of honor as a defence of state sovereignty against theories of noble resistance – and so explain Hobbes’s affection for the work.

auditPapers.title: Minimizing LIBS damage in the analysis of decorative tiles using RGB data clustering
auditPapers.abstract: • Dual-domain clustering integrates RGB segmentation with LIBS spectral mapping. • Achieves high match between visual and chemical similarity across sample regions. • Cuts LIBS shots and data size by more than one order of magnitude. • Minimizes surface damage while preserving chemical representativeness. • Scalable workflow applicable to other layered cultural-heritage materials. Spectral analysis of cultural heritage materials offers valuable insights into the restoration and preservation of historical artifacts, revealing details about the materials used and the manufacturing techniques employed. However, given their historical and artistic significance, the extraction of elemental information from these fragile samples poses a unique challenge, as these objects must be examined using minimally invasive methods to prevent irreversible damage. Laser-induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) is one such technique, providing a rapid and detailed elemental characterization. Yet, extensive LIBS analysis can still compromise the integrity of these delicate objects. In this work, a novel approach that integrates spectral and RGB data clustering to significantly reduce the number of LIBS measurements required is introduced. By segmenting the material into visually and chemically distinct clusters, this method enables targeted LIBS analysis using only a few representative shots per cluster, thus preserving the integrity of cultural heritage artifacts while still delivering reliable compositional insights.

auditPapers.title: Localised decorrelation stretch (L-DCS) for improved visibility of large, dense rock art scenes
auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: DStretch® is widely known within the study of rock art and is used across the field of archaeology to enhance the visibility of faded or difficult to see motifs. DStretch calculates enhancements based on all RGB values in an image and so often struggles to decorrelate local areas with high correlation, particularly if there is a wide distribution of RGB values such as in dense rock art scenes, orthomosaics, or 3D model textures. Local decorrelation stretch (L-DCS) automatically separates an image into overlapping windows, performing decorrelated stretching on each, and merging them back into a single image. The results retained greater fine details in motifs and improved significantly the visibility of “hidden” motifs in densely painted areas when compared to DStretch. The flexibility afforded by our approach and the consistency of results in different scenarios make L-DCS a robust approach for automated DCS on larger datasets without manual intervention. • A more robust method for enhancing rock art motifs in dense scenes. • L-DCS can handle large images more effectively. • L-DCS handles greater variation in pigment colours without the need for multiple filters.

auditPapers.abstract: Daniel Huws’s Repertory of Welsh Manuscripts and Scribes c.800–c.1800 was published in 2022 to widespread acclaim – a giant of scholarship which ... handed the world the keys to unlock the great riches of a thousand years of Welsh manuscript culture . Containing descriptions of c.3,300 manuscripts from sixty-eight repositories, along with detailed indexes and plates illustrating scribal hands, the Repertory is ... the kind of work upon which all others build . In his introduction to the Repertory, Huws immediately points to the future, writing that it ... belongs to that class of publication which can only reach maturity in a second edition . This case study describes work towards the production of that edition, not as an expanded or revised set of printed volumes but as a dataset. First, we set the Repertory in the context of catalogues of Welsh manuscripts, and in the wider context of digital resources derived from manuscript descriptions. Then we describe the process of converting the Repertory into a dataset, and how this process, while technical in nature, served as a close reading of its scope and purpose. We offer some practical guidance on the conversion of print volumes to datasets and outline some initial research findings. Finally, we suggest some possible next steps for the Repertory, covering issues such as access and sustainability, integration with other resources and minimal computing approaches to analysing and surfacing the data.

auditPapers.title: Facets of Friction: Investigating epistemological friction between computing and the humanities to support Digital Humanities computing education
auditPapers.abstract: Learning computing can often be challenging to Digital Humanities (DH) students because its knowledge-production practices and values do not necessarily align with those of humanistic inquiry. Further, the breadth of the technologies used in the field can make it difficult to identify which computational ideas and skills are most essential to teach in DH. This paper argues that, in order to teach students to enact a paradigm of 'humanistic computing' which is reflective of humanistic interests and ways of knowing, it is necessary to centre the epistemological friction that exists between computing and the humanities. It proposes a four-faceted framework to aid in the identification and exploration of that friction, with the intention that it be used by DH educators to structure their computing curriculum – regardless of the technologies or level of abstraction it engages with – and by students or even practitioners to scaffold a critical approach to computational DH work.

auditPapers.title: Do all politicians sound the same? Comparing model explanations to human responses
auditPapers.abstract: It is sometimes said that all politicians sound the same with their speeches mired in political jargon full of clichés and false promises. To investigate how distinct the plenary speeches of political parties truly are and what linguistic features make them distinct, we trained a BERT classifier to predict the party affiliation of Finnish members of parliament from their plenary speeches. We contrasted and compared model performance to human responses to see how humans and the model differ in their ability to distinguish between the parties. We used the model explainability method SHAP to identify the linguistic cues that the model most relies on. We show that a deep learning model can distinguish between parties much more accurately than the respondents to the questionnaire. The SHAP explanations and questionnaire responses reveal that whereas humans tend to rely on mostly topical cues, the model has learned to recognize other cues as well, such as personal style and rhetoric.

auditPapers.title: Virtual reconstruction and constructive modelling of the coffered ceiling in the Synagogue of El Tránsito (Toledo, Spain)
auditPapers.abstract: This article presents a work about the coffered ceiling of the Synagogue of El Tránsito (Toledo), an exceptional example of 14th-century Spanish-Muslim carpentry. Its structural model follows the typical geometric standards of the period which were common to both Christian and Muslim traditions in the 14th-century in Spain. This work includes, on the one hand, the analysis of the coffered ceiling geometric design: first, a basic module has been identified, as well as the several patterns that were developed with its variations and combinations; secondly, the whole design has been fit to the global dimensions to generate an idealised whole layout of the structure. Finally, a comparison with the actual geometry of the building has been carried out to analyse the reasons of the differences between them. On the other hand, a study of the coffered ceiling constructive configuration has been developed: the pieces that form the structure have been firstly individualized to study their assembling process later. The research has been possible thanks to a three-dimensional (3D) survey done in the building combining several techniques (laser scanning and photogrammetry). This generated a point cloud which has been the geometric basis for the latter analysis and for the generation of 3D parametric models of the coffered ceiling pieces. The main results are the geometric layout which could be used by carpenters to design the coffered ceiling, as well as the explanation of the wooden pieces and their assembling process. The paper is fully illustrated with two-dimensional (2D) drawings and images of the 3D models, thus helping to reach a better knowledge, conservation and dissemination of these types of historical wooden structures.

auditPapers.title: Armed Robberies in Colonial Asante: Official Denial, Private Speculation, and the Perpetuation of Stereotype, 1935–45
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Armed robberies that occurred in colonial Asante between 1935 and 1945 made life unbearable. This caused the colonial state and the restored Asante monarchy to try to find solutions to the growing insecurity. This article considers the various reactions to the armed robberies as a lens on the colonial state’s relationship with Asante society at the height of colonial power (1935–45). We argue that the colonial state was undercut by tensions, contradictions, and conflicts, which produced paralysis at times, rendering its approach inconsistent. This contention goes against the image of benevolence and goodwill presented by the colonial state in Asante historiography. This article draws on a previously unexplored set of records from the Kumase branch of Ghana’s Public Records and Archives Administration Department and the Manhyia Archives, newspaper articles, and state commission reports to make its case.

auditPapers.title: A Network View on the Big Exchange Project: Integrating and Analysing Heterogeneous Datasets
auditPapers.journal: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology
auditPapers.abstract: This study presents a proof-of-concept for integrating 14 datasets on 11 archaeologically relevant raw materials from the Big Exchange project into a heterogeneous information network (HIN), an informational structure explicitly modelling multiple object and relationship types. HIN-based approaches provide archaeologists with a powerful means of identifying structural and semantic patterns in material distributions. In this study, a spatial extension of the PathSim similarity measure is applied to the integrated HIN to quantify higher-order relationships (meta paths) between raw materials at different spatial scales. The results highlight overlapping material spheres as proxies for potential contact zones and social proximity in the Early Neolithic. They also reveal instances of spatial separation and limited interaction. The method additionally helps distinguish circulation patterns from potential taphonomic biases, such as artefact absence due to preservation conditions. The analysis reveals a particularly strong similarity between Rijckholt Flint and Actinolite-Hornblende Schist at all spatial scales. This suggests that there was sustained contact and low social distance between the communities associated with them. These findings show how spatially extended PathSim can reveal both expected and previously obscured interaction patterns, while also highlighting methodological limitations that result in localised variations in similarity scores being flattened by highly dispersed materials.

auditPapers.title: Galileo’s Three Repudiations of Copernicanism – Two Coerced and One Volunteered
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Up to 1616, when the Copernican theory of heliocentrism was prohibited, Galileo had never asserted its truth. But the pope and cardinals of the Roman Inquisition assumed that he had, and he was required to repudiate it. In contrast, Copernicus’s book was only lightly corrected and allowed to be read. Galileo continued his practice of not asserting the reality of heliocentrism in his Dialogue on the two world systems, but he was put on trial nevertheless, in 1633. However, instead of being charged with a crime to be proved, as required by canon law, he was subjected to pre-trial interrogation and intimidation, and he confessed to a made-up crime. His conviction entailed another repudiation of the static sun, on pain of harsh punishment. In subsequent years, even though he was reckless in expressing preference for the condemned theory, he still did not advocate it. In fact, in writing to the Tuscan ambassador to Venice in 1641, he insisted that the Copernican system was false, because theologians said so. However, he went on to say that the opposing Ptolemaic view was actually erroneous, while the other was merely insufficient – because stellar parallax (which would prove the earth’s orbit) could not yet be measured.

auditPapers.title: A linalool-based nanostructured fluid for the removal of alkyd paints
auditPapers.abstract: • Formulation of a linalool-based o/w microemulsion using a cationic surfactant. • Physicochemical characterization of the nanostructured fluid. • Assessment of the removal capability of tube paint and spray paint based on alkyds. • Evaluation of the removal action of vandalic tags in a real practical scenario. A linalool based microemulsion was prepared using a cationic surfactant, and its phase behaviour was systematically investigated. The morphology and structure of the micelles were also investigated and characterised by Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS). The system was tested on a laboratory scale using commercial tubes and spray paints applied on mortar mock-ups. Moreover, the system was applied on real case studies for the removal of unauthorized tags, from a cement-based facade covered with silicate-based outdoor paints. The promising results provide valuable insights into the potential application of linalool-based cleaning systems for conservation practice

auditPapers.title: Enduring Medical Knowledge in the Age of Slavery
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century slave management texts, plantation guidebooks, medical dissertations, and treatises on preserving health in hot climates functioned as authoritative sources on the specific traits, symptoms, and health complaints of enslaved Black people. That said, information found in these texts, especially specific physiological assertions about Black people’s bodies, were not always uniform. While doctors largely agreed that Black people had a high pain tolerance and ease during childbirth, there was less consensus around the amount of therapeutic bloodletting Black people should undergo, mainly owing to beliefs that their bodies were not so well suited for it. Scholars have done well to demonstrate the ways in which physicians and plantation doctors made and accepted claims about Black people’s susceptibility to disease, but less attention has been paid to how and why the need to bleed slaves sparingly failed to take hold as an unquestioned truth about Black people’s bodies in the way that Black people’s high tolerance to pain did. The broad question ‘what did doctors think a Black person’s body could withstand?’ provides an instructive framework for interrogating the selective acceptance of certain claims about Black people’s bodies and the factors that led plantation doctors to embrace or disregard them.
