auditPapers.title: Swimming without Water: Popular Physical Education in Berlin and Buenos Aires, 1880–1930
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract By the turn of the century, swimming had become an important activity for city dwellers who wished to participate in modern life. Considered essential for children and adults alike, it was a leisure activity for working people, as well as a sport best practiced in clubs. However, opportunities to swim in cities were limited, as urban infrastructure could hardly cope with the new size of booming cities, let alone provide them with swimming pools. Consequently, journalists, experts, politicians, and physicians developed the concept of “swimming without water” as a means of strengthening the body for urban life. This article examines the emergence of modern bodily exercise practices in urban contexts, focusing on how physical culture reflected social, technological, and cultural transformations in Berlin and Buenos Aires at the turn of the century. Through an analysis of popular magazines and self-help discourses, it demonstrates how bodies were shaped by transnational influences, technological innovations, and consumer capitalism. Debates about physical exercise show a globalizing body ideal characterized by muscularity, health, and resilience, which often transcended national identities. They also reveal an ambivalent and improvised relationship to modernity. The proponents of physical practices often rejected modern urban life rhetorically while relying on modern concepts such as science, medicine, or photography. Practices such as swimming without water and home-based workouts served as an improvisational response to infrastructure deficits. The body became a site of negotiating this ambivalent and improvised modernity as bodily cultures became a vital part of urban modernity.

auditPapers.title: A dual-path approach to emotional arousal and visual cognition in intangible cultural heritage: the case of Xiashi Pinprick Lantern Pictures
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract There is a limited empirical research on late Generation Z’s (Gen Z’s) experience and evaluation of Chinese intangible cultural heritage (ICH). Using a dual-path approach, this study conducted (1) a mixed-design ANOVA and semantic differential scale to analyze four themes and extract latent dimensions via factor and cluster analysis, and (2) an eye-tracking experiment to record fixation duration and count, thus assess their correlations with subjective ratings. These findings suggest that Gen Z’s preferences for traditional pinprick lantern art are theme-dependent and shaped by emotional and cognitive engagement. The study offers empirical evidence, through both subjective and objective measures, to better understand how ICH artworks are perceived by late Gen Z audiences, contributing to ICH transmission and the promotion of aesthetic education.

auditPapers.title: The Color of Family: History, Race, and the Politics of Ancestry. By Michael O’Malley
auditPapers.abstract: In The Color of Family, historian Michael O’Malley examines how the intertwined histories of genealogy, race, and state bureaucracy have shaped understandings of identity in the United States. Central to the book is the story of the author’s Irish immigrant ancestor, Patrick O’Malley, and his Virginian wife, Hester Holland—whose 1884 marriage certificate listed them both as “colored.” Using this document and the bureaucratic authority it represents, O’Malley explores how official records have defined belonging while enforcing exclusion. Bureaucratic recordkeeping and eugenic systems, he argues, imposed and distorted racial categories, turning state paperwork into a battleground over identity. The resulting study is an ambitious synthesis of family history, social theory, and intellectual history. O’Malley argues that genealogy is not simply personal or biological but fundamentally political. Modern bureaucracies—through censuses, birth records, and marriage licenses—created what he calls “administrative individualism,” rendering citizens both identifiable and controllable (4). This system conferred rights even as it reinforced racial hierarchies. Drawing on Barbara and Karen Fields’s concept of “racecraft,” O’Malley shows how bureaucratic rituals made race appear natural and self-evident. Reframing ancestry as history rather than biology can disrupt that illusion: to say one has ancestors from Africa or Asia, rather than is Black or is Asian, acknowledges movement and mixture over fixed identity.

auditPapers.title: Living the Global Tourism Boom “from Below”: People’s Expectations, Social Experiences, and Narratives of Modernization in Francoist Spain (1950s–70s)
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article analyzes the social effects of mass global tourism on Spaniards. Since the 1950s, and especially in the 1960s, the Franco regime promoted tourism policies that allowed the massive arrival of foreigners to Spain. At the same time, the regime’s propaganda conveyed that Spaniards, too, were part of this new situation of modern tourism. Scholarship has often treated tourism as an asset for breaking the hold of authoritarianism. Tourism symbolized social and economic modernity, which was seen as incompatible with a dictatorship like Francoism. Yet beyond these broad narratives, the social effects of tourism on Spaniards have rarely been studied on empirical grounds. This article argues that mass global tourism had a strong effect on Spanish society, but not the one described in prevailing modernizing narratives. The regime created high expectations that clashed with poor realities and left people resentful. By the mid-1960s, contrary to official propaganda, almost two-thirds of the Spanish population had no tourism experience at all. For those Spaniards who could travel, both in Spain and abroad, many felt like second-class tourists and perceived that tourism was designed mainly to please wealthy Europeans. Most recognized the economic benefits but separated them from the social consequences, which they often judged negative. Inside Spain, the flood of foreigners provoked scandals over “immorality” and even riots that disturbed public life. Catholic and conservative Spaniards protested against tourism and against the regime itself, accusing it of betraying the values it claimed to defend. Ironically, rather than liberalizing mindsets, tourism often reinforced traditional ones.

auditPapers.title: Imperial Sleep: Race, Climate, and Health in Late Nineteenth- and Early Twentieth-Century British India
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article argues that sleep is an understudied element of bodily experience in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century British India. Using the notion of “imperial sleep,” the article explores the ways in which the bodies of colonized and colonizer were enmeshed through medical, material, and technological cultures of sleep and sleeping. Sleep practices reveal complex interactions of imperial hierarchies of race and class as the British in India struggled to obtain a good night’s rest in the tropical climate. Looking to medical journals, advice books, and cultural representations of Anglo-Indian life, this article will consider how sleep played a crucial role in protecting white bodies from the perils of the tropical environment. Doctors and surgeons weighed in on how a careful regimen of “tropical sleep hygiene” could mitigate the degenerating influences of heat, wind, and bothersome insects. In turn, these medicalized sleep regimens encountered the indigenous sleep practices of colonized peoples, who were often forced to mold their own bodily need for rest to support that of their rulers. While typically represented as “laziness” by colonial rulers, the flexible sleep practices of Indian servants observed by Europeans might be viewed as a means of embodied resistance against the temporal violence of colonialism.

auditPapers.title: Sounds of Authority: The Cultural and Social History of Western Music in Japanese-Occupied Hong Kong
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article examines Japan’s cultural policies in occupied Hong Kong (1941–45), focusing on the promotion of Western music as a strategic political tool within the broader context of Japan’s imperial ambitions in East Asia. auditPapers.title: A GIS view of the word orders of numeral bases and numeral classifiers in Kuki-Chin languages
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Tibeto-Burman (TB) languages are known for their diversity in numeral systems and classifiers. This paper investigates the Kuki-Chin (KC, also called South-Central Tibeto-Burman) languages in TB’s Northeast Indian Areal Group and provides a comprehensive description of the four types of numeral systems: base-final, base-initial, base-split, and no-base, and the four types of classifier systems: CL-final, CL-initial, CL-split, and no-CL. A thorough survey of the literature, aided by fieldwork, enables a GIS view of the distribution of the different types of languages. Also, KC languages conform to Greenberg’s Universal 20A: N does not come between Num and CL, and the numeral base and classifier harmonize in word order. We propose the following hypothesis for Proto-KC (PKC) and Proto-TB (PTB) to account for the variation in numeral bases and classifiers in KC, that is, PKC, like PTB, is base-initial and without numeral classifiers, and the current variation in numeral bases and numeral classifiers in KC is due to horizontal external influence via language contact. Bayesian phylogenetic inference tests, however, show mixed results, as PKC is likely to be base-initial, as expected, but CL-initial, and PTB is likely to be base-final but CL-initial. Thus, we plan to conduct a comprehensive survey of all TB languages and further explore the state of PTB in terms of numeral bases and classifiers.

auditPapers.title: Seeding Empire: American Philanthrocapital and the Roots of the Green Revolution in Africa. By Aaron Eddens
auditPapers.abstract: Aaron Eddens's book is an original and informed invitation to reflect on the future of agriculture from a global perspective. Breaking from this convention, the author focuses on the transformation of the agricultural landscape in Africa, a region that has only recently entered the narrative canon of the Green Revolution. Eddens demonstrates that the Green Revolution narrative is so strong that even a region historically linked to global phenomena, such as Africa, is presented as a space of purportedly novel global integration based on the expansion of the Green Revolution's frontiers. The classic narrative of the Green Revolution suggests that genetically modified crops are the solution both to the lack of development in African countries and to the vulnerability that climate change imposes in contexts of drought. Reinforcing a colonialist tradition, this narrative presents Africa and genetically modified crop technology as the “final frontier” of the West's expansion project into places considered to be in crisis. In other words, it reiterates the idea that African farmers are behind the rest of the world and therefore desperately need more technology and more seed companies. Of course, this narrative distracts attention from the discussion of the conditions that have advanced underdevelopment on the continent.

auditPapers.title: The Bajío Revolution: Remaking Capitalism, Community, and Patriarchy in Mexico, North America and the World. By John Tutino
auditPapers.abstract: John Tutino’s new book is the culmination of a long and distinguished career in Mexican economic and social history. The book offers a deeply researched and sophisticated analysis of a crucial Mexican region that contained Mexico’s richest agricultural lands and most important silver mines. More provocatively, it also argues that the activities of the Bajío’s peasants and mineworkers were central to the changing economy of the nineteenth-century world. The book is based on many different types of sources. Some sections synthesize secondary sources, including some of Tutino’s own path-breaking works and books on other parts of the world. These sections are necessary for Tutino’s argument that the social unrest that began in the region in 1810 ended flows of silver and disrupted European trade with Asia, allowing the growth of industrial capitalism. Many other sections are based on deep research in primary sources. The most outstanding rely on Tutino’s careful, detailed analysis of the correspondence and business records of some of Mexico’s wealthiest nineteenth-century families. He incisively analyzes their business tactics, which combined investments in mining, commerce, and agriculture, but he does much more than that. Tutino shows that sophisticated reading of these elite-generated sources can reveal much about the lives of the ordinary Mexicans who toiled on the land or in the mines. This is unusual work. Generally, historians of Mexico have been more successful in probing the lives of indigenous peasants who lived in villages with communal lands because they litigated frequently, creating a rich documentary record. We have known much less about rural people living on large estates because they had little access to the judicial system. Tutino uses estate records to close the gap. These documents do not record the words of peasants, but Tutino convincingly shows that they tell us much about peasants’ economic choices and their efforts to feed their families under trying conditions.

auditPapers.title: Examining negativity and positivity bias in Pulitzer prize-winning news: a study across six subgenres
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Linguistic positivity bias (LPB) has been widely recognized as a universal linguistic phenomenon in various domains. To address this contradiction, we conducted sentiment analysis on a corpus consisting of over a thousand Pulitzer Prize-winning news articles spanning 26 years, covering six distinct news subgenres: Breaking, National, Local, Explanatory, Investigative, and International News. Additionally, we identified distinct patterns of sentiment across subgenres, also challenging the notion of LPB. A negativity bias is evident in several subgenres, while positivity is observed in others, implying nuanced differences of sentiment within news discourse. Furthermore, we found that although topic preference contributes to sentiment patterns, it is not the sole determinant.

auditPapers.title: CHRONOPOLITICS OF CLASSICAL PHILOLOGY THROUGH THE NON SEQUITUR
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article argues that classical philology can play a vital role in debates about the importance of philology now and configures a genealogy that may contribute to the quest for alternative philologies. Building on Werner Hamacher's definition of philology as “love of the non sequitur ,” I turn to founding texts of Western classical philology by Johann Joachim Winckelmann, Friedrich August Wolf, and August Böckh in order to interrogate their identification with modern classicism and historicism. Examining the science of philology as Altertumswissenschaft , I focus on a language of ambiguity and undecidability with regard to philology's classical object (Greek and Roman pasts) and the discourse of philological science that constructs it. This is grasped as the relation between a transcendental temporality that enunciated classical antiquity's wholeness and a kind of perturbation of time that destabilized philology's alignment with classicism and historicism. For Winckelmann, Wolf, and Böckh, the philologist's task required a conceptual and temporal leap toward the past that signaled the absence of philology's grounding. In this sense, it differed from evocations of a seamless movement across a unified horizon of time linking antiquity and modernity. This was conveyed by stressing the past's mutilation, absence, and accidental expression as the vanishing ground on which philology could build its classical vision. By configuring these notions as the self‐hollowing basis of its knowledge, classical philology came to be divided by a paradoxical appeal to sequential time and the non sequitur. Tensions produced in this context bring classical philology to the center of debates that seek to interrogate modern historical intelligibility and time. Far from perpetuating ideas of irreversible and linear time, classical philology claims to engage with an absent past, and as such, it disrupts sequential temporalities by desiring something that is always beyond presence or reach and therefore always available for times to come and for future emancipation from regimes of present time.

The initiative involved conservation issues, cleaning of the monument, investigating the origin of the raw materials used to build it, and determining the construction age. The characterisation of the mortars allowed us to know, for the first time, that several types of mortars were used during the construction of the bridge, clearly different to other ones used in historical repairs. In this study, a comprehensive analysis of these mortars provides key information for the use of optical stimulated luminescence (OSL) in their dating, to provide insights into the construction phases and historical development of the aqueduct. auditPapers.title: Influence of pulse duration on the effects induced by three Nd:YAG lasers operating at 1064 nm to tempera paintings mock-ups
auditPapers.abstract: • Under conditions of non-apparent damage, SFR (110µs) allows higher fluences. • Protective character of the binders: intense melting in orpiment temperas. • Rabbit glue based paints experienced greater color changes. • LQS (100 ns) was the best preserving of the original color as the fluence increased. Laser cleaning of soiled wall paintings is a conservation practice that has been adopted for decades. However, the increasingly widespread availability of laser technology highlights the need to optimize the choice of laser systems and, consequently, the parameters used on a case-by-case basis. In this study, three Nd:YAG lasers (1064 nm) with different pulse durations were tested: a short free-running system (110 µs), long Q-switched system (100 ns), and Q-switched (8 ns). These lasers were tested on tempera painting mock-ups made of one pigment (i.e. malachite, azurite, lead white, orpiment, or cinnabar) mixed with an organic binder (i.e. egg yolk or rabbit glue) applied to a lime mortar. Each laser was also evaluated in tablets composed solely of one pigment. The reference and irradiated temperas were studied using stereomicroscopy, spectrophotometry, attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR), and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX). The pigment tablets were also analyzed with micro X-ray diffraction (µXRD). All samples suffered blackening after laser irradiation, the intensity of which depended on the nature of the pigment and the binder. Overall, pigment susceptibility was broadly comparable across the three pulse-duration lasers. Cinnabar exhibited the highest level of susceptibility, followed by copper carbonates and orpiment, while lead white proved to be the least affected pigment. The binders exhibited a protective effect on the pigments, although this effect was more intense in egg yolk paintings. Regarding pulse duration, it was found that at low fluences, the laser with the longest pulse duration generated the lowest color changes, while at high fluences, this same laser generated the greatest impact on the temperas. Physical effects were observed in the samples (mineral melting and binder loss), though these were not proportional to the intensity of the blackening.

auditPapers.title: Spectroanalytical approach for analysis of archaeological objects related to personal adornment from Teruel Museum
auditPapers.abstract: • Multianalytical approach for personal adornment objects analyses. • p-XRF, LIBS, and µ-Raman spectroscopies allowed surface and in-depth composition. • Most historical personal adornment items material manufacturing have been assessed. • Update of Teruel museum catalog. • The proposed methodology could be extended to other Cultural Heritage objects. The immense variety of materials found in museum's archaeological collections often makes the tasks of cataloging and conservation difficult. This is even more challenging when dealing with objects related to personal adornments, such as jewelry or amulets, due to their extensive material diversity and complexity. For these reasons, the chemical characterization of this type of objects is crucial for linking the use of certain raw materials in the production of artifacts with commercial and influential spheres. The present study aims at the non/micro-invasive material characterization of a set of heterogeneous personal adornment pieces from a wide chronological period (2nd BC – 18th AD centuries) belonging to the archaeology collection of the Teruel Museum, Spain. A multi-analytical approach, without sample taking, was applied involving Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS), which allowed surface and in-depth elemental analysis of materials including the detection of trace elements. The LIBS results were complemented by using portable X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (p-XRF) and µ-Raman spectroscopy, which offered additional information on elemental and molecular surface composition, respectively, for accurate mineralogical identification. The analysis of the considered objects revealed the presence of a wide variety of both organic and inorganic materials that were used in the manufacturing processes, including red coral, black amber, glass, and iron, among others. This allowed for a comprehensive characterization and provided extensive details about the provenance and relative dating of the objects, information that will be useful in the elaboration of an updated catalog list and new conservation protocols for the archaeological collection of the Teruel Museum.

auditPapers.title: Understanding politicians’ attitudes to reusing built heritage: An experimental and behavioral approach
auditPapers.abstract: • Built heritage is being reused across the globe for a variety of purposes, often involving political decision-makers and policy goals. • Valuation tools are used to inform and rationalize the reuse decisions, but little is known about the actual effects of these tools on political behavior. • This experimental study shows that politicians are not significantly influenced by advice based on academic heritage expert consultation. • Citizen surveys indicating support or opposition have the strongest effect, whereas cost-benefit analysis only matters when the result is negative. • A behavioral and experimental approach is needed to better understand political behavior related to heritage preservation, including decisions to reuse built heritage. Across the globe, built heritage is being reused to serve specific policy goals of politicians. Such goals can include more efficiency, reusing built heritage to generate more income or reduce costs. They can also involve urban revitalization, reusing built heritage as community meeting centers for example. Noteworthy, decisions to reuse are not without controversy and have resulted in strong opposition from citizens and other societal actors. Within a political context, reusing historic buildings often serves different goals, which go beyond reasons of heritage preservation and protection. But which values drive politicians to make the decision to reuse built heritage? Are they influenced by economic, democratic or historical values? To answer this question, this paper engages in a survey experiment with 682 local politicians from Flanders (i.e. the northern, Dutch-speaking part of Belgium). In the experiment, a scenario is described where the local politician’s municipality is considering a potential reusing of a historic event hall as a movie theater (drawing from a real-world example). Different valuation tools are linked to the scenario, which measure economic, democratic or historical values. Specifically, politicians are randomly assigned to one of seven groups: a control group which receives general information about the reuse case, and six treatment groups which receive the same information as the control group but the results of valuation tools are added: a cost-benefit analysis ( economic value ) supports or rejects the decision to reuse, a citizen survey ( democratic value ) supports or rejects the decision to reuse, or a consultation of academic heritage experts ( historical value ) supports or rejects the decision to reuse. Afterwards, all groups are asked to indicate the extent to which they feel the built heritage should be reused. A range of balance, manipulation and attention checks are also included, and the experimental design was pre-registered and ethically approved. Results indicate that democratic values outweigh economic and historical ones, seemingly supporting the important role of citizens’ opinions in driving political behavior, compared to the role of more economic or scientific information. In line with behavioral economics and especially prospect theory, we also find that economic values only matter when they are negative – indicating a potential loss aversion and negativity bias among local politicians. These findings support an experimental and behavioral approach to cultural heritage and demonstrate the added value of survey experiments to elicit values preferences and causal mechanisms related to heritage decision-making by politicians and other stakeholders.

auditPapers.title: Developing a non-invasive approach for prehistoric rock art characterization based on smartphone imaging colorimetry and spectroscopy
auditPapers.abstract: The development of non-invasive archaeometric methods for the in-situ characterization of rock art panels is crucial for the archaeological study and the conservation of these unique remains. This study aims to test a non-invasive analytical approach based on smartphone imaging colorimetry and portable spectrometers for rock art characterization on experimental replicas made on slabs of carbonate rocks by employing iron (III) oxide as pigment and water, milk and marrow as binders. The painted areas and the supports were firstly characterized from the colorimetric point of view using a spectroradiometer and by smartphone imaging colorimetry to assess the potentials of this innovative technique. Furthermore, optical microscopy, and atomic and molecular spectroscopy were employed. A first methodological on-field test of imaging colorimetry was also carried out at the Levantine rock art site of Coco de la Gralla (Mas de Barberans, Spain), where smartphone data were cross-referenced to those from portable X-ray fluorescence. Data suggest that smartphone imaging could be a useful technique for a first colorimetric characterization of rock art, though several factors should be considered in the interpretation of the results, including not only painting materials, but also rock support characteristics and the variability of the conservation within the site. Furthermore, all the techniques revealed their potentials for the chemical and colorimetric characterization of the pictorial layer, while the limitations are caused by instrumental sensitivity, and by the influence of support features.

auditPapers.title: Protecting Soviet Muslims: Muhajir Activism and the Minority Treaties, 1917–1934
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract It is a historiographical convention to view interwar debates over the protection of vulnerable populations through the prism of ‘minority rights’, a regime fashioned by European empires, emerging nation states and the League of Nations. This article challenges that convention by widening the lens to recover actors who, in the 1920s–30s, contested the premises of international protection. Taking the transnational debate over the fate of Soviet Muslims as its principal case study, the article brings together two histories. First, it examines the strategies of Muslim émigrés from the USSR— sometimes in concert with, sometimes against, co-religionists across South Asia and the Middle East —to appropriate, resist and navigate that order in defence of Muslims inside the Soviet state. Second, it foregrounds the Soviet Union’s attempt to re-engineer the post-Versailles minority protection regime by appealing to Muslims under colonial rule. Whether advanced on behalf of ‘minorities’ or ‘majorities’, the language of protection became entangled with claims to sovereignty, the management of religious and social difference, and anti-colonial struggle. More broadly, the article argues that protection— not minority rights alone —offers a sharper and more inclusive framework for understanding the interwar international order and the political-legal templates it bequeathed to the twentieth century.

auditPapers.title: Rumour, Public Opinion and Print in Istanbul, 1780s–1830s
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Drawing on Ottoman official correspondence, an informer’s report, and palace-sponsored tracts and chronicles, this article challenges the widely-held notion that print is inherently linked to diversification, liberalization, and Enlightenment ideals. Against the background of rising tensions between the authorities and the Janissary army, Ottoman officials viewed rumours and political discussions in coffeehouses and other social hubs as threatening to their efforts towards centralization. To counter these perceived dangers, they sought to capture oral communication in written records and invalidate its credibility, relying on written and, later, printed texts. Government-sponsored tracts that targeted the Janissaries linked the supposedly unrestrained tongues of the common people with their unruly imagination, portraying both as antithetical to truth, reason, religion, and order. The Calendar of Events, the government gazette launched in 1831, was the culmination of this process. Rather than marking the emergence of an Ottoman ‘public sphere’, it reflected an effort to subjugate an already-existing realm of popular public opinion.

auditPapers.title: Introduction
auditPapers.abstract: This special issue of The Public Historian endeavors to situate places of burial, cemeteries, graveyards, and massacre sites within themes and methodologies of public history and historic preservation. Cemeteries and graveyards are sites that reflect the way a community memorializes its deceased and, in this sense, how it understands history in a profound and intimate way. There is purpose behind the placement of cemeteries. Many of these burial places were planned, not placed at random. Burial grounds allow for the public to see how families, friends, communities, and countries left a record of and paid their respects to the dead.What are the politics of preserving these sites? How do they change over time and vary over space? What is the role of the public historian in preserving and interpretating these sites? How can a consideration of the involvement of local community members, faith groups, historic societies, and professional caretakers in the creation and maintenance of burial sites help us reimagine community-based commemoration, preservation, and memory in understudied sites and communities? How might transnational comparisons help us understand practice, policy, and local history? What is the role of technology and digital history in documenting and preserving the history and legacy of our departed?The discovery of cemeteries, such as the African Burial Ground in New York City in 1991, has had a profound effect on public historical scholarship.1 The cemetery itself and the artifacts uncovered there have allowed collaboration among scholars in multiple fields such as history, archeology, and anthropology, and gave community members a window to interpret African life in New York City. What are the lessons of life and history that these spaces can offer, not only this example, but other cemeteries as well?2 This special issue considers subjects such as community reclaiming of unmarked graves and massacre sites; the politics of mining company motivations and the significance of land for Indigenous tribes; the response of communities in creating memorials when there are no remains to bury or when the colonial past overshadows the Native American story; and how massacres during wartime might be missed or overlooked by national institutions and their established methods of historic preservation. Research on cemetery sites simply takes a very long time because it requires extensive archival research as well as coordinated efforts between public historians, the local community, and descendants, who often need to be identified and located. These challenges, however, have not dissuaded scholars, nor reduced community interest in the topic.This special issue is intended to begin a conversation about cemeteries, graveyards, and massacre sites and the role of the public historian in researching and documenting those sites. These topics, and the role of cultural tradition in shaping rituals honoring the dead, have received popular attention, including from recent animated Disney films. Through box office hits Moana (2016) and Coco (2017), many people learned about ethnically specific rituals around death and remembrance for the first time. Although at best these films offered an incomplete portrayal of these traditions, the reality was that millions of people received introductory history lessons about the celebration of Dia de los Muertos (in Coco) or observed fictional Pacific Islanders caring for their dying family members and learning about their origins and their voyaging ancestors (Moana). As public historians, we recognize that further explorations on topics that examine everything from celebrations and cemeteries deserve our research attention.Technology has been a boon to cemetery studies by increasing accessibility. Satellite imagery has captured aboveground details of burial areas, and digital sites such as FindAGrave.com allowed community members to photograph pictures of headstones and cemeteries and upload them to the site’s crowd-sourced online archives.3 Having an accessible record online is particularly helpful when researchers are unable to travel to the cemetery themselves. Digitizing documents and images have helped to democratize the archives allowing everyone from family genealogists to the public the ability to access more information about the deceased and their final resting place. The site FindAGrave.com works well where there are known cemeteries with physical grave markers with names. However, not all people had a proper burial, and the archival paper trail may have gone cold or be nonexistent.In cases of limited archival information and a lack of a burial due to violence, war, colonialism, or massacre, the ethics of remembering the dead become complicated. In these cases, people have urged governments to intervene in the repatriation of human remains. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), passed by Congress in 1990, is one important response to concerns by the public and descendants. NAGPRA was designed to address the problem of the many Native American cultural items that were in museums or other institutions, items over which the descendants and tribes associated with them no longer held ownership or control.4 The cultural items included human remains, sacred objects, and funerary items, among other examples of material culture. To close some of the gaps in the law and to address issues specific to California, in 2001, the state legislature of California passed the Cal NAGPRA Act (California Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act) creating more oversight and tackling the issue of human remains of native peoples whose bones were studied by scholars in California’s public universities. As institutions offered public apologies while repatriating the bones of indigenous peoples, the politics of these interactions required knowledge of the oppressive conditions in that historical moment. Despite the federal and state requirements, which have been in place for decades, as of this writing in 2025, some universities have yet to comply fully with the terms of the law.5Memorializing the deceased can be a private activity and simultaneously something to be experienced collectively. On the national level, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, DC, and the 9/11 Memorial and Museum in New York City effectively captured the nation’s emotions and memories of those historic events by allowing the public to mourn the loss of lives through listing names of the individuals on a public memorial. For many, this provided a way for families and the country to heal.6 The elegance of these memorials lies in the simplicity of their design. National cemeteries have identical headstones for military veterans which allow visitors to take in the sweeping imagery of rows and rows of headstones against manicured grass.Often it is the smaller local cemeteries where family and community members are buried, however, that members of the public are most familiar with and connected to. One such local cemetery, the Japanese Cemetery of 1908, a county historic landmark in Ventura County, California (Historic Landmark #18), inspired me to research more about it, ultimately generating greater public support for its preservation.7 The cemetery and its location are well-known by the local community, but few are aware of its historical significance as one of the only known segregated Asian cemeteries in the US.I became interested in cemetery studies because of my training in history and ethnic studies and the intersection of my scholarly interests with the history of the people buried there as well as the community today. For many years, I attended community clean up events and met with community caretakers and some descendants. Through this work it became clear that the cemetery was a significant community space. My research incorporated digital archives as well as oral histories to piece together the cemetery’s history.8 Shreds of archival information and oral histories led to a fuller picture of the nearly 120 Japanese Americans buried in the cemetery. My research on this segregated cemetery centers a diverse community by elevating Asian American public history and historic preservation of an Asian American public space. Recognizing the need to put this research into conversation within public history was the next logical step.The special issue’s cover image comes from Cheryl Jiménez-Frei’s research on los desaparecidos (the disappeared) in Argentina. Jiménez-Frei’s article, “In the Absence of a Grave: Public Memory, Human Rights, and Argentina’s Disappeared,” examines two monuments, the May Pyramid and the Monument to the Victims of State Terror, and analyzes how the public memorialized the people who died from state sponsored violence. During the late 1970s to the early 1980s, the military dictatorship of Argentina murdered and disappeared nearly 30,000 people in what would later be known as Argentina’s Dirty War. Due to the disappearance of the individuals and lack of human remains to bury, most families did not get to participate in the communal practices of closure such as a funeral or burial at the end of their loved one’s life. These commemorative sites were important for the public to memorialize those who were denied justice and to provide a space for victim’s families to remember and mourn them. Jiménez-Frei’s analysis highlights monuments and how the public responded to violence when a traditional cemetery is absent, resulting in activism led by women.Twenty-five miles south of the Oregon-Nevada border in Humboldt County, Nevada, is Thacker Pass. This was the site of the 1865 Thacker Pass Massacre, and today is a contested mining site for lithium, an important component for electric batteries and green energy. Kelsey Hill’s article, “A Mine and a Massacre Site: Historicizing Violence at Thacker Pass/Peehee Mu’huh,” centers the politics of the site of a historic massacre of noncombatants of the Numu people by the Nevada Cavalry. Efforts to shift from fossil fuels to clean energy make lithium mining economically important locally and nationally. Native American groups of Numu, Newe, and Bannock descent and their allies, however, have protested the mine, contending that the Bureau of Land Management neither accurately evaluated the site according to the National Historic Preservation Act nor did they consult tribal nations meaningfully. The context of Thacker Pass provides insights for public historians at the crossroads of contested lands, Native communities, and the federal government.Kelsey Moore’s article, “Grave Matter(s): The Politics of Submersion in the Santee-Cooper Basin,” examines submerged Black cemeteries and “soiled archives” in a development in South Carolina. In 1934, as part of a New Deal era project to produce greater hydroelectric power and sites of leisure for recreation and tourism, the South Carolina Public Authority engineered two reservoirs. The decision to build a dam and divert the rivers flooded the basin where numerous known cemeteries and approximately eight thousand Black graves had been buried in the centuries prior. Some graves were exhumed and relocated; some were left behind and are still covered by water. Moore’s research juxtaposes the site ninety years later as a space of white leisure at the expense of Black memorials. Using a host of archives, reexamining the early surveyors’ methodology, and creating ArcGIS StoryMaps, the article addresses the erasure of Black graves and digital public history.Santa Clara University in California is the focus of Lee Panich, Amy Lueck, Lauren Baines and Isabella ‘Amne Gomez’s article, “We Are Here Because of Them: Co-Creating a Native Memorial at Mission Santa Clara,” which analyzes how to present Native American cemeteries within the history of the California missions. The university’s campus was built on the legacy of colonialism and enslavement of Native peoples in California. The authors presented the details of designing the interactive digital memorial exhibition which was co-created by the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe, Santa Clara University, and its students. The cemetery memorial allows visitors to learn about historic themes including labor, Native leaders, mission connections, resistance, and enslavement to contextualize the reality of colonial mission history that traditionally centers the Native Californios. Rather than focus on the university and the mission’s colonial past, with guidance from the Ohlone community, the process of co-creating the memorial reckoned with the over 7500 Native individuals whose burials were recorded in Mission Santa Clara from 1777 into the 1840s. This public facing educational memorial gave students the opportunity to engage directly with the community by incorporating rigorous research and digital methods to shape the memorial with respect and intentionality.Johnathan Thayer and Lori Wallach present the details of their research on the cemetery in Old Flushing, Queens, New York City, showcasing how cemetery research can be incorporated into classroom pedagogy and service-learning for public history students. The article, “Reclaiming the Olde Towne of Flushing Burial Ground Through Intergenerational Public History,” used the methodology of service learning to preserve community memory of a segregated and abandoned cemetery made up of primarily Black, Native American, and impoverished people from the 1840s to the early twentieth century. During the 1930s, the cemetery was eradicated to make a park for the growing city. While collaborating with community stakeholders and activists, the students used archival materials such as municipal death records to reclaim the burial ground and honor the deceased with a memorial wall imprinted with their names.In Elizabeth Clappin’s article, “Used to Good Advantage: The Challenges of Unearthing Atlanta’s History of Convict Leasing at the Chattahoochee Brick Company Site,” she examined the politics of the Chattahoochee Brick Company site today. Since the 1870s, Chattahoochee Brick company was one of the largest and still intact sites of leased convict labor. At its height, the brick company relied upon hundreds of mostly African American men to work in conditions nearly identical to antebellum slavery. Many were beaten, literally worked to death, and buried in unmarked graves on site.9 The article puts into conversation redevelopment and city politics, historic preservation, and environmental justice in the city of Atlanta.Desun Oka’s article, “The Mili Atoll Uprising and Massacre of March 1945: US Public History in the Marshall Islands and the Former Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands,” looks at the politics of historic preservation within Mili Atoll in the Marshall Islands. The article centers on the site of a World War II massacre of Korean conscripted laborers and Marshall Islanders by imperial Japanese forces. Due to the remote location of the atoll in the Pacific and the fact that it had changed hands from Japanese control during World War II to becoming part of the Trust Territories of the Pacific Islands in the postwar period, preservation of the site was complicated. Simply getting there from the mainland US to conduct research is difficult and costly. The Pacific is an underrepresented area in public history as evidenced by the National Park Service’s Asian American and Pacific Islander theme study.10 Noting that there are so few listed NRHP historic sites in the Pacific, Oka argues that the problems confounding historic preservation there are not just the distance from the US mainland, but also requirements that in order to overcome would necessitate examining public history guidelines and institutions and preservation law.Our final piece, Lynn Rainville’s “A National African American Cemetery Database Starts in Your Community,” advocates for a national database for African American cemeteries similar to the databases in place for Native American cemetery sites. Not surprisingly, Black cemeteries in the US have not received equal treatment to white cemeteries, particularly in places such as Virginia where Rainville’s research is based. It is clear that community advocacy is necessary in preserving and protecting these cemeteries, but infrastructure to support those community efforts is key. Preservation requires partnership. Based on her experience working with community organizations, Rainville argues for the importance of an online database to centralize information. This is multidisciplinary work that requires the collaboration of many people and entities including public historians, archaeologists, government, technology, local communities, and national organizations.With this special issue, we hope that the articles generate interest for public historians to consider the topic of cemeteries, graveyards, and massacre sites. This subject lends itself to incorporate methods to expand knowledge, collaborate with community stakeholders, and bring high impact teaching practices into the classroom to engage students. Further research on topics such as cultural commemorations such as All Saints Day and obon; the practice of picnics at cemeteries; the complex and ethnically necessary process of repatriating the bones of Indigenous peoples; and the tragic unearthing of graveyards of children in boarding schools, among others, still warrant our attention. Several authors in this special issue encourage readers by offering recommendations and a call to action.At each memorial site, specific details may have been lost, but historic memory, archives, and descendants fill the gaps. Historic cemeteries of formerly enslaved African Americans, colonial mission graveyards, and wartime massacre sites in the Pacific include both marked and unmarked graves. In some cases, during their lifetimes, the people in the burial grounds were brutalized, assumed to be disposable laborers, while those who were disappeared did not even receive a proper burial. The reasons for not marking a grave may be attributed to the lack of funding or duress, whether in wartime or peacetime. Each of the articles here reflects on the lives of the people and allows readers a window to view our common humanity. After reading this special issue, my hope is that you will come to the conclusion that cemeteries and burial grounds are not only about the people interred there, but also, like the rituals following someone’s death, they were just as much for the living as for the deceased.Thank you to Sarah Case, the editorial board of The Public Historian, and the reviewers who provided their input in improving the articles for this special issue. My gratitude goes to the authors of this special issue for your expertise and for your passion for this topic.

auditPapers.title: Editor’s Corner
auditPapers.abstract: Our special issue, “Cemeteries, Graveyards, and Massacre Sites,” guest edited by Lily Anne Welty Tamai, considers burial grounds and sites of mass violence as significant evidence for public historical research. The wide-ranging issue considers sites that have been ignored and repurposed for development or recreation, and as well as sites that have been claimed by survivors “in the absence of a grave,” in the words of our cover article. Articles in the issue range from the Marshall Islands, to Argentina, the US West and South, and the urban Northeast. They consider how communities, sometimes working with organizations, governments, or universities, might reclaim these sites and make new kinds of memorials and meanings from them. Many document success in this kind of collaborative public history work; others are calls to action. As our guest editor emphasize in her introduction, these articles represent just the beginning of possibilities for work in this subject area. We look forward to continuing conversation in this field.

auditPapers.title: Alexandra Kaloyanides. Baptizing Burma: Religious Change in the Last Buddhist Kingdom
auditPapers.abstract: Alexandra Kaloyanides’s book Baptizing Burma: Religious Change in the Last Buddhist Kingdom is a fascinating study of the Baptist Christian community in colonial Burma. Weaving together histories of art, religion, colonialism, and American missionary traditions, Kaloyanides provides a refreshing investigation of the little-known story of Christianity among Burma’s Indigenous minorities, such as the Karen, Kachin, and Chin, who became Christians in large numbers in contrast to the majority Buddhist Bamar (or Burman) population. This book is an intriguing and vivid history of religious material culture and how objects have shaped Burmese, American, and Baptist communities. Through examining the role of four primary objects—the sacred book, the school, the pagoda, and the portrait—Kaloyanides highlights transcultural, transnational, and interreligious histories. As she notes, most studies of Burmese religious history have focused primarily on Buddhism and the Bamar majority, while American religious histories rarely address missionaries in Asia that are not centered on forms of western imperial domination or American cosmopolitanism. In contrast, Baptizing Burma uses the study of religious material culture to move beyond elite monastic or royal scriptures to examine the lives of ethnic and religious minority groups through objects at a time when Buddhism and Christianity comingled in nineteenth-century Burma.

auditPapers.title: Evan P. Sullivan. Constructing Disability after the Great War: Blind Veterans in the Progressive Era
auditPapers.abstract: The past quarter century has witnessed an outpouring of interest in the welfare of disabled military veterans. In the United States, this concern can be chalked up to the nation’s latest wars in the Middle East, conflicts that resulted in more than 1.8 million disabled American veterans. To this day, organized veterans’ groups continue to raise alarms about the threats facing the latest generation of war-wounded troops. At the same time, American culture is awash in a kind of performative patriotism that prioritizes public ritual (such as “thanking” veterans for their service) over substantive action on vets’ behalf. None of this is new. Building upon David A. Gerber’s pathbreaking edited volume Disabled Veterans in History (2012), books like Beth Linker’s War’s Waste: Rehabilitation in World War I (2011), John M. Kinder’s Paying With Their Bodies: American War and the Problem of the Disabled Veteran (2015), and Sarah Handley-Cousins’s Bodies in Blue: Disability in the Civil War North (2019) reveal how Americans have always displayed complex attitudes toward disabled veterans, hailing them as icons of patriotic masculinity one minute, demonizing them as threats to national health the next. Often missing in this work, however, is a sense of how experiences of disability, stigma, and homecoming played out differently among various groups of disabled vets.

auditPapers.title: Expertise vs. statistics. A qualitative evaluation of three keyness measures (logarithmic Zeta, Welch’s t-test, and Log-likelihood ratio test) applied to subgenres of the French novel
auditPapers.abstract: This paper continues an ongoing investigation of measures of distinctiveness (also known as keyness measures), this time employing a qualitative, comparative evaluation of three different measures: logarithmic Zeta, Welch’s t-test, and Log-likelihood ratio test. Our domain of application is the contemporary French novel, more specifically four types of French novels from the period 1970-1999, namely: sentimental novel, crime novel, science fiction, and littérature blanche (literary fiction). Our evaluation proceeds in the following steps: First, we establish important abstract characteristics of specific literary subgenres based on a synthesis of close readings of scholarly literature on these subgenres, resulting in qualitative, expert-based subgenre profiles. Second, we use a purely statistical approach, namely three different measures of distinctiveness, to identify words that are expected to be statistically typical or characteristic of groups of texts such as subgenres, when compared to other texts. Finally, we compare expertise and statistics, that is, attempt to establish, for each of the four subgenres, a mapping between individual words found to be statistically distinctive of this subgenre and specific aspects contained in the relevant subgenre profile and count the matches. It turns out that each measure yields a different list of most distinctive words that therefore, relates differently to the subgenre profiles. The analysis of these varying degrees of overlap contributes to a better understanding of the characteristics of and differences between the three measures, while also serving as an example of a qualitative evaluation of a statistical measure.

auditPapers.title: Distinguishing pristine and conserved sediments in heritage sites: The Hathor temple at Timna Valley as a case study
auditPapers.abstract: • Microarchaeology distinguishes conserved backfill from pristine sediments. • Replicable approach for heritage sites with undocumented restorations. • Short-lived 14C from pristine Stratum IV context: 1496–1304 BCE. • Egyptian activity at Timna began in the 18D, not 19D; possibly Hatshepsut. Copper production in the Arabah Valley intensified during the Late Bronze and Iron Ages, particularly at Timna and Faynan. The Hathor Temple at Timna is especially significant for its Egyptian artifacts, including cartouches of Pharaohs from Seti I to Ramesses V (∼1300–1140 BCE), which provide key chronological markers. However, the site's complex stratigraphy—along with undocumented conservation work in the 1980s—complicates efforts to establish a clear occupational sequence for the site. To address this, we developed a method to distinguish between pristine archaeological contexts and contexts that underwent conservation using sediment morphology and mineralogy. Our analysis shows that restoration introduced carbonate-rich sand, differing from local geology, with iron oxide coatings and carbonate content serving as reliable indicators of modern disturbance. This approach enabled the secure identification of undisturbed contexts, including one that yielded a charcoal sample of the short-lived shrub Salsola baryosma , radiocarbon dated to ∼1500–1300 BCE (2σ). This new date suggests that Egyptian copper exploitation in Timna started already during the days of the 18th Dynasty.

auditPapers.title: Ageing-induced changes in varnish-coated oil paints: Surface and subsurface multi-technical analysis
auditPapers.abstract: Preventing varnish degradation is a major challenge in painting conservation. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms behind varnish alteration are not yet fully understood due to the complexity of the concurrent processes involved. Moreover, the extent to which organic and inorganic pigments, dispersed in various binding media within the paint substrate, influence this process remains unclear. Due to this complexity, detecting early signs of varnish degradation is a crucial step in protecting the underlying painting from irreversible damage. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of thermo-hygrometric and photochemical ageing at both surface and subsurface levels on natural (dammar resin) and synthetic (acrylic resin) coatings. These were analysed both as standalone layers and in combination with oil paint materials containing two common inorganic pigments: titanium dioxide and yellow ochre. A comprehensive suite of complementary, non-invasive techniques, spanning nano- to macroscale resolution, was employed. This optimized monitoring protocol, with potential in situ applicability, enabled high-resolution mapping of varnish degradation patterns, elucidating the complex interplay between compositional factors, environmental ageing conditions, and substrate-paint interactions. This study establishes a robust framework for evaluating material stability through the identification of early degradation markers, which can directly inform conservation strategies for painted artworks. Furthermore, it provides scientific support for varnish selection criteria, condition assessment protocols, and predictive conservation models.

auditPapers.title: The Oddy test applied to the study of fused deposition modelling additive manufacturing materials
auditPapers.abstract: In the recent years, Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies ―popularly known as 3D printing― have been introduced in different areas of daily life and nowadays a wide variety of polymeric printing materials are available. The term AM comprises a huge range of fabrication processes mainly characterized by the method employed during the transformation of the raw materials. Amongst them, Extrusion-based technologies, and specifically Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) have become very popular, affordable and widespread for many applications. Three-dimensional printing has demonstrated a relevant potential to contribute to the conservation and restoration of cultural heritage, as well as to artistic production. Some applications of AM in the conservation landscape are the design of display systems, the creation of storage structures and the reconstruction of missing parts. Thus, the interaction of new AM materials introduced in the proximity of cultural assets in a closed space could represent a risk of damage when gaseous pollutants are emitted from the printing material. In this context, a literature review was conducted, and the Oddy test was performed to assess a selection of 9 FDM PLA materials, evaluating their long-term behaviour in terms of Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) emissions and their suitability for use in heritage conservation and artistic production. Polylactic acid (PLA) is a widespread polymer used for FDM due to its cost and the rise of the social awareness concerning the relevance of using waste-recycling and biodegradable materials. This assay was performed both before and after subjecting the 3D printed samples to accelerated ageing in a Xenon-Arc chamber during 1080 h of exposure with 60 W/m 2 irradiance through a window glass filter, temperature of 60 °C and 10 % relative humidity. After the Oddy test, the FDM materials were evaluated, and their recommendation of use was classified based on the corrosion observed on the metallic coupons. Simultaneously, crystalline efflorescences emerged from the 3D printed samples exposed to the Oddy Test, motivating their observation through optical microscopy. Additionally, for the chemical characterization, inorganic fillers of the PLA filaments were analysed with Energy Dispersive X-ray spectroscope attached to a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM-EDX). The results allowed the classification of PLA filaments for their permanent or temporary use in an environment with cultural assets and reject those that released harmful pollutants. It is remarkable the effect of the additives and fillers when comparing the results in terms of corrosive VOC emissions of different composite PLA materials. The lower corrosion of the metals was promoted by PLA containing CaCO 3 fillers, while other PLA combinations were completely discarded. Nonetheless, crystalline efflorescences emerged from 3D printed samples containing mineral fillers. It is suggested that the combination of continuous high temperature and saturated relative humidity is a probable cause of these transformations. Thus, the potential for these minerals to grow at ambient conditions over an extended period and migrate to a cultural asset that is in direct contact with the 3D printed material should be also considered for their recommendation or rejection.

auditPapers.title: Joshua Nygren. The State of Conservation: Rural America and the Conservation-Industrial Complex since 1920 .
auditPapers.abstract: The steady exodus of farmers from rural America and the consolidation of their lands into fewer hands represent core transformations during the twentieth century. In The State of Conservation, Joshua Nygren explains those changes by analyzing a loose and decentralized coalition of well-positioned farmers, state actors, and industrial players that he calls the “conservation-industrial complex.” In a thoroughly researched and tightly argued narrative, Nygren shows how these public-private partnerships formed around soil and water conservation during the 1930s, became powerful social and economic forces after World War II, and persisted in the face of critiques from the 1960s through the end of the twentieth century. Nygren argues that the capital-intensive notions of conservation held by industry and wealthy farmers were tools of “social oppression and land confiscation” (7). As Nygren explains, the conservation-industrial complex formed in the wake of the 1927 Mississippi Flood and the Dust Bowl, when agricultural leaders such as Hugh Hammond Bennett argued that soil loss from erosion represented the single greatest threat to rural America. During the 1930s, agricultural leaders promoted cultivation strategies such as terracing and contour-strip cropping, embedding state-sponsored technical expertise into local soil conservation districts. While well-to-do farmers exercised a disproportionate share of control in these districts, Nygren argues that, prior to World War II, the social justice aims of New Deal thinkers such as Rex Tugwell held sway over purely developmentalist goals. Though Nygren’s argument is convincing, industry voices are absent in the first chapter.

auditPapers.title: Jason L. Newton. Cutover Capitalism: The Industrialization of the Northern Forest
auditPapers.abstract: As has happened to many of us, the book that Jason L. Newton originally planned to write is not the one he ended up writing. Newton originally turned to the history of timber workers in the Northern Forest—the forests stretching from upstate New York, through northern Vermont and New Hampshire, and up through Maine—hoping to tell a story about labor radicalism. He had good reason to expect there’d be a good history to tell. Radical unions, like the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), famously attracted thousands of members in the timber industries of the upper Midwest and Pacific Northwest, and Newton assumed, as just about any labor historian likely would, that those same radicals garnered a dedicated following in the woods of the northern Atlantic states. But rather than find stories of radical worker uprisings, Newton found almost no evidence of union activity at all. The IWW largely passed the Northern Forest over, and attempts to unionize the region’s loggers in the later twentieth century fizzled out just as soon as they started. Accordingly, Newton’s focus shifted, and his project became about trying to understand why labor radicalism was, more or less, nonexistent in the northern woods. While the labor sympathizers among us might mourn the lack of a sustained union presence in the Northern Forest, historians will be grateful that Newton did not find what he was originally looking for. That’s because, in trying to understand the dearth of union activity, Newton has written an innovative history of labor, environment, and capitalism that offers new ways of conceptualizing the relationship between work and nature that many historians—not just those who study the North American timber industry—will want to pay attention to.

auditPapers.title: Contemporary Parliamentary History and Petitioners in the Long Parliament, c. 1640–1642
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Studies of petitioning activity in the early years of the Long Parliament (1640–2) have often focused on the large-scale petitions which engaged with issues of high politics and religion in the charged atmosphere prior to the outbreak of Civil War. However, many subjects were drawn to petition the Commons and the Lords for relief in much more particular economic disputes. Utilizing overlooked manuscript petitions in the parliamentary archives and papers of the MP Bulstrode Whitelocke, this article re-examines petitioning activity between 1640 and 1642. It finds that, despite the absence of parliament during the Personal Rule, subjects eagerly embraced the calling of a new parliament, their perceptions of it shaped by its contemporary history. As MPs and peers increasingly utilized and preserved records, petitioners too evoked and confronted the parliamentary past. While some like the Merchant Adventurers’ Company glossed its presentation tactically, others including London-based glassmakers and merchants were driven by ideological beliefs in the historic role of parliament as a protector against arbitrary fiscal policies. This article contributes to post-revisionism by showing that subjects viewed parliament not as an event, but as an institution, fostering connections between past and present sessions as they petitioned for redress.

auditPapers.title: The Language of confiance and the French cahiers de doléances of 1789
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In the context of increasing historiographical attention to the emotional content of French revolutionary politics, the essentially unprecedented nationwide consultation that produced the cahiers de doléances of 1789, now available as a searchable digitised corpus, offers a route into exploring the hopes, fears, and concerns of thousands of French people who participated directly in the cahiers ’ composition. Mapping their uses of the concept of ‘trust’, and its manifold implications, offers new evidence on the nature and contours of the political relationships they believed they inhabited, and on the extent to which they were enacting agency over the prospect of change. It also provides material to contemplate the implications of the highly centralized, top-down reform processes actually initiated from the summer of 1789 onwards, and the violent complexity of their reception.

auditPapers.title: Furiose Interazioni Project
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: This article research introduces Furiose Interazioni project developed by the National Technological Cluster for Cultural Heritage (TICHE). The project’s main goal is to create a digital atelier centered around Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso and its imaginative world, particularly designed for school and preschool children. It emphasizes an interdisciplinary approach involving experts in Italian studies, literature, pedagogy, interface design, and technology. Each technological workstation in the project is analyzed in detail to ensure a satisfying user experience. Overall, Furiose Interazioni seeks to provide an immersive literary experience while preserving the essence of the original artistic work. Moreover, thanks to the integrated combination of this project and the restoration of the ancient Muriziano villa, new meanings of the iconographies of the frescoes are made possible, creating a further path of discovery (Stanze dell’Ariosto) through technology, for both adults and children.

auditPapers.title: Seasonality and the Practices of Illegal Trade in the Faroe Islands and the Northern and Western Isles, 1775–1785
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract By investigating 321 smuggling vessels that travelled between the Faroe Isles and the British Isles between 1775 and 1785, this article explores the regionality and seasonality of illegal trade in the north Atlantic. The article centres on a neglected oceanic region, thereby inverting historical geographies, shifting the focus from port centres like London and Copenhagen to the Scottish Northern and Western Isles, as well as the Faroe Islands. Epitomizing the ‘dichotomy of insularity’, in the eighteenth century these areas were located along maritime highways of global trade, and illegal trade flourished there, despite their challenging location. The article demonstrates that this illegal trade had different seasonal cycles from those of legal trade. While legal trade halted in the winter season, illegal trade continued throughout. Linking illegal maritime activities to more lawful ones, like fishing, the article suggests that the recurring nature of the contraband trade ought to be understood in relation to the broader coastal culture, in which maritime knowledge was circulated and the local relationship to the sea defined. The study suggests that illegal trade should be viewed not merely as an extension of globalization but as a rooted phenomenon, which developed in unison with the local environment.

auditPapers.title: THE WIND THAT MELTS THE ICE: REFLECTIONS ON THE SCALE OF PHILOLOGY
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT The global history of philology, like that of writing systems and other technologies, is characterized by diffusion and adaptation. These processes are made more difficult to grasp if we maintain a presentist focus on the Western philological tradition and its deeply Eurocentric legacy. Arguing against those who wish to resolve the problem by abandoning the term “philology” as irredeemably tainted, I propose that we introduce the notion of scale. Heuristically, it is helpful to think in terms of “small‐p” philology, the low‐level quotidian strategies and tools used by students and scholars to solve problems of textual interpretation, and “big‐P” Philology, a larger ideological edifice linked to metahistorical and transhistorical narratives about abstract concepts such as civilization, race, and religious truth. As a first step toward illuminating this issue of scale, this article excavates a highly specific moment of philological scholarship in twelfth‐century Japan and shows how a difficult word from a classical waka poem is explicated through the extension of an existing Chinese exegetical system. The example is taken from the Ōgishō , a pioneering treatise by the Heian period scholar Fujiwara no Kiyosuke (1104–1177).

auditPapers.title: Slavery and Capitalism: A New Marxist History. By David McNally
auditPapers.abstract: Slavery and Capitalism, by the political scientist David McNally, is not precisely a work of history. Rather, it is a revision to Marxist theory and its applicability to the study of enslaved labor in the Americas. McNally argues that transatlantic slavery played a pivotal role in the rise of capitalism, and that British and American plantations were capitalistic from their inception. His theoretical argument is that only Marxist analysis can provide the “concepts necessary to comprehensively theorizing [sic] capitalism and Atlantic slavery” (6). And yet, though history and theory cross-pollinate, historians and theorists ultimately have different scholarly projects, and different methodologies. Few historians commit to comprehensive theorising, at least to the watertightness on which McNally insists. The book is divided into two parts. In the first part, McNally analyses the careers of Richard Ligon, George Washington, and Edward Gibbon Wakefield. All three are well-known figures. Washington is universally familiar, and Ligon (a seventeenth-century colonist in Barbados, and the author of a history of English colonisation in the Caribbean), and Wakefield (a key figure in the British colonisation of South Australia) will be very familiar to specialists. The second part refutes claims about the place of enslaved labor and enslaved laborers in the history of capitalism that McNally considers evasions of, or challenges to, the applicability of Marx’s critique of political economy. For example, in one chapter, McNally argues that enslaved laborers, forced to work according to the industrial rhythms of clock-time, brutally and violented exploited, and wholly alienated from the products of their labor, ought to be considered "proletarians" despite not being wage-laborers. In another, McNally draws on histories of racial capitalism to insist that “racialization must be understood as, among other things, a modality of capitalist discipline” (83). These chapters are brisk and passionately argued, and McNally’s knowledge of Marx’s published work and correspondence is encyclopedic and impressive. Ironically, McNally often praises Marx’s own theoretical flexibility, quoting Engels, who wrote of Marx’s work, “It should go without saying that where things and their mutual relations are conceived not as fixed, but rather as changing … they are not to be encapsulated in rigid definitions, but rather to be developed in their process of historical or logical formation” (110).

auditPapers.title: TC-YOLO: An Improved Tai Chi Movement Pose Estimation Algorithm Based on YOLOv8
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: At present, the dissemination of Tai Chi is predominantly facilitated through offline instructional methods combined with video practice, lacking effective feedback on movement poses and exhibiting relatively low efficiency. This article proposes a novel algorithm named TC-YOLO for pose estimation based on YOLOv8. TC-YOLO enhances the efficiency through utilizing real-time detection of key points in Tai Chi practitioners’ movements to provide more accurate and intuitive feedback for instructional evaluation and pose correction. Focusing on the demonstration of the Essential Eighteen Movements of Chen-style Tai Chi as the research subject, Tai Chi movement dataset comprising 3,688 images is constructed. To enhance model efficiency, the backbone network is reparameterized through the Reparametrized C2f (RC2f) module, which optimizes feature extraction process by allowing more effective information flow and reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, a simplified neck network structure is designed to provide effective information transmission and multiscale feature fusion, thereby enhancing detection accuracy. Experimental results show that the TC-YOLO algorithm achieves a mAP of 97.2% and a recognition speed of 146.1 FPS with lower parameters and computational cost on the self-built dataset, which is better than YOLO-Pose and other models. TC-YOLO could make an instructive contribution to the field of sports science through the analysis of Tai Chi movement poses, promoting the inheritance and global dissemination of Tai Chi.

auditPapers.title: Curating New York’s “Raw Material”
auditPapers.abstract: In 1997, the literary critic Hans Ulrich Gumbrecht mused, “The real question behind the question of what to do with our knowledge about the past is not only the—more or less technical—question of how to write or represent history. It is above all the question of what we imagine the past ‘to be’ (the question about the past as ‘raw material’), before we even begin to think about possible forms of representation.”1 Gumbrecht aimed to chart the quotidian totality of a single year, 1926, jumping between topics as disparate as airplanes and murder. His book In 1926: Living at the Edge of Time invites readers to consider the “raw material” of history to make the historical environment of that year immediate for them—to make them feel as if they are “in 1926.” Gumbrecht’s aim of immersing readers in the materiality of the past is shared by public historians and museum curators, who often employ a range of sensory experiences—visual, textural, sonic—to stimulate different planes of historical thinking and rouse in audiences a sense of curiosity. At the same time, public history, like In 1926, provokes us to think about how “we” imagine the past, in effect making audiences co-producers of historical knowledge. Put another way, a historical museum exhibition usually emphasizes “showing” over “telling,” encouraging visitors to interpret historical change for themselves and, in the process, provoking emotional responses. Yet this approach also exists in tension with the craft of curation itself, which requires making narrative choices to create a cohesive exhibition.

auditPapers.title: Dig Where You Stand and International History from Below Movements
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article introduces the Swedish ‘Dig Where You Stand’ movement of the 1970s and 1980s as an workers’ and community history movement, and then explores Sven Lindqvist’s 1978 book Gräv där du står: Hur man utforskar ett job (recently translated for the first time in English as Dig Where You Stand: How to Research a Job) which acted as a handbook for historical research for the movement. The article then establishes how Lindqvist and the Dig movement were connected to and influenced similar movements in the UK and internationally such as History Workshop and the oral history movement, and how the ethos of ‘Dig Where You Stand’ remains an inspiration to this day.

auditPapers.title: Working-Class History in a Populist Age
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article considers the politics and possibilities of writing labour history in a context where ‘the working class’ has been so effectively co-opted and interpellated by the populist right. What might working-class and labour history tell us about the uses of class in the twenty-first century? How might we think anew about that historiographical tradition in light of right-wing mobilizations of ‘the working class’? What sort of working class history might we want to create in and for a populist age?
