auditPapers.title: Locating Geological Agency in a ‘Small’ Early Modern Anthropocene
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract What can anthropogenic interventions – set in a wetland backwater of England, long before the industrial era – tell us about the Anthropocene? How might contested interactions with earth, sediment, and water four hundred years ago lead us to reconsider not only when the Anthropocene began, but why and how humans have exerted geological agency in the past? In this article I shift the scale, location, and action of the story to examine a ‘small’ Anthropocene in early modern England, bringing into focus the human interests and values that gave rise to contested environmental politics and produced geophysical environments in wetlands past.

auditPapers.title: Predicting the Past
auditPapers.abstract: Absences pervade the historical record. The loss or destruction of material, redaction of documents, silence of participants, data embargoes, and poor record keeping present inherent difficulties to any understanding of the past. Gaps in the historical record pose significant challenges but they can also provide valuable opportunities. Instead of avoiding all gaps, historians can test the accuracy of some inferences about the past by carefully outlining their assumptions and explicitly predicting what they believe to have occurred in the absence of evidence. Subsequent discoveries or declassifications can then be used to assess the accuracy of these hypothesized explanations and, in turn, help us to evaluate the quality of historians’ thinking about the unknown past. Given enough examples, we can begin to learn more about how to make better predictions about the past or what we term “retrodictions.”1 The importance of prediction has been well documented across the social sciences for decades.2 Economists, political scientists, and psychologists regularly extol the virtues of making testable predictions for good scholarly practice and improved judgement. Although historians and historically minded scholars in the social sciences routinely rely on their own expert judgement when studying the past, few have considered making and testing explicit predictions when conducting historical research. Even fewer have considered the methodological demands and theoretical implications of retrodiction.3 This article considers why historians and social scientists should attempt to predict the past and explains how they can make and test retrodictions in a more rigorous manner. These conceptual and methodological insights are of considerable significance. Retrodiction is not an abstract or hypothetical subject. While some scholars may argue that accurate prediction of the past is irrelevant or impossible, many historians and social scientists regularly make inferences about undocumented history. Educated guesses occur across the discipline and beyond. There is nevertheless a tension between the widespread but often implicit employment of retrodiction, and the rarity with which it is deliberately considered and applied. Thinking more explicitly about retrodiction offers the chance to assess and refine historical interpretation. By understanding why some predictions about the past prove more or less accurate than others, we can think more clearly about how to manage empirical gaps, better adjudicate between competing interpretations, and gain greater confidence in our own retrodictions. This article proceeds in three parts before concluding. First, we introduce the concept of retrodiction and then reflect on the rewards and risks involved in making predictions about the past. Second, we consider different ways of making and testing predictions about the past, giving special attention to the important role of retrodiction tournaments. Third, we draw on key insights from research in the social sciences to inform the practice of retrodiction and highlight future avenues of research. Historical claims are built on evidence. From archival research and oral histories to archaeological investigations and satellite imaging, we have assembled much of our knowledge about the past from available data. Yet there are many gaps in the historical record and the pool of data available to experts is often very shallow. Experts who study the past rely on imperfect or incomplete information. In developing a broader interpretation of history, they may therefore need to speculate or “predict” the sort of picture that would emerge if or when more evidence ever became available. This attempt to predict the past—to engage in retrodiction—is thus one of the basic techniques that historians and social scientists use when they construct an interpretation of the past. Efforts to predict the past are commonplace. Scholars often make assumptions or reach conclusions about the past in the absence of direct evidence. Many historians and social scientists therefore already make retrodictions, albeit sometimes unknowingly or implicitly.4 For example, scholars have debated the status of the United Kingdom’s considerable war debts to the United States government following World War I. At least one historian has concluded that the war debt issue was effectively laid to rest in 1940 as a new and highly personal relationship emerged between Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt.5 In the absence of direct evidence, however, this conclusion represents an implicit prediction about what occurred in the past. Recent archival discoveries drawing on data from both sides of the Atlantic challenge this claim by showing that the United Kingdom’s war debts to the United States persisted as a source of diplomatic tension in the decades that followed and remain unpaid and outstanding.6 Some historians and social scientists advancing arguments about the past may seek to avoid making any explicit claims about gaps in the historical record and limit themselves to presenting the evidence they have found. Yet those scholars may have missed a valuable opportunity to test their historical judgement. Historians and historically minded scholars in the social sciences should instead accept that their interpretations of the past are often based on incomplete data and speculate about the sort of picture that would emerge if more evidence became available. They could then test their understanding of events by providing specific details about what we would expect to see if that missing evidence ever became public. Retrodiction does not alter the underlying logic of an historical argument but instead seeks only to make it clearer and more testable. Thinking more explicitly about retrodiction can therefore improve historical practice and our knowledge of the past. If historians and social scientists explain how they reach their conclusions, they and other scholars can better assess the quality of those arguments if new and important evidence ever comes to light. By making and testing enough examples, we may be able to determine how far the lessons of retrodiction can be generalized to other periods or fields of study. We accept that many scholars prefer to focus their attention on explanation rather than retrodiction. Analyzing what the available evidence says is a more familiar practice than speculating explicitly about what presently unavailable evidence might show.7 Yet explanation and retrodiction are cognate concepts.8 As an interpretation is developed—and historians and social scientists develop an interpretation by drawing on theories about how the world works—predictions are generated as a matter of course. “At any given point in an historical argument,” one of the authors of this article has previously explained, “the historian can ask, given what was said up to that point, whether it would be possible to predict how things would develop. This provides a useful test of the power of the argument: a strong interpretation should have a certain predictive force.”9 Retrodiction also provides the historian with a way to assess the validity of the interpretation taking shape in their mind. As historians or social scientists proceed with a project, they could ask themselves what might turn up when they read new material—whether material that has already been released, but which they have not seen yet, or material that is released later—if that tentative interpretation is correct. Those retrodictions about what new sources would show might be borne out, in which case the historian would have more confidence in the validity of that interpretation. Alternatively, the new sources might not be in line with what had been expected, in which case the historian might have to rethink their emerging interpretation, and maybe even question the assumptions or arguments on which it was based. We argue that it is important for scholars to consider and apply retrodiction consciously and thoughtfully, by explicitly stating what they would expect to see in as-yet-unexamined or unavailable sources. Historians and social scientists have advanced broader interpretations about what drove the collapse of the Soviet Union, for example, with a small number of scholars making educated guesses about the unknown past and what they would expect the archives to eventually reveal.10 The absence of evidence therefore serves as a way in which to test and potentially bolster a specific historical interpretation. Transforming explanations of past events into explicit, testable predictions enables historians and social scientists to shift from rationalizing events after they have occurred to formulating hypotheses in advance. Emphasizing a priori theorizing over post-hoc analysis can potentially lead to sharper, more robust historical narratives and help to strengthen the inferential power of interpretations or theories regarding causes of past events and historical trends.11 Retrodiction can also help scholars avoid hindsight bias—namely, the common tendency to incorrectly believe in retrospect that one correctly guessed how events would unfold.12 By making falsifiable claims, before new historical data comes to light, historians and social scientists can combat this tendency and increase accountability, thereby fostering scholarly rigor.13 Attempts to predict the past, however, do carry some risks. Retrodiction requires a degree of uncertainty about what has happened in the past. If we make educated guesses when the required evidence is unavailable to us, there is always the possibility that the missing data will never come to light. Assessments of historical judgement require the discovery of new, relevant evidence after a retrodiction has been made. Some predictions about the past, no matter how specific or well formulated, may be unverifiable. Crucial archival records have been destroyed in wars, for example, just as some individuals or organizations may have never written much down. Historians and social scientists should therefore try to focus their attention on areas where there is a reasonable possibility of testing their retrodictions. New data about the past can be anticipated in some cases. Some archives use “timed releases,” such as the National Archives in the United Kingdom, which embargoes many government documents for twenty years before releasing them to the public. We tend to know which government documents have been embargoed even if we do not know what they say. Not all government documents are released within twenty years, to be sure, but even in sensitive cases a release date is often agreed. Venturesome scholars can test their historical judgement by offering educated guesses about what these files contain and help us learn from their retrodictions by sharing how they reached these conclusions. Moreover, new data continues to emerge at a remarkable pace. Archives around the world regularly release new material. Previously closed archives have reopened, even if only temporarily, and archivists remain hard at work recovering lost data.14 Archival data represents one of many types of evidence that can emerge over time. Witnesses may eventually come forward, for example, just as leaked documents can shed light on the unknown past.15 Many exciting testing opportunities therefore exist for historians and social scientists. auditPapers.title: HISTORY AND THEORY AND PHILOLOGY NOW: TOGETHER IN THEORY
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT In English‐speaking academe, philology has virtually disappeared as a defined discipline, although its traditional array of skills and techniques for reading, editing, and interpreting texts are indispensable to fields ranging from biblical studies through every language and literature and are central to historical research. Philology's status “now” seems to be that the analytic skills for dealing with texts, skills developed over centuries, have been appropriated by multiple academic specialties while the framework that used to contain them has been dismantled and nearly forgotten. From a historian's viewpoint, I track the lively resistance movement pressing for a return to philology and a turn to a “new” philology, a revived, recovered, restored discipline with its own coherent identity. This movement of renewal and restoration is complicated by the need to come to terms with philology's deep entanglement with racialist thought and anti‐Semitism, a past that has indelibly stained the reputation of philology as a discipline. The guiding intent of this article is to bring philology, with all its complications, back together with history, its formerly yoked companion discipline, and inquire where and how theory emerges—a metaphilology analogous to metahistory.

auditPapers.title: The Colony and the Company: Haiti after the Mississippi Bubble. By Malick Ghachem
auditPapers.abstract: Malick Ghachem’s first book, The Old Regime and the Haitian Revolution (2012), examined the violent end of the French colony of Saint-Domingue and of the highly stratified, extremely exploitative model of plantation slavery that had made it France’s most lucrative overseas possession. In The Colony and the Company, by contrast, Ghachem is interested in beginnings rather than endings. He argues that the years 1715-1725 were particularly critical in the emergence of a distinctive “military-planter state” based on “militant slavery,” which he links to the rise of a new kind of finance monopoly capitalism, which burst onto the scene in France in the second decade of the eighteenth century with the rapid rise and dramatic fall of the financial system of the Scottish financier and fugitive John Law. As a result of this process, Ghachem argues, Saint-Domingue, hitherto something of a backwater of the French Caribbean, settled by pirates seeking quick riches through the plunder of Spanish treasure fleets, was transformed into a “bubble colony,” fueled by dreams of easy riches from the burgeoning sugar trade. The result was a dynamic but particularly unstable colony, characterized by rapid growth, periodic crises, and brutal repression, which would ultimately explode into the Haitian Revolution.

auditPapers.title: What Makes Transportation History
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The idea that societies progress from rickshaw to railroad has been ubiquitous in discourses of colonialism and technological determinism since the nineteenth century. While historians of colonialism have debunked these discourses in specific cases, the question of why transportation came to be such a common sense measure of historical change has been left untouched. This article argues that “transportation” has a history. From eighteenth- and nineteenth-century political-economic philosophy in Europe, Japan, and the United States, to rickshaw puller movements in early twentieth-century Japan, to the emergence of transport devices as museum objects in the 1960s, “What Makes Transportation History” shows how transportation came to be understood both as the foundation for economic life and as a measure and maker of linear and irreversible change over time. This process did not exclude those who approached transportation as a livelihood. Rather, battles with rickshaw pullers and other transportation workers naturalized the idea that the needs of transport’s producers must be subordinated to the needs of transport’s consumers for modern societies to progress.

auditPapers.title: Pattern Redesign Imitating Ethnic Clothing Color Styles via Palette-guided GAN
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: The digital regeneration of ethnic clothing colors is pivotal in fashion design. With advancements in information technology, machine learning techniques are increasingly being applied to the design of ethnic clothing. However, existing color transfer techniques often focus on single-color blocks, overlooking the complexity of color layering and proving inadequate for large-scale image colorization. To address these challenges, we propose an automatic colorization method guided by a color palette. The generative network is enhanced by incorporating a primary coloring network and a conditional network based on generative adversarial network principles. The conditional network integrates color palette inputs, while the primary network processes image data, enabling palette-guided colorization of non-colored patterns. Huber loss is introduced to the generator’s loss function to improve colorization precision. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing methods in structural similarity and peak signal-to-noise ratio values, with an average colorization time of less than 0.2 seconds per pattern. The proposed solution effectively supports the digital, intelligent mass design of ethnic clothing coloration, ensuring interactivity and style consistency, and offers valuable insights for fashion product colorization.

auditPapers.title: Social Media, Crowdsourcing and Everyday Life Information-Seeking: Cultural Heritage Preservation in Borneo Rural Communities
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Borneo’s diverse ethnicities in Sarawak face significant geographical and linguistic challenges, making it difficult to document and protect its rich cultural heritage. This study examines the impact of social media on Everyday Life Information-Seeking (ELIS) behaviours within these rural communities. By applying Chatman’s theory regarding the social and psychological aspects of information-seeking, along with Uses and Gratification Theory (UGT), we explore the reasons for media use in this context. Our approach, which combines qualitative crowdsourcing and expert evaluation, demonstrates that social media plays a crucial role in preserving Borneo’s cultural heritage. Over 8 months, we collected 342 verified entries related to Sarawak’s cultural heritage, with an impressive 88.4% reliability in the crowdsourced information. The data, primarily sourced from WhatsApp and Facebook, showcased a diverse range of cultural practices across different ethnic groups. These findings illustrate the effectiveness of social media as a platform for documenting and preserving cultural heritage in rural Borneo. Additionally, they provide valuable insights into the complexities of information-seeking in small, isolated communities and offer practical recommendations for using social media to support cultural heritage preservation efforts.

auditPapers.title: A Revolution of Letters
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Colonialism in Africa was a textual encounter, with writing operating as an essential tool for colonial governance as well as a visual embodiment of Western “rationality” and civilization. Somalis, a predominantly oral people spread out across five colonial territories in the Horn of Africa, resisted Latin-based orthographies for their language because of these associations, while anticolonial nationalism following the Second World War brought the orthography question to the forefront as Somalis vigorously debated the written form Somali should take. Following Somalia’s independence in 1960, the continued use of colonial languages for writing threatened the postcolonial nation-building project and its larger ambitions to unify the partitioned Somali territories into a Greater Somalia, a central objective of Pan-Somali nationalist politics. When General Mohamed Siad Barre seized power in 1969, the adoption of a Somali script became a priority for his socialist military government, as his authoritarian regime used visual practices of statecraft such as mass spectacles and textual production to establish a modern Pan-Somali nationalist identity. This article examines the history of the Somali orthography and the making of a nationalist discourse ecology that brought together text, sight, and spectacle in revolutionary Somalia at a time when the Somali state looked beyond its borders and mobilized for war.

auditPapers.title: Paula Fredriksen. Ancient Christianities: The First Five Hundred Years
auditPapers.abstract: Ancient Christianities is exactly the kind of general account of the early Christian centuries that we would expect from Paula Fredriksen: elegantly written, theologically rich, socially nuanced. Paul and Augustine loom large, as do intellectual histories of concepts like sin, salvation, god, and body. We are treated to Fredriksen’s cogent insights into the construction of “Jewish,” “Christian,” and “pagan” labels, not as fixed identities or groups, but as powerful rhetorical strategies that shift with time, situation, and audience. The plural “Christianities” of the title refers to diverse modes of religion and discourse just as much as to the diverse groups of Christ-followers that populate these centuries. The book consists of seven thematic chapters, organized more-or-less chronologically within each chapter. The first chapter, “The Idea of Israel,” and the last, “Pagan and Christian,” frame the book with the questions of religious transformation that shape the period we call late antiquity. In what ways does Christianity grow out of, appropriate, and/or reject both Judaism and the traditional Mediterranean religions of antiquity? How does a particular form of Christianity become the dominant religion of the Roman Mediterranean? The middle chapters address theological diversity (aka heresy and orthodoxy), persecution and martyrdom, apocalyptic eschatology, imperial Christology, and asceticism. This may sound like a lot of -isms and -ologies, but Fredriksen has a knack for making complex ideas clear and grounded in social realities. She treats each category as a capacious net for a variety of interrelated sub-topics.
topics: Globalization, Historical Perspectives, and International Relations

auditPapers.title: Revisiting the “Comfort Girls” of Report 49
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In 1944, a Japanese American intelligence officer stationed in Ledo, India, unwittingly composed a famous historical document: “Japanese Prisoner of War Interrogation Report No. 49,” which focused on twenty Korean comfort women captured near Myitkyina, Burma. In the decades since, most historians have regarded the report as evidence of the Japanese state’s responsibility for the comfort woman system, but it has also been embraced by revisionists arguing the opposing case. This essay reassesses the document to show how it emerged from a many-sided struggle over how women’s bodies should be used in the simultaneous conflicts of empire and decolonization that constituted World War II in Burma. Korean comfort women’s status as both Japan’s “own women” and colonized subjects meant that they could be exploited to a variety of ends—both on the battlefield and in the realm of information warfare—for audiences including Anglophone newspaper readers, American military officers, Japanese soldiers, and Burmese civilians. Removed from its specific geographical and temporal context, the document’s elevation as a generic piece of evidence has obscured a larger history in which concerns about “sex slavery,” a concept notably absent from this report, emerged, retreated, and reemerged over the course of the war.

auditPapers.title: The Plunder of Black America: How the Racial Wealth Gap Was Made By Calvin Schermerhorn
auditPapers.abstract: Numerous scholars have written about the racial wealth gap in the United States, often through social scientific approaches highlighting the ability of white families to transfer inheritance and other assets to their progeny across generations. In light of this existing literature, the critical contribution of Calvin Schermerhorn’s book, The Plunder of Black America: How the Racial Wealth Gap Was Made, is the intimate, poignant manner in which he bores into several Black families’ narratives across time and place to illustrate the fragility of African American household wealth and its interdependence with white racial domination and economic exploitation. Amid a surge of scholarly publications advocating reparatory justice for African American descendants of slavery, Schermerhorn also uniquely personalizes this demand. Built on discrete chapters spanning the colonial era to the present, the author depicts historical and contemporary families whose individual upward mobility foundered against “a new iteration of economic racism that emerged as they climbed” (2). Indeed, according to Schermerhorn, “[e]ach time Black Americans gained a little wealth, new policies or economic practices stripped a portion of that wealth and imposed new barriers to its creation and retention… peeling away assets in the present and obstructing opportunities for helping the next generation.” (2) Rather than constituting a parallel development to the acquisition of white wealth, the latter was premised on the former through successive periods of systemic dispossession, disinheritance, and decapitalization—a process that the nineteenth-century abolitionist Frederick Douglass identified as plunder. “Stolen Black labor value,” Schermerhorn argues, “became white wealth, passed down and increased in each generation, on average, while theft of African American work product became a loss that was compounded in each generation” (82). This dynamic developed in earnest between the 1640s and 1660s, when the initial possibilities for Black property ownership and wealth for colonial families like Mary and Anthony Johnson were eroded and African Americans “were forced out of places that held marginal opportunities to become free, generate income, and build resources and into places that held virtually no opportunities to do so” (73).

auditPapers.title: Glenn Dyer. The Era Was Lost: The Rise and Fall of New York City’s Rank-and-File Rebels
auditPapers.abstract: Organized labor is often treated as a cohesive unit. Phrases like “the labor movement” imply not only that there is an organized force but that it is unified. While this sense of solidity is useful when trying to understand the myriad forces stacked against workers’ organizations, it often oversimplifies complex dynamics at work within labor unions throughout US history. Sometimes the rank and file’s goals are not those held by union leadership. This dichotomy has only begun to be studied, and Glenn Dyer’s new book is a welcome addition to this literature. The Era Was Lost is a case study on New York City workers’ militancy in the 1960s and 1970s. During this period, which is detailed in Jefferson Cowie’s Stayin’ Alive: The 1970s and the Last Days of the Working Class (2010) and Kim Phillips-Fein’s Fear City: New York’s Fiscal Crisis and the Rise of Austerity Politics (2017), the United States became more conservative, and labor unions became substantially less powerful. While many of the unions and events discussed in the book have been told by other historians, Dyer claims his approach “provides a novel interpretation by foregrounding rank-and-file struggles” rather than “labor writ large” in the working-class struggles during this period (4). Making a distinction between union leaders and the rank and file, Dyer argues that the rank and file remained committed to advancing their cause of higher wages, better benefits, and better working conditions, even as union leaders became more conservative.

auditPapers.title: Self-Fashioning, Food, and Masculinity in George III’s Monarchy
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract George III was a family man, a modest eater, and a thoughtful ruler who wrote about the big questions of the day, from royal sovereignty to the best methods of agriculture to feed a modern nation. His writings provide a glimpse of his version of monarchy, which placed him at the head of a national family, where he embodied the habits of self-regulation and temperance in keeping with the sensibilities of late eighteenth-century manhood. This article brings together George’s meals and his essays, considering the histories of food, masculinity, and self-fashioning, to argue that George was a monarch who embodied a new form of masculinity, as marked by his agricultural interests and insistence on a modest diet. His eating habits, along with his intellectual interests and public persona, bring us to the intersection between the private man and the public monarch. Drawing on newly digitized data, alongside contemporary caricatures and descriptions, and George’s own writing, we argue that moderation was central to George’s creation of an image that appealed to the emerging British nation of the late eighteenth century; food was central to this image, highlighting both his masculine self-control and his ability to be useful to the nation.

auditPapers.title: Revolutionary Warfare: How the Algerian War Made Modern Counterinsurgency. By Terrence G. Peterson
auditPapers.abstract: The Front de Libération National was not the only revolutionary belligerent in the Algerian War (1954-1962). At least, that is how the French military viewed it. Since the 1960s, very few Anglophone studies have examined the truly revolutionary tones of the French Army’s guerre révolutionnaire doctrine, employed by a politically and militarily radicalized French officer corps, reeling from exposure and defeat to the Marxist Viet Minh in Indochina. It is perhaps more accurate to describe guerre révolutionnaire as more of an ideology than a strictly-military doctrine. Its proponents viewed the conflicts in Indochina and Algeria not as traditional colonial wars, but as part of a global conflagration against communism, which sought, in their eyes, to outflank and subsume the West via the colonies. The doctrine and its many proponents suggested that the French take a few leaves out of the Marxist playbook, and employ the methods of their communist foe. This included (but was not limited to) the use of psychological warfare: brainwashing, struggle sessions (autocritique), ideological re-education and political commissars: all utilized in Algeria in a desperate attempt to remake Frenchmen out of captured rebels.

auditPapers.title: The Colonial Metamorphosis of Egyptian Capital Punishment, 1884–1903
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article analyses how colonial rule remade Egyptian capital punishment. Around the turn of the twentieth century, British officials deliberately overturned the strong protections for defendants that Islamic law once offered, paving the way for a steady and sustained increase in execution rates. More executions meant more opportunities for ordinary people to practise the distinctive forms of ‘popular legalism’ that flourished on execution days. In keeping with established custom, the families of perpetrator and victim played leading roles on gallows days, defending kin and negotiating punishment. Women often took charge of these occasions, demonstrating and enhancing their social power while simultaneously directing the affective responses of the assembled crowds. Such public displays of gendered authority were anathema to Egyptian elites and colonial officials alike, turning both decisively against public punishment. The abolition of public executions thus erased a prominent manifestation of the social embeddedness of Islamic law.

auditPapers.title: Colonizing Accra
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Between 1886 and 1888, a series of dramatic events took place in the West African town of Accra, marking an escalation of colonial control and imperial state formation. This essay investigates three previously unknown, but profoundly important, political events through the perspective of narrative history. It asks how does storytelling change the way that historians approach the archive? What critiques of time, state, and power might narrative history offer the historian? This essay interweaves narrative storytelling with a critique of writing and archival practice. It argues that the events that took place in Accra in 1886–88 suggest a far later timeline for colonization than historians have previously accepted, and that these events—which were so crucial to Accra’s colonization by Britain—have perhaps been omitted from the historical record because historians mine the archives for data, not for stories. By approaching the archive for its storytelling potential, this essay suggests that historians may unearth not just compelling facts or anecdotes but a novel framework for understanding the movement of history.

auditPapers.title: Alison L. LaCroix. The Interbellum Constitution: Union, Commerce, and Slavery in the Age of Federalisms .
auditPapers.abstract: One major theme in histories of the American founding is imperium in imperio (sovereignty within sovereignty, government within government). This phrase is often treated as the framers’ original understanding of federalism: the new states sharing sovereignty with the new federal government. Before it was treated as a solution, it was the Latin name of a serious problem, an error, a contradiction, even an impossibility. Alison L. LaCroix and other American historians have cited Blackstone and eighteenth-century Whigs on sovereignty as “supreme,” “absolute,” unitary, and exclusive; and have quoted Alexander Hamilton’s famous description in 1774 of such attempts to split the sovereignty baby as a “solecism of politics,” an error. A year later, John Adams put the problem in theological terms: Two sovereigns could coexist in the same state no more than “two supreme beings in the same universe.” Nevertheless, the framers took the leap and embraced imperium in imperio as the solution to the same problem. However, it was just a new informal experimental solution, an abstract solution in theory. The problem would be how to solve the solecism in practice, and those practices from 1815 to 1861 are the deeply engaging stories in LaCroix’s The Interbellum Constitution: Union, Commerce, and Slavery in the Age of Federalisms. The last word in the subtitle is the most important: Each chapter shows how this formative era produced more complicated and more intriguing alternative models. Even if the framers had any single theory of federalism—which LaCroix rightly doubts—the theory soon multiplied into multiple doctrines and practices of federalisms, plural.

auditPapers.title: Pranks and the Viral Canon: On Top-Creator Content from YouTube to TikTok
auditPapers.abstract: Since the early 2000s, digital pranks—or filmed practical jokes—have earned a reputation for platform-based popularity. But how prominent are such pranks amongst other “viral” genres? And what might they reveal, more generally, about viral video as a cultural form? In this essay, I address these broad questions from a specific perspective: I consider the digital prank in the context of two datasets of video content by top-ranked English-language creators on TikTok and YouTube, 2020-2023 and 2012-2023, respectively. I find that digital pranks have been less prominent within this context than potentially expected, but that they have also reflected more general tendencies shared across the videos collected, like fixations on visual pleasure, materiality, and experimentation. I also engage in a more methodological discussion, considering complications that emerge when addressing platform-based media from this type of interpretive and generalizing perspective. I suggest that a (digital) humanistic approach to popular digital content can expand the types of new media canons available for analysis.

auditPapers.title: Joseph A. Seeley. Border of Water and Ice: The Yalu River and Japan's Empire in Korea and Manchuria
auditPapers.abstract: Joseph Seeley has produced an excellent book for historians interested in Sino-Korean border spaces, Japan’s 20th century continental empire and its infrastructure, and the entwined environmental legacies of both colonial Korea and Manchukuo. Border of Water and Ice: The Yalu River and Japan’s Empire in Korea and Manchuria is thematically ambitious but manages not to sprawl, in part through regular meditations on the tangible and environmental impacts of the seasonal changes on the Yalu River, the narrow watercourse flowing down for about 500 kilometers out into the Yellow Sea and separating the cities of Chinese Andong (today Dandong) and Korean Sinuiju. Seeley’s clear prose is carefully underpinned with sources in Japanese, Korean, and Chinese, and the book adds in-depth coverage of an important region to the increasingly transnational field of environmental history of Northeast Asia. Readers who wonder how the contemporary North Korean state managed to secure sovereignty over several strategic islands on the Chinese side of the Yalu estuary will find a fascinating origin story in Seeley’s first chapter. His detailed historical detective work demonstrates how Japanese efforts to harvest natural resources like reeds led to Korean (and then colonial Japanese) control being extended along the northern bank of the river. Seeley traces the emergence of one island from its origins in the upstream erosion and sedimentation flows of the late 1880s, moving through militia violence and an array of historical agents, including Chinese reed harvesters, Qing diplomats, Japanese local consular officials, Korean collaborators (Ilchinhoe), Japanese “continental adventurers,” and the ever-changing river itself.

auditPapers.title: Catherine Tatiana Dunlop. The Mistral: A Windswept History of Modern France
auditPapers.abstract: Those of us who have lived, worked, or travelled to Provence will have encountered the mistral. When this wind blows, the sky above turns the deepest blue while trees, crops, houses, and people are pummeled by the wind that sweeps down from mountains through the Rhône Valley and out to the Mediterranean Sea. The Mistral, Catherine Tatiana Dunlop’s slim yet punchy book harnesses the mistral in fascinating and generative ways. Tracking the wind’s impact through maps, illustrations, personal accounts and state records, alongside the landscape itself (such as wind-battered trees), Dunlop succeeds in showing how the mistral has shaped, but not determined, human and nonhuman life in this renowned and storied region of France. Beginning in the postrevolutionary era, she shows how successive governments have attempted to control, understand, and tame the wind through such things as the judicious planting of trees and new meteorological observatories (most famously on the top of wind-battered Mont Ventoux). Yet state attempts to contain the mistral were most often no match for the wind’s force: “the mistral became a forceful and bone-chilling reminder that provincial environments were not so easily quelled” (12).

auditPapers.title: Experimental and simulation studies on the mechanism of moisture-induced warping of traditional Japanese sliding doors
auditPapers.abstract: As a traditional Japanese fixture, fusuma is sliding doors, often displaying paintings on paper. However, because fusuma is also building components, it is often preserved and exhibited inside cultural heritage buildings, such as temples, shrines, and castles, which have low thermal insulation and airtightness; therefore, fluctuations in temperature and humidity may cause deformation of fusuma and tears in painted paper. This study focused on the deformation mechanisms of fusuma paintings preserved and exhibited inside cultural property buildings. Specifically, the study investigated the warping behavior of tobusuma —a type of fusuma made by attaching a support such as plywood or carbon fiber reinforced plastic (CFRP) board to one side to increase strength—when temperature and humidity differences occur on the front and back, clarified the warping mechanism, and evaluated the effect of different support types on warpage. In the experiment, an actual-sized tobusuma was prepared, and warpage was measured by subjecting its front and back surfaces to different temperatures and relative humidity. Additionally, we reproduced our experimental results using a finite element method (FEM) simulation and analyzed the effect of each tobusuma component on the warpage. The results showed that tobusuma tends to warp toward higher relative humidity if temperatures on both sides are the same, and that the direction and magnitude of warpage depend on the support type. For the plywood support, greater warpage occurred when the interior side was humid, whereas for the CFRP support, greater warpage occurred when the exterior side was humid because of its low moisture permeability; however, when the exterior side was humid, the amout of warpage was similar for both supports. In typical field environments, where the interior is generally more stable and less humid, the type of support may have a limited impact on warping. In the FEM simulation, the reproducibility of the simulation model was lower for the CFRP support than for the plywood support, which is considered to be due to uncertainties in the mechanical boundary conditions and moisture content input of the components. In particular, when the hygrothermal properties of components differ significantly, like CFRP, it is more important to perform coupling between moisture transfer and moisture-induced mechanical deformation simulation. The study results contribute to the selection of suitable support for preserving fusuma paintings and to investigation of environments in which they are installed. For a deeper understanding of fusuma paintings’ deterioration mechanism, it is necessary to investigate not only the warping of tobusuma but also the deformation behavior of painted paper and the discoloration/fading of the paintings. Since these phenomena are closely related to environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, illumination, and ultraviolet light levels, we consider that clarifying these deterioration mechanisms step by step will lead to the suggestion for optimal preservation and exhibition methods inside cultural property buildings with environmental fluctuations.

auditPapers.title: Using nanocellulose mixtures for the wood stabilisation of a Lilienthal glider
auditPapers.abstract: At the end of the 19th century, Otto Lilienthal (1848–1896) built humanity’s first airplanes. The Deutsches Museum Munich owns Lilienthal’s personal glider since 1904 and investigates preservation methods since the 1980s. The wooden fragments were severely damaged by the so called ‘woodworm’. Therefore, the frame of the glider needed to be stabilised in order to preserve it for future handling during conservation and exhibition. The choice of materials followed methods used at the University of the Arts Bern in Switzerland. In particular, the approach to reinforce Methyl cellulose with Nanocellulose was further investigated for the purpose of stabilising the infested wood of the glider. Pre – tests with celluloses showed that they meet the requirements of the conservation concept. Therefore, an object-related laboratory testing series was carried out in collaboration with the Leibniz Institute for Materials Engineering - IWT in Bremen, Germany. The laboratory results enabled the celluloses to be applied with respective to individual situations of the wooden fragments of the glider in 2024. They proved to be practical as wood stabilising agents, and the characteristic thixotropy of Nanocellulose was beneficial while using the mixtures on the fragments of the glider. The chemical properties of celluloses, their almost unchanged surface appearance after drying, and the non-toxic application of this natural polymer make these mixtures an attractive and sustainable wood stabilisation agent for the conservation of historic wooden artefacts.

auditPapers.title: Jonathan Lande. Freedom Soldiers: The Emancipation of Black Soldiers in Civil War Camps, Courts, and Prisons
auditPapers.abstract: Freedom Soldiers: The Emancipation of Black Soldiers in Civil War Camps, Courts, and Prisons by Jonathan Lande examines the protracted process of emancipation that Black Civil War soldiers engaged in as they transitioned from enslaved labor to military labor on their path to freedom. In doing so, Lande makes a powerful argument for seeing Black soldiers’ use of mobility as a larger struggle for Black self-determination and as a tool for renegotiating labor rights with the federal government. In Freedom Soldiers, Lande builds upon the arguments made in recent years by historians who argue that emancipation was a process and not an event and stress the important role that forging contractual relationships with the state played in defining and securing rights for newly freed people. However, Lande breaks new ground as he seeks to reframe the revisionist history of Black Civil War soldiers, which often aggrandizes their heroic deeds and loyalty while downplaying their acts of rebellion and desertion. Instead, Lande argues that the road to freedom for Black soldiers was multidimensional and that their acts of rebellion were not a departure from their fight for freedom but were, in fact, a defining feature. Lande argues that Black soldiers “leaves of freedom” or unauthorized departures were, in reality, ways in which these once enslaved men voted with their feet in their continuing fight for rights to familial bonds, equal labor rights, and in protesting unequal and coercive military labor practices. As such, Lande’s argument provides a unique perspective on Black soldiers’ desertion as a tactic to secure further freedoms and negotiate labor contracts with the US Army.

auditPapers.title: Avner Ofrath. Colonial Algeria and the Politics of Citizenship
auditPapers.abstract: Avner Ofrath’s scrupulously researched work focuses on the politics of citizenship in colonial Algeria. Algeria was France’s most important colony, with parts of it becoming an extension of the metropole. As such, the question of citizenship and empire is particularly pertinent in thinking about the relationship between the colonizer and the colonized. auditPapers.title: Dispelling ‘ das Herbert Butterfieldproblem ’: A Rereading of The Whig Interpretation of History
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Herbert Butterfield’s The Whig Interpretation of History (1931) is universally received as sceptical of ‘whig’ teleology in historical accounts and, therefore, of politically charged narratives of history. This view stands in need of a basic correction. Butterfield’s work targets teleological accounts which involve a determinate conception of progress such as would arm a partisan politics. He calls this the politics of the ‘general proposition’. Nevertheless, he does defend a conception of progress involving an indeterminate concept. The historian finds, intimated in the detail of the past, that progress is the fruit of interactions between opposing parties. The imperative for the statesman in the present, then, is to facilitate such interactions. In short, The Whig Interpretation of History is a positive work of political thought. Looked at this way, Butterfield’s later, controversial work, The Englishman & His History , does not appear to be in contradiction with the earlier book so much as a polemical expression of it. The two books together present what may be called Butterfield’s politics of historiography. Histories which present progress as a straight line, to be co-opted by one party, encourage precisely the political action which impedes progress. Butterfield, in short, is still a kind of ‘whig’.

auditPapers.title: Richard Reid. The African Revolution: A History of the Long Nineteenth Century
auditPapers.abstract: With this ambitious intervention, Richard Reid seeks to decolonize our understanding of the Scramble for Africa and its impacts. Drawing on his extensive knowledge of modern African history, Reid contextualizes the Scramble in terms of the political reformism and global commercial engagements that characterized much of Africa’s innovative yet volatile nineteenth century. The result is an impressive work of synthesis with its own revisionist agenda: to upend our understanding of the Scramble as a definitive “rupture” in African history (19). Reid presents his argument in The African Revolution in five parts, bookended by a prologue and epilogue. In part 1, he lays out the aim, scope, and arguments of the book. In part 2, he explores how the growth in trans- and intercontinental exchanges intensified political challenges in Africa and spurred much of the creative but violent political inventiveness of this epoch. Reid outlines a reoccurring “pattern … of fusion followed by fission” as polities were made and unmade through insurrections and violent reformism (54). These political developments were often entangled with socioeconomic reforms, and in the third part, Reid examines how “Africans, whether extant elites or entrepreneurial upstarts, sought to grasp the opportunities presented by intensifying global interaction” (116). Coercion and extraction underpinned many of the political and economic developments of this period, and as individuals attempted to position themselves advantageously, they created new urban spaces, forms of identity, and economic infrastructures that “ironically, facilitated global intrusion” (150).

auditPapers.title: Feminism, Artistry, Madness, and the Ghost of Valerie Solanas
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Valerie Solanas holds an unsettled place in feminist history, notorious for both her incendiary 1967 diatribe the SCUM Manifesto and her near-fatal 1968 shooting of Andy Warhol. This paper explores the tangled links between Solanas and women’s liberation: how the movement briefly commandeered her as a feminist martyr and how, on her release from psychiatric prison, Solanas sought to regain control of her story. In the process it asks how Solanas’s words, actions, and decades-long struggle with mental illness haunted a generation of women who came of age with the feminist movement and defined liberation in terms of art.

auditPapers.title: Zamira Abman. Coerced Liberation: Muslim Women in Soviet Tajikistan
auditPapers.abstract: In the 1920s and 1930s the Soviet government imposed a crash “liberation” campaign on the women of Central Asia, staging public shows of women burning their veils and putting husbands on trial for domestic violence. The literature on how women’s liberation unfolded in Uzbekistan is robust, but fewer historians have worked on other Central Asian republics, especially for the postwar decades. In Coerced Liberation, Zamira Abman makes a fine contribution to the field with her study, which considers the failure of women’s liberation in Tajikistan. Abman was born and raised in Tajikistan, and was able to gather dozens of oral histories in Tajik and Russian. She also gained unprecedented access to the Tajik Communist Party Archive, as well as state archives. She uses these archives to show not only why the liberation project in Tajikistan failed, but why the Tajik republic was anomalous within Soviet Central Asia. Abman’s argument rests on the sharp distinction between urban and rural life. Tajikistan’s capital, Dushanbe/Stalinobod, was built in the late 1920s; the only other town of note, Khujand/Leninobod, was much older but lacked political importance. The communists building revolutionary culture in the new capital were predominately Slavic, a situation that did not change until the 1960s. Meanwhile, more than 80 percent of the Tajik population lived in the countryside and did not speak Russian. A profound gap between urban and rural outlooks existed everywhere in the USSR, but the communists made less progress in overcoming it in Tajikistan than elsewhere in Central Asia. Abman does not spend much time investigating why this was, but it was partly rooted in the republic’s mountainous terrain that created very difficult conditions for industrial development. Tajikistan was consistently the poorest of the Soviet republics.

auditPapers.title: Political Equality and Economic Inequality in Étienne-Géry Lenglet’s Recipe for the Modern Republic
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Reflections on the legacy of ‘Jacobin egalitarianism’ in post-Thermidorian France can be seen as following one of three strands: conservative, communist, or democratic. By shedding light on the democratic trajectory, this article addresses the historiographical imbalance that has disproportionately focused on conservative and communist perspectives. This study thereby pursues a renewed understanding of the relationship between the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and the evolution of political economy. Through an analysis of Étienne-Géry Lenglet’s treatise, De la propriété (1798), the contexts and content of democratic political economy during the revolutionary decade are identified. Lenglet’s politics formed an intervention in the debates during the Directory on the dynamics of property, morality, the franchise, and the principles of modern polities. His thought exemplifies a Condorcetian egalitarianism that grappled with the dilemmas posed by the rise of commerce and standing armies. This analysis of Lenglet’s work challenges the notion that the radicals of the French Revolution operated outside of Enlightenment political economy: De la propriété was deeply rooted in Enlightenment and revolutionary rhetoric. Lenglet’s politics emerges as a crucial component of diverse reform projects that contradicts reified depictions of Enlightenment political thought.

auditPapers.title: La última guerra del Siglo de las Luces: Revolución Liberal y republicanismo popular en Ecuador (The Final War of the Age of Enlightenment: The Liberal Revolution and Popular Republicanism in Ecuador). By Valeria Coronel
auditPapers.abstract: Valeria Coronel’s La última guerra del Siglo de las Luces is the masterful culmination of efforts by a generation of scholars to rethink the nineteenth century in Latin America. The nineteenth century had long been understood as a time when popular actors, be they Indigenous communities, artisans, campesinos (small farmers), slaves, and freed people were ignorant of, and had no interest in, the newly independent Latin American nations and only entered the political sphere as clients of powerful patrons or cannon fodder. Their lot was to endure exploitation by an all-powerful oligarchy, occasionally engage in an atavistic rebellion, and await their political awakening with either populism or socialism in the twentieth century. A new historiography has slowly but surely worked to transform our understanding of the nineteenth century, exploring how plebeian actors created a popular republicanism to claim citizenship in the new nations, demand rights, and protect their interests. Ecuador has been mostly ignored in the historiographic revolution. Partly this is a matter of timing—while democratic republicanism was being dismantled by coalitions of liberal and conservative elites in most of Latin America by the 1880s, such as in Colombia and Mexico, in Ecuador it was surging. However, Coronel’s book is not only valuable for its focus on Ecuador (although this alone would make it a worthy read), but also because it builds on and perhaps even perfects the nation and state formation literature; it is a true social history of politics, linking the social history of popular groups’ everyday lives to their political discourse and actions.
topics: History and Politics in Latin America

auditPapers.title: Jess Whatcott. Menace to the Future: A Disability and Queer History of Carceral Eugenics .
auditPapers.abstract: Jess Whatcott’s Menace to the Future: A Disability and Queer History of Carceral Eugenics offers a provocative analysis of detention in California from the early twentieth century to the present. While Wendy Kline’s Building A Better Race: Gender, Sexuality, and Eugenics from the Turn of the Century to the Baby Boom (2001), Alexandra Minna Stern’s Eugenic Nation: Fault and Frontiers of Better Breeding in Modern America (2005), and Natalie Lira’s Laboratory of Deficiency: Sterilization and Confinement in California, 1900–1950s (2022) use archival research to highlight California’s place in the eugenics movement popular at the turn of the century, Whatcott takes a more theoretical approach. This makes sense: As a scholar working at the intersection of critical disability, prison, queer, and gender studies, Whatcott’s interest lies less in historical inquiry and more in using contemporary observations of carceral spaces and earlier scholars’ research to argue that “detention,” past and present, “is eugenics” (xiv). Whatcott is active in the prison abolition movement and explains how that work inspired their exploration of the racial, gender, and disability through lines in twentieth-century detention. Beginning with an examination of eugenics and disability institutions at the turn to the century and ending with an analysis of what Whatcott describes as the eugenics of the current carceral state, they “theorize how . . . confinement” of any kind has been and remains a form of “carceral eugenics” (3). They urge us to use their work as a playbook for abolishing “carceral logics and structures in all forms” (4).

auditPapers.title: Alan M. Stahl. The House of Condulmer: The Rise and Decline of a Venetian Family in the Century of the Black Death
auditPapers.abstract: The relationship between economic and political power is a central question for historians of late medieval Italian cities. Scholars have combed the archives of Florence, Venice, Padua, and Pistoia to examine how commercial success and merchant wealth did or did not allow individuals and families to ascend into civic government and gain control of political institutions. In the Venetian context, the question has been shaped by the closing, or Serrata, of Venice’s political class into a restrictive, hereditary oligarchy that ruled until the fall of the Venetian republic in 1797. While scholars traditionally dated the Serrata to 1297, Gerhard Rösch has argued that a more fluid political elite was defined as a ruling class in the early decades of the fourteenth century, and Stanley Chojnacki has extended the timeline of the social and legal consolidation of the Venetian patriciate to the early fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, arguing that the self-fashioning of Venice’s ruling class was a process of renewal and redefinition that spanned generations. While many studies of the Venetian patriciate focus on alliances and power dynamics between the most important patrician families, Alan Stahl’s The House of Condulmer: The Rise and Decline of a Venetian Family in the Century of the Black Death examines the fortunes of a family on the fringes of the nobility and tells five interconnected stories about individuals’ social, political, and economic strategies to gain access to patrician society.

auditPapers.title: Paul J. Kosmin. The Ancient Shore .
auditPapers.abstract: As the second century CE geographer Strabo noted, “We (humans) are, in some sense, amphibious, belonging as much to dry land as to the sea” (Strabo 1.1.16). With The Ancient Shore, Paul Kosmin sets out to explore the impacts of this duality on the development of ancient cultures and systems. Drawing from the late Bronze Age to the Roman Imperial period, the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, the work highlights the Hellenistic period with a truly innovative focus. Couched within Kosmin’s lyric, densely evocative voice, The Ancient Shore ambitiously seeks to situate the coast itself, rather than a specific, geographically discrete space, as a key locus for ancient history: “the single most significant setting in antiquity” (2) for contact, mobility, and exchange. The result is a sprawling work of sociocultural history, less successful at rigorous, comparative study than at exploring deep questions on the nature of the ancient world: What stimulates human social and cultural development? How much does environmental context impact intellectual, political, and economic processes? How has humanity confronted the slow passage of eternity symbolized by the ancient shore?

auditPapers.title: Benedito Luís Machava. The Morality of Revolution: Reeducation Camps and the Politics of Punishment in Socialist Mozambique, 1968–1990
auditPapers.abstract: After Mozambique’s liberation from Portuguese colonial rule in 1975, the Mozambique Liberation Front (Frelimo) became a Marxist-Leninist governing party led by President Samora Machel. Machel’s socialist vision for national development included top-down economic schemes, a desire to cleanse urban spaces of “bourgeois” Mozambicans living decadent lifestyles, and the widespread use of draconian policies meant to rapidly transform Mozambicans into revolutionary “New Men” and “New Women.” Machel’s ambitious revolutionary paradigm was meant to expedite Mozambique’s transition from a former colony into a modern postcolonial socialist nation. However, in The Morality of Revolution: Reeducation Camps and the Politics of Punishment in Socialist Mozambique, 1968–1990, Benedito Luís Machava contends that Frelimo’s moralistic impetus to reform “wayward” Mozambicans with the use of remote “reeducation camps” largely failed to achieve the state’s lofty revolutionary goals. As Machava deftly argues, officials in the “reeducation camps” not only struggled to “reeducate” and reform the incarcerated to the level of the revolutionary ideals set forth by Machel, but the perilous experiences of those in the camps generated bitter memories and animosities toward Frelimo that, for many, continue to this day.

auditPapers.title: Kate Stevens. Gender, Violence and Criminal Justice in the Colonial Pacific, 1880–1920
auditPapers.abstract: In Gender, Violence and Criminal Justice in the Colonial Pacific, 1880–1920, Kate Stevens offers an innovative study of the intersections between colonial law and sexual violence in the Pacific between roughly 1880 and 1920. The book focuses on three Pacific colonies—French New Caledonia, British Fiji, and the jointly ruled New Hebrides (now Vanuatu)—and provides a comparative history revealing the diversity in categorization and adjudication of sexual crimes across British and French colonial legal systems. Central to Stevens’ analysis are the ways imperial ideologies of race and gender impacted colonial jurisprudence, and the book focuses on sexual crimes as a way of understanding the contested introduction of European criminal justice in the Pacific. Stevens uses a variety of sources to uncover the marginalized voices of Pacific Islanders and indentured workers hidden in the colonial archives. Through her analysis, we see how colonial legal regimes developed in uneven and often ineffective ways. More importantly, colonial law was shaped into various hybridized systems largely determined by localized conditions and Indigenous responses to colonial rule.

auditPapers.title: Ontology-based federated information systems with NLP-enhanced retrieval
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Analysing large volumes of humanities data requires considerable time and resources due to the high and varied requirements of researchers in terms of data presentation. In addition, humanities scholars wish to enter their search queries in natural language, quickly synchronising distributed data. Efficient approaches, such as DBoD (DataBasing on Demand), can quickly transfer and insert research data into a database. Natural Language Processing (NLP) is used to make these systems more intuitive and user-friendly, and the use of Ontology-based Data Access (OBDA) ensures that the distributed datasets are mapped semantically correctly. In this article, we explain – using a large dataset from the field of epigraphy – how to build a federated information system that supports natural language queries and how OBDA ensures the semantically correct mapping of distributed datasets. We have significantly reduced the implementation time of information systems and a federated information system from months or years to hours. The research data are project-specific and published in a federated information system, complete with the required styles, allowing direct access to the information. In addition, we have a high usability of the federated information systems with NLP-enhanced retrieval.

auditPapers.title: DEAD LETTERS AND LIVING WORDS: IBERIAN ARABISM AS POLITICAL PHILOLOGY
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT A surge of Arabic studies in Spain and Portugal during the eighteenth century responded to specific anxieties connected to national identities. Philology offered a means to contend with Iberia's Islamic past through present‐day geopolitics that seemed to threaten national futures. A comparison of lexicographic projects from the last decades of the century shows how philologists relied on translation strategies of domestication and foreignization to recast the history of the Arabic language and its users in Spain and Portugal. Such strategies merged historical and ethnographic techniques that mapped peoples, places, and languages. Collectively, these projects contributed to a revised emplotment of al‐Andalus as a vital space for intellectual encounter and especially the translatio studii that was credited as a source of Enlightenment ideals. It became a transhistorical resource for nationalist claims within and beyond Spain and Portugal.

auditPapers.title: Vernacular development, drought, and US technical assistance in postcolonial Lebanon
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Between 1951–55, the US Bureau of Reclamation conducted research in Lebanon to plan a hydroelectric and irrigation scheme using Lebanon's largest river, the Litani. Their research would later form the basis of the Litani project, Lebanon's largest development scheme until the 1990s. In the shadow of that project, communities in the Litani River basin worked to enroll these US technical assistance researchers and their technologies into fulfilling their urgent needs for potable water. The article argues that these enrollments comprised ‘vernacular development’, a highly contingent, bottom-up strategy that the intended subjects of development deployed in their encounters with agents of international development. Vernacular development was a mode of interaction that interrupted and subverted the technological and temporal framework animating midcentury international development. That framework promised elaborate works in the future, which almost never materialized. Through vernacular development strategies, Litani communities identified their own material needs and goals and experimented with strategies to enroll international researchers into attaining them. They derived these strategies from their experience with successive imperial and corporate planning missions that had come and gone in the decades prior to the postwar development era. Exploring hitherto unexamined agrarian sources in the US National Archives, this article contributes to the historiography of international development and the postcolonial Middle East.

auditPapers.title: Chris Beneke. Free Exercise: Religion, the First Amendment, and the Making of America
auditPapers.abstract: Chris Beneke’s latest work, Free Exercise: Religion, the First Amendment, and the Making of America, serves as an excellent and remarkably readable survey of the political, intellectual, and social context in which the Constitution’s religious clauses emerged. The narrative starts from the genesis of the Bill of Rights as a text to then investigate how pragmatic and principled considerations—from the memory of religious violence to new ideas about free markets, nation-building, and “civility”—factored into the early republic’s option for free exercise, shaping both its terms and limitations. Such a comprehensive analysis of the “original meaning” of the First Amendment inevitably leads Beneke to address the contemporary debate opposing “separationists,” who argue that disestablishment was meant to create a secular republic, to “accommodationists,” who argue that its goal was the equal distribution of government support for religion (“nonpreferentialism”) rather than its wholesale suppression. The author’s ultimate case for separationism is more nuanced than his dismissal of accommodationism, which he bases on the First Congress passing up an explicit opportunity to incorporate nonpreferentialist language into the Constitution and on scattered evidence suggesting that public days of thanksgiving and laws on mandatory Sunday rest—commonly invoked by accommodationists as proof that the founding generation did not have a secular agenda—were considered at odds with the “spirit” of the Constitution from the get-go (32, 53–54). While conceding that attributing a modern secular sensibility to the founders, not to mention the average early American, would be an anachronism, Beneke emphasizes that those seeds were indeed being planted.

auditPapers.title: Steven C. Hahn. A Pirate’s Life No More: The Pardoned Pirates of the Bahamas
auditPapers.abstract: It is almost mandatory for any study of piracy to open with some mention of the hold that rogues like Blackbeard, William Kidd, and their compatriots have over our imaginations. Furthermore, authors frequently declare that their volume seeks to tell the true story of the “Golden Age of Piracy” of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. Yet, if only because they are so much better documented than their less infamous contemporaries, most accounts still focus on the most notorious marauders. Steven C. Hahn’s A Pirate’s Life No More: The Pardoned Pirates of the Bahamas is an impressive exception, focusing on “a list of mostly nobodies” of the sort that “actually constituted a majority of pirates” (2). The basis of Hahn’s study is a single document: a list of 209 pirates who accepted a royal pardon from Captain Vincent Pearse of the Royal Navy in the Bahamas in March 1718. Through research that draws on a prodigious array of local administrative records—primarily court records, shipping returns, deeds, and church records—from across British America, Hahn has managed to track the lives of 150 of these men before and after they accepted the pardon. While one can disagree with Hahn’s view that such records “are less subject to the agendas of writers seeking to impose their views on a wider audience” than the imperial records used in most pirate histories, these records open an unparalleled window into the lives of former buccaneers (11).

auditPapers.title: Lydia Walker. States-in-Waiting: A Counternarrative of Global Decolonization .
auditPapers.abstract: States-in-Waiting is a nuanced and meticulously researched exploration of knowledge, power, and legitimacy in the era of decolonization. The monograph opens with the story of India’s Jawaharlal Nehru handing a blank check to the Naga nationalist leader, Angami Zapu Phizo, and the rumored existence of this check within the archives of Naga nationalists. The catch is that these archives, much like many Naga nationalist leaders themselves, are in exile. Once handed to an international advocate for safekeeping, they have yet to be returned to the descendants of these activists. This opening vignette reflects one of the key tensions of the book: International advocates have played a critical role in preserving and promoting the knowledge of national claimants, yet colonial and paternal dynamics nevertheless pervade their relationships with those for whom they advocate. States-in-Waiting is driven by a core question: What makes a nationalist claim legitimate? Through exploring a range of case studies, this monograph reveals that the criteria for gaining legitimacy were not fixed, but were politically and temporally contingent. Walker argues that “international recognition [of nationalist claims] favored communities that had mobilized earlier under empire” and were able to leverage either colonial power structures or military strength and regional alliances to emerge as legitimate national actors when European powers withdrew (23). Nationalist claimants from supposedly peripheral regions, who surfaced during later periods, were often denied these forms of intervention and faced numerous barriers to gaining international recognition of their claims. Consequently, many states-in-waiting turned to transnational advocacy networks to legitimize and promote their struggles for national independence within international forums. The monograph follows a range of different struggles for liberation that reached their zenith in the early 1960s. Walker describes it as a connective rather than comparative history (7). Its narrative is situated at the level of the individual—allowing Walker to draw novel connections between a range of seemingly unrelated nonstate, state, and transnational actors. Amongst its diverse cast of characters are nationalist-claimants, postcolonial statesmen, humanitarians, intellectuals, peace activists, mining executives, missionaries, international civil servants, and government officials. Walker’s case studies are methodically researched and presented accessibly for a global history audience who may not have the regional knowledge to contextualize these actors or their networks. The chapters are written to work in isolation with detailed introductions and conclusions that reintroduce key figures and reinforce overarching arguments.

auditPapers.title: Jeremy Beer. Beyond the Devil’s Road: Francisco Garcés and the Spanish Encounter with the American Southwest
auditPapers.abstract: Since 1995, when Enrique Oltra Perales OFM published in Spanish the book entitled: Fray Francisco Hermenegildo Garcés Maestro: apóstol explorador y mártir de Arizona (1738–1781). Vida y diarios, the figure of this friar fell into oblivion as he was eclipsed by contemporaries such as Junípero Serra, Fermín Lasuén, or Fray Francisco Atanasio Domínguez and Silvestre Vélez de Escalante, the authors of what is known as the “expedition of Domínguez y Escalante” in 1776. This is why Jeremy Beer’s work acquires a special meaning today by rescuing the unjustly forgotten life of Father Garcés from oblivion. In a time when the actions of these missionaries, which were crucial in building Alta California and the region that became the southwestern United States, are being questioned, Beer’s book, Beyond the Devil’s Road: Francisco Garcés and the Spanish encounter with the American Southwest is a profound review of the heroic and iron will of this friar, who risked his life for a Hispanic and evangelizing project.

auditPapers.title: Tecnologías digitales para una arqueología integral: la recreación virtual de la domus del Bailío de Colonia Patricia Corduba
auditPapers.abstract: La documentación digital y en 3D del patrimonio arqueológico se ha convertido en las últimas décadas en una metodología de trabajo indispensable para la generación de conocimiento histórico, tanto en el ámbito científico como para la divulgación. No obstante, su puesta en práctica para el estudio de grandes espacios está condicionada a la conservación de estructuras accesibles y comprensibles desde un punto de vista arqueo-arquitectónico; ello ha llevado en muchas ocasiones a su aplicación mayoritaria en estructuras conservadas al aire libre o en ámbito rural como puedan ser las villae. En este sentido, el presente artículo lleva a cabo una lectura integral arqueo-arquitectónica y de los programas ornamentales de la casa romana de la calle Ramírez de las Casas Deza en Córdoba, denominada como casa del Bailío. Actualmente se conserva bajo el hotel Hospes Palacio del Bailío; el objetivo es definir arqueológica y visualmente las distintas fases de uso de la vivienda. Para tal fin, se ha llevado a cabo la documentación de los restos existentes mediante fotogrametría y aplicando diversas herramientas para el análisis y restitución de los programas ornamentales, como Dstretch y Adobe Illustrator. Junto a esto, los datos planimétricos se han integrado en plano que ha permitido ubicar la vivienda en la planta de la ciudad romana y generar un modelo 3D por fases mediante Blender. Este trabajo se posiciona como pionero en el análisis holístico que comprende un estudio sobre los pavimentos, los programas decorativos, la arquitectura y urbanismo, ofreciéndonos una nueva visión sobre la vivienda a nivel cronológico y constructivo; supone el primer caso aplicado en la ciudad de Córdoba. Ello permite disponer de un recurso de gran valor divulgativo para la comprensión del patrimonio arqueológico cordobés por parte de sus habitantes y visitantes.

auditPapers.title: Tracing ancient artisanal gestures: Digital applications and experimental archaeology on South Italian red-figure pottery production
auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: This paper explores how the integration of computational imaging and experimental archaeology can enhance the understanding of technological practices in South Italian red-figure pottery. Within the framework of the A.G.A.T.H.O.C.L.E.S. Project, funded by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions, this research focuses on the first and second generations of workshops active in Sicily and their connections with Campanian and Paestan ceramic production. Moving beyond traditional stylistic analysis, the study emphasizes the significance of Persistent Signs on Surfaces—such as incisions, brush marks, and pigment residues—as diagnostic indicators of workshop-specific procedures. Digital tools, including Reflectance Transformation Imaging (RTI) and digital portable microscopy, enable the detection and measurement of micro-traces otherwise invisible to the naked eye. When combined with experimental replication, these techniques allow researchers to reconstruct artisanal gestures, test hypotheses on pigment application (including a peculiar red-ochre, notably known as miltos ), and assess the chromatic challenges faced by ancient painters prior to firing. Ultimately, this study argues for a re-humanization of ancient technological processes by foregrounding the embodied experience of craft and the material consciousness of ancient red-figure vases’ painters.

auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: The VETTONIA project is focused on evaluating the rich Iron Age heritage of the western Iberian Peninsula and highlighting the recent archaeological research in the area with advanced technologies: virtual tours, 3D models, and immersive simulations. Its initiatives are presented during the annual archaeological interventions at the oppidum of Ulaca (Solosancho, Ávila, Spain), with excellent response by the attending public.
