auditPapers.title: Charles A. Sepulveda. Native Alienation: Spiritual Conquest and the Violence of California Missions .
auditPapers.abstract: Charles A. Sepulveda’s Native Alienation: Spiritual Conquest and the Violence of California Missions is a welcome addition to the field of mission studies. Sepulveda’s overall contention is that “conquest is gendered and sexualized violence, genocide, and land dispossession, all facilitated in California through spiritual domination, enslavement, and alienation from Native land and heritage” (xiv). The strength of this work is how Sepulveda underlines the strong connection between violability and possessability of Native bodies, souls, and lands. This history is personal for Sepulveda. Like thousands of Tongva-identifying peoples of Southern California, Sepulveda can trace his ancestry through digitized sacramental records of the California missions. Yet the archive is a by-product of the same colonial violence that Sepulveda critically analyzes. Nonetheless, using such records helps to reconnect the past with the present, preserving kinship through the centuries. Sepulveda offers what he calls an “Indigenous reading” of these archival sources, an interpretative approach that centers Native survival and refusal of colonialism (13).

auditPapers.title: Rachel M. Petrocelli. Transactional Culture in Colonial Dakar, 1902–44
auditPapers.abstract: How have cities worked? In one way or another, anyone working in urban studies tries to answer this question. For scholars working in the so-called Global South, one concept often haunts answers to this query: informality. Many observers deploy this term to describe often undocumented economic practices in postcolonial cities that defy the European and North American-based categories that experts use to plan cities and their economies. For decades, Africanists have pushed back against this characterization and the very concept of “informality.” Instead, scholars have explained the logics undergirding urban systems across the continent, calling into question the utility of deeming such complexly organized socioeconomic structures “informal.” However, most works present this alternative urbanism as a contemporary phenomenon or, at best, a product of the postcolonial era, a period that saw unprecedented urbanization across the continent as well as austerity imposed by international economic institutions like the World Bank. Rachel Petrocelli’s new book Transactional Culture deepens this history by looking at the colonial genesis of what she calls a “transactional culture.” In doing so, she reveals how people in colonial Dakar created urban economies rooted more in elaborately managed social relations than official plans.

auditPapers.title: Kit Kowol. Blue Jerusalem: British Conservatism, Winston Churchill, and the Second World War
auditPapers.abstract: The 1945 General Election has cast a long shadow over the history of contemporary Britain. In both popular and scholarly narratives, it is often evoked to tell a particular story about Britain’s wartime experience and the consequences that followed from it. At the center of this story is the idea of Conservative retreat. The apparent collapse of Conservative support at the hands of Clement Attlee’s Labour party, it seemed, signaled a rejection of the party’s assumptions and beliefs. As early as 1969, writers like Angus Calder referred to a “people’s war” that had been marked by a popular enthusiasm for collectivist change. It followed that Conservatism had only survived the 1940s by capitulating to a leftward turn that had rendered its traditional ideas redundant. Blue Jerusalem challenges this story. Prior to polling day in 1945, Kit Kowol argues, Conservatives had been remarkably successful in defending their beliefs and institutions. As well as reinvigorating their party with new ideas, Tories inculcated Britain from an ascendent socialism and introduced policies that had enduring legacies.
topics: World Wars: History, Literature, and Impact

auditPapers.title: Maria R. Montalvo. Enslaved Archives: Slavery, Law, and the Production of the Past
auditPapers.abstract: In Enslaved Archives: Slavery, Law, and the Production of the Past, Maria R. Montalvo poses a deceptively simple question: How did enslavers decide what to write down about the people they treated as property, and how have their choices affected what we can know today? Drawing on an analysis of over eighteen thousand civil court files created in New Orleans between 1813 and 1846—principally warranty disputes governed by Louisiana’s redhibition law and freedom suits—Montalvo argues that the legal archive of slavery was neither incidental nor merely administrative. Instead, she persuasively demonstrates that enslavers purposively constructed it to reduce human beings to fungible assets while foreclosing later efforts to reconstruct their lives. She sees enslavers employing “consistent, deliberate strategies and institutions . . . to control not only the lives of the enslaved but also what parts of their lives we can access from when and where we are now” (8–9). This work builds on Michel-Rolph Trouillot’s critique of archival power and echoes Walter Johnson’s insight that the marketplace can be read for enslaved people’s strategies and choices.

auditPapers.title: Merry E. Wiesner-Hanks. Women and the Reformations: A Global History
auditPapers.abstract: Women and the Reformations: A Global History by Merry Wiesner-Hanks is a broad survey of the experiences of women during the multiple Reformations. auditPapers.title: Keywords in Digital Humanities – A critical assessment of computational techniques for mapping security and freedom in historical debates
auditPapers.abstract: The article investigates the continued importance of keywords in digital humanities and especially their relation to recent machine-learning approaches. Different research practices related to digital humanities agree on the importance of keywords to present issues and/or provide the baseline for new stories about the past, about literature or media. Keywords are useful to target ideas that have no clear definitions and productive in describing contested categorisations that are key to humanities scholarship. At the same time, keywords are often employed used without considering specific contexts and how they are generated. To understand the diversity of keywords in digital humanities, we consider three approaches to computationally generating keywords, from traditional and established ones to state-of-the-art language modelling. With these three approaches, we analyse a case where keywords should be especially powerful, as underlying considerations are uncertain. We cover the relation between security, human-rights and freedom according to discussions in United Nations documents. Finally, we present a number of approaches to productively use keywords to tell a different story about the relation of security and freedom according to UN discussions.

auditPapers.title: Angela K. Parker. Damming the Reservation: Tribal Sovereignty and Activism at Fort Berthold
auditPapers.abstract: Historian Angela K. Parker (Mandan, Hidatsa, and Cree) offers an insightful history of the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation and the development of modern tribal sovereignty in Damming the Reservation: Tribal Sovereignty and Activism at Fort Berthold. This concise narrative introduces readers to the Three Affiliated Tribes that comprise the Fort Berthold Reservation—the Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara—and their adaptations to American colonialism and their own status as American and tribal citizens. Parker describes how EuroAmericans conceptualized sovereignty and applied their theories to Indigenous nations. She argues that colonial nations developed their sovereignty in opposition to the exercise of Indigenous sovereignty over Native homelands. She further explains that Indigenous origin stories legitimate authority over territory and contribute to the creation and continuity of sovereign communities. With this framework, Parker contends that “territories, places, and spaces narrated by our origin stories, populated by our peoples, and transformed through our physical and mental work” underpin modern tribal nations’ sovereignty (5).

auditPapers.title: Procedural Modelling of Aged Buildings: A Case Study of Mudbrick Houses in Cyprus
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Simulating aging effect phenomena on buildings, such as weathering or degradation, is a challenge for computer graphics that may bring great visual value for both realism and analysis of cultural heritage. We propose a system for procedurally generated aged buildings. Our system relies on a finite element analysis, which can simulate a wide range of common construction materials and consider in a simplified way a variety of aging mechanisms such as material degradation, weathering, and climate erosion. It can be fully integrated into any procedural building generator, seamlessly adding weathering effects to buildings as they are constructed. We illustrate the applicability of our method for mudbrick houses, taking typical constructions of Cyprus as a prototype. We analyze simulations according to parameter variations such as the material stiffness or the aging time. We also include internal structural stability for the study. We believe that extending procedural building modelling for aging inclusion could be an interesting avenue for cultural heritage visualization and analysis.

auditPapers.title: Methodologies in Indigenous History
auditPapers.abstract: With the emergence of Native American and Indigenous studies (NAIS) as a discipline in the early 2000s, growing numbers of historians who research and write American Indian and Indigenous histories have drawn from NAIS methodologies.1 This has begun to transform the way historians research and write Indigenous histories and the types of historical narratives that have been published. Yet even with this important methodological turn in the field of Indigenous history, there is still progress to be made at better incorporating NAIS methodologies in history and, for some historians, at recognizing the value of these approaches.2 Excited by the possibilities of this methodological shift in the discipline of history, the American Historical Review organized a roundtable discussion at the AHA’s 2024 conference in San Francisco, California. We assembled six historians whose scholarship successfully draws from both history and NAIS to discuss methodologies in Indigenous history. We then edited our conversation for clarity and cited some scholarship relevant to our discussion.

auditPapers.title: Allen James Fromherz. The Center of the World: A Global History of the Persian Gulf from the Stone Age to the Present
auditPapers.abstract: The Saudi actor and director Hisham Fageeh has described his nation as a digital Pangea, where the local culture and those from around the world interact with one another and sometimes clash, but without the resolving synthesis demanded by the Hegelian dialectic. In the twenty-first century, Fromherz observes, “many parts of the world exist in an economic system similar to the one the people of the Gulf have known for millennia: diversified, service centered, connected to global networks,” and “not dependent on agriculture as a primary industry” (10).

auditPapers.abstract: When the Fort Worth Narcotic Farm opened in 1938, it represented both the enormous expansion of the federal carceral state and the New Deal’s confidence in state solutions to social problems. “At a time when the country was firmly committed to crushing drug use through punitive measures,” writes historian Holly M. auditPapers.title: Gloria McCahon Whiting. Belonging: An Intimate History of Slavery and Family in Early New England .
auditPapers.abstract: In pursuing a project on the intimate lives of enslaved Bostonians, Gloria McCahon Whiting knew she would encounter problems of evidence. What she hadn’t foreseen was that hers would become a challenge not of silence but of “excess” (12). After indexes and catalogs initially turned up dry, Whiting adopted a strategy of exhaustive reading. Working page by page through voluminous probate records, court file papers, church records, diaries, and more, Whiting uncovered a wealth of details. A feat of research, the real mark of Whiting’s success is her ability to connect these fragments to produce richly textured stories of Black New Englanders and the families they made in slavery and freedom. Remarkable as a compendium of stories of enslaved families, Belonging: An Intimate History of Slavery and Family in Early New England deserves equal praise for its interventions into scholarship on slavery, family, and abolition. In the first five chapters of Belonging, Whiting illustrates how African and African-descended New Englanders forged families within the context of a form of smallholding slavery that made family formation challenging. Chapter 1 tells the story of Dorcas, a member of Dorchester’s First Church, who sought the “redemption” of her congregation in the 1650s to join her husband, Matthew, in Boston. Readers of Whiting’s earlier work will be familiar with the subject of chapter 2, the story of Jane and Sebastian, who in 1699 sought Samuel Sewell’s assistance in negotiating with their separate enslavers to marry. Chapter 3 focuses on Sue Black, who was sold as an infant for “the price of a petticoat” and removed from her mother in Boston to grow up enslaved in the seaside town of Manchester (90). In the fourth chapter, Whiting writes of a 1703 marriage between Thomas Bedunah, a freedman of African descent, and Lydia Crafts, an English woman, and how their children and Thomas crossed back and forth over the color line. Finally, chapter 5 considers a case in which Mark, Phillis, and Phoebe were accused of poisoning their master to interrogate the multiple “spheres of belonging” that enslaved people cultivated across nuclear families, communities, and households (156).

auditPapers.title: Vaughn Scribner. Under Alien Skies: Environment, Suffering, and the Defeat of the British Military in Revolutionary America
auditPapers.abstract: Despite nearly 250 years of historical study of the American War of Independence, scholars continue to find new lines of inquiry into the conflict. Vaughn Scribner’s Under Alien Skies: Environment, Suffering, and the Defeat of the British Military in Revolutionary America provides an example of how historians can examine a seemingly well-worn topic and offer fresh insights with new methodologies. In this case, Scribner interprets British and German soldiers’ wartime experiences through the lens of environmental history. Scribner argues that the encounter with the unfamiliar, threatening, and hazardous North American environment, the titular “Alien Skies,” undermined Crown soldiers’ morale and contributed to their failure to subdue the American rebellion. The author constructs “environment” broadly, with thematic chapters covering the experience of sailing to the New World; contending with the continent’s physical landscapes; grappling with its unfamiliar flora and fauna; suffering through its climate, weather, and diseases; dealing with the depression and anxiety resulting from service; and finally readjusting to civilian life after returning to Europe. Scribner covers an expansive geography in exploring these themes, gathering accounts from soldiers who deployed to theaters ranging from Quebec and New England to the Caribbean and Central America. The author also rightly recognizes that environment is not synonymous with “wilderness” or rural areas, and that urban places, too, constitute important environmental systems. The book thus devotes as much attention to soldiers garrisoned in New York and Newport as it does to those stationed in Canadian forests or Carolina swamps.

auditPapers.title: Involuntary Investors in British State-Building: Seamen’s Tickets and the Financial Revolution c .1700–1760
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article investigates the relationship between government liquidity, personal credit, and state practices in eighteenth-century Britain, drawing on a case study of seamen’s tickets: promises on paper issued to sailors by the Royal Navy to collect their wages at a future date. Because it was normal for tickets to remain unpaid for years, mariners and their households often sold them. To do so, they relied on an industry akin to modern payday lending. Tickets circulated within maritime communities and beyond, forming a financial market that existed in the shadows of the formal commercial paper economy sanctioned by the state. This article traces the contours of the ticket market in terms of its value, its actors, and its dynamics, as a crucial part of the invention of financial capitalism. It argues that British state-building and imperial expansion depended upon the involuntary investments of maritime labourers, whose wage debts were one of the largest categories of public debt in the eighteenth century. Focusing on the ticket trade expands the peripheries of Britain’s Financial Revolution, but it also complicates the agency and aspirations of the investors involved.

auditPapers.title: Adolfo Polo y La Borda. Global Servants of the Spanish King: Mobility and Cosmopolitanism in the Early Modern Spanish Empire
auditPapers.abstract: Today, Juan de Oñate is best known for leading the Spanish entrada into northern New Mexico at the end of the sixteenth century, a campaign that saw his men attack Acoma Pueblo where they killed 800 people, severed the feet of many adult men, and enslaved hundreds of survivors. Global Servants of the Spanish King: Mobility and Cosmopolitanism in the Early Modern Spanish Empire reveals that this expedition was a short episode in Oñate’s lifetime of service to the Spanish Crown as a mining expert. Oñate was born and raised in the mining center Zacatecas, and served as alcalde mayor of Mesquitique Potosí, the mining district, before his infamous expedition. In its aftermath, King Philip IV appointed him general inspector of Spanish mines in a wider effort to mobilize Novohispano knowledge to develop European mining. This is one of the book’s many examples of imperial careering that illustrate “the astonishing capacity (even by contemporary standards) of men and women to move across various regions” (2) in the service of the Spanish Crown. Imperial careering also challenges assumptions about how individuals and knowledge circulated in the Spanish empire, and the consequences of this mobility for how the empire was organized and conceptualized.

auditPapers.title: James M. Brophy. Print Markets and Political Dissent in Central Europe: Publishers in Central Europe, 1800–1870
auditPapers.abstract: James M. Brophy’s new monograph Print Markets and Political Dissent: Publishers in Central Europe, 1800–1870 is an impressive model of careful historical research based on extensive archival and printed sources from across the region. The book at once draws on and contributes to business, social, and cultural history, as well as the history of political thought. Brophy puts the spotlight on German publishers as innovative “entrepreneurs” who not only profited from the massive growth in readership in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries but also helped create that market and served as a necessary foundation for the flourishing of German literature and culture in that era (4). As he emphasizes, the growth of this market helped launch the careers of freelance authors in place of earlier court-centered patronage systems, and this, in turn, helped establish the importance of public opinion, whether in matters of taste or politics. Brophy goes on to investigate what he identifies as “the drama of early nineteenth-century print capitalism: the tension that lay between state authority and print markets” (9). The ongoing struggles between publishers and writers, on the one hand, and state censorship apparatuses, on the other, thus take center stage in the book. Brophy emphasizes the commercial and legal risks involved for publishers attempting to evade or contest the official bans and lauds the civic courage of those who made the effort. The publishers, he concludes, generally found clever ways to disseminate forbidden views in print, but the censors and officials could also point to successes in their campaign to stem that tide.

auditPapers.title: Sebastian Giessmann. The Connectivity of Things: Network Cultures Since 1832
auditPapers.abstract: The notion of the “network society” has been with us ever since a number of social scientists, most famously Manuel Castells, popularized the term in the 1990s. Social science studies of network societies, however, have often been criticized by historians, who have been dissatisfied with the lack of deeper interpretations of how network societies and network cultures emerged and evolved over longer periods of time. From this perspective, German media theorist Sebastian Giessmann’s book The Connectivity of Things: Network Cultures Since 1832 is a very welcome addition to the literature. The book was originally published in German a decade ago, but the English version is more than just a translation, as it includes references to recent events such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Giessmann, who identifies himself as an “East German dissertation writer,” compares a variety of network cultures and examines how they have taken shape over the centuries. The book astonishingly weaves together seemingly disparate human activities in science, technology, economics, and culture that at first glance may appear incompatible, but on closer inspection turn out to be related.

auditPapers.title: Lynn Hunt. The Revolutionary Self: Social Change and the Emergence of the Modern Individual, 1770–1800
auditPapers.abstract: Looking back, in 1797, at nearly a decade of revolutionary tumult, Charles-Guillaume Théremin memorably described what the French Revolution meant for those who had survived it thus far: “[E]veryone generally has been displaced from their original situation, and no one is what he was in 1789 or what, in the balance sheet of his life, he expected to be in 1796” (66-7). The observation, which Lynn Hunt cites midway through The Revolutionary Self, can be taken as the charter for the book as a whole. As Hunt acknowledges in her introduction, she is far from the first historian to address the impact that the French Revolution had on conceptions of individuality and selfhood. The novelty in her account lies in her suggestion that the emancipatory individualism of the period went hand in hand with the discovery of the shaping force of “society” and “social change” in a dialectical process for which the Revolution provided a spectacular demonstration-effect: “This book is about the origins of that paradox: the simultaneous discovery that individuals had a capacity for autonomy and that society had the power to sculpt that individuality” (2).

auditPapers.title: Nick Lloyd. The Eastern Front: A History of the Great War, 1914–1918
auditPapers.abstract: Nick Lloyd’s new book The Eastern Front: A History of the Great War, 1914–1918 is the second book in a trilogy covering the First World War, following the 2021 book The Western Front: A History of the Great War, 1914–1918, and to be followed by a subsequent volume on the wider war. As a result, the division of coverage across the three volumes is necessarily somewhat arbitrary. The Eastern Front naturally includes the Russian front, but in addition spends extensive time covering the Italian, Serbian, Salonika, and Romanian fronts. He begins with the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and carries the narrative through the Russian Revolution, and up to the final collapse of Austria-Hungary in the final months of the war. The campaigns in Africa, the Caucasus, Mesopotamia, and Gallipoli are left for the next volume. In trying to encompass a conflict as enormous as the First World War, even with three volumes of space with which to work, Lloyd has to choose the themes and aspects to emphasize. This is not to criticize his work for not being comprehensive, but instead to identify what he cares about. The best way to summarize the task Lloyd has set for himself is a chronicle: a strongly chronological, narrative story of decision-making by the highest-level military and political leadership on all sides. He has admirably sought out the primary sources to cover the military leadership of all belligerents, not merely the relatively well-known leaders of, say, Germany, Austria, and Russia. Italy, Serbia, Bulgaria, and Romania are fully represented, as are the British and French commanders of the seemingly remote and obscure Salonika front. Lloyd’s characteristic method of composition is to present generals and political leaders in their own words as they lay out their tactical and operational thinking, deciding when and how to risk their scarce and war-weary soldiers in new offensives. As a result, his book presents a vivid portrait of the personalities, pathological or otherwise, of the key commanders of all parties. His extensive use of their testimony is vivid and compelling. Despite the emphasis on military calculations, the book does not offer a particularly clear operational narrative. While it includes a number of maps, they do not offer much in the way of tactical and operational insight, and the military narratives do not provide much clarity.

auditPapers.title: Megan Moran. Gender and Family Networks in Early Modern Italy
auditPapers.abstract: Gender and Family Networks in Early Modern Italy offers a punctiliously researched archival study that also engages a broad sweep of modern scholarship relating to early modern women’s writing, family networks, and the interconnections between domestic and political realms of action. Moran intervenes in conversations at the vanguard of the historical field, contributing in particular to ongoing efforts to problematize “patriarchy.” Strange to say, even decades after Joan W. Scott’s field-transforming and now ubiquitously cited article “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis” (American Historical Review 91, no. 5 [1986]: 1053–75), scholars still have a tendency to conceptualize patriarchy as monolithic, failing to account for historical variability. Moran attends to those specificities and nuances exceedingly well, in a richly documented way. Several of the book’s chapters build productively on well-established lines of inquiry in Italian history, adding new and valuable empirical evidence to our current knowledge bases. Chapter 1, on women’s networking in their various capacities as wives, mothers, and widows, and chapter 3, on women’s associational work regularly breaching convent walls, offer fabulous new protagonists for us to consider as we continue to explore women’s active and positive contributions even in the face of premodern gender norms and patriarchal legal and social structures. These chapters, as Moran robustly acknowledges, in a way retrace interpretive tracks found in (among many others) Heather Gregory’s pathbreaking work on the redoubtable Florentine merchant’s widow, relentless network builder, and grassroots politician Alessandra Strozzi. So, too, there has been a flood of research in recent years on cloistered women’s cultural, medical, and political production, with K. J. P. Lowe’s magisterial Nuns’ Chronicles and Convent Culture: Women and History Writing in Renaissance and Counter-Reformation Italy (2003) and Sharon T. Strocchia’s Forgotten Healers: Women and the Pursuit of Healing in Late Renaissance Italy (2019) as just two instances of that important trend. auditPapers.title: Lori D. Ginzberg. Tangled Journeys: One Family’s Story and the Making of American History
auditPapers.abstract: Lori D. Ginzberg’s Tangled Journeys: One Family’s Story and the Making of American History traces the family lineage of Sarah Martha Sanders (1815–1850) and Richard Walpole Cogdell (1787–1866) from colonial Jamaica to South Carolina to post–World War II Philadelphia. It tells “competing stories, both traumatic and prosaic” of the Charleston slave owner Cogdell, and Sanders, the enslaved teenager who bore his children (121). Tangled Journeys is engrossing as a genealogy, pulling on tiny threads across centuries to build a coherent narrative of interconnected Black and white families, but Ginzberg presses against the usual narrative frame, confessing to the guesswork involved and inviting the reader to acknowledge their own interpretive role in telling “these stories together, while also telling them apart” (2). What Tangled Journeys reveals from Ginzberg’s deep readings of government documents, newspapers, and a remarkable family collection of letters, deeds, scrapbooks, bits of paper, and photographs, is the profound impact Sanders had on her children’s sense of possibility. “What Sarah Martha Sanders wrenched from her own commodification and abuse,” Ginzberg argues, “epitomizes resistance itself” (66). Joining scholars of nineteenth-century Black women’s social and intellectual history like Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham, Michele Mitchell, and Treva B. Lindsey, Ginzberg centers the lived experience of women whose names may not be well known, but whose commitments to one another, to their communities, and their faith have sustained Black Americans amid systematic oppression for centuries.

auditPapers.title: Stefanie Fischer and Kim Wünschmann. Illustrated by Liz Clarke. Oberbrechen: A German Village Confronts its Nazi Past .
auditPapers.abstract: Within the dense historiographical landscape of Holocaust studies, unexplored topics continue to come into focus alongside methodological innovations, the use of more visual and similarly accessible mediums, and a greater emphasis on inclusivity and contemporary relevance. The newest title in Oxford University Press’s Graphic History Series is a significant contribution to Holocaust and German Jewish studies, employing a microhistorical approach to the graphic storytelling format. Using three distinct mediums, the book chronicles the events of the Holocaust and its aftermath in a small village in western Germany, largely through the everyday encounters of Jewish and non-Jewish (mostly Catholic) residents, across several decades and generations. Fischer and Wünschmann maintain that the history of the Holocaust is not solely a story of grand political narratives and centralized state actions but also one deeply embedded in the everyday lives and local dynamics of seemingly ordinary communities.

auditPapers.title: J. Barton Scott. Slandering the Sacred: Blasphemy Law and Religious Affect in Colonial India
auditPapers.abstract: The publication of the Arya Samaj tract Rangila Rasool (Merry Prophet) in 1924 caused a stir in colonial India and led to the promulgation of Article 295A in 1927 to protect not religion as much as “religious feelings.” In Slandering the Sacred, J. Barton Scott takes readers on a quest to unpack the law’s origins, which he argues are not antithetical to liberalism or secularism, but very much rooted in these ideas. In the process, he helps us understand the term “secularism” itself as not just religious freedom, but quite as much the regulation of religious feeling and affect by the state. Scott meticulously details the emergence of what it terms “governmental” or “penal” secularism in colonial India as a means to contain and manage interreligious discord rather than conferring religious rights. Postcolonial India, which adopted secularism as a constitutional principle, rendered blasphemy a crime not against religion, but against secularism. The colonial and postcolonial states, thus, provided the language for groups to “inhabit outrage as legally actionable feeling,” thereby exacerbating the very conflict that the law set out to regulate (75).

auditPapers.title: Ann-Marie Foster. Family Mourning After War and Disaster in Twentieth-Century Britain.
auditPapers.abstract: In Family Mourning After War and Disaster in Twentieth-Century Britain, Ann-Marie Foster gives nuanced consideration to the emotional effect of mass-death events on surviving family members. The insertion of state or local bureaucracies disrupted preexisting family-centered death and mourning practices. auditPapers.title: Nancy S. Kollman. Visualizing Russia in Early Modern Europe
auditPapers.abstract: Between the early sixteenth and the mid-seventeenth century, European publishers in cities like London, Amsterdam, Gottorf, Augsburg, and Venice created a shared repertoire of images, words, maps, and tropes describing Russians and the peoples of Siberia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia. These representations were based increasingly on the first-hand accounts of European travelers who went to, and often through, Muscovy in pursuit of diplomatic and commercial ventures. With Visualizing Russia in Early Modern Europe, Nancy S. Kollmann identifies this conjuncture of encounter and a burgeoning print culture to explore why, how, and with what consequences societies west of Poland-Lithuania came to value new cartographic and ethnographic information about regions further east. She convincingly argues that a range of actors—courtiers, diplomats, merchants, engravers, and printers—contributed to and drew from stock representations to communicate information to European audiences. These actors articulated and sustained the durable idea that Russia and its peoples are sort of European but not quite, representing an ambiguous middle ground between East and West. Painstakingly tracing the trajectory of specific images and tropes through a thicket of publications, Kollmann reveals how these actors’ particular interests inflected the representations they sold. Business boomed. Russia was malleable.

auditPapers.title: Polly Zavadivker. A Nation of Refugees: Russia’s Jews in World War I
auditPapers.abstract: During the Russian Civil War between 1917 and 1921, White Russian armies and Ukrainian and Polish troops massacred at least fifty thousand Jews in western Ukraine and eastern Poland. The degree and extent of the violence specifically directed against Jewish civilians appeared unprecedented. Jews were targeted as collaborators of different enemies and soldiers systematically raped Jewish women, killed Jewish children, and looted homes and stores, often encouraging bystanders to join in the violence. Another feature of these attacks stands out: the post-1917 pogroms were often instigated by representatives of newly founded states and warlords. Several scholars who have examined the pogroms during the Russian Civil War in recent years have drawn a line to the Holocaust. Curiously, apart from Semion Goldin’s The Russian Army and the Jewish Population, 1914–1917 (2022) little has been written about violent attacks the Russian military committed against Jewish civilians before 1918. Even less was known about Jewish life during the war.

auditPapers.title: Christin L. Hancock. Unmentionable Madness: Gender, Disability, and Shame in the Malaria Treatment of Neurosyphilis
auditPapers.abstract: Christin L. Hancock’s Unmentionable Madness: Gender, Disability, and Shame in the Malaria Treatment of Neurosyphilis deftly explains why families and physicians, and sometimes patients, sought an excruciating, painful experimental procedure—malaria therapy—to try and cure neurosyphilis, which very rarely, if ever truly, led to success. Hancock brings a historical lens to questions that often feel impossible to answer because of their emotional weight: When and how do physicians recognize the failure of their proposed treatments for terminal illnesses? Why do families or patients consent to see out treatments that might prove more harmful than therapeutic? What qualifies as consent concerning patients with mental health issues? How do social meanings about abled and disabled bodies drive decisions? What role do perceptions of race and gender play in determining who gets what type of care and why? Hancock addresses these questions by studying a forgotten therapy of ultimately dubious efficacy at the Central State Hospital (CSH) in Indianapolis, Indiana, in the 1920s and 1930s. In doing so, she gives voice to the men and women, both white and Black, whose incarcerated bodies became research subjects and stitches their stories back into the historical record from which they were silenced.

auditPapers.title: Jennifer Ngaire Heuer. The Soldier’s Reward: Love and War in the Age of the French Revolution and Napoleon
auditPapers.abstract: Should soldiers marry? This question runs through The Soldier’s Reward, in which Jennifer Ngaire Heuer ably weaves political, social, and cultural histories of military service from the Old Regime to the Restoration. The issue was already under debate in enlightened circles in the decades preceding the Revolution, as discussed in chapter 1. The naturalist Jean-Baptiste Robinet argued that soldiering was incompatible with family life: “A bachelor soldier has married war” (33). He was opposed by Voltaire and Louis-Sébastien Mercier: Without someone to fight for, soldiers degenerated into vagabond mercenaries. As the former expressed it, “Tied to their families, they will also be tied to their patrie” (35). The Crown, worried about economic obligations to soldiers’ dependents, did not agree. The Revolution transformed the situation. Soldiers were now citizens who had rights including, once past their majority (reduced to twenty-one), the right to marry. The surge of “volunteers” in 1792–93 also brought thousands of married men into the armed forces. Given the republic’s inability to meet its own promises about supporting the families of absent soldiers, many volunteers’ wives accompanied them, sometimes in uniform themselves. Such women were, according to Lazare Carnot, a drain on resources and morale, and they were mostly expelled in April 1793, in what Heuer calls the “first demobilization” (65) of the revolutionary wars.

auditPapers.title: Ellen Hartigan-O’Connor. America Under the Hammer: Auctions and the Emergence of Market Values .
auditPapers.abstract: In our age of tariffs and greedflation, prices have never been more newsworthy, at least since the 1970s. But what actually is a price? Is it a value? A signal? A fantasy? America Under the Hammer: Auctions and the Emergence of Market Values is a history of early American auctions, but it is also a history of price as seen through the lens of those auctions. In her exciting new book, Ellen Hartigan-O’Connor makes a timely contribution to a growing literature that aims to historicize the capitalist relations we take as givens, from enclosure and commodification to monetization. With a focus on price, and closely attentive to the changing dynamics of gender and race, Hartigan-O’Connor breaks new ground and troubles old myths about property, supply and demand, and the “freedom” of choice. As Hartigan-O’Connor illuminates across six chapters, the notion that the price of a thing is its value has not always been a hard-and-fast truth. Rather, Americans’ equation of value with price was the outcome of a 150-year struggle over the nature of value itself. Over time, competing regimes of value “that allowed some things to be fungible and others not” gave way to the belief that everything and every life was reducible to a number, an economic fact, as it were (7). Auctions dramatized this alchemy. A constant fixture and emblematic institution of American markets through the end of the nineteenth century, auctions, more so than other modes of exchange, made visible the complex ways that nature, objects, people, and labor came to be regarded as commodities. But commodification was neither inevitable nor uncontested. On the contrary, the author argues, auctions served as spaces where “communities could sort out their ideas about value” (10). Though instituted by law and authority, their fundamentally social dimension demanded public participation in the production of economic knowledge.

auditPapers.title: Donald L. Fixico. The State of Sequoyah: Indigenous Sovereignty and the Quest for an Indian State
auditPapers.abstract: Donald L. Fixico has penned a concise and well-argued analysis of a statehood movement that has received little scholarly attention despite its importance as an overt expression of tribal sovereignty in pre-statehood Oklahoma. In The State of Sequoyah, Fixico demonstrates that, although efforts to form an Indigenous state proved unsuccessful, much can be gained by examining the historical context that spawned the movement. Heretofore relegated to a footnote in the march toward Oklahoma statehood, in this volume the State of Sequoyah takes center stage as a unique union of Indian and non-Indian partners in an attempt to thwart the aims of state and federal forces bent on imposing statehood upon a largely unwilling (or at least ambivalent) Native populace. Fixico begins by tracing the removals of the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee, and Seminole nations to Indian Territory and the alterations each made to its political structure as a consequence of forced relocation. While all five tribes remained matrilineal culturally, they reoriented themselves to function as patriarchal political systems similar to those of American states. This shift in governmental systems coincided with a more collective mindset of the Five Tribes brought about by conflicts with Native nations already occupying Indian Territory and later by a need to resist non-Indian incursions onto their reservations. Ironically, the same federal government that ultimately quashed plans for a separate Indian polity helped foster Native solidarity by sponsoring a series of intertribal councils in Indian Territory beginning in the 1830s. Apparently, the Great Father encouraged Native unity only up to a certain point and no farther.

auditPapers.title: Rachel Louise Moran. Blue: A History of Postpartum Depression in America
auditPapers.abstract: In Blue: A History of Postpartum Depression in America, Rachel Louise Moran offers an illuminating cultural and political history of postpartum mental illness. As the author notes from the outset, the book’s title term refers to a specific depressive disorder as well as to a wider constellation of conditions that manifest after birth, including depression, anxiety, mania, and psychosis. The naming and grouping together of these illnesses under one umbrella term, Moran argues, was the culmination of decades of activism carried out by grassroots and professional advocates, clinicians, and researchers. Braiding together a wide range of sources, including women’s magazines, medical publications, media coverage, parenting guides, and over thirty oral histories, Moran skillfully narrates this story of women’s suffering, treatment, and advocacy across ten chapters spanning the 1950s to the 2020s. The book opens in the post–World War II years, when a psychoanalytic medical discourse largely infantilized women troubled with the “baby blues,” framing their distress as a sign of immaturity. Popular advice, reflecting an expanding consumer culture of the era, encouraged women that a quick shopping trip and taking prescription “mood brightening” drugs like Ritalin would ease their adjustment to motherhood (32). With the rise of the feminist movement in the 1960s and 1970s, more women spoke out about their painful childbirth and motherhood experiences, linking their frustrations to broader critiques of social conditions—medical sexism, inadequate public resources for parents, and prescribed gender roles—that demanded reimagining. Such pointed challenges fueled feminist activism around a host of issues, including abortion, birth control, and child-rearing, but it was not until the 1980s that a movement focused on raising awareness about postpartum mental illness gained ground. Women organized support groups across the country, and an international network of, mostly male, psychiatrists pushed their profession to recognize the hormonal basis of postpartum conditions. These overlapping campaigns were part of a larger “quest for legitimacy,” as Moran characterizes it, with women increasingly turning to medical language to articulate their suffering (14).

auditPapers.title: Elise Franklin. Disintegrating Empire: Algerian Family Migration and the Limits of the Welfare State in France

auditPapers.title: Kate Merkel-Hess. Women and Their Warlords: Domesticating Militarism in Modern China
auditPapers.abstract: Standard narratives of China’s twentieth century typically minimize the lasting influence of the men who dominated politics following the 1911 collapse of the imperial system and preceding the rise of the Leninist party-state in the late 1920s. When mentioned at all, these men—usually characterized as junfa in Chinese, or “warlords”—are caricatured in a variety of cartoonish ways: some honorable and heroic, others petty and vicious. One of their only unifying characteristics is that their actions villainously split the nation apart, in contrast to heroic leaders like Mao Zedong or Chiang Kai-shek, who (depending on the historian) are often portrayed as struggling to unify China. The only thing more overlooked and understudied in the historiography of these warlords might be women in their orbit. In Women and Their Warlords: Domesticating Militarism in Modern China, Kate Merkel-Hess weaves together a wide range of sources to reconstruct the impact of these figures, both in their own time and after. While the literature has commonly implied that these warlords were overly concerned with material and military matters, or might have been shortsighted in managing their public image, Merkel-Hess shows that this is not the case. Furthermore, her book makes the long-overdue intervention of showing how stories about these men and women capture the attention of the Chinese public, both then and now, as historical myth and popular fiction. In other words, Merkel-Hess paints an empathetic portrait of her elusive subjects’ lives while simultaneously illustrating how they resonate in the present day as symbols of national duty, romantic love, and filial piety.

auditPapers.title: Caitlin Keliiaa. Refusing Settler Domesticity: Native Women’s Labor and Resistance in the Bay Area Outing Program
auditPapers.abstract: In Refusing Settler Domesticity: Native Women’s Labor and Resistance in the Bay Area Outing Program, Caitlin Keliiaa offers readers an intimate window into the lives of Native women who worked as domestic servants in the Bay Area in the early twentieth century. Analyzing over four thousand archival records, she pieces together the history of the Bay Area Outing Program (BAOP), which existed between 1918 and 1942. Outing programs worked with federal boarding schools to assimilate Native youth into settler culture and prepare them for work in the laboring classes. In consensus with recent scholarship on federal boarding schools and urban relocation, Keliiaa argues that, although these kinds of assimilation programs sought to eradicate Native culture and confine Native people to menial labor, participants resisted constraints on their lives and carved out futures for themselves while creating intertribal communities all over the United States. As a Yerington Paiute and Washoe tribal member who grew up in the Bay Area, Keliiaa approaches this project as a scholar and a descendent of women who participated in the BAOP. As such, the book connects the contemporary urban Indigenous community to the women who took up domestic work in the Bay in the early twentieth century in the homes of wealthy Bay Area families. The girls and women who took these posts did so for a variety of reasons. Some were teenage girls from boarding schools gaining experience in domestic labor, others were mothers who needed to earn wages for their families. In either case, the women who took these roles earned 47 percent less than the national average. They also navigated significant restrictions on their bodily autonomy, including curfews and sexual surveillance. Breaking expectations sometimes led to incarceration, child removal, and forced sterilization. Despite these challenges, women sought this work to earn wages for their families, experience the excitement of city life, and find community with other Native women. Keliiaa makes the case that these domestic workers were responsible for the first Native community organization in the Bay Area, the Four Winds Club, founded in the 1930s.

auditPapers.title: Ana María Otero-Cleves. Plebeian Consumers: Global Connections, Local Trade, and Foreign Goods in Nineteenth-Century Colombia .
auditPapers.abstract: There are many pleasures in reading Plebeian Consumers: Global Connections, Local Trade, and Foreign Goods in Nineteenth-Century Colombia. One is the writing. Ana María Otero-Cleves presents her arguments with clear and direct prose, even in sections touching on theory-driven social science literature. Another is that this is a material history grounded in considerations of political economy and social agency that does not drift into anthropomorphizing market forces, an unfortunate tendency in some works representing the new history of capital. Further, the study addresses a yawning historiographical gap. Though it has been decades since Benjamin Orlove’s The Allure of the Foreign: Imported Goods in Postcolonial Latin America (1997), few historians working on nineteenth-century Latin America have addressed the questions posed in that collection. There have been notable works on export commodities, cartography, and material culture, but little on imports and even less on people in Latin America as consumers with agency. Finally, the study contributes to the collective effort of moving beyond the conceptualization of Latin America as peripheral, a place subordinate to the core world regions that produced ideas, politics, and manufactured goods. Colombianists have made numerous contributions to this effort, but the focus has been on politics and ideas, not material culture. This examination of how Colombians—plebian, elite, and those somewhere in between—made choices as consumers based on their own tastes and understanding, and the implications of those choices for manufacturers in the United States, Great Britain, and France, is revelatory.

auditPapers.title: Seán Ó Hoireabhárd. The Medieval Irish Kings and the English Invasion
auditPapers.abstract: Modern scholarship has turned the year 1169 into either the start or end date of all studies of medieval Ireland. Such is the main point of Seán Ó Hoireabhárd’s first book The Medieval Irish Kings and the English Invasion, and it is an endeavor to disrupt this practice. This massive tome’s focus is the political (regnal power and relations) histories of the three “major kingdoms or hegemonies” on Inis Fáil during the twelfth century, when the island was invaded and English settler colonists first established their hold. These hegemons are Munster (Mumu), Connacht (Connachta), and The North (An Túaiscert). His preferred sources are the Gaelic annals, of which there are many, and thus he argues that they should be the main source for the history of Gaelic regnal politics. The book begins with a short mise-en-scène of events from 1167–71, a methodology chapter, and a historiography chapter. Next is section 1, “Connacht and the Shannon,” giving minute details about the rise of the Uí Chonchobhair and then a brief overview about the transition from the most powerful overking to English vassals. The latter has been covered in fine detail by Helen Walton (“The English in Connacht, 1171–1333,” PhD thesis, Trinity College Dublin, 1980) and Freya Verstraten (“Both King and Vassal: Feidlim Ua Conchobair of Connacht, 1230–65,” GAHS 55 [2003]: 13–37), so he does not need to rehash it here, but he should have cited them. Then comes section 2, “The Uí Néill and the North,” where the author covers the “phoney war” of Muirchertach Úa Briain and Domnall Mac Lochlainn (1088–1114); the fall of Uí Néill supremacy and the splintering of Uí Néill hegemony into several parts; and John de Courcy’s difficulties expanding his new colony. Section 3, “Munster and Leth Moga,” begins with the origins and origin legends of the dramatis personae, then pushes the study back to Cennéitig mac Lorcáin in 944 and traces the several rises and falls of the Dál Cais, ending with an examination of the historiographical depiction of Úa Briain-Mac Carthaigh relations. As another scholar who believes in providing copious detail, I think that these sections greatly support the arguments in the rest of the book and even could benefit from more context for the nonexpert reader.

auditPapers.title: Prithi Kanakamedala. Brooklynites: The Remarkable Story of the Free Black Communities that Shaped a Borough
auditPapers.abstract: The borough of Brooklyn as we know it today began its life as one of six former colonial towns in Kings County on the western tip of Long Island. The town itself was strategically located across the East River opposite the growing city of New York. However, unlike its more economically developed neighbor, Kings County remained largely agricultural, holding on to racialized slavery long after other emerging Northern urban areas were turning away from unfree labor. For example, the 1790 census reveals that about 33 percent of people of African descent in Manhattan were free compared to only 3 percent in Kings County. This is where Prithi Kanakamedala begins her study of Brooklyn’s free Black community. Brooklynites: The Remarkable Story of the Free Black Communities that Shaped a Borough focuses on the period between the end of the American Revolution and the beginning of Reconstruction. This was a time of transformation as Brooklyn grew from a village within a town to become the third-largest city in the nation. It was also a period when small but thriving free Black communities coexisted alongside bound labor. Brooklynites presents a social and cultural history of these communities as they created benevolent societies to meet their communal needs, schools to educate their children, and houses of worship to express their faith.

auditPapers.title: Isaac Stanley-Becker. Europe without Borders: A History
auditPapers.abstract: In Europe without Borders: A History, Isaac Stanley-Becker sets out to reframe the history of the Schengen Agreement as a foundational moment in European integration. According to the author, Schengen marked a departure from the market-oriented logic of the Treaty of Rome and reconnected with a humanistic paradigm of cross-border mobility rooted in personal liberty, rights, and cosmopolitan ideals. Stanley-Becker’s central claim is that Schengen redefined the freedom of movement in Europe by classifying its bearers not merely as workers but as persons, thereby elevating mobility to a symbol of democratic citizenship. This account ultimately founders on serious conceptual, empirical, and historiographical grounds. The book conflates distinct legal and political categories, misrepresents the chronology and substance of European mobility law, and bypasses the very scholarship it purports to supersede. Though elegantly written and occasionally insightful, Europe without Borders offers a misleading portrait of a well-studied subject and fails to deliver the archival and analytical rigor expected in a scholarly monograph.

auditPapers.title: Exploring chemical vs. enzymatic hydrolysis for fatty acid profiling of drying oils by liquid chromatography with high-resolution mass spectrometry
auditPapers.abstract: • Complete data on composition of free and total fatty acids in common drying oils. • Information on position and geometry (cis/trans) of C C double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids by a mild epoxidation reaction. • Comparison between Candida rugosa enzymatic and chemical hydrolysis. • Chemical hydrolysis in the presence of metal traces promoted isomerization, generating additional unsaturated species. Drying oils, rich in triacylglycerols with unsaturated fatty acyl chains, are widely used in artworks for their ability to transform them into cross-linked polymer networks upon exposure to oxygen, forming protective layers. However, over time, ester bond hydrolysis releases fatty acids (FAs) that can aggregate, migrate, and interact with pigments, causing artwork degradation. Understanding the lipid profiles of siccative oils is critical for preserving cultural heritage. This study investigated the composition of free and total FAs in common drying oils, including safflower ( Carthamus tinctorius ), linseed ( Linum usitatissimum L.), walnut ( Juglans regia ), and poppy seed ( Papaver somniferum ), using reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC) coupled with electrospray ionisation (ESI) and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) and tandem HRMS (MS/MS). To determine the position and geometry ( cis/trans ) of C C double bonds in unsaturated FAs, a mild epoxidation reaction with meta -chloroperoxybenzoic acid was applied. Oils were analysed under three conditions: without prior hydrolysis, after enzymatic hydrolysis using Candida rugosa lipase (0.25 mg enzyme per mL of extracted sample, incubated at 37 °C for 45 minutes), or following chemical hydrolysis (0.5 M HCl, 100 °C, 1 h). The results demonstrate clear differences between hydrolysis methods: chemical hydrolysis induced isomerisation in the presence of metal traces, yielding additional unsaturated species compared to enzymatic hydrolysis. These transformations were characterised by MS/MS diagnostic ions of FA epoxides and their retention times. To preserve the native FA profile and minimise artefacts, enzymatic hydrolysis or mild chemical conditions are recommended, with C. rugosa lipase providing a reliable reference standard. This approach was successfully applied to a 1970s oil-on-canvas painting by F. Rispoli, revealing lipid alterations associated with aging.

Additionally, British bankers frustrated American authorities by refusing to pay their overseas officials in dollars. auditPapers.title: Bethany Hughes. Redface: Race, Performance, and Indigeneity
auditPapers.abstract: Even today, the image of a muscular, bare-chested man in a feathered headdress remains instantly recognizable as “Indian.” How has this racialized portrayal been constructed and sustained in American culture? Why can we so easily identify what is performed as Indian while overlooking the continued presence of Indigenous peoples, nations, and cultures? Bethany Hughes’s Redface: Race, Performance, and Indigeneity responds to these long-standing questions by examining nineteenth- and twentieth-century American theater as a central site via which theatrical artists and audiences collaboratively defined “Indianness” through redface. This racial impersonation produced the Stage Indian—a curated, repeatedly performed figure in Indian plays that trained audiences to recognize the “Indian” on and off stage. Hughes’s analysis builds on substantial scholarship, including Robert F. Berkhofer Jr.’s The White Man’s Indian: Images of the American Indian from Columbus to the Present (1978) and Philip J. Deloria’s Playing Indian (1998) examining how Euro-Americans defined themselves through constructing and circulating stereotypical representations of Native Americans. Hughes extends this tradition by incorporating Chickasaw scholar Jodi Byrd’s view of representation as an imperial project that racializes and regulates Indigenous bodies. She illustrates that redface is not merely about costume and makeup; it is a settler colonial mechanism that erases Indigeneity, denies Indigenous sovereignty, and enacts the belief that the “Indian” is a vanishing race. Her extensive archival research, including theatrical posters, choreographic notes, and legal cases, combined with interdisciplinary insights, results in Redface, a provocative study that exposes the political and cultural dynamics that delimit and discipline Indigenous presence.

auditPapers.title: Lindsay M. Chervinsky. Making the Presidency: John Adams and the Precedents that Forged the Republic
auditPapers.abstract: Law reviews, courts, and podiums in the United States are alive with the sound of unbridled presidential authority, asserting an ever more imperial and unitary executive vested with authority to make and unmake law on matters foreign and domestic. Often these claims gesture toward a historical foundation, dressing up a drive for power with purported original meanings. The distance between this presidentialism, in practice and in the constitutional stories it summons, and the beleaguered presidency of John Adams is yawning—a discontinuity that confronts readers throughout Lindsay M. Chervinsky’s engaging political biography, Making the Presidency: John Adams and the Precedents that Forged the Republic. Chervinsky presents a sympathetic examination of the first post-Washington president through close attention to the wrangling and scheming of early national statesmen. Often a defense of Adams’s choices and character, the book affords a striking vantage of this chief officer’s authority as exercised and challenged. It shows a president without a legislative agenda who deferred to Congress; who did not exercise exclusive control over foreign affairs; who did not assert former royal prerogatives beyond constitutional specification; who was not the leader of his party; who faced competing claims to executive authority by ostensible subordinates; whose most common tactic against those claimants was inaction and silence; who commissioned another (Washington) as commander in chief and conceded military control; who could expect little loyalty based on his office; and who could not supervise and control a lean executive branch. Indeed, with his continuous eight-month retreat to Qunicy, Massachusetts, away from his ambitious cabinet’s activities amid international turmoil, the isolated figure of Adams gives new meaning to a unitary executive.

auditPapers.title: Jack Furniss. Between Extremes: Seeking the Political Center in the Civil War North
auditPapers.abstract: Between Extremes is a notable addition to a reassessment of the politics of the Civil War era in the United States that has been underway for a decade. Jack Furniss examines the politics of centrism—or, in the parlance of the war period, conservatism—practiced by Northern governors. His main focus is on state governors who affiliated with Union parties, ad hoc amalgams of Republicans, Democrats, and former Whigs. He argues that their successes lay in an ability to frame their support for the Lincoln administration around restoration of the Union, avoiding the revolutionary implications of emancipation and a consolidation of federal power. Furniss contends that governors engaged in realpolitik, acknowledging an electorate with no appetite for radical change but deeply invested in preserving the American republican experiment. Furniss situates Between Extremes within a gathering body of scholarship that views the Civil War–era party system as messy, factionalized, and fluid. Invoking J. Matthew Gallman, Adam I. P. Smith, Elizabeth Varon, and others, Furniss sets aside tidy Republican vs. Democrat binaries. The Republican Party, he observes, was in its infancy in 1860, still in the process of party-building by absorbing fragments of earlier organizations. Remnants of the Whig Party and the American Party (Know-Nothings) retained independence, and many conservatives voted for the Constitutional Union Party in 1860. The Northern wing of the Democratic Party, which supported Stephen A. Douglas for president in 1860, had more in common with Abraham Lincoln and the Republicans than with Southern secessionist Democrats. During the winter of 1860–1861, he points out, Northern state legislators acted across party lines to stave off secession. After Fort Sumter in April 1861, all but ardent peace advocates unified to support Lincoln’s limited war aim: restoration of the Union. The political center held and became a rallying point for Republicans, Democrats, and conservative Whigs, often via Union parties that sprang up across the North.

auditPapers.title: Tamara Chaplin. Becoming Lesbian: A Queer History of Modern France
auditPapers.abstract: It is time to put the notion of lesbian invisibility to rest. That is the primary take-away from Becoming Lesbian: A Queer History of Modern France, Tamara Chaplin’s outstanding history of lesbians in twentieth- and twenty-first-century France. The title of the book lets us know how this historian approaches the topic. In a wink to Simone de Beauvoir’s famous phrase, “one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,”(Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, trans. Constance Borde, [2011], 330) the “becoming” in the title shows an attentiveness to the idea that while same-sex sexual acts between women have existed since the beginning of time, an identity built around those acts did not appear until the late nineteenth century at the earliest, and that identity was far from static, but rather continued to become. There are reasons why at times historians, including me to be honest, have fallen prey to the idea that lesbians have been relatively invisible. Although there was an awareness of romantic and sexual attraction between women in twentieth-century France, it generally did not trouble the moral authorities of the time, so legal and political discussions of homosexuality were mostly limited to male homosexuality. This indifference among legal and political actors was to some extent rooted in prevailing stereotypes about female homosexuality, which suggested it was merely a passing phase or inherently less intense than male homosexuality. Such views were not limited to mainstream culture—they were also echoed within homosexual communities. For instance, in 1952, the homosexual journal Futur asserted that “female homosexuality is something essentially different from male homosexuality. There is a temporary and extremely fluid quality to it. The flames of that love are pale” (Claudie Lesselier, “Formes de résistances et d’expression lesbiennes dans les années cinquante et soixante en France,” Homosexualités expression/répression, ed. Louis-Georges Tin [2000], 105, translated by reviewer).

auditPapers.title: Sarah Lewis. The Unseen Truth: When Race Changed Sight in America
auditPapers.abstract: “How do we come to know what we think we know?” (99). This is the question at the heart of Sarah Lewis’s new book, The Unseen Truth: When Race Changed Sight in America. It is a question that can be addressed in case studies from countless times, places, and societies. Lewis tackles it across an extended moment of change in United States history: the period between the Civil War and World War I. In global history, this is a period known for its sharp rise in nationalist movements, usually forged in tandem with communal acts of “forgetting” pre-national pasts. Lewis tells us the story of another act of creation and forgetting at this time: in her words, the “transformation of vision that let obvious fictions remain at the basis of the [American] racial project and settle into a kind of truth” (2). Across five chapters, Lewis delves into topics including P. T. Barnum’s spectacles; Frederick Douglass’s lectures; elite museum curation; atlases, maps, and textbooks; and President Woodrow Wilson’s federal government files. She argues that an American public once understood that the Caucasus region—which German naturalist Johann Friedrich Blumenbach identified as the origin point of the white or “Caucasian” race in 1795—was in fact a territory of significant ethnic and religious diversity. She contends, for example, that Barnum’s famous Civil War–era “Circassian beauty” (who purportedly hailed from the Caucasus) was in fact a sideshow act meant to lampoon the idea of “Caucasian” whiteness. Barnum’s audience, Lewis explains, would have understood the evident mockery; they were familiar with the Caucasus through contemporary coverage of the Caucasian Wars (1817–1864), and they would have understood that Barnum’s “Circassian” was just another one of his fabricated, “freakish” figures meant for them to scrutinize and inspect. Put simply, Lewis asserts that Americans in the mid-nineteenth century did not take “Caucasian” whiteness seriously.

auditPapers.title: Samuel Agbamu. Restorations of Empire in Africa: Ancient Rome and Modern Italy’s African Colonies.
auditPapers.abstract: Romanità—a celebration of the memory of ancient Rome—was central to the self-image and ideology of Italy’s Fascist regime. In Restorations of Empire in Africa, Samuel Abgamu builds on the extensive scholarship on this topic and shapes it in two discrete directions. First, he focuses on how the ancient past was read specifically into Italian imperial ambitions in Africa, as the title of the book makes clear. Second, he begins his study in the late nineteenth century, demonstrating continuities in how Italians understood the connection between ancient Rome and the era of high imperialism between the liberal and fascist periods. A wide-ranging cultural history, this study infuses a combined history of romanità and the history of Italian imperialism with Agbamu’s deep understanding of the history of ancient Rome. The book is structured chronologically in nine substantive chapters and a brief conclusion. It starts with the early stirrings of Italian imperialism in East Africa immediately after national unification, but the main analysis begins with the invasion of Libya in 1911 and ends with reinterpretations of the ancient past in Italian connections with Africa in the postwar Italian republic. The chapters are generally divided by the various stages of Italian colonial expansion along the way. Each chapter also centers on the analysis of a set of cultural materials. The type of cultural materials under investigation shifts over the course of the book to reflect the changes in cultural production of the early twentieth century and the process of Italian imperial expansion. The early chapters of the book spotlight the literature of prominent figures like Enrico Corradini and Gabriele D’Annunzio, whose work imagined the future of Italian imperial expansion as a repetition of the ancient past. In 1914, we start to see cultural production shift to film, with Giovanni Pastrone’s Cabiria and, later in the book, Carmine Gallone’s highly influential 1937 film Scipione l’Africano. As the Fascist regime embraced grand public works programs and claimed greater control in the colonies, Agbamu turns his attention to physical manifestations of romanità in the cityscape of Rome, in colonial expositions on the peninsula, and—the one instance when the book actually takes us into the colonies—in the fascinating case of the Arco dei Fileni, a grand monument completed in 1937 at the halfway point of the road built to join together the Libyan colonies of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica. auditPapers.abstract: This book is a welcome addition to the scholarship on the subject of ruling elites and their interactions with larger society in Mughal and post-Mughal India. The sporadic appearance of monographic studies (by, for example, Farhat Hasan, Abhishek Kaicker, and Nandini Chatterjee over the past generation) serve to remind us of the subject’s importance and equally of its ongoing neglect. In Bankrolling Empire, Sheth approaches the subject by investigating, as he puts it, “state-capital relations” from the early seventeenth to the early nineteenth century. He does so through the prism of two Gujarat-based family firms engaged in trade and banking. Up to the mid-eighteenth century, the reasoning centers on the headmen of the Jain Jhaveri family of Ahmedabad. Thereafter, due to a dearth of pertinent sources on the Jhaveris, the focus switches to the Hindu Haribhakti family of Baroda. To advance the argument, the author draws on both literary and documentary sources in a range of genres, including histories, poems, travelogues, manuals, biographies, decrees, letters, and deeds, originally composed in a variety of local, regional, and European languages. The book’s substantive reasoning is framed explicitly in terms of the debate, initiated in 1979, between Karen Leonard and John F. Richards. This debate pivoted on the relationship (if any) between Indigenous family firms with expertise in trade, banking, and administration, and the revenue systems of the Mughal empire and of the smaller regimes that succeeded it. auditPapers.abstract: Marianne Kamp’s book Collectivization Generation is a landmark contribution to the social history of Soviet Central Asia, particularly to our understanding of Uzbekistan during one of the most transformative and traumatic periods of the twentieth century. Drawing on 120 interviews, Kamp reconstructs how rural Uzbeks navigated and made sense of the upheavals brought by Stalinist agricultural policy. What sets this book apart is its grounding in memory. While previous scholarship has leaned on archival materials and state documents, Kamp foregrounds the testimonies of the “collectivization generation” men and women born between 1900 and 1925 who experienced collectivization not merely as a policy, but as a rupture that reshaped the social, political, and emotional foundations of their lives. Her ability to weave these stories into an accessible yet analytically rich narrative is remarkable. As someone with personal ties to this history—my grandfather survived collectivization in Kokand and witnessed the execution of his father (labeled a quloq)—I was particularly moved by the book’s nuanced engagement with the paradoxes of memory. Kamp’s account of collectivization in Uzbekistan offers a compelling reflection on how oral histories illuminate the lived experiences and long-term recollections of Soviet rural transformation. Strikingly, as in my grandfather’s case, some of Kamp’s narrators ultimately came to embrace aspects of the very system that had once victimized them. Interviewed in the early 2000s, during Uzbekistan’s gradual and uneven retreat from collectivized agriculture, these individuals spoke with a candor largely unmediated by political incentives. This stands in contrast to many post-Soviet Eastern European contexts, where the pressures of privatization and political reckoning often shaped and constrained retrospective accounts.

auditPapers.title: Emmanuel Destenay. America’s French Orphans: Mobilization, Humanitarianism, and the Protection of France, 1914–1921
auditPapers.abstract: In Western humanitarianism, children have long enjoyed pride of place: quintessential subjects of innocence who tug at the heartstrings of distant spectators, their visuals and voices have prominently featured in myriad funding campaigns to help those in need in faraway lands. In America’s French Orphans: Mobilization, Humanitarianism, and the Protection of France, 1914–1921, Emmanuel Destenay illustrates this point by revealing how, during and after World War I, Americans became invested in helping children affected by the hostilities across the Atlantic. Told as a transnational story between the United States and France, but skewing heavily on the American perspective, the book focuses on two initiatives that have previously been relegated to the footnotes of humanitarianism: the Fatherless Children of France Society (FCFS) and the Committee Franco-American for the Protection of the Children of the Frontier (CFAPCF). Though short-lived, these groups raised enormous sums for French children who had lost their fathers during combat by matching them with American donors and safeguarded some 300,000 French children from conflict zones by sheltering, feeding, and educating them in so-called colonies throughout France. Combining American money and expertise with French local manpower, the FCFS and the CFAPCF were among the first to not only prominently feature children as recipients of aid but also, on the American side, draw on them as philanthropists. By thus mobilizing young citizens as active participants in the world of international relief even before America’s entry into the war in 1917, Destenay argues, they “paved the way for a new form of American humanitarian culture” (13).

auditPapers.abstract: In Savings and Trust: The Rise and Betrayal of the Freedman’s Bank, Justene Hill Edwards chronicles the promise and hope created by the establishment of the Freedman’s Savings and Trust Company at the end of the Civil War and the devastation caused by the appropriation of the depositors’ money and dreams. At its core, the book tells the story of people, the Black Americans who emerged from enslavement with aspirations of securing their full-fledged citizenship through the embrace of capitalism, and the white bank trustees who used their position for their own gain. With compelling writing that immediately piques the reader’s interest just as she hopes the plaque in Washington, DC, that commemorates the bank will do to those who note its presence near the White House, Edwards sensitively and poignantly documents the impact of white people’s theft of the funds on the lives and future prospects of those who lost everything due to managerial malfeasance.

auditPapers.title: Alberto Esu. Divided Power in Ancient Greece: Decision-Making and Institutions in the Classical and Hellenistic Polis.
auditPapers.abstract: It is no surprise that ancient Greece continues to inspire reflection on the nature and functioning of democracy. Alberto Esu has produced an excellent monograph that bridges the gap between traditional history and political science. Divided Power in Ancient Greece aims to explain how institutions were shaped by and, in turn, shaped the historical agents operating in Greek city-states. Esu deploys the methods of “new” historical institutionalism and shows us how an interdisciplinary approach to decision-making bodies in ancient Greece can achieve a nuanced yet simple way of accounting for historical change and continuity. Rather than reducing political regimes to stereotypes (i.e., “radical” Athenian democracy, iron-clad oligarchies), Esu provides convincing evidence and argumentation for a concept of “divided power” (itself a term borrowed from the work of P. Pasquino [“Democracy Ancient and Modern: Divided Power,” in Deémocratie Atheénienne—Deémocratie Moderne: Tradition et Influences, ed. Morgens H. Hansen (Fondation Hardt, 2010), 1–40]). “Divided power” refers to how political institutions delegated or shared respective deliberative and decision-making authority to/with different citizen bodies both as a safeguard to the stability of the particular constitution as well as its internal consistency. Unlike the modern notions of the “separation of powers” and “sovereignty” of one house or branch of government or another, divided power “is a constitutional order that distributes the power of making laws and binding norms among different institutions such as magistrates, assemblies, and courts” (11) in which no single institution had greater sway than another since it was “a form of decision-making that is the outcome of multi-institutional interaction between different bodies, each one playing a distinctive and relevant role in the shaping of decrees” (13–14).
