auditPapers.title: Assef Ashraf. Making and Remaking Empire in Early Qajar Iran
auditPapers.abstract: In the early nineteenth century, as the Near East was turning into the theater of the Great Game, the Qajar tribe, who descended from the Qizilbash confederacy of the Safavid military, rose to power in Iran. Russian expansionism brought war to the newly established Qajar Dynasty, and after facing defeat by Russia, the Qajars conceded some of their prized territories in the Caucasus and paid hefty indemnities to their northern neighbor. Meanwhile, as the British strengthened their foothold in India and the Persian Gulf, they turned into notable adversaries of the Qajars. Napoleon also had some interest in Iran as he envisioned a plan to approach India via Iranian territories. Few studies focus on the Qajar Dynasty in the opening decades of the nineteenth century without prioritizing how the Great Game unfolded within and beyond Iranian borders or examining how the Qajars’ political inefficacy and military setbacks started the process of modernization, which presumably led to the Constitutional Revolution (1901–1911) in Iran. Current works predominantly use modernization theories, focusing on the state and the elite, the interplay between the state and the Shiʿa ulema, or the political relations between the Qajars and Europeans. Especially after the Iranian Revolution of 1979, many scholars became interested in the roots of revolution and modernization in Iran. In Making and Remaking Empire in Early Qajar Iran, Assef Ashraf avoids modernization, Marxist, and postmodernist theories. Instead, he focuses on early nineteenth-century Iranian history by prioritizing what the historical actors did in their own historical time without expecting revolutions and modernization in the long run. Ashraf examines the “practices, customs, and relationships” that helped the Qajars consolidate their political power and remake a tributary empire after the fashion of the Safavids (296). Drawing on an impressive array of Persian, English, French, Russian, and Arabic published sources, as well as unpublished and archival documents in Iran, England, Russia, and Türkiye, Ashraf adopts an innovative sociological and anthropological approach that complements existing political histories in the study of early nineteenth-century Iran.

auditPapers.title: Rosamund Johnston. Red Tape: Radio and Politics in Czechoslovakia, 1945–1969
auditPapers.abstract: What is the role of media in society? What is the responsibility of reporters to the public? Of broadcasters? Under what conditions do the media operate? What is the relationship between the media and the state? These and other related questions have become top of mind in recent years in our ever-changing, globally inflected landscape, which continues to be transformed by ubiquitous streams of inexhaustible social media flows and their politics. Yet, as Rosamund Johnston argues in her fine-tuned investigation of postwar Czechoslovak Radio, Red Tape: Radio and Politics in Czechoslovakia, 1945–1969, “all media are social media” (20). Johnston’s compelling and vivacious book is filled with meaningful insights about the vibrating, ever-present conversation of radio, politics, and populace from the reconstruction of the Czechoslovak state in 1945 through the aftermath of the Warsaw Pact invasion, which crushed the Prague Spring. This is a story of how radio in its “second ‘golden age’” “established, stabilized, and reproduced” a nondemocratic society (2). It reveals the creation and sustenance of the rhetorical sound environment in which Czechoslovakia’s reporters, politicians, and listeners swam together. Her story leaves off as radio journalists refused to renounce their positions during the Prague Spring and were shuttled off into blue-collar jobs across the country.

auditPapers.title: Charles G. Thomas. Ujamaa’s Army: The Creation and Evolution of the Tanzania People’s Defence Force, 1964–1979
auditPapers.abstract: Charles Thomas’s book Ujamaa’s Army is a welcome addition to the history of East African military structures while also providing a necessary insight into the construction and formation of one of the more successful military institutions to emerge in the postcolonial era. Laser focused on the formation and reforms of the Tanzania People’s Defence Force (TPDF) from 1964 to 1978, Thomas illustrates the transformation of the TPDF from a small colonial infantry force to an effective modern military, all while being a part of Julius Nyerere’s vision of a “People’s Army” embedded within the social, cultural, and political life of the Tanzanian nation. And while Thomas admits the “TPDF proved to be an exceptional case,” its story helps illustrate the “extraordinary complexity involved in negotiating and balancing … postcolonial transitions” in this period of African history (5, 11). Hopefully, readers who have picked up this volume will already be aware of the general history that culminated in Nyerere and TANU’s victory and the achievement of uhuru (true self-government) in the early 1960s. However, Thomas makes a concerted effort from the outset to provide necessary historical background that helps place the TPDF in this environment of enormous change. After this moment, Nyerere sought “a Pan-African solution to his security dilemma” that would reflect the new nationalist vision of the new republic (45). How fitting that the first one thousand new soldiers of the TPDF were marched out at the same time as the announcement of the United Republic of Tanzania in September 1964. auditPapers.title: Nina S. Studer. The Hour of Absinthe: A Cultural History of France’s Most Notorious Drink .
auditPapers.abstract: Nina S. Studer’s book The Hour of Absinthe: A Cultural History of France’s Most Notorious Drink is a welcome and much-needed addition to the growing field of alcohol history. Studer tracks meticulously the social, cultural, and political ramifications of absinthe, starting from debates about its uncertain origins in the late eighteenth century and ending with an exploration of early twentieth-century bans. What Studer describes as “perhaps the most demonized drink in the world” (6) has yet to be given such holistic diligence in scholarly research until now. The book incorporates a wide range of primary source material, including newspapers, cultural texts, travel accounts, and psychiatric theses. Studer also engages frequently with existing scholarship, and it is evident how earlier research has informed this book. The book’s title arguably undersells its ambitious scope and downplays Studer’s most significant contribution to scholarship: absinthe drinking in French colonies, namely Algeria. The way that Studer interweaves the colonial context into this in-depth study of absinthe’s history is cogent and well versed. Such context is not included simply as a necessary nod to France’s past, as it sometimes has been in French historical scholarship. Instead, the colonization of North Africa by France is integral to understanding the history of absinthe. Studer compares colonial and metropolitan perspectives throughout, drawing important conclusions about attitudes toward absinthe. Notably, the dangers of absinthe in colonial contexts “predate the metropolitan focus on the dangers of alcohol” (171). After reading Studer’s book, I find it easy to agree with the introduction’s assertion that “the history of absinthe and the history of French imperialism are indivisible” (10). Class and gender are more familiar themes relating to absinthe, but both are entwined seamlessly throughout the book and appear as the primary themes of chapters 3, 4, and 5.

The relative impunity of pornographers (caused by the absence of a clear definition of obscenity and the tolerance of public opinion) fueled many conspiracy theories about the corruption of the republic. Collusion was assumed among pornographers, financiers, politicians, and the justice system, and the career paths of certain louche publishers (such as Victor Vidal, who had numerous connections with the financial and political elite) did lend some plausibility to these theories.

auditPapers.title: Mapping the intersection of digital technologies and humanities: a multidisciplinary scoping review of the digital humanities movement in Thailand
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Although digital humanities (DH) lacks a universally accepted definition, its boundaries are often shaped by local contexts and cultural factors. In Thailand, no formal DH programs exist, and only a few publications explicitly address the term “digital humanities”. At the same time, it is speculated that works considered as DH research have been sporadically produced. To gain a nuanced understanding of the Thai DH landscape, this study conducted a scoping review of scholarly works published between 2010 and 2019, using broad operational definitions and frameworks, and integrating quantitative and qualitative analyses. We identified a wide range of publications, frequently anchored in computer science and related fields, yet also involving humanities scholars and emerging “born-digital” disciplines. Many works focus on applying or developing digital tools, while relatively few emphasize long-term data stewardship or critical humanities-oriented methods. Patterns of collaboration remain mostly within or across departments, and conference proceedings dominate as publication venues, reflecting scholarly communication practices of Thai DH scholars. These findings suggest that a DH movement exists in Thailand without formal institutionalization or a cohesive community. By mapping the field’s scope and boundaries before the widespread adoption of generative AI, this study provides baseline evidence that can inform future strategies, encourage interdisciplinary dialogue, and situate Thai DH research within a broader international context.

auditPapers.title: Daniela R. P. Weiner. Teaching a Dark Chapter: History Books and the Holocaust in Italy and the Germanys
auditPapers.abstract: In Teaching a Dark Chapter: History Books and the Holocaust in Italy and the Germanys, Daniela R. P. Weiner undertakes the challenging task of analyzing how post–World War II textbooks in Italy, East Germany, and West Germany presented their Fascist and Nazi pasts, and their concomitant belief that education could influence a democratic future. This comparative and transnational study illuminates a previously understudied aspect of how these societies confronted their “dark chapters” through education—not during the often-cited watershed moments of 1968 or 1978, but considerably earlier, beginning in earnest with Allied occupation efforts in the immediate postwar period, although Allied plans for textbook revision had already begun as early as 1943. Through careful research spanning archives in five countries, Weiner demonstrates that textbooks served as critical instruments in reshaping postwar societies long before Holocaust discourse became prominent in public memory. Weiner’s methodological innovation lies in her “life cycle” approach to textbook analysis, which integrates three analytical frames: the process of textbook creation, the actual textbook content, and how students and the public received these materials. This tripartite approach represents a significant advance over previous studies that tended to focus solely on either educational restructuring or textbook content analysis. By examining the interplay among individual efforts, institutions, textbook narratives, and societal reception through a transnational framework, Weiner demonstrates how textbooks both reflected and shaped evolving national narratives about the Fascist/Nazi past.

auditPapers.title: Christa Dierksheide. Beyond Jefferson: The Hemingses, the Randolphs, and the Making of Nineteenth-Century America .
auditPapers.abstract: As a founding father, public servant, and political theorist, Thomas Jefferson’s impact on US history has long been the subject of discussion by scholars. Likewise, his personal life has attracted significant attention for embodying the grim realities of American slavery and freedom. Yet, rarely are these two worlds brought together to consider how the legacy of Jefferson’s family reflected and contributed to the complex realities of the nineteenth century. Christa Dierksheide’s engaging family biography, Beyond Jefferson: The Hemingses, the Randolphs, and the Making of Nineteenth-Century America, takes on that task by tracing the paths of Jefferson’s Black and white lineages to tell a deeply intimate account of the multiple histories of the United States. As she successfully demonstrates, Jefferson’s influence on early America was not simply political and intellectual but also personal and material through the actions of his descendants. For both branches of the Jefferson family tree, the patriarch’s death precipitated dramatic transformations. On the Hemings side, two of his four surviving children with Sally were manumitted in his will; Jefferson freed the other two several years prior. Freedom was thus hard earned, and neither the children nor Sally—who was herself never formally manumitted—had any substantial support from Jefferson’s estate after his death. This made life quite difficult for the Hemingses, not only due to financial limitations but also because of the challenges of navigating the color line in antebellum America. The children born from Jefferson’s marriage to Martha were also rocked by their father’s passing. The former president was in such terrible debt that many of his enslaved laborers were sold off, and eventually so too was the Monticello plantation. Desperate to recoup the family’s wealth and status, Jefferson’s white descendants undertook risky business endeavors that carried them across the world and into some of the most important geopolitical conflicts of the nineteenth century.

auditPapers.title: Meredith L. McCoy. On Our Own Terms: Indigenous Histories of School Funding and Policy
auditPapers.abstract: In the past forty years, historians have published a relatively large number of books and articles on the late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century experiences of Indigenous peoples in the federal boarding schools. With On Our Own Terms, Meredith L. McCoy adds to that scholarship, but also helps us better understand the less-studied Native encounters with public schools, where interacting with state and local governments, rather than just Washington, DC, was part of the experience. Still, even if the federal role in Indigenous education was different in public schools than it was in the boarding schools, federal policies and federal budgets have remained an ever-present reality, and one of this book’s added contributions are the impressive insights that it conveys about the inner workings of these legislative initiatives. McCoy adopts an appropriately wide chronological scope for this study, properly asserting that any history of Indigenous education should acknowledge its deep, precontact past. “Native people already knew how to educate their children,” she reminds us (24). From there, McCoy adeptly moves on to discussions of the various settler colonial impositions, from religious mission schools to government boarding schools. But, as alluded to above, she does not stop there. Most of the rest of the book examines Native experiences with federal legislation in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, from the Johnson-O’Malley Act of the 1930s, into the landmark policies of the 1960s and 1970s, and culminating with a look at the No Child Left Behind Act and the Every Student Succeeds Act of the 2000s and 2010s, respectively. Throughout, the book’s view is not only expansive in terms of time but also geography. The northern plains get special attention, but there are also examples from as far west as Hawai’i to as far east as the Mohegans of Connecticut.

auditPapers.title: Air Travel, Statelessness, and the Rights Claims of Ugandan Asians, c. 1973
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In the aftermath of Idi Amin’s expulsion of Uganda’s South Asians in 1972, some of those made technically stateless arrived in India unsupported by the United Nations or any national government. Eleven of them attempted to fly on via Sri Lanka, without the required paperwork, to join their families in the United Kingdom. As large colonial empires gave way to postcolonial nation states, and as the international community and the former colonial metropole shed responsibilities towards their former subjects, the various destinations to which such stateless persons were considered for deportation reflect the uneasy status of diasporic communities. Using what official records saw as the ‘problem’ of this international flight, this article explores how the sealed realm of air travel became a locus for the articulation of their rights as these peoples of the postcolonial world used the devices of deportation and ‘shuttlecocking’ against national and international actors to challenge the inequitable application of notionally universal principles to deny material assistance and recognition of their rights as refugees and stateless persons. In this way, individuals and non-state actors were able to use air travel to intervene bodily to influence national and supranational discourses designed to exclude them.

auditPapers.abstract: In this relatively new century with its curious social and political winds, Edward Anthony Polanco’s study Healing Like Our Ancestors is wonderfully direct in insisting that scholars can, and must, decolonize Indigenous histories, now. This book does not suggest that we decolonize just the past. It actively decolonizes Indigenous knowledge while using the same sources that so many have used to understand a colonized past.

auditPapers.title: The Utopia within Utopia (1516)
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The debate between Hythlodaeus and an English lawyer before Cardinal Morton in Book One of Utopia (1516) contains many proposals for socio-economic reforms. These have typically been interpreted as innovative proposals to counteract the corruption of Christendom which surrounds them. However, when placed into their legislative context, it is apparent not only that these reforms echo closely many socio-economic reforms passed in England in the decades preceding Utopia , but that corollaries for almost all of them were passed when Morton, in whose presence the debate took place, was lord chancellor. Recognizing this forces a reassessment of this debate, showing Hythlodaeus’s flaws, and reframing the contribution of the English lawyer. This very reassessment, however, realigns the entire dialogue before Cardinal Morton, which it is possible to identify as a mirror to the wider text. It is a Utopia within Utopia , or, a mise en abyme . By closing examining the reflection, it appears that this provides a structural indication of how Utopia should be read.

auditPapers.title: Catherine Kearns. The Rural Landscapes of Archaic Cyprus: An Archaeology of Environmental and Social Change
auditPapers.abstract: During the school year when a winter storm brings heavy snowfall or dangerous, subzero windchills to my suburban Wisconsin neighborhood, the district monitors what is happening in our town and adjacent communities and frequently closes the schools—a decision that triggers an array of political, economic, and social conditions. The district school board, elected by the community, is vested with the power to act according to policies and best practices, which are often ill-defined guardrails open to myriad interpretations and opinions (and often criticism). Parents with young children navigate work obligations and options—for example, lose pay, use sick leave or vacation time, work from home, or incur unplanned debt by hiring a babysitter. And kids get a snow day, taking to social media to arrange meetups at Starbucks or a sledding hill (or even online). Weather is local, uneven, and unruly, and its impact on the landscape, communities, and behaviors is layered. My excursive introduction to this review highlights a central aim of Catherine Kearns’s challenging and innovative new book, The Rural Landscapes of Archaic Cyprus: An Archaeology of Environmental and Social Change: to “consider more critically an archaeology of human-environment relationships” (17).

auditPapers.title: Robert L. Nelson. Frontiers of Empire: Max Sering, Inner Colonization, and the German East, 1871–1945
auditPapers.abstract: Max Sering, professor at the Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin from 1889 to 1925, was one of the leading agrarian economists of his time, and he had both the ambition and the ability to influence politics. It is thus surprising that it took so long for an intellectual biography of Sering to appear, and it is at the same time fortunate that Robert L. Nelson is the author of the inspiring one at hand. Through the lens of Max Sering’s academic and political career, Nelson’s Frontiers of Empire follows the trajectory of Germany’s settlement policies in the so-called German East, from their inception with the establishment of the Royal Prussian Settlement Commission for Posen and West Prussia in the 1880s, through the settlement projects pursued in German-occupied Baltic territories during the First World War, to their genocidal culmination in the Nazis’ lebensraum politics during the Second World War. Nelson offers neither a simple linear story nor a purely German story. He presents Max Sering as an internationally renowned agrarian economist and expert of settler colonialism, who developed his fundamental convictions as to what kind of agrarian policy Germany ought to pursue during a research trip to Canada and the United States in 1883—“the journey of a lifetime,” as Nelson calls it (41). The trip turned Sering into an admirer of the United States and convinced him that North America was the model that Germany should follow. Like many of his colleagues among the so-called kathedersozialisten, or “Socialists of the Chair,” Sering did not oppose capitalism, industrialization, and urbanization per se, but he was convinced that an industrial nation also needed agriculture to avoid becoming dependent on food imports, to slow down the migration from the countryside to the city, and to ensure that farming families would continue to produce the healthy young soldiers a great power like Germany required. In addition, Sering feared the creeping Polonization of Germany’s eastern provinces if the government did not implement a program of “inner colonization.” This consisted of breaking up large aristocratic land estates and transforming them into the kind of midsize homesteads of North America.

Gomez’s Picture Bride, War Bride: The Role of Marriage in Shaping Japanese America is a wonderfully original study that uses marriage as the lens to understand migration and diaspora. The control of Japanese women’s bodies was fundamental to the creation of Japanese America, their national status, and US-Japanese relations.

auditPapers.title: Hunter Price. Sacred Capital: Methodism and Settler Colonialism in the Empire of Liberty
auditPapers.abstract: Hunter Price’s Sacred Capital: Methodism and Settler Colonialism in the Empire of Liberty is the best book on the history of early American Methodism in nearly two decades. Methodism, Price convincingly shows, was a key player in the settler colonialism that expanded North America’s western frontier. In advancing this argument, Price hearkens back to the work of church historians like William Warren Sweet in the mid-twentieth century, borrowing from him and his contemporaries the conviction that the story of early American Methodism is intimately connected to the “chaos” of the western frontier and attempts to “bring order” to it. In contrast to Sweet, however, Price turns a critical eye to the memoirs, journals, and letters left behind by Methodist preachers, arguing that circuit riders were “much less self-sacrificing than historians have assumed and a fair amount more self-serving” (2). To make this argument, Price looks to recent work on settler colonialism, noting that Methodism’s itinerant preachers and lay migrants alike were key participants in the process. In this telling, “the Methodist Age and the Empire of Liberty converged.” He is careful to point out that Methodists were not often directly involved in “Indian removal, ethnic cleansing, or genocide.” Rather, Methodist networks were “easily adapted to core settler concerns,” including “land, work, marriage, [and] money.” Methodism thus “contributed institutionally to the phases of stabilizing and developing settler communities” (3–5).

auditPapers.title: Michelle Lynn Kahn. Foreign in Two Homelands: Racism, Return Migration, and Turkish–German Histor y
auditPapers.abstract: With this engaging first monograph, Michelle Lynn Kahn delivers transnational history at its most insightful. Foreign in Two Homelands centers on return migration, broadly defined to include cross-border flows of remittances, goods, discourses, images, and people. At its core, the book offers a long-overdue historicization of the migration wave triggered by the 1983 West German “Law for the Promotion of the Voluntary Return of Foreigners,” which encouraged so-called “guest workers” and their families to return to Turkey. In response, 250,000 Turkish citizens returned to their former homeland—“kicked out,” as Kahn puts it (9). Complementing studies that root Turkish–German history in German politics of identity, race, or gender, Foreign in Two Homelands argues that these return migrations—especially the often-alienated experiences of “returnees” in Turkey after 1983—were shaped by entangled, transnational dynamics. Two factors stand out in Kahn’s account. First is the racism—both everyday and structural—faced by migrants in West Germany, especially in the early 1980s. Second is a widespread belief in Turkey, dating to the early years of labor recruitment, that migrants had Germanized in behavior, consumption, and values, thus losing their Turkishness. For Kahn, this sense is captured in the term Almancı, translated here as “Germanized Turk” (5, 25). Commonly applied pejoratively to migrants in the Federal Republic in Turkish media and everyday discourse, Almancı implied they had become overly integrated. While German policy and public rejection of Turkish–German belonging rested on ideas of a biologically defined nation, this use of Almancı conveyed a commonsense belief in Germanness as acquired behavior and values. This meaning attached to Almancı surfaced in the condescending treatment Turkish Germans received from the Turkish state, in mocking portrayals in media, and in fraught interactions during visits or after return. For Kahn, being treated as Almancı complicated migrants’ belonging in Turkey, echoing the alienation caused by racism in West Germany. The result was a sense of betweenness. Through these meanings and their impact in both countries, Kahn shows that even Anatolian villagers who mocked visiting migrants as overly Germanized were actors in German history—shaping, from afar, “the contours of West German national identity” (317).

Racialized Commodities joins recent contributions to the history and historiography of race that argue that the concept can be fruitfully applied to describe the thinking and realities of premodern societies, long before its most well-known iteration in the context of Atlantic modernity. Following WWII, classicists rejected race as a framework for understanding Greek conceptions of appearance and culture, replacing it with “ethnicity.” Yet, “ethnicity was transferred many of the same meanings that race held prior to the war” (9). Although recent non-essentialist approaches to ethnicity have yielded results, the concept fails to capture the power dynamics embedded in emic descriptions of outgroups. Here, Parmenter argues, race proves a more effective analytical tool. The book contends that long-distance trade routes, and the commodities that circulated along them, helped shape Greek ideas of blackness and whiteness, and that these ideas were used instrumentally to rationalize aspects of status as well as structures of economic exchange and exploitation. As a result, blackness became associated with the prestige of Egypt’s Saite Kingdom while whiteness was linked with the enslaveable nomads of the Black Sea.

And the essays by Bain Atwood and Stefan Berger offer accounts of their troubling misuse of the past, the former in the case of the misrepresentation of the significance Australian aborigine activists’ contemporary references to the persecution of Europe’s Jewish communities; the latter with regard to current abuses of history by the radical right.

auditPapers.title: Timothy Brook. The Price of Collapse: The Little Ice Age and the Fall of Ming China
auditPapers.abstract: Timothy Brook’s book The Price of Collapse is a significant and thought-provoking contribution to climate history, price history, and global history. At its core, the book revisits a long-debated question with new methodological tools: why did the Ming Empire (1368–1644) fall? Drawing on the quantifiable evidence of grain prices, paleoclimatic reconstructions, and shifts in global economic flows, Brook, a pioneering historian for situating early modern China in a global context, argues that the onset and intensification of the Little Ice Age played a triggering role in driving the Ming toward collapse. Structured into five richly researched and cogently argued chapters, the book explores how grain prices, maritime policies, natural disasters, and imperial decision-making intersected under intensifying environmental stress. Brook brings to life a wide range of historical actors, ranging from emperors and officials to Jesuit missionaries, Buddhist monks, art collectors, and gazetteer writers. Chapter 1 introduces the late Ming crisis through the eyes of a local schoolteacher, Chen Qide, who witnessed it firsthand. Chapter 2 assesses the cost of necessities and standards of living in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Chapter 3 challenges the traditional explanation that an influx of New World silver caused a “price revolution” of high inflation. Brook maintains that the available price data does not support that conclusion, except in the luxury goods market. Chapters 4 and 5 offer his alternative interpretation: a sudden and dramatic grain price spike under the Chongzhen Emperor (1627–1644) coincided with the peak environmental volatility of the Little Ice Age in the mid-1600s.

auditPapers.abstract: Procedural modeling has become increasingly applied in the architecture field to address the high costs of manual methods in digitalizing architectural heritage. auditPapers.title: Chongololo : The Zambian Children’s Wildlife Magazine and the Making of an African Environmental Movement
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Created in 1972, the Chongololo magazine and wildlife clubs in Zambia broke with earlier examples of conservation advocacy and thought in the southern African nation. Nonetheless, by the 1990s, environmentalism in Zambia looked very different, in part as a result of the thinking and educating that Chongololo did.

auditPapers.title: Is Franz Kafka’s style simple, and Thomas Mann’s style complex? A quantitative comparative analysis
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In the field of German literature, it is widely recognized that Franz Kafka’s works are characterized by linguistic simplicity, whereas Thomas Mann’s writing style is more complex. This study investigates whether this perception reflects reality and explores the specific differences in their writing styles. A stylometric approach is employed to compare three key aspects: linguistic complexity and diversity, the use of parts of speech (POS), and POS N-grams. To examine these differences, we adopt a three-step analytical framework involving statistical tests, cluster analysis, and classification analysis, each based on indicators within these aspects. The results reveal that the most prominent difference lies in their use of POS, with Mann employing more adjectives and Kafka using more adverbs. Among the POS N-grams used by both authors, those exhibiting the largest differences in frequency also include adjectives and adverbs. The second most notable difference is that Mann’s writing demonstrates greater linguistic complexity and diversity than Kafka’s, particularly in terms of diversity. Overall, Kafka’s writing style can be characterized as simpler, while Mann’s is more complex. By incorporating the authors’ perspectives on linguistic style, their biographical backgrounds and interpretations of their works, this study further explores the reasons behind their stylistic differences.

auditPapers.title: Can digital humanities use microwork crowdsourcing in a fair manner? The effect of pedagogical training and multimodal instructions on annotation quality
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article explores the potential of microwork crowdsourcing for digital humanities. In contrast to volunteer-based crowdsourcing, microwork involves paying non-expert workers recruited through online platforms for their work. Microwork crowdsourcing is already an established part of the academic research infrastructure in many data-driven fields. However, previous research has identified numerous issues regarding worker treatment and experience, which range from sweatshop wages to unpaid labor. Building on previous research in human–computer interaction, this study evaluates two mechanisms designed to promote fairness: multimodal instructions, which combine language and visual content, and pedagogical training, which provides multiple examples and feedback. We tested their impact on data quality through two experiments, in which crowdsourced workers perform complex tasks that involve reasoning about primary school science diagrams. While pedagogical training did not lead to significant improvements, multimodal instructions had a positive effect on data quality. Our results suggest that microwork crowdsourcing has potential for digital humanities, especially in fields unlikely to attract volunteer communities. However, these findings highlight the importance of fairness-oriented task design and transparency in the responsible use of crowdsourcing.

auditPapers.title: Abandoned Land: Muslim Refugees’ Property in the Post-Ottoman Balkans
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article examines what happened to the ‘abandoned land’ of Muslim refugees in Bulgaria, Serbia, and Romania after the end of Ottoman rule in 1878. Circassians and Crimean Tatars from Russia, whom the Ottoman government had previously settled in the Balkans, were among them. As they evacuated for the safety of Ottoman Anatolia and Syria, never to return to the Balkans, they left behind their fields, pastures, and houses. The newly independent Romania and Serbia and autonomous Bulgaria built their land legislation upon the Ottoman land regime, asserting state ownership over large swathes of agricultural land. Local Christian populations and Muslim refugees laid claims to that land, contesting the government’s appropriation. The ‘abandoned land’ became a primary vehicle for ethno-religious homogenization in the post-Ottoman Balkans. The governments in Sofia, Bucharest, and Belgrade passed immigration laws to reassign the vacant land to Bulgarian, Romanian, and Serb immigrants arriving from the Ottoman, Russian, and Habsburg empires. Based on documents in Bulgarian, Serbian, Romanian, and Turkish archives, this study reveals legal mechanisms of land appropriation and redistribution as part of state-building in the modern Balkans.

auditPapers.title: Hand in Hand ; Strauss’ Kaiser-Walzer as a case study of interdisciplinary collaboration in digital musicology
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Johann Strauss Jr.’s famous Kaiser-Walzer (Emperor Waltz) has provoked frequent study. Our interdisciplinary investigation of the NYC series combines historical and systematic musicology, performance science, music informatics, and Web science. Our data, organized according to FAIR principles as a Linked Data corpus, support machine-readable references underlying our assertions via publishable URIs. This article presents a case study, both of our musicological research (exemplified using the Kaiser-Walzer), and of this novel approach to scholarly publication (using URIs included within the reporting).

auditPapers.title: TOWARD A CONJECTURAL HISTORY OF CONJECTURAL HISTORIES
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT Most intellectual historians use the term “conjectural history” to designate a new form of speculative history created in eighteenth‐century Scotland by Adam Smith and a few others. These writers traced the development of human society and culture through conjectural reasoning based on philosophers’ views about human nature and travelers’ accounts of “primitive” peoples. Their work had a deep impact on eighteenth‐century philology: it helped to shape such original and influential studies of the ancient world as Edward Gibbon's history of the fall of Rome, Johann Joachim Winckelmann's history of the rise of ancient art, and Friedrich August Wolf's demonstration that Homer was an oral poet. But the connection between conjectural history and classical philology began long before any of the varied Enlightenments conjured up by modern scholars came into being. Conjectures about the past were deeply rooted in the central humanistic discipline, rhetoric; this gave Lorenzo Valla the tools for his conjectural refutation of the legend of the Donation of Constantine. But these same tools were plied with similar skill and originality by many other humanists, from Valla's contemporary in the Roman curia, Leon Battista Alberti, to the Jesuit historian of the New World, José de Acosta, a century later. And they saw them not as an innovation but as part of the philological and historical tradition in which they were grounded. Valla, for example, saw Thucydides—whose histories he translated into Latin—as a conjectural historian and thus identified conjecture as a central feature of historiography in the classical tradition.

auditPapers.title: Fallen from Heaven: The Enduring Tradition of Europeans as Gods in the Americas. By Nicholas Griffiths
auditPapers.abstract: Nicholas Griffiths has produced a synthesis of the various myths and fantasies about Native people thinking Europeans were gods. No spoiler alert needed here. Griffiths makes it clear that he is aware that ethnohistory and the “new conquest history” of the last thirty years has debunked the idea that Hawaiians thought Captain Cook was Lono or that the Mexica thought that Hernando Cortés was the return of Quetzalcoatl or that New Guinea highlanders thought that twentieth-century Europeans were gods from heaven. Few readers will find these conclusions surprising. So what does this book offer? Fallen from Heaven purports to offer a synthetic overview of the myriad ways that Native peoples of the Americas made sense of European invaders and explorers. In reality, though, the book synthesizes the debates that Europeans had about themselves being or not being gods. Such an approach has the strange effect of reifying the counter-point—that, no, Natives did not believe the Europeans were gods. Here is a good example. Captain Cook is famous for having made it to the Hawaiian Islands, where the Hawaiians did or did not think he was a temporary manifestation of the god Lono. Griffiths claims that Native Hawaiians may very well have continued to believe in some version of this story because the Mo’olelo Hawaii, published in 1838, repeats some of this belief (239). But the devil is in the details. Griffiths credits the Calvinist missionary, Sheldon Dibble, for authorship, but it was probably David Malo who composed this early history. Malo was a Christian convert who was under pressure to produce a version palatable to his Calvinist overlords.

auditPapers.title: THE STAKES OF PHILOLOGY: REALITIES, ORIGINS, FUTURES
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT What does philology mean today? And what can it do in the future? In this article, I respond to these questions by performing—again—a “return to philology,” as Paul de Man proclaimed in the 1980s. To engage with the present and future of philology, I return to nineteenth‐century Germany and to some of the controversies that played out between the main proponents of the new discipline, including Gottfried Hermann, August Boeckh, Friedrich Nietzsche, and Ulrich von Wilamowitz‐Moellendorf. This was the time and place where philology came into its own and some of the discipline's stakes were spelled out for the first time. These stakes were both methodological and theoretical, phenomenological and ontological, and can be discussed according to their three main concerns: the struggle for the real, the possibility of origins, and the futures of the past. Invoking “Philology Now,” I argue, means bringing these stakes back into our discussion about history and theory.

auditPapers.title: PLANETARY CONCEPT‐WORK: PHILOLOGY, UNTRANSLATABLES, LANGUAGE JUSTICE
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT Starting with an example of philological method drawn from Leo Spitzer's essay titled “Linguistics and Literary History” (1948), which, for many years, served as a foundational text of the discipline of comparative literature, this article delineates some of the reasons why philology, especially in its most specialized guises, became an outmoded discipline in contemporary pedagogies of the humanities. A case is made, however, for “philology now” in the form of plurilingual concept‐work and translation theory. Crucial to forms of philosophizing across Western and non‐Western languages and traditions, recognized as an important fulcrum of global language justice movements, and repurposed in the emergent field of ecotranslation (which enlarges the semiosphere beyond human language even as it prioritizes language survival among humans), philology gains renewed traction in the contemporary translational humanities.

auditPapers.title: IMPLICIT COMPARISONS: VISUALITY AND THE INTERLINEAR MANUSCRIPT PAGE
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT A central question for European philology, informed by various agendas and ideologies, concerned comparison and the positing of hierarchies among languages. With this “traditional” question of philology in mind, but hoping to think in less traditional ways, this article asks how comparative understandings of Arabic and local languages of the Indonesian archipelago may have been reflected in nineteenth‐ and twentieth‐century Islamic manuscripts that contain interlinear translations. These Islamic interlinear translations contain a text written in Arabic with a translation into Javanese or Malay appearing in between the lines of Arabic text. Such translations often follow a word‐for‐word model, striving to replicate the source down to the level of prepositions and word order even when the result is far from idiomatic. Many questions could be asked about the translation of doctrine, values, and stories through these bilingual manuscripts. However, although I have been trained to examine texts for their content and literary dimensions, I will attempt to put these dimensions aside momentarily in favor of considering “sensory translation.” Doing so, I explore what visual aspects (including script size, ink color, and writing angle) might tell us about the “implicit comparisons” between languages as reflected on the page.

auditPapers.title: The Last Door: A History of Torture in Mexico’s War against Subversives. By Gladys I. McCormick
auditPapers.abstract: Gladys McCormick’s new book opens with a content warning about the graphic depictions of torture to follow. It is well warranted. Relying on a combination of archival documents from Mexico’s security agency (Dirección Federal de Seguridad, DFS) and oral histories from those subjected to state violence, McCormick brings the reader into the gruesome reality of torture as state policy, modernized and institutionalized in the context of the Cold War. While the book focuses on the long 1970s, which she dates from the late 1960s until 1982, McCormick begins her analysis by situating the institutionalization of torture as policy in the early 1950s. Further, she brings us to the present to reveal the persistence of torture and impunity in Mexico and to explore Mexico’s failure to reckon with state crimes or seriously undertake a truth and reconciliation process. There are risks, of course, to writing a history of torture and extreme state violence. However, McCormick artfully navigates the potential pitfalls of sensationalizing violence or rendering victims as one dimensional recipients of torture. She systematically builds a historical narrative that encompasses the entire experience of the torture victim—arrest, torture, and detention—and elucidates recurring patterns: clearly defined roles for those participating, the repetition and escalation of torture methods, the medicalization of torture, and the creation of a public narrative that legitimized torture as a necessary practice to safeguard Mexicans from the subversive threats of Cold War dissidents. Further, McCormick shows that while state violence was a common experience across Latin America’s Cold War, Mexico’s dirty war was unique in including the families of alleged subversives. Family members, like elsewhere, mourned their disappeared and cared for those who were tortured and imprisoned. But only in Mexico, McCormick argues, were family members systematically included in the torture itself—as witnesses, as subjects threatened with torture, and as victims themselves—for the crime of relation to alleged subversives.

auditPapers.title: Abraham Bäck, Scarcity, and the Racial Anatomy of Skin
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In February 1744 in Paris, the Swedish physician Abraham Bäck (1713–95), better known as Carl Linnaeus’s best friend, dissected the cadaver of an unidentified sub-Saharan man. In contrast to the widespread exploitation of the enslaved dead in North America, cadavers of dark-skinned Africans remained rare in the anatomical theatres of eighteenth-century Europe. Scarcity not only increased their market value in medical circles interested in skin colour: in Europe, empirical anatomists often used these rare remains for building their medical authority. This article explores the rise of an empiricist social culture of racial anatomy in the European Enlightenment by following the case of Bäck, whose research on ‘black’ skin also provides a little-known counterpart to Linnaeus’s racial anthropology. Bäck’s case illustrates not only how European anatomists often wrote accounts of skin colour which best showcased their medical skills but also how the production of racial pseudoscience became increasingly driven by the authoritative rise of empiricism, the expansion of the slave trade, and the Enlightenment’s fascination with human differences.

auditPapers.title: Historic Failures, Failures of History: ‘Necessitous Gentlewomen’ Reconsidered
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract A chance encounter with the records of a local charity has re-opened the question of middle-class female poverty and dependence in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, in ways which seem to have been ignored by many historians. Studies on topics ranging from financial speculation to the expansion of education for women have often left unexplored the extent of middle-class precarity, and the wreckage left in the wake of the myth of the male ‘provider’. Can stories of inactivity, non-achievement and unheroic failure among ‘necessitous gentlewomen’ become subjects of serious and sustained research?

auditPapers.title: History Workshop: A South African Movement
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In its nearly 50 years of existence, the History Workshop at the University of the Witwatersrand (Johannesburg) has played an influential role in the development of social history and public history in South Africa. This article provides an overview of the collective’s contributions to the production of new, counter-hegemonic histories from the mid-1970s, when popular resistance against apartheid gained momentum, to the early years of the transition to democracy and the more recent period of deepening structural crises. It has negotiated these historical periods while attempting to maintain a commitment to researching and writing histories of and with subaltern groups.

auditPapers.title: Culture War: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis?
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Now ubiquitous in public debate, the term ‘culture war’ has become increasingly unmoored from models that were developed when the concept first shot to popularity in the specific context of the United States in the 1990s. This article retraces the conceptual history of culture war over the long term, questions some of the assumptions about the normal course of history and politics that are often implicit in its usage, and reflects on the place of the American paradigm in discussions of the subject. It argues that historians could adopt a more explicitly Gramscian perspective to develop a robust historical concept of culture war.

auditPapers.title: Dame Janet L. Nelson (28 March 1942 – 14 October 2024)
auditPapers.abstract: Jinty Nelson left a strong mark of her presence in every institution that she was ever a part of, and there is none which does not regard its association with her as a source of deep pride. Past and Present is no exception. She was an immensely valued member of the Editorial Board for nearly twenty years, starting in 1995 and leaving in 2013, when she reached the mandatory retirement age of seventy. 1. Jinty Nelson c.2019 (Phil Fisk). Jinty studied at Newnham College, Cambridge, where she was a star student, made the University Challenge team, and later wrote her Ph.D. dissertation under the direction of Walter Ullmann.1 Ullmann did not approve of the way the thesis turned out, and their relationship was a fraught one, though it was eventually repaired. When discussing him later in life, she would sometimes quote what he had reportedly fumed to someone praising her work, after they were no longer on speaking terms: ‘Do not speak to me of that girl!’ (she emphasised ‘girl’, which is probably revealing, whether he had originally done so himself or not). At the root of their clashes was her evolving sense of a need to approach early medieval royal rituals as something other than the top-down communication of political ideas; to her they were also about negotiation, about meeting unspoken expectations. In this she was under the influence of anthropology, which at the time was a particularly active force in French medievalist academic circles, and was gaining ground in Britain among a younger generation of scholars, and a few older ones — even though, or perhaps because, it meant breaking out of some established patterns of thought. Despite this strong streak of intellectual independence from the start, it took her about a decade to really find her voice. In 1970 she was hired as a lecturer in the Department of History at King’s College London, where she would remain for the rest of her long and distinguished career. Six out of her first seven articles came out in Studies in Church History, the proceedings of the annual conferences of the Ecclesiastical History Society, to which she remained characteristically loyal throughout her career, publishing in it twelve times between 1971 and 1994. The sixth of these early articles, ‘On the Limits of the Carolingian Renaissance’ (1977), was her first classic, landmark article, and others followed hot on its heels over the next couple of years: ‘Kingship, Law and Liturgy in the Political Thought of Hincmar of Rheims’ (1977); ‘Inauguration Rituals’ (1977); and ‘Queens as Jezebels: The Careers of Brunhild and Balthild in Merovingian History’ (1978).2 The latter heralded a new aspect of her research, which would remain a stable feature from then on: women and gender — at this point still restricted to queens, but soon to branch out from there. During the 1980s and 1990s her strong and long-standing personal commitment to feminism became a more intrinsic part of her historical practice. She played a key role in setting up the Women’s History Seminar at the Institute of Historical Research in 1986. She was interested in engaging in dialogue across periods, but strongly resisted giving the early Middle Ages any special periodization job to do. She did not see it through rose-tinted glasses as a golden age for women, as many did who felt their duty lay in using the Middle Ages to show up modernity. She never lost sight of, nor took for granted, the deep seam of gender-based injustice running through the period she studied. But she did not dismiss the importance of women during it, nor discount the way some of them managed to leverage the small range of roles and privileges granted to them in this world of ‘little patriarchs’ in order to make their voices, their sense of their own rights, heard.3 As she showed in many articles, women were never simply not there; and accordingly, from this point until the end of her career, they would always form a part of any historical picture she put together. This was also, of course, a battle that still needed to be fought in the present: it took gumption then simply to demand to be taken seriously as an academic and an intellectual at the same time as being the mother of two small children. During these years, feminism, and a sense that the personal really was political, that the distinction between public and private was something that needed to be questioned, began to supply an increasingly crucial angle of approach for her historical work — and, unusually for the time, in relation not only to female subjects, but also to male ones. Two key male subjects for Jinty were Charles the Bald and Alfred, two ninth-century figures traditionally credited with the creation of (respectively) France and England. She roundly dismissed ahistorically nationalistic readings of their place in history, but without diminishing their role within it: rather than cutting them down to size, she cast them in a more realistic and a more interesting light — as makers of new political communities on more unfamiliar, contingent, and above all non-national terms. The culmination of this recurrent thread in her work was the series of addresses which she gave as President of the Royal Historical Society, in which she made connections and comparisons between England and the Continent in the ninth century in the broadest cultural as well as political, social, and economic terms.4 These lectures were given during a decade of professional triumphs. Between the 1990s and the mid-2000s she gained practically every accolade that it is possible to get as a member of the historical profession. In 1990 she joined the History Workshop Journal collective; in 1993 she became a professor at King’s; in 1993–4 she was President of the Ecclesiastical History Society; in 1995 she joined the Editorial Board of Past and Present; in 1996 she was elected a Fellow of the British Academy, serving as Vice President for Research from 1999 to 2001; she became the first female President of the Royal Historical Society in 2001; and in 2006 was awarded a DBE in recognition of her services to history. From the point of view of Past and Present, the 1990s were an important decade: it, and she, came not a moment too soon. In 1977, when Jinty’s first major article came out, Joan Thirsk had been the first and for the previous twenty years the only woman on the editorial board. In the late 1970s she was joined by Olwen Hufton and Judith Herrin, so the 1980s started strong, with three whole women on the board (and twenty men). At some point during the early 1980s, a daring proposition was made that perhaps a fourth woman might be asked to join the board, and that this might be Jinty. The suggestion was rejected, and there would in fact be a near ten-year gap before another woman did join (Joanna Innes, in 1988). Despite some significant renewal in membership, the editorial board remained quite strongly patriarchal in flavour and character, and a number of its members were yet to be convinced that women’s history or gender history were worthwhile pursuits. In view of this, it is not altogether surprising that the journal never became the natural home for gender history that one would wish, looking back, it had been able to become.5 The 1990s saw this atmosphere start to change. In 1990 the gender ratio had barely altered, with four women (non-administrative) editorial board members and twenty-two men; by 2000, there were nine women and sixteen men. Jinty, alongside the other women on the board at the time, was part of bringing about that important change in the character of the journal. At meetings she was an engaging and charming presence: someone with strong views about new directions the journal should take (not least on the need to encourage more articles by women and about women, family, gender, or masculinity), but by all accounts also someone one would always feel lucky to be sitting next to at lunch. Her reports on article submissions reflected her fierce standards, but she was immensely supportive and constructive wherever she saw potential. Two things happened during that era which I think had a big influence on Jinty’s practice as a historian: one was a professional caesura, when she started to assume those various positions of genuine influence in academic leadership; and the other in her life cycle, when she first became a grandmother in 2000. The latter led her, at this most busy time of her professional life, to scale back, and to turn Thursdays into inviolable, work-free ‘Granny days’.6 These two concurrent and major developments in her life — grandmotherhood and academic leadership — pulled against each other, if only in competing for her time; and together, of course, pulled against her own research time. But they both also seem to me to have enriched her historical practice profoundly. 2. Jinty’s staff page photograph: on a ‘Granny Day’ with grandson Eli, c.2002. The ease with which she made friends, and her ability to feel genuine admiration and respect for people with quite different values from her own, translated, in more official settings, into real political skill. As she experienced academic leadership there was a subtle change — not, I think, coincidentally — in the way she thought about Carolingian government. Her early years as a historian had been spent fighting back against a top-down reading of history, where kings, states, and governments were the ones that got their way and made things happen. She wrote about the limits to their ambitions, about the distance between their aspirations and the reality of their power; she was sceptical about the ‘Carolingian Renaissance’ and the ability of kings to force through change. In time, though, she became more attentive and more sympathetic to the sheer act of striving; and she laid ever greater emphasis on, and appreciation for, working towards a common purpose, of reform being not a test of royal power, but something that was brought closer to reality through the work of many people, lay and ecclesiastical. Her attention to the individuality of historical actors, strong from the beginning, had always led her to question the power of abstract ideas on their own to effect change, and to focus more on individuals’ own sense of their place in the world and the work they had to do in it. At first this led her to stress their scope for resistance. By the time of her later writings, though, she had come to see the part that these same individuals, with complicated personal histories and entanglements, could play in building something lasting: in establishing values and building institutions and communities, even in the face of ineffectiveness and defeat. This will likely chime with many readers’ experience of academic life in the UK and elsewhere, and this growing emphasis in her work went hand in hand with the process of learning to wield power herself within that world (in a way that was surely even more limited than that of the Carolingians). Grandmotherhood enriched her work in other ways. Her treatment of people became richer and more intimate: she started listening out for the ‘voice of Charlemagne’ in his legislation, and stressed the importance of family and how it was experienced, especially calling attention to the importance of small children within it — what she once called la politique de la crèche. Her last book included a memorable discussion of a story about Charlemagne losing his first milk tooth.7 These developments all leaned towards the highly personal, but were not reductive: they were intended to enrich her subjects, to open them up, to show how the conditions and structures of personal intimacy interacted with ideas about the self, about power and about the right order of things, but also about its disruption, in other areas — all of which came together in a genuinely embodied history of political ideas. Situating Charlemagne within that context is one of the major achievements of her biography of him, which was to be her last great work. It is symptomatic of her attention to individual experience that the only two books she wrote were biographies, of Charles the Bald (1992) and of Charlemagne (2019).8 Those were the projects that made her feel the need to expand beyond the length of a research article, which was otherwise her preferred format, and the one in which she made her mark.9 Even in this shorter form, she always turned her subjects, male or female, into real people: famous figures including Nithard and Dhuoda, but also obscure ones, such as Erkanfrida and Agintrude, who in someone else’s hands might have remained bit players but in hers were given a star turn.10 Curiously, almost none of these research articles came out in journals. Discounting Studies in Church History (every issue of which is more like an edited volume on a particular theme), you could count on the fingers of one hand the journal articles in her enormous bibliography: one in the English Historical Review, one in Speculum, one in Past and Present; that is pretty much it.11 She did contribute to journals, but mainly review articles, or short contributions to debates, or to special issues, or every now and then a published version of an annual lecture: in other words, she contributed to them principally in their capacity as a forum for exchange and debate. The overwhelming majority of her most important articles were published in the context of collective enterprises, in a wide range of edited collections published in many different countries. This was the context in which she most enjoyed working, and it reflects the breadth of her personal and intellectual connections. Forster’s ‘Only connect!’ was one of her favourite phrases, and she managed to live by it more than most. In her early career she had been combative and iconoclastic, but never a loner: she forged strong relationships, remembered and took to heart every personal fact and confidence, and was a fiercely loyal friend, who also made people feel loyal towards her. In the 1990s the Transformation of the Roman World project, funded by the European Science Foundation, helped to create a much denser and better-connected network of European scholars; she thrived in that setting. International connections in Europe and North America were important to her, and she to them. The collection The Medieval World which she published with Routledge in 2001, co-edited with Peter Linehan, was unusually broad in its outlook for the time — long before the global turn, when not many textbooks about the medieval ‘world’ had a chapter about Timbuktu — and it included contributions from academics working in North America, in the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and in Japan.12 She was interested in creating links with many different people, and was famously supportive of junior scholars in particular: she supervised no fewer than thirty-two Ph.D. students herself, but a great many more who were supervised by others found her to be just as unstinting in her attention.13 Visiting scholars often stayed at her house, and her kitchen table was a key intellectual magnet for early medievalists in London. These collective enterprises sometimes had a human focus rather than an intellectual one: some of her most field-defining articles, for instance, came out in Festschrifts, of which she co-edited quite a few herself.14 She edited papers and brought projects to completion for friends and colleagues who died prematurely.15 In historians and in historical subjects she was strongly preoccupied with recognizing the human beings behind the works, and not letting their contributions be forgotten. She was also extremely faithful to institutions: to King’s College London, to the Ecclesiastical History Society, to Past and Present, to History Workshop Journal, to the Institute of Historical Research in London. (Sometimes she was loyal to a fault, as in the case of her unswerving fidelity — to others unfathomable — to Pizza Paradiso, the little Italian restaurant on Store Street where the Earlier Middle Ages seminar felt duty-bound to go every Wednesday after the paper, until even her unconditional support proved unequal to the task of keeping it in business.) I was surprised, even a little bit shocked, to discover her rebellious streak in stories I heard about her youth, some of which she told me herself. Walter Ullmann, for instance, always smoked cigars during doctoral supervisions, which rather annoyed Jinty; one day, after they had sat down and he had taken out and lit his usual cigar, she took out and lit one of her own. (I like to remember she said it was a bigger cigar, though that may be wishful thinking rather than an actual memory: the point was made all the same.) Several people who knew her at the time talked about her as being ‘formidable’, and I can well imagine that. auditPapers.title: Reconstrucción 3D histórica y difusión digital del patrimonio arquitectónico en peligro: el caso del Monasterio de Nuestra Señora del Risco (Amavida, Ávila)
auditPapers.abstract: Este trabajo presenta un enfoque innovador para la valorización y difusión del patrimonio arquitectónico en peligro, tomando como caso de estudio el Monasterio de Nuestra Señora del Risco. A través de imágenes generadas a partir de un modelo tridimensional (3D) y de una visita virtual 4D, se busca conectar la reconstrucción histórica del monasterio en su momento de máximo esplendor, el siglo XVIII, con su estado actual, mostrando las transformaciones sufridas a lo largo del tiempo. La reconstrucción virtual integra diversos aspectos del edificio: elementos arquitectónicos, características del emplazamiento y posibles funcionalidades. Asimismo, se ha incorporado a la visita virtual información relativa a la actual ubicación de elementos arquitectónicos originarios del monasterio, actualmente deslocalizados. Este enfoque demuestra las capacidades interpretativas y divulgativas de las técnicas digitales que, a pesar de sus limitaciones, contribuyen significativamente a una mejor comprensión del pasado. De igual forma, se plantea como objetivo la identificación de bienes deslocalizados originarios de un bien patrimonial en peligro. Este proyecto, además de transmitir la riqueza arquitectónica del monasterio, resalta su importancia histórica y cultural. La cuidadosa representación de los elementos decorativos, mobiliario e iluminación interior permite recrear la atmósfera de oración, trabajo y vida comunitaria que caracterizó a este espacio monástico. Con ello también se ofrece una visión enriquecida del legado histórico y se promueve su valorización y conservación. El edificio estudiado presenta una singular distribución en planta, fruto de lo accidentado del terreno y de su origen ligado al culto a la roca de la cueva. Esto ha supuesto un particular reto en la reconstrucción, precisando un análisis de los restos (incluyendo adquisición de datos geométricos con fotogrametría); además, se realizó su comparación con otros ejemplos de patrimonio abulense que, si bien presentan elementos comunes, tienen en su mayoría plantas más canónicas que el caso de estudio planteado.

We carefully selected and prepared the data, reflected on potential biases and trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) accordingly. Our model architecture was designed to process sets of images instead of only one individual image, which enables us to experiment with different combinations of image segments. This forms the basis for an analysis framework, which allows us to go beyond mere painter attribution and to explore the ambiguity of image similarity itself.

auditPapers.title: The Vortex: An Environmental History of the Modern World. By Frank Uekötter
auditPapers.abstract: The Vortex is an ambitious reinterpretation of modern history that foregrounds the natural world. Over the past five centuries, human societies have expanded, fought, oppressed, rebelled, traded, and built in ways that have profoundly shaped life on Earth. Throughout, the environment itself has been a dynamic sculptor of world history, etching or foreclosing paths often beyond the intentions of our species. The book captures this thesis in its title and central metaphor of a vortex: “The key is that the vortex highlights the powers of the nonhuman world and their unrelenting inclination to push humans around” (11). The Vortex is an unapologetically anthropocentric book in which the environment constitutes perhaps the most important player—one that humans seek to master at their peril and whose instability in the face of modernity threatens increasingly to lead to collective catastrophe. Frank Uekötter is the author of several important books about the environmental history of Germany. Here he broadens his canvas. This book’s temporal sweep concentrates on the years between 1500 and 1970. The geographic scope covers all of planet Earth, with particular areas of focus, backed up by original archival research, on Germany, the United States, and the United Kingdom. In prose running across forty chapters and more than six hundred pages, Uekötter combines the tools of global history and environmental history to weave a provocative argument about what we can and cannot know about the modern world. He places The Vortex in dialogue with several other major syntheses of global environmental history, most prominently J.R. McNeill’s Something New Under the Sun and Joachim Radkau’s Nature and Power. Uekötter’s principal intervention is to emphasize disorder. “The best one-sentence summary of this volume,” he writes, “would be that it is all a big mess, and we are stuck in the middle of it” (611). Against the comparatively neat narratives of McNeill and Radkau, Uekötter asserts a more chaotic vision.

auditPapers.title: Transnational Whiteness and the Elite Backlash to Reforming the Australian Immigration Control System in the 1950s and 1960s
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In the 1950s and 1960s, changes in the international situation, such as decolonization in Asia, led some Australians to question the usefulness of keeping the ‘White Australia Policy’, the basis for the country’s immigration system since Federation in 1901. Some argued that Australia’s international reputation, especially with newly independent countries in Asia and Africa, could be harmed by the maintenance of this policy. Events such as the Sharpeville Massacre in apartheid South Africa in 1960 caused further introspection into Australia’s racialized system. However, as pushes to reform the policy grew, others used international events to resist reforms. Using speeches by politicians and documents produced by policymakers, this article will show how events, such as the Notting Hill riots in Britain, the Little Rock controversy in the United States, and the Sharpeville massacre, were used as warnings about Australia potentially introducing similar ‘racial problems’ if it allowed more non-white migration. This article argues that these concerns tapped into a transnational whiteness that shared anxieties about decolonization, civil rights and non-white immigration in the post-war period, bringing a racialized solidarity forged at the turn of the twentieth century into the Cold War era.

auditPapers.title: A Forgotten Migration: Black Southerners, Segregation Scholarships, and the Debt Owed to Public Black HBCUs. By Crystal R. Sanders
auditPapers.abstract: In A Forgotten Migration: Black Southerners, Segregation Scholarships, and the Debt Owed to Public Black HBCUs, Crystal Sanders presents a compelling study of the intersections between segregation and the development or underdevelopment of graduate and professional school opportunities for African Americans and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). She incorporates suggestive vocabulary like “intellectual warfare” to depict the determination of civil rights lawyers like Charles Hamilton Houston and Thurgood Marshall, and the courage of African American test plaintiffs like Lloyd Gaines, Ada Sipuel, and George McLaurin, who legally dismantled the focus of her book—segregation scholarships. The term “segregation scholarships” echoes the definitive ideological themes like slavery as a “peculiar institution” and Jim Crow having a “strange career.” Southern and border state governments defended their racially discriminatory decision to allocate significant funds for sending Black citizens out of state, primarily to the North, for graduate degrees by citing the United States Supreme Court’s 1896 ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson, which established the “separate but equal” doctrine. However, in 1938, the Gaines v. Canada Supreme Court case stipulated that “separate but equal” meant either admitting African Americans into white, in-state public graduate schools or establishing and funding a “separate but equal” graduate program for African American students within the state, often at a Negro college. Sanders’ book highlighted enforcement challenges, as states ignored the Gaines v. Canada ruling and continued to offer segregation scholarships, along with significantly inferior funding for graduate programs at HBCUs, leading to a wave of litigation. Ironically, in 1921, Walthall M. Moore, the first African American to serve in the Missouri General Assembly, introduced the original legislation for segregation scholarships as an attempt to help Black’s attain higher education. As noted in Sanders’ central contention that “the burdens Black southerners withstood in the quest for advanced study functioned as a double tax levied on account of racism,” meaning African Americans contributed taxwise to funding state and federal education but due to anti-Black racism were illegally penalized for attempting to access that same educational system, particularly on the graduate level (7).

auditPapers.title: ON CONCEPTS AS HISTORICAL FORMS
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT What are the consequences of holding fast to the axiom that words are not the same thing as concepts? This article explores some of them in relation to the tensions between two different but overlapping approaches to the history of concepts: philology and computationally informed historical semantics. The methods utilized were developed in the Cambridge Concept Lab and essentially comprise a measurement for word associations that can then be exported into comparative frameworks for tracking the evolution of concepts over time. Some examples are provided using the dataset Eighteenth Century Collections Online that are intended to demonstrate the fecundity of computational approaches to the history of ideas and concepts. Throughout the article, a distinction is held between two interconnected terms: meanings and concepts—or to put that more pointedly, the hard case of distinguishing between a change in meaning of a word and a change in conceptual form is addressed. Although the article comes to the conclusion that hard‐and‐fast distinctions between words and concepts are extremely difficult to maintain, it nevertheless insists on the benefit of supposing that such distinctions can be held. This enables one to characterize concepts in terms of their functions rather than their meanings, and some examples of these functions are provided. In conclusion, the article returns to the issue of historical approaches to words and concepts and suggests that a conceptual history formulated through the lens of conceptual function complements philological accounts of how words and meanings inform us about the past.

auditPapers.title: Computation and Form, Reconsidered
auditPapers.abstract: Throughout the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, critics have continually reconsidered the compatibility of computation and the humanities. Often, questions of “form” have played key roles in these conversations. In the 1940s, for example, critics asked whether word-counting might capture “formal units” of poetry like style. By the 2010s, scholars debated with new fervor whether computational methods could—or should—be used to track aesthetic structures like narrative, character, or genre, and especially without eliding rich socio-historical contexts. Today, these debates are by no means over. But they look different after a half decade of new work, and a cascade of theoretical and technical developments—perhaps most prominently, increasing attention to audiovisual materials and the explosion of transformer-based generative AI. In this special issue, we bring together scholars from across multiple disciplines to reconsider the intersections between computation and form for this emerging technological and critical moment. Together, their work represents a digital humanities in multiple types of transition. The essays collected in this issue refine existing computational critical methods to enable more nuanced and contextualized formal analysis; they apply these methods beyond literary or aesthetic canons to broader ranges of audiovisual, pop-cultural, and technical artifacts, from comics and conspiracy theories to viral TikToks; and they consider prompt-based LLMs, not only as new tools of aesthetic analysis, but also as cultural and technical “forms” in their own right. The articles in this special issue will be published in groups on a rolling basis over the coming weeks.

auditPapers.title: Beyond Computational Formalism or, Architecture Matters
auditPapers.abstract: Despite frequently avowed commitments to formalist methodologies, computational literary studies (CLS) has insufficiently accounted for the importance of the formal architectures of the computational models it employs—particularly deep learning neural networks. By examining the genealogy of neural network architectures—from Frank Rosenblatt’s Perceptron to contemporary transformer-based models—this article demonstrates how these architectures materially shape the capacities, outputs, and interpretive possibilities of machine learning models.
