auditPapers.title: Parler Games: A Narrative Framework Analysis of Parler Conspiracy Theories and the January 6th Insurrection
auditPapers.abstract: Parler, a prominent right-leaning "echo platform," became a forum in late 2020 for Trump supporters convinced the 2020 election was fraudulent as they abandoned or were banned from Twitter. This study suggests that a narrative analytical approach to the discussions on Parler in the period from the 2020 presidential election up to the violence at the Capitol on January 6th, 2021 can provide some insight into the relationship between storytelling and real world action. We deploy a computational pipeline combining natural language processing and network analysis to uncover the underlying narrative framework, based on an actant-interaction model. We use a topic modeling approach to further reduce the complexity of the narrative framework; various community detection methods afford a macroscopic view onto the discussions, allowing one to both trace the development of narratives and subnarratives over time, and to explore at various levels of granularity the make-up of narrative subgraphs. The main narrative framework of Parler is redolent of conspiracy theory, and portrays a profound threat to America and her patriots from deep state actors, "globalists," and Democrats. This threat necessitates a response. Beyond expressing anger, people posting to the site developed strategies for fighting back. Analyzing shifts and connections in conversations reveals an emergent real-world conspiracy to take violent action on January 6th, demonstrating how online conspiracy theorizing fostered an emergent real-world conspiracy.

auditPapers.title: Beyond Plot: How Sentiment Analysis Reshapes Our Understanding of Narrative Structure
auditPapers.abstract: Sentiment analysis, particularly with the advent of large language models, is reshaping our understanding of narrative. Emotional arcs in both fictional and non-fictional narratives surface latent structures that challenge traditional notions of plot and character. One reason is that feature extraction correlates with passages often selected for close reading, suggesting the role of emotion in passage selection has been undertheorized. Case studies, moreover, show that common critiques of sentiment analysis are misplaced, and the method can identify and contrast cultural differences, locate translation effects, and illuminate collective emotional experiences. Both the strengths and limitations of sentiment analysis in understanding affect and emotion in literature are detailed to help address misconceptions. The method, as it turns out, now offers a powerful tool for highlighting emotional structure in narrative, complementing traditional literary analysis and reshaping our understanding of what constitutes a story. Sentiment analysis for literary studies asks us to reconsider not just how we analyze individual texts, but how we conceptualize the very nature of narrative itself.

auditPapers.title: A site-wide and comprehensive assessment of salt-induced tuff deterioration in the Archaeological Park of Herculaneum
auditPapers.abstract: The Archaeological Park of Herculaneum, buried by the 79 CE eruption of Mount Vesuvius, faces a significant conservation challenge, the degradation of the volcanic tuff walls. Building upon previous studies, this work presents the first large-scale assessment of this degradation phenomenon, employing a comprehensive analytical approach that extends across the entire archaeological park. In detail, this study combines in-situ and laboratory analyses to investigate the origin and composition of the soluble salts that take part in this degradation process. Thermographic imaging identified moisture accumulation at the base of walls, confirming the capillary rise of humidity from the soil. Raman and FT-IR spectroscopy revealed that sodium sulfate, in both anhydrous (thenardite) and hydrated (mirabilite) forms, is the predominant salt, with additional contributions from calcium sulfate and minor nitrates. Ion chromatography of soil samples confirmed significant spatial and seasonal variations, with sulfates more concentrated in northern areas and increasing overall in winter. The results demonstrate that a combined approach using ion chromatography, thermographic imaging, and handheld Raman spectroscopy provides an efficient diagnostic tool for assessing salt-related deterioration. This protocol could be extended to other archaeological sites to guide conservation strategies and mitigate the impact of salt-induced decay on built heritage.

auditPapers.title: Quantifying the faithfulness of poetry translations in four closely related Slavic languages
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Translating poetry is notoriously difficult—some would claim impossible—because it inherently requires making triage decisions what to preserve and what to sacrifice if necessary. Both form and meaning contribute to the esthetic effects of the original, but translations that faithfully preserve the metrical versification principles of the original might struggle to fully preserve lexically conveyed meanings and connotations, and vice versa. Other esthetically relevant sound-related features (e.g. phonemic patterns) are particularly challenging to preserve. This paper presents a pilot study to empirically test this intuition by assessing the faithfulness of translations to their original. Quantifying aspects of the beauty of sound and meaning, that is, the sonority and the esthetic affective potential, of selected poems and their translations in/from Russian, Polish, Czech, and Slovak, that is, a sample controlled for linguistic and cultural context, we measure the degree to which translations correspond to their originals along these dimensions. The results suggest that, for the poems and languages considered, the beauty of sound and meaning are preserved to varying degrees, which can be sensibly interpreted against specific features of the poems, linguistic distances, and cultural prestige. The study thus serves as a proof of concept that demonstrates the basic feasibility of the method applied and foreshadows its potential for advancing empirical studies in the field of comparative poetics.

auditPapers.title: Geotropes: Situating Postcolonial Bestsellers in the Global Literary Marketplace
auditPapers.abstract: Conceptions of the literature of the Global South, and of India in particular, have been powerfully shaped by the work of a small number of well-known authors writing in English. The possible distortions resulting from this limited canon have garnered significant scholarly attention in the past two decades, which has typically focused on how works produced by these writers are shaped by their own positionality as well as the exigencies of catering to an Anglo-European metropolitan audience. The concern expressed in such reflections often boils down to that of offering incomplete, skewed, or overly accommodationist representations of the cultures and countries being represented. A corollary of this position is that these same metropolitan readers would be confronted with a different, and potentially quite valuable perspective on the countries and cultures for which these authors have been presumed to speak, were they to encounter a broader swath of the writing produced by local authors writing in indigenous languages. This essay attempts to evaluate and concretize this presumption by way of a computationally assisted analysis. We compare a collection of contemporary English-language novels written by authors of South Asian descent with a corpus of contemporary fiction translated from South Asian languages into English. Using a series of quantitative proxies for two qualities seen as typical of English-language originals — literariness and cosmopolitanism — we aim to establish 1) whether and how the works of the authors writing in English can be seen to constitute a distinctive corpus vis-à-vis the translated works and 2) whether and how the former converge with literary fiction translated from two languages considered to possess high literary capital: French and German. By situating the postcolonial bestsellers within this broader context, we intend to provide a starting point from which to understand the differential pressures exerted by the “otherness industry” on literary production, as well as how reader perceptions of South Asia might be different if they were exposed to a broader range of translated texts.

auditPapers.title: Communications
auditPapers.abstract: Dear colleague, I am writing in response to a review of my book, A Slave Between Empires, that a colleague, Odile Moreau, contributed to the March 2025 issue of your journal. Usually, I do not reply to reviews of my books in academic journals. But the problematic nature of this review compels me to do so; it is biased, misleading, and full of mistakes. The book was awarded the Alf Andrew Heggoy Book Prize (from the French Colonial Historical Society) in 2021 for the best volume published in the preceding year dealing with the modern French colonial experience. It was also a finalist for the 2021 African Studies Association Best Book Prize. Yet in this instance, either the author did not understand the argument of the book, or she did not have the proper historical expertise to engage it. The reviewer does not discuss at all the argument of the book: namely, how to interpret the colonial history of North Africa and more precisely the history of colonial Tunisia through its own Ottoman legacy. She insists instead on details that are not relevant to the book’s core argument and goals. For instance, Moreau writes that “In addition to being very vague, however, the title is misleading, by fixing the category of slave in a static manner, whereas the book shows that Husayn’s trajectory and his status were very dynamic.” Titles are by definition very broad, and in this case, the title precisely highlights the main figure’s “in-betweenness.”

auditPapers.title: Susannah Gibson. The Bluestockings: A History of the First Women’s Movement
auditPapers.abstract: Susannah Gibson’s The Bluestockings: A History of the First Women’s Movement explores the lives of the renowned Bluestocking women—an informal association of mostly upper-class women whose shared pursuit of intellectual study challenged contemporary beliefs of appropriately gendered behavior and capabilities. For Gibson, the Bluestocking salons enabled these women to “prove […] that they were capable of so much more than anyone believed possible” (4). Gibson possesses a power of description that works to transport readers to the Bluestockings’ salons, leading the reader to feel as if they are dining and conversing with guests, as if the reader knows each woman—her thoughts, feelings, and character—­­on a most intimate level. This style makes Bluestockings both informative and delightful, and it is written in such a way as to appeal to any reader interested in eighteenth-century histories of women, gender, and intellectualism. Gibson deploys a number of thematic lenses across eleven chapters, with something to interest readers from a wide range of scholarly backgrounds. A significant proportion of Gibson’s research is ­­centered, for example, around contemporary medi­­cal thought and practice; Bluestockings frequently includes detailed descriptions of ailments with which eighteenth-century women contended and the treatments they applied to cure themselves, their families, and friends. The seventh chapter of Bluestockings, “Motherhood,” is especially rich with such detail, explicating the remedies and practices applied, often seemingly in vain, by Bluestocking Hester Thrale to heal herself and her family from myriad afflictions. From her many uncomfortable pregnancies and the frequently fatal illnesses her children suffered to the sexually transmitted infections repeatedly contracted by her husband, Thrale oversaw the family’s care and often personally administered the recommended treatments of the time (159, 174–75). Gibson’s work offers critical insights to researchers of eighteenth-century English society that extend far beyond the salons of the Bluestocking women, and draws us into their sickrooms, still-rooms, and bed-chambers.

auditPapers.title: Bayley J. Marquez. Plantation Pedagogy: The Violence of Schooling Across Black and Indigenous Space
auditPapers.abstract: Each generation since Reconstruction, it seems, rediscovers Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute. Turning to cultural geography, critical theory, and archival history, Marquez examines how Armstrong and Richard Henry Pratt, founder of Carlisle Indian Industrial School, believed African slavery in the United States held civilizing lessons for conquered Indigenous nations. Marquez distills this discourse into a heuristic she calls “plantation pedagogy” and its two tenets: 1) that proximity to whiteness promoted civilization, and 2) that manual labor transformed people into productive subjects who would, in turn, transform land into productive property. This pedagogy aimed to reform Black and Indigenous peoples by teaching both “slavery and settlement” (3).

auditPapers.title: D. Fairchild Ruggles. Tree of Pearls: The Extraordinary Architectural Patronage of the 13th-Century Egyptian Slave-Queen Shajar al-Durr.
auditPapers.abstract: With a frankness that characterizes Tree of Pearls: The Extraordinary Architectural Patronage of the 13th-Century Egyptian Slave-Queen Shajar al-Durr, D. Fairchild Ruggles muses, “In writing Shajar al-Durr’s story, I have often struggled with the problem of genre. Is this biography? Social history? Art history? Melodrama?” (146). Narrating the lives of premodern Islamic women poses unique challenges that can only be partially solved through reading sources against the grain and employing interdisciplinary methods. Often, as in the case of Shajar al-Durr, the written record of elite women is produced by men who are concerned with their lives only when they intersect with politics and, as I have argued, through motifs and tropes as a way to praise or critique the state. Ruggles contextualizes such sources, as well as the later legends and myths that surround this exceptional figure, by putting them in conversation with material culture. Writing the story of Shajar al-Durr is doubly challenging. Not only was she a woman, but she was enslaved. Therefore, biographical information about her family history is completely unknown because her slave status erased those relationships. She enters the historical record as concubine to the Ayyubid Sultan Salih (d. 1249), as Ruggles notes, “as an object of exchange between men” (19). Negotiating the diverse array of source material necessary for excavating a history of this woman is where her analysis shines. Translated excerpts from textual sources are juxtaposed with detailed descriptions of urban space and the exterior and interior of key buildings, including Salih’s madrasa (school), his tomb, and Shajar al-Durr’s tomb. Scattered through the pages of the book are images of buildings, manuscripts, coins, architectural plans, and reconstruction drawings as well as maps of Cairo, inviting the reader to traverse the city as Ruggles imagines that Shajar al-Durr might have done. What makes a biography of the slave-queen possible is the abundance of material culture that gives evidence to her political role, especially the coins minted in her name, one of the signs of leadership in the premodern Islamic world, and the commemorative architecture that she built for both her deceased husband Salih and, later, herself.

auditPapers.title: Shelby Johnson. The Rich Earth Between Us: The Intimate Grounds of Race and Sexuality in the Atlantic World, 1770–1840
auditPapers.abstract: Burials haunt the narratives assembled in Shelby Johnson’s The Rich Earth Between Us: burials in earth and water, burials deferred or denied, burials of knowledge and subaltern desire beneath the weight of imperial records and ontologies. One that lingers with me still is a brief story about reburial in William Apess’s (Pequot) Eulogy on King Philip (1836), in which an unnamed Native man disinters his son’s body, carrying it 200 miles away after finding his white neighbors apathetic to his grief. Johnson presses on questions history cannot answer: What was this child’s name? How did he die? What paths did his heartbroken father take? And what else remains buried in colonial archives, either hidden or distorted beyond recognition? While much remains unknowable, Johnson reads the father’s journey north to an Indigenous community in Canada as an act of “worldmaking”: “the father must, impossibly, improvise a world out of a shattering loss and an unsettled grave” (107).

auditPapers.title: Thomas W. Smith. Rewriting the First Crusade: Epistolary Culture in the Middle Ages
auditPapers.abstract: Much of what we used to know about the First ­­Crusade is becoming complicated by ongoing research. What was the catalyst? What was the goal? Who was in charge? Where does it fit within a developing ideology of holy war? One thing is clear: The voluminous textual record produced during and after the events of 1096–1099 constitutes an unprecedented documentary response driven by intense contemporary interest, raising vital questions about why and how such texts were made, and what kinds of evidence can be distilled from them. Moreover, because they were shaped by the various material and embodied media through which news and (mis)information circulated, these texts are a tremendous resource for studying medieval modes of communication, regardless of their veracity. In Rewriting the First Crusade: Epistolary Culture in the Middle Ages, Thomas W. Smith makes an important contribution to our understanding of the manuscript milieu that conveyed these narratives, and to the process of reassessing how historians should be reading and teaching them now.

auditPapers.title: Rajbir Singh Judge. Prophetic Maharaja: Loss, Sovereignty, and the Sikh Tradition in Colonial South Asia
auditPapers.abstract: Prophetic Maharaja: Loss, Sovereignty, and the Sikh Tradition in Colonial South Asia by Rajbir Singh Judge revisits the efforts of Duleep Singh, the youngest son of Ranjit Singh (d. 1839), the ruler of the Greater Punjab State centered in Lahore, to return to Punjab and reclaim his inheritance in the 1880s. Utilizing psychoanalysis as a core analytic, the author tells us that there is “no ‘real’ Duleep Singh nor an authentic story to tell” (2); Singh instead should be seen “as a struggle to constitute meaning” (138).The author’s aim, then, is not to recover the history of Duleep Singh, but to understand how the idea of Singh circulated in late nineteenth-century Punjab, and the British empire more broadly, among Punjabis and colonial officials alike. The book thus highlights the unknowability of the colonial subject, which “oscillated between contradictory interpellations” (89). Still, it is not entirely clear how different the author’s approach to Duleep Singh is from already existing explorations of the multiple and contested views of this figure, such as Tony Ballantyne’s, despite the author’s disregard for it (and for history as a field). Frequent declarations of ambiguity, instability, contingency, and a “contested and discrepant tradition” may not be sufficient to differentiate this approach (120).

auditPapers.title: Marion Girard Dorsey. Holding Their Breath: How the Allies Confronted the Threat of Chemical Warfare in World War II.
auditPapers.abstract: The Allies did not deploy poison gas during the Second World War, but its potential use is the subject of this fascinating work of comparative diplomatic and mili­­tary history. Despite international attempts to limit or ban the use of gas after 1918, the Western Allies (the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada) ­­continued to explore the ethical and practical use of gas on the battlefield. This is an important study with a rich archival foundation that details the complexities of creating a common policy among three democratic countries. It also shows that, despite the wider efforts to outlaw the use of poisonous gas, each country was sometimes prepared to use gas if deemed necessary. Marion Girard Dorsey’s Holding Their Breath begins in 1925, when signatories of the Geneva Gas Protocol agreed to ban the use of chemical weapons and biological weapons. Britain and Canada signed the Protocol; the United States did not. Even so, it still posed a powerful check on the use of gas for all three countries. International opinion mattered. Dorsey draws from Susan Grayzel’s work to detail how the British government tried to prepare for gas attacks that never came. Dorsey is on firmer ground when exploring how gas became a powerful diplomatic and propaganda tool. British diplomatic notes to belligerents (and less trustworthy Allies) were worded carefully to avoid any sense that, if a gas war ensued, the Allies were responsible. It was a delicate balancing act. As Dorsey notes, after 1941 “Would a warning [against the use of gas] deter Germany? Would the same announcement backfire and incite Russia, bringing about the very outcome—gas warfare—that Britain hoped to avoid? And, on top of this, what was Britain willing to promise a dubious ally?” (105). Ultimately, in May 1942, Winston Churchill promised publicly that if “we are satisfied” that the Germans had used poison gas against the Russians, the Allies would launch “gas warfare on the largest possible scale far and wide upon the towns and cities of Germany” (105). For their part, the Americans broadened ­­Churchill’s warning, promising “full and swift retaliation in kind” if the Axis deployed gas in Europe or Asia. As Dorsey concludes, the Americans “may have deterred or risked—a global gas war” (107).

auditPapers.title: Mistakes I Carried
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract My critical mistake as a historian was ignoring the physical body as a site of knowledge production. For years, I analyzed fitness history in archives and images while overlooking the value of embodied experience. Recognizing this blind spot offers historians a powerful new lens—namely, that bodies can serve as historical archives that capture dimensions of the past inaccessible through traditional sources. In this article, I explore this approach by connecting my personal weight training journey with J. C. Hise, an American strength figure from the 1930s. By examining parallel experiences of extreme body transformation during periods of economic instability—Hise during the Great Depression and myself following the 2008 financial crisis—the article explores how masculine identity crises repeatedly manifest in physical culture. Through my own experience with Hise’s grueling twenty-rep squat program, I discuss how physical practices reshape both bodies and worldviews. This embodied knowledge explains, in part, how fitness cultures reinforce the very insecurities they claim to address while transforming masculine anxiety into profit. By positioning the transformed body as a site where personal metamorphosis intersects with broader social and economic forces, historians can access a more complete understanding of how physical culture has shaped masculine identities across generations.

auditPapers.title: David Yee. Informal Metropolis: Life on the Edge of Mexico City, 1940–1976
auditPapers.abstract: Over the last two decades, the idea of “Third World” deviant cases of urbanization—that is, gigantism, corruption, cronyism, political clientelism, poverty, informality, and inequality—has been surpassed by a growing historiography showing the inevitability and co-substantiality of the formal/legal/planned and the informal/illegal/chaotic in twentieth-century megalopolises, in either Mexico City or Kolkata. David Yee builds on and advances this historiography with a remarkable contribution displaying imaginative research—from notary records to rare local municipal archives, from presidential papers to cultural traces left by all sorts of intriguing characters (urban speculators, union leaders, Jewish immigrants converted into urban speculators and show businessmen). Readers will find in the book a thorough examination of the politics of housing, informality, and space, mostly centered on the largest and most important “informal settlement” in twentieth-century Mexico City: Ciudad Netzahualcóyotl (Neza)—Yee significantly expands previous pioneer studies by Carlos G. Vélez-Ibañez (Rituals of Marginality [1983]) and Maribel Espinosa Castillo (Ecatepec y Nezahualcóyotl [2010]).

auditPapers.title: Amy Sodaro. Lifting the Shadow: Reshaping Memory, Race, and Slavery in U.S. Museums.
auditPapers.abstract: Lifting the Shadow: Reshaping Memory, Race, and Slavery in U.S. Museums by Amy Sodaro argues that museums like the National Museum of African Ameri­can History (NMAAHC) in Washington, DC; the Legacy Museum in Montgomery, Alabama; and the Greenwood Rising Museum in Tulsa, Oklahoma represent a new category of African American memorial museum specific to the post-2016 Trump presidency. Amid the turmoil of white nationalism, these new museums implicated the present as intimately connected to the past, which in Sodaro’s view, presented new narratives that differed from previous African American history museums. Sodaro argues that these new museums are heavily influenced by memorial museums to other tragedies, like the 9/11 museum and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, borrowing on their storytelling methods and affective design elements to tell hard-hitting stories about the United States’ racist past. Lifting the Shadows is organized in five chapters. The first chapter offers a brief history of the Black museum movement before launching into three chapters dedicated to one of the three museums mentioned above. A fifth chapter explores the concept of the “new memorial museum.” She defines “the new memorial museums” as “hybrid commemorative forms that infuse their historical exhibits with memory … They are driven by narrative” (33). Each of the three museum case studies explore the relationship that the museums have with local communities and beyond.

auditPapers.title: Panagiotis Delis. Notions of Violence and Ethnic Cleansing on the Eve of the First World War: The Balkan Wars of 1912–13
auditPapers.abstract: The Balkan Wars, fought as two distinct but closely interrelated conflicts between October 1912 and August 1913, reshaped the political map of Southeastern Europe and led to the expulsion of the Ottoman Empire from most of the Balkan Peninsula. Unlike the nineteenth-century Balkan revolutionary wars of national liberation, waged by local notables, peasants, and brigands against Ottoman rule, the Balkan Wars were launched by independent, modernizing Balkan states, grouped together in the Balkan League (Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro, and Serbia) against an increasingly beleaguered Ottoman state. These conflicts were waged by modern armies, supported by paramilitaries and other irregular forces, and characterized by internecine violence that often targeted noncombatants. They reshaped borders, communities, and identities, and in many respects, these wars prefigured the mass violence that characterized European history in the first half of the twentieth century. The centenary of the Balkan Wars occasioned several academic conferences and monographs that revisited these two wars, their origins, course, and legacies. While earlier studies had focused on the high politics of the Balkan Wars and small-power imperialisms of the region’s states, these newer works have examined the dynamics of local violence and how communities in the multiethnic and multiconfessional Balkans navigated the contentious and increasingly violent state policies of irredentism, occupation, and assimilation. This is certainly no easy task, as it involves working in multiple languages across regional and national archives in several countries, as well as having a solid understanding of local historiographies. Panagiotis Delis’s Notions of Violence and Ethnic Cleansing on the Eve of the First World War is one of the most recent studies in this vein and builds on the earlier works by Dimitar Tasić, Ryan Gingeras, Eyal Ginio, John Paul Newman, and others.

auditPapers.title: Mary Ellen Curtain. She Changed the Nation: Barbara Jordan’s Life and Legacy in Black Politics.
auditPapers.abstract: In She Changed the Nation: Barbara Jordan’s Life and Legacy in Black Politics, Mary Ellen Curtin offers an ambitious and nuanced biography of Texas Congresswoman Barbara Jordan (1936–96). Even though Shirley Chisholm was the “first” Black woman to serve in Congress, it was Jordan who was the first Black woman elected to the House of Representatives from the South, where she had to battle stubborn legacies of disfranchisement. Jordan ably navigated a Black, Latino, and white electoral coalition in Houston, winning election to the state house in the 1960s, where she served for six years, and then to Congress in 1972 for three terms. While she was often overshadowed by Congresswoman Chisholm, Jordan commanded the nation’s attention in her star-making speeches at the Watergate hearings and the Democratic National Convention, becoming the very first Black woman to deliver a keynote address in 1976. Even though she was most famous for her speeches, Curtin argues that Jordan was a highly effective legislator, and her book chronicles that more hidden history. Drawing on archival collections, newspaper articles, biographies, and oral histories, Curtin critically analyzes Jordan’s public career and private life, rightfully situating her in the pantheon of Black political leaders in the twentieth century.

auditPapers.title: Robert M. Owens. Killing over Land: Murder and Diplomacy on the Early American Frontier
auditPapers.abstract: Imperialism, colonization, competition for land, and murder go hand in hand. With the arrival of ­­Europeans on North American shores, an adversarial mindset developed between Indigenous and settler colonial communities. These contentious relationships often led to miscommunication, conflict, and, in some cases, murder. From the Pequot Massacre in 1637 and colonial cross-cultural frontier raids to the terror of Pontiac’s Rebellion and the horrors of removal in the 1830s, Indigenous and early American communities searched for stability in an ever-­­changing world. Murder impacted communities across the racial divide on the early North American frontier. Murder, like trading relationships, created an avenue for both sides to seek redress, forced them to communicate with one another in the cause of justice, and produced a shared space where the parties could potentially find common ground. This is the main argument of ­­Robert M. Owens’s book Killing over Land: Murder and ­­Diplomacy on the Early American Frontier. Over the course of fourteen chapters, Owens methodically unpacks the nature of cross-racial murder in early American history and its connections to power, land, natural resources, and empire building in the ­­eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

auditPapers.title: Charlotte Lydia Riley. Imperial Island: An Alternative History of the British Empire
auditPapers.abstract: Critical histories of Britain’s relationship with its imperial past have become commonplace in recent years, which is hardly surprising given the ongoing position of the empire in the country’s rabid culture war discourses of recent years. Charlotte Lydia Riley’s Imperial Island (originally published in the UK by Penguin last year and now appearing in the US ­courtesy of Harvard University Press) joins other recent works—by the likes of Hakim Adi, Priyamvada Gopal, and Sathnam Sanghera—in providing a historically detailed, yet highly readable, riposte to unpleasant waves of imperial nostalgia and apologia promoted by a coalition of right-wing politicians and nonexpert academics. Taking readers on a journey from the throes of the Second World War to the ferocious contestations over Brexit, Imperial Island convincingly demonstrates the near-inescapable presence of imperialism in British society, politics, and culture since the 1930s. As this core argument suggests, the book is a history of empire in Britain over the last ninety-odd years and not a new history of the British Empire (as the rather misleading Harvard edition subtitle of An Alternative History of the British Empire might imply). Riley focuses particularly on ordinary people—a category that is acknowledged as imperfect in the introduction—and builds her case using a well-established canon of sources. Newspapers and political pamphlets rub shoulders with government documents, diaries, oral histories, and popular culture artifacts (ranging from BBC sitcoms to anarcho-punk songs). A brief historiographical discussion in the introduction helps situate Riley’s work within a broader movement toward decolonizing and repositioning modern British history.

auditPapers.title: John Ma. Polis: A New History of the Ancient Greek City-State from the Early Iron Age to the End of Antiquity
auditPapers.abstract: The city-state (polis) is undoubtedly one of the most fundamental aspects of Greek history. John Ma’s Polis: A New History of the Ancient Greek City-State from the Early Iron Age to the End of Antiquity is a monumental study of the history of the Greek polis in the very long term. It starts from the collapse of the Bronze Age palaces around 1200 BCE and takes the story to the end of ancient poleis around 600 CE; alongside the immense temporal extent, Ma impressively covers the whole of the Eastern Mediterranean. In my view, this is unquestionably the most significant contribution to the study of Greek history over the last two decades. Until the 1980s, the study of the Greek polis was dominated by a simple narrative: The polis emerged around 700 BCE as a result of major social, economic, and political transformations. The late archaic and the early classical period (600–400 BCE) constituted the golden age of the polis; during these centuries the polis provided the framework for all important achievements of Greek history. By the fourth century BCE, though, the polis could no longer cope with growing economic and social crises, or compete geopolitically with larger actors, like the Macedonian and Hellenistic kingdoms; accordingly, the postclassical polis was either dead, or in serious malaise. As a result of these assumptions, most studies of the polis have focused on the archaic and classical periods. In recent decades, Hellenistic historians have seriously challenged this narrative and have shown the vitality of the Hellenistic polis; furthermore, they have documented the remarkable phenomenon that Hellenistic poleis overwhelmingly described their political systems as democracies: Were Hellenistic poleis the golden age of democracy rather than classical Athens?

auditPapers.title: Riina Turtio. State-Building and National Militaries in Postcolonial West Africa: Decolonizing the Means of Coercion, 1958–1974.
auditPapers.abstract: Riina Turtio performs a valuable service by re-centering the link between militaries and state building in the history of African decolonization and early postcolonial politics. This link is not well developed in the relevant historiography, and Turtio’s State-Building and National Militaries in Postcolonial West Africa should stand as a key reference work in the coming years for anyone working on the subject. Indeed, given the core imperative of political—and at times personal—survival common to nearly all postcolonial leaders, the role of the military in the history of both state building and the political economy of decolonization ought to be a central one. Turtio’s work offers deeply researched insights into these questions as they pertain to what was once known as French West Africa. One of the book’s themes is the impact of foreign military assistance (chiefly French and Soviet) on the character of national militaries and the political fragility of states. The book examines the politics and impact of military assistance and the development of national militaries across four categories: autonomy, sovereignty, legitimacy, and governance, with four lengthy chapters addressing each. In particular, the book challenges simplistic narratives emphasizing the strength of French neocolonial control over former West African colonies in the early postcolonial decades. It highlights the ability of a number of African governments to buck French pressure and exploit French geopolitical vulnerabilities to maximize their strategic autonomy and limit Paris’s ability to dictate policies in its former colonies.

auditPapers.title: David N. Livingstone. The Empire of Climate: A History of an Idea.
auditPapers.abstract: Global warming has restored climate and weather as serious topics for historians and social scientists. Yet after decades of avoiding these subjects, are scholars now succumbing to the same crude climate determinism that seduced writers of the late 19th and early 20th centuries? Geographer David Livingstone believes they are, and in The Empire of Climate: A History of an Idea, he argues for a direct continuity of ideas about climate and society from ancient Hippocratic thinkers through the Enlightenment to apologists of slavery and imperialism and down to present-day pundits projecting catastrophic effects from global warming. Though erudite and forcefully written, Empire of Climate ultimately fails to persuade. If anything, the breadth and depth of Livingstone’s subject emphasizes the diversity of past and present ideas about climate and society and the inadequacy of the single label “climate determinism.” Following a substantial introduction, Livingstone’s monograph is structured around four themes. Part I (“Health”) traces ideas about climate’s influence on human constitutions. The first of its three chapters examines the humoral theory of medicine and the search for salubrious climates from Hippocrates to modern health tourism. The following chapters turn to tropical medicine, acclimatization theories, and fears of tropical disease in the context of 19th-century British imperialism, and then to the intersection of biometeorology, pseudoscientific racism, and eugenics in the United States at the turn of the 20th century. Part II (“Mind”) first discusses recent science and speculation about links between Pleistocene climatic variability and human evolution, while implying that these theories are little more than 19th-century “environmental determinism reborn” (156). It next situates concerns over the mental health impacts of global warming within a longer history of ideas about seasons and moods, from early modern notions of weather and “melancholy” to 20th-century theories about temperatures and temperaments. Part III (“Wealth”) examines ideas throughout the centuries associating economic success with temperate latitudes as well as theories associating tropical climates with poverty and servitude. Finally, in part IV (“War”) Livingstone compares present fears about global warming and global conflicts to 19th-century climate determinist explanations for the US Civil War.

auditPapers.title: Hamid Dabashi. An Iranian Childhood: Rethinking History and Memory.
auditPapers.abstract: Memoirs are effective sources in gaining rare insight into the history of peoples and places where typical primary sources or theoretical analyses lag. That’s why they have become a “house” of their own, to borrow from Anna Green and Kathleen Troup, beside the standard “houses of history,” such as the Annales, Marxist history, and others. Although most academically informed memoirs are useful, one can argue that they are especially valuable in demystifying aspects of non-Western societies. By historically contextualizing personal experiences, as Hamid Dabashi does in An Iranian Childhood: Rethinking History and Memory, memoirs can strengthen our ability to look from the bottom up. Written in four chapters and including a prelude and an epilogue, the book also shares paintings and film posters that contextualize the text better; it is a must-read for those interested in mid-twentieth-century provincial Iran and anyone who wants to take cues about how to successfully integrate scholarship into creative memoir writing.

auditPapers.title: Surviving the Bomb in Diaspora
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Uncovering the voices of the Korean diasporic atomic bomb survivors across multilingual and transimperial spaces in archives and memories in East Asia and the Americas, this article explores the historical meaning of compensatory justice for those who have been deprived of their national right of redress. Their lifelong struggles for survival after World War II have hinged on their confrontation with multiple forms of colonial and state violence across national borders that have severely compounded their redressability. Their history exposes the fundamental limits of the postcolonial discourse on human rights that has privileged justice adjudicated by nation-states. The voices of these survivors of multiple generations across the transpacific diaspora also offer powerful insights into the role of the United States in the interimperial history of not only the bombs but also their victims, spanning a longer period than customarily assumed by historians. To gain such insights, this article elucidates how Korean survivors have formed their diasporic identities, memories, and activism as they have grappled with the fraught, US-centric notion of compensatory justice and, by extension, offered textured critiques of the dualistic notion of the war between Japan and the United States that has circumscribed the bomb’s historiography.

auditPapers.title: Matthew H. Sommer. The Fox Spirit, the Stone Maiden, and Other Transgender Histories from Late Imperial China
auditPapers.abstract: In The Fox Spirit, the Stone Maiden, and Other Transgender Histories from Late Imperial China, Matthew H. Sommer delves into a rich array of materials on gender-variant individuals in late imperial China (ca. 14th–19th centuries). His study sheds new light on an often-overlooked aspect of gender and sexuality in premodern China while also offering insights that deepen our understanding of challenges faced by today’s transgender movement. Methodologically, Sommer adopts a distinctive approach pioneered by Susan Stryker, who emphasizes transgender practices over the subjective construction of transgender identity in studying transgender history. Rather than limiting his analysis to individuals who might self-identify as transgender—a relatively modern and elusive concept—Sommer applies a more expansive definition of transgender to include anyone who deviated from their assigned gender roles at birth. This practice-based approach enables Sommer to encompass a broader range of individuals, such as eunuchs and clerics, who would not be considered transgender under contemporary identity-based definitions. By doing so, Sommer offers a more inclusive and nuanced account of gender nonconformity in imperial China, capturing the complexity of gendered behavior beyond modern categories.

auditPapers.title: James Barnaby. Religious Conflict at Canterbury Cathedral in the Late Twelfth Century: The Dispute between the Monks and the Archbishops, 1184–1200
auditPapers.abstract: The history reconstructed in James Barnaby’s Religious Conflict at Canterbury Cathedral in the Late Twelfth Century, a fascinating exercise on monastic microhistory, is uniquely English—that is to say, it could only have occurred in medieval England because of the peculiar circumstance that some medieval English cathedrals were staffed not by chapters of canons, as was the case everywhere in continental Europe, but by Benedictine monks. This situation, which arose from the reforms of English monasticism in the tenth century, meant that some bishops were also exofficio abbots. Archbishops of Canterbury, whether they were themselves monks or not, were also abbots of Christ Church, the Benedictine community that served as a chapter for the cathedral. Tensions between bishops and their cathedral chapters were, of course, a regular feature of episcopal life, but when the chapter was a monastic community, the stakes could be higher and the fallout more serious. For one thing, the Rule of Benedict required abbots to be elected by the community, but few kings—or popes, for that matter—were willing to permit the head of the Church of England to be elected simply by the monks of Christ Church. Then there was the question of resources. As episcopal governance became increasingly sophisticated and demanding, bishops needed an increasingly specialist household, for whom provision had to be made from the resources of the bishopric. Whereas this could be done in a chapter of cathedral canons by using prebendaries, this was not possible in a monastic chapter. Disputes over the proper use of the community’s resources were inevitable. One twelfth-century bishop, Hugh de Nonant, bishop of Coventry, even expelled the monks of his chapter in 1186 and replaced them with regular canons, an act that occasioned an assault on his person by one of the monks wielding a crucifix.

auditPapers.title: Deborah Sutton. Ruling Devotion: The Hindu Temple in the Imperial Imagination, 1800–1946
auditPapers.abstract: Deborah Sutton’s Ruling Devotion: The Hindu Temple in the Imperial Imagination contributes to the growing literature on Hindu temples in historical, art historical, and political contexts. Sutton is not concerned, however, with Hindu temples and their complex archeology, intricate carvings, and plentiful devotees; nor does she address the range of rituals that take place therein (though, of course, she acknowledges their importance). Rather, it is how the temple—which was variously understood in colonial history as “a site of enviable wealth, compelling depravity, architectural wonder, political sensitivity, and aesthetic appeal” (2)—and how the idea of the temple was mobilized variously throughout colonial history that Sutton expertly explores through deep archival research. In other words, Sutton explores the idea of the Hindu temple as it appears in historic, literary, and academic discourses in order to demonstrate how this discourse was utilized to justify continued colonial rule in South Asia. Sutton’s history of the Hindu temple in colonial discourse begins in the years following the eighteenth-century Carnatic wars in south India. Focusing on three temples in particular—the Srirangam, Jambukeswarar, and Thayumanar temples, all located in present-day Tiruchirapalli district—Sutton demonstrates the way that the British East India Company’s failure to understand elements of the temple (such as the organizational structure, financial management, and rituals) affected their (mis)management of the temples. The ambivalence of British authorities toward Hindu temples, which both fascinated and disgusted them, resulted in an overall discomfort that comes across in the archives as racially coded malice toward local temple managers. Despite this discomfort, the Company still benefited from these very same temples until Evangelist missionary campaigns eventually succeeded in ending the Company’s support of “idolatry” (and thus, Company involvement in temple administration altogether) in 1841.

auditPapers.title: Douglas Pretsell. Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century
auditPapers.abstract: In a few short years, Douglas Pretsell has made important contributions to nineteenth-century LGBTQ+ studies by publishing two incredibly useful primary source collections translated into English from German. Now he returns with his first full-length publication, Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century, examining the ground-­­shaking discursive impact that the pioneering LGBTQ+ activist Karl Heinrich Ulrichs had when he coined this term in the 1860s to describe same-sex-attracted men. Somehow Ulrichs was missed by Michel Foucault when this French philosopher first observed that the concept of the homosexual only entered into Western discourse at the end of the nineteenth century. During the 1980s, however, a whole wave of historians helped to return Ulrichs to the spotlight. Even more recently, Robert Beachy featured Ulrichs quite prominently in the first chapter of his 2014 book Gay Berlin: Birthplace of a Modern Identity. With decades of research into the emergence of LGBTQ+ identities in Germany behind us, it is a little surprising that anyone could show us anything new about the topic. And yet even scholars familiar with Beachy’s book and other relevant literature will be pleasantly surprised at how much can be learned by a real in-depth study of Ulrichs’s work as a writer and an activist. Specifically, in the debate going back to Foucault about whether “the homosexual” was an identity created largely by psychiatrists or by LGBTQ+ peoples themselves, Pretsell makes a compelling case for the latter. He does this by mining the letters sent to Ulrichs by his readers, which together with Ulrichs’s pamphlets created a kind of “community of correspondence,” Pretsell argues. A close reading allows him to highlight the ways that their inner lives were utterly reconfigured by the exposure to the term “urning,” years before psychiatrists were injecting their own ideas into public discourse. In the process, he is successfully able to trace the transformation of the urning from being a “strategic identity,” crafted, Pretsell suggests, largely at first for rhetorical purposes, into a “new, sexually modern social identity” in the course of the decade (39).
topics: Historical Studies on Reproduction, Gender, Health, and Societal Changes

auditPapers.title: Shane Bobrycki. The Crowd in the Early Middle Ages
auditPapers.abstract: Crowds are a universal phenomenon. Throughout history and across all societies, crowds have emerged and continue to do so, particularly in urban settings, where they serve as a prominent expression of public life. Crowd dynamics are deeply interwoven with social, political, cultural, economic, and religious developments, making them a subject of great interest to societal leaders. Effective crowd management and control remain crucial for authorities tasked with overseeing the organized or spontaneous activities of large gatherings. Traditional modern scholarship on the early medieval period (500–1000 CE) has often portrayed this era as devoid of crowds. While crowds were undeniably a prominent feature of the Roman world and reemerged noticeably in the High Middle Ages, they seem to have receded into the background, almost as if they had vanished in the period in between. In The Crowd in the Early Middle Ages, Shane Bobrycki challenges this conventional perspective, aiming to demonstrate that the Early Middle Ages were in fact full of crowds.

auditPapers.title: Jane Ohlmeyer. Making Empire: Ireland, Imperialism, and the Early Modern World
auditPapers.abstract: In December 2020, amid the Black Lives Matter and Rhodes Must Fall protests, Professor Jane Ohlmeyer published an article in The Irish Times arguing that Ireland had yet to come to terms with its imperial past, citing, among several examples, the ownership of enslaved persons by eighteenth-century philosopher George Berkeley, which occasioned a “denaming” and eventual renaming of a library by Ohlmeyer’s university, Trinity College Dublin. The article prompted much debate and some backlash, as a trawl of social media and the Times’ letter pages will show. In Making Empire: Ireland, Imperialism, and the Early Modern World, Ohlmeyer returns to these key questions of ­­Ireland’s place in early modern imperialism, in a sweeping and impressive account that spans four ­­centuries of global history. Based on her James Ford lectures in 2021, Ohlmeyer presents a compelling synthesis of current scholarship and approaches to Ireland and empire, while making some important interventions based on original research. The book is thus simultaneously a masterful overview of this broad field, while advancing some new insights for those already engaged in its intricacies. Using Brian Friel’s 1988 play Making History as the overarching frame, the book literally sets the stage for a discussion of the complexities of Ireland and the Irish relationship with empire: the ideological underpinnings that were tested and honed on the island; how its people went out—both willingly and unwillingly—to participate in it; and what effects early modern imperialism had “back home,” evocatively captured in a 1660s recipe that evoked “the world in a potato pie” (176). As Friel’s Archbishop Peter Lombard declaims, it is “the time for a critical assessment” and “another history”—something that Ohlmeyer evidently firmly believes in, demanding that historians “change the questions we ask” of Ireland’s past (19). This framing, while offering some interesting vignettes, also has its limitations: It feels as if there is no real introduction or conclusion, and this together with the book’s inconsistent approach to explaining and engaging with chronologies may be off-putting for the nonspecialist.

auditPapers.title: Prachi Deshpande. Scripts of Power: Writing, Language Practices and Cultural History in Western India.
auditPapers.abstract: Prachi Deshpande’s cultural history of the Modi script—a “visual symbol” of current Marathi identity and an “opaque text” within Marathi language historiography (2)—anchors it “within a field of writing and documentation” that straddles the “early-­­modern” and the “colonial modern” to explore the social, multilingual contexts of usage and deployment at critical junctures (5). Deshpande’s “middle durée” perspective on Marathi literate practice and regional linguistic formation reveals “multiscriptality” in documentary practices, and bi/multi-lingual oral and literate usage that overturns modern linguistic boundaries. Deshpande urges us to rethink the easy equation between an objectified, “natural” deshi (local) language and its uninterrupted connection with history, territoriality, and identity. Spread over two parts and six chapters, Scripts of Power offers a rich narrative of the multilayered intricacies of writing practices in a plurilingual world. The work tracks the tousled trajectories of scripts; the conflicted notions of “roots”; the evolving ideals of scribal comportment and correct writing; the imperatives and impact of administrative and devotional documentation; and the perennial multilingual, regional, and transregional entwining in quotidian practice of language and script that incited debates over etymology, orthography, grammar, and pedagogy. All this shaped current Marathi language and script.

auditPapers.title: Ruby Lal. Vagabond Princess: The Great Adventures of Gulbadan.
auditPapers.abstract: Vagabond Princess explores of the life of Gulbadan Begum (d. 1603), whose father, Babur (d. 1530), founded the Mughal Empire (1526–1857). Gulbadan penned a memoir, Humayunnama, in response to a command given by her nephew, the Emperor Akbar (d. 1605), in 1587. Akbar had asked those who knew his father, Humayun (d. 1556), and grandfather Babur to write down their recollections for his royal historian Abu’l Fazl (d. 1602), who was compiling a chronicle of Akbar’s reign. The first half of Vagabond Princess builds upon Ruby Lal’s earlier work on Gulbadan, which was based on a close reading of the Humayunnama, and the second half traces Gulbadan’s life as a matriarch within the empire and includes an account of her pilgrimage to Mecca in the mid-1570s. The only extant manuscript of the Humayunnama is incomplete and ends maddeningly in mid-sentence; it does not cover Gulbadan’s years abroad, and Lal’s creative reconstruction of these years is welcome, especially as they traverse “the vast terrains, people, animals, and sacred geographies of Mughal India, the Red Sea, and the desert land of Arabia” (13).

auditPapers.title: Christoph Rosenmüller. Viceroy Güemes’s Mexico: Rituals, Religion, and Revenue.
auditPapers.abstract: Since the 1980s, the Bourbon Reforms stood as a watershed in Spanish American history. Scholars debated the extent to which they were successful, their scope and reach, whether they formed a coherent project, and their relationship to Spanish American independence. But there was little disagreement that change began in the aftermath of the Seven Years’ War (1756–63) and that, culminating during the tenure of José de Gálvez as minister for the Indies (1776–87), Spanish authorities had embarked on an effort to significantly transform imperial governance, revenue collection, and naval and military structures in Spanish America. Bourbon reformism came to define the region’s history during the late eighteenth century. That consensus began to crumble as, from the mid-2000s, a growing volume of scholarship focusing on the earlier and largely ignored part of the century highlighted a long series of previous reforms. These have been characterized as precursors of, laying the foundations for, and often more effective and successful than those introduced after the 1760s. In Viceroy Güemes’s Mexico, Christoph Rosenmüller adds to this scholarship, boldly suggesting that “it is now hard to say what the term ‘Bourbon Reforms’ should mean, and when they began or ended” (148), inviting us instead to think about imperial reform as an ongoing process stretching as far back as the late seventeenth century.

auditPapers.title: Mistakes I Dare Not Admit
auditPapers.abstract: History Unclassified’s first special edition is dedicated to mistakes. That is fitting because History Unclassified began in failure and rejection. In 2017, Kate Brown submitted a screenplay to the American Historical Review. It was not necessarily a good play, but it was all history, footnoted with newly-unearthed archival sources. Why, Kate asked, does history in the AHR generally appear in the same format? Why can’t, for example, nonfiction take fictional form? She found the format of a screenplay useful to narrate actions that occurred in different times and places simultaneously on stage. The stage helped frame the Chernobyl tragedy more reliably than chronology, she argued, because one effect of radioactive contaminants was to both slow time and speed it up. The readers rejected the play, but what was meant as a provocation started a conversation between Kate and Alex Lichtenstein, then AHR editor, and led to the launch of the History Unclassified section in June 2018.

auditPapers.title: The Peculiarities of Cambridge History: Some Comparative Thoughts on the Historical Tripos
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This study develops and expands some of the arguments of a lecture I delivered on the occasion of the 150th anniversary of the foundation of Cambridge’s Historical Tripos. Its central proposition – that it is meaningful to talk about ‘Cambridge History’ and to discuss its distinctiveness – remains central to this published version of the lecture, as does the idea that the Tripos has always embodied that distinctiveness as a form of social memory. Both the Tripos as a structure and the Faculty archive as a source come into play in helping to make sense of the Cambridge trajectory over the past half century. The lecture lays stress on some persistent legacies from the Cambridge tradition, identifies some strands that developed internally after 1945, and considers the impact of external influences on Cambridge History. Taking the story up to the ‘new’ Tripos of 2022, the lecture concludes that the legacy has exercised more control than has innovation and that the Historical Tripos is best understood as a continuing conversation with its own past.

auditPapers.title: The Monarchs’ History Men: What Has Changed over Three Centuries?
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Since its foundation in 1724, the regius chair has been held by twenty-two men. auditPapers.title: Preserving the contemporary mural “Musica Popolare” by Orticanoodles in Milan, Italy: Deterioration processes and protection performance of commercial coatings
auditPapers.abstract: • Six commercial coatings were applied on a real street artwork and monitored over 1-year of natural ageing. • In-situ testing protocol was set up for assessing protection efficacy and durability. • Acrylic-based coatings in sheltered areas showed adhesion issues and a tendency to attract PM. • None of the commercial coatings offered optimal protection after 1-year. This study aims to investigate the possibility of protecting real street artworks in urban outdoor conditions. Specifically, this paper focuses on a testing experimental work carried out on the mural “Musica Popolare” (2016) in Milan by Orticanoodles and includes: i ) the assessment of the state of conservation through in-situ and micro-invasive techniques; ii ) the set-up of an in-situ testing protocol to assess the compatibility and efficacy of protective treatments; iii ) the one-year monitoring testing campaign. This study investigates the deterioration processes of the paint and evaluates the protective performances of various commercial coatings, which were previously tested under laboratory conditions. Notably, the mural experiences three distinct exposure conditions (fully exposed, partially exposed, and sheltered) allowing for a comparative evaluation of their effects. The coatings performance was evaluated by using a testing protocol including: portable digital microscopy, VIS reflectance spectroscopy, glossmetry, and vertical water contact angle measurements. After one year of natural ageing, the monitoring results indicate that acrylic-based coatings offered only limited protective action of the painted surface, ensuring a moderate colour retention but an insufficient protection towards liquid water. In sheltered areas, the application of protective coatings had a negative effect, making the treated surfaces more unstable than the original paintings without significantly improving water repellency (WCAs). An increase of particulate matter (PM) adhesion to the surfaces was also observed. Contact angle measurements indicated that only the fluorinated coatings achieved and maintained good water repellency over the one-year period. However, none of the tested coatings provided satisfactory protection over the monitoring period, highlighting the need for more innovative and effective preservation strategies for these artworks.

auditPapers.title: The Battles Over Addiction Treatment
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract To the extent that it is remembered today, the controversial California commune Synanon is known for two things—(1) attempting to murder attorney Paul Morantz by putting a rattlesnake in his mailbox and (2) spawning an addiction treatment model with violent and totalizing tendencies: the therapeutic community (TC). My book, The Recovery Revolution: The Battle Over Addiction Treatment in the United States, omitted the rattlesnake in the mailbox and glossed over the details of Synanon’s spectacular decline. According to some critics, including Morantz himself, this was a major mistake, and a small but highly vocal cadre of activists went online to publicly question my historical objectivity and reframe what I had intended as a nonpartisan history of Synanon’s public relations campaigns as an endorsement of therapeutic violence. The omission led me, then a closeted person in long-term eating disorder recovery, to a mental breakdown, psychoanalytic psychotherapy to treat it, and, with this approach, fresh insight into the value of analysis as well as synthesis in the development of historical knowledge. I conclude by exploring “reparatory history” as both a method and a way forward for our impossible profession.

auditPapers.title: Ian Atherton. Britons and Their Battlefields: War, Memory, and Commemoration since the Fourteenth Century.
auditPapers.abstract: With Britons and Their Battlefields: War, Memory, and Commemoration since the Fourteenth Century, Ian Atherton sets out to chart a longue durée history of British commemoration. Using battlefields across eight centuries, he argues that the traditions of Bri­tish remembrance, so intertwined in popular thought with the world wars of the twentieth century, not only predate Remembrance Day but also draw heavily on Britain’s long martial traditions, the politics of nation and empire, and religious reformation. Britons and Their Battlefields employs a broad definition for both its title categories. Britons here include, at various times, the English, Scots, British, and various populations across the empire. This big-tent approach is particularly intriguing in Atherton’s analysis of battlefields and commemoration traditions from the English Civil War, the Jacobite Rebellion (1745–1746), and other conflicts that spilled blood on the soil of the British Isles, where monuments and commemoration take on even more loaded political implications and rivalries than they normally do. The definition of “battlefields” is equally broad. Atherton does an excellent job of demonstrating how what makes a battlefield has changed over the centuries, along with the changes in commemorations tied to such events and locations. Some of these evolutions are due to changing societal and religious mores, of course, but they are also influenced by the nature and locations of Britain’s conflicts.

auditPapers.title: Holly Miowak Guise. Alaska Native Resilience: Voices from World War II.
auditPapers.abstract: In Alaska Native Resilience: Voices from World War II, Holly Miowak Guise (Iñupiaq) provides readers with a crucial reframing of Indigenous-US relations and World War II in Alaska. Drawing on her extensive oral history work and interviews with Alaska Native elders, Guise joins the proliferation of recent scholarship that challenges “simplistic, incomplete, often nationalist U.S. portrayals” of the “Good War” (3). Following the 1942 Japanese invasion of the Aleutian Islands of Attu and Kiska, the US government executed the forced removal of over eight hundred Unangax̂ from their homelands and justified their internment in southeast Alaska as a necessity of wartime exigencies. Challenging this narrative, the book situates the militarization of Alaska as the expansion of US empire to which Alaska Natives from diverse tribal geographies responded as nations. Upending one-dimensional tropes that portray Indigenous peoples as the reactive recipients of colonialism, Alaska Native Resilience demands that Alaska Native actions throughout the war be understood as more than resistance. Rather, Guise brings into focus an Indigenous wartime political geography in which she demonstrates that the subversive strategies employed by Alaska Natives represent assertions and affirmations of Indigenous sovereignty, diplomacy, and nation-­­­­to-nation alliances.

auditPapers.title: Joseph Berger. Elie Wiesel: Confronting the Silence.
auditPapers.abstract: Even a brief perusal of the history section in one of the few remaining general interest bookstores quickly reveals the popularity of biography as a genre of historical writing. Indeed, among general audiences, biography may be the most popular form of history. This makes sense. Biography has a built-in narrative through line, a David Copperfield structure, from birth through the prime of life to the inevitable end. It offers a central protagonist whom the reader may admire or condemn. It easily takes on the form of a morality play, with clear heroes and villains. But aside from these essentially literary virtues, what does biography offer to students of the past, particularly to academic historians? For lesser-known figures, the answer may be largely informational. The biography presents new empirical information. One might think of this as the “hidden figure” type of biography, often accompanied by outsized claims for the underappreciated significance of said figure.

auditPapers.title: Mónica A. Jiménez. Making Never-Never Land: Race and Law in the Creation of Puerto Rico.
auditPapers.abstract: In January 2025, Puerto Rican singer Benito Martínez Ocasio, known by his stage name Bad Bunny, released his sixth solo studio album titled Debí tirar más fotos (I Should Have Taken More Photos). Musically, Bad Bunny’s work blends reggaeton with older Puerto Rican genres such as salsa, bolero, and plena. Thematically, it explores Puerto Rican history and the seemingly never-ending state of crisis that Puerto Rico has endured in the first quarter of the twenty-first century. In the powerful but grief-stricken “Lo que le pasó a Hawaii” (“What happened to Hawaiʻi ”), for example, the rapper addresses gentrification in the Caribbean archipelago, where American real estate companies and tourists are displacing Puerto Ricans from their own land. Bad Bunny’s album shares with Mónica A. Jiménez’s Making Never-Never Land a profound, even desperate, need to make sense of Puerto Rico’s current situation. In her book, Jiménez reminds the reader how difficult life has been for Puerto Ricans over the past two decades: the onset of a years-long economic crisis in 2006; a prolonged debt crisis since 2015; the devastating effects of Hurricane Maria in 2017 and the swarm of earthquakes in early 2020; population loss owing to migration to the United States; and the harm brought by overtourism in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. While the artist offers his interpretation of these intertwined problems and tragedies through music, carefully curated visuals, and even a short film, the scholar uses legal history to deliver hers.

auditPapers.title: Anastasia C. Curwood. Shirley Chisholm: Champion of Black Feminist Power Politics.

auditPapers.title: Brian D. Laslie. Fighting from Above: A Combat History of the US Air Force
auditPapers.abstract: Brian Laslie takes a long view in Fighting from Above, arguing that “an American air force existed long before the United States Air Force [USAF] became a separate and independent service.” He breaks this long view into just four epochs (compared to ten or even twenty-seven “propositions,” “attributes,” or “dicta” of airpower proposed by some scholars), enough to demonstrate significant trends, but not so many that readers lose track of meaningful conclusions. This is also more than just another chronological or topical survey of airpower or USAF history. Instead, Laslie asks: “is it possible to discern a unique ‘way of war’ for the Air Force?”(4). This question shapes both the periodization and content of his excellent study. Epoch 1, “Period of ­Discovery, 1907–1941,” begins when the US Army Signal Corps established its aeronautical branch and ends when the United States entered World War II. This section describes the fumbling invention of various roles for military aviation during World War I, along with the interwar ascendance of the yet-unproven concept of strategic bombing. Epoch 2, “Strategic Dominance, 1942–1975,” encompasses the costly evolution of US strategic bombing from optimistic theory to brutal practice during World War II, followed by decades of single-minded focus on this mission, with long-range bombers providing both nuclear deterrence and the raison d’être for an independent postwar USAF. ­Laslie aptly describes Korea and Vietnam—including the repeated need to reinvent tactical air support for ground troops—as “aberrations that the Air Force was not prepared to accept” (114). During Epoch 3, “Tactical Ascendancy, 1975–2019,” the “fighter generals,” who as junior officers had fought the air war over Vietnam, finally displaced the postwar “bomber mafia” stranglehold on USAF leadership (128). Under their direction, the USAF shifted to a tactical-strategic mix in which fighters and bombers filled both roles using a combination of air-to-air missiles, precision-guided munitions, and stealth technology. A chapter on Desert Storm and the Balkans campaigns, and another on US military intervention in Afghanistan and Iraq, highlight the capabilities, achievements, and limitations of USAF airpower in recent conflicts. Finally, “An Unmanned Future?” ventures into current events, speculating that “even now the Air Force is entering into or, at the very least, moving toward a fourth epoch that could fundamentally alter its current way of war: that being the era of the unmanned aerial vehicles and a second space age” (5).

auditPapers.title: Waitman Wade Beorn. Between the Wires: The Janowska Camp and the Holocaust in Lviv
auditPapers.abstract: Waitman Wade Beorn is one of the best experts on the history of the Holocaust in the occupied territories of the Soviet Union. Beorn’s earlier work traced the murderous deeds of the Holocaust in Eastern Europe over large areas, but the work to be presented here is a microstudy. Between the Wires: The Janowska Camp and the Holocaust in Lviv examines the Janowska camp on the outskirts of Lwow, one of the largest cities in Galicia. It belonged to Austria-Hungary until 1918 and then became Polish in 1918, but in 1939, the territory fell into the Soviet occupation zone as a result of the ­­Hitler-Stalin Pact. Before the start of the Second World War, Lvov had just over 300,000 inhabitants, around 100,000 of whom belonged to the ­­Jewish minority. Due to the flight of Jewish people from the German-occupied area of Poland, however, there were probably 160,000 Jewish people in Lwow when the Wehrmacht occupied the city on June 30, 1941. An SD-Einsatzgruppe carried out a first pogrom in the city with the help of Ukrainian nationalists. But the National Socialists did not assign the city to occupied Ukraine. Rather, it was ceded to the Generalgouvernement under the leadership of Hans Frank.

auditPapers.title: Jody Benjamin. The Texture of Change: Dress, Self-Fashioning, and History in Western Africa, 1700–1850
auditPapers.abstract: The eighteenth to mid-nineteenth century witnessed transformations of the political and economic landscapes in West Africa. The Islamic reformist movement spread eastward from the Senegal River valley, establishing theocratic states. Meanwhile, the Atlantic slave trade peaked and gradually declined in response to the abolitionist movement in Western Europe and North America. Concurrently, the cash crop trade, or so-called “legitimate commerce,” expanded in response to the British industrial revolution. Historians and economic historians have demonstrated that the growth of West Africa’s maritime trade, whether in slaves or in other items, was intertwined with an increasing inflow of European and Indian textiles. Recent scholarship highlights the crucial role of African consumers’ taste in these trades, showing that demand for textiles was deeply embedded in local production as well as social and cultural contexts. auditPapers.title: Nora E. Jaffary. Abortion in Mexico: A History
auditPapers.abstract: Abortion is a hot-button topic in US culture and politics. Politicians are made and unmade over the issue. Families are admonished to avoid the subject at Thanksgiving dinner. The Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, and some states like my own (Arkansas) enacted some of the strictest abortion restrictions in the nation. Some might believe that nations like Mexico, rooted in Catholicism and stereotyped as steeped in machismo, would also severely restrict abortion. On the contrary, Abortion in Mexico reveals that tolerance and a more nuanced assessment have characterized Mexican abortion laws and prosecution. Indeed, Nora E. Jaffary convincingly demonstrates that continuity with small bumps and valleys rather than dramatic change has characterized the history of abortion in Mexico from 1519 to 2000. It was not until the mid-twentieth century that more Mexicans, including women, disapproved of abortion and lobbied for criminalization of the procedure. By the mid-1970s, Mexican society shifted to greater receptiveness, culminating in the 2023 federal decriminalization of abortion during the first twelve weeks of pregnancy. Mexico City had decriminalized abortion in the first trimester in 2003 and 2007. Only the United States among North American nations has moved the opposite way: from decriminalization to criminalization. Engaging a wide range of primary sources and literature, Jaffary provides a highly readable, concise, and intellectually compelling historical synthesis of abortion in Mexico.

auditPapers.abstract: Reading William Max Nelson’s masterful Enlightenment Biopolitics amid the portentous atmosphere of the 2024 US presidential election campaign was at once an alarming and revelatory experience. Through the history of biopolitics Nelson opens a window into broader, ongoing historiographical debates about the nature of the Enlightenment itself. He urges historians to abandon a Manichean view of the 18th century as either exclusively emancipatory or totalitarian, pointing to the manifold ways in which “the Enlightenment was characterized by the formation of new conceptual and practical foundations on which modern inclusions and exclusions were built” (4). auditPapers.title: David Stefan Doddington. Old Age and American Slavery
auditPapers.abstract: In 1852, Harriet Beecher Stowe published Uncle Tom’s Cabin. While Uncle Tom’s age is never clear, representative of the uncertainty that most enslaved people had about their age, he was not elderly. Still, scholars, writers, and activists over the years attributed his subservience and passivity to his aging. “His type of goodness,” wrote James Weldon Johnson in his 1912 autobiography, could be found in “lots of old Negroes as foolishly good as he” (The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man, 39). Older people and their treatment have always been part of the story of American enslavement, and yet their experiences within enslavement have most often been portrayed as similar to those felt by other enslaved peoples regardless of age. Experiences as aging enslavers have been largely overlooked as well. Although middle-aged and elderly “Aunties” and “Uncles” were consistent and influential presences within slave communities, treatments of the history of enslavement through age has been nearly absent from the literature. Only in recent decades, with the works of Wilma King, Mary Niall Mitchell, Anna Mae Duane, and Daina Ramey Berry, has age, albeit youth, become useful as an interpretive lens. In fairness, Berry also attended to the elderly, but her interpretations, like those of a handful of other scholars who paid attention to the aged, were more focused upon the support and respect granted them by other enslaved persons and their diminishing monetary value to enslavers. Few historians have sought to understand American enslavement through the physical decline, social isolation, and acquiescence to enslavement experienced by the aging.
