auditPapers.abstract: Anyone who has visited an Italian city such as Florence has experienced its unique sonic ambience—a cacophony of voices, shouts, songs, bells, sirens, doors opening and shutting at all hours—whose echoes are made more poignant somehow by the architecture. This noisiness isn’t just confined to the modern moment, however. If anything, early modern Italians were noisier; from early modern sources, we know that they made a great deal of noise, shouting insults at one another, crying their wares, calling out gride or official government proclamations, serenading one another, shouting the news, and in general fare baccano, or making a din. Julia Rombough’s A Veil of Silence: Women and Sound in Renaissance Italy explores this world and is a well-researched, ably argued, and insightful investigation of an understudied topic: the intersections between soundscapes, gender, and space in early modern Florence. Rombough sets the stage in the first chapter by discussing the striking demographics of women’s ­religious institutions in early modern Florence—approximately 19 percent of the female population lived in an enclosed institution, and there was roughly one nun for every seventeen residents, according to the 1632 census, many of whom were unwilling residents or women who forcibly professed for familial and economic reasons. As Rombough points out, the networks of religious institutions were extensive, and many Florentines had a female relative in one of these houses. This was particularly true for women of the aristocracy, but grand ducal policies toward women of mala vita, or ill fame, also pushed women believed to be at risk for the sex trade or repentant prostitutes into the growing number of charitable reforming institutions. Interestingly, Rombough has found that institutions like the Convertite and the Malmaritate were surrounded by active sex work zones and working-class enclaves. In such an atmosphere, concerns about unruly behavior seeping inside institutional walls were perhaps inevitable. Moreover, post-Tridentine reform stressed women’s silence as a crucial component of religious practice.

auditPapers.title: Matthew Neufeld. Early Modern Naval Health Care in England, 1650–1750
auditPapers.abstract: Historians write about the formation of the early modern English state in one of two ways. One group describes a fiscal-military state focused almost exclusively on money and war, implementing an increasingly intrusive and efficient system of taxation to fund the increasing expense of sustaining armies and, especially, navies. Matthew Neufeld’s Early Modern Naval Health Care in England, 1650–1750 identifies an instance where the state reached in to manage the customary practice, usually left to local authorities, of providing relief for the “deserving poor”: A small state bureaucracy emerged to provide health care for sick and wounded sailors, ensuring the navy could man its ships. Neufeld’s book explores the development of that system of care over the century between the civil wars and the War of Austrian Succession. He argues that the system, overseen by a handful of centrally appointed commissioners for sick and wounded seamen, embodied a “preservative ethos” with three objectives: “saving seamen’s lives, saving money, and keeping men in sea service” (11). The system grew to include three parts—care in the community, care in contracted hospitals, and care in navy-operated hospitals—each of which arose as the solution to a problem. This story is not simply about modernization, however; rather than replacing its predecessor, each new method simply augmented the existing system and operated in parallel, and the final transition to a fully “modern” system of state-run hospitals did not occur until long after the book closes.

auditPapers.title: Vince L. Bantu. Those for Whom the Lamp Shines. The Making of Egyptian Ethnic Identity in Late Antiquity.
auditPapers.abstract: Vince Bantu’s Those for Whom the Lamp Shines reads Egyptian sources through the lens of ethnicity, arguing that a latent ethnic identity emerged immediately after the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) and reached maturity around 700 CE (126, 141). The study charts the collapse of ethnic and religious identities—hence, “Egyptian” became synonymous with “Miaphysite”—and it promotes ethnicity as the optimal paradigm for reading the sources of this era (10–12, 129). Chapter 1 introduces ethnicity as a methodology, while dismissing older nationalist readings. Chapter 2 explores the universal Christian ideal of community and empire that dominated until Chalcedon, after which “ethnic thinking” emerged, deepening the Chalcedonian Schism; chapters 3 to 5 detail this evolutionary process. The last chapter identifies ethnic consciousness as the source of tensions even between Syrian and Egyptian Miaphysites. The volume raises new questions and thoroughly employs its chosen methodology, though it also poses many interpretive challenges. Methodologically, it groups and analyzes texts pertaining to the same historical figure(s) to demonstrate continuity in ethnic rhetoric. Nonetheless, the focus is typically on the period when the historical figure lived, not when a source was drafted. This dilutes historical context and ideological shifts within each cluster of texts, which—not infrequently—contains documents separated by centuries (e.g., Samuel of Qalamun’s dossier in chapter 5). Inconsistent historiographic discussions exacerbate this problem across the volume. For example, the precursors to the History of the Patriarchs are not discussed, and the work is glossed as a 10th-century composition of Sawirus ibn al-Muqaffa‘ (101), though it should be read as a late-11th-century work by Mawhub ibn Mansur (see publications by Johannes den Heijer, Perrine Pilette, and Mark Swanson).

auditPapers.title: Thomas M. Larkin. The China Firm: American Elites and the Making of British Colonial Society
auditPapers.abstract: “In February 1784, little more than a month following the end of the War of Independence, the American ship Empress of China departed New York for Canton,” Thomas M. Larkin explains in the introduction to The China Firm: American Elites and the Making of British Colonial Society. “This voyage anticipated a century-long wave of American mercantile interest in China” (1). Over the next 100 years, US merchants joined the international push to expand foreign trade with the Qing Empire. First at Canton, and then at Hong Kong and treaty ports along China’s coast, US firms positioned themselves to capitalize on the further opening of China to foreign trade and influence. This experience brought these US companies into competition, but also into different forms of accommodation, with foreign and Chinese merchants and officials. Most important was the relationship with the British, whose colonial culture and authority heavily influenced the lives and commercial activities of Americans in China, along with their sense of national and racial identity, and their attitudes toward Chinese people.

auditPapers.title: Emily Conroy-Krutz. Missionary Diplomacy: Religion and Nineteenth-Century American Foreign Relations.
auditPapers.abstract: In Missionary Diplomacy: Religion and Nineteenth-Century American Foreign Relations, Emily Conroy-Krutz offers a careful examination of the relationship between Protestant missionaries and the US State Department. Indeed, Conroy-Krutz demonstrates that in the 19th century, American “evangelistic work was deeply entwined with diplomatic work” (13). In this period, she shows, missionaries served as “trusted experts” about the world to a wide array of US audiences. They wrote about the “world and its people” for lay audiences and increasingly took on more official roles: as translators, consuls, and advisers, in some cases even “testifying before Congress about international affairs” (3). As Conroy-Krutz argues, the State Department and the US mission movement each powerfully shaped the other’s growth over this period. The book is divided into three parts, which allows Conroy-Krutz to trace the evolving and complicated connections between the US State Department and the Protestant mission movement. The book’s first part covers the period between 1810 and 1840, “when the United States diplomatic corps was small, weak, and focused on European and Latin American affairs” (11). Yet—as the author ably demonstrates—US missionaries in this period trained their attention on the world’s “heathen,” who resided in places that “mattered less” to the State Department: places like India, China, and Hawaii. In doing so, they positioned themselves in such a way as to become “experts” on these regions and their people. Protestant missionaries wrote prolifically about their labors around the world. If they primarily aimed to drum up support for their evangelistic efforts, they were also frequently “quite earthbound and concerned with practical and political questions about peoples, governments, and civilization” (41). Thus, in their works for US audiences, they wrote not just as missionaries, but as “historians, scientists, and explorers” and endeavored to persuade Americans about the kinds of “issues, places, and peoples they should care about” (41). Their writings and their roles as “experts” about the world’s people and places created a situation in which missionaries began to influence the course of US diplomacy.

auditPapers.title: Jessica O’Leary. Renaissance Masculinities, Diplomacy, and Cultural Transfer: Federico and Ferrante Gonzaga in Italy and Beyond
auditPapers.abstract: Federico Gonzaga (1500–1540) must count among the best-traveled children of the Italian Renaissance. Son of Mantuan rulers Francesco Gonzaga and ­Isabella d’Este, Federico became a bargaining chip in his parents’ dealings with allies and enemies alike during the Italian Wars (1494–1559). As a boy, Federico was coveted as a hostage by French King Louis XII, and he spent almost a quarter of his life as a guest-detainee at the courts of Pope Julius II and King Francis I before returning to Mantua as its lord. Effectively a resident teenage diplomat, Federico absorbed knowledge, language, habits, and perspectives in this youthful tour that served him well for the rest of his life. In this stimulating study of the Gonzaga dynasty’s diplomacy in the first half of the sixteenth century, Jessica O’Leary’s Renaissance Masculinities, Diplomacy, and Cultural Transfer examines Federico’s life alongside that of his younger brother Ferrante (1507–1557), whose status as a cadet child brought him to different European environs from his brother: first to the court of Emperor Charles V and then a series of imperial appointments in Milan and Sicily as an adult. The book sets the two brothers’ lives and careers in the context of the Italian Wars to demonstrate the nimble and imaginative adjustments the ruling family of Mantua—a well-connected but diminutive Italian principality—made to insulate themselves from the ensuing political tumult. The book proposes that the Gonzaga boys’ cultural immersion in foreign courts trained them in new forms of sixteenth-century manhood and cultural diplomacy. The lordly fifteenth-­century “bluster” (54) of the boys’ father Francesco had little effect at the courts of major European monarchs after 1500, nor could the “crisis diplomacy” (20) the house of Gonzaga practiced in the early Italian Wars function effectively in later decades. The book charts transformations between generations as the men of the dynasty confronted the wars’ new challenges over decades, and O’Leary’s analysis of these shifting political and cultural terrains is particularly insightful. In tracing the evolutions of familial strategies of clientage and statecraft between parents and children, the author outlines the limitations of ­fifteenth-century lordship in new political realities and suggests how the Gonzaga adapted their approaches to the next century.

auditPapers.title: Chloe Wigston Smith. Novels, Needleworks, and Empire: Material Entanglements in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World
auditPapers.abstract: Chole Wigston Smith brings the interior worlds of romantic fiction and the so-called low arts of domestic needlework—pictorial embroidery, marking, mending, the sewing of a shirt, samplers—and other objects long seen as outside the epicenter of “taste and commodity culture” to the forefront of 18th-century global conceptions of empire and colonialism in the Atlantic World in Novels, Needleworks, and Empire: Material Entanglements in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World (7). In a rich and complex study of the entangled lives of women and girls—including Black and Indigenous women and girls—the small objects they made and used, visual sources they were exposed to, and the novels they read, Smith offers new insight into the complex relationship between the material of the home and changing global boundaries. As she convincingly argues, “education and instruction were both embedded in making practices and novels focused on romance and marriage” and this knowledge was not solely manual, but also intellectual (9–10). While these goods were made and used in the home, the words, images, and materials they were made of were part of broader conversations on national and racial identity in the global 18th century.

auditPapers.title: Baijayanti Roy. The Nazi Study of India and Indian Anti-Colonialism: Knowledge Providers and Propagandists in the ‘Third Reich.’
auditPapers.abstract: That the Nazis had a special interest in India is immediately apparent. As part of their self-mythologization, they linked themselves to the Indian subcontinent—think of the swastika—within the framework of their pseudoscientific theories about the Aryan race. As is now well known and thoroughly researched, this Nazi appropriation of India was the culmination of a long German tradition of Indomania, which originated in German Romanticism and unfolded in multiple directions throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. We can even pinpoint quite precisely when this particular German-language interest in India began: with Friedrich Schlegel’s Über die Sprache und der Indier (1808). Schlegel’s treatise sparked an enduring interest in Indian thought, broadly construed—sometimes purely philosophical, religious, or spiritual; sometimes infused with colonial fantasies; and, most consequentially, giving rise to a radicalized, antisemitic vision of an Indo-Germanic bond that the Nazis eagerly adopted and expanded in their ideology. This long and complex chapter has been examined by numerous scholars, most notably Suzanne Marchand, Doug McGetchin, and Perry Myers, each of whom has explored different aspects of Germany’s intellectual engagement with India. Yet one key question remained unanswered: What did the Nazis actually know about India? Thanks to Baijayanti Roy’s new book titled The Nazi Study of India and Indian Anti-Colonialism: Knowledge Providers and Propagandists in the ‘Third Reich’, we now have an answer.

auditPapers.title: Kalyani Ramnath. Boats in a Storm: Law, Migration, and Decolonization in South and Southeast Asia, 1942–1962.
auditPapers.abstract: Twenty years of tumult across the Indian Ocean provide the backdrop for Kalyani Ramnath’s fascinating study of decolonization in South and Southeast Asia, Boats in a Storm. This region, as many historians have highlighted, was long defined by the circulation of labor, capital, people, and commodities. In 1942, this world of motion was shattered by the Japanese invasion of Burma. The end of the war offered little respite. The British Empire unraveled rapidly, a bloody Partition tore apart the subcontinent in 1947, and the colonial state launched a ferocious war in Malaya. Postcolonial states were established in this context of fatigue, trauma, and suspicion, and faced the monumental task of sorting the former empire’s subjects into national citizens. In a few years, the legal landscape of the region utterly transformed. How did ordinary people, whose lives and livelihoods had long stretched between intertwined and interconnected geographies, navigate these drastic and paradigmatic changes? Ramnath takes this question up in her first monograph. Set between the Japanese occupation of Burma in 1942 and General Ne Win’s coupe état there in 1962, the book describes the “banal encounters with law” of migrants navigating new legal frameworks in postimperial South and Southeast Asia (1). Ramnath mines a wealth of legal and administrative records from India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Singapore, and Burma to excavate stories of ordinary people as they applied for citizenship ­­certificates and passports, settled debt repayments, contested taxation schemes, claimed or disputed property, and tried to avoid detention and deportation.

auditPapers.title: Richard Stone. Bristol and the Birth of the Atlantic Economy, 1500–1700.
auditPapers.abstract: As its title suggests, Bristol and the Birth of the Atlantic Economy, 1500–1700 by Richard Stone contributes to the “Atlantic” turn in the study of the early modern world, including the revived debate regarding the role of slavery in fueling European, especially British, economic growth. Although relatively short and elegantly written, with no econometric jargon or formulae and relatively few statistical tables, this highly important work nevertheless rests its argument on a detailed quantitative analysis of the port books (and related wharfage accounts) for Bristol, whose status as “metropolis of the west” of England (and Wales) long predated the eighteenth century. As its lucid technical appendix explains, it is now possible to translate the immense detail of the customs records into convincing estimates of the values (as well as volumes) of the imports and exports of a major port, even though patchy survival and highly complex issues of valuation mean that any figures remain estimates. Using this data, Stone successfully develops, and challenges, existing arguments regarding English overseas trade in the sixteenth through eighteenth centuries, showing that a London-based account is not sufficient and has led to an overemphasis on the crisis in England’s traditional export of cloth into northwestern Europe as a driver of economic change and an underestimate of how early first Iberian and then English American colonies began to transform the English economy.

auditPapers.title: Jacob Dlamini. Dying for Freedom: Political Martyrdom in South Africa
auditPapers.abstract: Dying for Freedom is an innovative and thought-provoking study that places important conversations about death on the intellectual table. Death defined honor, dignity, heroism, loyalty, and status. Many men of South Africa’s liberation struggle viewed death heroically. It represented the path to the afterworld and beyond. Dlamini uses several historical examples to support his analysis. They include the AmaXhosa cattle-killing episode (1856–57), the British invasion of the AmaZulu Kingdom (1879), and the Mendi’s sinking (1917). Each of these historical episodes conveys different meanings about death that revolved around cosmology, cleansing rituals, and ancient sayings and Christian beliefs. Dlamini incorporates these examples to demonstrate that the political use of death in southern Africa predated apartheid. He even asserts that freedom fighters invested in death for its use as a vehicle to manhood. In some cases, as Dlamini demonstrates, death spelled celebration as decendents entered the spiritual realm whereas in other cases, it connoted mortalization and the end of one process for another.

auditPapers.title: Todd H. Weir. Red Secularism: Socialism and Secularist Culture in Germany 1890 to 1933
auditPapers.abstract: Todd H. Weir’s Red Secularism: Socialism and Secularist Culture in Germany 1890 to 1933 explores the subculture of “red secularism” that emerged during interactions between the German socialist thought collective and secularism, both of which themselves were the products of various intellectual trends in European culture, particularly Enlightenment, Protestant “free religion” tradition, and Catholic rationalist dissent. For example, by the 1860s, in Germany, many members of so-called Free Religious Congregations, who formally continued to function as legacy churches, already abandoned Christianity and came to embrace a naturalistic view of the world (5). Incidentally, in his earlier Secularism and Religion in Nineteenth-Century Germany (2014), Weir has already researched in detail that and related themes. Red Secularism represents a follow-up volume that examines how the ideas of German free religion, free thought, and popular scientific materialism were related to major segments of the contemporary German Left collective (social democrats, independent social democrats, and communists) after 1890. Overall, these interactions (red secularism) provided a potent backdrop for the rise of socialism. At the same time, according to Weir, red secularism was a broader phenomenon that went beyond membership in conventional socialist parties or free-thought associations. It was a countercultural state of mind that operated in many levels of society, ranging from pop science print media to radical women associations, nature reform movements, gay rights’ clubs, vegetarian, and nudist groups.

auditPapers.title: Luca Zenobi. Borders and the Politics of Space in Late Medieval Italy: Milan, Venice, and their Territories.
auditPapers.abstract: A poor man spent the summer of 1457 harvesting crops in fields near Lodi. Perhaps a day’s walk from his home near Bergamo, he had petitioned a local official for safe passage to allow him to travel through lands that were subject to the Republic of Venice; however, his route also took him through areas bound to the Duchy of Milan. On his return home later that summer, ducal officials seized the wheat he was bringing back to his mother, as he had not secured similar approval to travel through Milanese lands. The Venetian governor intervened. His letter, now in Milan’s Archivio di Stato, emphasized the difficulties travelers faced, as this route frequently crossed territorial borders between the two states. This episode is completely ordinary in its details of an otherwise unknown peasant seeking to improve his family’s situation. At the same time, it reflects the ubiquity and complexity of medieval territoriality that Luca Zenobi excavates in Borders and the Politics of Space in Late Medieval Italy. Focusing on the frontier between Milan and Venice established by the Peace of Lodi (1454), he shows how territorial borders were clearly identified and controlled. This argument challenges earlier scholarship that has presumed premodern borders lacked precision and were at best porous, before states demarcated clear boundaries. Zenobi also emphasizes their contingent nature, which he argues was characteristic of medieval Italian spatial politics. Strongly grounded in documentary evidence and adopting insights from contemporary geography and international relations theories, his book reveals how medieval people from all classes created, reimagined, and negotiated political boundaries that were both spatial and social.

auditPapers.title: Andrés I. Prieto. The Theologian and the Empire: A Biography of José de Acosta (1540–1600)
auditPapers.abstract: There is no need to repeat that José de Acosta (1540–1600) was one of the pioneering Jesuits who established the general missionary policy in colonial Spanish America during the second half of the sixteenth century, a policy that continued until the end of the eighteenth century. His “religious and intellectual significance is comparable only to that of the Dominican friar Bartolomé de Las Casas (1484–1566)” (1). He is also world renowned as a protoanthropologist and naturalist, primarily because of his publication Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590). However, The Theologian and the Empire written by Andrés I. Prieto focuses on a different aspect: Acosta’s role as a “colonial” or “imperial agent” (1, 5). In reality, “Acosta focused on the necessity to create and maintain an adequate colonial superstructure supported by native labor that would allow for a robust colonial church to emerge” (7). In other words, Prieto’s book is highly valuable for shedding light on Acosta’s political activism, particularly focusing on his other famous soteriological treatise on the Indigenous people of the Americas, De procuranda Indorum salute (1588). As Prieto notes in his book, the discussion in De procuranda was adopted beyond the Americas, in regions such as South Asia and Africa (1).

auditPapers.title: Malcolm Ebright and Rick Hendricks. Pablo Abeita: The Life and Times of a Native Statesman of Isleta Pueblo, 1870–1940.
auditPapers.abstract: By the start of the twentieth century, three hundred years of settler colonialism in modern Canada and the United States reached an apogee. Conquest, capitulation, and genocide resulted in the wreckage of Indigenous economies, the reshaping of cultures and social relations, and the loss of political independence to direct colonial rule. Indigenous nations also faced a renewed, reorganized, and intense national program of cultural genocide, with federal schools and federally subsidized church-run schools as a centerpiece. Amid resistance and adaptation, a relatively small but growing class of Indigenous people with high levels of formal Western education emerged, and some of them went on to become national activists. Much of their voluminous writings survived and ultimately fed good biographical scholarship. Recent work includes David Martinez, My Heart Is Bound Up with Them: How Carlos Montezuma Became the Voice of a Generation (2023), and two biographies by the late Tadeusz Lewandowski: Red Bird, Red Power: The Life and Times of Zitakala Ša (2016) and The Life of Sherman Coolidge, Arapaho Activist (2022). More broadly, historians have spent decades studying the Society of American Indians (SAI) and other national Indigenous activist organizations from the early twentieth century.

auditPapers.title: Chloe L. Ireton. Slavery and Freedom in Black Thought in the Early Spanish Atlantic
auditPapers.abstract: One of the most astounding statements about slavery and freedom comes from a Black slave named Diego de la Cruz in New Spain in 1651. De la Cruz declared to the Inquisition in Mexico that he had spent a night out with friends, playing music and having a late-night dinner before returning to work the next morning. The Inquisition later discovered it was all made up. Slaves in the early modern Americas did not simply go out like that. The interesting point, however, is that the issue of freedom is fundamental here: Diego fantasized about being free, and by telling the inquisitors, that fantasy became more real. It was not merely a case of picaresque behavior but rather escapism from reality. I initially considered the case of Diego de la Cruz an exception, presuming that there were few such individual testimonies—until I read Jennifer L. ­­Morgan’s book Reckoning with Slavery and now Chloe L. Ireton’s new book, Slavery and Freedom in Black Thought in the Early Spanish Atlantic. Both books reveal a vast amount of testimonial material on the daily lives and self-fashioning of slaves about whom we knew little. Until recently, we could count the ships on the Middle Passage and analyze plantation economies, but we lacked access to personal data. Ireton’s book fills this gap by weaving together countless ego-­documents, fragmentary testimonies, and case studies. As the author stresses: “From a free Black mother’s embarkation license to cross the Atlantic as a passenger on a ship, or an enslaved Sevillian woman’s letters to her freed husband in New Spain, or an enslaved man’s negotiations for credit arrangements with prospective buyers on the auction block in Mexico City, to a Black man’s petition to a royal court in an attempt to reclaim his liberty after his illegitimate enslavement, Africans and their descendants were important intellectual actors in the early modern Atlantic world” (16–17).

auditPapers.title: Marion Turner. The Wife of Bath: A Biography.
auditPapers.abstract: “Alison of Bath is a middle-aged woman—a reasonably happy older woman (even if she might prefer to be younger)—still sexually active, still attractive, someone who works, goes on holidays, and enjoys life.” So Marion Turner begins chapter 1 of The Wife of Bath: A Biography, an imaginative and learned “biography” of one of Chaucer’s most famous characters. Better known for her moniker than her name, Chaucer’s Wife of Bath is an unusual choice for a biography, yet Turner reveals how Alison is indeed worthy of such a study. Part biography, part microhistory, and part literary reception study, Turner first explores this famous pilgrim in Chaucer’s own late fourteenth-century milieu and then in her cultural longevity and popularity as a figure who migrates out of The Canterbury Tales and into other authors’ creative works. Turner’s main question is “why this character from a fourteenth-­­century poem has had such a dramatic impact across time?” (2) In short, she answers, it is because the Wife of Bath is “the first ordinary woman in English literature” (2); in her ordinariness, Chaucer’s Alison is extraordinary.

auditPapers.title: Whose Revolution?
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This essay grapples with the concept of categories in historical writing: When are they useful, and when do they lead us astray? Covert recounts an episode in their own research that began with a mistaken assumption based on predominant ideas in the historiography about who was “revolutionary” and who was “counterrevolutionary.” Upon realizing the mistake, Covert recalibrated their project, resulting in a more nuanced interpretation of the subject. The essay acknowledges the utility of categories for making comparisons and broad claims, but also reminds the reader that many major historiographical breakthroughs have occurred as a result of revisiting or questioning previously accepted categories. It therefore makes the case for a more expansive approach to categories as dynamic, rather than static, and reminds historians to embrace contingencies and always go back to the historical context to understand what those terms meant to the individuals who used them.

auditPapers.title: Barbra Streisand. My Name is Barbra.
auditPapers.abstract: “What is so offensive about a woman taking control?” Barbra Streisand asks on page 472 of her 2023 memoir My Name is Barbra. Her context is the fierce opposition she encountered in her quest to direct a film rather than simply star in it, but the question is a broader one and sadly resonant today as top ranks of the United States Armed Forces are purged of hard-working, qualified, and talented female leaders on no basis other than their identity as women. Uncannily, even defiantly, sure of herself since, apparently, birth, Streisand hasn’t exactly gone unheralded. Her accomplishments are legendary and legion: she is a member of the highly exclusive EGOT club, meaning her trophy shelf includes an Emmy (5), a Grammy (5), an Oscar (2), and a Tony (1). She has received both the National Medal of the Arts (2000) and the Presidential Medal of Freedom (2015). Her performance as Fanny Brice in the movie of Funny Girl earned her an Oscar at age twenty-one; legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael titled her review of the movie simply “Bravo!”

auditPapers.title: Nico Slate. The Art of Freedom: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and the Making of Modern India.
auditPapers.abstract: In The Art of Freedom: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and the Making of Modern India, Nico Slate introduces his readers to one of the most important and influential South Asian women of the twentieth century. It is said that—until relatively recently—there were more autobiographical writings by South Asian women themselves than biographies written about them. (It has been the other way round for South Asian men.) The process of recovering and piecing together the life stories of individual women—whether well known or not—was slow to get going, though now there is a growing corpus of publications that collectively addresses this historical deficit. In many cases, the challenge for biographers has been how to reconstruct lives from what are often scant or fragmented materials, sometimes only discovered by family members after the subject herself is no longer alive. A paucity of sources, however, does not apply in the case of Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay (or Kamaladevi, as Slate decides to call her). Prior to the appearance of this well-crafted biography, there have been others, both in Hindi and in English, testifying to Kamaladevi as a woman of substance whose achievements demand that proper attention be paid to her. Moreover, there is no shortage of her own words on which to draw. During the course of a long and extremely active life (1903–88), Kamaladevi wrote prodigiously in the form of published articles and reports, letters, and her own memoirs, all of which provide direct access to her thoughts and actions on a myriad matters.

auditPapers.title: Bryan Banks. Write to Return: Huguenot Refugees on the Frontiers of the French Enlightenment
auditPapers.abstract: In Write to Return: Huguenot Refugees on the Frontiers of the French Enlightenment, Bryan Banks has written a fascinating and significant study of how Huguenots formulated an identity as refugees and advocated for religious toleration. At the heart of Write to Return are three arguments. First, Banks contends that the concept of suffering in Huguenot writing drifted away from a principle of faith built on religious foundations. In its place, Huguenot writers increasingly explained suffering in terms of its political meaning. Second, Huguenot writers in dialogue with the French Enlightenment adopted arguments supporting religious toleration, often in terms of the metaphor of the body politic. While community and universality animated their writing, theology did not entirely fade, and the limits of toleration led—by 1789—to demands for religious liberty. Third, the visibility of Huguenot refugees made possible new forms of sentimentalism that influenced the French Enlightenment. In the context of the 18th century, the increased attention to Huguenot experiences fostered conversations about rights that were universal, sentimental, and religious.

auditPapers.title: Nina Janz. Remnants of Wehrmacht Soldiers: Burial and Commemoration Practices of German Soldiers of the Second World War in Russia and Europe, 1941–2023
auditPapers.abstract: Roughly eighteen million German men served in Hitler’s armies, the Wehrmacht and the Waffen-SS, in World War II. Five million of them did not survive the war and were buried across Europe and North Africa, most of them in the Nazi-occupied territories of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. At the beginning of the war, the Nazis went to great lengths to honor German war deaths individually and collectively through military ceremonies and intricate rituals of burials and commemoration, taking up the cult of the fallen soldiers that had started with the rise of nationalism, drafted armies, and the concept of the citizen-soldier around 1800. But the abundance of losses since 1943, especially on the Eastern Front, left most of the graves unattended and often purposefully neglected or destroyed as symbols of German aggression, crimes, and genocide—until the end of the Cold War. While the West German Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge (VDK), or German War Graves Commission, assumed authority to recover and ­­cultivate the remains of German soldier across the battlefields of Western Europe and North Africa, only the end of the Cold War and a German-Russian war grave agreement established in 1992 allowed for expanding these activities into the Eastern hemisphere, including Russia. The activities, which culminated in the recovery of the remains of one million German soldiers through 2023, are at the core of Nina Janz’s Remnants of Wehrmacht Soldiers.

auditPapers.title: William Gow. Performing Chinatown: Hollywood, Tourism, and the Making of a Chinese American Community.
auditPapers.abstract: Performing Chinatown: Hollywood, Tourism, and the Making of a Chinese American Community explores two related but distinct developments. The first is a local one: the way different members of Los Angeles’s Chinese American community attempted to shape Chinatown tourism and participate in the movie industry in the 1930s and 1940s. The second is far broader in scope: “the role that Chinatown performances played in shaping, challenging, and creating dominant ideas about Chinese Americans in the popular conscience, the ways these performances constructed ideas about race and, in turn, how these ideas shaped the lives of everyday Chinese Americans” (3). William Gow tackles these subjects in a series of roughly chronological chapters that examine aspects of Chinatown tourism nationally and in Los Angeles; the 1930s demolition of LA’s Old Chinatown, as well as the construction of rival replacements; the work Chinese Angelenos found as extras and bit players in the emerging Hollywood film industry; and the way World War II transformed that work and the larger portrayal of Asians and Asian Americans.

auditPapers.title: Nathan Perl-Rosenthal. The Age of Revolutions: And the Generations Who Made It.
auditPapers.abstract: Nathan Perl-Rosenthal’s ambitious new synthesis makes a novel contribution to the crowded field of comparative revolutions. Attuned to the Tocquevillian continuities that lurk beneath dramatic ruptures, The Age of Revolutions: And the Generations Who Made It charts the “long tail of political turning points” (465) like the American Declaration of Independence. Perl-Rosenthal’s longer durée approach stretches the “age of revolutions” back to the Stamp Act crisis of the mid-1760s; he then broadens its geographic ambit to include both familiar and “offbeat” (11) cases from across Europe and the Euro-American empires, culminating with Peruvian independence in 1825. What makes the work especially innovative is the onus it places on generational transitions to explain why revolutionary movements across the Atlantic World played out in the halting and often illiberal ways they did. Privileging practices over principles, Perl-­­Rosenthal argues that “what makes a revolution happen” (3)—and then endure—is a movement’s ability to mobilize the masses by building inclusive communication networks, public spaces, and institutions like political clubs and conscript armies. The first cohort he identifies—“gentlemen revolutionaries” who grew up in fixed societies where “birth was usually destiny” (29)—proved incapable of establishing durable alliances with their social inferiors. Drawing on Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of “habitus” (4), Perl-Rosenthal attributes this generation’s “top-down” tendencies to their formative experiences in a hierarchical world. From Túpac Amaru’s doomed Andean rebellion to the Constitutional Convention’s elitist coup in Philadelphia, the book’s opening half contends that George Washington, Maximilien Robespierre, and even Toussaint Louverture lacked the “mobile social imaginary” (292) and practical skills to operate across class and caste lines, much less dismantle them.

auditPapers.title: Jacob Flaws. Spaces of Treblinka: Retracing a Death Camp.
auditPapers.abstract: Among the countless sites of brutality and criminality associated with the Holocaust implemented by Nazi Germany, the extermination camps associated with Operation Reinhard are perhaps the most notorious and enigmatic. Jacob Flaws’s Spaces of Treblinka: Retracing a Death Camp offers insights into one of those camps. Located approximately eighty kilometers northeast of Warsaw in the German-occupied General Government district, the Treblinka extermination camp operated between July 1942 and October 1943. During that relatively short time, an unfathomable 700,000 to 900,000 men, women, and children, predominantly Polish Jews from occupied Polish territories, were murdered in Treblinka’s gas chambers and proximate spaces. Together with Operation Reinhard’s two other main extermination camps, Belźec and Sobibór, SS troopers and their auxiliaries carried out the murder of approximately 1.6 million people, the deadliest phase of Hitler’s Final Solution to exterminate Jews and other groups regarded as subhuman by Nazi ideology. Flaws delves into this dark chapter and takes readers beyond the shocking and mind-numbing numbers to explore how perpetrators, victims, survivors, and various types of witnesses experienced Treblinka and how those experiences extended far beyond the barbed wire, guard towers, and anti-tank obstacles that defined its perimeter.

auditPapers.title: Vanessa Wilkie. A Woman of Influence: The Spectacular Rise of Alice Spencer in Tudor England.
auditPapers.abstract: Biographical studies of Tudor-era figures are hardly few and far between. Yet the oversaturation of the genre makes the addition of lesser-known subjects especially welcome. Alice Spencer Stanley Egerton, Countess of Derby (1559–1637), is one such subject. A Woman of Influence: The Spectacular Rise of Alice Spencer in Tudor England, by Vanessa Wilkie, originates from a PhD thesis exploring the lives of the countess and her three daughters, where their relationships were reconstructed primarily to supply additional context for the infamous trial of the Earl of Castlehaven in 1631. In this iteration, the same material has been transformed into a more traditional biography. As the title suggests, it is Alice herself who is given center stage: Her name alone is in the title, and the story begins with her earlier life and ends with her death. The book is structured to trace first her rise, then her role at the heart of a Renaissance family, and finally her success in steering her offspring through what the author labels “secrets and violence.”

auditPapers.title: Pete Millwood. Improbable Diplomats: How Ping-Pong Players, Musicians, and Scientists Remade US-China Relations
auditPapers.abstract: Improbable Diplomats takes us into the world of US-China relations in the 1970s through the stories of athletes, musicians, and scientists who traveled between the two countries during the tricky diplomatic period of rapprochement. During this time, US-China relations remained stuck in diplomatic limbo as leaders from both countries sought to achieve full diplomatic relations after more than twenty years of isolation. Pete Millwood is interested in how people from both China and the United States connected with one another and rebuilt ties. He looks, in other words, at the “Ping-Pong” aspect of the decade’s infamous “Ping-Pong diplomacy”: at cultural ties, not just high politics. One of the core arguments of the book is that these cultural exchanges and academic ties influenced diplomatic relations. He does not look at these exchanges only as moments of interpersonal connection; rather, he makes an argument about causality. “These interactions also exerted a powerful influence on the diplomatic relationship between the two governments,” Millwood writes. They were “a critical factor” in the “success and failures” of rapprochement negotiations (3). Millwood repeatedly shows how the diplomatic summits between political leaders were preceded, and aided, by cultural ties. President Richard Nixon and Chairman Mao Zedong’s much-lauded February 1972 meeting was made easier by the Ping-Pong exchanges that took place months earlier. Millwood balances the usual narratives of this moment by drawing out the “return leg” of the Ping-Pong saga, pointing out that not only did the US team travel to China, but a few months later, the Chinese team visited the United States too. The end of rapprochement was similarly eased by the efforts of a US scientific delegation that traveled to China in 1978, Millwood shows.

auditPapers.title: John H. Arnold. The Making of Lay Religion in Southern France, c. 1000–1350
auditPapers.abstract: At once sweeping and granular, John H. Arnold’s The Making of Lay Religion in Southern France opens with the question of how Christianity “change[d] for ordinary people between the turn of the millennium and the coming of the Black Death” in Southern France (1). The introduction outlines both the historiographi­cal traditions with which he tangles, from the nature of “popular religion” to the Peace of God, Gregorian Reform, and Feudal Revolution, as well as his goal to reconstruct a complex lay piety that places the hete­rodox alongside the orthodox, the lukewarm alongside the devout, and individual devotion alongside community practice. He argues that there was a profound change in lay piety in this period, toward increasing emotion, interiority, and enthusiasm. This change was not exclusively the result of top-down institutional efforts to impose observance, nor can it be attributed to the emergence of “natural” lay pious feeling (gesturing inevitably toward the Reformation). Rather, Arnold presents a multivalent picture of change, always grounding his claims in concrete examples from the Southern French evidence.

auditPapers.title: Rob Waters. Colonized by Humanity: Caribbean London and the Politics of Integration at the End of Empire
auditPapers.abstract: In Enoch Powell’s often quoted 1968 “Rivers of Blood” speech, the Conservative Party politician warned against the dangers of rising immigration from Britain’s former colonies. Powell claimed that there was “a ludicrous and dangerous misconception” that the “great and growing majority of immigrants” demonstrated a desire to integrate within the British nation. Powell’s speech no doubt whipped up racial antagonism, but he was far from the first British politician to focus on the limits and possibilities of integration. MP Roy Hattersley’s now famous aphorism summed up state responses to immigration in the 1960s: “Without integration, limitation is inexcusable; without limitation, integration is impossible” (12). For the ­­Minister of Education, Sir Edward Boyle, “the problem of race relations, and of integration versus segregation, would continue for generations to be one of the most important issues facing the free world.” Figures from across the political spectrum have therefore acknowledged the importance of integration within histories of modern Britain, yet it has until now received scant ­­scholarly attention.

auditPapers.title: Kathryn L. Mahaney. Feminism, National Identity and European Integration in Modern Spain: Defining a Democracy, 1960–Present
auditPapers.abstract: In Spain, feminism has been central to the construction of a society bent on turning the page on the Franco dictatorship. In this thought-provoking study resulting from her doctoral research, Kathryn L. Mahaney analyzes the complex political democratization of Spain in an international context, placing the accent on the advances in gender equality. Despite the fact there is already plenty of literature on the feminist movement during the Spanish Transition—in this ­connection, references to key works in the field of Spanish historiography are missing—Feminism, National Identity and European Integration in Modern Spain offers an unquestionably interesting historical perspective. First and foremost, because it interweaves feminist struggles with the reconstruction of national identity and the efforts to appear before Europe as a modern democracy. Second, because it does not take for granted that greater gender equality was a result of the feminist struggle, the book introduces another variable that assumes a leading role in her account: the opportunism of the country’s political parties and their quest for democratic legitimacy. Third, it warrants noting how Mahaney has managed to frame her study in an international context that fleshes out and gives depth to her analysis.

auditPapers.title: Jorge Marco. Paradise in Hell: Alcohol and Drugs in the Spanish Civil War.
auditPapers.abstract: In Paradise in Hell: Alcohol and Drugs in the Spanish Civil War, Jorge Marco does an outstanding job of highlighting the use, and abuse, of alcohol and drugs during the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939). The topic of psychoactive substances in the early twentieth century is currently a popular topic among historians, as seen in the recent publication of two other excellent books: Norman Ohler’s Blitzed: Drugs in Nazi ­Germany (2017) and Edward B. Westermann’s Drunk on Genocide: Alcohol and Mass Murder in Nazi Germany (2021). According to Marco, propagandists during the Spanish Civil War created the idea of the “new man,” one imbued with idealism, who worked toward victory and looked after his own physical and moral health (9). Additionally, Marco describes the rise of the concept of “respectable masculinity,” where drinking ­alcohol—particularly Spanish wine, as opposed to “Protestant beer”—was deemed important. An example of “respectable masculinity” was a man who could hold his liquor, but who would not devolve into a sloppy drunk. Many Republican soldiers and militiamen accused foreigners in the International Brigades of this latter condition. Marco also notes that some proponents of this new “respectable masculinity” considered not drinking wine as a sign of weakness, a lack of virility, and, as a result, of homosexuality.

auditPapers.title: 張娟芬 (Chang Chuan-fen). 流氓, 王信福 (Hooligan, Wang Xinfu).
auditPapers.abstract: In April 2024, the Constitutional Court of Taiwan heard arguments against the constitutionality of the death penalty. Hooligan, Wang Xinfu describes how the system of martial law in Taiwan had criminalized Wang throughout his youth and eventually led to a conviction for a murder Wang did not commit. Although constructed around an individual life, Chang Chuan-fen’s genre-defying book is not a biography of a man so much as a scrupulous examination of a corrupt police investigation and a reconstruction of a trial convened over a decade after the crime. auditPapers.title: Elizabeth D. Leonard. Benjamin Franklin Butler: A Noisy, Fearless Life.
auditPapers.abstract: He wore nicknames including “Devil,” “Damnedest Yankee,” “Beast,” and “Spoons” for his treatment of Southern gentility and his alleged theft of silverware. Loathing for him by white Southerners rivaled that for Abraham Lincoln and William T. Sherman. Meanwhile, when removed from command during the Civil War, adoring and saddened Black soldiers sent him off with cheers and tears. Decades later, Black veterans feted their former general at his funeral. The effusive emotional responses to Benjamin Butler speak to his contentious life and personality. Such people can make for difficult subjects of biography. The strong responses test the biographer. Evocative sources demand the writer account for many political biases and wade into divergent accounts. But if successfully understood, a character like Butler presents the biographer the rewarding opportunity to offer a thrilling account of a person and the past. In Benjamin Franklin Butler: A Noisy, Fearless Life, Elizabeth D. Leonard accomplishes this, providing a complex view of the complicated politician, general, and family man.

auditPapers.title: Marc-William Palen. Pax Economica: Left-Wing Visions of a Free-Trade World.
auditPapers.abstract: Who’s afraid of free trade? In Pax Economica, Marc-William Palen argues that the contemporary tendency to link free market and free-trade ideas with right-wing politics fails to recognize their roots in a very different context: the world of left-wing socialist, liberal, feminist, and internationalist peace activists. Between 1850 and 1950, he contends, such activists developed a theory that linked free trade with global interdependence and, consequently, world peace. They have been forgotten, but not because they failed: Palen argues that the supranational organizations set up to oversee a free-trade world after the Second World War represent their political and ideological triumph. However, that triumph would be overtaken by Cold War politics and then obscured by the ideological shifts that soldered free trade to neoliberalism in the guise of Reaganomics toward the century’s end. Pax Economica makes an important contribution to the emerging body of historiography reconsidering the roots of key concepts in contemporary economics. This work unsettles modern orthodoxies by demonstrating the diversity of past ideas and alliances.

auditPapers.title: Daniel J. Feather. British Cultural Diplomacy in South Africa, 1960–1994
auditPapers.abstract: The election of the National Party in 1948 and the subsequent implementation of its apartheid policy of racial discrimination saw South Africa gradually drift to assume pariah status in the late 20th-century international order. The country had firmly been in Britain’s sphere of influence since the early 19th century, despite much of the white minority population originating from earlier Dutch, French, and German immigrants. These Afrikaners, as they became known following their defeat by the British Empire in the Second South African War (1899–1902), had long chaffed at British political control, and the decision by the National Party government to withdraw from the Commonwealth in 1961 threatened to fatally undermine British influence in the region. Daniel J. Feather’s well-written and timely book, British Cultural Diplomacy in South Africa, 1960–1994, analyzes how British policymakers viewed South Africa’s exit and their subsequent attempts to keep cultural links alive between the two countries to ensure that South Africa remained in, what recent scholarship has termed, the “British World.”

auditPapers.title: Janaki Bakhle. Savarkar and the Making of Hindutva
auditPapers.abstract: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar (1883-1966) was the progenitor of Hindutva (Hindu-ness/Hindu nationalism). Today, he is at the centre of an Indian culture war that seeks to displace Nehru and Gandhi as leaders of India’s freedom movement, and with them, the principle of non-majoritarian pluralism. Savarkar’s life and ideas conceived Hindu majoritarianism not as religious fundamentalism but as a “way of life” rooted in India in opposition to internationalist Islam. This is the ideology of India’s governing Bhartiya Janata Party today. Savarkar’s interventions prefigure the Euro-American Zeitgeist, where so-called “Christian atheists” appeal to an exclusionary “Christian civilization” equally preoccupied with demonizing Muslims. To say that Janaki Bakhle’s new biography of Savarkar is timely, then, would be understatement. It comes as the boom in intellectual biography-writing has reconstructed the politically imaginative ways Indians reckoned with the subcontinent’s diversity. Alongside works that have reconstructed the intellectual life-worlds of several thinkers at once, these biographies have been crucial to recovering Indian political thought as both national and global. Bakhle’s important contribution to this new canon shows how Savarkar’s legacy was demonized and valorized depending on the regional, linguistic, and aesthetic perspective people took. Bakhle self-consciously eschews the hagiographic or condemning tone of the voluminous writing on the man and instead uses his political treatises, speeches, historical works, and crucially, his poetry up to 1937 to paint a “kaleidoscopic” portrait. In so doing, Bakhle expertly reveals how Savarkar’s legacy has been so contested, interpreted as both modernist and reactionary, rational and dogmatic, upper-caste and anti-caste, pro women’s rights and defending sexual violence.

auditPapers.title: Jenny Shaw. The Women of Rendezvous: A Transatlantic Story of Family and Slavery.
auditPapers.abstract: In the summer of 1686, a “great and numerous family” sailed from Barbados to London. They included 2 enslaved African women, an English female servant, 11 children, and the children’s father. John Peers, ­­Barbados’s largest landowner, member of the island’s council, enslaver of 180 people, and master of 8 white servants, had business to attend in London. Three years earlier, 9 of the children had been baptized on the same day in the same church, their names and the names of their parents duly recorded. Their mothers were the enslaved women Susannah Mingo and Elizabeth Ashcroft and the English servant Dorothy Spendlove; their father was Peers, who already had 5 older children, born to two English women whom he had married in succession and who had not survived. After first lodging in London’s fashionable West End, the group from Barbados took up residence in a grand, finely furnished manor house five miles away in the small village of Streatham. There, the enslaved and servant women and their children continued to serve the white members of the family in their new home. Peers’s Eurafrican son may have worn, with his fine livery coat, a locked metal collar similar to those on dogs, as did many enslaved boys at the time in England. In 1689, still in London, the ailing Peers drafted a will and then, three days later, died. Though the amounts bequeathed differed according to the race and status of the recipients, in an unusual move, Peers recognized his entire, multihued family. The will provided for all of the Peers children and all three of their living mothers.

auditPapers.abstract: There are two common conclusions about the 1988 presidential contest between Vice President George H. W. Bush and Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis. auditPapers.title: Beeta Baghoolizadeh. The Color Black: Enslavement and Erasure in Iran.
auditPapers.abstract: Iranians enslaved East Africans too. That simple yet significant intervention made by Beeta Baghoolizadeh in The Color Black challenges both the historiographic erasure of slavery in Iran and the collective denial that slavery became distinctly racialized from the latter half of the 19th century until its abolition in 1929. ­­Ensla­­vement in what is now Iran stretches back to the Achaemenid Empire (550 BCE–330 BCE), and those ensnared in the trade came from bordering areas, including the Caucasus, Central Asia, South Asia, and East Africa. As the number of enslaved people from areas outside of East Africa dwindled, the status of being enslaved in Iran became increasingly synonymous with being East African and Black, which, in turn, solidified the whiteness of non-Black Iranians.

auditPapers.title: Julia F. Irwin. Catastrophic Diplomacy: US Foreign Disaster Assistance in the American Century
auditPapers.abstract: Hurricane Flora churned through the Caribbean Sea in late September 1963, killing 7,193 people in the region, among them 1,750 Cubans. Almost exactly one year after the Cuban Missile Crisis, Flora opened another front in the Cold War struggle between the United States and Cuba: a contest over the meanings of a disaster and its implications for statecraft. One Kennedy administration official saw the chance to offer disaster aid as a route to gaining a “psychological advantage” among the distraught Cuban population. According to long-standing tradition, the American Red Cross (ARC) initiated aid, and was rebuffed by their Cuban Red Cross peers, who rejected out of hand this “hypocritical offer of assistance.” Recriminations, anger, and—at last—diplomacy followed when a small delegation of American Quakers were permitted to deliver $92,000 in food and medical supplies—a small win for the soft power catastrophe diplomats. This superbly strange tale of hurricane realpolitik is one among hundreds of local disaster cases across more than a century—from East to West and all points in between—animating Julia F. Irwin’s densely researched and fast-paced new book Catastrophic Diplomacy: US Foreign Disaster Assistance in the American Century. Disasters may emerge from the weather, geology, or technological failures, but they are fundamentally social phenomena, and therefore political, and in no way separable from the broader forces shaping US foreign policy since the founding of the nation.

auditPapers.title: Elisa Camiscioli. Selling French Sex: Prostitution, Trafficking, and Global Migrations.
auditPapers.abstract: In Selling French Sex: Prostitution, Trafficking, and Global Migrations, Elisa Camiscioli tells a sweeping story of global migration in the early 20th century that centers the French sex worker. Camiscioli shows how French women were a hot commodity in brothels across the Americas, where they frequently outnumbered and outearned women of other nationalities, benefiting from an image of Parisian vice culture that underwrote the idea that French women were more likely to offer “perverse” sex acts. But if “French sex” seemed to be desired much like a luxury good with a certain je ne sais quoi, migration for the purposes of selling sex also made French women undesirable in a moment when American countries like the United States were working to bar immigrants intending to enter the country for “immoral purposes” (45). That is to say that individuals found French sex workers desirable. States did not. Thus, in the eyes of both clients and immigration officials across the Americas, the French sex worker did not look much like a trafficking victim, despite the widespread circulation of stories about French women kidnapped into sexual slavery in Buenos Aires and other destinations around the globe, which have been well-studied by historians. Breaking with historical and contemporary framings, Camiscioli rereads the archive of the “white slave trade” as one of migration and transforms women characterized as both trafficking victims and “undesirable” immigrants into individuals making informed—if always constrained—decisions about their working lives. Much like Philippa Hetherington and Julia Laite, in their introduction to a special issue of the Journal of Women’s History on “Migration, Sex, and Intimate Labor” (33, no. 4 [2021]: 7–39), Camiscioli finds trafficking to be—if not a “useless ­­category of historical analysis”—a category that masks more than it reveals about women’s movement to sell sex across national borders.

auditPapers.title: Brian Patrick McGuire. Bernard of Clairvaux: An Inner Life
auditPapers.abstract: Brian Patrick McGuire’s Bernard of Clairvaux: An Inner Life promises to take up the “state of mind” or the “inner conviction[s]” of Cistercian monk and abbot Bernard of Clairvaux (1090-1153), who was among the most creative thinkers of the Middle Ages and who exerted unparalleled influence on the major intellectual and institutional developments that rocked 12th century Europe. His sharp, sensual, reasoned, and imaginative writings shaped centuries of Christian spirituality. Attuned to the extreme reactions Bernard elicits among modern readers, McGuire is committed to presenting a portrait of Bernard that neither dismisses him as “intolerant and unsympathetic” nor reduces him to a saint cast in saccharine hues and instead aims to unveil the monk in his complexity (2). McGuire’s commitment to holding together Bernard’s subtle and sublime insights with his frequently brusque and brutal interventions is much needed and commendable. The book is divided into two major sections. The first section travels through Bernard’s life in rough chronological order, and a second section, “Fifteen Questions,” provides what McGuire calls “the background” for this study (xv). The book also contains a chronological list of significant events in Bernard’s life, a bibliography, and two maps, one of Champagne and Burgundy (Bernard’s home territory) and one of Cistercian monasteries—whose number explored under Bernard’s influence—established by the time of the abbot’s death. It is a real misfortune that McGuire restricts notes to “Fifteen Questions,” an omission he explains as in service of maintaining “the integrity of the text” (xv).

auditPapers.title: Charles Wilkinson. Treaty Justice: The Northwest Tribes, the Boldt Decision, and the Recognition of Fishing Rights
auditPapers.abstract: Charles Wilkinson’s Treaty Justice begins dramatically on the banks of Tacoma’s Puyallup River in the summer of 1964, where violent clashes erupted between Indigenous fishers and Washington State police. These confrontations marked the opening salvos of the “fish wars”—a period when Puget Sound tribes actively resisted state attempts to deny them access to waterways where they held treaty-protected fishing rights. Written at the urging of fishing rights activist Billy Frank Jr. and funded by the Northwest Indian Fish­eries ­Commission, the book commemorates the fiftieth anniversary of the Boldt Decision, positioning it as “a landmark in the American civil rights movement” (8). Indeed, Wilkinson boldly asserts that the case “belongs in the same company as Brown v. Board of Education.” As a scholar renowned for making complex Indian law and policy accessible through elegant prose, Wilkinson adds to his distinguished body of work that includes Blood Struggle: The Rise of Modern Indian Nations (2005) and The People Are Dancing Again: The History of the Siletz Tribe of Western Oregon (2010)—the latter written in close collaboration with the Siletz Indian Nation. His reputation for ethical scholarship and meaningful research return to Indigenous communities makes him particularly well suited to tell this story.

auditPapers.title: Rebecca L. Davis. Fierce Desires: A New History of Sex and Sexuality in America
auditPapers.abstract: In Fierce Desires: A New History of Sex and Sexuality in America, Rebecca L. Davis offers a breezy narrative that centers stories of gender nonconformity, sexual diversity, efforts to control reproduction, and attempts to regulate sexual expression. She argues that over four centuries of American history, sexual behaviors shifted from being seen as “a reflection of personal preferences or values” to “an essential part of what makes a person who they are” (x). To support this argument, Davis structures each of her eighteen chapters around one or two individuals whose experiences highlight the major trends or exceptions of different eras. This narrative-driven approach makes the book enjoyable to read. However, for scholars of sexuality, many of Davis’s stories will be familiar, drawn as they were from the last fifty years of published research on sexuality and its intersections with race, class, and gender. This raises the question: what is new about this “new history of sex and sexuality”?

auditPapers.title: William Gee Wong. Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America.
auditPapers.abstract: William Gee Wong’s Sons of Chinatown is a memoir rooted in Oakland’s Chinatown. It spans more than one hundred years from 1912, when Wong’s father arrived at the Angel Island immigration station, to the recent past, when the author travels to his father’s ancestral village in Guangdong with his adult son. In the process, Sons of Chinatown spans much of Chinese American history—from the exclusion era through World War II, to the long Asian American movement. It traces Wong’s father’s life through various jobs, dubious dealings, marriage, and raising a family of seven children: six girls and, finally, the longed-awaited boy, William. Interleaved with this history, the book explores the author’s life: Growing up as the valorized only son in the secure “bubble” of Oakland’s Chinatown, attending the University of California, Berkeley, in the 1950s as opportunities began to open for Chinese Americans, and breaking ground as one of the first Asian American print journalists. About one-third of the book focuses on his father’s life, and two-thirds on Wong’s coming of age and career.

auditPapers.title: Tamrala Swafford Bliss. Wilma Mankiller: A Life in American History.
auditPapers.abstract: Tamrala Swafford Bliss’s book Wilma Mankiller: A Life in American History examines how Wilma Mankiller’s life (1945–2010) intersected with some of the most significant policies and events in Indian Country in the latter half of the twentieth century. Mankiller became the first woman principal chief of the Cherokee Nation at age forty in 1985, when, as deputy chief, she replaced resigning chief Ross Swimmer. In 1987, Mankiller became the third popularly elected principal chief since Oklahoma’s statehood in 1907. She served in the office until 1995. Much of the book is devoted to the characteristics of Mankiller’s leadership style. Mankiller’s skills in organizing and motivating her community members came both from an adherence to Cherokee beliefs and from on-the-ground training in grassroots organizing. Throughout the text, Bliss returns to the Cherokee practice of gadugi. Bliss notes that the “most current usage of the term” means “working together for the good of the community” (xiv). Gadugi can also refer to “work crews” of Cherokee people who perform services for the community—including building and maintaining churches and stomp grounds, supporting elderly and sick community members, and rebuilding homes damaged by fire or floods (66). Gadugi is thus an active term, and practicing interdependence means getting things done for the betterment of the community.

auditPapers.title: Todd Presner. Ethics of the Algorithm: Digital Humanities and Holocaust Memory
auditPapers.abstract: In Ethics of the Algorithm: Digital Humanities and Holocaust Memory, Todd Presner seeks to respond to what he sees as a “big problem”: how to use computational methods “in ethical” ways to distant read vast Holocaust testimony archives (vii). While the book is rich in discussions of a range of current digital humanities methods and tools, its focus is very much on a core set of ethical concerns that persist regardless of the precise, ever-changing technologies deployed. Although working with a particular source—collections of oral history interviews with tens of thousands of Holocaust survivors—the central question in the book is one of wider significance for humanists: “How can we think, listen, compose, and interpret ethically with algorithms and computational methods?” (19) While Presner is the main author, the book includes the words of others from the UCLA lab. Collaborative and interdisciplinary ways of working are the norm in the digital humanities, and the book draws on this wider team to good effect, mixing Presner’s overarching narrative with shorter, focused sections that delve into particular projects coauthored with or by others. These multiple texts are further enhanced by QR codes that enable further exploration of the data under discussion. Both signal new ways of working and publishing that are to be welcomed more widely in the discipline.

auditPapers.title: Franklin Rudolf Ankersmit. Representation: The Birth of Historical Reality from the Death of the Past.
auditPapers.abstract: Historians should have no more trustworthy a philo­­sophical companion than Frank Ankersmit. For the past five decades, he has been the historicist’s philosopher, defending the ambition of historians to represent historical reality against literary spoilers and epistemological skeptics. Ankersmit has advanced the two-pronged argument that history consists in 1) true statements about the past, and 2) historical representations that, though composed of true statements about the past, are independent from that past. The full title of his new book, Representation: The Birth of Historical Reality from the Death of the Past, reflects these dual components. Representation announces the need to zero in on the concept that in previous works is qualified (Historical Representation, 2001; Political Representation, 2002). The subtitle, The Birth of Historical Reality from the Death of the Past, reinforces the message that to talk of “past reality” is meaningless. Historians trade in historical reality and it comes into existence only because the past is no longer.

auditPapers.title: Chanelle Delameillieure. Abduction, Marriage, and Consent in the Late Medieval Low Countries
auditPapers.abstract: Abduction, Marriage, and Consent in the Late Medieval Low Countries is a fascinating analysis of an intriguing medieval phenomenon: abduction with marital intent. Although its title claims to cover the entire Low Countries, this book has a narrower focus and deals with three cities in Flanders and Brabant—namely, Ghent, Leuven, and Antwerp. Nevertheless, Chanelle Delameillieure was able to trace no less than 650 abduction cases during the fifteenth century. A thorough analysis of this extensive corpus allows her to critique traditional narratives that portray abductions and clandestine marriages solely as acts of rebellion by young women seeking autonomy. Delameillieure convincingly challenges conventional views on medieval marital conflicts and highlights the unique sociolegal environment of the Southern Low Countries. In fact, Middle Dutch had a specific term to distinguish abduction with marital intent (schaec) from rape (vrouwencracht). Furthermore, the Southern Low Countries had a unique legal regime with a secular age of consent, strict anti-abduction laws, and a high age threshold for marriage without parental approval, setting it apart from other regions in late medieval Europe. ­Delameillieure also exposes the tension between the church’s consent-based marriage doctrine and traditional customs favoring family-controlled marriage strategies. This conflict led to legal disputes and family conflicts, showing that marriage choices were highly contested areas. This distinctive legal and social landscape made marriage a matter of negotiation, both within families and the broader social fabric of cities in the Southern Low Countries.

auditPapers.title: Charles C. Bolton. Home Front Battles: World War II Mobilization and Race in the Deep South
auditPapers.abstract: Within the field of World War II history, more scholars are approaching the United States home front as an area as deserving of study as the Pacific and European theaters of the war. While histories of women entering the workforce, cultural trends, censorship and surveillance, Japanese American incarceration, and race relations from the Double V Campaign to the racially motivated violence of 1943 abound, recent works integrate these topics into synthetic studies that detail the experiences of life beyond the combat zones. But as Charles C. Bolton demonstrates in his most recent book Home Front Battles: World War II Mobilization and Race in the Deep South, historians should continue to recognize the importance of regionalism in understanding the varied experiences of Americans who did not serve overseas. Perhaps it makes more sense for scholars to think of multiple home fronts rather than one home front, a notion that Bolton presents in his study of the war’s impacts on the economic, racial, and political landscapes of the American South.

auditPapers.title: Michael D. Hattem. The Memory of ‘76: The Revolution in American History
auditPapers.abstract: Michael D. Hattem’s book The Memory of ‘76 offers a much-needed and timely account of the meaning and legacy of the American Revolution in American culture from the nation’s beginnings to the present. As Hattem notes, despite the importance of the Revolution to American national identity, the memory of the Revolution as a whole has received surprisingly little attention from scholars. While there have been studies of specific aspects of that memory, such as Sarah Purcell’s Sealed with Blood: War, Sacrifice, and Memory in Revolutionary America (2002) or Alfred Young’s The Shoemaker and the Tea Party (1999), the only other broadly synthetic account of the memory of the Revolution comparable to Hattem’s is Michael Kammen’s A Season of Youth: The American Revolution and the Historical Imagination (1978). But where Kammen emphasizes how the Revolution was “de-revolutionized” and given a conservative cast, Hattem highlights the contested meaning of the Revolution throughout the nation’s history, showing how it was used to at once uphold and challenge the established social order. Consequently, Hattem departs from Kammen’s focus on mostly high culture—art, literature, and theater—in favor of more overtly politicized areas of contention such as political rhetoric, commemorative activities, and historic preservation, with the aim of integrating public history, formal historical writing, and popular culture.

auditPapers.title: Scott Gac. Born in Blood: Violence and the Making of America.
auditPapers.abstract: Born in the Blood was written as a response to Richard Hofstadter’s pronouncement that the United States “has a history but not a tradition of domestic violence.” To the contrary, Scott Gac argues, American history illustrates a “process-oriented, ideological tradition centered on slavery, colonization, Whiteness, and hostile difference” (267). Though there may have been “moments of justice in the American past,” in the United States, violence has been the successful tool of racial oppression and capitalist exploitation (268). The book is divided into three parts: “Early Manifestations,” focused on the eighteenth century; “Evolutions,” focused on the 1850s and the Civil War; and “Modern Traditions,” focused on the postbellum decades and the beginnings of the Gilded Age. It is in the immediate postbellum period that Gac sees a confluence of military discipline, labor coercion, and the emergence of new post-emancipation forms of racial order and plantation discipline. In this combination, Gac sees the emergence of a coherent culture of violence at the heart of modern industrial capitalism. He goes on in part 3 to elaborate on the manifestations of this new order in the form of the crushing of the Railway Strike of 1877, the violent subversion of reconstruction, and the acceleration of lynching. Gac does a good job of capturing this incredibly grim period in the history of American political violence in all its atrocity.
