auditPapers.title: Timothy C. Hart. Beyond the River, Under the Eye of Rome
auditPapers.abstract: Timothy C. Hart’s Beyond the River, Under the Eye of Rome, a welcome addition to the field of Roman borderland studies, skillfully combines close reading of Greco-Roman ethnographic texts with environmental analysis and new archaeological data. The book’s geographic focus is on the Danube River and its watershed, with special attention to the Hungarian Plain and Pontic Steppe. Its chronological range is primarily from the second through fifth centuries CE, with some forays back to classical Greece and the early principate. It raises compelling and timely questions about the destructive power of ethnic stereotypes and the persistent tendency of societies like Rome to build borders out of a perceived need to protect themselves from being overrun by outsiders seen as threatening or inferior. At its core, Hart’s argument is straightforward—the Romans repeatedly failed to recognize the environmental and cultural realities of the Danube borderlands they sought to dominate. Indigenous people who lived in the region before the Roman arrival didn’t see the river as a dividing line; rather, the Danube lay at the center of a unified ecological and cultural zone. Rome’s establishment of a militarized border along the river in the first century CE—the Danube limes—thus profoundly disturbed the region’s migratory patterns and rhythms. Although force and ideology enabled the empire to maintain its imposed boundary for centuries, Roman policy was ultimately self-­­defeating for two main reasons. First, the navigable tributaries and traversable plains that defined much of the region extended on both sides of the Danube and undermined its suitability as a barrier against north-south migration. Second, the dated and inaccurate ethnographic tropes that the Romans used to categorize the various “barbarian” peoples who lived beyond the river led them to make disastrous policy decisions when confronting groups such as the Tervingi Goths or Huns, whose behavior did not align with expectations. Roman blindness to the environmental realities of the Danube watershed and the actual characteristics of the people who occupied the region, especially during late antiquity, ultimately led to the destruction of the limes system.

auditPapers.title: Rachel Gross. Shopping All the Way to the Woods: How the Outdoor Industry Sold Nature to America
auditPapers.abstract: Rachel Gross opens her book Shopping All the Way to the Woods: How the Outdoor Industry Sold Nature to America with a short tale of her adventure spending a year hiking across four continents. With no real camping experience, she did what many Americans do when preparing for such a venture into the outdoors, she went shopping. Outfitted with what she believed was the correct clothing and equipment, she hit the trails, only to discover that she was far from the expert her gear made her appear. Gross masterfully places this paradoxical mixture of consumerism and identity at the center of her study of the outdoor industry and how it, over the course of the past century and half, has sold the idea of nature to the American public. Over nine tightly written chapters, Gross traces how outdoor equipment, and clothing in particular, shaped Americans’ views of both nature and of their own identity through consumerism, as well as the outdoor industry’s evolution from a small cottage industry into a powerful global economic force.

auditPapers.title: Charmian Mansell. Female Servants in Early Modern England
auditPapers.abstract: It is fitting that one of the central themes of Female Servants in Early Modern England is labor, since the book itself is the product of painstaking archival research described by its author as “needle in a haystack work” (297). Mining the records of nearly nine thousand legal actions before church courts across five dioceses in southwest England between 1532 and 1649, Charmian Mansell recovers the experiences of the largest sample of female servants yet considered in the study of women’s work in early modern England. The book’s chief contention—that service in early modern England was neither the static nor the stable institution described by prescriptive sources and by generations of historians—is persuasively argued and meticulously supported by qualitative and quantitative analysis, the latter yielding thirty-four tables that catalog female servants’ ages, work activities, relationships, movements, and much more. Mansell’s findings contribute to the historiographies of gender, marriage, patriarchy, work, and memory and have significant implications for the way scholars understand the early modern economy both within and beyond the household.

auditPapers.title: Jessica Marie Otis. By the Numbers: Numeracy, Religion, and the Quantitative Transformation of Early Modern England
auditPapers.abstract: “Numbers were a socially pervasive technology of knowledge,” writes Jessica Marie Otis in By the Numbers, “with the power to shape modes of thought” (158). Yet one of the key points of this excellent book is that numbers were no more a single technology than mills. As Otis carefully shows, the use of numbers was complex, multifaceted, and dynamic, involving a number (so to speak) of techniques; tools; media; and social, cultural, and intellectual commitments. Reading this book, one quickly begins to wonder whether numeracy itself is too broad and too blunt a concept to have much purchase in any such fine-grained historical analysis of early modern ideas and practices of counting, measuring, calculating, or recording. Like the “quantifying spirit” that haunts many studies of these topics but is not conjured here, it encompasses too much and explains too little. Otis, for her part, uses the introduction to make the case for “recogniz[ing] early modern English numeracies, plural, within the overarching formula of early modern numeracy, singular” (10). Important to this case is a set of distinctions maintained throughout the book between the various linked but separately moving parts that “numeracy” tends to collapse: numbers as symbolic systems, numerical practices, mathematical education, and the wider, dynamic contexts of literacy and communications technology. The first chapter enriches this immensely via an in-depth survey of different systems, from performative systems of hand-counting and oral numeration through object-based systems involving slates, tally sticks, and counting boards (lovingly explored and explained here), through to written systems, including number words and Roman and Arabic numerals.

auditPapers.title: David Cowan. Politics of the Past: Inter-war Memories and the Making of British Popular Politics, 1939–2009
auditPapers.abstract: How can we trace the histories of stories? This excellent monograph by David Cowan charts how the memories, histories, and stories of the interwar period in Britain have been shaped and have influenced politics and society since. Politics of the Past brings together history, politics, and the family in new and fascinating ways, making several important contributions to the field of modern British history. There are three key points made by the book: that stories have a history that must be interrogated; that politics is an everyday practice made in conversations between family members, workmates, and friends; and bringing those two points together—that the twentieth century was by no means a period of increasing political apathy, but one in which individuals were often deeply engaged in political matters. By looking beyond political parties and other institutions and instead delving into the intimate spaces of the family, Cowan shows a different way of thinking about individual politics. The home and family, as he puts it, “facilitated forms of political thinking rooted in everyday discussions” (103). Cowan forges an approach of not only bringing together but also better understanding the “reciprocal relationship between family and politics” (10). Through reused social research materials, Cowan gives many fascinating examples of how “recollections became mutual productions between family members” (153). It’s a convincing argument: that politics is less what happens in debates between MPs but is what is thrashed out, argued about, between relatives and friends, between different generations, over kitchen tables.

auditPapers.title: Matthew Rowley. Godly Violence in the Puritan Atlantic World, 1636–1676
auditPapers.abstract: Between the outbreak of the Pequot War in the mid-1630s and the conclusion of King Philip’s War four decades later, Puritans on both sides of the Atlantic perpetrated more than their fair share of violence. By the end of the 17th century, Native Americans, English royalists, Irish Catholics, and Scots Presbyterians had all experienced firsthand the brutality of which hot Protestants were capable when they unsheathed their swords. Matthew Rowley’s new monograph, Godly Violence in the Puritan Atlantic World, asks how this violence was justified and seeks to uncover the complex processes by which the godly imposed providential meaning on their experiences of warfare. If all Christians in the 17th century could agree that God spoke through dramatic military events, what exactly was he saying? Which biblical and theological resources were enlisted to help interpret the divine messages that were spelled out in blood? These are undoubtedly important questions, not least since historians over the past few decades have demonstrated just how central providentialism was to political decision-making during the 1640s and 1650s. After an opening section setting out the book’s structure and methodological approach, Godly Violence shows how Puritans went about establishing when conflict was legitimate and outlines some of the problems they contended with when doing so. As well as confronting countless New Testament injunctions to peace, charity, and mercy, the godly were consistently discomforted by the multivalence of providence. Was God on the side of victors in battle? Or was he merely using them as instruments to admonish his chosen, sinful people? Almost any event could be—and was—read as evidence of God’s continued favor. The Presbyterian minister Edward Gee recognized after the Battle of Dunbar in 1650 that each side would interpret the result “as the respective quarrel of each unto them hath led them” (182). However, there was also a broader Protestant anxiety about Christians claiming divine inspiration when taking up arms. Hence, as Rowley shows clearly, most Protestant theologians were eager to argue that a holy war was a just war and vice versa. Parliamentarians in the 1640s claimed that their campaign against the king was both defensive—and therefore just—and supported by the dictates of scripture and providence.

auditPapers.title: Iryna Vushko. Lost Fatherland: Europeans between Empire and Nation-States, 1867–1939
auditPapers.abstract: Lost Fatherland: Europeans between Empire and Nation-States, 1867–1939 is a broad tableau of lives and political-ideological lineages stemming from Habsburg Austria—dissolved in 1918 after it lost the First World War—to its successor states: Italy, Yugoslavia, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and Soviet Ukraine. Iryna Vushko selected twenty politicians of various convictions and nationalities, whose life trajectories following the collapse and during the development of the successor states reflect, she argues, important continuities of what was once the empire. In this regard, Vushko’s book is undoubtedly and admittedly part of a larger trend of reevaluation. Unlike classic national narratives, Lost Fatherland—together with works by Pieter Judson, Dominique Reill, Natasha Wheatley, Kamil Ruszala, Máté Rigó, Judit Pál, and Vald Popovici, to name a few—argues that Austria-Hungary’s successor states were not created in opposition to the empire’s legacy. Rather, the heritage of Austria-Hungary had a positive influence on how its successors were organized and how they operated.

auditPapers.title: Priscilla McCutcheon, Latrica E. Best, and Theresa Rajack-Talley, eds. Beyond the Kitchen Table: Black Women and Global Food Systems
auditPapers.abstract: Beyond the Kitchen Table: Black Women and Global Food Systems, edited by Priscilla McCutcheon, Latrica E. Best, and Theresa Rajack-Talley, provides an in-depth examination of Black women’s roles in global food systems. In this volume, Black women’s lived experiences are the prism through which food justice, food security, and sustainable agricultural practices are evaluated and understood. The chapters of this book collectively articulate the intersections of the personal and political dimensions of food systems. This book draws on interdisciplinary research methods to amplify Black women’s often-overlooked voices and contributions to global food systems. This book is structured into three distinct parts: “From the Fields,” “Food and Social Justice,” and “Food Security, Health, and Well-Being.” These sections examine themes of labor, justice, and health and highlight the interconnectedness of race, gender, and socioeconomics. Each section illuminates women’s pivotal roles in simultaneously shaping food systems and addressing systemic inequities that have historically marginalized their contributions.

auditPapers.title: Sanjay Subrahmanyam. Across the Green Sea: Histories from the Western Indian Ocean, 1440–1640
auditPapers.abstract: Sanjay Subrahmanyam’s Across the Green Sea studies the western Indian Ocean’s maritime-terrestrial space through polycentric views from different spatial units. The book juxtaposes a set of analytical incisions to discuss interstate relationships, political economy, social history, and cosmopolitanism in the western Indian Ocean from the 15th to the 17th century. There could be many readings of this book. My review explores how these incisions read together. The book’s approach is of connected histories—a methodology Subrahmanyam outlined in other works—whose crucial aspect is to grasp whether our current geographies are fit for our research questions. Drawing on the approach of French historian Jean Aubin, Subrahmanyam stresses the need to interrogate a wide gamut of European and non-European sources to study the western Indian Ocean. We might imagine this book as analogous to a musical polyphony, where multiple counterpoints produce a harmonic texture. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss interstate systems, political legitimacy, and transition in the western Indian Ocean between the 15th and 16th centuries, and ramifications of Portuguese violence on its political economy. Symbolic political legitimacy, a contentious issue in the 15th century, saw the Mamluks and the Timurids competing for control over the Kaaba’s rituals. Then, the Ottomans defeated the Safavids and the Mamluks and dispatched victory bulletins to western Indian Ocean powers including Gujarat, while the Portuguese Estado da India regularly attacked western Indian Ocean shipping and changed the scale of violence. Chapter 2 analyzes an Arabic text, Kitab Nail al-muna, produced by the Islamic scholar Jarullah ibn Fahd al-Makki (d. 1547), which described the impact of the 1530s Gujarati-Portuguese struggle in the Hijaz: The local Ottoman officials and the Ottoman top brass extorted the Gujarati court elite seeking refuge in Mecca during Bahadur Shah’s conflict with the Portuguese. The episode culminated in an unsuccessful Ottoman expedition against the Portuguese. So, Subrahmanyam argues, the complexity of the western Indian Ocean’s political balance in the early 16th century needs further consideration.

auditPapers.title: Ruth Larsen, Alice Marples, and Matthew McCormack, eds. Innovations in Teaching History: Eighteenth-Century Studies in Higher Education.
auditPapers.abstract: Innovations in Teaching History: Eighteenth-­Century Studies in Higher Education consists of collected contributions from nine UK and Australian-based specialists of Britain’s “long eighteenth century” (1688–1832). Given these geographical and temporal origins, the question arises: Should this book find a wider readership with the audience of the AHR? The answer is a resounding yes. When allowances for the educational terminology unique to the UK are made, readers will find that the lessons offered here have a wide and general application. A strength of this collection is that the contributions take the form of self-reflective accounts of a single experience in course design. This is a universal experience for history teachers, and it is here enhanced by the restraint the authors show in not descending into excessive detail about the century that they love. The focus instead has been on presenting clear narratives of course design and outcomes assessment. Thematically, the volume is structured to address digital history, student-centered learning, and material culture. All contributors take advantage of the eighteenth century’s unique positioning with respect to the ­digital archive—that is, that the extent of archival digitization, and the accessibility of those collections to students, is perhaps greater than for most periods.

auditPapers.title: Laura Frances Goffman. Disorder and Diagnosis: Health and the Politics of Everyday Life in Modern Arabia
auditPapers.abstract: In Disorder and Diagnosis: Health and the Politics of Everyday Life in Modern Arabia, Laura Frances Goffman offers a social and political history of how medicine, disease, and public health transformed the Arabian Peninsula and the Persian Gulf from the late 19th century until the 1973 oil boom: A behemoth undertaking, but not unsurmountable. The book is structured into six chapters, each exploring key themes through specific institutional or social settings: contagion, hospitals, childbirth, experiments, nurses, and folk medicine. Goffman’s research draws on a range of archival collections in India, Kuwait, the United States, and the United Kingdom, as well as online repositories, such as the Indian Foreign Office Records via the Qatar Digital Library and the Arabian Gulf Digital Archive. Early chapters focus on quarantine stations, hospitals, and childbirth practices, demonstrating how British and US medical interventions sought to define and regulate health. Quarantine stations, positioned within the framework of empire, exemplify the imposition of sanitary controls that sought to discipline bodies in transit, while the latter chapters showcase spaces of contested authority, where missionary doctors, regional experts, and local communities negotiated medical practice and gendered access to care. Hospitals, for example, contrast the quarantine stations discussed in earlier chapters to show how “ordinary people . . . played a powerful role in institutionalizing modern health services” (54). ­­Nonetheless, Goffman highlights how the persistence of home childbirth despite missionary efforts to medicalize the ­­process underscores the limits of institutional authority while showcasing the agency of local women.

auditPapers.title: Jane Webster. Materializing the Middle Passage: A Historical Archaeology of British Slave Shipping, 1680–1807
auditPapers.abstract: The year 2023 was good for historians of Britain’s Atlantic slave trade. It saw the publication of two important studies that have deepened and extended our knowledge of that grisly commerce. Jane Webster’s Materializing the Middle Passage is one of them. It is a handsomely produced volume that synthesizes an extensive literature in a clear, confident fashion. It should be read alongside Nicholas Radburn’s landmark Traders in Men: Merchants and the Transformation of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2023), which provides a bold overview of how British merchants ruthlessly streamlined the trafficking of Africans in the 18th century. Webster details the material underpinning of that transformation. She loses no time in laying her theoretical cards on the table. She does not see the Middle Passage as an instance of “social death” that “stripped transported Africans of their culture and identity” (12). Nor does she view the slave ship as “a conduit by which African ethnicities were transferred, virtually unmodified, to the Americas” (12). Following the lead of Stephanie E. Smallwood, whose book Saltwater Slavery: A Middle Passage from Africa to American Diaspora appeared in 2007, she invokes instead a “mid-Atlantic creolization” (12). Webster argues that the shipboard experience of enslaved Africans was formative.

auditPapers.title: Henry Reece. The Fall: Last Days of the English Republic
auditPapers.abstract: Henry Reece’s The Fall seeks to explain the end of the republican period of English history, between the death of Oliver Cromwell in September 1658 and the proclamation of Charles II as King in May 1660. As these basic details suggest, the fall of the English republic and the restoration of the monarchy were dramatic and profound political developments that occurred suddenly and stunned many contemporary observers. This is in many ways the first book to take on as a distinct research topic the difficulty of explaining why England’s only experiment with non-­monarchical government came to such an abrupt and dramatic end. A different historian writing nearly two decades after the publication of William H. Sewell’s Logics of History and similar works might have approached the task of accounting for the fall of the republic by asking whether it was a Sewellian event in which an important structural transformation occurred, thereby avoiding the false dilemma between structure and agency present in both structuralist narratives of inevitability and histories premised on strong individual agency. Such a historian might have begun by delving systematically into the difficult but fascinating question of whether the revolutionary regime ever existed on a structural or institutional foundation, a question with implications for the nature of the regime’s downfall.

auditPapers.title: Corey Ross. Liquid Empire: Water and Power in the Colonial World
auditPapers.abstract: Liquid Empire is a wide-ranging and sweeping book covering the length and breadth of European colonial engagement with water. In Corey Ross’s words, the book tries to tell “the intertwined stories of water and Europe’s modern imperial enterprise” (6). Ross attempts to bring together what he labels terra-acques histories of the European empire across irrigation schemes, hydropower, fisheries, urban waterworks, navigation, floods, land reclamation, and groundwater exploitation, among other colonial technologies of improvement. When taken together, the imprint of European empire, technology, and power becomes apparent, and to bring together these disparate histories is no easy task, but one that Ross accomplishes in a complex yet highly readable account. The core argument of the book shows how colonialism was as exploitative as it was contradictory, frail, and yet also a remarkably resilient system that lived well past its official end date. Ross places water and hydro-systems at the center of European empires, emphasizing connectedness, both of water as a substance and colonialism as a project at large across geographies. As Ross notes, a 200-year sweep requires generalizations, and in this sense one can think of this book as a critical rethinking of classic works such as Daniel Headrick’s Tools of Empire (1981), but where the frailties of empire and the materialities of nature are as important as the power exerted by European imperialism.

auditPapers.title: Kevin Padraic Donnelly. The Descent of Artificial Intelligence: A Deep History of an Idea 400 Years in the Making.
auditPapers.abstract: Despite its title, The Descent of Artificial Intelligence is not really about what we think of today as AI. The author, an intellectual historian whose previous book was a study of influential nineteenth-century Belgian ­­statistician Adolphe Quetelet, is instead concerned with “the descent of the idea of artificial intelligence” (259, emphasis mine). The real focus of this genealogy is on constructions of human intelligence and agency that have “reduce[d] the complex thought and behavior of human beings to a level where they might be studied by a variety of tools and methodologies ­borrowed from the natural sciences.” In other words, this is not a history of computing technology or information theory, but rather of the preconditions for believing that thinking machines or artificial intelligence (AI) are possible or desirable. Over the course of nine chapters divided into three historical acts, Kevin Padraic Donnelly carefully traces a trajectory of mechanical and mathematical reasoning from 17th-century natural philosophers like René Descartes and Isaac Newton (Part I), through debates about education and social values in the French Enlightenment and post-revolutionary France (Part II), and into the construction of nineteenth- and twentieth-­­century approaches to the “sciences of man” grounded in positivism, quantification, and statistical prediction (Part III). The central argument of the book is that, ever since Descartes famously suggested that living beings are machines, a tension has existed between mechanical and mathematical accounts of human intelligence and behavior—a “geometric spirit”—and those who emphasize the inherent complexity and irreducibility of human thinking and action.

auditPapers.title: Esther Elizabeth Adaire. Neo-Nazi Postmodern: Right-Wing Terror Tactics, the Intellectual New Right, and the Destabilization of Memory in Germany since 1989
auditPapers.abstract: Imagine a young neo-Nazi in the early 1990s—likely with shaved hair and wearing a bomber jacket, maybe sitting on an overturned beer crate in a depressing prefab building deep in the East German countryside, now a makeshift youth club—eagerly reading Discipline and Punish to wash away his worries about ­raging unemployment and national humiliation. A bit too far-fetched? Maybe not, if we follow the arguments that Esther Elizabeth Adaire develops in her book Neo-Nazi Postmodern. Does the notion of a hostile takeover of postmodern theory by the far-right help us better understand the massive political shifts of the last years? This important book aims to explore these intellectual connections, linking them to a broader story about the transnational rise of right-wing politics during the last forty years. The seemingly endless comparisons of rising ­populism—in the shape of US Trumpism or the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Germany—with the fall of the Weimar Republic and the rise of National Socialism have, as Adaire argues, dominated the reflections of journalists and historians. Consequently, they often disregard lesser-known histories of radical right-wing thought, organization, and action after 1945. At the same time, the myths of a successful “Peaceful Revolution” and an altogether seamless unification of Germany obscured what went wrong after 1989. It is precisely at this intersection that Adaire’s study examines the recent history of German right-wing radi­calism, populism, and terrorism.

auditPapers.title: Sugata Bose. Asia After Europe: Imagining a Continent in the Long Twentieth Century.
auditPapers.abstract: This is a heartfelt and thought-provoking book by a distinguished scholar of South Asian and Indian Ocean history. It shows how some of the best minds in East, South, and West Asia imagined “Asia as an abstract entity transcending the imperial and national frontiers … [that were] etched by colonial powers onto the physical and mental maps of the colonized” (3). It tracks the “intersecting journey of Asian intellectuals and subalterns alike” to ask under what conditions a distinctively non-European idea of Asia and Asian solidarity was “forged” and then, unfortunately, “fractured” (6). Sugata Bose emphasizes that for many Asians, the continent of Asia was far more than a mere product of western cartographic invention. Instead, it was a creative space infused with emotion. In other words, this book is about how, if Europeans imagined Asia as a space—a cartographic invention—many Asian intellectuals imagined it as a place. Bose argues that against significant odds, Asian intellectuals like Rabindranath Tagore, Benoy Kumar Sarkar, Okakura Tenshin, Yone Noguchi, Yokoyama Taikan, Ananda Commarasamy, Xu Beihong, and Liang Qichao—to name just a few—tried to realize an Asia that was radically different from European ideals of nationalism, unitary sovereignty, and regionalism. These imaginings were developed as part of a shared network of interactions that was not mediated by Europe. It is perhaps not important that the lofty ideals of this strand of Asianism failed to materialize. Indeed, Bose recognizes how the complicated relationship between Japan and China and China and India made such solidarities difficult to sustain. But what is important is that some of Asia’s finest minds spent considerable time and energy conceptualizing an Asianism based on principles of “Asian universalism”—an idea I wish was unpacked more explicitly in the book. One of Bose’s central contentions is that if a notion of a European or Western identity could survive the mayhem of the two world wars, then ­­Japanese imperialism and Chinese and Indian expansionism, too, should not mean that in the future, a larger Asian identity based putatively on Asian ideals cannot be forged. I am convinced by this argument. In fact, I would venture to say that it is this point—that Asian solidarity is possible and plausible even in the age of inter-Asian national conflicts, as long as Asians try to (re)activate non-­­European or precolonial modes of Asian universalism—is the most significant argument of this important book. Whether one agrees whether non-­­European, precolonial, or Asian universalism is imaginable or desirable is beside the point.

auditPapers.title: Dorit Brixius. Creolised Science: Knowledge in the Eighteenth-Century Indo-Pacific.
auditPapers.abstract: Dorit Brixius’s Creolised Science places the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius at the center of an analysis of how plants were transported and transplanted across the Francophone Indo-Pacific. Brixius succeeds in decentering French science by demonstrating that the quest for useful or profitable plants to cultivate on Mauritius extended from Madagascar to China and island Southeast Asia, and relied on experts ranging from Southeast Asian plant collectors to enslaved expert gardeners from Réunion and India. The book is based on extensive archival research, demonstrating one of the author’s key arguments; that the agency of diverse actors is best revealed through unpublished records. Mauritius was under French control from 1721, following a period of Dutch occupation. The island was originally administered by the Compagnie française pour le commerce des Indes orientales and became a possession of the French crown in 1763. French ambitions for the island ranged from using it as a naval base to support Pondicherry against British rivals in India, to a plantation that would break into the Dutch stranglehold on the nutmeg and clove trade from the Maluku Islands. These aspirations often clashed with the practical needs of the settlers in Mauritius to feed themselves and the large numbers of enslaved people, who came from Madagascar and East Africa, with smaller numbers from West Africa and South and Southeast Asia.

auditPapers.title: Langston Hughes. I Wonder as I Wander: An Autobiographical Journey.
auditPapers.abstract: The first volume of Langston Hughes’s memoir The Big Sea (1940) may be more widely known, but I Wonder as I Wander (1956) is its indispensable second half. Across eight gripping chapters, Hughes—that great American poet and scion of the Harlem Renaissance—recounts his wide-ranging international travels during the 1930s, when the world was sliding toward catastrophe. This kind of nonfiction belongs to a distinctive genre of memoir writing that thrived between the world wars: autobiographical travelogues by foreign correspondents and other globetrotting intellectuals who raced to bring first-person glimpses of faraway conflicts to the reading public. Recently, similar work by Hughes’s white American contemporaries, such as Dorothy Thompson and John Gunther, have drawn extensive interest from historians. Yet written by a Black social commentator, and written in retrospect, on the other side of World War II and amid an accelerating civil rights movement and a Cold War–era Red Scare, I Wonder as I Wander in many ways exceeds the bounds of the genre and emerges as a much more interesting and layered source.

auditPapers.title: José Antonio Piqueras. Derecho antiguo y esclavitud moderna: Los esclavos, la ley y la justicia entre Europa y el imperio español de América
auditPapers.abstract: José Antonio Piqueras skillfully captures the reader’s attention with the title Derecho antiguo y esclavitud moderna. With polished precision, he formulates the subtitle: Los esclavos, la ley y la justicia entre Europa y el imperio español de América. This work can be viewed as a continuation of his book La esclavitud en las Españas: Un lazo transatlántico (2011); interrelated, both aim to reveal the reality of slavery in Spanish America, which sharply contradicts and disproves the official narrative. In Derecho antiguo y esclavitud moderna, the author expands his analysis to include the experiences of Indigenous people, who, while being protected as subjects of the Crown in discourse, were also subjected to slavery in practice. He also addresses the official disregard for the transatlantic slave trade that continued until the nineteenth century. Piqueras presents the ancient phenomenon of slavery in its entirety and temporality as the first form of appropriation of the labor capacity of others through the appropriation of the person, approaching the history of slavery not as a continuous narrative but rather as a fabric that undergoes continuous moments, ruptures, jumps, and recoveries, where slavery experiences phases of revitalization following phases of decline. He highlights that in the former phase, history was utilized to legitimize the new forms of domination, while in the latter, abolitionists believed slavery had ceased to correspond to the changing spirit of the age.

auditPapers.title: Javier Fernández-Galeano. Maricas: Queer Cultures and State Violence in Argentina and Spain, 1942–1982
auditPapers.abstract: Maricas: Queer Cultures and State Violence in Argentina and Spain, 1942–1982, by the brilliant historian Javier Fernández-Galeano, covers queer cultures and state violence in Argentina and Spain in the second half of the 20th century and fills a gap in the historiography of LGBTQ+ people. National studies on these topics in Argentina and Spain already exist, but there was not yet a comparative study that included both countries. In this sense, Maricas is a welcome addition to the literature, but it will also be appreciated by a wider readership who may be interested in Spanish and Argentine LGBTQ+ cultures because the book is written in a pleasant and accessible style. Maricas also has an almost iconic cover design by artist Miguel de Molina, which will certainly help make this book a classic. The word maricas refers to working-class men who adopted a feminine attitude in their interactions in the queer subcultures of these spaces, which stood in contrast to the entendidos who tended to come from the wealthier upper classes of society and who did not adopt a feminine attitude, but rather the opposite. Based on Fernández-Galeano’s dissertation, this book uses a wide variety of sources, including correspondence, memoirs, and interviews, as well as judicial, police, medical, military, and literary records. However, the author acknowledges varied access to research sources in Argentina and Spain. For example, there were significant differences in the judicial archives of the vagrancy courts in Spain and the judicial records available in Argentina, located at the Classification Institute. Similarly, the military archives in Argentina are kept in a civilian archive because of projects to clarify the role of the army in crimes against humanity, while in Spain, these archives are held at military bases. Fernández-Galeano relates how the colonel in charge of a base archive he visited did not show much interest in assisting with access to sources related to the subject matter. Fernández-Galeano shows monumental work in archives on both sides of the Atlantic, in spite of the peculiarities of each country. In this sense, the archival research is outstanding.

auditPapers.title: Juan F. Cobo Betancourt. The Coming of the Kingdom: The Muisca, Catholic Reform, and Spanish Colonialism in the New Kingdom of Granada
auditPapers.abstract: This insightful book explores a crucial aspect of Spain’s early colonialism: the Christianization of Indigenous communities in its overseas territories. Using the Muisca—inhabitants of the central highlands of New Granada (roughly present-day Colombia)—as a case study, the author sheds light on a colonial region often overlooked in historical narratives, especially compared to the better-documented areas of Mexico and Peru. These regions are frequently seen as models for the Spanish colonial project, an assumption that this book challenges. Focusing on the century following the first encounters between Spaniards and the Muisca, the study spans from the 1530s to the 1650s. During this period, particularly in the early seventeenth century, colonial officials, religious leaders, and Jesuit missionaries launched an ambitious reform effort aimed at Christianizing the Indigenous population, a process thoroughly examined in The Coming of the Kingdom. Drawing from a wide array of sources—including correspondence, ecclesiastical reports, petitions, legislation, legal documents, and related materials—found in archives and libraries both in Colombia and abroad (Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom, and the United States), the book traces the complex dynamics of Christianization. Cobo Betancourt reveals this process to be coercive yet deeply negotiated, contested, contingent, and uneven. Despite its shortcomings and obstacles, the Christianization effort was persistent, closely tied to Spain’s identity as a newly unified kingdom and reinforced by its use of Christian evangelization to justify the conquest, occupation, and control of colonial territories, with legal backing from the papacy. The preservation of Catholic orthodoxy in colonial enclaves was an additional driving force.

auditPapers.title: Oz Frankel. Coca-Cola, Black Panthers, and Phantom Jets: Israel in the American Orbit, 1967–1973.
auditPapers.abstract: Oz Frankel’s book Coca-Cola, Black Panthers, and Phantom Jets: Israel in the American Orbit, 1967–1973 is a sprawling and exciting work of social, economic, and political history. The breadth of topics to which the unwieldy title gestures is a mere fraction of what Frankel manages to cover in the nearly 400 pages of smart and engaging prose. Frankel delivers a keen, critical, and affectionate take on the themes of consumerism, race and ethnicity, and what he calls “ambivalence and resistance” (10), the latter being represented by fears over “being drawn too far, too quickly into the American orbit” (11). Included among the many topics are things and people both delightful (the all-Hebrew version of Fiddler on the Roof, professional basketball) and hateful (the racist ideologue and founder of the Kach party and movement, Meir Kahane, the prejudicial treatment encountered by the Black Hebrew Israelites). Certainly, the 1960s and early 1970s was a fertile period for Israel adopting US cultural reference points. On the heels of Israel’s stunning victory in the Six-Day War (1967), Israelis were primed to consider new ways of living. The Yom Kippur War (1973), which concludes the formal period under investigation in Frankel’s book, represented a failure of imagination (Israel’s security establishment was under the spell of what became known by analysts as the conceptzia—a false conception of their enemies’ resolve and capabi­­lities to try to undo what Israel had gained in 1967). The months after the Six-Day War was also when France turned away from Israel, and the United States became its main arms supplier. All this solidified what we today call the Israeli-American “special relationship.”

auditPapers.title: Omar Valerio-Jiménez. Remembering Conquest: Mexican Americans, Memory, and Citizenship
auditPapers.abstract: In his new book Remembering Conquest, Omar Valerio-Jiménez powerfully illuminates how the US-Mexico War (1846–1848) and the dispossessions, displacements, and disenfranchisements that colored life for Mexican Americans in the postwar era are not distant historical events but living legacies that persist in contemporary struggles. In turn, he effectively argues how the war’s conquest, as part of ongoing colonial structures, continues to shape the identities, livelihoods, and citizenship rights of Mexican Americans. While this argument may not be entirely new to scholars and students of Mexican American and Chicana/o Studies, Valerio-Jiménez innovatively and effectively explores this argument through a rigorous analysis of collective memories of the US-Mexico War across multiple generations of Mexican Americans since 1848. To do so, he examines, among many other sources, transnational oral histories, Spanish and English language newspapers, and political organizations on both sides of the border, searching for alternative war memories. These memories, he shows, urgently challenge official narratives on the US-Mexico War and the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo that ended this conflict. In doing so, Remembering Conquest offers a remarkably comprehensive cultural and intellectual history on the politics of memory as it pertains to the US-Mexico War. The book’s driving concern, however, is not simply how Mexican Americans have remembered this war in shared, distinct, and varied ways; perhaps most importantly, it is concerned with “the role of collective memories in processing the trauma of war and fomenting social transformation through political involvement” (8). The book therefore importantly adds to the wealth of literature on the US-Mexico War, the many (deliberate) failures of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, and the living history of Mexican American political organizing in response to these failures.

auditPapers.title: Robin Bernstein. Freeman’s Challenge: The Murder that Shook America’s Original Prison for Profit
auditPapers.abstract: Robin Bernstein’s book, Freeman’s Challenge, centers on the life of William Freeman, an Afro-native man who lived in Auburn, New York, from the 1820s to the 1840s and served a prison sentence there. Its ten chapters are organized into three sections. The first section introduces readers to Freeman. We learn that his parents struggled with alcohol abuse, that he stole chickens as a child, and was later found with a stolen horse in a nearby town. As an alibi, the then sixteen-year-old said that he had been sent on an errand with the horse by a man named Jack Furman, a fellow Black resident of Auburn. Authorities cross-examined Furman and ultimately believed the latter’s testimony. Young Freeman was subsequently held in the nearby Cayuga County jail to await trial, but he escaped with another inmate before it commenced. This probably contributed to the longer-than-usual sentence he received after his capture: five years in Auburn State Penitentiary.

auditPapers.title: Anne Berg. Empire of Rags and Bones: Waste and War in Nazi Germany
auditPapers.abstract: Anne Berg’s rich new monograph, Empire of Rags and Bones: Waste and War in Nazi Germany, provides readers with a unique perspective on the relationship between waste, race, destruction, and environment in Nazi Germany. Focusing on the period from the introduction of the Four-Year Plan in 1936 to the Allied ­liberation of the camps in 1945, Berg traces the evolution and violence of the Nazi regime. She boldly claims, “The Nazi Empire was a waste regime,” and then ­clarifies that it developed an economic rationale ­linking waste utilization, or recycling, and internal purging (3). In doing so, Berg connects Nazi policies about reducing and reusing waste for economic ­purposes—and to achieve autarky—to racial policies that sought to eliminate undesirable populations from Germany or German-occupied territory. Empire of Rags and Bones highlights the materiality of death and destruction in the Third Reich by illuminating the using and reusing of waste in the search for a “zero-waste,” or closed circuit, economy. Berg contends that the “alignment of racial and economic fanaticism took time, practice, and war” and altered physical environments across Europe (36).

auditPapers.title: Tapati Guha-Thakurta and Vazira Zamindar, eds. How Secular Is Art? On the Politics of Art, History, and Religion in South Asia
auditPapers.abstract: How Secular Is Art? brings together thirteen essays that probe the subject of secularity by looking at “the politics of art, history, and religion in South Asia,” as is stated in the book’s subtitle. In their introductory essay, Tapati Guha-Thakurta and Vazira Zamindar write that the book aims to “[chase] the secular as a shadow as it moves and lingers across the modern worlds of art and architecture, monuments and icons, in the Indian subcontinent” (9). The introduction situates the book’s genesis and publication between a conference at Brown in 2018 and the aftermath of the CAA-NRC protests in India in 2019, which urgently foregrounded issues of the secular, secularism, and secularizing in the Indian political sphere. Indeed, Akeel Bilgrami’s essay in part 1 (“Secularity and Its Art”) offers a definition of these three terms—secular, secularism, secularizing—and lays a foundation for the book. Secularism, as Bilgrami explains it, comes with three commitments: (a) a commitment to the freedom of religion; (b) a commitment to certain fundamental constitutional rights that neither mention religion nor opposition to religion; (c) a third commitment in which if commitments (a) and (b) were to come in conflict, commitment (b) would be given greater weight (36). Secularization is the process through which a society transforms into the secular; implicit in such a transformation is the decentering of belief systems and cultural practices associated with religion(s). The secular, to put it inversely, is the outcome of secularization, or as Bilgrami writes, the secular is something “to have come out from under the shadow of religion” (39). Already in the first two essays, the secular is cast as a “shadow”—and in a roundabout way, the book reveals its main subject to be religion: the thing that is casting the shadow. The book is thus asking the parallel question: How religious is art (in South Asia today)?

auditPapers.title: Nathaniel Mathews. Zanzibar Was a Country: Exile and Citizenship Between East Africa and the Gulf.
auditPapers.abstract: Zanzibar Was a Country is the best book written on Zanzibar political history in over a decade. Beyond that, this work clearly has larger implications for other histories by enriching historians’ understanding of diverse subjects such as identity, diaspora, memory, and the interplay between decolonization and national belonging in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Nathaniel Mathews tells the story of the muwalladūn, individuals of mixed Arab and African descent who were born in the Zanzibar Protectorate but who were forced to flee in the wake of the 1964 Zanzibar Revolution. Before the arrival of the British, the isles were ruled by an Omani Arab dynasty; when the British departed in December 1963, they left in place a constitutional monarchy that was quickly overthrown in a bloody revolution a month later by African nationalists who deposed the sultan and incited an anti-Arab pogrom. Mathews chronicles the lives of these exiles from the years leading up to the revolution until the present day. While parts of this narrative have been told by scholars of both East Africa and Oman, such as James Brennan and Abdel Razzaq Takriti, respectively, Mathews is the first scholar to center this history on the diasporic Zanzibaris themselves and comprehensively tell the story from their perspective—a retelling only made possible by Mathews’s mastery of both Arabic and Kiswahili, allowing him to draw on the rich source materials from both languages and regions. In the process, he has illumined the complicated phenomena of the untangling of empires and the re-entanglement of peoples across postcolonial borders.

auditPapers.title: Robert Shea Terrell. A Nation Fermented: Beer, Bavaria, and the Making of Modern Germany.
auditPapers.abstract: Beer and German culture are closely linked in the ­popular imagination, both in Germany and abroad. ­Robert Terrell’s book A Nation Fermented explores the social construction of “German beer” and its changing ­cultural meaning since the late nineteenth century. The study builds on recent interest in commodity ­histories and the transnational history of brewing, but Terrell focuses on the political and cultural significance afforded to the beverage in an effort to write “a history of [modern] Germany revealed through beer” (4). In particular, he asks about the role of regional Bavarian influences in shaping German debates on beer and broader perceptions of Germany in the twentieth century. In doing so, Terrell contributes to an important strand in the current historiography of modern ­Germany, which seeks to understand the nation through its “provincialism” and regional diversity. Contemporary German understandings of what should count as proper beer, Terrell contends, were shaped prominently by Bavarian actors. Indeed, Bavarian-style lagers became popular across the nation during the second half of the nineteenth century, and while beer production grew in many regions, Bavarians led the nation in per capita consumption and production. In contrast to large industrial brewing concerns further north, the Bavarian brewing industry long remained decentralized with many smaller breweries. In addition, Bavaria early on codified the traditional Reinheitsgebot (a beer purity regulation dating back to the fifteenth century), which stipulated that beer could only be brewed with four ingredients: water, malted barley, hops, and yeast. The possible inclusion of additives such as sugar would become a bone of contention between Bavarian brewers and those further north throughout the twentieth century, particularly in times of shortages induced by crisis and war.

auditPapers.title: Don H. Doyle. The Age of Reconstruction: How Lincoln’s New Birth of Freedom Remade the World
auditPapers.abstract: Rumors of US diplomats “negotiating with Denmark over the sale of Greenland” and Canada “peacefully and cheerfully” joining the United States might sound exclusively like a fever dream of the ­twenty-first century (117–18). These anecdotes, however, appear in Don H. Doyle’s account of how many Europeans interpreted the United States’ purchase of Alaska from ­Russia in 1867 as betokening a rising tide of republicanism in the Western hemisphere and beyond that followed the US Civil War. A sequel to Doyle’s The Cause of All Nations: An International History of the American Civil War (2014), this book ­considers the international dimensions of a period in US history that until recently was most often discussed and taught within a purely national frame. Like most scholars of Reconstruction for half a century and more, Doyle acknowledges his indebtedness to W. E. B. Du Bois, suggesting that this present book is merely an outworking of Du Bois’s intuition a century ago that “America’s racial divide [w]as part of a global clash between European whites and the ‘colored’ races, African, Asian, and all non-whites” (6). Doyle’s thesis is that there were two Reconstructions: the familiar, domestic version focused on rooting out slavery politically and economically, as well an international version aimed at “creating a zone of friendly, independent, ideally republican nations” (6–7). To substantiate this argument, Doyle details how the ­legacy of the US Civil War and the concurrent developments of Reconstruction loomed large in some of the era’s most important events, ranging from the Second French Empire’s interventions in Mexico and the Ten Years’ War in Cuba to the Canadian confederation, Britain’s Reform Act of 1867, and Italian unification. In the Western hemisphere, Doyle contends, international Reconstruction amounted to a “muscular new version of the Monroe Doctrine” backed up by the military prowess that the United States demonstrated in the Civil War (7). Elsewhere, the desire to remake the world in America’s image was largely contained to “inspiration and indirect influence, not foreign policy or government propaganda” (9). In other words, a victorious Union became a canvas onto which foreign liberals, socialists, and other radicals projected their conflicting hopes. At the same time, Radical Republicans shoehorned seemingly every incoming headline from foreign capitals into their preferred narrative that the United States heralded the democratic future in store for all nations. For example, Americans and ­Russians plausibly compared Lincoln and Tsar Alexander II, who abolished serfdom in 1861, as great emancipators, but it strained credulity when Senator Charles Sumner lauded the tsar for overseeing a “program of Radical Reconstruction by elevating twenty million serfs to full citizenship” (106).

auditPapers.title: Paul Nugent. Race, Taste, and the Grape: South African Wine from a Global Perspective
auditPapers.abstract: The twentieth century witnessed a profound transformation of the global wine industry when it collapsed the binary of Old World versus New World. In Race, Taste, and the Grape, Paul Nugent offers a compelling exploration of how South African wine played a pivotal role in this shift, situating itself at the intersection of cultural exchange, technological innovation, and sociopolitical reform. Nugent’s work deftly demonstrates how South African wine exemplified the global currents that redefined the industry. The book highlights how South Africa’s wine communities skillfully blended tradition with innovation, underscoring the centrality of terroir as a concept that intertwines ecological significance with cultural heritage. South African wines became emblematic of a new wave of winemaking that balanced terroir-driven authenticity with the technological advancements demanded by international markets. The concept of terroir, which encapsulates the intersection of soil, climate, and human tradition, became foundational to South Africa’s transformation. Nugent shows how the post-apartheid period marked a renaissance for South African wine, with exports skyrocketing from 24.5 million liters in 1993 to over 525 million liters by 2013. This remarkable growth was underpinned by a strategy that combined the preservation of traditional viticulture—rooted in terroir-driven practices and old vine cultivation—with aggressive market adaptation. South African winemakers emphasized the quality and diversity of their wines, leveraging the country’s unique climate and soil diversity to appeal to a global audience. The adoption of terroir as a branding and production philosophy allowed the wine industry to craft a narrative that resonated with international consumers, while simultaneously rooting itself in the cultural and ecological heritage of the Cape region.

The author’s familiarity with his city is a portal to exploring its painful and generative contradictions.

auditPapers.title: Elizabeth R. Williams. States of Cultivation: Imperial Transition and Scientific Agriculture in the Eastern Mediterranean.
auditPapers.abstract: What does it mean to talk about the “post-Ottoman” period? That is, when, how, and where have Ottoman legacies and antecedents shaped the modern Middle East? Across five chapters, Williams explores “scientific” or “modern” agriculture as a key element of state-making and knowledge production, first in the late Ottoman Empire and then under the French Mandate. Williams uses this approach to trace discourses and approaches to development from the Ottoman into the Mandate period, and to compare the Ottoman and French imperial projects in the Levant. This approach offers an alternative to the framework of “Ottoman colonialism,” especially insofar as it enables Williams both to situate the Ottomans within the global context of 19th-century state-building, and to contrast ­­Ottoman rule with the clearly colonial context of the Mandate (5). Essentially, she argues, the transition to the Mandate meant more intense extraction and increased tension between technocrats and imperial authorities, but less protection from foreign capital and decreased attention to environmental constraints (7). Williams follows those transitions by looking at how agriculture fit into larger projects of administration (chapters 1 and 5) and the politics of expertise (chapters 2 and 4).

auditPapers.title: Patricia Cleary. Mound City: The Place of the Indigenous Past and Present in St. Louis

auditPapers.title: Galen Brokaw and Pablo García Loaeza, eds. The Nahua: Language and Culture from the Sixteenth Century to the Present
auditPapers.abstract: The study of Nahuatl, best known as the language of the Aztecs but regionally spoken across northern Mesoamerica, has transformed historical approaches to Indigenous and Spanish colonial Mexico over the past half century. In the United States, linguist R. Joe Campbell has played a key role in this process. The Nahua: Language and Culture from the Sixteenth Century to the Present pays fitting homage to Campbell’s life’s work. For historians who may be most familiar with James Lockhart’s “New Philology” developed at the University of California, Los Angeles, in the 1970s–90s, the volume is an exemplary guide to other schools of thought and disciplinary approaches, from several generations of leading scholars in the United States, Mexico, and Europe. The first two chapters lay the necessary groundwork and demystify the term “Classical Nahuatl,” which refers to the variant of the language dominant in central Mexico at the time of Spanish invasion and should not be confused with the archaeological “Classic” period of Teotihuacán and the Maya lowlands from 300–800 CE. As Galen Brokaw and Pablo García Loaeza explain, this variant formed the bedrock of a new standardization created by Nahua and Spanish intellectuals in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The stakes could not have been higher; in a context of religious repression, imperialism, and demographic disaster, ancient and unique writing systems that constituted rare examples in world history of the independent development of script were replaced by a single Latin-based standard that only partially succeeded in capturing the richness of Nahuatl and other Mesoamerican languages. Brokaw and García Loaeza survey this transition in the early Spanish colonial period from semasiographic Mesoamerican to alphabetic European writing. They also survey the major schools of Nahuatl studies in Mexico and the United States (Europe and other parts of the world are not addressed, although some of their practitioners are cited).

auditPapers.title: Melissa Teixeira. A Third Path: Corporatism in Brazil and Portugal.
auditPapers.abstract: Prior to the 1990s, when a rebranded left presented itself as defending a Third Way between socialism and neoliberalism, corporatist ideas that strengthened the role of governmental regulations on capital-­­labor relations and advocated for a central role for the state as an economic actor guiding society toward a higher nationalist future helped reshape countries around world. Corporatism had a logic of its own that, largely due to its own conceptual malleability, left lasting impacts on nations across the world.

auditPapers.title: Renée Poznanski. Propaganda and Persecution: The French Resistance and the “Jewish Question.”Translated by Lenn J. Schramm
auditPapers.abstract: In this abridged and translated version of her original book, Renée Poznanski offers readers a unique opportunity to think about the French Resistance and its stance on Jewish persecution. The author is not concerned with the measure of antisemitism in France or within the French Resistance, but rather the French social imaginary as it elaborated various responses to the so-called “Jewish question.” Instead of a black or white approach to antisemitism in this period, Poznanski uses close reading of the underground press and broadcasts from London to discover how they dealt with Nazi and Vichy persecutions against Jews in France. In the opening of Propaganda and Persecution, the author argues that “[w]hat is at issue here is the Jews’ place in the French cultural imaginary—not among the overt antisemites but among those who committed themselves, at their mortal peril, to fighting against the camp that harbored the antisemites” (xv). Poznanski tackles this question in chronological order, by starting in the 1930s, where she highlights the centrality of the “Jewish question” to texts—so much so that this Judeophobic rhetoric appeared in the writings of people who were ostensibly opposed to antisemitism. Naturally, the proliferation of antisemitic literature was sped up by the creation of the Vichy regime, normalized by its many laws and decrees targeting Jews, and supported by the historical legacy of “reasonable antisemitism” in France. It was into this landscape that the early resistance organizations, both metropolitan and overseas, were forced to decide how they could, on the one hand, wage war on Nazi narratives, and on the other, win over French public opinion. To be clear, one did not need to oppose the antisemitic measures of the day to be opposed to Nazism—we know from decades of research, including Poznanski’s, that many resisters had no ethical issue with many of Vichy’s antisemitic laws, beyond the fact that they seemed to be imported from Nazi Germany; however, all resistance organizations felt the need to counter Nazi propaganda (and Vichy propaganda that seemed to support Nazi goals). Thus, we find early references to antisemitism in Resistance messaging, often couched in broader attacks on the Nazis.

auditPapers.title: Kathleen DuVal. Native Nations: A Millennium in North America
auditPapers.abstract: In the book Native Nations: A Millennium in North America, historian Kathleen DuVal attempts two herculean tasks. The first is tackling a thousand years of Indigenous North American history in a single monograph. The second, and far more challenging, is reshaping the general public’s perception of that history. Despite some blind spots, this well-written and engaging effort achieves the first goal; yet only time will tell if it can undo centuries of misinformation regarding Indigenous life on the continent before and after European invasion. Duval’s work contends with early American historiography’s reliance on well-familiar tropes regarding Indigenous America, such as Natives being changeless people outside of history with little power to stop the overwhelming tide of colonization and progress, whose story ends with the 1890 massacre at Wounded Knee. In traditional versions of US history, Indians play the dual role of the savage/victim, both terrifying and pitiable, depending on the immediate psychological needs of colonizers and their descendants. To combat these long-outdated frameworks, Native Nations emphasizes the existence of strong, stable, and diverse Indigenous cultures that existed long before, and crucially, long after Europeans invaded North America. DuVal demonstrates profound change over time, undermining those assumptions and revealing that European domination, be it from Dutch, Spanish, English, or French colonizers, was neither immediate nor inevitable.

auditPapers.title: Amanda Lanzillo. Pious Labor: Islam, Artisanship, and Technology in Colonial India
auditPapers.abstract: Pious Labor reconstructs an important and largely untold history of Muslim labor in late colonial India (1858–1947). Lanzillo has assembled a remarkable archive of Urdu and Persian texts that she reads with acuity alongside colonial sources to show how north Indian Muslim karigars (artisans) in six trades—bookmaking, metalsmithing, tailoring, carpentry, boilermaking, and stonemasonry—contended with the rapid economic and social changes of British colonialism. The book focuses on how Muslim artisans (predominantly male, though Lanzillo addresses questions of female labor and the gendering of labor in a chapter on tailoring) adapted to changes in the materiality and technology of their trades, and to the transition from artisanal production to wage-labor precipitated by industrialization. The centrality of Urdu sources allows Lanzillo to tell this story largely from the perspective of artisans themselves. She adeptly uses a combination of technical manuals that explained how to do tasks such as electroplating, maintain a steam engine, or use new construction technologies, and histories of artisans in a particular trade, which she refers to as community histories. Both types of texts were written mostly by artisans themselves and published by small commercial presses across north India. Although the artisanal communities studied through these texts (barring scribes) were largely illiterate, Lanzillo shows how these texts were directed at such communities, who would have accessed them through their being read aloud—a practice common of vernacular literatures in India during this era.

auditPapers.title: Kate Imy. Losing Hearts and Minds: Race, War, and Empire in Singapore and Malaya, 1915–1960
auditPapers.abstract: With the publication of her award-winning book Faithful Fighters in 2019—a study that addressed British attempts to maintain loyalty in the colonial Indian Army—Kate Imy established herself as not only an expert in British colonial military policy but also of the psychological, emotional, racial, and gendered dimensions of colonial militarism in general. Her second monograph, Losing Hearts and Minds, therefore promised to bring this expertise to bear on colonial militarism in Singapore and Malaya. It absolutely fulfills this promise. Losing Hearts and Minds examines the lives of soldiers and civilians in Singapore and Malaya from the 1915 Singapore Mutiny through to the end of the British colonial period during the 1948–1960 Malayan Emergency. Its central argument is that while colonial power and white supremacy rested upon racial and gendered hierarchies, they also relied on the loyalty and service of Asians and Eurasians, both in the military and civilian spheres. This contradiction meant that, despite the colonial state’s understanding that it needed to win the “hearts and minds” of its subjects, each conflict in the region resulted in a series of betrayals to reassert colonial hierarchies. Imy frames the book around the now-infamous “hearts and minds” expression used by Sir Gerald Templer during the Emergency to reinforce the futility of colonial attempts to inspire loyalty: the colonial state’s supremacist mandate ensured that its promises of belonging would inevitably result in betrayals. These betrayals are precisely what hastened the empire’s demise.

auditPapers.title: Anthony H. Minnema. The Last Ṭa’ifa: The Banu Hud and the Struggle for Political Legitimacy in al-Andalus

Minnema’s book The Last Ṭa’ifa: The Banū Hūd and the Struggle for Political Legitimacy in al-Andalus offers a comprehensive exploration of the Andalusī dynasty’s political strategies and ideological claims to legitimacy in the turbulent landscape of medieval Iberia. Minnema’s close analysis of primary sources in Latin and Arabic, including chronicles, coins, and diplomatic documents, shows how the Banū Hūd balanced dynastic pride with strategic alliances to sustain their rule across generations. This meticulously researched work is essential reading for scholars of medieval Spain and al-Andalus, medieval Islamic political culture, and the broader Mediterranean. Minnema sets the stage by framing the Banū Hūd as a unique Andalusī dynasty with a “second act”—a recurring ability to reassert power through careful claims to lineage and allegiance. He critiques conventional historiographical views of the ta’ifa periods as chaotic or politically unsophisticated, as influenced by a preference for centralized imperial regimes. He instead suggests that these fragmented times allowed smaller polities, such as the Banū Hūd, to develop distinctive forms of statecraft. The central question for the book is how the Banū Hūd deployed their dynastic identity and claims to legitimacy to maintain power over three centuries in the face of multiple challenges.

auditPapers.title: Andrea Wright. Unruly Labor: A History of Oil in the Arabian Sea.
auditPapers.abstract: Andrea Wright’s timely monograph traces the consolidation of the nation-state through labor struggles in the oil-producing countries encircling the Arabian Sea in the waning days of the ­­British Empire. Unruly Labor opens with a chapter on oil work and oilfield mobilization in 1930s and 1940s Iran, where the Tudeh, the Iranian communist party, held significant influence and an internationalist orientation. Wright notes the extent to which noncitizens—especially Indian migrant workers—took part in a 1946 Tudeh-led strike to improve the labor and living conditions they shared with Iranians. Confronted with an anti-imperialist form of class solidarity that crossed ethnonational lines, representatives of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company advanced a paternalistic form of national development for Iranians—the “cultivat[ion] of workers into good citizens” through education and noncommunist union membership—combined with the deportation of “undesirable,” often communist, Indian workers (32–34). From here, Wright’s argument tacks across the Arabian Sea, encompassing labor struggles in Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Yemen from the 1940s through the early 1970s. Chapter 2 traces how the Kuwaiti state’s attempts to advocate for Kuwaiti oil workers amid mobilizations by a diverse workforce comprising local and migrant workers prompted a more restrictive definition of Kuwaiti citizenship. Chapter 3 details efforts by highly skilled Indian chemists to protest their subordinate status within the racialized labor hierarchies established by a US-owned oil company in Bahrain, which spurred the intercession of the newly independent Indian state on behalf of its citizens in the late 1940s. ­­Chapter 4 examines a cross-class hunger strike by Indian workers at a British refinery under construction in Aden. This strike drew from a nationalist tradition of protest against racial and religious discrimination targeting Indians—especially Hindus—laboring abroad, prompting Indian state intervention to defend the new nation’s honor. Chapter 5 returns to Bahrain, tracing growing pan-Arab nationalism among Arabic-speaking local and migrant workers in the mid-1950s. Pan-Arab, pro-Palestine, and anti-imperialist organizing prompted a crackdown against labor organizers and the passage of a labor law that constrained unions’ ability to make international affiliations, placed restrictions on noncitizens’ union activities, and limited unions’ right to strike. Chapter 6 examines a series of strikes in 1960s Qatar that specifically aimed to increase the rights of Qatari workers vis-à-vis noncitizens—including other Arab workers—amid drives to Qatarize the workforce and restrict non-Qatari capital. But by the end of the decade, a large majority of the oilfield labor came to be performed by South Asian migrants, while Qataris themselves increasingly abandoned such work as they began to receive growing shares of the country’s oil wealth via patronage. Chapter 7 moves to Abu Dhabi, where strikes against a ruler regarded by his British patrons as ineffectual led to a British-backed coup and an increasingly securitized approach to oilfield labor, including a more ready recourse to police and military force to suppress strikes and the passage of a labor law that banned labor actions in the public sector that might pose risks to “persons and property” (187). By 1970, a recognition that national governments throughout the region would ultimately assert control over their petroleum industries led international oil companies to move toward contracting services rather than owning and operating assets. This final shift laid the groundwork for the labor regime that emerged across the oil industry in much of the region: state employment in nationalized oil companies for citizens of Arab Gulf states, lucrative contracting work for Europeans and ­­Americans, increasingly limited opportunities for non-Gulf Arabs, and highly securitized manual labor for South Asian migrant workers.

auditPapers.title: David Carey Jr. Health in the Highlands: Indigenous Healing and Scientific Medicine in Guatemala and Ecuador.
auditPapers.abstract: In 1996, Jennifer S. H. Brown and Elizabeth Vibert’s edited volume, Reading Beyond Words, argued that it takes patience to recover and communicate the experiences and perspectives of those for whom the historical record is lacking or limited by the interpretation of others. In his work Health in the Highlands, David Carey Jr. takes on this challenge through an examination of public health within Indigenous communities in Guatemala and Ecuador. The book positions at its center the experiences of indígenas, teasing out their perspectives and interactions from outsider sources during an intense period of labor coercion and land colonization between the 1870s and 1930s in Latin America. Although Indigenous experiences with health care have been difficult at best to ascertain, Guatemala and Ecuador provide critical case studies, as these two countries have high proportions of Indigenous populations that make their erasure from the national archives impossible. The book is organized thematically over six main chapters, weaving together the connections among modernization, indigeneity, and medicine. Through an examination of the interactions among an array of actors, Carey’s research like roots of a tree tap into social, economic, and political soils. Beginning with the assertion that conceptions of health were bound up with concepts of the nation, Carey pursues a transnational analysis that destabilizes states and corporate entities as interpretive lenses in favor of analyzing power dynamics through body experiences and Indigenous encounters with illness and healing, along with the circulation of theories of race and racial difference. This work draws from a variety of archives, including the Rockefeller Archive Center, the Archivo General de Centroamérica and Academia de Geografía, Revista Militar, Revista Agricola, Government and Public Health Memorias in Guatemala, and the Museo de Medicina and the Archivo Nacional del Ecuador in Ecuador.

auditPapers.abstract: In his new book North Korea’s Mundane Revolution, historian Andre Schmid tackles the subject of North Korean social history. First and foremost, it contests the Western caricature of communist economics as a strictly top-down enterprise that simply grinds down humanity with Stakhanovite brutality to meet ridiculous quotas. Schmid highlights how the workers of the nascent Kim family regime voiced their concerns and criticism of national economic policies. For instance, they criticized the party-state with their choice of living quarters. Despite Party pleas for rural workers to remain in the countryside, many from those regions moved to urban areas for higher wages and better job opportunities.

auditPapers.title: Eram Alam, Dorothy Roberts, and Natalie Shibley, eds. Ordering the Human: The Global Spread of Racial Science.
auditPapers.abstract: When discussing the origins of race and racial science, historians regularly have looked to the Americas and the Anglo-Atlantic World. In this framework, slavery and the conquest of the Americas provided a laboratory for the construction of the scientific race concept, which naturalized the enslavement of Africans as healthy and the dying out of Native Americans as an inevitable consequences of their bodily weakness in the face of novel illnesses. What this narrative does not always emphasize is how racial science was a product of emergent globalization. Racial science’s global nature and consequences, though, are the subject of a compelling new collection of essays, Ordering the Human: The Global Spread of Racial Science, edited by Eram Alam, Dorothy Roberts, and Natalie Shibley. Including scholarship from anthropologists, historians, and public health scholars, Ordering the Human covers diverse locales, times periods, and disciplines, with chapters ranging from late 18th-century ­­German naturalism to the consequences of racial thinking during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States and India. Collectively, what emerges is a much larger and more complicated study of racial science, one where its practitioners are ethnically and disciplinarily diverse and engage with such populations as government officials, academics, and health care providers. In short, expanding to a global framework highlights the true horrors of racial science, a knowledge system uncritically adopted by a range of academic disciplines and nations.

auditPapers.title: Gale L. Kenny. Christian Imperial Feminism: White Protestant Women and the Consecration of Empire

Whether they were raising money for overseas evangelism or trying, vainly, to open US borders to Jewish refugees during World War II, the missionary women and churchwomen consistently labored to create “an appealing and modern Christian cosmopolitanism that linked the hierarchical power dynamics of White women’s rescue fantasies of liberating religiously oppressed women to their seemingly more egalitarian vision of a Protestant and transnational community of women” (9). Put bluntly, these women wanted to achieve the best of all possible worlds through management by the best of all possible women—themselves. “Christian” meant their specific type of Protestantism; “imperial” meant global, but with a clearly demarcated center and periphery; and “feminism” meant not liberationist activism but gendered moral authority.

The Nahua culture that is the subject of Indigenous Science and Technology is one that, in the fifteenth century, produced the famous Aztec Empire, which, a century later, was invaded by the Spaniards and turned into a colony called “New Spain” (part of today’s Mexico). Although in subsequent decades the vast majority of these territories’ Indigenous populations perished in wars, epidemics, and forced labor systems, the Nahua culture has survived to this day. Consequently, the scholarly discourse about the past (precontact and colonial) Nahua affects their living descendants. Mindful of that, McDonough describes her approach as “grounded in the interdisciplinary field of critical Native American and Indigenous studies” (19). Instead of writing about the Nahua, as the traditional scholarship tends to, she chooses to write with or for the Nahua.
