auditPapers.title: David Reeve. To Remain Myself: The History of Onghokham.
auditPapers.abstract: Indonesian historian Onghokham was “the best guide to Indonesia,” and he could be “the serious historian, the public intellectual, the sexual being, the quiet lover, or the hedonist and party host” (298). Ong died in 2007, too late to see the book, but Reeve, an Australian researcher with deep connections to Indonesia, has done a marvelous job of fulfilling Ong’s wish to tell the full story. Reeve coedited Onze Ong, a posthumous recollection by Ong’s friends, which was a key source for reconstructing Ong’s life; Reeve also relies on interviews and letters Ong wrote to his Cornell friends, such as Benedict Anderson, Daniel Lev, and Herbert Feith. The result is an affective narrative with a multiplicity of voices speaking to Ong’s emotional life, his identity, his worldview, and his lifestyle. We cannot help but admire Ong, who shows us how to remain oneself in the time and space within which one is embedded. As such, Ong’s biography is a critical intervention into the political establishment and cultural assumptions of Indonesian society.

McCleary’s Staging Buenos Aires: Theater, Society, and Politics in Argentina, 1860–1920 offers a well-researched study of Argentina’s popular theater from its origins to its golden age in the early twentieth century. This is a particularly important contribution for English-language readers, as few monographs on Argentine theater have focused on this time period. The book examines the development of popular theater in this era and argues that, as the city’s main form of leisurely activity, it was not only a reflection of Argentina’s political and social processes but also a key site for their unfolding—including the formation of a national identity; modernization; democratization; and, most importantly, as the author argues, the emergence of a middle-class consciousness. The book begins with a historical overview of the development of Argentine theater, from colonial times to the 1920s, tracing how colonial practices, such as censorship and proselytism (political or religious), were still in effect in the early twentieth century. Through the analysis of various cases of censorship—ranging from popular theater’s beginnings to its massification—the first chapter attempts to show how theater was seen and used as a tool to force and instill ideas of nationhood and citizenship. Interestingly, McCleary reveals throughout the book, that censorship was often accompanied and resisted by “democratic spaces” (84)—created by practitioners and audiences alike—from public exchanges and negotiations surrounding censorship, to the formation of writers’ and actors’ guilds that defended their rights, as well as the social critique and satire conveyed on the stage.

auditPapers.title: John K. Bardes. The Carceral City: Slavery and the Making of Mass Incarceration in New Orleans, 1803–1930
auditPapers.abstract: Scholars and students in a plethora of fields will benefit from John K. Bardes’s outstanding book The Carceral City: Slavery and the Making of Mass Incarceration in New Orleans, 1803–1930. Superbly researched and written, this study contends that the nation’s carceral crisis is more than two centuries in the making, with origins long predating the Jim Crow era. State power and the post-Civil War prison complex did not simply replace the institution of slavery and private plantations, as popularly understood; rather, the author argues, “many antebellum slaveholders were fiercely committed to and deeply reliant upon, the use of police and prisons to coerce enslaved and free labor” (3). Bardes’s introduction includes a thorough historiographical discussion of the myriad ways The Carceral City engages scholars past and present and works to steer various disciplinary debates. Prison histories, for instance, have been too focused on the Northern United States, northern Europe, and the post-Civil War and Emancipation South, excluding slave societies and their tangled “interplay of race, slavery, and the growth of state power” (6). Studies of urban slavery have overemphasized “the relative freedoms that enslaved people accessed within cities, rather than the particular policing and carceral systems that cities developed to counteract those freedoms” (5). The author also furthers ongoing efforts to inject slavery and the American South into histories of the state and capitalism. But most impressively, each of the seven chapters and the epilogue include numerous historiographic interventions that greatly enrich readers’ understanding of the content while not interrupting the flow and readability of the text.

auditPapers.title: Rafał B. Reichert. Wood, Trade, and Spanish Naval Power (c. 1740–1795).
auditPapers.abstract: How did Spain manage to become the second naval power in the world, just 20 years after its disastrous involvement, alongside France, in the Seven Years’ War? This is the big question that Rafał B. Reichert, a regarded scholar of the Spanish colonial empire, has chosen to place at the heart of his latest book Wood, Trade, and Spanish Naval Power (c. 1740–1795). To answer this question, the author draws on several of his recent publications on the issue of timber supplies for the Spanish Navy, which was sourced from two strategic regions: the Baltic Sea and the Caribbean. The book is highly interesting due to the wealth of perspectives it opens. Indeed, the issue of supplying royal navies has already been the subject of a very rich historiography, which the author masters thoroughly and of which he offers an exhaustive review at the end of the work (except for its French side, where he could find useful points of comparison in the recent work of David Plouviez and Caroline Le Mao). The main interest of the book lies in its ability to situate a classic topic in the historiography of the early modern period at the crossroads of various scientific debates, which have been particularly active in recent years. Through its focus on the descriptions of forest resources provided by various investigators dispatched by the Spanish crown to the relevant areas, the book aligns fully with the field of environmental history, and as such it is a fitting addition to Brill’s Environmental History series. In addition, the book is inspired by imperial history, as it places the Spanish-British rivalry at the center of its analysis. The comparative method it employs, meanwhile, is drawn from global history. The focus on the various forms of contracts established between the Spanish Navy and the merchants responsible for provisioning it, with the participation of other institutional actors enlisted to support it (notably ambassadors and consuls), is unquestionably an interesting contribution to the social history of institutions and commercial practices. Finally, Reichert’s overall conclusion—that the Baltic did better than New Spain because it was better integrated into the commercial circuits of early globalization and because it offered more advantageous services than America—constitutes an important contribution to the more general reflection on the dynamics of globalization in the early modern era.

auditPapers.title: Secrecy and sovereignty in the Age of Revolutions
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Transparency, or publicity as it was then called, became a fundamental value linked to popular sovereignty in the late eighteenth century. Those who advocated greater publicity, particularly of legislative deliberations, did so as part of an overarching vision of political representation as a process by which the popular will was to be continuously reflected in government. Publicity, in short, would make popular sovereignty possible. But when elected officials in the early United States and revolutionary France made claims to speak for the people, the use of secrecy actually strengthened those claims by temporally dislocating disagreement to after the passage of unpopular policies rather than during the deliberative process. This reality created a paradox at the heart of representative government: secrecy was bolstering a type of regime to which it was simultaneously deemed anathema. Placing procedural decisions about publicity and secrecy front and center, this article addresses questions long plaguing historians: how did the American framers secure what Edmund Morgan called the “fiction of popular sovereignty”? And why were French revolutionaries unable to do the same? One answer, which has long been neglected despite its significance, is the procedural practices of constituent bodies in each context. This article undertakes a comparison of the procedural decisions in the American Constitutional Convention and subsequent legislature and the establishment of the French National Assembly and successor legislatures. It argues that there is nothing mystical about the legitimacy of popular sovereignty through representative government: it was the result of deliberate decisions about the procedures of governance.

Mary E. Hicks follows the journeys of enslaved Black mariners who traversed the South Atlantic serving in multiple positions both aboard slave ships and at coastal ports, for instance, as cabin boys, carpenters, cooks, interpreters, healers and surgeons. Dubbed “captive cosmopolitans,” these Black mariners demonstrated how they were frequently cognizant of laws, which they might employ to secure their liberty from the bonds of slavery.

auditPapers.title: Metricizing diaspora dualities: a comparative quantitative analysis of poetry and prose in Southeast Asian Chinese literature
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The intersection of quantitative literary studies and diaspora research presents critical opportunities for examining linguistic divergence between immigrant literatures and their cultural origins. While digital humanities scholarship has increasingly embraced computational methods, systematic applications in comparative diaspora studies—particularly those focusing on Southeast Asian Chinese communities—remain underdeveloped. This study bridges this gap through a corpus-driven analysis of 372 literary works (comprising 240 poems and 132 prose pieces) using natural language processing pipelines, hierarchical clustering, and one-way analysis of variance. The common features we proposed have played a greater role in distinguishing Southeast Asian Chinese diaspora new poetry from Chinese mainland poetry. We found that the new poetry of Southeast Asian Chinese diaspora new poetry is not as natural as that of Chinese Mainland, showing greater freedom and diversity in vocabulary selection. Specifically, the vocabulary usage rate of Southeast Asian diaspora new poetry is relatively high, while the grammar usage rate is low. These computationally derived patterns not only establish measurable criteria for distinguishing diaspora literatures through machine-learning classifiers, but also challenge conventional assumptions about linguistic “naturalness” in cross-cultural contexts. Our methodology, which integrates computational stylistics with diaspora theory, provides a replicable analytical framework for studying literary migration phenomena, thereby advancing both digital humanities methodologies and Southeast Asian literary studies.

auditPapers.title: “A golden bridge for republican consciences”? The Simon-Gagern Pact and the Frankfurt Constitution of 1849
auditPapers.abstract: The Simon-Gagern Pact of 1849 is mentioned by nearly every historian of the Frankfurt Parliament, but seldom with much explanatory detail. It is presented as a simple quid pro quo, which fulfilled its short-term function but failed to satisfy anyone. Under the pact, Heinrich Simon (1805–60) and his democratic supporters agreed to vote for a hereditary emperor as head of state in return for significant changes to the German constitution, which was then undergoing its second reading. It was only with the votes of Simon and his followers that the hereditary emperorship was narrowly approved on March 27, 1849, and with it the entire constitution. However, when King Friedrich Wilhelm IV declined the imperial title and the revolutionary flame of 1848–49 was extinguished, both centrist liberals and exiled radicals sought to downplay the significance of the pact, portraying it as an ignoble episode in an era otherwise characterized by high ideals and heroism. Even though the 1849 Frankfurt constitution would later be recognized as a significant milestone in German history and an important influence on both the Weimar constitution and the Basic Law of the Federal Republic, it was not until 1954 that the first detailed study of the pact was published; no new research has appeared in print since then. This article employs sources from British as well as German archives to shed new light on Heinrich Simon’s actions during the crucial months of 1849.

auditPapers.title: “When all the liquid World was one extended Thames”: Early Modern British Prospects in West African Estuaries
auditPapers.abstract: This essay examines how cross-cultural politics and local ecologies shaped early modern British imperial structures by focusing on the Royal African Company’s efforts to exploit West African estuaries for economic and political advantage. Company agents pursued two strategies to integrate these tropical estuaries into a mercantilist imperial framework: prospecting, which sought to render estuarine productivity legible from across the Atlantic, and settling, which involved manipulating local trade dynamics and mobilizing both human and nonhuman forces to serve company interests. Environmental obstacles and African and European competition, however, hampered these ambitions. The result was the formation of hybrid waterscapes that reflected the entanglement of British imperial aspirations with local power dynamics and estuarine ecologies. In response to these challenges, a grassroots coastal trade emerged in the late seventeenth century to offset the difficulty of controlling any single river system. This evolving structure strengthened Britain’s Atlantic slave trade by facilitating the movement of captives, improving access to labor, and reducing shipboard mortality. It also encouraged a shift toward an aggregate estuarine strategy centered on the more secure, nonestuarine outpost of Cape Coast Castle. Drawing on the company records, travel narratives, and environmental histories, this essay argues that attending to the political ecology of estuaries reveals the adaptive and contested nature of British imperial expansion in West Africa.

auditPapers.title: Fixing Early Modern Identity in the Mobile Mediterranean
auditPapers.abstract: What did it mean to have religious and spatial mobility serve as both a professional asset and a legal liability? This article addresses the question through the lens of an early seventeenth-century Venetian inquisitorial trial involving agents who served as brokers and interpreters for Ottoman and Persian merchants in the city. The brokers’ backgrounds were marked by geographical and religious mobility. Their profession required competence in Turkish and/or Persian, which many had acquired while living periods of their lives as Muslims in the eastern Mediterranean. Like other early modern European commercial hubs, Venetian policy was driven by twin imperatives: on the one hand, the imperative of facilitating the movement of people and goods across religious and jurisdictional boundaries for reasons of commerce, and, on the other, the imperative of ensuring the fixity of identity, particularly religious identity. The Venetian state was a complex bureaucratic entity, and each of these imperatives was pursued by different magistracies at different times. The case demonstrates that while the brokers were valued by certain state institutions for their perceived ability to move between the worlds of Latin Christendom and Islam, that mobility proved a liability before other institutions that insisted upon fixity of religious identity. The case points to a set of strategies the brokers employed to negotiate the tension between mobility as an asset and a liability.

auditPapers.title: Parallel Revolution: Hungarian Peasants during the Upheavals of 1918–1920
auditPapers.abstract: This article is the first study of Hungarian peasant revolutionism during the political upheavals that immediately followed the First World War and the collapse of the Habsburg Empire. Historians of Hungary have charted the revolutionary movements that brought to power Mihály Károlyi’s liberal regime in November 1918 and Béla Kun’s communist regime in March 1919, but they have mostly neglected the rural revolution that unfolded in parallel with events in Budapest. Communist tactics vis-à-vis the countryside, which have preoccupied many Hungarian historians as well as scholars of revolution in other overwhelmingly agrarian societies, appear less significant than peasants’ own radical expectations. The evidence from Hungary in 1918–20 demonstrates the critical importance of wartime mobilization and the role of rural veterans as instigators of political unrest in triggering modern peasant uprisings.

auditPapers.title: Iconicity in large language models
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Lexical iconicity, a direct relation between a word’s meaning and its form, is an important aspect of every natural language, most commonly manifesting through sound-meaning associations. Since Large language models’ (LLMs’) access to both meaning and sound of text is only mediated (meaning through textual context, sound through written representation, further complicated by tokenization), we might expect that the encoding of iconicity in LLMs would be either insufficient or significantly different from human processing. This study addresses this hypothesis by having GPT-4 generate highly iconic pseudowords in artificial languages. To verify that these words actually carry iconicity, we had their meanings guessed by Czech and German participants (n = 672) and subsequently by LLM-based participants (generated by GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet). The results revealed that humans can guess the meanings of pseudowords in the generated iconic language more accurately than words in distant natural languages and that LLM-based participants are even more successful than humans in this task. This core finding is accompanied by several additional analyses concerning the universality of the generated language and the cues that both human and LLM-based participants utilize.

auditPapers.title: The War People: A Social History of Common Soldiers during the Era of the Thirty Years War. By Lucian Staiano-Daniels
auditPapers.abstract: In recent decades the influence of social and cultural history has transformed the writing of war history. For both modern and pre-modern Europe, the study of politics, diplomacy and the military now sits alongside a new military history that explores the wartime experiences of ordinary soldiers and civilians, the material and psychological impact of conflict, and postwar memory and commemoration. As the title of a recent essay collection edited by Tryntje Helfferich and Howard Louthan suggests, historians of war now spend much—possibly even most—of their time “Beyond the Battlefield.” Staiano-Daniels’ The War People is a very welcome addition to this literature. It traces in microscopic detail the history of a regiment raised in Electoral Saxony in 1625 by Wolf von Mansfeld in the service of Philip IV of Spain. At its strongest the Mansfeld Regiment comprised 2,545 infantrymen and 979 horses. In the summer of 1625 it travelled from Dresden to northern Italy, but arrived too late to participate meaningfully in the conflict over the Valtellina that was resolved by the Treaty of Monzón in March 1626. Its members remained in northern Italy until 1627, when the regiment gradually mutinied and collapsed due to a lack of money. Staiano-Daniel’s study was made possible by the unusually rich collection of surviving archival sources relating to the regiment: muster rolls, records of passage and quartering, and, most importantly, court books containing all manner of legal records. In keeping with the traditions of microhistory that Staiano-Daniels cites, trial records play a key role in his study. The author has also done an impressive job of mining local printed and archival sources to examine the impact of the regiment’s presence on the communities through which it passed.

auditPapers.title: Digital betrayals: "translating" the ancient drawings of the Monastery of Nossa Senhora da Rosa
auditPapers.abstract: The research described in this paper used digital technologies to study the ethical and philosophical implications related to the analysis and interpretation of historical sources of cultural heritage. As the described technologies used are not neutral tools, they actively shape heritage narratives, influencing how we perceive and represent the past. Thus, reconstructing the past through heritage fragments cannot be objective or universally accepted, as it is inherently shaped by contemporary social, cultural, and political contexts. The past, therefore, can only be analysed from the unique perspective of the present. In this regard, the American historian David Lowenthal suggests “the past is a foreign country,” and therefore, its language, customs, and traditions cannot be fully understood. Since heritage is irreconcilable with the past, or more precisely —quoting Lowenthal again—since heritage is a “distortion” of the past, cultural heritage studies should combat those simulacra that define the past as objective, unambiguous, and unquestionable—definitions often protected by academia. The case study this paper focuses on is the Monastery of Nossa Senhora da Rosa of the Order of São Paulo da Serra de Ossa (Caparica, Portugal). It represents an opportunity to reflect on the ambiguity implicit when reading historical sources, always involving a certain interpretive and creative component. Borrowing the semiotic concept of translation, it is possible to say that reading any source is comparable to translating a document from an obscure and mysterious “language”, that of the past, to the contemporary world “language”. During the process of transferring word meanings from one language to another, many nuances inevitably end up being twisted, lost, or otherwise altered. Consequently, “translating” the drawing into the real building (as well as into a virtual replica) is, to use a famous 16thcenturyanalogy, a sort of “betrayal,” a departure from the initial idea represented on the sheet. This is particularly pertinent when the building no longer exists, as is the case with the Monastery of Nossa Senhora da Rosa. What are the limits of interpretation, its criteria, and the freedom that the "reader/interpreter" can take? What is the role of digital technologies in this theoretical framework? This research, rather than extolling the photorealistic results of digital heritage visualisations and their uniqueness, focuses on the process that led to certain interpretations, emphasising their subjective and context-dependent aspects.

auditPapers.title: On proximity—exploring experiences of bias and discrimination in digital humanities
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article explores proximity as a critical feminist methodology in digital humanities, emphasizing its role in addressing bias in digital technologies. In line with the proximal approach, interviews were conducted with community groups and organizations as well as researchers, academics, artists, coders, activists, and software developers. By centring marginalized voices, the article proposes a proximal approach as a means to counteract digital bias and foster more just digital landscapes. auditPapers.title: Minority’s History: Tracing an Equivocal Social Category through the Twentieth-Century United States
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article traces the long career of the term “minority” in the United States, tracking both its continuities and its shapeshifting in the twentieth century American vernacular. I argue that the changing uses of minority reflected a protean politics of language that reflected changes in racial ideology across the twentieth century, which I explore by analyzing the evolving tension between ascriptive language and demands for self-description by Black and Latino Americans in particular. The earliest usage of minority as a social category emerged after the First World War, when Black journalists and advocates argued that African Americans needed protection as a “racial minority” in the U.S. Social scientists popularized a broader version of the term in the 1930s—which included immigrants and their offsprings—that held sway until a postwar shift in racial schema enabled second- and third-generation European ethnics to escape the minority category. The phrases “disadvantaged minority” and “underprivileged minority” gained currency around that time, entangling Black, Latino, and other “non-white” Americans in a shared but fragmented marginalized status. While the development of affirmative action policies in the late 1960s lent minority status an important form of leverage, the category continued to signal exclusions from the benefits of full citizenship. Even by the late twentieth century, members of groups labeled minorities still resided figuratively and often literally on the periphery of American society, a position from which many continued to critique and rework the language of minority to challenge its normative power.

auditPapers.title: Spaces of Treblinka: Retracing a Death Camp By Jacob Flaws
auditPapers.abstract: One of the most disturbing characteristics of the Treblinka extermination camp is what Gitta Sereny described in her book “Into That Darkness: An Examination of Conscience,” (New York, 1983) as the “terrible smallness of the place.” The Treblinka (II) camp was only 42 acres in size but was responsible for the mass murder of as many as 925,000 Jews. It was, perhaps, one of the deadliest places on earth. It is more than a little surprising, therefore, that more scholarly books have not appeared covering Treblinka. In this book, Flaws contributes to the so-called “spatial turn” in Holocaust studies that approaches the topic from a more geographical perspective, considering the meanings of space and place. He sets out to explore the spaces of the camp both literally and figuratively. Importantly, he examines not only the spaces within the camp but also the spaces around the camp. In this way, Flaws situates the camp in its surroundings, not a space completely sealed off from the outside world, but rather one deeply connected with it. For him, it is a space “in which ‘distinct trajectories’ of experience, ideology, and perception from any different people—Germans, Jews, and Poles—coalesced around the focal point that was the camp” (xix). Flaws, thus, also rises to Saul Friedländer’s challenge for Holocaust scholars to write an integrated history that includes all participants. The prominence of first-person Polish accounts is noteworthy and enlightening.

auditPapers.title: Worlds of Labor on Georgetown’s Waterfront: Work, Freedom and the Labor Question in Guyana, c. 1890–1966
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article examines conflicts over the meaning and organization of work on the waterfront of Georgetown, Guyana. In the Anglophone Caribbean, “free” wage labor was a key component of the post-emancipation civilizing mission. Afro-Caribbean peoples, however, had their own ideas about the place of wage labor in their individual and collective lives. For many freed peoples and their descendants, wage labor was often one “livelihood strategy” among many, and it did not always take priority over other individual needs, or familial and communal concerns. This article investigates how these different understandings of wage labor shaped the multifaceted worlds of Georgetown’s Afro-Guianese waterfront workers. The first part examines the social relations and hierarchies that mediated the organization of work on the waterfront, influenced waterfront workers’ attitude toward wage labor and its relationship to other aspects of their lives, and facilitated episodes of industrial protest, including strikes when Afro-Guianese and Indo-Guianese workers co-operated in defiance of British Guiana’s racialized political economy. The second part focuses more narrowly on the workplace and the colonial authorities’ ongoing search for answers to the labor question. The article contends that decasualization—which complemented the wider post-1945 development and welfare agenda—represented a new iteration of the post-emancipation project to organize Afro-Guianese peoples’ lives around wage labor. Against the backdrop of rising anti-colonial sentiment and the subsequent split within the nationalist movement, the article demonstrates that although the colonial authorities had some success in creating a cohort of regular waterfront workers, decasualization was no panacea for the labor question.

auditPapers.title: Lac dye colours: A review of the origin, history and identification techniques in textiles
auditPapers.abstract: Lac dye, the dyestuff derived from Kerria scale insects, has been valued for millennia by various civilizations, which have appreciated its deep red shades in textiles, paintings, and other cultural artefacts. The colour derived from lac dye is complex both in structure and history, and has been the topic of numerous discussions addressing its origin, history and multiple uses as a dyestuff, medicine or cosmetic. However, there is still a significant lack of cohesion between sources, and no publication to date has offered a comprehensive overview of lac dye. This review aims to fill this knowledge gap by exploring the biological sources from which lac dye derives; the historical importance in Asia and the Mediterranean area; and the variety of processing techniques according to technical written sources. Particular attention is given to the use of lac dye on textiles by comparing the existing dyeing manuals and identification in historical textiles by analytical methods such as high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) coupled to diode array (DAD) and mass spectrometry (MS) detectors or surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS). The review also offers an updated overview on the taxonomy of Kerria lac insects, highlighting their geographical diversity and suggesting future perspective of research. The discussion provides new insights into the complexity of lac dye and its use in the dyeing traditions worldwide, by intersecting sources from history, science and art.

auditPapers.title: Recognizing past shapes: sex differentiation through deep learning on European Upper Palaeolithic hand stencils
auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: This study explores the application of advanced deep learning techniques in analyzing Upper Palaeolithic hand stencil representations, focusing on sex classification of individuals involved in prehistoric rock art activity. auditPapers.abstract: Juan Cobo Betancourt’s masterwork, The Coming of the Kingdom, is an important contribution to historical scholarship that will shape the study of the Catholic Church during the first century of Spanish colonization in America. However, this force did not lead to a straightforward transformation. Instead, the Muisca interacted with Catholicism in ways that reveal resistance, adaptation, and ingenuity, as well as their limitations.

auditPapers.title: Blue: A History of Postpartum Depression in America By Rachel Louise Moran
auditPapers.abstract: In this well-written and engaging monograph, Rachel Moran captures the struggles and triumphs to define, diagnose, and raise awareness about postpartum depression in the United States. Though a certain percentage of new mothers have undoubtedly experienced mood fluctuations since the ancient times, the term “baby blues” emerged during the postwar baby boom era, when motherhood was celebrated as the ultimate goal of womanhood. And yet, as exemplified by Betty Friedan’s bestselling The Problem that Has No Name, motherhood could be a struggle. Moran traces the condition’s evolution from the 1950s to the present, as various stakeholders attempted to frame the baby blues as a legitimate medical condition worthy of research and treatment. As Moran aptly demonstrates, suggesting that the experience of new motherhood could be anything other than pure joy was contentious enough (particularly in the 1950s); understanding the causes and determining treatment when things went wrong was even more so. If a new mother struggled to bond with her child, for example, was this a sign of selfishness and immaturity? An indication of a traumatic birth? An unhappy childhood? A rejection of gendered expectations? Or a psychiatric disorder? It could, of course, be any of these, depending upon who you asked, which accounts for the cacophony of voices weighing in on the matter. Moran walks us through the decades, demonstrating how cultural influences (from pronatalism to feminism to celebrities and social media) shaped the debate over time.

auditPapers.title: Money, Value, and the State: Sovereignty and Citizenship in East Africa By Kevin P. Donovan
auditPapers.abstract: In the first pages of Kevin Donovan’s thorough and thought-provoking book, he asks what is national (as in sovereign) about a national currency when its value is determined by the amount of foreign currency that nation holds? That foreign currency is procured with a rickety seesawing of national and international markets. African states sell cotton or coffee or sisal on the international for foreign currency; they convert that currency to local currency—taking a percentage for the costs of marketing—with which they pay local producers. Postcolonial African states, Donovan insists, are therefore moneychanger states, because they do not fully control the value of their own currencies. Just as states are canonically defined by the ability to monopolize violence within their borders, they are also defined by their ability to monopolize the power to establish the value of the money that is used within their borders. Postcolonial African states, not being fully capable of controlling the value of their currency, thus find that their sovereignty—postcolonial, economic, and in contrast to development—is limited. This hinders the ability of residents to practice “economic citizenship,” one of several kinds of citizenship described in this book.

auditPapers.title: Demos Rising: Democracy and the Popular Construction of Public Power in France, 1800-1850 By Stephen W. Sawyer
auditPapers.abstract: The French Revolution created a democratic society, one in which all adult males were in principle equal before the law. The new state of affairs raised a novel question: what kind of political regime was best suited to govern such a society? The answer, it might be thought, would hinge on a range of political technologies—constitutions, representative bodies, electoral procedures—and how they were made to work together to reconcile the contrasting demands of freedom and stability. But, as it turns out, there is another way to conceptualize the problem. For the Revolution also created the modern state, and it had projects of its own, to develop or preserve the nation’s resources, the better to enhance its own power. Citizens might see the virtue of such schemes or experience them as an imposition. Citizens too, free and equal beings that they were, might have projects they wanted to pursue, coming together for this purpose or that, and the state had an interest in making sure that such associational initiatives dovetailed with its own ambitions. How the state and its citizens interacted required management, regulation in a word, and regulation, as Stephen Sawyer notes, might take all kinds of forms, some more top-down and expert-driven in nature, others more participatory with folks on the ground claiming a say over how rules were applied. That see-saw battle between the experts and what Sawyer calls the demos over the command of the state’s regulatory power was ground zero, as he sees it, in the struggle for democracy in France under the Restoration and July Monarchies. Given Sawyer’s angle of approach, the time frame is an apt one. This was a period when the state conceded a measure of liberty to its citizens but was at pains to circumscribe its practice through censorship and disenfranchisement. The people were excluded from public life but had some room to maneuver, to bang, that is, at the state’s regulatory gates and demand entry.

auditPapers.title: Detecting pigments of cave paintings hidden beneath calcite layers: The potential of magnetic susceptibility and visible-to-infrared (400-2500 nm) reflectance spectroscopy
auditPapers.abstract: • Iron-based pigments in prehistoric rock paintings may be masked by calcite layers. • Magnetic susceptibility and reflectance spectroscopy (400–2500 nm) are non-invasive. • We propose MS and RS techniques associated with advanced statistical analysis. • Laboratory experiments detect iron-bearing pigments beneath up to 7 mm of calcite. • Prehistoric rock art is detected under 3 mm of calcite on a cave wall by MS and RS. Detecting cave paintings, protected but hidden beneath calcite layers, is an important step in completing the inventory of prehistoric art, yet it poses significant challenges. The mechanical removal of calcite is often invasive; image enhancement is often of limited effectiveness. This study investigates two non-invasive, complementary approaches to detect these hidden paintings: magnetic susceptibility and visible-to-infrared reflectance spectroscopy (400 to 2500 nm). Reflectance measurements give detailed insights into pigment composition, while magnetic susceptibility measures the magnetic properties of materials and is particularly effective in detecting iron-based pigments such as hematite and goethite. The two methods were first tested in the laboratory on a limestone slab painted with various pigments and covered with calcite speleothem masks of varying thickness. This setup was a proxy for prehistoric cave paintings covered by opaque calcite speleothems. Both reflectance spectroscopy and magnetic susceptibility were used to assess pigment detectability. Results showed that magnetic susceptibility could detect iron-based pigments beneath thin calcite layers (up to 7 mm in laboratory conditions), while reflectance spectroscopy analysis identified the spectral differences between all the materials tested, although the signal decreased with speleothem thickness. These findings were then validated in field tests at the Grande Grotte (Arcy-sur-Cure, France) where three prehistoric red ochre paintings covered by calcite were analysed. Both techniques were suitable for non-invasive detection: magnetic susceptibility was more effective for iron-based pigments, while reflectance spectroscopy provided broader mineralogical information. While these methods are not yet fully operational for field use, this preliminary study shows that it should be possible to use both magnetic susceptibility and reflectance spectroscopy probes to detect and delineate paintings hidden (and protected) beneath opaque calcite layers.

But for both, the ghostly world was part of their spiritual and social fabrics. Traditional Bengali ghosts were social beings, engendering ecumenical participation: both Hindus and Muslims warded off evil spirits, invoking Krishna and Allah. auditPapers.title: Comparative analysis of classics book review data created by users across Douban and Goodreads
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract While empirical research on online book reviews has advanced our understanding of book reception and everyday reading, more cross-platform and comparative analyses are needed to cross-examine and enrich existing perspectives on these topics. With book tagging, rating, and reviewing data collected from the two platforms, we examined how 144 classics identified by users on Goodreads and 141 classics on Douban were characterized and received across platforms. Our analysis reveals how book reviewers’ interests in and opinions about classics differ across platforms and demonstrates the necessity of gaining a more comprehensive understanding of classics. We also contribute a parallel dataset of classics across Goodreads and Douban for future investigations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first parallel classics dataset across Anglophone and non-Anglophone platforms. In addition, we identify three primary challenges in aligning and comparing cross-platform data regarding metadata quality, rating systems, and multi-lingual data processing. We present these challenges and discuss how we managed to overcome them. Our case study furthers existing conversations on the characterization and reception of classics online and informs future cross-platform online book review studies.

auditPapers.title: The chelation of silicone-treated wood artifacts to address sulfate precipitation
auditPapers.abstract: • Iron corrosion causes sulfate generation in artifacts treated via siloxane polymers. • Chemical chelation effectively penetrates siloxane-treated artifacts. • EDTA and ammonium citrate are effective in chelating siloxane-treated artifacts. • Ammonium citrate causes leaching of siloxane polymers. While the generation of sulfuric acid and iron sulfates has been known for at least 25 years in water-logged artifacts conserved with a mostly-reversible polyethylene glycol treatment, it has not previously been reported or treated in artifacts conserved using other methods. The issue is at least partially related to the presence of iron and iron corrosion products in the wrecks, and is therefore often treated through chelation to remove chemically iron from the artifacts. Now, sulfate salts and sulfuric acid have precipitated in artifacts from the 1686 La Belle wreck, which were conserved using silicone oil polymerization, a currently irreversible conservation technique. To determine whether the silicone would allow direct chelation of the iron, archaeological samples from the Heroine wreck were conserved using silicone polymerization and chelated for three months using ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and ammonium citrate. The chelated solutions were tested weekly with inductively coupled plasma-mass spectroscopy (ICP-MS) to determine the quantity of iron removed. Both EDTA and ammonium citrate were able to remove iron in similar quantities, with ammonium citrate initially removing it at a slightly faster rate. However, the ammonium citrate disrupted the silicone used to preserve the samples, making it an unviable method for treatment.

auditPapers.title: The Morality of Revolution: Reeducation Camps and the Politics of Punishment in Socialist Mozambique, 1974–1990. By Benedito Luís Machava
auditPapers.abstract: Benedito Machava’s The Morality of Revolution is an essential and engaging account of the post-colonial Mozambican government’s ill-fated attempts to impose a moral code via re-education camps to guide the revolution it sought to fulfill. Based on a tremendous depth of research, it provides a deep immersion into the creation of postcolonial Mozambique. It will be vital reading for anyone interested in Mozambican history or the wider story of postcolonial Africa. Machava’s introduction presents the book’s primary argument: that studying the intellectual history of public morality is essential in understanding postcolonial Mozambican politics. The introduction effectively shows that this history deserves to be read within African and global contexts, arguing that understanding Mozambican history contributes to a broader perspective on the interplay between morality and power in post-revolutionary political systems. The first chapter begins the intellectual history of Mozambique’s revolution, providing a background into the moral code of Samora Machel, Mozambique’s first President. It further shows how Machel’s moral code extended into his leadership of Frelimo (Mozambican Liberation Front), the rebel movement turned political party that fought for, and subsequently governed, independent Mozambique. The chapter convincingly locates Samora Machel’s ideology within religious ideals of salvation and rebirth as well as revolutionary (especially Chinese) ideas of complete social transformation. It also shows the depth of his commitment to this ideology; indeed, the book recounts Machel’s decision to sentence his younger sister and his children to moral reeducation, an astonishing illustration of his ideological devotion. Chapter 2 shows how Samora’s philosophy of revolutionary social redemption was put into practice soon after independence via the start of show trials and reeducation camps, initially targeting Frelimo’s political opponents. In the years following Frelimo’s takeover, the government dramatically expanded the camp system, as it began relocating hundreds of thousands of Mozambicans from urban to rural areas, both as a means of reforming morally suspect city dwellers and of furthering state-led development projects. Chapter 3 provides a detailed reconstruction of how the Frelimo government implemented this policy, culminating in the 1983 launch of Operation Production, a huge effort to dramatically expand the number of forced deportations; as the operation’s title made clear, the government’s objective was to further its goal of cleansing Mozambican society by remaking deportees into productive citizens who could contribute to the broader goal of national development. The enormous campaign transformed both the machinery of the Frelimo government and the lives of ordinary Mozambicans, as the forced migrations profoundly altered conceptions of citizenship in the reborn Mozambican state. Chapters 4 and 5 move beyond the ideologies and practices of high-ranking officials to examine how the deportation campaign shaped the actions and ideas of ordinary Mozambicans in their everyday lives. Chapter 4 is about how Mozambicans reproduced the ideology of moral cleansing and acted on that ideology by denouncing their neighbors. Chapter 5 explores the reeducation camps, to demonstrate how the lofty ambitions of social rebirth were totally divorced from the austere, isolated camps at which detainees arrived. Chapter 6 further pursues this analysis through an examination of the punishing daily life of camp inmates; cold, sick, and forgotten, they were the victims of widespread disease and terrible torture meted out by camp guards. Chapter 7 takes the history of the camps forward into the 1980s, when many camps were shut down and the detainees resettled into development villages, joined by a new wave of individuals sentenced under Operation Production. This history intersected with the expansion and intensification of the Mozambican Civil War—the country’s more well-known postcolonial tribulation—which brought even more tragic consequences for its citizens.

auditPapers.title: New Generations and the Hopes of Empire: Youth Premilitary Training in Early-Twentieth Century Eurasia
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In the early-twentieth century, state institutions and voluntary associations in the Ottoman, Habsburg, and Romanov empires envisioned a “new generation” of imperial subjects to reinvigorate patriotism serving as the bond between state and society. Premilitary training caused frictions between ministries and raised new issues of belonging and loyalty in those multiethnic societies. Eventually, the envisioned militarized imperial youth did not prove particularly effective in the framework of the First World War. However, those initiatives reveal a crisis in politics of difference as they reinforced activism in the name of empire albeit mostly limited to the empire’s respective “dominant” group: Sunni Turks, Catholic Germans, and Orthodox Russians. In so doing, premilitary training tested forms of mass mobilizations and remained a reference with which post-imperial societies in the republics of Turkey and Austria as well as the Soviet Union had to reckon.

auditPapers.title: Research on the authorship identification of The Tale of Genji based on quantitative analysis
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Numerous scholarly contributions have enriched our understanding of The Tale of Genji; however, the question of its authorship remains a subject of debate, with no definitive resolution to date. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of various linguistic indicators within The Tale of Genji, encompassing aspects such as distribution of part-of-speech, function words, word length, N-Grams, and sentence-segments. These characteristic parameters were subsequently utilized to perform principal component analysis, perform non-parametric tests, calculate relative entropy, and assess relative distances. The findings of this analysis reveal a remarkable consistency in writing style between Chapters 43–54 and the preceding Chapters 1–42 of The Tale of Genji. Consequently, the quantitative statistical examination presented in this study provides robust evidence to support the conclusion that a single authorship underlies the entire text of The Tale of Genji, refuting the hypothesis of a second author.

auditPapers.title: Report on the Development of Digital Humanities in China (first volume) （Zhongguo Shuzi Renwen Fazhan Baogao (Diyiji)). Huiling Feng
auditPapers.abstract: In 2004, Susan Schreibman and colleagues first brought together a wide range of theorists and practitioners to consider the significance of digital humanities as an independent discipline and reflect on its relationship with traditional humanities (Schreibman et al. 2004). In 2009, the concept of “digital humanities”—an imported term—was first introduced to Chinese academia by Professor Wang Xiaoguang from Wuhan University. Although many scholars such as Chen Jing have pointed out that there were already numerous digital humanities practices in China before this, facing the need for innovative research methods in the humanities and social sciences, it is crucial to systematically disseminate the latest content, research directions, and emerging frontiers of international digital humanities to domestic scholars in the humanities and social sciences, so as to expedite the evolution and transformation of research paradigms in China’s humanities disciplines (Wang 2010). Combining the reality in Chinese academic research, “digital humanities” is defined as a set of approaches to formulating, redefining, and answering academic questions. That is, humanists can use digital technologies, especially computer databases, as external tools to address academic questions they have previously posed, or to explore new issues inspired by digital technologies, and even to develop new research paradigms (Xu and Chen 2017). Edited by Feng Huiling, with Xia Cuihong and Liang Jihong as associate editors, Report on the Development of Digital Humanities in China (First Volume) is a work that demonstrates Chinese academia’s response to the global trend of digital humanities and its successful transformation of academic research in the digital era. In addition to the preface and appendices, the book is divided into four main parts, aiming to showcase the “remarkable journey of China’s digital humanities in its infancy” (Feng 2024) to the academic community. Led by the Institute for Digital Humanities at Renmin University of China, the book’s authors come from a wide range of backgrounds, including forty-seven educators and researchers from eighteen universities or research institutions across China, representing diverse disciplines.

auditPapers.title: Empire of Rags and Bones: Waste and War in Nazi Germany. By Anne Berg
auditPapers.abstract: Today, people value recycling as a public good—important both for environmental sustainability and as a way to demonstrate care for one’s community. In reality, such a view of recycling practices is idealistic at best. “Recycled” garbage largely goes to landfills; “donated” used clothing undermines local manufacturing in developing nations. Most people, however, prefer not to think about the waste they are creating, as long as it disappears weekly from the kerbside. The meanings and motivations behind waste management is thus a subject that warrants closer analysis. In the case of Nazi Germany, the topic speaks to three issues that have long captured the attention of scholars: the Nazi fixation on purity and hygiene; the regime’s support for initiatives that appear to anticipate the environmental movement; and its engagement of most citizens in ways that belie the ferocity of the dictatorship. Empire of Rags and Bones interrogates Nazi Germany as a “waste regime.” The book examines the myriad ways the German state and individual citizens sought to turn trash into usable resources, such as the collection of kitchen scraps to feed livestock or the abhorrent Müllwurst (trash “sausage’)—made from pulping waste—that was fed for a time to Mauthausen prisoners. It also offers a framework for understanding the nation’s leaders’ obsession with recycling, or as Berg puts it, the internal logic of the regime’s “quasi-religious hunt for junk” (3). Her argument unfolds over three roughly chronological sections, beginning in earnest with the Four-Year Plan in 1936 and ending with the first wave of post-defeat clean up. Berg maintains that the recycle-mania she describes reflects the regime’s “extractivist” imperial agenda fueled by an annihilationist worldview that pitted purity and order, represented by “Aryan” culture, against impurity and disorder, represented chiefly by Jews and Bolshevism.

auditPapers.title: The Two Princes of Mpfumo: An Early Eighteenth-Century Journey Into and Out of Slavery. By Lindsay O’Neill
auditPapers.abstract: This book tells the story of two princes, James Chandos Maffoom and his brother John Twogood Maffoom, who came from the Mpfumo area of Maputo Bay in modern Mozambique. In 1716 they and six attendants bearing gifts boarded an English ship as honored guests, intending to go to England on a diplomatic trade mission. The ship sailed first to Madagascar to fill its large hold with slaves, then Jamaica. During the voyage, the captain enslaved the princes and sold them in Jamaica—not the only time this happened to princes in the eighteenth century. The English lawyer who “discovered” them was shocked that elite African princes were being enslaved like common Black people on Jamaica. He purchased and freed the princes, and together they sailed with other ships for London. After a terrible shipwreck on the coast of Cuba that cost hundreds of lives, the princes arrived and remained in England for six years, first in London and then in Middlesex, where they became celebrities, yet were treated as curiosities, not equals, as was often the case with African princes in England during the eighteenth century. Meanwhile, the Royal African Company, the East India Company, and the Society for the Propagation of Christian Knowledge jostled over plans to manipulate the princes into assisting their projects in southeast Africa. Eventually, English reporting noted that the two brothers were fighting. Their ship departed for Maputo Bay in 1722 but foundered in the English Channel in a storm, and during the subsequent extended stay in Exmouth for repairs, James tried to kill his brother and then hanged himself. When the ship reached the Cape of Good Hope, imperial rivalry with the Dutch threatened the mission. Nevertheless, upon arrival in Maputo Bay, the missionary-trade project began well, and the English outperformed the Dutch, with the assistance of John, the nephew of the local ruler. Eventually, however, John, his uncle, and others changed their minds and ejected the British from their lands.

auditPapers.title: Colonial world-making and global knowledges at the early modern Cape of Good Hope
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract As the Cape of Good Hope was integrated into early modern colonial world-making projects, it came to be regarded as ‘the western part of the East Indies’. Exploring the causes and consequences of the Cape’s integration into the East Indies, this article underlines how contingent geopolitical designations reshaped scholarly descriptions of natures and cultures in southern Africa.

auditPapers.title: The conservation soft box (CSB): An innovative, versatile, and low-cost technique to preserve cultural heritage

auditPapers.title: Papyrus Economies and the Experience of Early Medieval Papal Documents
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The medium of papyrus, a ubiquitous, state-sponsored product in the Roman world, was turned by the empire’s loss of Egypt in the 630s–640s into a comparatively rare, high-status good in the early medieval northern Mediterranean (though not in the early caliphate, where it continued to have more or less the same value and associations as it had in the Roman period). The significance of papyrus altered radically as its economic value outside the Islamicate world shifted from a relatively easily obtainable, state-sponsored bulk product to a commodity available only at a few well-connected, wealthy centres: probably Constantinople and certainly Rome. The papacy continued to use this now precious commodity for its written communications. This was a crucial strategy in projecting its unique claims to authority across Latin Europe through the changing world of the late seventh to early eleventh centuries. Consequently, the sudden decline and disappearance of the Egyptian papyrus industry in the 950s-970s had its role to play in the transformation of papal government of the following century.
topics: Historical and Religious Studies of Rome

auditPapers.title: Integrating AI in historical research: a new method to analyzing national narratives
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a human-machine collaboration method to integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into historical research, specifically in the analysis of national narratives. Using President Ronald Reagan’s portrayal of America as a case study, the paper demonstrates how AI tools like natural language processing, BERTopic., and generative large language models, when guided by historians, can streamline the analysis of national narratives, significantly enhancing research efficiency. While AI tools have been successfully implemented in social science research, historical research requires more nuanced methods due to its emphasis on language and imagery within narratives. This study seeks to address this gap. This paper also examines the potential impact of AI on historical methodology, while acknowledging the challenges and limitations of integrating AI into historical research. Despite its promising capabilities, the paper argues that AI should be viewed as a research partner that assists historians with repetitive tasks, but underscores that human interpretation remains crucial for producing meaningful historical analysis.

auditPapers.title: Beyond Keeping the Lights On
auditPapers.abstract: This article reviews the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on public history sites and museums along the Lower Mississippi River Valley between 2020 and 2024. Constructed from interviews with sixty-seven sites across a four-year period, it uses a regional approach to examine how pandemic closures, reopening processes, and adaptations impacted public history sites and museums in the short-, medium-, and long-term, arguing that the pandemic created lasting changes through adaptation rather than large-scale closure of public history institutions. It concludes with an assessment of what can be learned from the pandemic period’s effect on public history.

auditPapers.title: The Practice of Simultaneously Curating Physical and Virtual Exhibits to Resist Against Institutional Memory Loss
auditPapers.abstract: Institutional memory, particularly on university campuses, is difficult to maintain. Preserving the institutional memory related to the activism, work, and community building done by marginalized communities, such as LGBTQ2S+ communities, is important to protect the communities’ histories, maintain the strides these communities have made, and inspire ongoing activism. I argue that curating exhibitions simultaneously in physical and virtual spaces as a public history practice relieves some of this burden on individuals having to maintain institutional memory and works to overcome some of the root causes of institutional memory loss. In addition to discussing the specific case study of the LGBTQIA2S+ McGill Student, Faculty, and Staff Activism physical and virtual exhibitions, this article includes guidelines for other institutions.

auditPapers.title: Being Like Mayberry
auditPapers.abstract: While the current controversy over Confederate monuments is a well-known aspect of Southern collective memory, less considered are the seemingly neutral sites of quotidian commemoration—named spaces that celebrate town founders, prominent residents, or local connections to a larger history—that dot the landscape of Southern localities in the United States. By uncovering the silences of named memorial sites in Avondale Estates, a historic suburb outside Atlanta, Georgia, this essay explores the ways in which such sites naturalize the white spatial imaginary and efface the presence of racialized power, with implications for contemporary placemaking and heritage.

auditPapers.title: Charting a Path Toward Historic Sites Sustainability
auditPapers.abstract: In 2021, Connecticut Landmarks worked with Museum Insights to create a model for assessing its twelve historic houses and developing new operating models that met the organization’s commitment to preservation and its goal to tell more of Connecticut’s stories through dialogic interpretation. This report will review the status of historic house museums and the perception that they are a moribund type of museum before explaining the development of the assessment frameworks, how the results of the assessment have been implemented at Connecticut Landmarks, and how the assessment frameworks could be adapted at other historic house museums to improve their operations.

auditPapers.title: Editor’s Corner
auditPapers.abstract: The four articles in this August issue examine preservation in many aspects, including the racial implications of historic commemoration and preservation; the preserving of historical sites affected by the COVID-19 shutdowns; recommendations for the preservation and management of historical house museums and sites; and the preservation of precarious records created by campus organizations.First, we feature Kathryn E. Wilson’s “Being like Mayberry: Memory, Landscape, and the White Spatial Imaginary in an Atlanta Suburb.” Wilson asks us to look beyond Confederate memorials and tributes to the Civil Rights Movement to consider how more “modest forms of quotidian commemoration” shape local history in the South and the nation. As she argues, street names, plaques and other signage, community celebrations, and other everyday parts of the built and cultural environment create and support “versions of history that produce normative and naturalized relations of power.” Often, as in the Atlanta suburb of Avondale Estates, these power relations are implicitly or explicitly racialized, equating order, safety, and cleanliness with whiteness. Wilson considers how local and national preservation law and practice has served to bolster a vision of the past and present that justify white supremacy while at the same time masking it in a language of race neutrality. The “white spatial imaginary” (a phrase of George Lipsitz employed by Wilson) continues to shape Avondale Estates today, as Wilson’s graduate students found through interviews with local residents.Next, “Beyond Keeping the Lights On: COVID-19’s Impact on Lower Mississippi River Valley Museums and Public History Sites,” by Liz Skilton and Ian Beamish, examines the short- and long-term effects of pandemic shutdowns on the area’s historic sites. Skilton and Beamish had planned to take students on a study-travel course on the Mississippi River in late March 2020. Instead, they worked with their students to “start answering a question we were preoccupied with: were the public history institutions we were set to visit at risk of permanent closure due to the shutdown? And, if so, what would public history sites and museums (or public history as a profession) look like at the end of the closure period?” Skilton and Beamish used the results of class research to track the effects of the lockdown period on Mississippi River Valley historical sites during and for several years after the shutdowns. Their work shows that although an estimate that 30 percent of all museums would close permanently circulated widely, the actual number of closures was quite small. At that same time, museums and historic sites were significantly impacted by the shutdown, in terms of loss of income, staff layoffs, and reliance on virtual programing.Additionally, this issue brings two Reports from the Field. The first, “Charting a Path toward Historic Sites Sustainability: Mission, Money, and Meaning,” was co-authored by representatives of Museum Insights, a museum consulting firm, and Connecticut Landmarks (CTL), a preservation organization. The authors, Sara Patton Zarrelli, Guy Hermann, Aaron Marcavitch, and Shaelyn Amaio together examine the issues facing historic properties and offer concrete, actionable recommendations to help historical organizations “make thoughtful decisions about management of resources (properties, finances, and people) in times of relative calm that will, thereafter, lead to the development of an operating model that will sustain the organization long-term.” They first describe the process they used and then propose a toolkit that can be applied to other, similar organizations across the country.Alex Ketchum, in “The Practice of Simultaneously Curating Physical and Virtual Exhibits to Resist Against Institutional Memory Loss: Keeping LGBTQIA2S+ Campus Histories Alive,” also offers a roadmap. Here Ketchum demonstrates how curating physical and virtual exhibitions together help prevent the kind of “memory loss” that is prevalent in in university settings, with their frequent turnover of faculty, staff, and especially, students. Ketchum argues that “digital humanities strategies such as distributed knowledge production, collaboration, multimodal creation and distribution, animating the archive, accessibility, and sustainability, curating of physical and virtual exhibitions at the same time works to overcome some of the root causes of institutional memory loss.” As she stresses, this kind of work is especially essential for marginalized communities, including the LGBTQ+ community at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, the focus of the exhibition.Our review section also focuses on Montréal, the host city of this year’s annual meeting of the National Council on Public History. Featured are four reviews of sites or tours highlighted for conference attendees.

auditPapers.title: An Unformed Map: Geographies of Belonging between Africa and the Caribbean By Philip Janzen
auditPapers.abstract: Philip Janzen’s innovative, insightful book offers new perspectives on the modern Black Atlantic by foregrounding African diasporic exchanges heretofore occluded by official archives. An Unformed Map takes the form of a collective biography of some 500 individuals who were born in the Caribbean and served as colonial officials and administrators in French and British African colonies from the 1880s through the 1940s. Some of these officials are well-known to historians—the eventual governor of Chad, Félix Éboué, for example—while others were otherwise anonymous schoolteachers, sanitary inspectors, and railway employees. What bound them together was a shared experience as onsite intermediaries between European colonial administrations and African societies, inflected by these civil servants’ status as double outsiders: too Black and too Caribbean to be accepted as European; too foreign and too associated with colonial hierarchies to be accepted as African. The result was a class of individuals “isolated on two fronts” (32). Such isolation, Janzen demonstrates, led this group of Caribbean-born African officials to engage deeply with the contradictions of empire. In the process, they created new “geographies of belonging” that drew upon the interconnected histories and shared experiences of the Black Atlantic.
