auditPapers.title: EDITORS’ INTRODUCTION: TRANSLATION, MIGRATION, NARRATIVE
auditPapers.abstract: Empirical, positivist approaches have long dominated migration history and migration studies and shaped these fields with their research questions, theoretical approaches, and methodologies. However, the data, interpretations, explanations, and narratives of migration and society produced in this framework have come under criticism in recent years. This critique includes challenges to methodological nationalism, the construction of migration as a problem requiring intervention and regulation, the production of sedentarism as the normal, the use of categories and concepts that place migranticized people in subaltern positions, and the reproduction of colonial knowledge structures by privileging Western perspectives.1 Decolonizing research on migration, mobility-induced social change, and diversity that considered migration societies (Migrationsgesellschaften) as the norm and understood mobility and migration as constitutive elements of the conditio humana took different forms and paces within different disciplines, in different academic communities in the Global North and South, and across the Atlantic and Pacific. It also led to a growing number of interdisciplinary initiatives. The reflexive turn in migration studies transformed vague critique at the margins into a dynamic drive for a paradigm shift at the center of migration research, demanding fundamental transformations to long-established epistemologies, power structures, and disciplinary traditions in this multidisciplinary, international, and often highly politicized field.2 Our own intellectual trajectories reflect these shifts. As historians of migration policies and societies, we began collaborating to explore connections between histories of labor migration in Europe (Christoph Rass's expertise) and in the United States (Julie M. Weise's expertise). As we worked, we realized that the largely empirical research methodologies on which we both usually relied left too much unexplained. We needed a better way to analyze the circulation of ideas about migration management around the Atlantic and beyond—not just among policymakers but also among migrants themselves. As we engaged with theories of translation on a broad register, we were better able to interpret the documents in front of us, but more than this, we were pushed to rethink the ways we narrated migration history as a whole.3 We were fortunate to enlist leading German and US historians and literary, cultural, and ethnic studies scholars to join us in this critical reflection and methodological and narrative experimentation in the interdisciplinary field of migration history. Our shared foundation is an understanding of “translation” as a broad theoretical umbrella that includes all activities transposing sensual data into tangible and communicable—that is, social and aesthetic—forms. Inspired by Alexandra Lianeri's June 2024 reading of Theo Hermans's Translation and History: A Textbook,4 we explore these concepts of translation as parts of a fundamental paradigm that can enrich migration research not just as a methodological tool but as a critical force in shaping social reality and producing the knowledge we study and perform. Reflexive migration research demands a critical assessment of our epistemologies, our methods, and our roles as authors coproducing migration—or migrantization—through the choices we make while creating translations of the world into text.5 In her work on the reflexive turn, cultural theorist Doris Bachmann-Medick has highlighted how sociocultural and disciplinary frameworks and research practices themselves eventually co-constitute and re-produce the categories of difference that they claim to merely describe.6 At the same time, Bachmann-Medick has conceptualized translation as a transformative cultural practice that includes, but is not limited to, linguistic transfer. Translation is a continuum of ongoing acts negotiating and reconfiguring contested and contingent meanings across cultural, disciplinary, and temporal boundaries. It reshapes not only the original “object” of translation but also its contexts of origin and destination. This view configures translation as an analytical tool and metaphor for understanding cultural contact zones, power differentials, and knowledge production. As a methodology in practice, this equips us with a pragmatic model for navigating the complexities of interdisciplinary and intercultural scholarship. Understanding knowledge production as a translational effort makes ambiguities, hybridity, and contested meaning-making legible within a productive space for dialogue. This changes how we, as scholars, approach and analyze our source materials, represent the knowledge we produce, and do interdisciplinary research.7 Overall, this “Translation, Migration, Narrative” forum uses the framework of translation studies to make two principal arguments. First, we argue that theories of translation can point the way toward a critical self-reflexive approach to understanding ourselves, historians of migration, as not merely interpreters but also translators of history. In this endeavor, our authors have particularly appreciated the work of Thomas Nail, Theo Hermans, and Andrew Abbott. Nail's concept of “kinopolitics” creating the “figure of the migrant” demonstrates how the production of such figures, including by scholars, generates subaltern positions in a hierarchical social order and points out how translation becomes materially and politically consequential.8 Additionally, Hermans merged historical scholarship and translation studies by arguing for the inherent translingual dimension of the sociohistorical process, the study of knowledge production, and our doing knowledge while translating the past into history.9 Abbott has gone further to challenge disciplinary traditions privileging narratives structured by dominant choices and institutionalized practices; his “lyrical sociology” advocates for epistemological emancipation through his search for alternative modes of translating complex social realities into knowledge.10 Second, we argue that greater attention to linguistic and cultural translations, as found within typical historical sources, can yield penetrating insights into migrant agency and experiences that would otherwise remain hidden. We have found it particularly fruitful to draw on theoretical reflections and scholarship at the intersection of translation studies and postcolonial studies (for example, Paul F. Bandia, Homi K. Bhabha, and Mary Louise Pratt) in interpreting migrant archives and experiences. Both Bandia11 and Bhabha12 expanded translation from a linguistic process to a broader cultural process of negotiating meaning and identity in asymmetric colonial and postcolonial power relations. Whereas Bhabha stressed the outcome by focusing on hybridity and ambivalence, Bandia conceptualized the diasporic struggle for agency between being translated and translating the self. Indeed, this tension between translation as a way that society's most powerful actors (including scholars) attempt to control mobile human beings and translation as a way for migrants to engage in creative self-invention marks both dimensions of our forum's argument. In the forum's opening intervention, literary scholar Laura A. Zander (University of Münster and Osnabrück University) theorizes from an analysis of Nigerian author Helon Habila's 2019 novel Travelers.13 She shows how Habila's novel brings to the fore the ways in which intellectuals (in this case, the novel's protagonists) translate lived human experience into a limited set of migrant “types”—or, in Nail's words, “figure[s] of the migrant”—that are legible to the surrounding society. Zander's essay challenges historians of migration to reflect on how our own practices inadvertently mimic this reductionism and to consider how our texts could instead function, like the literature she analyzes, as a “contact zone” between migrants’ creative self-translations and the legal narratives that objectify them.14 Building on Bachmann-Medick's conceptualization of translation as a cultural and analytical practice, ethnic studies scholar Catherine S. Ramírez (University of California, Santa Cruz) and historian Christoph Rass (Osnabrück University) explore in their forum contribution how “integration” is constructed, translated, and institutionalized in Germany and the US.15 Their approach, which combines translation theory with conceptual history, challenges the traditional understanding of the evolution of what “integration” means. They demonstrate how political, economic, and historical forces actively shape the meaning of integration, using it as a medium to translate individuals into “migranticized figures.” They also interrogate underlying processes of knowledge production and meaning-making as acts of translation that both regulate belonging and reinforce social hierarchies. Translation theory makes “integration” legible not as a neutral category but as embodying historical power relations that contribute to the reproduction of exclusionary mechanisms and the perpetuation of unequal power dynamics. Three forum contributions, two coauthored by German and US scholars, then engage in interdisciplinary analyses and methodological experiments that focus on moments of linguistic translation to situate migration history as a “contact zone” between migrant agency and discursive and structural control by states and capitalists. These pieces show how translation can be operationalized as a mode of interpreting typical historical sources: migrant political expressions, archival documents, and autobiographies. Historians Albert Manke (Ca’ Foscari University of Venice) and Fredy González (University of Illinois Chicago) use multiple theories of translation to reexamine the political self-representation of Chinese migrants’ sworn brotherhood organizations over a century and a half of diasporic evolution.16 In particular, the organizations’ strategy of self-representing as “masonic lodges,” and even shifting their visual iconography to reinforce this image, expanded their political space for operation and challenged outsiders’ representation of them as threatening. By following Hermans's thoughts on the fundamental power of translation to shape social reality, these moments of linguistic translation become, for Manke and González, ways of understanding the brotherhoods’ creative agency and the powerful constraints within which they operated in an era of overt anti-Chinese racism. Cultural studies scholar Peter Schneck (Osnabrück University) and historian Julie M. Weise (University of Oregon) focus on a single 1954 document from the archives of the labor recruitment agency for the South African Chamber of Mines to conceptualize the archives of migration as repositories of translation.17 They look beyond physical mobility to see the ways that linguistic translation implicated the Malawian migrants’ “left-behind” family members whose translated words appear in the document. Bandia's concept of migrants as “beings in translation” creates a unifying frame for understanding migrants and their family members as part of a single process, even as analyses of two contrasting works of literature from the Mexico–US border point to the ways that Malawian migrants themselves experienced creative agency through translation while, for their family members, translation was primarily a constraint. Historian Anand A. Yang (University of Washington) then reconsiders heavily cited migrant self-writings through the lens of translation.18 He shows how the testimonies of North Indian contract laborers Totaram Sanadhya and Munshi Rahman Khan disrupted official colonial accounts and highlighted migrants’ lived experiences as both “translated beings” (Bandia)19 and self-translators forging new identities (Bhabha). Language choices—especially in Hindi—and personal perspectives emerge as key to understanding how migrants translated experiences of suffering, their advocacy for abolition, and their diasporic selves into their life-writing. By complicating historians’ treatment of these rarely preserved voices, Yang underscores their significance for a deeper, noncolonial understanding of how marginalized communities shaped their own narratives and identities in global migration histories. Even as the four middle pieces apply translation as a methodology to rethink familiar topics and sources in migration history, they also point the way toward critical acts of self-reflection for the historian. Indeed, just as German and US scholars, politicians, and bureaucrats, Chinese sworn brotherhood leaders, mine labor recruitment agents, and former Indian contract laborers engaged in power-laden acts of translation, so too do we as scholars of history. In the forum's final piece, literary scholar Kirsten Silva Gruesz (University of California, Santa Cruz) offers yet another provocation to historians of migration and their audiences.20 Whereas Zander's opening essay asks us to engage in critical self-reflection to push against our tendencies to order migrants as capitalists and the state have done, Gruesz's closing intervention asks us to consider entirely new forms of scholarly communication. Drawing on literary inspiration and Abbott's demand to move from structured narrative to lyrical representations of knowledge, Gruesz presents list, interruption, and assemblage as alternate modes of translating the migrant experience beyond “story.” Indeed, if the “figure of the migrant” (as conceptualized by Nail) is produced by a constellation of discourses, then the stories that historians tell are surely among them. Methodological case studies work in concert with Gruesz's call for new forms of translating migrant experience, together challenging us to find new possibilities within the inextricable ambiguities of our archives, narratives, and interpretations.

auditPapers.title: FROM HOFSTADTER TO LEPORE: NATIONAL HISTORY FOR THE AMERICAN PUBLIC
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT Nick Witham's Popularizing the Past: Historians, Publishers, and Readers in Postwar America provides cogent and accurate accounts of the careers of five American academic historians of the post‐World War II era who won large popular audiences for national narratives: Richard Hofstadter, Daniel Boorstin, John Hope Franklin, Howard Zinn, and Gerda Lerner. Witham omits, without explanation, the highly relevant case of Oscar Handlin, author of the 1951 work The Uprooted: The Epic Story of the Great Migrations That Made America . He also fails to engage the heavily Jewish ethnoreligious matrix of popular American historiography of the postwar era. In Popularizing the Past , Witham is directly concerned with today's challenges for writing popular national histories, and he argues that the very idea of a single, national audience has been rendered anachronistic by ideological polarization and media fragmentation. Whereas Witham insists that works resembling Jill Lepore's 2018 book These Truths: A History of the United States should no longer be attempted, he upholds Ibram X. Kendi's 2016 volume, Stamped from the Beginning: The Definitive History of Racist Ideas in America , as an example of what is appropriate today: a narrative for a certain community of readers, and not for other readers. Witham's essentially sound account of major features of postwar American writings about history is marred by his jejune comments about the early twenty‐first century. He leaves us with only a shadow of the witness that each of Witham's subject‐historians bore with distinction to the mission of discovering and disseminating the truth about American history in the interests of a national community.

auditPapers.title: The First Amerasians: Mixed Race Koreans from Camptowns to America. By Yuri W. Doolan
auditPapers.abstract: Once considered a personal and apolitical act, transnational adoption has been reconceptualized by scholars of U.S. history, gender, and postcolonialism as a practice whose origins lie in Cold War geopolitics, particularly as Asia became increasingly central to U.S. strategic interests in the mid-twentieth century. Yuri W. Doolan’s The First Amerasians: Mixed Race Koreans from Camptowns to America extends this line of inquiry by urging a critical reassessment of the term “Amerasian,” used to describe children of mixed parentage born to Asian women and U.S. soldiers, many of whom became among the first internationally adopted children. Doolan contends that the Amerasian is not a neutral racial category but “an important figure in U.S. political culture—a Cold War construct—that has helped Americans to explain and promote, both at home and in the world, the dominant ideas undergirding the Cold War” (2). In this thoroughly researched and attentively written book, Doolan traces the evolution of the Amerasian category from the onset of the Korean War in 1950, a pivotal moment that positioned South Korea as a key site of U.S. military and humanitarian intervention, to the passage of the Amerasian Homecoming Act in 1982, which legally defined Amerasians as primarily biracial children from Korea and Vietnam. In doing so, Doolan underscores Korea’s centrality to understanding U.S. postwar modernity (12).

auditPapers.title: The Eastern International: Arabs, Central Asians, and Jews in the Soviet Union’s Anticolonial Empire By Masha Kirasirova
auditPapers.abstract: The Eastern International has been so long anticipated by historians of Central Asia, the Soviet Union, and the Middle East that it had already been cited widely in manuscript or dissertation form well before it appeared as a book. The long anticipation is warranted: this is the type of work that launches a thousand dissertations, and it speaks to the book’s importance that its lacunae present less as deficiencies than as opportunities. Kirasirova’s book is, at least on a surface level, a kind of begriffsgeschichte, a history of the idea of the “East” throughout the Soviet period and across its geographical span. Kirasirova’s analysis thus entails a sizable amount of intellectual and cultural history: for example, it parses the arguments of Old Bolshevik Konstantin Troianovskii about the “East” and its potential for revolution in the years immediately following 1917 (chapter 1) and analyzes the films of Uzbek actor and director Kamil Yarmatov in the Cold War era of postcolonial cultural diplomacy (chapter 6). Across the book’s chapters, which span the entire Soviet period in chronological order, Kirasirova foregrounds the constructed and contested nature of the “East,” a nebulousness that made the category both powerful and dangerous. For Troianovskii, writing in the years immediately following the 1917 revolution, the “East” held massive potential as a driver of world revolution beyond Europe: it could spearhead an “Eastern International,” bringing together the newly Soviet, but historically Muslim regions of the Caucasus and Central Asia with the territories of the former Ottoman Empire, of South Asia, and even of China and Southeast Asia. As ephemeral as Troianovskii’s career may have been, Kirasirova argues, his geopolitical ideas “run like a thread” through the Bolshevik institutions designed for promoting world revolution (57). By the time Kamil Yarmatov made his mature body of work in the 1960s, a new kind of geopolitics was at play, situating Yarmatov as a crucial Cold War intermediary for the many foreigners who visited Tashkent for the Afro-Asian Film Festival of 1968. Billed as a participant in the Revolution and an authentic Easterner, Yarmatov brought together the ideological and geopolitical priorities of his time, but he struggled to bridge the contradictions between Soviet ideas and global ideas of decolonization. Both of these case studies emphasize the constructedness of the category of the “East” and its malleability in the context of shifting geopolitical priorities and of the longer history of Orientalism in the Russian Empire.

auditPapers.title: ‘Liberal’ Virtues and Values, Women’s ‘Genius’, and the British Literary Reviews, c. 1750–1795
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In 1764, while discussing female authors one critic suggested that the views of ‘the liberal’ were normative. But what did it mean to be a ‘liberal’ at this time? This article examines the ‘liberal and enlightened’ patterns of thought popularized by reviewers who belonged to the network of friends and acquaintances of the founders of the Monthly Review , the dissenters Ralph Griffiths and William Rose. Opposing different forms of ‘tyranny’, or authoritarianism, critics promoted ‘liberal and rational’ political principles and a social morality comprising the values of open-mindedness, reason, toleration, and ‘equity’ or justice as fairness. Focusing in particular on issues relating to gender, this article shows how conceptions of the ‘liberal spirit’ informed accounts of women’s capabilities, of their ‘genius’ and rationality. By the 1780s, the language of ‘liberal sentiments’ had spread within print culture, appearing in the New Annual Register , founded by Andrew Kippis, a leading critic at the Monthly , and in the work of political and social theorists such as Major John Cartwright or James Mackintosh. Yet, defeating stereotypical notions of gender could be complicated even for men who aspired to a place within the elite of the ‘enlightened’ or ‘liberal and philosophical’.

auditPapers.title: No Country for Old Age: America's War on Aging from Valley Forge to Silicon Valley By Mischa Honeck
auditPapers.abstract: The 2024 election cycle revived a longstanding American concern with old age. I don’t mean a concern with actually existing older people and their need for Social Security and adequate nursing care. That population remained, as usual, an afterthought. The concern, in 2024, was about the gerontocracy: the idea that older people have too much power, and need to make way for the young. That concern has been present in America since the founding. In No Country for Old Age, Mischa Honeck explores that long history—tracing, as the subtitle promises, a history of a prejudice from the eighteenth century to the present. This is a brisk book, moving in nine chapters and just over two hundred pages through a vast historical terrain. The first chapter, entitled “Phoenix Rising,” gives a flavor of Honeck’s method. It begins with William Barton’s quixotic attempt to make the phoenix, rather than the bald eagle, the symbol of the nation. America, Barton insisted, was a land of longevity—understood not as a celebration of old age, but as an extension of youthful dynamism, as represented by the phoenix. He attempted to prove this scientifically, too, participating in the new science of demographics to show the remarkable longevity of American citizens. Honeck starts the book with Barton because he perfectly encapsulates Honeck’s own method, which brings together cultural history and the history of science.

auditPapers.title: The Second Battle for Africa: Garveyism, the U.S. Heartland, and Global Black Freedom By Erik S. McDuffie
auditPapers.abstract: “This book is a manifesto,” writes Erik S. McDuffie in the first sentence of his impressive new monograph, The Second Battle for Africa: Garveyism, the U.S. Heartland, and Global Black Freedom. McDuffie really means it! Drawing on research conducted over ten years, in nine countries, including interviews conducted with more than 100 subjects, The Second Battle for Africa sets out to fill in a number of gaps—some distressingly wide—that hamper our ability to understand the full scope of the Black liberation struggle. McDuffie makes a convincing case for the enduring significance of Garveyism specifically, and Black nationalism generally, as a political formation. He demonstrates the centrality of the U.S. Midwest as a place of Black politics-making. And he shows how these political threads were held together by the organizational genius of the Black women, many little-known, who populate his story. Despite a renewed scholarly focus on Garveyism in recent years, there remains a discordance between our awareness of the global importance of the movement and our understanding of what Garveyism’s political success tells us about the innumerable communities it mobilized. McDuffie shows that Black Midwesterners, like Black people everywhere, were captivated by Marcus Garvey’s message of deliverance: a call to Black people to resist the assimilationist premises and promises of the Eurocentric domestic (and global) order, to look to their own communities for the resources to survive, and to embrace the principles of Black pride, diasporic solidarity, and race-based organizing. Black Midwesterners pursued this vision by eagerly joining, and doggedly sustaining, local divisions of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA), the organization founded by Garvey and Amy Ashwood (Garvey) in 1914. McDuffie’s book, which traces the work of the UNIA in the Midwest from World War I to the election of Ronald Reagan (and up to the present in the conclusion), is the first to tell the history of the organization from start to finish, and the first to show how the UNIA continued to shape Black liberation politics for several decades after the organization’s 1920s heyday. McDuffie also shows how the influence of Garveyism far outstripped the reach of the UNIA and became manifest in what he calls the “midwestern Garveyite front”: the labyrinth of political, religious, and cultural organizations that were influenced by—and gave new shape to—the Black nationalist politics propounded by Marcus Garvey and Garveyites, and that surged again during the Black Power era. This presentation of Garveyism reveals both its flexibility and its enduring appeal. McDuffie shows how Garveyism was mobilized, in different moments, toward radical and conservative ends; how, in the form of the “Garveyite front,” it could be refashioned to meet new needs and serve new political purposes. What remained consistent across the twentieth century was that, again and again, Garvey’s Black nationalist message succeeded in galvanizing Black people to action, spurring organizational growth, and shaping the contours of midwestern politics. “Garveyism,” writes McDuffie, “was the most potent political, cultural, and social force in the twentieth-century Black world.”

auditPapers.title: Recent advances in the analytical and experimental study of mineralised textiles
auditPapers.abstract: Mineralised textiles — altered remnants of organic textiles preserved by the diffusion of metallic cations from nearby artefacts or the environment — have gradually emerged as an essential source of information on the production and use of textiles in prehistoric and antique societies, as well as on their implication on the economy, technological developments and trade. In many contexts, they are the only evidence of productions known either indirectly through tools or not at all. In this review, we highlight the contribution of analytical methods in recent years to their study, an evolution that began with the emerging use of optical and then electron microscopy in the 1960s and 1970s. In particular, we describe the most recent period, which has seen (i) the widespread use of digital optical microscopy in laboratories and museums, (ii) the adoption of approaches aimed at characterising molecular signatures, even for highly altered textiles, and (iii) the development of micro-imaging methods, particularly using synchrotron radiation or laser sources. We are finding that these methods are making an increasing contribution to the field of archaeology. We outline possible prospects for the research and documentation of mineralised textiles and the possible impact of imaging methods on museum displays.

auditPapers.title: The Poetry of Failure
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Institutional records and reports, letters, and logbook entries are often the bread and butter of historical research, and the experience of extracting the depth and texture of these resources draws us back to the archive. Still, creative inspiration can wax and wane throughout a long project. In this essay, Johnson explores the utility of poetic inquiry as a method for getting “unstuck” in the face of waning inspiration. Poetic inquiry relies on a close reading of the source material, followed by the extraction and artful rearrangement of words and phrases that highlight themes in the original text. Johnson deploys poetic inquiry to analyze the student records of influenza orphans at Girard College. Accentuating the original texture and color of the sources, Johnson assembles three short, haiku-style poems distilling the resilience of influenza survivors, whose relationships ably stretched across new geographies and institutions following separation in the pandemic aftermath. Ultimately, the practice underscores how poetry and historical analysis connect us to the depth of human experience.

auditPapers.title: The Weak and the Powerful: Omar Torrijos, Panama, and the Non-Aligned Movement in the World By Jonathan C. Brown
auditPapers.abstract: Jonathan Brown has written an insightful study of Panamanian General Omar Torrijos’s long struggle to gain control of the Panama Canal Zone from the United States to make his country a truly sovereign nation. The central problem Torrijos faced upon seizing power in a 1968 military coup was confronting the world’s most powerful state—which had reduced Panama to a neo-colony for nearly seventy years though its mastery of the Canal and the enclave that surrounded it. Panama had a population of only 2 million and territory smaller than South Carolina. The ingenious strategy that Torrijos adopted was to take advantage of the international environment of the 1960s-1970s as smaller states in Africa, Asia, and Latin America broke free of imperial domination to chart their own independence. Brown focuses the bulk of his study on the personality and vision of Torrijos, who was born in obscurity, the son of rural schoolteachers. Through twenty years of service in the Panamanian National Guard, Torrijos developed a strong sense of solidarity with the majority of his country’s impoverished population. He adopted a center-left political stance contrary to most of the hard-right caudillos of Latin America during the Cold War. While certainly a dictator, Torrijos proved far less repressive than the bloody tyrants of his era and pushed for moderate land and labor reforms. He moved to construct a populist base in contrast to the oligarchic rule of Panamanian elites—the so-called rabiblancos—who generally accommodated the hegemonic U.S. presence on the isthmus.

auditPapers.title: Identification of low-concentration tar in wood samples from archaeological contexts by ATR-FTIR
auditPapers.abstract: The investigation of pine tar residues in wood recovered from a waterlogged historic pine tar production site is presented. The site is a wood tar kiln constructed in a mire, a mode of production distinct to Central Norway. Due to lack of surviving visible wood tar, this study involves a non-invasive and micro-destructive approach. Samples taken from the wood were analyzed by a combination of fluorescence microscopy, attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR), and Scanning Electron Microscopy coupled with Energy Dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). Due to low concentrations of surviving wood tar, the study aimed at developing a method to reliably identify and differentiate the scarce tar residues from the wood substrate in the specimens. The results were compared against known reference materials of modern pine tar, as well as tar residue extracted from a medieval archaeological textile.

auditPapers.title: ENTANGLING KNOWLEDGE AND IGNORANCE
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT This review essays situates Alain Corbin's Terra Incognita: A History of Ignorance in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries within current discussions of knowledge and ignorance related to intellectual history, the history of science, and the history of knowledge. These varying approaches have drawn the borderland between knowledge and ignorance divergently. After a brief critique of the Corbin's positivist approach in Terra Incognita , I sketch some well‐known ground in the history of science over the past two generations. I then point to how recent discussions of the relationships between intellectual history, the history of science, and the history of knowledge have tended to sidestep that history. I conclude by suggesting how indigenous studies and Corbin's own previous work might serve to better entangle knowledge and ignorance in ways that might draw on the strengths of all three fields.

auditPapers.title: Taken for granted? Investigating constructivist principles with Bayes’ theorem in Digital Humanities scholarship
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article investigates the intersection of constructivist principles and statistical methods within Digital Humanities (DH) scholarship. While constructivist principles are foundational, albeit often implicit, in DH scholarship, the increasing use of statistical methods, especially Bayesian approaches, introduces epistemological tensions. Therefore, this article examines the latent constructivist assumptions in DH and explores how these principles resonate with or diverge from the epistemic premises of Bayesian statistics. It argues that there are interferences between Bayesian statistics and constructivism. The main aim is to reveal how epistemological assumptions shape knowledge production, in order to pave the way for a more reflective epistemology of DH scholarship.

auditPapers.title: The ‘People of the Pagoda’ and the 1963 Buddhist Mobilization in Huế, Vietnam
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract A new, ground-up narrative of the Buddhist Mobilization of Huế in central Vietnam in the summer of 1963 highlights the voices of its participants – the ‘People of the Pagoda’. Drawing on local records and personal narratives, the article explores the process of how the ‘People of the Pagoda’ forged a collective identity from daily activism and protests for religious equality. Months of various nonviolent collective actions – in the form of demonstrations, hunger strikes, and self-immolations – developed a strong, broad community within the distinctive spaces of Buddhist temples. The article emphasizes the relevance of culture, morals, emotions and identity in the Buddhist Mobilization’s enduring impacts on personal awareness and community networks. In contrast to much top-down, politically-oriented, and Sài Gòn-centric scholarship on this event in Vietnam War historiography, this essay examines the mobilization as a social movement in its own right and seeks to restore Huế’s significant historical role as the birthplace of this movement.

auditPapers.title: Canoes in the Early English Caribbean: The Role of an Indigenous Technology in Making Mercantilism Work
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The Caribbean, with its focus on cash crop production, played a major role in the rise of England’s Atlantic trading system and the making of modern capitalism. Yet, there remains poor understanding of the processes by which the early colonizers built the economic and social capabilities necessary to extract wealth from an alien environment, and a common assumption that they relied overwhelmingly on metropolitan skills and knowledge. This article addresses these issues through a study of the canoe, an Indigenous transport technology. The first imperative of successful settlement was to construct robust regional supply networks and, although the colonizers were fortunate in that the fragmented Caribbean island-scape possesses abundant land and marine resources, they lacked the knowledge and tools necessary for effective extraction and distribution. The newcomers turned to native residents to develop the skills required to manage local geography and soon recognized the utility of canoes, dug out of single logs, with their low cost, shallow draft, speed, and agility, and learned how these boats should be made and used. Canoes in a range of sizes became objects in everyday use among the English colonists and played a central role in moving people, goods, and information around the region, with its shallows and tyrannical wind system; served as platforms for resource extraction; and provided a necessary defence capability. Understanding the challenges encountered in managing the Caribbean environment, and bringing canoes into the picture, pulls Indigenous people into sharper focus and highlights some of the transcultural exchanges that made mercantilism work.

auditPapers.title: The Guardian Angels: Anticrime Activism and “Popular Neoliberalism” in Crisis-era New York City
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Recent historical scholarship has begun to explore the agency of grassroots actors in the ascent of neoliberalism in late twentieth-century New York, uncovering a history of neoliberalism “from the bottom up.” This article builds upon this scholarship by addressing the work of the Guardian Angels, an anticrime patrol group of Black and Latino youths led by Curtis Sliwa, in developing a form of “popular neoliberalism” in the 1970s and 1980s that complemented emergent approaches to crime, policing, and urban citizenship while connecting with the histories and everyday experiences of ordinary residents. Providing a close reading of the ideological content of the group’s activism and its wider public reception and dissemination within a context of high crime and municipal austerity, dysfunction, and neglect, it argues that the Angels and their patrols performed important ideological work: normalizing the pivot to private and voluntarist initiative in the resolution of social problems and enfranchising new ideas integral to neoliberal governance and governmentality on the ground. Overlooked in the scholarship on New York’s neoliberal turn, the Guardian Angels serve to illustrate the extent of popular participation in, even validation of, New York’s late twentieth-century transformation.

auditPapers.title: Impacts of sea-level rise and wave inundation in the Tongariki Complex, Rapa Nui
auditPapers.abstract: Sea-level rise (SLR) threatens both modern assets and the irreplaceable, tangible heritage of past coastal settlements. Assessment of SLR inundation on coastal cultural sites has been a topic of growing interest but the distribution of research is globally uneven and particularly scarce in Pacific Islands. Using XBeach in 2D non-hydrostatic mode we simulate the wave environment under future SLR scenarios in the Tongariki Complex, Rapa Nui, to estimate the extent of wave- and SLR-induced inundation. We model the extent of SLR-induced flooding at current mean higher high water and SLR scenarios of 1.2 m and 3 m. Wave modeling is accomplished using 1-yr and 100-yr swell event return periods. We find that cultural assets are within the reach of wave run-up at current sea level and the number of assets impacted could triple by 2100. Particularly, we estimate that the iconic Ahu Tongariki , part of the Rapa Nui National Park UNESCO world heritage site, could be reached by seasonal waves as soon as 2080 under a High SLR scenario (1.2 m SLR). The results suggest urgency for SLR-related assessments in other coastal cultural sites in the Rapa Nui National Park and encourage community consultation for adaptation and mitigation efforts.

auditPapers.title: Studying archaeological iron corrosion in the ground – Sample handling to avoid undesirable changes
auditPapers.abstract: This paper evaluates sampling and storage methods for the study of iron archaeological artifacts, aiming to minimize unwanted changes. The selected methods will be used to handle samples in multiple studies utilizing neutron and X-ray computed tomography (NX-CT) to monitor 3D transformations in artifacts during time series experiments. It is thus important to keep full control of the parameters that could induce such changes. Two main approaches were tested: 1. imaging iron nails with their surrounding soil to maintain quasi-in-situ conditions and 2. imaging iron nails with a limited amount of soil to improve imaging resolution, also applicable for fully excavated nails. The highly variable soil moisture levels caused option 1 to be discarded, due to difficulties in reconstructing the tomograms. For the nails from setup 2, image reconstruction was successful. Additionally, to prevent unwanted changes occurring during storage, various short-term anoxic storage options were tested. Results showed that keeping the samples in Intercept® bags with RP-K oxygen scavengers and shortening the waiting time between experiments effectively minimized alterations like moisture loss, microcracks, and material displacement. In contrast, prolonged storage in the imaging sample holder caused noticeable unwanted changes. The findings emphasize the importance of optimized handling and storage to distinguish changes caused by external factors of interest. These protocols ensure accurate assessments of post-excavation conditions and conservation treatments, providing valuable insights into the preservation of archaeological iron artifacts and advancing the study of long-term corrosion processes.

auditPapers.title: The lost altar of the Ptolemaic Sanctuary at Hermopolis Magna (Egypt): hypothetical reconstruction and publication of the Rizkallah Makramallah excavation work
auditPapers.abstract: The research tackles the study, publication, and hypothetical three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of a mudbrick construction from the Ptolemaic period, situated within a Hellenistic sanctuary at Hermopolis Magna in Middle Egypt. The sanctuary site was excavated in 1945 by Rizkallah Makramallah, a former lecturer at Alexandria University, whose findings remained largely unpublished and obscure until the present study. This study enhances our understanding of the reconstruction potential of the mudbrick construction, proposed as a lost Hellenistic altar, in relation to the broader sanctuary complex. Furthermore, it elucidates the architectural and spatial planning dynamics between Hellenistic sanctuaries at Hermopolis Magna and Alexandria; this provides novel comparative insights into the religious, civic, and ceremonial functionalities of such monuments throughout the Ptolemaic period. With the inaugural academic publication of Makramallah’s excavation findings, derived from his photographic archives now preserved at the British Museum, the Hermopolis Magna sanctuary is reconstructed with enhanced detail and coherence, significantly transforming scholarly interpretations of both the monument and its functional context. The significant challenges faced included the absence of field notes, architectural drawings, or published plans; thus, it was necessary to rely on meticulous visual analyses of the photographic evidence captured from multiple perspectives and in different preservation conditions. These images underwent interpretative and comparative scrutiny; they were integrated into advanced 2D and 3D digital modelling software to reconstruct the monument's form, proportions, layout, and architectural characteristics. The reconstructed structure is subsequently examined in relation to typologically analogous Hellenistic altars discovered in Egypt, mainland Greece, and Asia Minor. This multidisciplinary approach not only revitalises an overlooked aspect of the sanctuary, but also enhances the broader understanding of the topographical, urban, and religious landscapes of Hermopolis Magna during the Graeco-Roman period. This research also proposes novel hypotheses concerning spatial organisation, monumentality, cultic accessibility, and ritual practices within provincial Ptolemaic sacred architecture.

auditPapers.title: Simulación de movilidad viaria en la región minera de Sisapo y Almadén en época romana: aplicación de análisis de redes (SIG)
auditPapers.abstract: Este artículo analiza la movilidad en época romana en la microrregión minera de Almadén y su articulación territorial, centrándose en las redes de caminos que permitieron la evacuación del cinabrio (minium). Mediante el modelo de acumulación de desplazamiento óptimo (MADO) y tecnologías de Sistemas de Información Geográfica (SIG), se simula la red secundaria de vías, esenciales para comprender la circulación en un territorio cuya infraestructura primaria dejó escasa huella arqueológica. Considerando los factores de transporte y orografía, junto con las fuentes antiguas y la cultura material, se han reconstruido rutas posibles para el transporte del mineral hacia Córdoba, principal centro redistribuidor. Además, se revisan los asentamientos jerarquizados de la región, destacando el papel del yacimiento del Cerro de las Monas como eje económico y logístico clave. Paralelamente, se subraya la relevancia de Sisapo: capital administrativa del cinabrio hispano y responsable de la gestión y explotación de este recurso estratégico. El objetivo principal de la investigación es resaltar el papel fundamental que jugó el Cerro de las Monas en la organización económica de esta región minera; además, se exploran las posibilidades interpretativas que ofrecen los análisis SIG, como los modelos de redes de movilidad. Los resultados obtenidos aportan nuevas perspectivas sobre la organización territorial en contextos mineros y abren líneas de investigación comparativa que podrían ayudar a identificar patrones de movilidad en otras regiones productivas del Imperio.

auditPapers.title: Evaluation of the reversibly cross-linked polymer-consolidated waterlogged archaeological woods from Zhangwan No.1 shipwreck
auditPapers.abstract: Zhangwan No.1 Shipwreck, excavated in 2012, urgently requires the application of conservation materials to protect its waterlogged archaeological woods. In this work, reversibly cross-linked polymer (RCP) is employed as conservation materials to consolidate the waterlogged archaeological woods from Zhangwan No.1 Shipwreck and its corresponding consolidation effect is thoroughly evaluated. RCP-based conservation materials are constructed by penetrating 2-formylphenylboric acid modified polydimethylsiloxane (PPBA) into the waterlogged wood samples, and then in-situ reversibly cross-linking by N-coordinated boroxines (NCBs). In-situ formed reversibly cross-linked conservation materials (PNCB) can support the structure of the archaeological woods to improve their dimensional stability. The shrinkage rate of the PNCB-consolidated archaeological woods is ∼2.1% and its anti-shrinkage efficiency is ∼85.6%. Moreover, the PNCB-consolidated archaeological woods exhibit the excellent humidity stability and thermostability due to the stable cross-linking network of PNCB. Even under the environment with relative humidity of 100%, the equilibrium moisture content (EMC) of the PNCB-consolidated archaeological woods is only ∼0.4%, significantly lower than that of un-consolidated and polyethylene glycol-consolidated archaeological woods. Because the NCB cross-linkers can be broken by ethanol, the PNCB conservation materials within the archaeological woods can be depolymerized into PPBA and eliminated from the archaeological woods after ethanol immersion.

auditPapers.title: The non-destructive characterization of a rare Liao silver reliquary from the Museum of oriental art in Turin (Italy)
auditPapers.abstract: The present research study focuses on the archaeometric investigation of a delicate silver object. The artefact may be stylistically attributed to the Chinese Liao dynasty (907–1125 AD) and exhibits some peculiar aspects. It is made up of five overlapping and untied silver foil components, which may have been taken from unrelated artefacts and reassembled in ancient times. However, very little provenance information is available, and its manufacturing process is unknown. In addition, the reliquary was found in a highly fragmentary state, with advanced corrosion, extensive yellowing of the silver foils and severe embrittlement, which highly compromised its structural integrity and the legibility of its decorative features. Thus, a non-destructive and multi-analytical approach, based on surface spectroscopic techniques and structural characterization, was carried out on micro-fragments detached spontaneously from the reliquary. This study investigates the materials and manufacturing techniques, the conservation history, and the coherence of the five assembled components of this unique reliquary. Moreover, the investigation allowed us to gain insight into the silver microstructure and the possible causes of the observed alteration phenomena The results provide new knowledge on the metalworking practices of the Liao dynasty and might be valuable for developing and optimising strategies to restore the structural integrity of brittle ancient silver artefacts.

auditPapers.title: The impact of the pandemic on musicologists’ use of technology
auditPapers.abstract: This paper discusses findings of a global survey of nearly 600 musicologists in 35 countries in 2022, asking about their uses of technology during the pandemic. The survey focused on participants’ frustrating and rewarding experiences, risks, limitations and benefits of technology, and highlighting changes they would keep after the pandemic. There was a preference for digital resources over physical counter-parts, apart from where physical books were more popular than e-books. Zoom and other video conferencing software were frequently mentioned in both positive and negative terms, particularly around music performance and fieldwork, conferences and collaborations. Access and availability of online resources was positive, due to availability, and negative due to losing the analogue experience. Methodologies had also been impacted on, allowing researchers to ask new questions, while shaping and limiting these questions. There was impact of technology on community-building and enhancing the ability to meet across borders while limiting networking opportunities. The shift to teaching online impacted on teaching music performance, and heavy teaching loads were prioritised over research, highlighting the interconnected roles of the musicologist researcher in teaching and learning. This research contributes towards an understanding of the complex nature of the information behaviour of musicologists. Insight into how musicologists‘ attitudes and practices have changed and fulfil their multiple roles suggests they are moving closer to the digital humanities field in their practices.

auditPapers.title: Sediments surrounding waterlogged archaeological wood: could arsenic be involved in preserving wooden pile dwelling from microbial decay? The Gran Carro case study (Lake Bolsena, central Italy)
auditPapers.abstract: • WAW conservation depends on the properties of the environment surrounding it. • Climate change and anthropic impact may affect cultural heritage conservation. • Gran Carro sediments show elevated As concentration in stable chemical forms. • As is inversely related to sediment enzymes and directly to microbial stress index. • Monitoring sediments helps to preserve heritage from natural and anthropic pressures. Waterlogged archaeological wood (WAW) conservation depends on several abiotic properties related to water and/or sediments (temperature, pH, redox potential, salinity, heavy metals or pollutants) and biotic factors (amount and type of microorganisms and their metabolic activity). All these factors may be altered by anthropic activities and/or climate changes thus accelerating or decreasing wood decay rates. Regardless of its rate, the decomposition and alteration of submerged material can be expected to leave traces in the surrounding sediment properties. Gran Carro is an archaeological site, located at Lake Bolsena (central Italy) and characterised by the presence of wooden pile dwellings (WPD). According to the most recent archaeological evidence, the site dates back in the period spanning from Middle Bronze Age (XV century BC) to the Early Iron Age (IX century BC). The study of waterlogged WPD, particularly those located in Mediterranean areas, was the object of WOODPDLAKE project financed by JPI-CH19. Lake Bolsena sediments chemical, biochemical (enzymatic activities) and microbiological properties (EL-FAME profiles), discriminated in the portion in tight contact with WAW (WSed) and the sediment in the surrounding area (Sed), are reported in this article with the aim to highlight any “wood effect”. Most properties showed a clear “wood effect” indicating that WSed was strongly influenced by the processes occurring within WAW. The chemical properties of Gran Carro sediments showed a consistent amount of arsenic deriving from the volcanic lithological substrate whose fractionation showed, however, that it was mostly present in stable and immobilized forms. The presence of sulphate reducing bacteria suggested, in fact, the use of arsenic to form insoluble sulphide mineral-like phases that precipitated in the sediment and in wood structure. Arsenic was also highly concentrated within WAW, negatively impacting microbial biomass and activity, in terms of enzymatic activities, which were significantly decreased in WSed. The geochemistry and mobility of arsenic ion depend on environmental factors that may be impacted by climate changes. Therefore, it is advisable to monitor the current variations of environmental matrices such as soil, sediments, water in contact with archaeological material to understand the potential effects on the conservation of cultural heritage. A possible mechanism explaining the processes occurring in the vicinity of waterlogged archaeological wood. Arsenic is immobilized into wood porous structure thus acting as a likely «protection» factor from microbial decay.

auditPapers.title: Landscaping Patagonia: Spatial History and Nation-Making in Chile and Argentina By María de los Ángeles Picone
auditPapers.abstract: María de los Ángeles Picone’s Landscaping Patagonia examines the myriad ways that people understood and experienced space, place, and nature in northern Patagonia, and the impacts of these spatial imaginaries on nation-state formation in both Argentina and Chile. Picone traces these shifting conceptualizations of Patagonian landscapes over a fifty-year period, from the late nineteenth century (as Argentina and Chile concluded their respective military campaigns against Indigenous populations in the region) through the mid-twentieth century. In line with the broader frameworks of spatial history, Landscaping Patagonia demonstrates that geographical knowledge is far from an objective category. On the contrary, the diverse populations who inhabited, governed, and traversed Patagonia developed different—and often clashing—perspectives on the region’s natural and built environment. These diverging experiences of Patagonian space inflected contemporary discourses on identity, citizenship, immigration, patriotism, and modernity. Landscaping Patagonia is part of a growing body of transnational scholarship on the Argentine-Chilean cordillera region and builds productively on English- and Spanish-language scholarship, such as that of Susana Bandieri, Alberto Harambour, and Kyle Harvey. Additionally, Picone’s work is in conversation with the theoretical frameworks of borderlands history and spatial history. Picone employs both of these theoretical frameworks in order to unsettle traditional narratives of national history, highlight alternative ways of conceptualizing space and place, and bring a diverse array of historical actors into the frame of vision. In doing so, Picone is able to tease out the fascinating ways in which borderlands populations (elite and non-elite, Argentine and foreign-born) experienced and sought to shape the natural world.

auditPapers.title: An Encroaching Sea: Nature, Sovereignty and Development at the Edge of British India 1860–1950. By Devika Shankar
auditPapers.abstract: Environmental histories, not only of British India but of European colonialism more broadly, have been concerned with establishing how, why, and with what effects empire encroached on ecologies and indigenous or local communities. Devika Shankar flips this dynamic on its head. In her fastidious and engaging account of the development of the port of Cochin in southwest India, European empire is less encroacher than encroached upon; the active agents are not British colonizers, but littoral princely states and environmental objects like sand and seawater. “Encroachment” figures in this book as both actor’s category used by colonial administrators, and analyst’s category used to comprehend ecological-political developments around Cochin. Through this device, Shankar reveals the danger of reproducing colonial self-representations as the primary shaper of environments. An Encroaching Sea instead describes a cautious, fractious, and forgetful British Indian state buffeted by both the vibrant terraqueous environs and equally energetic local polities pioneering “a fundamental transformation of [their] princely power” (113).

auditPapers.title: The Age of the Borderlands: Indians, Slaves, and the Limits of Manifest Destiny, 1790-1850. By Andrew C. Isenberg
auditPapers.abstract: Was the early United States a confident, expansionist nation? That depends on where you look and who you ask. Certainly, many early federal leaders and ordinary people shared a vision of continental expansion that became increasingly providential over the first decades of the early nineteenth century. Expansion was baked into the revolutionary settlement, and federal officials imagined that Indigenous land reaching west to the Mississippi River (and soon beyond it) would underpin the financial stability of the new nation. And yet, they also knew that expansion was a source of instability. Expansionists they may have been, but confident they were not. Indigenous people thwarted land theft at every turn. Even in the earliest decades of the new republic, some white Americans who we might expect to have been invested in expansion were troubled by its implications. And by the 1830s Indigenous leaders were supported in their efforts to counter Indian removal by a vocal white and black minority. As many scholars have recently shown, expansion was never inevitable.

auditPapers.title: FIRST PERSON SINGULAR? NORTH INDIAN MIGRANT NARRATIVES FROM THE ERA OF INDENTURE
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT Between the early nineteenth century and the early twentieth century, over one million people from India served as indentured laborers in European‐dominated colonies scattered across the Indian Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and Caribbean. To understand this mass migration at the individual and micro‐level, scholars have recently turned their attention to the autobiographies of two “translated” people, Totaram Sanadhya and Munshi Rahman Khan, because their texts offer firsthand accounts of indenture from within that system. Sanadhya spent twenty‐one years in Fiji after arriving there in 1893, and Khan went to Suriname in 1898 and stayed there for the next seventy or so years of his life. Their reminiscences, which translate into words the lived experiences of migrants from North India, offer crucial insights into the language practices they had to negotiate and the different subjectivities they had to assume (or were assigned) not only while en route to indenture but also during and following their period of indenture. Such information cannot be extracted from the official archives that historians typically rely on to compile macro‐ or meso‐histories of mobility in colonial India. But migrant self‐writing also has limitations: many personal stories of indenture are organized solely around the theme or plot of suffering and coercion, as demonstrated in Sanadhya's testimonio , and many self‐narratives represent the experiences and thoughts of a single historical agent, as evidenced by the autobiographies of both Sanadhya and Khan.

auditPapers.title: Surgery and Salvation: The Roots of Reproductive Injustice in Mexico, 1770-1940. By Elizabeth O’Brien
auditPapers.abstract: Progress on reproductive health has never been linear or easy. Even under liberal governments, women have faced restrictive policies, and medical professionals have often exercised their authority in paternalistic—and at times harmful—ways. In Surgery and Salvation, Elizabeth O’Brien takes a long chronological view of reproductive injustice in Mexico, tracing the roots of what she calls “obstetric violence” from the end of Spanish colonial rule through the Mexican Revolution. Over more than two centuries, priests and physicians intervened surgically in the name of saving fetal souls, women’s honor, and the nation’s reputation. Religious ideology and discourse, far from being displaced by modern medicine, became deeply intertwined with forms of institutionalized medical violence against women, whose bodies were used both for clinical experimentation and social regeneration. The book is structured chronologically and thematically, divided into five sections. A 1749 royal decree mandated that priests throughout the Spanish empire perform caesarean operations on dead or dying women to save the fetus’s soul. This practice—especially common on missions of the Californias—was more widespread in the colonial period than previously understood and laid the groundwork for a medical culture that often prioritized the unborn fetus over the mother’s physical health. During the liberal Reforma era (1840s–1870s), physicians were trained in an environment in which Mexico City’s hospitals remained largely under the care of religious women. When they diagnosed conditions of hysteria and complications from pregnancies, they frequently located disease in the reproductive organs, leading to therapeutic abortions or, in some cases, the surgical removal of ovaries.

auditPapers.title: Language in times of COVID-19: lexical and morphopragmatic analyses of two Austrian media corpora
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract We investigate frequencies of (1) new vocabulary and (2) evaluative-expressive morphopragmatic forms such as expressive compounds and diminutives in two corpora of German in Austria in the first 22 months of the COVID-19 pandemic: (1) the amc (Austrian Media Corpus), a corpus of newspaper articles using more formal registers and (2) the stf (STANDARD forum corpus), a corpus of user-generated content of more informal forum posts on the COVID live ticker of an online newspaper. Results show significant correlations between frequencies of new COVID-19 vocabulary in both corpora despite the different registers used. However, the timing of emergence and of frequency peaks differs in both corpora, as will be illustrated by the three COVID-19 neologisms Babyelefant ‘baby elephant (= distance measure)’, Covidiot_in ‘covidiot’ and Corona-Leugner_in ‘Corona denier’: New lemmas tend to emerge and increase in the formal amc first before being picked up by the users of the informal stf, leading to later but mostly higher frequency peaks of the lemmas in the stf. The results show also significant correlations between daily new COVID-19 cases and numbers of forum posts as well as between daily new COVID-19 cases and frequencies of morphopragmatic forms produced by forum users, indicating a higher posting activity and the use of more emotional vocabulary in more problematic periods of the pandemic.

auditPapers.title: Visualization of time in a digital edition: the example of the imperial diet of the Holy Roman Empire of 1576
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract By providing structured data as well as documents, digital editions offer new tools for historical research, which this paper intends to demonstrate by making reference to two different visualizations of dates included in the edition of the records of the Imperial Diet, a form of premodern parliament of the Holy Roman Empire, that took place in Regensburg in 1576. As the edition presents information of various kinds, such as transcriptions, document descriptions, and metadata, a large number of dates was recorded and tagged with the standard of the Text Encoding Initiative, and thus made machine-readable. Moreover, there are seven different categories of dates which need to be analyzed differently: dates that head the entries of minutes, dates mentioned in texts and comments, dates that indicate when documents were sent, dates indicating when they were received, or dates indicating when they were copied by the diet’s participants, dates indicating when participants arrived at the diet, or dates concerning the duration of archival units in which the diet’s files are stored. Visualizations like those presented in this paper help researchers to navigate their way through this mass of dates to identify and investigate those that help answer their research questions, or even to recognize patterns not apparent at first sight, which might lead them to ask new questions.

auditPapers.title: British Colonial Rule over Littoral Space and Watercraft in Hong Kong, 1841–1898
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Proposing ‘the littoral’ as a subject of historical enquiry, this article centres on British rule over the waters, isles, and shores in nineteenth-century colonial Hong Kong. It argues that similar and connected to its rule over urban space, the British government endeavoured to regulate the colony’s watery fringes out of racial and other concerns. Commensurate with the growth of shipping, colonial rulers demarcated particular littoral spaces as mirrors or even extensions of land spaces. In the late nineteenth century, an emerging hierarchy of delineated navigational, anchorage, and quarantine spaces was discernible in Hong Kong’s littorals. Despite their efforts to structure littoral space, British colonial authorities failed to direct its actual usage. Not only did stakeholders compete and negotiate over using Victoria Harbour, but also, many Chinese watercraft countered official control by venturing across administrative boundaries. More broadly, the case of Hong Kong suggests perspectives for addressing the complexity of the littoral history of colonial port cities in Asia. First is the examination of connections between different areas within littoral space. Second is the inseparability between littoral space and urban space in terms of government policies. Third is the contrast between colonial designs and actual negotiations regarding the use of littoral space.

auditPapers.title: Letizia Osti. History and Memory in the Abbasid Caliphate: Writing the Past in Medieval Arabic Literature.
auditPapers.abstract: Letizia Osti’s History and Memory in the Abbasid Caliphate: Writing the Past in Medieval Arabic Literature is a tightly argued investigation of a court operative who flourished during the ʿAbbasid caliphate (r. 750–1258). The subject, Abū Bakr al-Ṣūlī (d. 947), often appears in scholarly treatments of the period, but rarely does he receive the spotlight. At court, with access to caliphs, and both as a participant and eyewitness to caliphal power, he was a courtier-­­scholar of many dimensions. Al-Ṣūlī wrote about the chancery, turned his hand to poetry (as a writer and collector who collated other poets’ works—including the caliphs’), and gained a reputation as a skilled chess player. He taught Abbasid princes. After decades supported by caliphal and courtly patrons—especially the caliph al-Rāḍī (r. 934–40)—the caliphate’s unraveling proved to be his own too. He ultimately finished his life in Baṣra, selling his notebooks to survive (“the written word, accumulated over long years” was “precious currency at the end of al-Ṣūlī’s life” [81]). He inspired no editor to collect his poetry. A personal story runs throughout this book: of a man striving to win payouts, proud of his connections and foresight and unhappy with a dumbing down of educational standards, who witnessed the caliphate’s financial troubles and rivalries, as well as the insecurity experienced by the population of Baghdad. Still, this is no “life and times” story. Rather, across five chapters Osti goes to unusual lengths to situate her work within scholarship relating to the Abbasid period as she uses a well-­­documented, but rarely remarked on, person to give a wider account of Arabic literature and historiography. Osti’s critical treatment introduces readers therefore not just to al-Ṣūlī and the ʿAbbasids, but to the many fields that encompass him. The book is therefore also an efficient introduction to court life under the Abbasids.

auditPapers.title: Mathematical approach for sample projection in linguistic landscape studies
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This study presents a novel approach to addressing methodological challenges in linguistic landscape (LL) research through the development of an advanced algorithm for language pattern sample projection. Leveraging fuzzy number-based generation with Mersenne number principles, our proposed algorithm offers a sophisticated solution for projecting the number of language signs in diverse LL contexts. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy and reliability of our proposed algorithm in accurately capturing linguistic diversity within LL environments, contributing to improved methodological objectivity in LL research. We recommend the widespread adoption of our algorithms to enhance linguistic analyses in public spaces and advance our understanding of language dynamics and sociocultural interactions.

auditPapers.title: Housing and the Peripheralization of Race Politics in Britain, 1948–1977
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The idea that there was a ratio of people of colour to white people that, if exceeded, would prompt a white backlash was a tenet of folk sociology in Britain. This belief was the basis of strategies of ‘dispersal’. In the 1940s and 1950s, officials counted on the labour market to spread people from the Caribbean, South Asia, and Africa around the country. However, the housing market had the opposite effect. It ‘concentrated’ Black and Asian people in run-down parts of British cities. Later, as urban authorities began to demolish these neighbourhoods and to integrate public housing, some (most notably Birmingham) introduced formal dispersal programmes with racial quotas. Dispersal in particular and housing policy in general illustrate the way central government devolved contentious matters involving race to local councils. Examining this process of ‘peripheralization’ brings two distinct concerns in the historiography — national policy on immigration and local social processes — into the same frame. City and regional authorities in France and West Germany pursued dispersal in parallel ways, despite the differences in the three countries’ migration histories and citizenship regimes. The similarities in the project of dispersal and its failure point to a common European history of the origins of multiculturalism.

auditPapers.title: PRODUCING INTEGRATION: THE TRANSLATION OF NON/BELONGING IN GERMANY AND THE UNITED STATES
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT This essay examines how the concept of integration has been produced, translated, and institutionalized in Germany and the United States as a key element of policy frameworks that migranticize some people and, thus, translate them as outsiders. By combining conceptual history and translation theory, we analyze how the meaning of integration has evolved within academic and political discourse, tracing its emergence as a key category in migration governance. We argue that the production of what integration means can be read via and as translation, resulting in an ambiguous medium that structures access to belonging in a way that facilitates the reproduction of exclusionary hierarchies. We begin by outlining our theoretical framework, linking cultural translation with conceptual history to examine how integration operates as a dynamic but historically contingent concept. We then explore integration in Germany, tracing its genealogy from racializing notions during the Nazi years to its institutionalization as a migration policy in a multicultural society during the twenty‐first century. Next, we turn our attention to the US, where integration remains undefined in official policy but is shaped through differential inclusion in the market and illegality. Focusing on Duldung and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, we argue that the German and US systems translate older forms of exclusion into contemporary governance structures. Far from a neutral or inclusive concept, integration becomes operative as a tool for regulating mobility and non/belonging through a twofold translation: the production of what integration means determines how the concept translates people.

auditPapers.title: MIGRATION, MOBILITY, AND BEING IN TRANSLATION
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT Drawing on an expanded concept of translation as process and practice, this contribution to the “Translation, Migration, Narrative” forum explores how migrants, as described by scholars such as Paul F. Bandia, embody “translated beings” who are marked both by agency and by constraint. We argue that translation serves as a literal and metaphorical framework for analyzing archives of migration by illuminating the interplay between migrants’ identities, their larger social networks, and the legal, cultural, and linguistic translations they enact and endure. The piece begins by developing theoretical insights from two works of literature: Valeria Luiselli's writings about her experiences as a volunteer interpreter for child migrants and Yuri Herrera's novels reflecting on migrancy as a form of evolving self‐translation between languages and cultures. These literary perspectives on translation as an essential component of migrant experience emphasize the hybrid, translational experiences of migrants and the paradoxical, but also resilient, nature of their identities and agency. We then bring these theories to bear as methodology and analyze a 1954 document from the archives of South Africa's Witwatersrand Native Labour Association (WNLA) that translated and transcribed Malawians’ messages to their mineworker family members in South Africa. We consider how the lived experience of “being in translation” was both common and differentiated between migrants and their “left‐behind” family members. Ultimately, our intervention offers an interdisciplinary approach to migration studies that bridges literature, history, and cultural analysis. This perspective not only underscores how translation practices are essential to the experience of migration but also helps to (re)constitute migration histories, in turn contributing to the archives and narratives that navigate the complex terrain of mobility, identity, and cultural mediation.

auditPapers.title: TRAVELERS IN TRANSLATION: OF “LIMINAL SPACES” AND “LITERARY CONTACT ZONES”
auditPapers.abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the global visibility of the migrant as a key figure in discussions of human rights, the contours of the migrant as a subject of rights still remain unspecified. However, global human rights fictions, which are often rooted in autobiographical and biographical accounts, offer alternative subjectivities by producing narrative forms that contrast with dominant “migration literatures.” Literature emerges as a contact zone where migrant voices engage with host cultures, facilitating dialogues that challenge stereotypes and reshape cultural imaginaries. In these spaces, language becomes the central medium to navigate and negotiate liminality. Processes of translation are the most obvious means of this negotiation, as translation bridges personal experience, political ideologies, and social imaginaries. By translating precarious migrant experiences into narratives, literature reconfigures the migrant as a central figure of human rights while also challenging dominant political discourses. Helon Habila's 2019 novel, Travelers , exemplifies these dynamics by mapping migrancy through a network of interconnected characters whose fates illuminate the complexity of migrant experiences and challenge received notions of migrancy. As individual narratives intersect and transform into a collective story, Travelers reflects the potential of literary contact zones to mediate cultural exchange and envision alternative migrant subjectivities. By moving beyond tropes of cultural clash and identity struggles, such narratives reimagine migration and its connection to human rights.

auditPapers.title: Graph schema validation at last? Work towards a StemmaREST ontology with Neo4J, RDF-STAR, and SHACL
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract As of 2023, there have been two intriguing developments in the Semantic Web world that are especially relevant to digital humanities projects that are anchored to graph technologies, such as the StemmaREST repository for variant text traditions. The second is Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), a language whose purpose Is to define a set of constraints against Ih RDF graphs can be validated. auditPapers.abstract: In 2006, Neil MacGregor, the former Director of the British Museum, asserted that “repatriation is yesterday’s question.” But recent history has proven this declaration to be highly inaccurate. Repatriation and restitution have become hot topics in recent years, in part due to a revival of interest in two well-known cases: that of the Benin “bronzes” looted by the British in 1897 from the ancient kingdom of Benin in Nigeria, and the Parthenon marbles (still controversially referred to as the Elgin Marbles after their eponymous extractor, Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin). Not only have there been more public calls for restitution and repatriation in recent years; the rate of successful claims has increased exponentially. Bénédicte Savoy’s Africa’s Struggle for its Art, Dan Hicks’s The Brutish Museums, and Barnaby Phillips’s Loot: Britain and the Benin Bronzes all focus on marshaling historical evidence for the ethical necessity of restitution. While drawing her readers’ attention to the longue durée of repatriation and restitution struggles in Africa, Bénédicte Savoy suggests in Africa’s Struggle for Its Art that the current focus is in large part due to the report she published together with the Senegalese economist Felwine Sarr in 2018 at the behest of the French president Emmanuel Macron. More than this, she suggests that many current claims have been able to gain traction in ways that earlier demands failed largely due to their joint research and the moral arguments advanced in their report. In many ways, what has become known as the Sarr/Savoy report was indeed a milestone. However, I would argue that the report was part of an established trend, and that a much wider set of political and economic circumstances have contributed to the current resurgence of calls for the return of cultural property.
