auditPapers.title: From coin to data: the impact of object detection on digital numismatics
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In this work, we investigate the application of advanced object detection techniques to digital numismatics, focusing on the analysis of historical coins. Leveraging models such as Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP), we develop a flexible framework for identifying and classifying specific coin features using both image and textual descriptions. By examining two distinct datasets, modern Russian coins featuring intricate ‘Saint George and the Dragon’ designs and degraded first-millennium CE Southeast Asian coins bearing Hindu-Buddhist symbols, we evaluate the efficacy of different detection algorithms in search and classification tasks. Our results demonstrate the superior performance of larger CLIP models in detecting complex imagery, while traditional methods excel in identifying simple geometric patterns. Additionally, we propose a statistical calibration mechanism to enhance the reliability of similarity scores in low-quality datasets. This work highlights the transformative potential of integrating state-of-the-art object detection into digital numismatics, enabling more scalable, precise, and efficient analysis of historical artefacts. These advancements pave the way for new methodologies in cultural heritage research, artefact provenance studies, and the detection of forgeries.

auditPapers.title: Remembering Anne Beach: Love, Scandal, and Sickness in Eighteenth-Century Britain By Carolyn A. Day
auditPapers.abstract: Carolyn Day begins this short but impactful microhistory by recounting how what began as research into the life of Princess Amelia led to the story of Anne Beach (1749-1771), a young woman allegedly imprisoned by her family for falling in love with local clergyman William Wainhouse (1738-1797). auditPapers.title: The Revolutions that Consolidated Empire: A Reconsideration of 1830
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract There is a world of imperial connections and consequences of the revolutions of 1830 that historians hardly ever mention. The relationship between these revolutions and empire needs to be investigated, not from a viewpoint of isolated, national histories, but as a European phenomenon. These revolutionary events engulfed empires, reshaped their mutual relations, and altered the face of European imperialism itself. With a specific focus on France, Belgium, and Great Britain, this article argues that the revolutions of 1830 were not simply events coincidentally affected by their imperial context, but were themselves transformative of the imperial landscape. They gave a boost to European expansion, ushered in more direct forms of colonial dominion, and initiated an era of heightened trans-imperial co-operation. The continuation of the Congress System that arose out of the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with its frameworks of multilateral diplomacy and collective security, is key to this development. Rather than destroying the post-1815 system, the revolutions of 1830 demonstrated its adaptability and durability. Old and new faces within the system swiftly adjusted to the political changes and accommodated the imperial ambitions of liberal elites, wherever they came to power.

auditPapers.title: Detecting authorship between generative AI models and humans: a Burrows’s Delta approach
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The distinction between artificial intelligence (AI)- and human-generated texts has become increasingly significant with the emergence of ChatGPT and other generative AI models, which have garnered millions of users. In this study, we assess Burrows’s Delta, a well-established algorithm in authorship attribution, as a potential AI detector in argumentative essays. Our results prove that Burrows’s Delta is an effective tool for detecting AI-generated content. In addition, the accuracy of distinguishing between AI- and human-generated texts exceeds 80 per cent across varying text lengths, from short excerpts approximately 100 words to full essays of approximately 550 words. However, the accuracy is influenced by both text length and the number of features selected by Burrows’s Delta. More importantly, our findings indicate that AI exhibits distinct linguistic and stylistic authorship markers, which can be identified using conventional authorship attribution methods. We discuss these findings in relation to authorship attribution, stylometry, and the role of large language models in language teaching and learning.

auditPapers.title: The Impact of Human Decision-Making on the Research Value of Archaeological Data
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: ‘ Good data in, good data out ’ is a well-known adage, often used to consider the ‘precision’ of data entry rather than other human activity when inputting information into a database. These could be omissions or errors, but are just as likely to be inconsistencies in data recording. This is especially relevant when thinking about the efficiencies that recorders might make (i.e., to make their work easier) and what this could mean for end users (e.g., researchers). For example, a recorder of an archaeological object might do things differently based on their knowledge or understanding of the value of recording certain types of data (e.g., the various characteristics of the object) and how this information is likely to be used by others. With this in mind, this article will consider the research question of how can advancing Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable (FAIR) principles be used to contextualise the impact of human decision-making on the research value of archaeological data, taking (as a test case) the Portable Antiquities Scheme (PAS) database of archaeological finds from England and Wales. The methodology used here examines data recorded within the PAS database directly and through a separate web application demonstrator (PASampo) that is being developed. The latter, in particular, enables ease-to-use visualisation of the data to provide an analytical evaluation of how data is inputted into the PAS database and, more significantly, how the researcher might extract this data. Through a series of case studies exploring aspects of material culture, we will highlight how data quality is affected by human decision-making alongside elements of the database framework. We will then argue that this provides the basis for new learning alongside adopting FAIR principles that could benefit the development of a wide range of future archaeological and cultural heritage databases, including the PAS database itself.

auditPapers.title: The medieval stained glass in Catalonia: Girona cathedral
auditPapers.abstract: • 13th and 14th century stained glass is of the potash lime type, similar to north-west France. • 15th century stained glass is of the potash-lime type, similar to north-eastern France. • 16th century stained glass is of the soda-lime type from Barcelona. • The production of stained glass moved from France to Barcelona at the end of the 15th century. The production and distribution of stained glass in Mediterranean Europe during the Middle Ages remains inadequately understood. This article focuses on Catalonia, where local glass production is documented as early as the 13th century, but little is known about the production of window glass. This study analyses a collection of stained glass fragments from Girona Cathedral, dating from the 13th to the 16th century, some of which is the work of renowned master glassmakers. The data obtained is compared with contemporary stained glass documented from other parts of Europe, and with a collection of 15th and 16th century archaeological window glass from Barcelona. The data is also contrasted with historical documentation on glass production in Catalonia. The findings reveal that the glass from Girona from the 13th and 14th centuries is of the potassium-lime type, similar to that produced in the workshops of north-western France. By the late 14th and 15th centuries, the composition aligns more closely with that of north-eastern France. In the 16th century, however, the glass changes to a soda-lime composition, similar to the glass found in Barcelona, suggesting a transition from central European to Mediterranean sources, and indicates a change in the raw materials involving the use of soda-lime plant ash instead of potassium-lime forest ash. These results indicate that the production of window glass shifted from France to Barcelona at the close of the 15th century.

auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Recent years have seen a growing number of studies devoted to short video platforms, including TikTok. We show the reliability of the scheme by testing and evaluating it on a corpus of twenty TikTok videos representing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. We conclude the article by sketching possible future applications of the scheme in studies on larger corpora.

auditPapers.title: The art of positive reporting in media discourse: Time magazine’s linguistic positivity bias over the 20th century
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Linguistic positivity bias is widely examined in spoken communication and written academic communication. Existing research proposes that this trend of favoring positive language use is common and universal in human communication. However, to date, no existing study has confirmed this tendency to use more positive words than negative ones in media discourse. By examining a list of positive and negative words and how they are distributed in the Time Magazine Corpus of American English, a large diachronic corpus with nearly 100 million words, the study reveals a greater increase in the use of positive words compared to negative ones in journal articles published in Time magazine between the 1920s and the 1990s. Finally, such an increased use of positive words in media discourse may be a result of the general tendency for positive communication, the shift toward constructive journalism, the application of positive psychology in media discourse, and the post-war socio-economic and technological development coupled with media commercialization.

auditPapers.title: Machine Learning Applications in Use-Wear Analysis: A Critical Review
auditPapers.journal: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology
auditPapers.abstract: Use-wear analysis examines the macroscopic and microscopic patterns of traces left on tool surfaces as a result of use. Recently, machine learning (ML) has been employed as a promising method for automating and standardizing the identification of these traces. While the number of use-wear analysts using ML continues to grow, discussions regarding the effectiveness and appropriate implementation of these methods are ongoing. The main aim of this literature review is to provide recommendations for the more effective application of ML in use-wear analysis and archaeological research, by identifying trends, research gaps, and evaluating the quality of the models developed. There are three key challenges identified. Firstly, the limited adoption of open science practices restricts the creation of large datasets and hinders reproducibility and transparency. Secondly, research efforts are concentrated within limited institutions, focusing on certain research questions, algorithms, raw materials, and use-wear traces. Thirdly, the inadequate quality, quantity, and diversity of data affect the performance of the models being developed. To address these challenges, this paper advocates for the promotion of open science and the systematic gathering of experimental and analytical data. Involving a broader range of institutions can improve research quality and promote greater diversity of perspectives. Collaboration with computer scientists and computational archaeologists is essential to integrate the expertise necessary for designing and implementing effective ML methods. By addressing these factors, this paper facilitates the effective use of machine learning, enabling use-wear analysts and archaeologists to develop robust models that automate, accelerate, and improve their research.

auditPapers.title: ‘Due Diligence’ and the British Government’s Response to Confederate Ship Procurement in Britain during the American Civil War
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The British government’s stance towards the American Civil War belligerents, while professedly neutral, has often been seen by historians as leaning, more or less strongly, towards the Confederacy. Its failure to prevent the Confederates from procuring warships in Britain during the war is regularly cited as supporting this viewpoint. This article examines in detail Britain’s response to the vehement demands from the US government to shut down the Confederates’ ship procurement programme in the context of Britain’s administrative machinery in the 1860s. It concludes that the state apparatus at the time was not fit for purpose, and in particular that it lacked central direction, was hidebound in its procedures, and was too dependent on individuals’ competence and integrity to rise to meet the challenge to British law and governance mounted by a determined Confederacy. However, Britain did make considerable efforts to prevent the Confederates from obtaining warships and did not set out with the deliberate intent to aid and abet the Confederate States by providing them with a navy, did not turn a blind eye to Confederate activity, and did not demonstrate a negligent disregard for its own laws.

auditPapers.abstract: This article examines the pedagogical adaptation of Textual Communities, a digital tool originally developed for collaborative research in textual scholarship, to teach paleography at the undergraduate level within a liberal arts context. Prompted by the exigencies of remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic and the broader framework of critical digital pedagogy, the course-design reimagined the tool’s primary research-focused function — edition-making — as a dynamic teaching and learning environment emphasizing transcription, engagement, and student autonomy. The article presents a specific example of the use of a digital tool in teaching paleography, detailing its purpose and impact on student learning and engagement. The article offers a concrete case study of hybrid- and flexible-by-design pedagogy, showing the value of using scholarly digital tools in undergraduate settings.

auditPapers.title: A Dunhuang mural restoration network based on mask guidance and Transformer architecture
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In the process of Dunhuang mural restoration, models often struggle to focus on damaged areas, leading to issues such as color deviation and blurred lines. To address these problems, we propose a Dunhuang mural restoration network based on mask guidance and Transformer architecture, named MGTNet. First, we design a mural focus attention module to dynamically optimize both channel and spatial information in an adaptive manner. Next, we introduce a mural enhancement module that leverages the long-range dependency capturing capability of Transformers to improve restoration quality. Finally, a mask-guided downsampling module is proposed, which fuses the mask image as prior knowledge with downsampled features, enhancing the model's ability to perceive damaged areas. Experiments on a publicly available Dunhuang mural dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms comparison algorithms in terms of objective evaluation metrics such as PSNR and SSIM, validating the effectiveness of the algorithm. This study demonstrates the practical application potential of the algorithm in Dunhuang mural restoration and contributes to the significant advancements of artificial intelligence in the field of digital humanities.

auditPapers.title: Online Reviews as Communal Formations. A Corpus Linguistic Approach
auditPapers.abstract: Within the framework of our research we intend to show how online reviews could be seen not only as texts, but as digital practices and as part of “communal formations”. In order to justify our claim, we have collected extensive data from different literary review resources as well as reviews of museums and exhibitions, and general discussions of cultural objects from different reviewing platforms. Implementing traditional methods of corpus linguistics, we analyzed the digital review processes by comparing average review and sentence length, normalized distribution of parts of speech and subordinate clauses, and the use of keywords and phrases. As a result, we established that online reviewing is based on platform specific patterns and can be described as a form of “communal formation” that consist of shared knowledge and shared practices.

auditPapers.title: Immobility
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Increasingly, since the early years of the twenty-first century, some have questioned the relevance of historians’ ‘fetishization of mobility’ in an era of closing borders. This has led to greater attention being placed on systems of ‘regulation and intervention’ that shape global migration. Shifting away from the narratives centred on movement and fluidity, we argue that immobility is not a mere lack of movement: it is about the power relations and barriers that enforce, experience, and resist stillness. By delving into the archives of Past and Present, we aim to construct a conversation around the processes of enforcing, experiencing, and challenging immobility. We have found that immobility shapes the experiences of both the historical actors found in the journal and the historians and scholars who write these histories. This issue explores immobility through three interconnected sections: ‘Spaces’ examines the physical and metaphorical places where movement is arrested, revealing the lived experiences within these confines and the technologies that facilitate and enforce stillness; ‘Shadows’ delves into the legal and administrative categorizations that produce and sustain immobility, focusing on the policies and ideologies that mark certain bodies as immobile; finally, ‘Aftermath’ reflects on the consequences of enforced immobility, exploring how displaced and immobilized individuals navigate and shape their identities and communities in the wake of restrictions.

auditPapers.title: Does the “Indo-Pacific” Have a History?
auditPapers.abstract: The “Indo-Pacific” is supplanting the South China Sea as an arena of geostrategic concern among liberal democracies. The emergence of the “Quad”—the “Quadrilateral Security Dialogue” among Japan, Australia, India, and the United States—has led to a geographical pairing of the Indian and Pacific Oceans to spatially naturalize a new security community predicated on notions of a “rules-based maritime order” and “peace and stability” in the region, notions that ostensibly are threatened by a militarily aggressive China. This essay ponders whether this constructed geography has a history and whether that history will prove conducive to the forging of new political identifications. It will focus on the early modern and modern port polities of Southeast Asia, which served as vital nodes in trade networks that connected the vast, commercial economies of East and South Asia. Europeans imagined this maritime configuration as the “East Indies” while the Chinese labeled it the Southern Seas (“Nanyang,” among other terms). Both configurations emerged from commercial ambitions and strategic anxieties that similarly animate the maritime imaginary of the Indo-Pacific today.

auditPapers.title: Integral Outside: The Financial Curb Market, the Electric Telegraph, and the Politics of Pricing in Second Empire France
auditPapers.abstract: Financial markets in nineteenth-century France were far more complex than an analysis of the official Bourse or its state-authorized brokers would suggest. Most financial transactions occurred on an illegal yet tacitly tolerated curb market called the coulisse, which played a vital role in expanding market liquidity during the Second Empire while also attracting controversy as a site of complex speculative activity. Existing historiography attributes the 1859 suppression of the Paris coulisse to aggravated competition between state-authorized brokers and coulissiers following the market downturn of 1857–58. Based on police, ministerial, prefectoral, and judicial archives, I present an alternate account that stresses the twin roles of financial innovation and the telecommunications revolution in breaching the limits of the state’s tacit toleration for the coulisse. I emphasize the lesser known coulisse in Marseille, suppressed at the height of a bull market in 1855, to formulate an alternative explanation of the 1859 suppression of its counterpart in Paris. I conclude that the rising importance of the curb markets in both cities reflected the robust, short-term options market developing among coulissiers. Public attention given to the coulisse price lists—distributed via newly opened telegraph lines—challenged the legitimacy of official brokers as authoritative sources of price information and compromised the political interests of the Bonapartist state, which proved decisive in the crackdown.

auditPapers.title: Beyond Antisemitism: Rethinking Stalin’s Anti-Jewish Campaign, 1948–1953
auditPapers.abstract: This article focuses on a single major affair within modern Jewish history whose antisemitic context is unequivocally recognized by most historical scholarship, namely, the murderous persecution of Soviet Jews during the final years of Joseph Stalin’s rule (1948–53). I argue that alongside events and actions on the part of the regime that appear obviously antisemitic in nature, one can point to a certain distinct trend in Stalin’s “Jewish” policy at the time that the concept “antisemitism” does not help to unravel or understand. Historians were unaware of this trend until the Soviet archives were opened following the collapse of the Soviet Union. I address it here for the first time after perusing relevant archival material that has yet to be assessed by scholarship. After presenting and analyzing this unknown stratum of Stalin’s policy toward Soviet Jewry during the time of the persecutions, I argue that both this element, which is unassociated with the phenomenon of antisemitism, and the familiar murderous components of Stalin’s ostensibly antisemitic policy should from now on be analyzed and interpreted against a phenomenological and theoretical backdrop other than the paradigm of antisemitism.

auditPapers.title: Jessica L. Lamont. In Blood and Ashes: Curse Tablets and Binding Spells in Ancient Greece.
auditPapers.abstract: In Blood and Ashes: Curse Tablets and Binding Spells in Ancient Greece by Jessica L. Lamont is a study of curse tablets in ancient Greek religion and magic. As Lamont defines them, curse tablets are “small, thin sheets of lead inscribed with maledictions, spells, and prayers against rivals, lovers, wrongdoers, or otherwise threatening persons” (3). Numbering almost two thousand, curse tablets are ubiquitous across the Greco-Roman world; appear in a variety of contexts (for example, commercial, domestic, and competitive); and are inscribed in multiple languages, mostly Greek and later in Latin, often with references to local contexts or gods, especially Egyptian but also Judeo-Christian. This book closely examines the objects themselves, which combine invective speech with the ritual actions of transcription and placement in specific locations, and tells the history of curse practices more broadly in Greek antiquity from 750–250 BCE. The book also provides fairly comprehensive examples of individual curse tablets from published and forthcoming works. By juxtaposing actual images and drawings of curse tablets side by side as much as possible with their inscriptions and translations, Lamont allows the reader to consider not only the content of the curses but also visible features, material manipulations (such as folding or nailing), and findspots (for example, at graves sites, in wells, and in temple precincts) to build a full picture of how they were used and were meant to operate.

auditPapers.title: Christian R. Burset. An Empire of Laws: Legal Pluralism in British Colonial Policy.
auditPapers.abstract: Christian R. Burset’s deeply researched study, An Empire of Laws: Legal Pluralism in British Colonial Policy, is a notable addition to the legal history of the British Empire. While there is a rich historiography on the legal history of the early modern British Empire, the role of legal thought in the intellectual history of eighteenth-century British imperialism still remains understudied, especially compared with the prominence of Jeremy Bentham, Henry Maine, and James Fitzjames Stephen in histories of the Victorian empire. An Empire of Laws analyzes changing British policies toward colonial law in the 1760s and 1770s, revealing how questions about what kinds of legality were appropriate to different colonies became central to imperial political thought. The book also intervenes in historical debates about legal pluralism. Lauren Benton’s influential book Law and Colonial Legal Cultures: Legal Regimes in World History, 1400–1900 (2002) focused attention on the plural legal environments of early modern empires and on the role of jurisdictional politics in shaping new colonial forms of legal pluralism. Burset’s study defines legal pluralism in a different way than Benton, as a legal system allowing for radically distinct forms of law rather than one with multiple jurisdictions and varied sources of legal authority. In contrast to Benton’s more practice-oriented, colony-centered approach to legal change, Burset’s study explores how elite British policymakers in London and the colonies reimagined imperial law in territories conquered during the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763). It argues that British elites before the mid-eighteenth century aspired to an ideal of legal uniformity, a “common-law empire” in which English law provided the broad template for judicial administration in colonial spaces, though with regional variations. Imperial policymakers only embraced “strategic legal pluralism” (7) with the incorporation of French civil law by the Quebec Act (1774), and of colonial versions of Muslim and Hindu law in Bengal after 1772.

auditPapers.title: Comment by Hyunhee Park
auditPapers.abstract: In today’s academic landscape, the growing emphasis on globalization has amplified the demand for non-Western curricula, prompting a reexamination of how Asian history is framed. Increasingly, institutions incorporate Asian studies into broader world history frameworks, grouping diverse histories into regional surveys that highlight Asia’s cultural, political, and economic diversity while emphasizing its historical connections to global processes. These approaches challenge the outdated notion of Asia as a collection of isolated civilizations, presenting it instead as a dynamic, interconnected region. The think pieces in this forum expand on this shift, urging a reconsideration of Asia’s historical boundaries and interactions. This commentary contributes to that dialogue by exploring “Big Asia” as a framework to move beyond static portrayals and uncover the region’s diversity, fluidity, and integrative contributions to global history. To begin with, the concept of “Big Asia” compels us to rethink Asia’s boundaries and historical definitions. As Nile Green observes, Asia has never been a fixed entity; its meanings and contours have shifted across time and cultures, shaped by the priorities of those who conceptualized it. With regard to my own research, premodern societies like China and the Islamic caliphates developed “geoconcepts” that situated Asian regions within broader frameworks of world understanding. Building on flourishing trade connections across Asia, their scholars crafted geographical texts and maps that divided the world into vast regions rather than defining Asia as a distinct entity. This integrative approach is exemplified by Sima Qian’s (145–86 BCE) official histories, which categorized foreign societies and described them in relation to China, as well as in the geographic works in the Islamic world, which synthesized knowledge into comprehensive worldviews, centered on their respective societies.1

auditPapers.title: Ari Şekeryan. The Armenians and the Fall of the Ottoman Empire: After Genocide, 1918–1932.
auditPapers.abstract: The challenges of understanding the road(s) to mass atrocity, the dynamics of the crime, and its prevention continue to engender a regular stream of multidisciplinary scholarly output. Less attention is focused on what comes after, even though it is no less compelling a subject, combining the complications inherent to genocide with the questions the preposition after introduces. Ari Şekeryan takes up this challenge for the Armenian Genocide in The Armenians and the Fall of the Ottoman Empire: After Genocide, 1918–1923. Şekeryan is not entirely in uncharted waters. Two monographs in particular illuminate the path for him: Talin Suciyan’s The Armenians in Modern Turkey: Post-Genocide Society, Politics and History (2015) and Lerna Ekmekçioğlu’s Recovering Armenia: The Limits of Belonging in Post-Genocide Turkey (2016). Both compellingly explore—through different theoretical lenses, archival pools, and spatiotemporal focus—how genocide survivors who remained in Turkey tried to navigate the crime’s aftermath. Şekeryan’s interest in sociopolitical history and ethnic relations overlaps with the former, and the period he covers overlaps with the latter. However, The Armenians and the Fall of the Ottoman Empire surveys larger territory—the length and breadth of a crumbling empire from where a resurgent republic emerges in 1924—and offers new insights into the political maneuvers of the decimated Ottoman Armenian community.

auditPapers.title: Aditya Balasubramanian. Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India.
auditPapers.abstract: A critical, though somewhat underappreciated aspect of late colonial South Asian history is the fact that neither the anti-colonial movement nor the visions of postcoloniality that were routinely advanced by several leaders of this movement were synchronous or homogenous. Deep ideological and political differences characterized the debates not only about the colonial state but also about all aspects of Indian life, such as the bureaucracy, economy, culture, laws, and impact of foreign affairs, to mention only a few. While the dominant political force of late colonial and the early decades of postcolonial India remained the Indian National Congress (a political party founded in 1885), and the thought and legacy of its two towering leaders, Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948) and his political successor and India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru (1889–1964), the subcontinental landscape was actually dotted by innumerable “minor” figures who played a pathbreaking role in shaping the life of the country. In Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India, Aditya Balasubramanian masterfully traces the life and legacy of one such oppositional force in postcolonial India, which espoused a powerful economic alternative to state-led developmental projects of the Congress and instead advocated an economy that would be unfettered to individual economic pursuits. Balasubramanian documents their emergence and transformation into a political party, notes their brief electoral success and subsequent formal demise, and reflects on their enduring legacy in the twenty-first century. In doing so, he provides a detailed account of the promises and perils of a movement that challenged the orthodoxy and became a testament to the deepening roots of democracy in a fledgling republic.

auditPapers.title: Ana Lucia Araujo. The Gift: How Objects of Prestige Shaped the Atlantic Slave Trade and Colonialism.
auditPapers.abstract: The Gift: How Objects of Prestige Shaped the Atlantic Slave Trade and Colonialism is the latest piece of dogged historical detective work from Ana Lucia Araujo, a prolific historian of slavery, memorialization, and material culture in the Afro-Atlantic World. Unique among Araujo’s many books, The Gift takes a single object as the basis of its investigations: a silver ceremonial sword that has been held at the Musée du Nouveau Monde in La Rochelle, France, since 2015. The Gift retraces this object’s journey over the course of a little more than a century. Likely smithed in 1776, only a few blocks from its current location in La Rochelle, the sword emulates the form of a kimpaba, a material insignia associated with rulership in West Central African polities like Kongo and Loango. By mid-1777, La Rochelle slave trader Daniel Garesché gifted the sword to mfuka (a kind of commerce minister) Andris Pukuta of Cabinda. By the book’s end, Araujo has convincingly argued that the silver kimpaba was transported back to La Rochelle following Andris Pukuta’s death in 1786 and then gifted once more to elites on the Bight of Benin before being seized by the forces of the Kingdom of Dahomey. The kimpaba remained in Dahomey’s capital city of Abomey until its 1892–94 conquest by the French and afterward was, once again, transported back to France.

auditPapers.title: Masha Kirasirova. The Eastern International: Arabs, Central Asians, and Jews in the Soviet Union’s Anticolonial Empire.
auditPapers.abstract: In the first years after the Russian revolutions, the Bolsheviks came to imagine the “East” as an area of people once or still under imperial rule whose struggles for liberation were interconnected, and who required a particular non-European kind of revolutionary politics. This “East” encompassed the formerly Russian imperial territories in the Caucasus and Central Asia that would become part of the Soviet Union, Ottoman territories near the Soviet borders, and any “other parts of the colonial world” in Asia and Africa “that might eventually decolonize within the framework of a global transition to communism” (10). auditPapers.title: Joy Schulz. When Women Ruled the Pacific: Power and Politics in Nineteenth-Century Tahiti and Hawai‘i.
auditPapers.abstract: When Women Ruled the Pacific is a consequential and instructive read for scholars of Pacific Island history. It provides a gendered history of female Polynesian queens in the context of a rapidly changing eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Pacific. Joy Schulz’s focus is Hawai‘i and Tahiti—two Polynesian chiefdoms that became sovereign nations. The queens—Purea and ‘Aimata in Tahiti, and Ka’ahumanu and Lili’uokalani in Hawai‘i—exercised female spiritual and strategic power to shape the first hundred years of encounter with the West. Past historians have written histories of contact focused on a male world of chiefs, kings, and visiting traders and missionaries; women of high chiefly status who also negotiated with Western visitors are downplayed as minor characters. Schulz turns this trope around by recounting the complex political histories of four Polynesian women who ruled Tahiti and Hawai‘i. Her novel examination of gendered political and spiritual power opens new possibilities for reexamination of Polynesian history.

auditPapers.title: Elizabeth Gansen. Natural Designs: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo and the Invention of New World Nature.
auditPapers.abstract: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo (1478–1557) is best known as the author of the Historia general y natural de las Indias (General and Natural History of the Indies), a path-breaking work that both celebrated the early achievements of Spain in the Americas and conveyed to a European audience one of the first accounts of the lands and peoples of the New World. Oviedo’s efforts to compile systematically a complete human and natural history of the Indies, mainly from first-hand experiences, forced him to forge new ways of incorporating the models of antiquity and the Renaissance into an encyclopedic presentation of plants, animals, and other phenomena that Europeans had never witnessed before. His writings, and the choices he made to organize, categorize, and present the subject matter, proved influential for generations of chroniclers and historians. Elizabeth Gansen’s book Natural Designs: Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo and the Invention of New World Nature makes clear that Oviedo’s writings and drawings underwent nearly continuous revision over the course of his life as he struggled to convey as effectively as possible, using written text and visual representations, the abundance of constantly increasing new information about American plants and animals. Gansen argues that it is necessary, therefore, to trace each stage of Oviedo’s writings and examine the evolving contemporary influences in the world around him. Her book is a significant contribution to the scholarship on Oviedo specifically and sixteenth-century European encounters with the Americas more broadly.

auditPapers.title: Lewis Wade. Privilege, Economy and State in Old Regime France: Marine Insurance, War and the Atlantic Empire under Louis XIV.
auditPapers.abstract: The home page for Lloyd’s of London, an institution once at the core of mercantile risk management amid early modern England’s Financial Revolution, boasts a subsection entitled “Our past” that proudly claims ownership of “nearly 350 years of history … at the heart of making progress.” The early modern French marine insurance institutions explored in Lewis Wade’s Privilege, Economy and State in Old Regime France benefit from no such contemporary corporate hagiographies. The Chambre générale des assurances et grosses aventures (1668–1686, the “Chamber”) and the Compagnie générale des assurances et grosses aventures (1686–c. 1710, the “Company”) lasted for only a few decades in Louis XIV’s reign. Apart from a handful of mid-twentieth-century French-language works, they have been forgotten to early modern French scholars focused on state power in the age of “absolute” monarchy. Among economic historians, neoinstitutionalists—from Douglass North to Ron Harris—have focused their efforts on exploring the so-called “Little Divergence,” or why northern European countries like England and the Netherlands produced durable, supposedly modern economic institutions, and countries like France failed to do so. Per Harris, this owed to a lack of “credible commitment”: French shareholders avoided investment in commercial institutions—from insurance to trading companies—because they feared expropriation at the hands of a strong, meddling absolute monarchy. These institutions are reduced in this formula to overburdened agents of state power, rather than private ventures designed to maximize shareholder profit. But, as Wade points out, this neoinstitutional model ignores decades of scholarship (by William Beik, James Collins, and others) that undermined any possible notion that the louisquatorzien monarchy was indeed absolute, capable of imposing its will from above without negotiation with elites. It has similarly neglected the contentions of scholars like Philip Stern, Rupali Mishra, or Oscar Gelderblom, who have shown that supposedly free-market, Anglo-Dutch commercial institutions were political bodies in their own right, both benefitting from and subject to political winds in their home states.

auditPapers.title: Makhroufi Ousmane Traoré. Slavery, Resistance, and Identity in Early Modern West Africa: The Ethnic-State of Gajaaga.
auditPapers.abstract: Nearly a century ago, W. E. B. Du Bois examined the impacts of the slave trade on Africa, which he referred to as “a rape of a continent” (Africa, Its Geography, People, and Products; and, Africa, Its Place in Modern History, 2007, 40.) In the vast historical literature that has subsequently taken up this complex question, many aspects of Africa’s economic, political, and demographic history have been explored in efforts to illuminate how the continent was affected by more than 400 years of violence and human trafficking in the form of the transatlantic slave trade. Despite this rich historiography, it remains difficult to understand how the impacts of the slave trade were experienced at the local level, within smaller-scale and less centralized societies that constituted the majority of Africa’s population prior to the 20th century. This is where Makhroufi Ousmane Traoré’s book, Slavery, Resistance, and Identity in Early Modern West Africa: The Ethnic-State of Gajaaga, makes its greatest contribution. It explores the slow and subtle changes that shaped one West African society during the 17th and 18th centuries as a people connected primarily by a shared ethnic identity struggled to protect themselves and glean benefits from their situation at the intersection of the trans-Saharan and transatlantic trading networks through which vast numbers of captives were bought and sold.

auditPapers.title: M. T. Howard. Black Soldiers in the Rhodesian Army: Colonialism, Professionalism, and Race.
auditPapers.abstract: Following the imposition of colonial control, European powers recruited local forces in Africa to maintain internal order within these colonies. Most of these forces were then involved in the larger and complex process of decolonization, and many then entered into a period of negotiation or protest with the new state—such as the Royal West African Frontier Force becoming the national armies of Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Gambia. However, the path to decolonization was not always a smooth one, and for those regions of southern Africa, such as the colonies of the Portuguese Empire and South Africa, the desire for local majority rule demanded the use of organized violence. In these cases, the locally raised military forces and gendarmeries had a much different path to walk, becoming part of the armed forces fighting to maintain white minority rule within their colonial states. M. T. Howard’s book Black Soldiers in the Rhodesian Army explores the challenging and contested history of the locally raised African forces of the state of Rhodesia, investigating their experiences serving a racist state and drawing out how and why these personnel served throughout the lengthy liberation war that birthed Zimbabwe, and ultimately why these soldiers of the Rhodesian African Rifles (RAR) became integrated into the state now run by their former enemies. To achieve this, Howard manages to weave together an impressive series of interviews with former members of the RAR with archival sources and current social theory undergirding military professionalism and identity. The ultimate product is an extraordinary book, one that offers a deep analysis of the experiences of Black soldiers in one of the last colonial states; the social structures that maintained their group identity; and the RAR’s conception of professionalism, which shaped their relationships with their peers, their government, and their enemies throughout the 15-year liberation war.

auditPapers.title: The Death of Woman Guo Big Asia and the Anthropocene
auditPapers.abstract: One chilly night in December 1937, somewhere in Keshan, a county in Japanese-occupied Manchukuo, Mrs. Guo (née Sun)—no given name recorded—woke up in her adobe farmhouse with crippling head and chest pains. As a 26-year-old with no prior history of serious illness, she should not have had such severe symptoms. When local clinicians examined her three days later, they noted that Guo was in so much distress that they could not ascertain her heart rate or blood pressure, only that her skin had turned white and her limbs blue from the lack of oxygen in her blood. By this point, she was vomiting yellow bile. Five hours later, she was dead. Guo only exists in the imperial archive because Japanese epidemiologists documented her autopsy in a medical journal, alongside those of several other casualties from this mysterious sickness.1 Her death had followed a sudden and terrifying outbreak that had killed over a hundred people in Keshan two years earlier. The alarmed doctors at first wondered if they had encountered a new variant of pneumonic plague but ultimately decided to classify the disorder as a “climatic disease,” implying that its cause lay in the interaction between the environmental setting and cultural practices of a particular area. They named the ailment Keshan Disease after its place of origin.2

auditPapers.title: Jennifer Lofkrantz. Ransoming Prisoners in Precolonial Muslim West Africa.

auditPapers.title: Aaron W. Marrs. The American Transportation Revolution: A Social and Cultural History.
auditPapers.abstract: The role of the railroad industry in nineteenth-century United States history is unchallenged, and the literature exploring it is vast and vibrant. In The American Transportation Revolution: A Social and Cultural History, Aaron W. Marrs uses the framework of steam transit to innovatively connect railroads with another powerful technology, steamboats. He argues that the two changed the cultural and social landscape of antebellum America. Through this approach, Marrs provides an important reminder of the interconnectedness of modes of transportation. Historians have tended to draw a line, admittedly quite porous, between water-borne travel and the iron road. Railroad historians include canals as competitors and lake transport as complements, but books systematically linking water and rail are rare. Marrs argues that unlike exponents of, for example, the New History of Capitalism, foregrounding steam transit in the big picture of economic transformation allows us to understand how and why steamboats and railroads shaped American culture and society. Building on works like James A. Ward’s Railroads and the Character of America 1820–1887 (1986), H. Roger Grant’s Railroads and the American People (2012), Robert H. Gudmestad’s Steamboats and the Rise of the Cotton Kingdom (2011), and especially A Most Magnificent Machine: America Adopts the Railroad, 1825–1862 (2010) by Craig Miner, Marrs asks how steam transit became naturalized in the American imagination. His answer is to show that steam-powered transportation fostered cultural and social change, arguing that “steam transit influenced the creation of popular, artistic, and educational artifacts consumed by Americans” (4).

auditPapers.title: Las Que Van Quedando en el Camino (The Women Who Are Left by the Wayside)
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article examines a recently discovered oral history interview of a woman peasant (campesina), Emelina Sagredo, who was a leader of Chile’s most important campesino uprising, the 1934 Ránquil rebellion. The article explores Sagredo’s 1965 interview with the Chilean playwright Isidora Aguirre to raise questions about how to write the history of largely illiterate women, gender, and sexuality and the limits of both archival and published sources. I read the oral history and Aguirre’s 1969 theatrical dramatization of the Ránquil rebellion together to demonstrate how the Left’s “Communist morality” imposed limits on historical representations of women’s lives. I argue that the interview is valuable both because it provides a unique view of women’s historical experience and because it exposes the limits of the available archival and published material. Finally, the article raises questions about the historian’s ethical obligation to respect the privacy of their subjects even in the face of extraordinary archival discoveries. The interview was never intended to be made public and was found among Aguirre’s papers posthumously. I ask: What responsibility does the historian have to keep private aspects of a life history, a conversation, as valuable as it may be as a source?

auditPapers.title: Jack Crangle. Migrants, Immigration and Diversity in Twentieth-century Northern Ireland: British, Irish or ‘Other’?.
auditPapers.abstract: For most of the twentieth century, immigrants were invisible in Northern Ireland. This is the starting premise of Migrants, Immigration and Diversity in Twentieth-century Northern Ireland, Jack Crangle’s rich and timely exploration of the small communities of Italians, Indians, Chinese, and Vietnamese who have made Northern Ireland home. From that premise, a number of consequences followed. Immigrants’ invisibility meant there was no major backlash against them in the twentieth century; unlike in Britain, immigration never became a central issue in Northern Ireland politics. But their invisibility also meant immigrants did not enjoy the same support systems, public and private, that their counterparts in Britain did. Instead, they were forced upon their own resources, developing an entrepreneurial ethos that was strong even by the standards of other immigrant communities. As Northern Ireland becomes more diverse in the twenty-first century, and as it struggles to address some of the challenges attendant upon that diversity, it has become ever more urgent to understand the region’s prior history of immigration. This book is a major contribution to that effort.

auditPapers.title: Paraska Tolan-Szkilnik. Maghreb Noir: The Militant-Artists of North Africa and the Struggle for a Pan-African, Postcolonial Future.
auditPapers.abstract: Today, the most viral images of the Maghreb are of it as a setting for revolutionary activity. Photographs of the Black Panther Party in Algiers in 1969 and clips of Senegalese director Ousmane Sembène explaining that Europe was irrelevant to him at a film festival in Tunis receive thousands of likes on social media platforms. These depictions circulate because they are inspiring. They remind us of brief moments in history where incredible transnational solidarities formed. Yet inherent in the circulation of these images, excerpts, and clips is also a flattening. They are presented without history or context. Viewers have no sense of what facilitated these Black revolutionaries’ presence in the Maghreb, what treatment they encountered, who they engaged with, and how they were encouraged or constrained by their time there. Enter Maghreb Noir, a thoughtful history of the height of the Maghreb’s revolutionary ethos from the 1950s to the 1970s by Paraska Tolan-Szkilnik.

auditPapers.title: Elizabeth Campbell. Museum Worthy: Nazi Art Plunder in Postwar Western Europe.
auditPapers.abstract: The Museum of Art and History of Judaism (mahJ) in Paris features multiple displays related to art looted from France during the Second World War, including an installation of works photographed for art dealer Paul Rosenberg’s gallery, which were crucial to the postwar restitution of hundreds of his stolen pieces. There is also a room dedicated to the looting of Chana Orloff’s Parisian home studio featuring a wooden sculpture of her son, finally returned to the Orloff family in 2022. Additionally, a self-portrait by Max Liebermann bears a stamp identifying it as MNR-978. In 1967, Liebermann’s portrait was entrusted to the French National Museums as an unclaimed artwork (MNR) recuperated after the Second World War. The portrait found its way from the Louvre to the Orsay Museum and the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art in Strasbourg before becoming a long-term loan to the mahJ. Elizabeth Campbell traces the history of looted pieces such as these in France, the Netherlands, and Belgium in Museum Worthy in order to demonstrate the lasting legacies of cultural theft and how institutions benefited from unclaimed artworks while “the dispossession of Jewish Holocaust victims is an injustice that has yet to be fully rectified” (9).

auditPapers.title: Thomas D. Conlan. Kings in All but Name: The Lost History of Ōuchi Rule in Japan, 1350–1569.
auditPapers.abstract: In Kings in All But Name: The Lost History of Ōuchi Rule in Japan, 1350–1569, Thomas D. Conlan does not shy away from posing provocative questions. He challenges the typical historical periodization of medieval Japan, which characterizes the sixteenth century as the “Warring States period” and Kyoto as the geopolitical capital. Instead, he argues for an earlier “Age of Yamaguchi,” a city in western Japan that was the seat of power for the Ōuchi family. Conlan makes thorough use of Japanese and Korean sources to piece together a timeline of nine Ōuchi leaders and their methods of rule. In doing so, he demonstrates the strong impact that the Ōuchi had not only in western Japan but also in Kyoto and even in interactions with Korea and China. The monograph follows the rise and fall of the successive Ōuchi leaders. Conlan’s main focus is on how each ruler consolidated his power and influence, and he highlights several key themes: the Ōuchi’s ethnic ties with Korea, the use of religious rituals to legitimize rulership, and waxing and waning connections with military and royal institutions in Kyoto. The first topic in particular has not previously been deeply explored in the English-language historiography. Conlan demonstrates how the Ōuchi leaders actually tended to flaunt their ancestral ties (both real and imagined) with Korean peninsular royalty and used those ties to legitimize their leadership in Japan, challenging historical ideas of ethnic homogeneity in Japanese rulership. He further delineates how the Ōuchi skillfully used their connections to promote trade with the mainland, sometimes usurping the role of official trade carried out by the central powers in Kyoto and using the profit to strengthen their own position. In particular, Conlan suggests that the Ōuchi leveraged their political authority to develop copper mining, as opposed to the typical narrative emphasizing agriculture as the main source of income.

auditPapers.title: Rama Sundari Mantena. Provincial Democracy: Political Imaginaries at the End of Empire in Twentieth-Century South India.
auditPapers.abstract: Rama Sundari Mantena’s Provincial Democracy: Political Imaginaries at the End of Empire in Twentieth-Century South India is a history of liberalism and anti-colonialism in South India primarily concerned with analyzing discourses of self-determination, federation, and civil liberties. By taking a regional approach and focusing on Telugu-language source material, Mantena seeks to decenter imperial and national frameworks by attending to the development of Indian democracy within a vernacular context. This regional approach also allows Mantena to explore how anti-colonialism grappled with and sought to transcend the boundaries between the princely state of Hyderabad and the British Indian province of Madras. Provincial Democracy consists of an introductory chapter on liberalism and anti-colonialism in South India followed by two chapters apiece on federation and civil liberties. The opening chapter on liberalism maps out the pre–World War I history of social reform movements in colonial Andhra, and the subsequent development of a regional political identity, public sphere, and civil society in the crucible of the interwar period. The main figure here is J. Gurunatham, a little-known but founding figure of the Andhra movement, who, Mantena argues, “understood the necessity of training people to become citizens” (35). In pursuit of preparing Telugu-speaking people for democracy, Gurunatham sought to couple late nineteenth-century social reformism with an explicitly political agenda. Mantena argues that early articulations of a separate Andhra state were the product of the “cultivation of public reason” (43) and that the interwar Andhra movement subsequently, and successfully, engaged in a deliberate project of extending “civic institutions for nurturing Telugu political life and public spirit” (53). Provincial Democracy offers a rich sense of the broad range of ideas and initiatives that were indeed recognizably liberal or, at the very least, liberal-adjacent. Mantena’s capacious understanding of liberalism includes nearly all shades of Indian political opinion, which has the advantage of illuminating shared liberal sentiments, but also the effect of muddling the ideological stakes and dissensions. The book deploys more contemporary terms to categorize its subjects: Individuals are often described as either “progressive” or “conservative.” Overall, the global expansion of liberalism, within a context defined by imperialism and nationalism, is understood as largely unidirectional. One wonders what unique contributions these regional figures may have added to a global history of liberalism and liberal ideas, or how their ideological innovations, to borrow from C. A. Bayly’s Recovering Liberties: Indian Thought in the Age of Liberalism and Empire (2012), “cannibalised, reconstructed and re-authored” (3) ideas from the Western liberal tradition.

auditPapers.title: Selim Güngörürler. The Ottoman Empire and Safavid Iran, 1639–1682: Diplomacy and Borderlands in the Early Modern Middle East.
auditPapers.abstract: Selim Güngörürler’s The Ottoman Empire and Safavid Iran, 1639–1682: Diplomacy and Borderlands in the Early Modern Middle East is a meticulously researched study that sheds light on the intricate diplomatic and political dynamics between two powerful empires in early modern history. The relationship between the Ottoman Empire and Safavid Iran, which had been largely characterized by recurring waves of military conflict and subsequent peace treaties, underwent a profound transformation following the signing of the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639. As Güngörürler demonstrates, the Treaty of Zuhab not only delineated a stable territorial boundary between the two empires but also set the stage for a remarkable shift in how both states managed their relations. Güngörürler emphasizes that the treaty’s significance lies not merely in its creation of a physical boundary but in its inauguration of a new era of diplomatic interaction—one marked by bureaucratic correspondence rather than military confrontation. This era of relative peace, which spanned more than eight decades until the fall of the Safavid Empire in the 1720s, saw both states adhering to the terms of the treaty, exchanging ambassadors, and engaging in diplomatic missions that fostered what Güngörürler calls a friendly “harmony” between the two empires. Güngörürler’s book examines the first four decades of this period, with a particular focus on diplomatic exchanges.

auditPapers.title: Lauren Lassabe Shepherd. Resistance from the Right: Conservatives and the Campus Wars in Modern America.
auditPapers.abstract: Lauren Lassabe Shepherd has joined a growing number of scholars reconsidering the history of US higher education in recent years. That work has offered critical reevaluations of landmark federal laws (such as the 1862 Land Grant College, or Morrill, Act and the 1965 Higher Education Act), proprietary schools, once-celebrated university presidents (including Southern liberal Frank Porter Graham and California pluralist Clark Kerr), and campus expansions into low-income Black and Brown neighborhoods. Much of that research has shown the darker side of the liberal policies behind the academy’s storied expansion, but Resistance from the Right: Conservatives and the Campus Wars in Modern America explores the links between campuses and the growth of modern conservatism, a topic that has dominated the field of twentieth-century US history since the mid-1990s. Shepherd focuses on conservative and far-right students. That group has received far less attention than the broad student left, some of whom became the tenured radicals writing the history of Berkeley’s Free Speech Movement, Students for a Democratic Society, and other radical groups. Shepherd’s short account of conservative campus activism between 1967 and 1970 helps explain why. Most undergraduate and graduate students went to class. Only a small subset protested the Vietnam War, demanded integration, tried to stop left-wing demonstrations, or mocked efforts to start Black Studies programs. Yet the Young Americans for Freedom, Intercollegiate Studies Institute, College Republicans, and Campus Crusade for Christ International proclaimed themselves the voice for a silent student majority who wanted to learn, not be indoctrinated. They had a lot of help from powerful conservative groups, including the Foundation for Economic Education, the Mount Pelerin Society, and National Review. As such, Shepherd argues the conservative movement on college campuses across the country was better understood as “an astroturf backlash” (189). Such top-down support provided fellowships, instruction manuals, and jobs after graduation, which led many into careers in politics and policymaking, not academia. Yet conservative alumni found themselves with a lot of power over colleges and universities, which relied on federal funding that declined in the decades after this set of conservative activists graduated.

auditPapers.title: Trevor Burnard. Writing the History of Global Slavery.
auditPapers.abstract: Although the institution of slavery has been continuously practiced in the world since its ancient origins, enslavement lacks a comprehensive unifying model that includes most or all of the forms of slavery that exist or have ever existed. In Writing the Global History of Slavery, Trevor Burnard not only advocates for expansive denotations of the condition of enslavement and the institution of slavery; he also suggests pathways that might lead to the possibility of cross-society and cross-temporal comparisons of slavery. Burnard proposes focusing on similarities such as the possession of people and the maternal inheritance of the status of being enslaved as two promising approaches. Furthermore, he advances the idea of shifting slavery’s paradigm in the scholarship “from sociological models and with a heavy reliance on slavery in nineteenth-century America as the norm from which all enslavement might be analysed” to an archetype rooted in historical methods of inquiry (1). Ultimately, he argues that a new historical perspective of slavery should perhaps be considered in conjunction with empire.

auditPapers.title: Catherine Volpilhac-Auger. Montesquieu: Let There be Enlightenment.
auditPapers.abstract: In “The Translator’s Task,” Walter Benjamin remarks that the “history of great works of art knows about their descent from their sources, their shaping in the age of the artists, and the periods of their basically eternal continuing life in later generations” (154). Catherine Volpilhac-Auger’s biography, Montesquieu: Let There be Enlightenment, and her ongoing reproduction of Montesquieu’s complete works do precisely this. She injects new life into our understanding of Montesquieu and his writings. Her biography is a product of the monumental study of Montesquieu’s life and archive that includes his published and unpublished writings, correspondence, and library. Together these have brought to light new information and created a fresh, yet classic, portrayal of Montesquieu’s life, writings, intellectual and historical contexts. This biography does not seek to replace earlier ones produced by Robert Shackleton (1961) and Louis Desgraves (1986). Rather, it aims to fill in gaps, to rethink his ideas based on evidence that has recently come to light and to dispel false or embellished narratives. As such, her biography ought to be read in conjunction with these earlier ones.

auditPapers.title: Erin Pettigrew. Invoking the Invisible in the Sahara: Islam, Spiritual Mediation, and Social Change.
auditPapers.abstract: How to write about the invisible, the esoteric, the magical in a place like Mauritania? As in many other contexts, both in the past and in our own times, people in Mauritania appear to either believe in, or at least find credible, the possibility that there are unseen forces that can act on the visible, or human, world. Efforts to control these forces, for good or for ill, are called l’ḥjāb in Hassaniya Arabic, a term that Erin Pettigrew translates as “Islamic esoteric sciences.” These include a wide range of systematic knowledge and techniques that specialists use to access powers of the unseen world in order to manipulate the visible world. In Invoking the Invisible in the Sahara, Pettigrew traces a history of these ideas and techniques in Mauritania using as her sources the Islamic literature written in Arabic in Mauritania since the 17th century, French colonial accounts, and her own ethnographic work in the postcolonial period. Not only does she clearly demonstrate that l’ḥjāb has long been understood to be extremely important by people in this region at least since the time that we have written records, but she also shows that there can be a history of l’ḥjāb, in that it has changed over time from a knowledge and practice embedded in Sufism to a postcolonial perception that esoteric knowledge is subject to abuse by those who claim mastery of it. In contemporary Mauritania, TV shows and media entrepreneurs regularly focus on the uses and misuses of l’ḥjāb.

auditPapers.title: Sandra McGee Deutsch. Gendering Antifascism: Women’s Activism in Argentina and the World, 1918–1947.
auditPapers.abstract: Sandra McGee Deutsch was interviewing an elderly Argentine woman about her life when the interviewee happened to recall her participation in an Argentine women’s antifascist political organization called Junta de la Victoria (Victory Board). This memory raised new questions for Deutsch and led to a long research process involving archival research in several countries. The results of her work are reflected in Gendering Antifascism, a major contribution to the historiography of antifascism, gender studies, and political history in the countries of the Southern Cone of South America during the interwar period. Deutsch presents a study of the Junta de la Victoria, which was created in 1941 as a result of the German invasion of the Soviet Union. This organization remained active until 1947 and gave visibility to women’s political participation. The growth of this group was remarkable, from 16,000 members in 1942 to eventually 45,000 members across the country. It was a socially heterogeneous community that included upper-class women as well as factory workers and peasants. It also included women of varied religious, ethnic, and political backgrounds who developed formal and informal democratic practices within their organization. Unity was achieved through pluralism, social ties, and culture, as women from these varied origins shared books, music, and other artistic expressions and gathered together to sew and knit for the Allies, which had a strong political significance. The author argues that the Junta de la Victoria was the most important Argentine women’s political movement before Peronism, an unprecedented local experience characterized by pluralism, coalition building, and mobilization that constituted a democratic microcosm promoting women’s participation in the world of politics. Curiously, this experience has been forgotten because historians have not taken into account the impact it had on sympathizers, the wider antifascist movement, and its detractors.

auditPapers.title: Choon Hwee Koh. The Sublime Post: How the Ottoman Imperial Post Became a Public Service.
auditPapers.abstract: While as teachers we constantly advise our students to first think about the questions they want to ask of the past and then find the relevant sources that might answer them, it is no shame to admit that as researchers we often experience the opposite. We discover a body of sources and wonder what questions they might answer. I imagine this is how Choon Hwee Koh’s materially rich and conceptually insightful study The Sublime Post was conceived. It is based on archival documentation of the Ottoman postal or courier system in the 18th century, hundreds of registers produced by bureaucrats in the capital Istanbul and by postmasters at relay stations from Belgrade to Baghdad. These unnervingly factual registers meticulously record expenses ranging from horseshoes to barley; the comings and goings of horses, couriers, and other travelers; and fees collected and waived. This body of sources seems to contradict commonly held assumptions about the Ottoman Empire. It shows that the central government paid a lot of attention to an important imperial infrastructure during an era that is usually thought of as a time of decentralization and weakness of the center. In contrast, the scarcity of sources suggest that Istanbul wasn’t as focused on this infrastructure during the 16th century, a time when the central state was thought to be most powerful.

auditPapers.title: Kathryn Taylor. Ordering Customs: Ethnographic Thought in Early Modern Venice.
auditPapers.abstract: Francis Bacon’s trio of key early modern technologies—the compass, gunpowder, and print—famously underpinned the explosive growth of Europeans’ awareness of, access to, and power to influence the wider world from the late fifteenth century onward. That empire, new technology, and sustained direct contact with distant peoples new to Europeans were sufficient to explain the equally rapid transformation in the scale and structure of European ethnographic thought has longed seemed natural. Kathryn Taylor, however, in Ordering Customs: Ethnographic Thought in Early Modern Venice, challenges such unexamined assumptions by focusing on a parallel tradition that operated significantly in manuscript, followed old routes to familiar places, and was bound up with the sliding relative power of a slowly crumbling empire. In Taylor’s account, the practices and institutional forms that developed out of Venice’s attempts to navigate a newly hostile world that threatened to undermine its prosperity and cherished independence generated genres in which sustained engagement with the manners and customs of other peoples, which Taylor characterizes as ethnographic thought, was expected. The center of this vein of the history of ethnography, then, lies in another classic pair of early modern stories: the growth of the state and its increasingly formalized practices of diplomacy and information gathering. Based on these premises, Venice—famously cosmopolitan, a towering early center of print, and the leading exemplar of new diplomatic practices—emerges as a naturally central site for the development of ethnographic thought.

auditPapers.title: “Survival in an Age of Revolution”
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract While great effort has been invested in analyzing the role of revolutionary intellectuals in history, much less attention has been paid to the counterrevolution and its guides. This is especially the case in the former colonial world in the era of decolonization, where anticolonial politics are often portrayed as having been the default position. Lebanese philosopher and statesman Charles Malik was a candid opponent of what he theorized as the “great Asian and African revolution” against imperial rule. Instead, he advocated consciously counterrevolutionary politics that sought to purify the corruptions of “collectivism, materialism, and secularism” brought forward by an age of anticolonial and socialist revolutions. Primarily known as a principal author of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, it was in the Lebanese arena that his global political commitments were most directly expressed. This included his decisive role in securing US military intervention during Lebanon’s 1958 civil war, and more fundamentally in his founding role in the Front for Freedom and Man in Lebanon (FFML), the counterrevolutionary, Christian-supremacist alliance in Lebanon’s international civil war (1975–90). Malik’s praxis highlights an overlooked philo-colonial trend in the era of decolonization: native advocates for continued imperial sovereignty over a dependent and rigidly stratified nation-state without equal citizenship. Malik’s ideological and material entanglements on multiple scales foreground the defining part of counterrevolutionary networks in shaping the global history of twentieth century and its inheritance.

auditPapers.title: Big Asia
auditPapers.abstract: In recent years, after decades of increasing specialization, new approaches have emerged in Asian studies that focus on larger units of analysis. Some are predicated on transnational or transimperial spaces, whether based around language (the “Persianate world” and “Sinosphere”), geography (the Indian Ocean or “Silk Road”), or networks (whether forged by commercial, political, or cultural actors). This attention to networks has in turn fostered interest in “inter-Asian” developments, and in methods that are at once micro and macro in scale by following small numbers of people, concepts, or commodities across the continent at large. Correspondingly, the rise of not only global history but also environmental and “big history” has encouraged studies of the entire continent, or large sections of it, by way of steppes and mountain ranges as much as river systems and seas. Such big spaces have in turn linked the study of individuals and communities in Asia to their associates or counterparts in the Americas, Europe, and the Pacific, framing Asia within the larger geography of the “Pacific Rim,” “Asia-Pacific,” “Indo-Pacific,” and “Eurasia”—concepts that have found political as much as scholarly purchase. “Big Asia,” then, begs big questions about not only the methodological how but also the fundamental where and who of Asia’s past, and their implications for the geopolitical present.

auditPapers.title: Caleb Wellum. Energizing Neoliberalism: The 1970s Energy Crisis and the Making of Modern America.
auditPapers.abstract: Energizing Neoliberalism is a provocation to those of us who think about the 1970s energy crisis. Caleb Wellum effectively connects the event to many strands of the new ways that energy history has guided us to reconsider and evaluate these events, which becomes essential as our energy story progresses to reveal that maybe something important did, in fact, transpire in humans’ approach to energy use after this critical decade. As a provocation, though, Wellum’s work introduces insights without necessarily carrying them to completion. With its emphasis on neoliberalism, Energizing Neoliberalism is best categorized as a work of political history even though it states its emphasis as the cultural story. Readers expecting a complete consideration of the politics of the era, though, might best be served by Meg Jacobs’s book Panic at the Pump and other titles that broadly source the events of the period. However, what Wellum offers is a most insightful consideration that will introduce many readers to the approach of the developing line of inquiry known as “petrocultures.”

auditPapers.title: Elizabeth Garner Masarik. The Sentimental State: How Women-Led Reform Built the American Welfare State.
auditPapers.abstract: In The Sentimental State, Elizabeth Garner Masarik expands our understanding of sentimentalism from a cultural phenomenon to a crucial political tool wielded by white and Black reform-minded women in the Gilded Age and Progressive Era. The language of grief and emotion served as the conduit through which American women could make demands on local and federal governments. By tracing the formation of private-run organizations and their connection to nascent legislation protecting the sanctity of children and motherhood, Masarik provides an alternative history of the formation of the modern welfare state. The voluntary, unpaid, and often unrecognized labor performed by middle-class white and Black women not only facilitated the creation of these national welfare programs but also continues to define modern debates over their impact. Throughout the book, Masarik demonstrates that private, local, and voluntary reform organizations have never been separate from the state-building process. Redefining infant mortality, grief, and sexuality as concerns central to the state allowed reformers to influence local policy, acquire funds, and participate in political debates. These issues emphasized the mother-child bond and intimately connected the personal to the political. Importantly, the book locates the origins of the modern welfare state well before the New Deal. Masarik describes the process through which voluntary organizations in the late nineteenth century constituted an “associative welfare state” that later merged with local and state governments (10). The grassroots work of middle-class women created the foundation for social policies but also provided emotional legitimacy for their implementation. Crucially, Masarik acknowledges and centers the experiences of African American women and the unique conditions under which they engaged in maternalism and social reform work at the turn of the century. Contributing to the new and growing field of the history of emotions, she utilizes a variety of institutional and governmental documents, newspaper records, and cultural artifacts like popular fiction to craft a narrative of sentimentalism.

auditPapers.title: Benjamin Carp. The Great New York Fire of 1776: A Lost Story of the American Revolution.
auditPapers.abstract: Stories of wars and revolutions, when abstracted to their ideological impact, can elide the daily horrors experienced by people unable to escape the violence. Narratives of the American Revolution are particularly susceptible to this framing. Unbeknownst to rebels and patriots, the United States would become a global superpower whose present-day citizens find in the Revolution the source of their country’s “exceptional” character. But many revolutionary actions, when explored as microhistories, reveal new lessons about a tumultuous era. Benjamin Carp offers just such a careful and nuanced study in The Great New York Fire of 1776. Carp’s investigation demonstrates that patriots could be vindictive, destructive, and cruel. His conclusion is clear and convincing—in the fall of 1776, American rebels torched New York in a coordinated effort to burn the city to the ground before the British could take it. Carp’s thesis, which is supported by a careful reading of extant sources, is important because he settles a debate that animated citizens and officials in Britain and the rebellious colonies at the time but was subsequently written out of revolutionary history. His conclusion that patriots set fire to New York complicates the founding story of the United States by reminding contemporary Americans that patriots “skulked and deceived, burned and massacred, unleashed campaigns of terror, and denigrated people as less worthy of citizenship” (5). Over the course of fourteen tight chapters, Carp recreates the world of New York in 1776—describing its buildings and streetscapes, its inhabitants, and the city’s role as a character in the revolutionary drama. New York was divided along class, gender, and racial lines in ways that are unfortunately familiar today; it was also a city where violence was not uncommon. Fire was a constant threat in crowded settlements across North America, especially given the ease and economy of building structures of wood rather than stone. In 1776, patriots from George Washington to nameless sympathizers considered torching New York to keep it from falling into British hands. Washington himself later regretted not giving official orders to burn the city—Congress had instructed him not to—but he must have taken solace in the fact that his orders were unnecessary. Patriots set the fires nonetheless.
