auditPapers.title: Andrew Seaton. Our NHS: A History of Britain’s Best-Loved Institution.
auditPapers.abstract: In the spring of 2024, theatergoers in London had a choice of two star-studded plays commemorating the birth of Britain’s National Health Service (NHS). One, The Human Body, told the story of the NHS’s foundation in 1948 through the eyes of a socialist woman doctor. The other, Nye, celebrated the politician commonly credited as its architect, the Labour Minister of Health Aneurin Bevan. The ovations greeting these performances were not for the actors alone but spoke also to the affection in which the public still holds the service. This compound of nostalgia and hope that attends the service today owes less to its current performance than to its talismanic features. These are universal population coverage, cradle-to-grave medical provision, and “free at the point of use” funding based largely on graduated general taxation. In contrast, Seaton’s focus is on retrieving attitudes and feelings toward the service to establish its place in popular and political culture.

auditPapers.title: Amy Godine. The Black Woods: Pursuing Racial Justice on the Adirondack Frontier.
auditPapers.abstract: Since its founding, the American nation has predominately been an agricultural society infused with notions of freedom, independence, and economic advancement through farming labor. The small independent farmer became a romantic symbol, which was most popularly referenced by Thomas Jefferson, to epitomize the ideal American citizen. However, such agrarian traditions were often denied to millions of African Americans and their descendants. The “forty acres and a mule” became the symbol of this obstructed promise of mass landownership after freedom. As the preeminent scholar W. E. B. Du Bois once wrote, “The vision of ‘forty acres and a mule’ . . . was destined in most cases to a bitter disappointment” (The Souls of Black Folk [1903], 26). Amy Godine explores an earlier short-lived pursuit of this Black agrarian vision in The Black Woods: Pursuing Racial Justice on the Adirondack Frontier. The Black Woods examines a little-known history of a land giveaway project of forty-acre plots to Black New Yorkers. Implemented from 1846 to 1853, this project was created by the abolitionist and large landowner Gerrit Smith, who broke up 120,000 acres of his land located in the remote northern New York wilderness of Adirondack. This land was intended for farming and gifted to three thousand Black people. Though eventually viewed as a failure, an analysis of this land giveaway reveals the earlier aspirations of Black agrarian pursuits.

auditPapers.abstract: In The Sonoran Dynasty in Mexico, Jürgen Buchenau explores how eleven politicians from the northern state of Sonora significantly influenced national politics during and after the Mexican Revolution (1910–20). The literature on the revolution has tended to cast this group, known as the Sonorenses, in a negative light. “Winning the revolution,” writes Buchenau, “came at the price of blame for its shortcomings, including the persistence of authoritarian governance and widespread corruption; the failure to achieve social justice; and the inability to diminish the influence of the United States” (9). Consequently, historians initially avoided in-depth analyses of the Sonorenses, preferring to focus on the revolution’s defeated agrarian forces and their leaders. Weaving together biography, political history, intrigue, and superb storytelling, Buchenau has crafted the first comprehensive and archivally based study on the Sonorenses and its members—a regional dynasty that dominated Mexican politics from 1920 to the mid-1930s. This work represents the “culminating synthesis” of a senior scholar who has established himself as the premiere authority on the political lives of Sonoran Presidents Álvaro Obregón (1920–24) and Plutarco Elías Calles (1924–28) (ix). In this latest book, however, Buchenau expands his analysis beyond these two patriarchs and considers the political rise and fall of the larger and influential Sonorense group. This group hailed from a state with “less than 2 percent of Mexico’s population [but] accounted for an estimated 11.4 percent of the governing elite” (4). Buchenau contends that the personal relationships and rivalries within this group contributed to Mexico’s process of centralization through institutionalization but also led to the formation of opposing “social and political movements” that fueled successive bloody civil wars and rebellions (6–8). The group “also brought about important reforms and innovations, in addition to defending Mexican sovereignty and political stability” (13).

Elijah, the Gaon of Vilna (1720–1797), who imparted it directly to Rivlin’s own ancestors, who, in their turn, mobilized the students of the Gaon to emigrate and thus “laid the foundations for Zionism” (1) decades before the first secular “pioneers” established the New Yishuv. auditPapers.title: Jamie L. Jones. Rendered Obsolete: Energy Culture and the Afterlife of US Whaling.
auditPapers.abstract: The concept of an energy transition is a powerful and deceptively simple one that has captured the attention of energy and environmental historians writing amid climate crisis. The result has been a spate of excellent work on the economic, social, and political implications of the modern era’s major energy transition: the shift from a world defined by renewable flows of energy (muscle, sun, wind, and water) to one defined by the production and use of fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas). Many of these studies have offered nuanced accounts of transition, noting that it is always contested, uneven, and overlapping to such a degree that the term transition may not even be appropriate. But few scholars have approached the question in the compelling way that Jamie L. Jones does in Rendered Obsolete: Energy Culture and the Afterlife of US Whaling. Most accounts trace either the rise of new fuels or the persistence of old ones, but in this densely argued book, Jones focuses on a declining resource—whale oil—to explore the “cultural afterlife” of a fuel rapidly losing its original economic significance (5). The result is a history of energy that deepens our understanding of how energy transitions work culturally and politically. Jones’s overarching argument is that the representation, memory, and artifacts of US whaling helped mediate the nineteenth century’s bewildering transition to fossil fuels, functioning as a yardstick of modernity and a site of nostalgic longing for a fictive past that helped remake social and political life in the United States.

auditPapers.title: Hannah Forsyth. Virtue Capitalists: The Rise and Fall of the Professional Class in the Anglophone World, 1870–2008.
auditPapers.abstract: Global history often renders down the histories of modern British settler colonies into generic settler colonialism. In works with a global scope, it’s easy to lose the particularities of the interactions between the social, cultural, and environmental circumstances of a place, especially when settlers seem to be broadly British in their cultural and political aspirations. In contrast, each modern former British settler nation’s local history-writing traditions deal with the consequences of the specific encounter between what settlers and immigrants bring, and Indigenous institutions and environments. Here, the opposite is at stake: national historiographies seek what marks them out from neighbors, antecedents, and the rest of the world. This contrast between a totalizing global history of modern settler colonialism and the parochial historiographical traditions of modern settler colonies is often frustrating for those of us with an interest in both. Because of this, Hannah Forsyth’s book Virtue Capitalists is a refreshing, fun, and interesting book that integrates the local with the global without losing track of what is important about local detail or global scope. Forsyth argues that, far from being extensions or the margins of fundamental changes in modern work and class structures, Australia, Aotearoa New Zealand, Canada, and the United States were where the modern professional-managerial class (defined broadly and vaguely) was born. This was not an accident or coincidence; in fact, Forsyth argues, setter colonialism was central to the processes that created modern work and class, because of the settler need to marginalize Native claims to sovereignty, autonomy, and stewardship. The experiences of Anglo settlers, the experiences of the Native and non-Native groups whom they exploited and alienated, and the process of settler colonialism, therefore, made the professional-managerial class and modern bureaucratic institutions. To understand the dominant class dynamics of the twentieth century, Forsyth suggests, historians must invert the traditional perspective and provincialize Britain.

auditPapers.title: Susan Gaunt Stearns. Empire of Commerce: The Closing of the Mississippi and the Opening of Atlantic Trade.
auditPapers.abstract: Empire of Commerce: The Closing of the Mississippi and the Opening of Atlantic Trade by Susan Gaunt Stearns gives a clear view into the complex history of the “Mississippi Question.” In 1784, Spain closed the Mississippi River to European Americans triggering a national crisis for the United States. Stearns masterfully unpacks the ramifications of this decision for Indigenous peoples, the Chickasaw Nation in particular, as well as European American farmers, traders, merchants, and politicians. With astute observation and captivating historical examples, Stearns showcases the economic importance of the Mississippi River to these diverse groups and the fluidity of their affairs on the waterway. Stearns divides her history of empire and commerce into three parts. The first explores economic activity along the Mississippi River prior to the American Revolution through 1783. Indigenous peoples, like the Chickasaws, had long used the river as a center for long distance trade. Meanwhile an influx of European American settlers into the trans-Appalachian west, whom Stearns calls “westerners,” hoped to access Atlantic markets via the Mississippi to finance the region’s developing land market. Part 2 centers on events following Spain’s closure of the Mississippi River until its eventual reopening in 1795. Though no single power, Indigenous or imperial, could fully command the river, the Chickasaw Nation’s strategic position at the Chickasaw Bluffs near modern-day Memphis and Spanish policies in New Orleans made traveling and trading on the Mississippi a daunting task. The ramifications of this nearly divided the newly founded United States. Stearns culminates her work with the integration of the trans-Appalachian west into the Atlantic World. Pinckney’s Treaty in 1795 opened the Mississippi to American trade, working to reinforce the bonds between westerners and the rest of the United States. The economic benefits this brought to the national economy cleared the way for the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, ensuring the Mississippi became an “American river.”

auditPapers.title: Comment by Cemil Aydın
auditPapers.abstract: Contributions to the AHR History Lab on “Big Asia” collectively summarized the critical scholarly wisdom on the origins, achievements, internal contradictions, limitations, and futurity of the idea of Asian geocultural unity since the height of Western hegemony in the 1880s. While we have a rich critical literature among both the scholars of Asia and Asian intellectuals about the invented and constructed character of Asian unity and Asianism as a project, why do we still talk about Asian identity and projects of Asian civilizationism in the early twenty-first century? These History Lab essays show us how we need a similar critical inquiry of Europe and Western civilization to complement our reflection on the idea of Asia. As long as the European master narrative of civilization stays alive and politically mobilized, there will be some form of imagining “Big Asia.” As Nile Green notes, the term “Asia” entered from its European origins into vernacular languages from Ottoman intellectual circles to China as early as the sixteenth century, yet it was in the late nineteenth century that the idea of Asia spread more widely amid spaces and people it designated in Asia. A synchronization and convergence of epistemologies occurred by the turn of the twentieth century, when European etic ascription of Asia was embraced by Asians themselves as a capacious emic concept, strategically formulating a humanist discourse of civilization, internationalism, and globalism. Since then, there have been multiple ways to describe an Asia beyond the negative unity against the European colonial hegemony and Orientalist discourses, with references to shared Asian geography, religion, language, culture, and art. In the age of steam and print as well as transportation and communication infrastructure built by Western empires, proximity was felt among Chinese, Indians, and Arab populations due to inter-Asian connectivity of trade, travel, and anticolonial solidarity, similar to the proximity felt among different Asian activists today, as discussed by Jeffrey Wasserstrom. But proximity was also imagined because of the problem space of colonial racism, with Persian and Afghans seeing Japanese in very distant lands as fellow Asians compared to Russians next door.

auditPapers.title: Huang Pumin, Wei Hong, and Xiong Jianping. A History of Traditional Chinese Military Science. Translated by Fan Hao.
auditPapers.abstract: The field of Chinese military history in the West has grown considerably in the last couple of decades but remains extremely small. Consequently, despite the growing interest in the contemporary Chinese military and the history and culture that informs its thinking, there are no reliable overviews in English of Chinese military history, military thought, or military culture. This is not peculiar to scholarship in English, however, as the field is similarly limited in Chinese (which the authors note), Japanese, or any European language. The few academic studies that do exist are highly specialized, with most books or articles confined to research on narrow issues and very limited times and places. There are several brief overviews of Chinese military history or Chinese military thought available in Chinese as well as a few massive, broad, but unreliable surveys, but there are no high-quality general surveys. A History of Traditional Chinese Military Science is therefore valuable if only because there isn’t much else. Its primary value is in presenting a Chinese view of the history of Chinese military thought. To some extent, it is a fair representation of what many Chinese scholars think about war in Chinese history and the history of Chinese military thought. It does not engage any scholarship outside China, or even much Chinese scholarship. A History of Traditional Chinese Military Science does not attempt to present the state of knowledge of the academic field of Chinese military thought in China. It relies upon a very narrow set of modern Chinese scholarship and a selective use of primary sources. Indeed, most of the secondary Chinese works cited are at least twenty years old.

auditPapers.title: Father Pepe’s House of Cards: Jesuits, Cheap Print, and Material Devotion in Eighteenth-Century Catholicism
auditPapers.abstract: This article examines the impact of the rise of cheap print on devotional practice in eighteenth-century Catholicism. It offers a case study of Francesco Pepe (1684–1759), a Jesuit missionary active in Naples from the 1730s through the 1750s, and the media empire he built to popularize a religious practice steeped in material objects among the city’s poor. Mobilizing the technology of the printing press and innovative labor arrangements, Pepe mass-produced paper-based devotional objects whose use he promoted through another cheap print: best-selling booklets touting the miraculous interventions effected by his devotional articles. Participating in the “war on books” that the church had declared on enlightened tomes, Pepe swamped the market with tracts that rekindled a belief in the mediating function of devotional objects as a way of addressing the problems besetting the poor and women in an increasingly overcrowded early modern metropolis. Borrowing the notion of cheap print from book historians, the article suggests that historians of religion treat books not as repositories of ideas inherently at odds with material religion, but as an integral part of a media ensemble in which the borders between inexpensive books and paper objects remained porous. In an age when prints of all sorts could be produced at unprecedented rates, books and portable objects mutually reinforced each other, laying the groundwork for a new material piety for the uneducated and women that would survive well into the twentieth century.

auditPapers.title: Jeffrey Schneider. Uniform Fantasies: Soldiers, Sex, and Queer Emancipation in Imperial Germany.
auditPapers.abstract: In Uniform Fantasies: Soldiers, Sex, and Queer Emancipation in Imperial Germany, Jeffrey Schneider explores the entanglement of the male queer emancipation movement in Imperial Germany with the country’s fascination with military uniforms and the military itself. To do so, Schneider engages with fantasies involving queer men and the military. Engaging with psychoanalytic theory, Schneider shows how fantasies can reveal the structures and conflicts surrounding social formations. In this specific case, they demonstrate the power that the military exerted on how Germans imagined their society. Openly articulated, these fantasies also had the potential to complicate gender dynamics, especially for bourgeois commentators who already viewed the fantastical uniforms of the pre-1914 Germany military as suspiciously effeminate. While concerned with the military, the book thus contributes just as much to the larger discussion of the strictures of liberal bourgeois society, which themselves could complicate homosexuals’ infatuation with the military as much as the aristocratic army elite itself.

auditPapers.title: David de Boer. The Early Modern Dutch Press in an Age of Religious Persecution: The Making of Humanitarianism.
auditPapers.abstract: David de Boer’s book, The Early Modern Dutch Press in an Age of Religious Persecution: The Making of Humanitarianism, seeks to demonstrate the broad argument that those advocating for religious minorities, especially in the Dutch Republic, were fundamental in the process of establishing a humanitarian culture in Europe (2). De Boer pursues the notion that print media were used to raise awareness of religious persecution and, more significantly, were used to make universal arguments that went beyond confessional boundaries. The book is divided into five substantive chapters, arranged chronologically, that address a wide array of historical contexts. Chapter 1 begins with the print coverage of the 1655 massacre of Reformed Waldensians in Piedmont. De Boer shows that advocates for the Waldensians employed various strategies depending on their audiences. The Waldensians could not simply appeal to religious solidarity, because they depended on the goodwill of both Protestant and Catholic powers. Thus, they needed to demonstrate their own passivity as victims and frame the massacre as illegal and inhumane, thereby making a humanitarian argument rather than a solely religious one.

auditPapers.title: Gendering the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere
auditPapers.abstract: Asia has peoples and languages, mountains and rivers, religions and civilizations. In many historical conceptions, it also had a gender. This is not entirely surprising, since the idea of “Asia” was often imagined in opposition to the idea of “Europe,” and binaries invite gendered thinking. If “Asia is one,” as Okakura Kakuzō famously proclaimed, then it must also have had one gender. The question was, which one? For twentieth-century Japanese Pan-Asianists, whose visions of a unified Asia were inextricably linked to the state’s imperial ambition, the answer was clear: Asia was male. As the state extended its reach into Hokkaido and Okinawa, seized colonies in Taiwan and Korea, and expanded into Manchuria, they imagined Asia as an all-male patriarchal family with Japan at its head. Analogizing the order of colonial expansion to birth order, the state often told Okinawans, “Okinawa is the eldest son, Taiwan the second, and Korea the third.”1 During the Asia-Pacific War (1937–45), a book called China’s Children (Shina no kodomo) reimagined China—often constructed as a menacing, demonic threat—as a “younger brother country.” In this vision, China was a failed patriarch who required Japanese guidance to properly raise his own children.2 Elsewhere, the war created new sons for the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere (1940–45): Manchukuo, Indonesia, Burma, and the Philippines. A wartime foreign minister, Tani Masayuki, explained, “Relations between the empire and member nations are like relations among relatives. It is our ideal to bring them closer, like a big family, so there will be no need for so-called diplomacy.”3

auditPapers.title: Anna Bonnell Freidin. Birthing Romans: Childbearing and Its Risks in Imperial Rome.
auditPapers.abstract: Anna Bonnell Freidin’s Birthing Romans: Childbearing and Its Risks in Imperial Rome is a study of birthing, risks, expectations, and ideology surrounding births and procreation in the Roman Empire. The text is structured as follows: an introduction, five thematic chapters, followed by conclusions, bibliography, and index. The thematic chapters are: “Veturia at Scale: Kinship, Community, and Empire”; “Cornucopia and Rudder: Imagining Generation, Embodying Risk”; “Bodily and Social Order in Soranus’s Gynecology”; “Technologies of Hope: Amulets, Materiality, and Affect”; and “Fate and Fortune: Living with Uncertainty, Understanding Loss.” The period covered by the study is from the age of Augustus and roughly over the first three centuries CE (4). The focus is on the Latin-speaking West and North Africa, but the Greek-speaking East is not entirely left out. The text is accompanied by twenty illustrations. The broader picture takes its point of departure from a microhistory of a woman named Veturia. She is introduced in chapter 1 and is recurrently referred to throughout the book, in a mixture of facts and the author’s speculations. The facts are that Veturia lived and died in Acquincum, Pannonia, in the second century CE. She passed away at the age of twenty-seven and was commemorated by her husband Fortunatus, a Roman legionnaire, and buried in a sarcophagus with an inscription giving a brief outline of the life of Veturia (CIL 3.3572; fig.1.1; Hungarian National Museum, Budapest). From the inscription, we learn that Veturia died after sixteen years of marriage, during which she experienced at least six pregnancies, perhaps from the age of fourteen. At Veturia’s death, however, only one of her children was still alive. From this harsh reality, which was shared by many women in the Roman Empire, Bonnell Freidin contextualizes birthing over three centuries and exemplifies how Romans tried to handle and control risks and anxieties related to childbirth. A legal marriage (matrimonium iustum) was required for having legitimate children, and as such, marriage and childbirth were the most prominent social duties for Roman women. As surviving children were a necessity for the continuity of a family line and for society at large, it was an issue constantly present in the lives of women from a young age. A first marriage followed by pregnancy was a reality for Roman female teenagers. Sometimes it could occur at a very young age, as in the case of Veturia, who appears to have been married at eleven, which was early even for the Romans. Given the risks and high mortality rates of both pregnant women and of newborns, across social hierarchies, all kinds of assistance and support were vital to make a pregnancy end with the survival of both mother and child. Bonnell Freidin gives extensive examples of how birthing women and mothers were supported by networks of family and kin (chapter 1), and how protections for pregnant women and unborn children were sought in a variety of ways, spanning from material objects such as amulets (see fig. 2.2 and 2.3. for examples of uterine amulets; chapter 4), by divinities, especially Fortuna, the goddess of fortune and luck (especially in chapters 2 and 5), and oracles.

auditPapers.title: Lauren Braun-Strumfels. Partners in Gatekeeping: How Italy Shaped U.S. Immigration Policy over Ten Pivotal Years, 1891–1901.
auditPapers.abstract: US immigration historians have long demonstrated that antipathy toward Italian immigrants and opposition to widespread Italian immigration were key ingredients to both elite and working-class expressions of nativist politics in late Gilded Age America and proved central to restrictionists’ efforts to pass and implement increasingly harsh Progressive Era federal immigration measures. Italian authorities rarely occupy center stage in such tellings, more often appearing as major actors in (seemingly separate) scholarship on sending states’ responses to mass emigration. In Partners in Gatekeeping: How Italy Shaped U.S. Immigration Policy over Ten Pivotal Years, 1891–1901, Lauren Braun-Strumfels reveals the fundamental inseparability of these American and Italian histories of migration law and politics. Comprising five chapters (plus an introduction and epilogue), the book proceeds briskly. Chapter 1 identifies 1891 as the nadir of late nineteenth-century US-Italian relations, centering on the fallout of the mass lynching of eleven Italian migrants in New Orleans and the recall of Italy’s ambassador from Washington. Chapter 2 reveals how Italian diplomats and bureaucrats swiftly and successfully rebuilt relationships with American immigration officials, winning approval for the establishment of a unique office at Ellis Island—the Office of Labor Information and Protection for Italians—run by Italian representatives themselves. Chapters 3 and 4 emphasize the limits of Italian officials’ powers of persuasion, exemplified by the difficulties they encountered trying to direct migrants to and support them in rural settlements in the US South (through a case study of one such locale: Sunnyside, Arkansas), along with the repeated refusal of American lawmakers and bureaucrats to clearly define excludable categories of migrants such as “alien contract laborers” and those “likely to become a public charge.” Chapter 5 illustrates how lawmakers in Italy responded to these and related challenges (such as the forced closure of their government’s Ellis Island office) by adopting a range of emigration policies—most concretely the Italian Emigration Act of 1901—that sought to prevent the departure of those likely to be denied entry to the United States while offering increasingly tangible legal protections to would-be migrants vis-à-vis recruiters and shipping companies.

auditPapers.title: Kai Jun Chen. Porcelain for the Emperor: Manufacture and Technocracy in Qing China.
auditPapers.abstract: Recent scholarship on the Qing dynasty (1644–1912) has illuminated how the Manchu minority rulers forged a multiethnic and multilingual early modern empire through various strategies, including bureaucratic reforms, military campaigns, and fiscal policies. Situated in this line of scholarship on Qing empire-building, Porcelain for the Emperor poses a long-awaited question: How did the Manchu court expand its authority into the domain of technology? Centering on the personal journey and career trajectory of Tang Ying (1682–1756), a bannerman who oversaw the Imperial Porcelain Manufactory for over twenty years and who was also a prolific playwright, Kai Jun Chen insightfully characterizes Tang Ying as a technocrat who seamlessly “combined technological expertise and managerial power” (3). More importantly, given the long-established hierarchical division between intellectual and manual labor in the Confucian tradition, Tang Ying’s public identification as an imperial potter—a craftsman—signifies the emergence of a new identity in the Qing dynasty. Porcelain for the Emperor argues that bannerman specialists like Tang Ying instantiated a distinct mode of knowledge production. While bannermen technocrats emphasized hands-on and practical knowledge through “empirical and often nontextual experience,” the “literati-bureaucrats’ ways of knowing and making gravitated toward textual knowledge” (11–12).

auditPapers.title: Randy M. Browne. The Driver’s Story: Labor and Power in the World of Atlantic Slavery.
auditPapers.abstract: In The Driver’s Story: Labor and Power in the World of Atlantic Slavery, Randy M. Browne gives us a fascinating study of the multifaceted power dynamics on plantations by focusing on drivers, the enslaved people who supervised field labor. Rather than reducing power dynamics to theoretical “abstractions,” he focuses on how they “played out in the messy, everyday interactions among individuals” (142). His chapters examine, thematically, the plantation labor regimes in which drivers worked, the expectations and challenges that drivers faced as they were caught between enslavers and enslaved, the authority and privileges they held within the enslaved community, and the ways in which they facilitated or opposed widespread rebellions. The last two of his five chapters are case studies. One is built around an enslaved driver named January in early nineteenth-century Berbice who had been demoted but who still commanded what the plantation owner called “unbounded authority over the gang of slaves” (100). The other examines the role that drivers played in a “little-studied uprising” of enslaved people in Berbice in 1813–14 (114). Browne shows that “most drivers, most of the time, were not rebels” (131).

auditPapers.title: How Mediterranean Economies Were Shaped in the Early Middle Ages
auditPapers.abstract: The clichéd image of the premodern Mediterranean economy is stagnation until the twin forces of capitalism and Industrial Revolution kick-started growth and the modern world. Yet the premodern Mediterranean economy fluctuated significantly over time with two significant trade cycles. First, the Roman Empire united the Mediterranean together for the first four centuries CE before its political economy broke down. Second, people and states, starting around 1000 CE, wove together local trade networks into trans-Mediterranean connections, leading to a Commercial Revolution. Chris Wickham’s 2005 book, Framing the Early Middle Ages, explained how the first trade cycle ended and trade atrophied from 400 to 800 CE. Framing sketches out the workings of the late Roman Empire’s tax system, whose extracted revenues based largely on agricultural produce funneled wealth toward the imperial administration in a capital city and, above all, to pay standing armies on its frontiers. The elites controlling the tax system simultaneously used these economic networks to piggyback trade in bulk goods around the Mediterranean. Elites thus both administered the tax system as bureaucrats and used the system’s networks to create massive wealth for themselves, leading to a booming late Roman economy.

auditPapers.title: Mesopotamian Words for “Slave”
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The emergence of slavery in Mesopotamia is of crucial importance for historians who study ancient cultures as well as for comparativists interested in its influence on later societies. But the social, economic, and legal contexts in which “slaves” appear in cuneiform texts differ so widely not only between ancient and modern forms but also within intracultural contexts, such that the nature of the underlying concepts and practices are hardly clear. Given these indistinctions, the Mesopotamian terms for “slave(ry)” warrant closer scrutiny. Remarkably, the relevant words in both Sumerian and Akkadian are etymologically opaque and semantically uncertain, obscuring the precise status denoted by the words arad/ardu. This paper delves into philological problems in order to argue that the ambiguity of these terms was deliberately perpetuated by structured linguistic choices. Definitional vagueness generated and permitted nonspecific meanings for personal status, legal object, and economic institution, which enabled slavery to change and thrive across the ages. This deliberate ambiguity allowed slavery and mastery to persist in legal and commercial practice untroubled by social logic or critical definitions—as concepts whose protean meanings were transmitted to successive historical cultures as both profoundly ambivalent and natural.

auditPapers.title: Quito Swan. Pasifika Black: Oceania, Anti-colonialism, and the African World.
auditPapers.abstract: The islands and peoples of Melanesia, a region that etymologically means “islands of Black people,” were racialized as Black by various European colonizers who violently conquered these communities. Not only do these communities self-identify as Black, but they have also been included in the Africana world by many Black scholars and leaders of the 20th century. Colonization and racialization produced a common experience whereby peoples were marked either for extinction or forced labor. Pasifika Black by Quito Swan focuses on how these common experiences also meant that anticolonial movements in Oceania were connected to the late 20th-century discussions of decolonization in other parts of the African and diaspora world. It aims to show not only those common colonial strategies of racialization, forced migration, and land and labor expropriation that knit Black peoples of the Atlantic and Pacific together but, equally, that anticolonial movements in Oceania “embraced African freedom struggles” and contributed their own perspectives to Black Power, negritude, Pan-Africanist, peace, and women’s movements. And, rightly, rather than set up a contest between Black Atlantic and Black Pacific frameworks, the book sets out to illuminate the Pacific “via the lens of African Diaspora studies and Black intellectual history” (3).

auditPapers.title: Steven Peach. Rivers of Power: Creek Political Culture in the Native South 1750–1815.
auditPapers.abstract: An ongoing predicament in the Native South centers on how to make sense of the political organization and governance of Creek Indians during the eighteenth century. In multiple explorations attempting to identify the seat of Creek authority, historians have proposed organizational structures based on regional affiliations, trade alliances, town-based localism, and burgeoning nationalist institutions. In Rivers of Power: Creek Political Culture in the Native South 1750–1815, Steven Peach proposes a novel approach centering Creek political organization on four distinct provinces defined by four corresponding waterways in Alabama and western Georgia. Across six chapters, an introduction, and conclusion, Rivers of Power flows chronologically, focusing on the experience of the Abeikas and Tallapoosas from the mid-1700s through the first quarter of the nineteenth century. As the book unfolds, Peach widens his examination across Creek country, incorporating the coalescence of the Alabamas and Lower Creeks as distinct provinces. When looking regionally, Peach addresses the intersecting political and cultural web of the Native South’s diverse Indigenous people and intensifying colonial incursions. The book chapters are evenly paired in three corresponding parts. Part 1 discusses the period from 1750 through 1776 and centers on the turmoil resulting from the Seven Years’ War. Peach pays close attention to both Indigenous-colonial friction as well as the cascading conflicts between Native communities. Part 2 focuses on the Revolutionary era in the Native South and addresses the motivating factors leading to the development of alliances among the Abeika, Tallapoosas, and Lower Creek. Part 3 commences with the start of the nineteenth century as the Creek navigated increasing settler incursions on their eastern borders. Through these final two chapters, Peach focuses on the expanding influence of the Alabamas in Upper Creek politics and the discord surrounding the 1813 Creek War.

auditPapers.title: The Nature and Politics of Talent in West Germany, 1950–1970
auditPapers.abstract: The article examines shifts in West German understandings of talent (Begabung) from 1950 to 1970. It analyzes debates about school and education reforms and explains how politicians, education reformers, and business representatives moved away from strict hereditarian understandings of talent to assumptions that there were significant talent reserves among socially disadvantaged sectors of the population that could be mobilized for the benefit of the economy and wider society. In this process, promises of upward social mobility based on talent and performance merged with the perceived imperatives of an advanced industrial economy that needed to adjust to two different kinds of competition: (1) the competition with other capitalist countries for market share, and (2) the system competition with the socialist Eastern Bloc with its growing numbers of university and engineering graduates. Both required significant efforts to identify and foster new talents.

auditPapers.title: Jonathan Huener. The Polish Catholic Church under German Occupation: The Reichsgau Wartheland, 1939–1945.
auditPapers.abstract: Jonathan Huener’s The Polish Catholic Church Under German Occupation: The Reichsgau Wartheland, 1939–1945 is a significant scholarly achievement. Huener demonstrates a meticulous command of a wide variety of Polish and German sources to describe in harrowing detail the largely successful Nazi efforts to cripple the Catholic Church in annexed Polish territories as part of making a new “model Gau” of Wartheland. After their victory over Poland, the Nazis carved up much of western and central Poland to create the largest and most populous Gau in an expanded Third Reich. The Nazi official in charge of Wartheland, Gauleiter Arthur Greiser, who played a key role in initiating the Shoah with his assaults on Wartheland’s Jews, also facilitated the mass murder of the region’s Polish gentile cultural and spiritual leadership. In addition to these crimes, the Nazi authorities enslaved and expelled much of the remaining Polish population and began the colonization of this territory by Germans to change the face of the region—particularly religiously. This work is especially strong in its analysis of the impact of first two years of the occupation on both this pioneering Nazi administration and the fate of Poles whom it sought to subjugate spiritually as well as physically. As a thick description of how the Nazis tried—and failed—to enslave a people spiritually, this is a model of careful scholarship.

auditPapers.title: Peter Elmer. Medicine in an Age of Revolution.
auditPapers.abstract: Completed in the thick of a global pandemic that saw health care fractured by partisan concerns, this study proves the adage that the past is prologue. In Medicine in an Age of Revolution, Peter Elmer examines the myriad ways that British medicine was politicized, c. 1640–1688. He assays received wisdom as well as offering fresh insights, complicating if not revising our understanding. The study reconsiders the thesis championed by Charles Webster that puritanism—Protestant dissent—was largely responsible for driving innovation in natural philosophy, medicine included. By the same token, it is often assumed that a tendency to professionalism by some later seventeenth-century healers—physicians, surgeons, and apothecaries—made for distancing from political debate or religious controversy, if not also an intellectual conservatism. Whether latter-day acolytes of the iconoclastic Paracelsus or followers of the more respectable Jan Baptist van Helmont, Elmer demonstrates quite convincingly that repudiation of a Galenic orthodoxy was not the preserve of puritans-cum-dissenters. Thus, the failure to establish a Society of Chemical Physicians in the mid-1660s, which would rival if not usurp the Royal College of Physicians, cannot be attributed simply to the marginal status of many would-be members or their demise when trying to treat victims of London’s Great Plague. Vice versa, too, sectarians and radicals did not necessarily abandon organicist political ideology. Many sought, in their own way, to recuperate it.

auditPapers.title: Xin Zhang. The Global in the Local: A Century of War, Commerce, and Technology in China.
auditPapers.abstract: In the most dramatic passages of Xin Zhang’s The Global in the Local: A Century of War, Commerce, and Technology in China, we read of the panic within the city walls as British troops approached Zhenjiang in July 1842, near the culmination of the Opium War. The city-dwellers’ fear of the foreigners was based on rumors of atrocities they had already committed and experiences of marauding soldiers in earlier conflicts. Paranoid Qing officials further terrorized those trapped in the city, publicly executing innocent people—including children and a monk—for aiding the enemy. When the nine thousand British troops arrived, the largest force mustered thus far in the war, they saw a group of women drown their children before being drowned themselves by Chinese soldiers, who then committed suicide en masse rather than face the unknown horrors anticipated of the enemy. Protecting women’s chastity at the cost of their lives had a long tradition in China, but Zhang stresses that this kind of mass “mercy killing” (a problematic term, not problematized in the book) was “sui generis” here (76). The British then unleashed a wave of looting and burning on the city, joined by some Chinese opportunists. This kind of drama is not, however, typical of the book, which charts the interaction of Chinese society with foreign steamships beyond that initial shock of war to long-term commercial and technological changes. Zhang warns in the introduction that he pays “a significant amount of attention to specifics” (12), which reads more as a threat than a promise, but the details enrich the history.

auditPapers.abstract: Sam Ottewill-Soulsby’s The Emperor and the Elephant: Christians and Muslims in the Age of Charlemagne reflects the global turn in Carolingian studies, focusing on the diplomatic interactions between Carolingians and different Muslim rulers during the eighth and ninth centuries. The third chapter deals with Carolingian-Abbasid relations, involving the most famous episode, alluded to in the title, the Indian elephant sent by the Abbasid caliph to Aachen. Christian Arabic apocalyptic writings, discussed by the author in this context, are a welcome addition to the usual sources taken into account for the reconstruction of this episode. The author is an expert on Carolingian-Umayyad relations, which are discussed in two chapters. Treatment of these relations involves a detailed consideration of the Frankish frontier with al-Andalus, involving the border lords on both sides; shifting constellations in Catalonia as well as in the three marches controlled from Mérida, Toledo, and Zaragoza; and the varying strength of the Umayyad emirs in Córdoba, who were frequently faced with rivals and rebellions. The last chapter turns its attention to the central Mediterranean, comprising Muslim polities in Northern Africa, Sicily, and on the Italian mainland.

auditPapers.title: Matthew D. Lassiter. The Suburban Crisis: White America and the War on Drugs.
auditPapers.abstract: For a subject as well-trodden as race and the drug war, framing new work within the existing literature can be a challenge. Numerous studies have explored the US war on drugs as a system of social control targeting urban minority populations through the expansion of aggressive policing and the carceral state. As the story goes, Republicans, obsessed with law and order, designed punitive antidrug policies while Democrats kept their focus on treatment and rehabilitation. By focusing on white suburbia and the drug war, Matthew D. Lassiter offers a revision to the conventional narrative, demonstrating that the war on drugs operated through a reciprocal paradigm of criminalizing blackness (and foreignness) while decriminalizing whiteness. White middle-class youths consumed illegal drugs, to be sure. Lassiter’s aim though is to examine how the government helped them maintain clean criminal records. He argues that the government saw them as “victims,” creating strict laws and crime control measures that instead targeted nonwhite and foreign “predators” (4, 15). The racial state-building project chronicled in The Suburban Crisis intensified from the 1950s to the 1980s through policies enacted at the local, state, and national levels.

auditPapers.title: Paul Hillmer and Ryan Bean. Inappropriation: The Contested Legacy of Y-Indian Guides.
auditPapers.abstract: While many cultures have been subjected to cultural appropriation, Native American communities have been a primary target in the United States. Some might dismiss critiques of cultural appropriation as “mere identity politics,” or, in an effort to stem discussion, they might point out—rightly—that cultures are not static, and that people have always adopted ideas, practices, and objects from others. However, the structures and ideologies that facilitate cultural appropriation as such reflect unequal power dynamics and engender significant historical and material consequences. This is underscored in an excellent new contribution to this conversation, Inappropriation: The Contested Legacy of Y-Indian Guides by Paul Hillmer and Ryan Bean. Inappropriation is the first book-length study of the YMCA’s popular Y-Indian Guides program. Initially developed as a program for fathers and sons, a large portion of its participants were historically white and from middle-class families. As a core component of the program, participants “played Indian,” a longstanding practice described by Phil Deloria in his important 1998 book Playing Indian. As Hillmer and Bean document, non-Native participants in the Y-Indian Guides program organized themselves into “tribes,” adopted “Indian” names, crafted and wore clothing that was meant to mirror Native garb, and engaged in rituals and ceremonies that, whether or not they actually resembled any, were inspired by Indigenous beliefs and practices. The authors describe the cultural context out of which the program emerged, recount its (somewhat mythic) origin story, trace its growth and demise, and consider its legacy. Their intention is to offer a complex picture of the program—to account for its development and popularity while highlighting the damaging aspects of the forms of cultural appropriation perpetuated (or perpetrated) by the Y-Indian Guides.

auditPapers.title: Simon Devereaux. Execution, State and Society in England, 1660–1900.
auditPapers.abstract: In 1706, Roger Lowen’s corpse was gibbeted (hung in chains post-execution) in Turnham Green, a suburb southwest of London. The decaying corpse swung in chains in view of the house where Lowen’s victim had lived, a practice that underlined the retributive force of execution and post-execution punishment. Any sense that this proximity gave succor or satisfaction to relatives of Lowen’s victim was undercut by a petition from the victim’s widow and her neighbors asking for the gibbet’s removal, as it was causing nuisance to the local area. Simon Devereaux offers this example in Execution, State and Society in England, 1660–1900 as perhaps constituting the first surviving recorded example of a suburban “not in my backyard” attitude in England. The disturbance caused by Lowen’s gibbeted corpse is just one illustration of how what Devereaux terms “urbane” culture was important to driving changes in English execution culture. As cities expanded, better-off suburban residents voiced their discomfort with or distaste for the sight (and, indeed, sound and smell) of the gallows and the gibbet. These residents were not from the ruling class, but in a constitutional monarchy like England, their views and feelings mattered.

auditPapers.title: Arang Keshavarzian. Making Space For the Gulf: Histories of Regionalism and the Middle East.
auditPapers.abstract: The study of the Persian Gulf has been invigorated over the past two decades. A flourish of studies and histories of labor, social movements, the environment, migration, cultures, and political economies of the region have proliferated, breathing scholarly life into a part of the world that, with the exception of a handful of earlier pioneering scholars such as Fred Halliday, had mostly been the preoccupation of security studies, students of and advocates for Western power, and those enamored with the region’s oil. Newfound interest in the Gulf’s complexities has been critical to rethinking the fields of Middle East studies and southwest Asia. Even so, the Gulf—including the name itself—remains somewhat inscrutable. The communities around it, as well as those connected to it and one another, are complex, varied, and, most importantly, have changed over time, rendering the Gulf historically contingent and ever-shifting. How should we think about the interconnections, forces, and histories that have shaped the making of the Gulf, including the very idea that it possesses the kind of territorial coherence that makes it a place and space?

auditPapers.title: Oscar Sanchez-Sibony. The Soviet Union and the Construction of the Global Market: Energy and the Ascent of Finance in Cold War Europe, 1964–1971.
auditPapers.abstract: He did it again. Oscar Sanchez-Sibony fundamentally challenges our understanding of the Soviet attitude toward the capitalist world economy—this time by looking at The Soviet Union and the Construction of the Global Market. Sanchez-Sibony convincingly argues that the Soviet Union played a crucial role in the gradual globalization of energy and financial markets since the early 1960s—that is, at the apex of the Cold War. Large-scale energy projects initiated by the Soviet Union with Western European countries catalyzed the emergence of international credit relations—with the Soviet Union becoming a virtuous player and taker of (international) credit. The link of energy and finance is crucial for Sanchez-Sibony’s argument since it was ultimately the pipeline deals that led the Soviet Union to effectively “helping” (9) to dismantle the system of Bretton Woods. This “help” consisted of undermining the relatively strict international barter and trading list system of Bretton Woods, which did not allow for much free circulating credit or internationally floating currency since this would have affected the fixed exchange rates between the US and the other major international currencies. The Soviets, however, who were excluded from the system of Bretton Woods, pushed their Western European partners for international long-term credits in order to finance its energy infrastructure in and to Europe. Thanks to the international Soviet deals of the 1960s, capital controls became something of the past, and the unleashing of the petrodollar became the future—such is Sanchez-Sibony’s bold argument.

auditPapers.title: Hanne Elliot Fønss Nielsen. Brand Antarctica: How Global Consumer Culture Shapes our Perceptions of the Ice Continent.
auditPapers.abstract: To enter a historic hut from the heroic era of Antarctic exploration is to be taken, perhaps a little unexpectedly, into a world of household English brands from the early twentieth century. At Shackleton’s hut at Cape Royd’s, for example, Colman’s Mustard Powder sits on the shelf, General Electric Co. dry batteries stand in a box on the floor, and tins of John Moir and Son chicken and veal pâté await a brave consumer. Many of these products were taken on the expeditions as the result of sponsorship arrangements that helped to cover the costs, while others were home comforts that helped make Antarctic exploration a little more bearable. Given the pedestal on which heroic era explorers are often placed, there can be something slightly disappointing about this commercial encounter: Antarctic heroism is not generally associated with selling Heinz Baked Beans. But as Hanne Elliot Fønss Nielsen argues in her fascinating study Brand Antarctica, commerce has been an integral part of human engagement with Antarctica, almost from the very beginning.

auditPapers.title: Amy Absher. Fritzie: The Invented Life and Violent Murder of a Flapper.
auditPapers.abstract: When thinking of the “Roaring Twenties,” what most have in mind are flappers in scanty dresses dancing to the sounds of jazz, brazenly challenging both social norms and the law as they sip some bootleg alcohol in defiance of Prohibition officers. Fritzie: The Invented Life and Violent Murder of a Flapper has all of these components, but it manages to rise above the tired cliches of the period to present a refreshing look at the culture that defined this decade, revealing “how and why the Jazz Age celebrated women while simultaneously destroying them” (5). Partly a microhistory, partly a true-crime mystery, Fritzie is an engaging read. In twelve short chapters, Amy Absher provides her readers with a detailed look at the short life, police investigation, and subsequent trials of the murder of Frieda “Fritzie” Mann, a young Jewish immigrant woman turned flapper showgirl who was murdered while pregnant. Mann’s story has everything a good Hollywood script would include: murder, abortion, a dramatic trial, and a scent of glamour and fame. But her story is also a story of how consumer culture and media in the early twentieth century enabled people—and particularly women—to reinvent themselves and become modern. Mann’s story is a story of promises and possibilities even if, in the end, they remained unfulfilled.

auditPapers.title: Proximity Matters
auditPapers.abstract: The activist was devoted to doing all he could to improve the situation in the Asian country that was his homeland. He felt it was on the wrong path. It was being ruled in too autocratic a fashion, and he wanted to do what he could to move it in the right direction. He followed the news about other parts of the world hoping to find models that could be adopted and adapted to further this end. While he was open to discovering inspiring or useful ideas in the work of all kinds of foreign thinkers and the histories of all kinds of foreign movements, he took particular interest in things happening in other parts of Asia. He found it especially valuable to pay attention to events in relatively nearby places even when the political situation there was very different from that in his own country. When activists in bordering lands or even ones that were a bit farther away managed to score a victory, this fascinated him. It gave him hope. And proximity made it easier for him to interact with people who had taken part in those struggles rather than in similar ones unfolding farther away. At an important point in his life, thanks partly to proximity, he was able to meet up with some of the activists from another part of Asia whose actions had inspired him. And even though there were major cultural differences between their homelands, and one was in East Asia and the other in Southeast Asia, he convinced some of these people that he and they had much in common and should collaborate.

auditPapers.title: The Opiated Ocean
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In December 1853, British officials at Hong Kong amended the Passenger Acts to allow the substitution of “opium for tobacco” on voyages taking indentured laborers, or “coolies,” from China to the Caribbean. Authorities in the US, Cuba, and Peru followed suit by legalizing and mandating opium in what became known as la trata amarilla. By using fresh evidence to explore the genesis of this little-known cluster of regulations, this article explains the process through which Western officials authorized the provision of opium as a prophylactic against shipborne contagions, linking the circulation of opium with the global movement of Chinese labor. Whereas scholars have tended to present smoking opium either as a harmless restorative or as a tool of social control, this study calls attention to the prevalence of comorbidities between opium dependence and infectious illnesses such as cholera and typhoid to suggest that, above all, the drug served as a volatile resource necessitated by the exigencies of epidemic risk.

auditPapers.title: Comment by Sebastian Conrad
auditPapers.abstract: In April 1881, the Hawaiian King Kalākaua visited the mighty empire of the Qing. He attempted to convince Li Hongzhang, the minister of the Office of Foreign Affairs (Zongli Yamen), of their shared Asianness, despite their many differences. “We are Asian, as are you,” the surprised Li heard, and Kalākaua went on to explain the necessity of a common front against European imperialism. As related by Rebecca E. Karl, Li did not take either the warning or its carrier seriously. Allegedly, he had only learned from his secretary, on the morning of Kalākaua’s visit, that a country named Hawaii even existed. Li Hongzhang operated within the notion of a Chinese cultural sphere, a “common civilization” (tongwen) defined by script, Confucianism, and cultural tradition. Between the Great Middle Kingdom and the small, geographically and culturally distant Hawaii, there could be no similarities. But Kalākaua was unfazed. “[I] have warned the Japanese emperor, and now [I] am cautioning you, Li: if we were able to unite so as not to leave foreigners a single opening, would this not be the best way to arouse our brown Asian peoples? I eagerly await for this to happen.”

auditPapers.title: Kirsten E. Wood. Accommodating the Republic: Taverns in the Early United States.
auditPapers.abstract: Kirsten E. Wood’s Accommodating the Republic adds to a body of historical scholarship on taverns and drinking spaces, including works by Madelon Powers, Sharon Salinger, and most recently, Vaughn Scribner. Wood focuses on the social, economic, and political roles of taverns from the late eighteenth century through the mid-nineteenth century. Though not neglecting tavern drinking and the controversies it engendered, Wood takes a more expansive view of taverns’ political and economic functions over time. She argues that from “individual pursuits of happiness to collective efforts to promote the general welfare, tavern encounters helped shape Americans’ relationship to the republic itself” (2). Examining who could drink, eat, stay, vote, and conduct business at taverns, Wood detects a formative influence on racial, class, and political identities. Accordingly, Accommodating the Republic eschews defining exactly what constituted a tavern, focusing instead on “how patrons and keepers used the places they called by that name, how they made meaning from those uses, and how those meanings advanced competing visions of the republic and its citizens” (3).

auditPapers.title: Maximilian C. G. Lau. Emperor John II Komnenos: Rebuilding New Rome, 1118–1143.
auditPapers.abstract: John II Komnenos (r. 1118–1143) had a grand plan. He aimed to rebuild “New Rome,” securing and substantially expanding its territory from Dalmatia across the Danube frontier to Northern Syria. John built on his father’s achievements, and his son Manuel continued his. He built a vast network of fortresses for ideological and logistical purposes. As far as he can be considered a “crusader,” John wished to visit Jerusalem as a pilgrim and appear as a legitimate overlord of all Christians of the East. But John’s premature death hindered him from reuniting a universal church. His results required a lot of effort for little gain or long-lasting effect. Lau describes John as having a dynamic personality: He was ambitious, family-centred, and merciful, and he promoted the cult of the Theotokos as a crucial element of his religiosity. Lau’s work is welcome, being the first monographic discussion of John II’s reign since Ferdinand Chalandon’s second volume from 1912, part of his volumes on Komnenian Byzantium (Chalandon, Ferdinand, Les Comnène : études sur l’empire byzantin au XIe et au XIIe siècles. 2, Jean II Comnène (1118–1143) et Manuel I Comnène (1143–1180), 1912). The author successfully tackles two significant challenges: First, John II’s reign is attested by the Byzantine historians John Kinnamos and Nicetas Choniates, whose narratives were written from a distance of four decades after the events with a specific authorial agenda. Second, Choniates described John as a second Marcus Aurelius and a soldier-emperor in favorable terms. Choniates’s positive portrayal has been echoed by scholars, who accepted this image of John with varying degrees. This volume, by contrast, attempts to make a holistic approach to the internal (Byzantine) source material, considering all available sources and genres. More importantly, Lau examines John’s reign in a Mediterranean context, considering various non-Byzantine sources. Lau’s use of Syriac and Armenian sources is a case in point, providing a more nuanced understanding of John’s roles. After preparatory research trips to the Balkans and Anatolia, Lau complemented his study of the written testimonies with archaeological case studies. The book is well structured, according to chronology, which is a justified approach, as it serves the purpose of a more profound analysis. The transitions within and between chapters are well crafted, enhancing the reading experience. I find the index helpful, and the key terms are well defined. Maps occur to the reader when visual explanation is needed. In this review, I want to assess Lau’s attempt to present a more complex image of John than a soldier-emperor by focusing on three chapters dealing with John’s education, his military profile, and church policy.

auditPapers.title: Katlyn Marie Carter. Democracy in Darkness: Secrecy and Transparency in the Age of Revolutions.
auditPapers.abstract: Katlyn Marie Carter’s Democracy in Darkness is an important and engaging study of political information, access, and institutions in revolutionary France and in the nascent United States. It will be essential reading for historians of the early US and the French Revolution, as well as those interested in how political theory and practice informed one another as modern democratic politics took shape. Toggling between her two revolutionary contexts, Carter highlights a “paradox” at the heart of modern representative democracy, noting that “at its origins, [representative democracy’s] legitimacy and stability depended upon a degree of secrecy that was simultaneously deemed anathema to this form of government” (4). Building on this insight, she demonstrates that political transparency and public access to government were not foundations on which representative government could easily be built, but vexing questions that would have to be settled in both principle and practice. The book is organized in three parts and unfolds in a roughly chronological fashion, even as its attention moves back and forth across the Atlantic. The first part (chaps. 1–2) establishes the centrality of debates over state secrecy and political publicity in the tumultuous 1770s and 1780s. As British colonial subjects and French reformers began to reimagine the relationship between the people and the state, they returned frequently to questions about who needed to know what, when, and to what end. Carter shows that these concerns about publicity were at the heart of debates over sovereignty, the separation of powers, the role of the press in a free society, and the character of representative government. As she notes, calls for reform often included condemnations of state secrecy and demands for greater transparency, even among those who operated largely behind closed doors.

auditPapers.title: Kelly Lytle Hernández. Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands.
auditPapers.abstract: Ricardo Flores Magón is a widely-known historical figure in Mexico, yet has been little-known in the United States, until now. Kelly Lytle Hernández, a historian of immigration, race, and incarceration, seeks to inform Americans about the importance of Flores Magón and his followers, magonistas, in her book, Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands. Lytle Hernández describes the efforts of the magonistas at the turn of the twentieth century to resist and overthrow Mexican dictator Porfirio Díaz. During his administration, Díaz centralized his power over the Mexican government, aided in establishing American dominance over the economy, and suppressed labor and indigenous movements in the country. Rather than making this a Mexico-centric story, the author intertwines the role of the United States into this story of the magonista revolt. Bad Mexicans therefore argues that the magonistas are as important to the history of the US as they are to the history of Mexico. Lytle Hernández explains that it is impossible to understand the history of the US as a world superpower without understanding its imbalanced relationship with its neighbor to the south. She also states that one cannot understand the American West without comprehending the long-standing presence of Mexicans in the region. Lastly, she details how Mexican Americans resisted a racialized social order that white Americans imposed upon them. Lytle Hernández argues that “the magonista revolt threatened key sectors of U.S. society at the turn of the twentieth century. US authorities, agents, and settlers mobilized to stop them,” and as a result, “the campaign to crush the magonistas opened a new chapter of policing in the United States” (11).

auditPapers.title: Amy Harris. Being Single in Georgian England: Families, Households, and the Unmarried.
auditPapers.abstract: Being single did not mean being alone in Georgian England. Or, at least, being single never meant being alone for the close-knit Sharp siblings of clerics, professionals, amateur musicians, and philanthropists, who serve as the collective subject of Amy Harris’s book Being Single in Georgian England: Families, Households, and the Unmarried. Although this is as much a history of the Sharps as it is a study of English adults who married late, never married, or became widows and widowers, Being Single provides important, original insights into family and social history. Harris argues that historians’ emphasis on eighteenth-century marital and parental relations has overshadowed other equally important emotional bonds—namely, that between single people within kin networks. Beginning with Lawrence Stone’s The Family, Sex, and Marriage in England, 1500–1800 (1977), historians have emphasized marriage as people’s primary emotional bond in adulthood. Yet marriage was far from a universal state: In the eighteenth century, one-fifth of English adults never married and, as Amy Froide emphasizes, at least one-third of urban women were single at any moment (Never Married: Singlewomen in Early Modern England, 2005). Harris bridges the gap between the marital household and the state of being single by analyzing the Sharp siblings and cousin networks, showing that “[f]amilies did not just adapt to or accommodate their single members; they were shaped by them” (6).

auditPapers.title: Olufemi Vaughan. Letters, Kinship, and Social Mobility in Nigeria.
auditPapers.abstract: Olufemi Vaughan’s book Letters, Kinship, and Social Mobility in Nigeria examines an important aspect of the social history of modern Nigeria. The book, which is part prosopography, uses the letters that were preserved by Abiodun Vaughan to provide a detailed empirical account of the emergence and consolidation of a Yoruba Western-educated elite in Ibadan who were members of the Christian Missionary Society (CMS). The book focuses on the letters written by four generations of Vaughan’s extended family at the national and transnational levels in Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and the United Kingdom, as well as letters written by friends and professional colleagues. Virtually all of the letter writers were associated with the CMS Church and schools with the bulk of them connected with the CMS Church, Aremo, Ibadan, and Ibadan Grammar School. The idea of kinship, whether at the natal family level or friends and colleagues, dominates the letters. The themes discussed in the book show the complex ways that the newly emergent Yoruba Western-educated elites negotiated their position in society at the intersection between modernity and traditionalism. This was clearly demonstrated in Abiodun’s biological family. With the death of their father in 1930, Samuel Aribiyi Vaughan, the eldest son who graduated from the first secondary school in Nigeria, CMS Secondary Lagos, and was 20 years older than Abiodun, assumed the role of the head and provider for the family. His letters to Abiodun were mainly instructions on issues such as sharing remittances to other members of the family, paying the school fees and other financial needs of Samuel’s two children, and ensuring that his houses at Ibadan were well maintained and rents collected. On the other hand, Abiodun’s letters to Samuel were respectful. This type of relationship changed when Abiodun graduated from Ibadan Grammar School in the 1920s and secured a job with the department of agriculture. The letters became more transactional and collaborative. As the two most successful sons of the Vaughan family, they were responsible for providing for other family members, that is, their widowed mother, their brother who had severe health challenges, and two married sisters, as well as maintaining the family home. The situation in Abiodun’s nuclear family reflected the gendered nature of education, work, and status that was promoted by Christian and colonial modernity during the early colonial period in Nigeria. Apart from Dorcas Olayinka Brainerd, Abiodun’s eldest sister who had a secondary school education, Mariam O. Vaughan, Abiodun’s mother, and Jadesola Juliana Odebunmni, Abiodun’s elder sister, only had primary education. This therefore put most of the women, as family matriarchs, in the position of protecting the interests of the family and ensuring the promotion of kinship ties and interpersonal relations among various family members while also partly dependent on remittances from the male elites. Abiodun’s relationships and letters to his mother-in-law, Rachel Ayodele Akinloye, and brother-in-law, Adisa Akinloye, reflected “the moral order on which obligations are negotiated” in the Yoruba kinship system and “reciprocal marriage relations” during this time of social change (153).

auditPapers.title: Aaron George. When Cowboys Come Home: Veterans, Authenticity, and Manhood in Post-World War II America.
auditPapers.abstract: Aaron George’s book When Cowboys Come Home: Veterans, Authenticity, and Manhood in Post-World War II America presents a sweeping analysis of American manhood in the wake of World War II and sheds new light on how American veterans’ wartime experiences undermined traditional notions of manhood and laid the foundations for new, alternate models of male behavior in the midst of a cultural emphasis on hetero-domesticity in post-World War II American society. Grounding his analysis in the lives and work of three prominent midcentury American writers who served in World War II—the author James Jones, the screenwriter Stewart Stern, and the poet Edward Field—George examines how the realities of wartime service cast doubt on the “frontiersman masculinity” of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Dubbing the rebellion against these traditional masculine traits the “veterans’ critique,” George explores how Jones, Stern, and Field tapped into widespread skepticism of traditional notions of manhood and came to view frontiersman masculinity as inauthentic during World War II, which led them to champion a softer, more emotional manhood that emphasized male camaraderie and authenticity.

auditPapers.title: Nadège Ragaru. Bulgaria, the Jews, and the Holocaust: On the Origins of a Heroic Narrative. Translated by Victoria Baena and David A. Rich.
auditPapers.abstract: First published in French in 2020, Nadège Ragaru’s Bulgaria, the Jews, and the Holocaust: On the Origins of a Heroic Narrative deploys different rhetorical genres—detective story, philosophical treatise, film essay—to offer an exacting exploration of memory work in the Balkans. The book dives deep into the omissions, elisions, and illusions of post–World War II Bulgarian self-fashioning, tracing how national pride and geopolitical pressures have interacted to produce a savior narrative stubbornly shared by a supermajority of Bulgarian citizens. Ragaru’s investigation acknowledges two well-established and thoroughly documented facts: 48,000 Bulgarian citizens of Jewish faith survived the Holocaust, while 11,434 Jews in formerly Greek or Yugoslav territories under Bulgarian administration were deported and murdered in spring 1943. The former fact distinguishes Bulgaria from almost all other European countries allied to or occupied by Nazi Germany, highlighting defiance to German demands and solidarity across religious difference. The latter fact instead suggests either complicity or impotence and draws attention to the Bulgarian state’s discriminatory and antisemitic policies.

auditPapers.abstract: Aztec Latin. Renaissance Learning and Nahuatl Traditions in Early Colonial Mexico portrays in detail the influence of Renaissance humanist education, particularly the Latin language, on the cultural development of New Spain. The book has nine chapters, some of which center around particular Latin texts written by missionaries. Others focus on rhetoric and Latin as important models for the development of written texts in indigenous languages, such as grammars, catechisms, and other evangelistic sources. At the same time, it is important to bear in mind that in the end, texts were molded to fit Nahua language, beliefs, and ways of thinking, not to preserve humanist principles or Latin models. The first chapter addresses the work of early missionaries such as Zumárraga, de Quiroga, and Garcés, while chapter 2 reviews other figures in relation to their works written in Latin, such as las Casas, Focher, Valadés, and Cabrera. Chapter 3 describes the grammatical Latin models employed in the creation of the Artes of Amerindian languages, although only two are presented in greater detail. The fourth chapter deals with the known facts about the Imperial College of Santa Cruz at Santiago de Tlatelolco, stressing that this was not a school to train Indigenous clergy but rather to furnish Indigenous nobility with a humanist education that missionaries believed would enable them to become leaders in their communities. Additionally, the school produced evangelistic texts, with many translated from Latin into Nahuatl, but there were others created directly in Nahuatl. With this in mind, it would seem that the assertion that “the active translations those Indigenous scholars helped to produce from Latin are by far the most important legacy of their training and led to the creation of a written literature in Nahuatl” goes a bit too far because it seems to imply that without Latin, the Nahuatl language would not have thrived (148). This chapter also neglects to mention that after completing their formal preparation, Indigenous scholars also performed other tasks in addition to collaborating with any of the priests. Indeed, they served as scribes, interpreters, teachers, litigants, mayors, councilors, and authors in their own right. It should also be emphasized that the claim that the Tlatelolco scholars were better versed in Latin than in Nahuatl is an overstatement.

auditPapers.title: David C. Porter. Slaves of the Emperor: Service, Privilege, and Status in the Qing Eight Banners.
auditPapers.abstract: In Slaves of the Emperor: Service, Privilege, and Status in the Qing Eight Banners, David Porter makes a significant contribution to the fields of Chinese history and early modern history. The thesis of this book is twofold: First, Porter argues that the Eight Banners of the Qing empire (1636–1912) was a status group. Through a case study of the Hanjun banners, Porter then presents status as the most important organizing principle of the Qing empire, where banner people and commoners formed the two most prominent examples. Second, he puts forward specific characteristics that made the banners “service elites,” which he defines as “groups that provided military and administrative service to a ruling dynasty and received in exchange institutionalized legal privileges” (14). As highly bureaucratized service elites, the banners helped meet Qing rulers’ demand for centralized bureaucracy and military service in their expanding empires. As Porter notes in chapter 1, Qing historians seldom employed status as an analytical category. Drawing on studies on status in Edo Japan, the Russian Empire, and the Ottoman Empire, Porter lists five characteristics of status: It is defined by law, has implications for rights and obligations, is linked in law to occupation, is heritable with hard inter-status boundaries, and is historically contingent. These characteristics make status distinct from—and for Porter, more useful than—other categories such as class, ethnicity, and caste. The rest of the chapter shows how status operated in Qing at the household level and functioned as a basic identifying feature in official documents.

auditPapers.title: Joshua Ehrlich. The East India Company and the Politics of Knowledge.
auditPapers.abstract: Joshua Ehrlich’s book The East India Company and the Politics of Knowledge offers an original and densely populated intellectual history of the changing ways that the East India Company’s sovereign obligations and its enduring interests as a merchant came to be tied to the cause of “enlightenment.” Ehrlich reminds readers that eighteenth-century Britons were committed to the Baconian “advancement of learning” as much as they were to the plundering conquest of foreign lands, and, consequently, that it is necessary to take the age’s appetite for knowledge seriously if we are to make sense of how officials of the “world’s most powerful corporation” saw themselves as members of “the world’s most enlightened one” (2). The East India Company and the Politics of Knowledge underscores, in particular, how the Company’s initial patronage of Indian learning and, later, its role as an inconsistent and inadequate purveyor of education were inextricably tied to the political debates and the constitutional rearticulations that marked the Company’s tumultuous institutional history. Attention to the wrangles surrounding the Company’s contested charter renewals allows Ehrlich to show that the relation of the Company to knowledge was not merely one of instrumental legitimization: Debates about the proper relationship of government and trade to the provision of learning helped to define the substantive content of the idea of knowledge itself. Similarly, fierce arguments about what kind of knowledge the Company ought to patronize implicated and called into question the hybrid nature of the company-state.
