auditPapers.title: Emily M. Brooks. Gotham’s War within a War: Policing and the Birth of Law-and-Order Liberalism in World War II-Era New York City.
auditPapers.abstract: The field of policing history continues to grow through the new publication of case studies outlining the origins, nature, and consequences of rising police power in twentieth-century American cities. Focusing on New York City in the 1930s and 1940s, Emily Brooks’s book Gotham’s War within a War: Policing and the Birth of Law-and-Order Liberalism in World War II-Era New York City contributes to the field by showing how foreign war—in this case, WWII—helped police administrators solidify the expansion of police power on the home front. While Brooks is not the first scholar to show how so-called liberal politicians and administrators helped shape repressive policing regimes in the twentieth century, her book advances the field by showing how police boosters exploited wartime conditions to advance their law-and-order agenda. According to Brooks, “This book argues that [Mayor Fiorello] La Guardia and [Police Commissioner Lewis] Valentine crafted a new model of liberal law-and-order policing in New York City in the 1930s. It contends that this vision of policing thrived during the militarized moment of World War II when the space for criticism shrank and the NYPD received ideological and material support from the federal government” (6). As developed by La Guardia and Valentine, liberal law and order involved the belief that “some residents were law-abiding and deserved respect, while others were criminals who should be met with repression and violence” (37). Evoking a rhetorical commitment to colorblind justice, however, liberal law and order also enabled rank-and-file officers to perpetuate unequal treatment against marginalized populations. “Despite claims of impartiality,” Brooks argues, public officials “encouraged NYPD members to rely on the racialized geography of the city as well as visual signifiers associated with distinctions of gender, race, class, and sexuality when identifying criminality” (57). Not surprisingly, the political leaders of 1930s New York City embedded discriminatory practices within their professional model of policing despite their allegedly progressive credentials.

auditPapers.title: Karen Auman. The Good Forest: The Salzburgers, Success, and the Plan for Georgia.
auditPapers.abstract: Karen Auman’s book The Good Forest: The Salzburgers, Success, and the Plan for Georgia casts a spotlight on the experiences and contributions of an often-overlooked aspect of colonization in British North America: the role of non-British colonists. She focuses on the Salzburgers, a group of German Protestants who were removed from Salzburg in the early 1730s because of their Protestant beliefs. While most Salzburg Protestants moved to other German states, a minority migrated to the new British colony of Georgia. Forty-five Salzburgers arrived in 1743; by the end of the Trustee era in 1752, they lived in three towns, including Ebenezer, the second largest colonial settlement after Savannah, and accounted for about one-third of Georgia’s population. This sizeable minority population within Georgia became, as Auman argues, shining examples of the Georgia Trustees’ vision for their colony as a refuge for the worthy poor and morally upright. Georgia’s Trustee era has often been painted as a failure, with scholars arguing, as many British colonists did, that it was impossible and foolish to attempt a colony in the Lowcountry that did not utilize and depend upon slave labor. Auman argues that the Salzburgers’ example proved that Georgia’s transition to a slave economy was not inevitable, and that those communities thrived for several decades before Georgia adopted slavery and continued largely without a major reliance on slave labor in the years immediately afterward. Auman also contends that focusing only on economic factors in Georgia’s development underplays both the Salzburgers’ and the Trustees’ overriding concern with the moral character of Georgia’s citizens. Ultimately, a discussion of Georgia’s Trustee era needs to include its German citizens, and Auman’s book serves as a case study for other scholars seeking to grapple more seriously with other minority groups in colonial America.

auditPapers.title: Janet Martin-Nielsen. A Few Acres of Ice: Environment, Sovereignty, and “Grandeur” in the French Antarctic.

The French government only formalized the claim in 1924 in response to British and Australian territorial ambitions and diplomatic inquiries, and it was not until 1950—110 years after discovery—that an official French party would again set foot on this territory. Terre Adélie has had mixed fortunes since, with wavering official interest, fluctuating intensity of scientific research, and uneven public appreciation. auditPapers.title: Andrea Benvenuti. Nehru’s Bandung: Non-Alignment and Regional Order in Indian Cold War Strategy.

In Nehru’s Bandung, Andrea Benvenuti underscores Bandung’s significance through a diplomatic history of India’s reasoning behind, involvement in, and contribution to that historic meeting. Combing archives from India, Britain, the US, and Australia to fashion a narrative that darts between Asian and global capitals, the book seeks to remedy the paucity of scholarship on Nehru and the Indian government’s route to Bandung. Why did Nehru, initially cautious about even the idea of an Asian-African conference, change his mind to the extent that the Indian government would eventually become one of its main proponents? In eleven chronologically sequenced, impressively detailed, and carefully reasoned chapters, much of them devoted to the three years preceding the conference, Benvenuti painstakingly solves this “central puzzle” of Nehru’s journey from Bandung skeptic to architect (5). The book argues that the transformation was caused by three factors: The United States’ defense partnership with Pakistan and its anti-communist regional military alliance in Southeast Asia (seen by New Delhi as threatening and destabilizing respectively); China’s seeming abandonment of international revolution and apparent adoption of the principle of peaceful coexistence in 1954 (which Nehru viewed as propitious); and Nehru’s overarching aim of using the Asian-African conference (initially an Indonesian proposal) as a means to secure his vision of “areas of peace,” understood as a region of nonalignment amid the Cold War, bound together by the “Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence.” Challenging the commonly held view of Nehru as a lofty idealist on the international stage, Benvenuti instead contends that “Cold War concerns—not Afro-Asian unity—drove his actions” (8). Viewed from New Delhi, Bandung was “first and foremost an exercise in regional security” (53).

auditPapers.abstract: Andrew Denning’s Automotive Empire is a rich and significant contribution to the comparative history of how colonial regimes conceived and implemented their policies on road construction in Africa. The concept of “automotive empire,” which underpins the book, is centered on how technology, infrastructure, and mobility shaped colonial policies and how these interventions transformed Africa in turn. Denning aims to develop a theoretical framework connecting European technopolitics development with imperial projects—French, Italian, British, and German. At the heart of his analysis lies the fixation of colonial regimes on road building and automotive culture. The author explores how colonial administrators envisioned their automotive empires, their inherent fragility and limitations, and their challenges in confronting Africa’s landscapes, particularly regarding resources, territorial extension, and labor. Although the issue of African forced labor is addressed only tangentially, Denning compellingly examines the intersection between colonial ambitions and the practical realities of roadbuilding, offering valuable insights into the technopolitical dimensions of European imperialism.

auditPapers.title: Uğur Zekeriya Peçe. Island and Empire: How Civil War in Crete Mobilized the Ottoman World.
auditPapers.abstract: In this book, Uğur Zekeriya Peçe considers a question of profound historical and contemporary significance: When, why, and under what circumstances do the displaced become displacers? To trace that process, Island and Empire follows the trajectories of some 70,000 Cretan Muslim refugees who, after fleeing conflict on the island in the 1890s, brought the “Cretan question” to the forefront of Ottoman mass politics following the Constitutional Revolution of 1908. The book sheds light on an underexamined episode in the mass displacements that forged the modern Middle East and models an approach to examining historical coexistence alongside intercommunal violence. Peçe’s discussion of violence and his success in narrating the political participation of nonelite refugees emerges through virtuosic use of published materials and archival collections located in seven countries. His interweaving of sources in English, French, German, Greek, Italian, and Ottoman Turkish/Turkish serves as a constant reminder of the shared Greek vernacular of Cretan Muslims and Christians and of the polyglot spaces Cretans inhabited in Ottoman cities from Hania to Izmir.

auditPapers.title: Gabriella Romano. Italian Fascism’s Forgotten LGBT Victims: Asylums and Internment, 1922–1943.
auditPapers.abstract: Gabriella Romano’s Italian Fascism’s Forgotten LGBT Victims is a fascinating and original book. It covers a vast amount of ground but does it with great care. The book is focused on LGBT patients in Italian psychiatric hospitals during the years of fascism in Italy. But, in reality, it also touches on a number of other crucial issues of history, medical history, and queer history. These include: the history of psychiatry in Italy and Europe; the understanding of homosexuality by psychiatrists and others in Italy, Europe, and elsewhere; the impact of fascism on psychiatry and psychiatric hospitals; the persecution of homosexuality in Italy (and elsewhere) by fascism but also before fascism; the management and institutional culture inside Italian psychiatric hospitals and the differences between various psychiatric hospitals and their cultures (also geographically); and personnel and psychiatric management. Moreover, the book is extremely reflective in terms of methodology and archival access, and it draws a number of interesting conclusions around its sources and the use of sources of this kind in the general and specific. It would not be an exaggeration to call this a pathbreaking work, which breaks new ground in a whole series of areas.

auditPapers.title: Shellen Xiao Wu. Birth of the Geopolitical Age: Global Frontiers and the Making of Modern China.
auditPapers.abstract: In China’s arid far western region of Xinjiang, there is no shortage of monuments commemorating the reclamation campaigns that transformed landscapes and bound this border region more closely to the state. One such monument in a leafy park in the capital city of Urumqi, located a distant 1,700 miles from China’s capital of Beijing, features two brawny men grappling with the earth and a quote from a Chinese Communist Party official who proclaimed that it was the labor of men like these that made Xinjiang green and, implicitly, connected it more closely to China. In her new book The Birth of the Geopolitical Age: Global Frontiers and the Making of Modern China, Shellen Xiao Wu offers a new global perspective on the campaigns that transformed this and other border regions in China—and indeed around the world. In it, she centralizes not the blood and sweat of settlers but rather the plans, maps, and surveys of geographers, agronomists, and other scientists who were charged with the task of recasting imperial frontiers into national borders.

auditPapers.title: Tabitha Stanmore. Love Spells and Lost Treasure: Service Magic in England from the Later Middle Ages to the Early Modern Era.
auditPapers.abstract: Tabitha Stanmore’s examination of late medieval and early modern English “service magicians” builds usefully upon the foundations established by several generations of scholars such as George Kittredge, Keith Thomas, Alan MacFarlane, and Owen Davies. The book concerns actual magic practitioners who were employed in their local communities for a variety of tasks. Like Davies, although in a narrower timeframe, Love Spells and Lost Treasure focuses on those who provided remunerated services. The book pursues a strategy similar to prior studies of common magic by assembling a large body of examples and treating them thematically. Thus, the overall orientation of the project is conventional, although Stanmore has collected a significant body of previously unexamined evidence. As Stanmore writes in the conclusion, the volume serves in broad strokes more to confirm what has been suggested about the subject by prior scholars than to break entirely new ground, although it significantly expands the number of known magicians, provides considerably more evidence and detail, and makes some quite significant contributions in more focused ways.

auditPapers.title: Alvita Akiboh. Imperial Material: National Symbols in the US Colonial Empire.
auditPapers.abstract: What binds an imperial community? This question animates Alvita Akiboh’s Imperial Material: National Symbols in the US Colonial Empire. The book’s title suggests the answers it provides. Objects (flags, stamps, paper currency), Akiboh argues, mediated the fractious, uneven, and malleable process(es) of Americanization in the United States’ Caribbean, Pacific, and Southeast Asian colonies. In their pervasiveness, they served paradoxically as a circulatory system for communicating (Euro)American culture and as conduits for reimagining and rearranging colonization. By mapping the banal nationalism of these objects, the book illustrates how the “stuff” of everyday colonial life became a site for negotiating citizenship, subjecthood, and the spaces in between. Like in other notable works on US overseas colonies, Akiboh uses the 1901 Supreme Court’s so-called Insular Cases as a departure point. Unlike them, however, she shows how the distances and proximities produced in their wake were articulated through symbols of the United States. Imperial material produced the imperial immaterial that culturally constituted colonization. In staking these claims, the book dialogues with not only the robust scholarship on the US empire but also work on a host of other empires.

auditPapers.title: Kelly L. Marino. Votes for College Women: Alumni, Students, and the Woman Suffrage Campaign.
auditPapers.abstract: Just as the College Equal Suffrage League (CESL) sought to reinvigorate the fight for the vote in the early twentieth century by adding new players and new energy to a movement that had stagnated, Kelly Marino hopes to reinvigorate suffrage scholarship with her book Votes for College Women: Alumni, Students, and the Woman Suffrage Campaign. The little-studied CESL, established by Maud Wood Park and Inez Haynes Irwin in 1900, started as an effort to mobilize female college graduates before turning its attention to on-campus faculty and student recruitment. Eventually, about five thousand women became affiliated with the organization through roughly fifty chapters scattered across the county. Marino documents the CESL’s creation, expansion, and impact while also tracing how reluctant college administrators and students, male and female, came to embrace the cause by the 1910s. Rather than dismissing the early twentieth century as the doldrums of the suffrage fight as historians so often have, Marino deems this an essential period. As progress stalled, leaders sought new strategies and new constituencies, and the CESL fit well into these revitalization efforts. She argues that the CESL’s work to help pass a state suffrage amendment in California in 1911—an effort that won by less than four thousand votes but that doubled the number of women voting in the country—was especially crucial and deserves more attention. Aligning itself with the National American Woman Suffrage Association, the CESL was not flashy, and it did not draw the kind of headlines that followed the more radical National Woman’s Party, but the professional prestige and gravitas its members offered helped turned the tide to make ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment possible. During these years, suffrage became a mainstream cause, and Marino emphasizes that smart, articulate, and reasoned college women were essential to the transformation.

auditPapers.title: Jane Mumby. Dismantling the League of Nations: The Quiet Death of an International Organization, 1945–48.
auditPapers.abstract: Jane Mumby’s book Dismantling the League of Nations: The Quiet Death of an International Organization, 1945–48 places itself in a broader body of literature that has emerged over the last decade or so, looking at this first experiment in global governance and institutionalized international cooperation from the perspective of its staff. Just within the last couple of years, Emil Seidenfaden has published the first study of the Information Section of the League, Benjamin Auberer has written a monograph on the Australian and New Zealander officials of the Secretariat, and Myriam Piguet defended a thesis on the integration of women in the League and UN Secretariats. This is a relatively new chapter in the historiographical saga, which first saw the League as a failure, then as a mere stage upon which great powers locked horns, then as an important node in broader transnational networks of embryonic global governance, and now as a bureaucratized multilateral organization with its own dynamics and history. These perspectives are, of course, both overlapping and complementary—and there are many more to come.

auditPapers.title: Navyug Gill. Labors of Division: Global Capitalism and the Emergence of the Peasant in Colonial Panjab.
auditPapers.abstract: When formal British rule arrived in the province of the Panjab in 1849, the colonial state immediately directed its energies toward extracting land revenue. The effect of this endeavor on Panjabi society has often been viewed positively, but Navyug Gill challenges this narrative of “colonial benevolence” in his book Labors of Division: Global Capitalism and the Emergence of the Peasant in Colonial Panjab. Rejecting the claim that cultivators remained “largely unscathed if not deliberately empowered” (4) under British rule, Gill sets out to show how colonial technologies of rule instigated an “internal contest for social and economic primacy among different groups of Panjabis” (261). The book is divided into five chapters, flanked by an introduction and a conclusion. Chapter 1 begins Gill’s investigation into how the seemingly obvious category of the “peasant” was the contingent product of colonial governance. To maximize revenue, the state used mathematical methods to assess lands based on criteria such as their productive “capacity” and the quality of the labor working it. Usually, such assessments were greater than what the land produced and/or the revenue that cultivators had hitherto paid. Gill concludes that the “peasant” who emerged through colonial rule was “irreducibly distinct and modern” (65) and that colonial benevolence was a claim produced to “conceal the novelty of a discordant accumulation” (66).

auditPapers.title: Lindsey Dodd. Feeling Memory: Remembering Wartime Childhoods in France.
auditPapers.abstract: In Feeling Memory: Remembering Wartime Childhoods in France, Lindsey Dodd continues her inquiry into children’s experiences of war. In this new work, the author breathes new life into oral interviews she conducted previously for a different project, focused on reconstructing children’s memories of the Second World War. Right from the start, she makes it clear that this is not a book on the official or collective memory of the Second World War, nor is it a prosopography, nor even, she warns, a work of history in the canonical and academic sense of the term. Instead, Dodd focuses on two questions that guide her investigation: What does it mean to be a child during the war? How can oral sources be used to tell the story “from the inside out” (2)? Following what has been called the “affective turn,” Dodd has taken up the challenge of weaving together a sensitive, “affective” history of the war by paying attention to the multiplicity and heterogeneity of individual memories and childhood experiences of the war. She explains that the more traditional historical methods prevented her from seeing that all her interviews were saturated with emotions, feelings, and sensations. In this respect, she starts from the premise that “memories of experiences must be memories of feeling” (52). Using an “ideological positioning” (2) and an “affective methodology” (11), she advocates for a much more empathetic approach to witnesses, listening to them with renewed attention and without overlooking them. The focus is therefore on individuals and their singularities rather than on the collective or the analysis of structures. In her view, the usual methodological reflexes of historians are inadequate insofar as they too often impose a chronological ordering of memory, which does not sufficiently take into account the challenges of the disordered, multiple, and complex dimensions of memory. Her approach is therefore both critical and reflective, offering a revision of her own work as well as a rereading of her personal use of oral sources. She draws on an impressive corpus of 120 oral testimonies produced between 1982 and 2017, fifty-two of which she conducted herself. By choosing an “impressionist” methodology (17), which seeks to fit the blurred and complex contours of the oral source, the author justifies her choice not to adhere to the traditional methodologies of the historical discipline.

auditPapers.title: Samuel Dolbee. Locusts of Power: Borders, Empire, and Environment in the Modern Middle East.
auditPapers.abstract: The history of the Jazira, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, finds new expression and creative resuscitation in Samuel Dolbee’s book Locusts of Power. The toponym, Jazira, is not often found on contemporary maps, Dolbee notes. Yet, by tracing the movement of peoples and insects across this geographic region from 1858 to 1939, Dolbee reveals the Jazira’s place in Ottoman and Middle Eastern history while also describing the limits of state power, the increasing influence of market forces, and the productive and destructive qualities of borders. The first two chapters of Locusts of Power focus on Ottoman efforts to control and benefit from the Jazira, a region that grew in strategic and economic value from the mid-19th century due to the US Civil War and the construction of the Baghdad Railway. Dolbee explains how the Jazira’s aridity and nomadic groups’ mobility affected Ottoman visions for settlement and agricultural expansion. The Jazira’s ecologies and physical geography take a backseat in these discussions as Dolbee foregrounds the movements of the book’s primary actors. An impressive array of sources furnishes vibrant descriptions of nomads, Ottoman reformers, warlords, deported Armenians, and European imperialists. The analysis is at its best in moments of synthesis, when the Shammar herdsmen, the armies sent to subdue them, and the insects and starlings, all kinetic and moving in “a choreography of locusts and nomads,” come together (39). The examination of the locusts’ economic effects and their reverberation through politics and society is also excellent. Moreover, the careful juxtaposition of material and political borders produces paradoxes that help to illuminate intertwined human and insect fates, as when Dolbee notes, “Regions remained beyond settlement because that was where the locust laid their eggs, and locust eggs could not be destroyed because they were located in regions beyond settlement” (134). More information about the locust itself and its reproduction would have made these juxtapositions that much keener.

auditPapers.title: Manisha Sinha. The Rise and Fall of the Second American Republic: Reconstruction, 1860–1920.
auditPapers.abstract: When Eric Foner’s Reconstruction: America’s Unfinished Revolution came out in 1988, reviewer Michael Perman wondered whether historians would have anything left to say about the post-Civil War era. He need not have worried. Since then, Reconstruction has captured the interest of a growing number of Americans, including historians who have expanded the study of this pivotal era and taken it in new directions. In The Rise and Fall of the Second American Republic: Reconstruction, 1860–1920, Manisha Sinha, a Foner-trained expert on the history of abolition, offers her own single-volume account of this period. Uncovering and amplifying “the voices of abolitionist and radical critics of mainstream society,” Sinha immerses readers in the abolitionist vision and activism of Reconstruction (xxiv). The Rise and Fall of the Second American Republic explains how American interracial democracy was built and then broken during and after the Civil War. Stressing the racialism of emancipation and Reconstruction, Sinha introduces first-time readers to a new set of historical protagonists, centering freedpeople, women, and antislavery and feminist activists. The book effectively emphasizes the centrality of emancipation and interracial democracy—through the expansion of political rights and grassroots efforts led by Black Americans and their allies—to the major successes of Reconstruction. Rather than a new phase of America’s longstanding quest for a more perfect Union, the Civil War, Sinha argues, was the catalyst for the full-scale “destruction of the ‘first’ American republic and [the birth] the second” (xix). Borrowing from the history of French republicanism, Sinha puts the Civil War and Reconstruction in conversation with other nineteenth-century political revolutions in Europe and Latin America.

auditPapers.title: Mark Boulton and Tobias T. Gibson, eds. Red Reckoning: The Cold War and the Transformation of American Life.
auditPapers.abstract: Scholars have documented a rise in Cold War nostalgia among policymakers and everyday Americans in recent years. Apparently longing for the days when the United States identified its domestic and international goals in distinction to the Soviet Union and communism, some Americans idealize that Manichean division of the world in which the sides and the stakes were clear, if not comforting. Red Reckoning, a new volume edited by Mark Boulton and Tobias T. Gibson, offers a reminder of just how misplaced that nostalgia is and how fundamentally the Cold War remade the United States. Boulton and Gibson have assembled an impressive collection of essays from scholars across several disciplines to chart the ruptures that opened in US society across four decades of the twentieth century. The Cold War may have never turned hot on US soil, but that does not mean that American society, culture, and politics escaped unharmed. Red Reckoning traces the wounds inflicted by that conflict and reminds readers how the after-effects of the Cold War still linger in the present day.

auditPapers.title: Laurence W. Marvin. The Damietta Crusade, 1217–1221. A Military History.
auditPapers.abstract: The “classic” Crusades to the Near East between the 11th and 13th centuries are one of the best-studied fields of medieval history. Each major military campaign has been covered in several monographs and chapters of standard synopses. The “Fifth” Crusade (1217–21) is no exception, particularly as it has attracted increased scholarly attention during the past decade. However, with the last comprehensive monograph published in 1986, Laurence W. Marvin’s The Damietta Crusade offers a welcome revision of this classic subject, incorporating four decades of scholarly progress. Marvin’s primary thesis posits that the crusaders initially conceived a sound and quite achievable “grand strategy”: By invading Egypt and threatening or even conquering the economic power base of the Ayyūbids, they aimed to compel the surrender of Jerusalem to the Christians. Due to its strategic and economic importance, the Mediterranean port city of Damietta became the crusaders’ initial target and maintained its central role throughout the campaign, which is thus often called the Damietta Crusade.

auditPapers.title: Tomás Irish. Feeding the Mind: Humanitarianism and the Reconstruction of European Intellectual Life, 1919–1933.
auditPapers.abstract: Tomás Irish’s Feeding the Mind unearths a fascinating chapter in the post–World War I relief and reconstruction of Europe: the rescue and rehabilitation of intellectuals and intellectual life. The war-produced crisis of civilization caused governments, the new League of Nations, epistemic bodies, nongovernmental organizations, philanthropies, and the concerned individual to undertake a variety of interventions in the name of humanitarianism to favor the intellectual and repair the damage done to intellectual life. This is a valuable account of how civilizational projects and intellectuals and knowledge production combine into a form of humanitarianism unlike most. The book is organized into six chapters plus an introduction and epilogue. The introduction and chapter 1 lay out the major twin themes of the argument. Once the war ended, Europe turned to the labor of repairing the physical and emotional damage wrought by the war. This was a period of introspection. Ideas of progress were central to the meaning of European civilization, but the very fact of the war and its immense destruction cratered such beliefs. Indeed, in many conflict zones, the armed parties aimed to destroy the pursuit of knowledge and the preservation of culture by burning books, libraries, academic institutions, and museums. Irish notes how civilizational discourse served multiple functions: It is what kept Europe from descending into conflict and collapse; it represented a form of universalism that transcended borders and nationalisms; and it placed an emphasis on high culture. Intellectuals were central to these functions as they became the symbols of civilization and could help overcome national differences and continuing resentments toward ex-enemies.

auditPapers.title: Tristan G. Brown. Laws of the Land: Fengshui and the State in Qing Dynasty China.
auditPapers.abstract: Tristan G. Brown’s book Laws of the Land: Fengshui and the State in Qing Dynasty China breaks new ground in Chinese legal history by considering the roles played by the knowledge system of fengshui—which literally means “wind and water” and concerns the orientation of structures following cosmological principles—in the governance and social fabric of late imperial China. The historiography of late imperial China has long moved away from Orientalist narratives that blame indigenous traditions such as fengshui as obstacles to reason and development. In the past few decades, as historians sought to demonstrate the rationality, pragmatism, and dynamism in many facets of Qing China’s governance, social life, and intellectual world, fengshui and other “superstitions” that were once at the center of the narrative of China’s backwardness have now gone backstage in the historiography, as if they were only the insignificant components of a rational, secular society. Brown makes a valuable contribution by demonstrating that fengshui was not marginal but pervasive and persistent in Qing China, not because people were superstitious or irrational, but because this system of cosmic knowledge was deeply entwined with Qing law as a technology of administration and embedded in social practice as a language of power.

auditPapers.title: Adam Zientek. A Thirst for Wine and War: The Intoxication of French Soldiers on the Western Front.
auditPapers.abstract: Ever since Norman Ohler’s book Blitzed: Drugs in Nazi Germany was published in 2015, there have been a number of monographs covering elements of drugs use in war. Adam Zientek’s book A Thirst for Wine and War: The Intoxication of French Soldiers on the Western Front is among the very best of these and deserves a place on many a bookshelf and reading list. Histories of soldiers and drinking are, of course, nothing new. Paul Fussell, in Wartime: Understanding and Behaviour in the Second World War, wrote vividly of traumatized soldiers salving their psyches with large quantities of alcohol. In Fussell’s work, the debauched drunkenness of soldiers was just one more sad absurdity of modern (or indeed, any) war. Zientek, on the other hand, treads a middle ground, giving us a history with substantial interest to social, cultural, and intoxicant historians (should such a designation exist), while also showing a nuanced understanding and respect for military history and the history of war.

auditPapers.title: Caryn Cossé Bell. Creole New Orleans in the Revolutionary Atlantic, 1775–1877.
auditPapers.abstract: Caryn Cossé Bell’s new book is an interesting, smart, at times truly original—if at other times rather flawed—work that serves as a potent and meaningful follow-up to her excellent first book, Revolution, Romanticism, and the Afro-Creole Protest Tradition in Louisiana (1997). The first part of the book, “Revolutions,” follows a band of “itinerant revolutionaries aspiring to a new world order” who, displaced by the Haitian Revolution and inspired by republican independence movements across the circum-Caribbean, formed “an influential interracial refugee coalition” based in New Orleans by the 1830s (34). Sowed by their participation in, yet the denial of citizenship after, the Battle of New Orleans and a shared dedication to revolutionary spirit throughout the wider gulf area, this coalition took up the mantle of republican revolution and equal rights in the decades that followed. Importantly, and certainly historiographically novel, New Orleans becomes part of something bigger than the francophone circum-Caribbean. It becomes a waypoint for Atlantic radicalism—the same revolutionary ideas that gave rise to names like Pétain, Bolívar, and Lafayette.

auditPapers.title: Leyla Amzi-Erdogdular. The Afterlife of Ottoman Europe: Muslims in Habsburg Bosnia Herzegovina.
auditPapers.abstract: Leyla Amzi-Erdogdular’s new book, The Afterlife of Ottoman Europe: Muslims in Habsburg Bosnia Herzegovina, begins with a simple premise: The end of the Ottoman Empire’s rule over its Balkan provinces did not mean the end of an Ottoman presence. The radical remapping of the Ottoman Balkans at the end of the 1877–1878 Russian-Ottoman war created independent states, such as Romania and Serbia, the quasi-states of the vassal Bulgarian principality and autonomous province of Eastern Rumelia and Bosnia Herzegovina, which was placed in a novel legal limbo: The Ottoman sultan remained officially sovereign, but the Habsburg monarchy assumed administrative rights and responsibilities. It took a year to hammer out the details, but the essential feature was already fixed by the 1878 Treaty of Berlin: An Ottoman presence would be maintained not through the informal momentum of local practice but was to be formally guaranteed by international law. The Afterlife of Ottoman Europe offers a fresh perspective on what happened next by concentrating on Bosnia’s Muslim population who, unlike their Catholic and Orthodox neighbors, remained uniquely tethered to the Ottoman sultan as both sovereign and caliph. The province’s status left Bosnian Muslims trying to maintain their close relationship to Istanbul while adjusting to the Habsburg’s increasingly thorough and definitively Christian administration. For Austria, the occupation was a preliminary to annexation; the Ottomans viewed it as a temporary anomaly requiring innovative support for people who continued to be Ottoman subjects; and while Bosnian Muslims hoped for a provincial repatriation, they also seized all available tools to determine their future. “To the Habsburgs,” writes Amzi-Erdogdular, Bosnian Muslims “insisted on the execution of Ottoman laws and practices and ties with the sultan-caliph. To the Ottomans, they appealed for protection as Ottoman subjects and as part of the umma, stimulating Ottoman diplomatic activity in their direction and often trying to attract international attention” (166).

auditPapers.title: Kirsten Schultz. From Conquest to Colony: Empire, Wealth, and Difference in Eighteenth-Century Brazil.
auditPapers.abstract: Scholars of the Portuguese Atlantic empire are well acquainted with Kirsten Schultz’s work. Her first book, Tropical Versailles, showed how the early nineteenth-century events leading to the Portuguese Court’s transfer to Rio de Janeiro in 1808 influenced Portuguese perceptions of the empire and the colonization process. This second major work, From Conquest to Colony, consolidates Schultz’s place as a major figure in the field. Schultz argues that the discovery of gold in late seventeenth century Brazil and the economic decline of colonies in Asia led the Portuguese court to develop new ideas about sovereignty and governance in Brazil, and to find new ways to govern the territory. This shift transformed Brazil from being a “conquest”—where Portuguese dominion was based on the incorporation of new lands through frontier expansion and new persons through evangelization—into a “colony.” This redefined Brazil’s status within the Portuguese Empire and created a specific social, political, and economic order.

auditPapers.title: Andreas Zeman. The Winds of History: Life in a Corner of Rural Africa Since the 19th Century.
auditPapers.abstract: Andreas Zeman’s book The Winds of History: Life in a Corner of Rural Africa Since the 19th Century is a meticulously researched microhistory of Nkholongue, a small village on the shore of Lake Niassa in northern Mozambique. Across 10 densely argued chapters, Zeman evokes the disruptions and adaptations that have marked Nkholongue’s past, stretching from the village’s foundation in the shadow of the Indian Ocean slave trade to the economic and social reconfigurations caused by ecotourism resort construction in the 21st century. The title is aptly chosen, as the “winds of history” is a recurring motif that captures much of the book’s central argument. Zeman introduces the term by evoking the social impact of mwera, a wind that comes off Lake Niassa: an external, structural, and powerful force that changes “everyday reality in Nkholongue” (36) and which thus offers “an appropriate metaphor to describe life in Nkholongue since the 19th century” (37). Zeman’s work charts the impact of large-scale historical trends—the slave trade, colonization, independence, civil war—on the people of Nkholongue, in order “to demonstrate that it is not possible to analyze the lives of people in this corner of rural Africa without spotlighting the frequent and often violent ruptures they were confronted with during their lifetimes” (39).

auditPapers.title: Neeti Nair. Hurt Sentiments: Secularism and Belonging in South Asia.
auditPapers.abstract: What makes secularism an enduring idea and a catchall phrase in contemporary South Asia? In Hurt Sentiments, Neeti Nair ventures to answer this question through a historical study of secularism in most of South Asia in the twentieth century—particularly the postcolonial nation-states of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. Nair’s book tells a terrific tale, excavating the multilayered lives of South Asian secularism. South Asian secularism, as Hurt Sentiments shows, is a contingent idea constructed and reconstructed through a wide range of political practices. In a painstakingly detailed narrative, Nair argues that in order to study secularism we need to return to the founding moment of the three postcolonial nation-states and trace how being secular was an iteration of belonging in twentieth-century South Asia. In an astounding achievement, Nair forges a connection between intellectual history and social history in tracking the career of secularism in modern South Asia. The book consists of four chapters that present multiple iterations of secularism in the wake of crucial turning points in the history of South Asia. Drawing on Partha Chatterjee’s suggestion, Nair shows that pitting secularism against “Hindu majoritarianism” is not a useful framework, in the case of South Asia. Rather, Nair argues, the “hurt Hindu” and the “hurt Muslim,” on the ascendant, has in fact shaped state ideologies of secularism in modern South Asia (6, 14).

auditPapers.title: Anne O’Donnell. Power and Possession in the Russian Revolution.
auditPapers.abstract: After assuming power in October 1917, the Bolsheviks went on to seize a “dazzling array of resources,” as Anne O’Donnell notes in Power and Possession in the Russian Revolution (2). Though this would later be portrayed as an integral part of the revolution, in fact, they planned little in advance, and dispossession occurred largely in the absence of laws. Examining these seizures in Moscow and Petrograd during the first few years after the revolution, her book tries to make sense of this “unprecedented quest to abolish private property and the search for an alternative system of political economy—socialism—that grew out of it” (2). Dispossession drew upon prerevolutionary trends, the subject of the prologue. A turn toward “municipalization”—that is, the abolition of property rights in buildings and their transformation into state property—began during the First World War under the Provisional Government. Housing became a site of social conflict as evacuees and refugees arrived in cities from the front, leading to the creation of “building committees” to resolve grievances, which would later be exploited by the Bolsheviks. Early Bolshevik seizure orders also drew upon prerevolutionary legal language, referring to them as “requisitions” just like those intended to help the war effort.

Misers figured, he insists, in these intellectual and cultural shifts in complicated and revealing ways. Alborn investigates misers’ role in giving rise by the nineteenth century to “self-help” as a dominant British ideology. He investigates what misers have to offer us in understanding the consolidation of classical economics in the wake of the publication of Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations as well as the novel’s emergence as a central organizer of British social and gender relations (8). Moreover, the changes over time that Alborn’s study investigates and explores in misers’ stories—their transformations from characters exhibiting meanness, hoarding, and avarice to the economic and affective reformation of their characters and emotions exhibited in credit, savings, and investment as economic engines of growth—underscores how economic and literary genres “converged on the same awkward embrace of capitalism,” albeit, by different means (5).

Ultimately, Roy argues that child abolitionists did not simply consume antislavery readings but rather “came to develop their own understandings of abolition, deploying surprising degrees of agency in the process” (6).

auditPapers.title: George Roberts. Revolutionary State-Making in Dar es Salaam: African Liberation and the Global Cold War, 1961–1974.
auditPapers.abstract: In Revolutionary State-Making in Dar es Salaam: African Liberation and the Global Cold War, 1961–1974, George Roberts studies the politics of Cold War rivalries, African liberation movements, and socialist state-building in Tanzania. In focusing on these three elements, Roberts intricately weaves the Cold War and decolonization histories to show how the Tanzanian city of Dar es Salaam was part of a larger network of global Cold War and anticolonial cities, including Hong Kong, Mexico City, Accra, and Algiers. The book details how Dar es Salaam became a nerve center of anticolonial African movements and how the Tanzanian government’s hospitality created powerful enemies, which forced the government to become authoritarian to defend itself. Even though the book prioritizes Julius Kambarage Nyerere’s primary role in making postcolonial Tanzania, Roberts emphasizes how other elites often challenged his views. Drawing from archival materials from Tanzania, Britain, France, Germany, Portugal, the United States, Belgium, the Netherlands, South Africa, Australia, India, and Poland, as well as newspapers, oral interviews, official publications, and memoirs, the book details how Cold War powers sprinted to set up embassies in Dar es Salaam following Tanzania’s independence in 1961. This rush, Roberts notes, turned Dar es Salaam into a “revolutionary city,” “Cold War hotbed,” “city of hopes and dreams,” “mecca of liberation,” “a dangerous staging ground for communist penetration,” “city alive with grand visions of Africa’s postcolonial future,” “center of revolutionary subversion in Africa,” and “epicenter of [African] radical politics.” These descriptions provide a mosaic picture of a busy city with strong characters and whose interests intersected and diverged. After introducing the city, Roberts zooms in on Nkrumah Street, decorated with signs of African nationalist parties: ANC, PAC, SWAPO, ZANU, ZAPU, and FRELIMO. Dar es Salaam’s residents included journalists, guerrilla leaders, Cold War diplomats, foreign embassy staff, Chinese booksellers, radical academics, and Tanzania postcolonial elites.

auditPapers.title: Anthony Gregory. New Deal Law and Order: How the War on Crime Built the Modern Liberal State.
auditPapers.abstract: In fall of 2024, Americans are entering an unprecedented presidential election season. One reason, though far from the only one, that this election differs from recent historical convention can be found in the divergent visions of crime policy presented by the two mainstream parties. In this 2024 clash, we can see the breakdown of a bipartisan commitment to what historian Anthony Gregory calls a “war on crime” that has dominated American politics since the 1930s. Gregory’s book New Deal Law and Order: How the War on Crime Built the Modern Liberal State is a thorough and convincing explication of the process of building this framework that will prove essential to historians of the New Deal, political and legal historians, historians of the carceral state, and readers who wish to understand one of the central building blocks in the political order that preceded our contemporary moment. New Deal Law and Order is an ambitious political and legal history of the formative years of twentieth-century American liberalism at the federal level. Gregory argues that welfare liberalism and what he dubs war-on-crime liberalism developed together in the 1930s. He contends that “the New Deal war on crime delivered political legitimacy to the modern state through the transformation of liberal ideas, liberal governance, and constitutional structure” (5). In this argument, Gregory makes an important intervention in a growing historiographic subfield, exploring the relationship between liberalism and state mechanisms of imprisonment, policing, and punishment. Gregory methodically reframes the role of the war on crime in 1930s state building, contending that 1930s crime policies enabled the political alliances and expansions in federalism that made the New Deal possible. The author clearly shows that New Deal policies built carceral capacity at every government level, which is a useful point that other scholars have referenced but few have taken the time to systematically prove. Gregory’s most groundbreaking and unsettling argument is that support for war-on-crime policies, including the introduction of new federal crimes and a massive expansion of federal crime-fighting infrastructure, brought adversaries together in a coalition that generated important liberal political capital, some of which translated into support for New Deal policies.

auditPapers.title: Patrick William Otim. Acholi Intellectuals: Knowledge, Power, and the Making of Colonial Northern Uganda, 1850–1960.
auditPapers.abstract: In 1953, Lacito Okech published the first history of the Acholi written by an Acholi. Tekwaro ki Ker Lobo Acholi, or History and Chiefly Tradition of Acholiland, was wildly popular among his contemporaries, not because it was the first book written by an Acholi or because an influential hereditary chief had written the foreword—both explanations offered by European missionaries—but because the author was a respected leader. As a royal messenger, la or Pa rwot, Okech was part of an elite cadre of “intellectuals” who held prominent positions as court officials in various Acholi chiefdoms. The history and significance of their labor is skillfully mapped out in Patrick William Otim’s powerful new book, Acholi Intellectuals: Knowledge, Power, and the Making of Colonial Northern Uganda, 1850–1960. Otim argues that the men who held these important positions as war leaders, royal messengers, royal healers, priests, and poet-musicians—most of these persons were indeed men—were not the ordinary or marginalized citizens that European colonizers and missionaries assumed them to be, but instead, sophisticated and highly trained members of the precolonial political elite. These intellectuals played “a pivotal yet overlooked role in the transition to, and spread of, Christianity and colonial rule” (7).

auditPapers.title: Adeeb Khalid. Central Asia: A New History from the Imperial Conquests to the Present.
auditPapers.abstract: In an illustrious career spanning some four decades, Adeeb Khalid has explored the effects of Russian and then Soviet rule on Central Asian (especially Uzbekistani) Muslim societies. Khalid begins his text with an insistence on the centrality of Central Asia. Growing up in the 1970s in Pakistan, he tells us, although his hometown of Lahore was only twelve hundred kilometers from Tashkent, “it might as well have been on a different planet” because travel was difficult and news in short supply (2). He provides other anecdotes about how, from US diplomatic practice to Japanese documentary makers and British comedians, Central Asia was seen as inscrutable, exotic, timeless and unknown. This general level of ignorance is arguably no longer the case, and an early-career scholar embarking on a similar project today would be less likely to place their argument in such a framework. But it makes sense of Khalid’s formative experiences, and he uses it to compelling effect to insist that Central Asia “has experienced every current of modern history, every achievement of modernity and every one of its disasters, and every extreme of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries” (3).

History is not a court of law, and pleading ignorance cannot protect us. In other words, what we don’t know will kill us. We cannot always anticipate what the past holds in store for us. This vision of abundant but exploited and underutilized natural wealth influenced Miguel Hidalgo, José María Morelos, Vicente Guerrero, and Agustín Iturbide, the last the erstwhile loyalist who switched his allegiance to Guerrero and helped the rebels claim victory. Despite the differences among them, all these independence leaders promised that independence would limit access to Mexico’s riches to the country’s own nationals. But over the next forty-six years, Mexico experienced a devastating conflict with the United States, which robbed it of half of its territory, and suffered three foreign invasions, one from Spain and two from France. Foreigners continued to control much of Mexico’s wealth. At the same time, and in part because of endemic political instability, the Mexican economy lagged behind that of the United States and also behind those of larger South American nations.

auditPapers.title: Technical advantages bridging the preservation limits of painted decoration of Neolithic ceramic figurines
auditPapers.abstract: Painting on ceramic objects is one of the most outstanding features of visual narration of the Neolithic material culture in Southeastern and partly in Central Europe. Unfortunately, post-firing painting is usually poorly preserved due to deposition conditions. Moreover, it may have been damaged or contaminated during post-excavation and conservation processes in the past. This project studies how new methods of pigment traces visual detection bring about a more successful identification of pigment traces and reconstruction of motifs; this leads to both more targeted protection without contaminants and a broader understanding of the motifs preferred by Neolithic societies in their narrative expression. Decorrelation algorithms have been widely used to analyse rock art and wall paintings, but their application to fragile pigments on mobile artefacts remains limited. DStretch, a key tool in this process, enhances colour contrasts in digital images to detect faint pigment traces, which are often overlooked in standard macroscopic analysis. By applying DStretch to high-resolution photographs or 3D model textures, pigment residues can be identified without damaging the object. The algorithm’s versatility extends to different colour channels, making it possible to detect subtle traces across different pigments, improving overall data preservation and analysis. 378 fragments of Neolithic ceramic figurines from the Lengyel culture site Těšetice-Kyjovice – Sutny, the largest known collection in central Europe, have been studied. The DStretch results were verified using reflected-light microscopy, and samples of the most commonly used pigments were analysed by Raman spectroscopy. In the past, painting the figurines was considered a minor practice, which led to believe that only 25 % of them were painted. Thanks to the methods applied in this project, it is revealed that, despite the intensive removal of pigments during post-excavation surface cleaning, almost 60 % of figurines were painted. New data on the structure and origin of pigments were collected as well as data concerning the nature of the motifs.

auditPapers.title: Line Drawing-Guided Progressive Inpainting for Mural Damage
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Mural image inpainting is far less explored compared to its natural image counterpart and remains largely unsolved. Most existing image-inpainting methods tend to take the target image as the only input and directly repair the damage to generate a visually plausible result. These methods obtain high performance in restoration or completion of some pre-defined objects, e.g., human face, fabric texture, and printed texts, etc., however, are not suitable for repairing murals with varying subjects and large damaged areas. Moreover, due to discrete colors in paints, mural inpainting may suffer from apparent color bias. To this end, in this article, we propose a line drawing guided progressive mural inpainting method. It divides the inpainting process into two steps: structure reconstruction and color correction, implemented by a structure reconstruction network (SRN) and a color correction network (CCN), respectively. In structure reconstruction, SRN utilizes the line drawing as an assistant to achieve large-scale content authenticity and structural stability. In color correction, CCN operates a local color adjustment for missing pixels which reduces the negative effects of color bias and edge jumping. The proposed approach is evaluated against the current state-of-the-art image inpainting methods. Qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in mural image inpainting. The codes and data are available at https://github.com/qinnzou/mural-image-inpainting .

auditPapers.abstract: Mosses are one of the most widespread and dominant biological diseases that damage stone cultural relics. Therefore, to detect the moss coverage rate and growth rate, we constructed a semantic segmentation model for moss segmentation on rock surfaces. Subsequently, the local and texture information extracted by the shallow structure of the convolutional neural network was combined with Swin Transformer to enhance feature diversity. Next, transfer learning was performed on similar large-scale datasets. The effectiveness of the model was validated using a public dataset and the moss dataset. auditPapers.title: The Political Crisis of British Keynesianism, 1973–1983
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In histories of Western political economy in the 1970s–1980s, Keynesianism is conventionally depicted as a victim of neoliberal ascendancy. Building on revisionist scholarship, this article looks beyond neoliberalism to explain the fate of Keynesianism in the transforming political economy of the United Kingdom in its global contexts. It explores a neglected case study: the intense controversies sparked by the Keynesian policy makers Wynne Godley and Francis Cripps. Responding to stagflation and strikes, Godley and Cripps demanded sweeping import controls to forestall mass unemployment and reverse Britain’s ‘decline’. They became celebrity economists, attracting admiration and opprobrium from government ministers and officials, political parties, journalists, and the City. Their arguments raised thorny questions, not just over economic policy, but also over Britain’s domestic statecraft and geopolitical relations after empire, during the Cold War, and inside the European Community. Revisiting these debates underscores the destabilizing impact of de-industrialization. It also reveals that (geo)political calculation determined the fate of Keynesian policy making more directly than neoliberal ideology. Godley and Cripps’s failure therefore illuminates a deeper political dilemma for fin-de-siècle Keynesians across Europe: upon which territorial order could they, and should they, exercise demand management as globalization accelerated? This question continues to shape Western politics in the twenty-first century.

auditPapers.title: Sibling-texts keyword analysis: exploring topic and register keywords
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article introduces a novel method for refining approaches to distant reading by proposing a procedure that categorizes prominent units (keywords) into two types: those pertinent to the topic and those associated with the genre/register of a text. auditPapers.title: Making sugar out of opium: A narco-plantation regime in early modern Southeast Asia
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In the early modern period, while slavery became firmly entrenched in the Atlantic’s sugar economies, Southeast Asia witnessed the rise of distinct plantation regimes. Unlike their Atlantic counterparts, these Asian plantation regimes relied not on enslavement but on addiction — particularly to opium smoking — as a means to control and exploit plantation labour. Existing research has highlighted how such opium-driven regimes, along with Asian ‘coolie’ labour, proliferated globally in the nineteenth century following the abolitionist movement. Yet, their early modern origins in Southeast Asia remain largely unexplored. As a result, a deep plantation labour history outside the Atlantic World is still lacking, and researchers often continue to essentialize early modern plantation capitalism as inherently tied to slavery, while overlooking other, often more insidious, forms of plantation labour control that existed beyond the Atlantic. This article seeks to address this gap by examining the emergence and development of a narco-plantation regime on the sugar frontier of rural Batavia (Jakarta) from the late seventeenth to the early nineteenth centuries.

auditPapers.title: The purposeful workhouse of England’s Old Poor Law
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract It has long been recognized that the English workhouses of the Old Poor Law era (1601-1834) were important precursors to institutions of the modern social services, but what kind of places were they? Integrating recent work that has revealed much about material conditions and the agency of workhouse inmates, this article reassesses work in Old Poor Law workhouses, focusing especially on houses of industry in the county of Norfolk. We find a new perspective on these poor law institutions by recognizing their serious and sustained efforts to keep inmates working productively. Simply put, workhouses worked in the long eighteenth century. To house the infirm, embed work habits in the young, provide temporary shelter and confinement for the able-bodied or unsettled poor, parishes poured time and resources into their local and regional workhouses. In their multifaceted nature, workhouses most resembled not the prisons or hospitals to which they are sometimes compared, but rather the institution of the household-family that was the bedrock of society in the long eighteenth century.

auditPapers.title: Silent Echoes
auditPapers.abstract: The National Park Service subtly employs a colonial ideology in managing history, ecological conservation, and public perception, marginalizing Native American histories, notably observed in wayside signs in Yellowstone Park. Adding a balanced memoryscape that includes Native American histories is crucial for fostering a more inclusive and accurate representation of the past and the park’s ecology.

auditPapers.title: Assessment of the impacts of climate change on a world heritage site in Greece
auditPapers.abstract: Climate change is exacerbating the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, threatening cultural heritage sites. This research focuses on the Dion monument in Pieria, Greece, a significant cultural heritage site historically affected by severe rainfall. Trends in temperature and precipitation over both historical (1971–2000) and future (2021–2100) periods are analyzed through extreme climate indices analysis, using data from the Coordinated Downscaling Experiment for European Domain (EURO CORDEX) under the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 (RCP8.5) emissions scenario. Historical analysis provides a baseline for past climate variability, while future projections reveal emerging cultural heritage risks. This analysis identifies critical climate risks, such as rising temperatures and an increased frequency of intense rainfall events that contribute to flooding. To achieve high-resolution insights into extreme rainfall dynamics, dynamical downscaling is applied using the Weather Research and Forecasting model with the Advanced Research WRF dynamic solver (WRF-ARW). By simulating the 2017 Medicane in Greece, the model demonstrates its efficacy in capturing complex precipitation phenomena at a fine spatial scale (1 km resolution). The integration of extreme climate indices analysis for long-term trend assessment with dynamical downscaling for event-specific simulations provides a comprehensive assessment of climate-induced hazards, facilitating the development of informed conservation and risk management strategies aimed at safeguarding cultural heritage sites under evolving climate conditions.

auditPapers.title: Titanium dioxide-based nanocoating to conservation of rigid PUR foams on cultural heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Several studies have investigated the conservation of polymers, as rigid polyurethane (PUR) foams, in cultural heritage. These materials are highly susceptible to various environmental conditions within museum environment, including hydrolytic, thermal, and photo-oxidative processes, affecting its structural stability and promotes discoloration and/or yellowing. In response to these challenges, this research proposes the development of nanocoatings based on titanium dioxide surface functionalization with different organosilanes to protect artworks from degradation processes caused by the museum environmental conditions. For this, two surface modifiers were employed: (3-aminopropyl)triethoxysilane, that enhances chemical affinity with the foam; and (n-octyl)triethoxysilane, that contributes to increase the hydrophobicity of the samples. The functionalization reactions involved varying ratio of organosilanes, and the spectroscopic and thermal analyzes confirmed the successful modifications. Subsequently, the modified titanium dioxides particles were added to a surface of rigid PUR foam based on polyether and polyester using an ethanol dispersion. The nanocoated samples then were submitted to an artificial aging process in a climatic chamber under controlled temperature, humidity, and exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Comparative evaluations were conducted before and after treatment, employing visual, morphological, spectroscopic, and dynamical mechanical analyzes. The results demonstrated that the different formulations exhibited good surface adhesion to the foam and effectively limited visual degradation while preserving the foam’s properties. These findings serve as a promising starting point for the development of innovative approaches to preserve PUR artistic works.

auditPapers.title: Recolonization dynamics of lichens after biocidal treatments: A limitation in the spreading of water-based solutions beneath thalli as species-specific influencing factor
auditPapers.abstract: Recolonisation by lichens of recently cleaned heritage surfaces is a major issue for conservation, but subtending processes were only partially unveiled, particularly with respect to species with a low potential of propagule dispersal, for which a rapid ingress from external sources is rather unlikely. In this work, recolonisation by lichen species of Megasporaceae and Verrucariaceae was investigated on the marble balustrades of two residences of the Royal House of Savoy (UNESCO-WHS 823bis; NW Italy), cleaned approx. 20 and 12 years ago, respectively. The work aimed to verify if (i) lichen recolonisation started immediately after the conservation interventions and if (ii) this may depend on a scarce effectiveness of devitalization treatments. With regard to this latter point, a possible specific resilience due to a high depth of hyphal penetration within the substrate and/or a limitation in the biocide spread and penetration beneath thalli -due to stone properties and/or a lichen-related effect- were experimentally evaluated. The calculation of growth rates and minimum age of thalli on the balustrades indicated that recolonisation started immediately after the conservation interventions. Blocks of marble from the ancient quarry sites were used to verify the spread and penetration of water-based solutions, mimicking those of quaternary ammonium salt biocides, in presence and absence of Megasporaceae and Verrucariaceae lichens. Lichen cover was shown to influence the capillary water absorption, but the depth reached by the water-based solution (visualised with fluorescein dye) was still higher than that of hyphal penetration structures. On the other hand, some hydrophobic volumes were detected just beneath/below lichen thalli. The applications of water-based biocides do not likely affect lichen structures observed in these rock volumes, which may thus act as viable remnants rapidly starting recolonisation process. Such scenario may thus account for the frequent occurrence of species of Megasporaceae and Verrucariaceae, having a low potential of propagule dispersal, on recently cleaned marble heritage surfaces.

auditPapers.title: A Spatiotemporal Examination of Confederate Monuments in the Former Confederacy
auditPapers.abstract: This article examines Confederate monuments, statues, and plaques in the eleven states of the former Confederacy based on the Southern Poverty Law Center’s “Whose Heritage” data. Focusing on commemorative trends over time, this research seeks to undermine certain assumptions about the history of Confederate monuments in the South. First, there is significant variation across the eleven states of the Confederacy. Second, Confederate monuments continued to be dedicated throughout the 1920s and 1930s in some states, and in others, across the twentieth century. Finally, there are more Confederate monuments standing today than there were in 1980. This research proposes some speculative interpretations of these findings, but its objective is to provide researchers with avenues for further research into divergent trends in monumentation with the goal of crafting interpretations of a varied Southern commemorative landscape.

auditPapers.title: Structural properties of 19th century phonograph discs by photogrammetry and terahertz imaging
auditPapers.abstract: • Photogrammetry has been used to measure 19th century phonograph disc deformations. • THz pulse time-of-flight has been used for measuring disc layer thickness. • Gluing cardboard to deformed discs worsens warping over time. • Durium disc deformation is associated with a thinner Durium layer. • Lacquer discs are produced by spinning liquid resin. This study investigates two types of phonograph discs from the 1930s to 1960s, conserved at the Institute for Sound and Audiovisual Heritage (ICBSA) in Rome, Italy: Durium cardboard discs and instantaneous discs (Decelith and lacquer). Durium discs, composed of synthetic resorcinol-formaldehyde resin on a cardboard substrate, often exhibit bending deformations due to aging and environmental factors, rendering them unreadable on standard turntables. Attempts to mitigate these deformations by gluing a secondary cardboard layer to their backs resulted in further deformations over time. Instantaneous discs, such as Decelith (polyvinyl chloride) and lacquer (metal base coated with cellulose esters), also face preservation challenges like plasticizer migration, cracks, and deformation. Two non-invasive techniques were employed to address these issues. THz time-domain spectroscopy measured layer thickness, and Structure from Motion-Multi-View Stereo (SfM-MVS) photogrammetry analyzed Durium disc deformations, even on featureless, reflective surfaces. Photogrammetry revealed that Durium discs exhibited bending deformations, with deviations from planarity of up to 2 cm, which worsened after the removal of the glued secondary cardboard. Applying a central weight effectively reduced deformation to within 2 mm. THz imaging associated Durium disc deformation with thinner resin layers (0.20–0.25 mm). The Decelith disc were thinner at the edges and thicker near the center (1–1.3 mm), while lacquer disc showed inhomogeneous dielectric layers (0.14–0.28 mm), thicker at the edges most likely due to centrifugal deposition of liquid resin. This study provides valuable insights into material composition, degradation, and historical production techniques, informing conservation strategies critical to preserving phonograph discs and ensuring access to their sound heritage.

auditPapers.title: Editor’s Corner
auditPapers.abstract: This issue features two research articles and two reports from the field. The two articles both consider the meaning of representation and “memoryscapes” (physical spaces that shape understandings of both history and contemporary identity). Thomas Rust’s “Silent Echoes: History, Ecology, and Yellowstone Park’s Colonial Memoryscape Through a Critical Examination of Wayside Signs” examines the underrepresentation of history, and particularly of Indigenous history, in the park’s educational signage. Surveying over 480 wayside signs in Yellowstone Park, Rust found that less than 2 percent examine Native American history (mostly discussing the Ni’imupu/Nez Perce) or the ongoing cultural significance of the area to Indigenous peoples. Rust argues that the “memoryscape” created by the National Park Service’s wayside signage presents a “muted understanding of Indigenous people’s history in the world’s first national park and their role in its ecological systems.” Although former Department of Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna and the first Native American to serve in a cabinet position, made tribal consultation and inclusion of Indigenous voices a goal of her administration, much of that work moved slowly within the department’s large bureaucracy. Notably, under Haaland’s direction, the National Park Service increased its representation of Indigenous stories on its website, perhaps reflecting the relative ease of updating a website when compared to physical signage. Chillingly, however, much of that progress has been reversed—many of the hyperlinks cited in this article were dead or erased by March 2025 when reviewed before the issue was sent to press.Our second research article, Ben Roy’s “A Spatiotemporal Examination of Confederate Monuments in the Former Confederacy,” uses statistical evidence to consider memoryscapes. Roy’s careful use of data produced by the Southern Poverty Law Center demonstrates a wider variation in region and across time in monument-building than studies that have focused on monuments to Confederate leaders such as Robert E. Lee and Jefferson Davis and on the 1890s through the First World War. Roy finds that most Confederate monuments honor the “common soldier” rather than a military or political leader, and that monuments continued to be built across the twentieth century—even well into the twenty-first. Although he acknowledges that more research is necessary before establishing a definite link between the two, Roy intriguingly notes regional variations both between and within states that seem to link increasing cotton production in the 1920s and 1930s with Confederate monument building.The two Reports from the Field explore collaboration between museums and Indigenous communities. Although geographically far apart—one is in New Hampshire, the other in California—both museums offered exhibitions that would counter the colonial legacies of their institutions. To do so, curators at both institutions created a collaborative process that involved Indigenous partners’ participation from the start and foregrounded survivance (survival plus resistance) and the continuing presence of their people and communities. Interestingly, virtual programming created during the COVID-19 lockdown inspired programs that remain an important part of both museums’ outreach.In “Deep History and Continuing Presence: Strawbery Banke Museum’s Abenaki Heritage Initiative,” co-authors Alexandra Martin and Anne Jennison examine Portsmouth, New Hampshire’s Strawbery Banke Museum. The museum is located in a collection of buildings across nearly nine acres of space and has traditionally interpreted several time periods at once but has given little attention to Indigenous people. Jennison, an educator of Abenaki heritage and Martin, an archaeologist at the museum first created educational programming at the museum focused on the Abenaki with Jennison present, demonstrating traditional arts, and later, a permanent exhibition, “People of the Dawnland” (2019). Working with others in their community, they later created an exhibition featuring work created by contemporary artists as well as archaeological objects. The exhibitions evolved into the Abenaki Heritage Initiative, which includes videos created during the pandemic shutdown, a reconstructed wigwam, a teaching garden, and educational programming.Sarah FitzGerald, former curator at the Rancho Los Cerritos in Long Beach, California, worked with local Tongva community members from the start to develop our second Report from the Field, “Tevaaxa’nga (Te-vaah-ha-nga) to Today: Stories of the Tongva People.” Rancho Los Cerritos, constructed in 1844, has generally focused its interpretation on the wealthy landowners who ran the rancho. As the curator, FitzGerald created an exhibition centering the history and presence of the Tongva people. FitzGerald’s report is candid about the challenges she faced, including a lack both of funding and of Indigenous objects in the collection, a situation created in part by the museum’s focus on landowners. Additionally, FitzGerald acknowledges that one of the first challenges she faced was deciding which representatives of which local Indigenous communities to work with. Choosing to work with those who identified as Tongva, she found a positive collaboration and valued that they “ma[d]e decisions about the goals, parameters, structure, and approaches of the exhibition” throughout the process. As with the Strawbery Banke Museum, contemporary objects and oral histories underscored the presence of Indigenous communities in Long Beach and Southern California today. Further, the relationships extended well beyond the completion of the exhibition.

auditPapers.title: Impact of storage conditions on the preservation of taphonomically altered human skeletal remains: Insights from ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and DNA analysis
auditPapers.abstract: • The effects of storage conditions on bone samples are substantial. • Changes in DNA at room temperature were linked to mineral and collagen alterations. • Changes in DNA in the freezer were associated with changes in mineral. • Freezer storage mitigates degradation by minimizing mineral and collagen loss. • Room-temperature accelerates changes, particularly in collagen quality and quantity. The preservation of skeletonised human remains is crucial for successful archaeological and forensic analyses, yet it is influenced by various intrinsic and extrinsic factors. While numerous studies have addressed preservation states and their implications, the effects of storage conditions on taphonomically altered remains have been largely overlooked. This study examines the impact of storage conditions—freezer and room temperature—on bone samples from 21 femur shafts excavated from a World War II mass grave over a period of 1, 2, and 3 years. Changes were analysed using ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and DNA analysis to explore correlations between molecular alterations and DNA preservation. Results demonstrate that storage conditions significantly affect bone preservation. Freezer storage showed minimal degradation, primarily characterised by changes in mineral crystallinity due to the loss of loosely bound ions, while collagen quality improved initially, likely due to molecular reordering. In contrast, room-temperature storage accelerated both mineral and collagen deterioration, with pronounced effects on collagen quantity and quality correlating with increased crystallinity and apatite domain proportions. DNA quality and quantity exhibited similar trends under both conditions, though correlations with mineral and collagen changes varied by storage environment. Over three years, freezer storage mitigated degradation by limiting mineral and collagen loss, whereas room-temperature storage accelerated changes, especially in collagen. These findings highlight the importance of controlled storage conditions, as significant molecular and structural alterations were observed within a relatively short period. This has important implications for the long-term preservation of forensic and archaeological samples, emphasising the need for appropriate storage strategies to ensure sample integrity for future analyses.
