auditPapers.title: People’s Control and the Morality Quest of the Late Soviet Economy
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract “People’s Control” was a centrally controlled institution of economic and social regulation widespread in state socialist countries and, particularly, in the Soviet Union between 1965 and 1991. The ideology underpinning the institution, however, insisted on its vernacular nature and framed its actions in terms of a democratic approach to economic problems. The offices of people’s control proliferated as part of a system that covered the whole country, empowering controllers with an impressive array of rights codified in high-level legislation. Endorsed by the system as moral and honest citizens, controllers inspected factories, farms, grocery shops, and other production and management units to reveal acts of crime, fraud, and low-quality work. Controllers denoted these phenomena as deviations from “normal” economic behavior and explained them in terms of a purported lack of morality. This article examines the place of morality in the late Soviet Union through the lens of political regulation of socio-economic relationships. People’s control, it argues, exposed a particular notion of morality as a range of norms and obligations for revealing and struggling against what the state deemed improper individual economic behavior. It served as one political attempt to mobilize society and tackle growing problems of the planned economy, which came to be described in terms of deviation. In the end, however, the ambit of people’s control remained largely limited to nominal public criticism.

auditPapers.title: Evaluation of archeological heritage exposure to wildfires through simulation techniques. A study case in Galicia (Northwestern Spain)
auditPapers.abstract: • Wildfire simulation tools for analyzing exposure of archeological heritage sites. • Impossibility of fire control for a large portion of the study area. • Distinct exposure levels in typical and atypical meteorological conditions. • Modifications to vegetation structure reduce fire exposure. • Tool for prioritizing fire management in landscapes with abundant heritage sites. Wildfires are one of the most prevalent hazards to which archeological sites are exposed. Wildfire regimes are expected to intensify in coming years in terms of frequency, severity and burn area, leading to an increased number of extreme wildfire events. In this context, it is essential to develop strategies for protecting cultural heritage from fires. These strategies involve exposure assessments which take inventories of cultural assets and evaluate how they would be impacted by fires. This study presents a workflow for analyzing the exposure of archeological assets to wildfires when these assets are dispersed throughout a landscape. In this study, a forested landscape with 692 granite-based cultural-heritage elements (mainly petroglyphs and dolmens) was analyzed. The workflow uses a wildfire simulation software that predicts variables related to wildfire behavior. In the study area, a total of 355 systematically distributed ignition points were simulated for both typical and atypical meteorological conditions. The output values analyzed were the flame length (FL), the rate of spread (ROS) and the fireline intensity (FLI), all variables related to the damage that the cultural elements could incur and to the feasibility of fire control. Outputs were analyzed in the immediate surroundings of archeological elements, deemed the paleointerface area. Additionally, simulations were also performed with virtual modifications to the vegetation structure in the paleointerface areas to determine whether this type of fire management strategy could help reduce the exposure of these elements to wildfires. Different behaviors were encountered in typical and atypical meteorological conditions. In typical conditions, controlling a fire would be nearly impossible in 53 % of the total paleointerface area. In atypical conditions, this was the case for 100 % of the paleointerface area. This reveals the great exposure of these archeological elements to wildfires, even in typical conditions, and indicates that fire management strategies are needed to protect them. The different results obtained also highlight the importance of considering both meteorological situations when performing exposure assessments. The results of the modified-vegetation-structure simulation revealed that fire management strategies focused on decreasing the height of shrubs, in shrub areas, and of the understory, in forested areas, can help to reduce wildfire exposure in both typical and atypical meteorological conditions. Finally, this workflow represents a tool that fulfills essential parts of a fire management plan: exposure analysis, emergency preparedness, and the design of fire reduction strategies. Specifically, this is a tool for prioritizing elements in need of management in landscapes with abundant scattered archeological elements where executing comprehensive preventive actions, although ideal, is not affordable.

auditPapers.title: Digitizing Guardianship Registers in Senegal (1895-1910): Naming as Evidence and Ethical Concern
auditPapers.abstract: Drawing from research on liberated minors, formerly enslaved children whom the colonial state in Senegal entrusted to guardians following their emancipation, this article describes the process of building a database consisting of identifying information about formerly enslaved children in early colonial Senegal based on data originally collected in the early twentieth century, and it uses the database to ask both historical and ethical questions about naming practices and aliases, experiences of unfreedom, and the agency of marginalized African children. Of the 1,324 liberated minors who entered guardianship in Saint-Louis from 1895 to 1910, for example, at least 114 of them took on another name at some point, a fact that raises interesting questions about naming, name changes, and agency. I argue that names contain fragmentary evidence about their bearers' cultural or linguistic background or geographic origin, and, more importantly, that aliases can offer insight into social networks or self-fashioning. Yet reproducing names from colonial inventories in digital history projects could reinscribe oppression and violence and, in some circumstances, could contribute to stigma and shame among descended communities. As such, scholars should include them in databases and other digital history projects, but only if ethical concerns can be addressed and resolved.

auditPapers.title: Descendants and Ethical Considerations when Documenting the Names of Enslaved People in Datasets on the Internet
auditPapers.abstract: This paper examines the ethical implications of public, internet-based history projects that list enslaved people by name. It does so by considering the appropriateness of the ethics statement written by the Principal Investigators at Enslaved: Peoples of the Historical Slave Trade (or Enslaved.org). Enslaved.org directly addresses the urgent call to document the history of people of African descent more fully. Housed at Michigan State University, the project centers the Black experience globally, with most projects to date focused on North America. Contributors to Enslaved.org tell the stories of named enslaved individuals by extracting what is often fragmentary information (names, ages, skills, injuries, African ethnicities, etc.) from a vast range of primary source documentation and by assembling that data into datasets. The Enslaved.org team makes the datasets available, searchable, and understandable on its open-source platform (https://enslaved.org/) and through its peer-reviewed journal, The Journal of Slavery and Data Preservation (https://jsdp.enslaved.org/). The Principal Investigators are committed to identifying by name as many enslaved people as possible and to representing individual and collective experiences in an international, humane, and ethical frame and to working collaboratively with researchers and descendant communities to continually develop and follow practices that respect the lives of enslaved people. The paper considers the appropriateness of the Enslaved.org ethics statement for datasets focused on slavery in a variety of places and concludes with a call for historians to work closely with descendant communities in compiling and publishing data that names enslaved individuals.

auditPapers.title: Naming Slavery in a Digital Public History Project in Mali in the Context of Increased Violence Against Those Who Refuse to Be Called Slaves

auditPapers.title: Naming Names of Enslaved People in the Senegal Liberations Project
auditPapers.abstract: Enslavement is linked to enduring and systemic inequalities, hierarchies, and to the erasures of enslaved people's histories, including their names. Such erasures meant and continue to mean different things to different populations of formerly enslaved people. Descendants of enslaved people, especially in the diaspora, turned to well-established means of genealogical research and new forms of DNA research to trace their ancestors. However, in West Africa and in other parts of the world where obvious racialized markers do not automatically hint at an enslaved ancestor, many former enslaved people would rather forget their enslaved past or that of their ancestors, precisely because descent from enslaved ancestry remains stigmatized. Ethical considerations of conducting digital historical research on slavery and emancipation have been hotly discussed for a number of years, and given the public-facing character of many of these digital projects, the stakes of naming versus anonymity are high. This article suggests a way forward for those people recorded in the Registers of Liberation in colonial Senegal.

auditPapers.title: ChatGPT as speechwriter for the French presidents
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence proposes several large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate a message in response to users’ requests. Such scientific breakthroughs promote new writing assistants but with some fears. The main focus of this study is to analyze the written style of one LLM called ChatGPT by comparing its generated messages with those of the recent French presidents. To achieve this we compare end-of-the-year addresses written by Chirac, Sarkozy, Hollande, and Macron with those automatically produced by ChatGPT. We found that ChatGPT tends to overuse nouns, possessive determiners, and numbers. On the other hand, the generated speeches employ less verbs, pronouns, and adverbs and include, in mean, too standardized sentences. Considering some words, one can observe that ChatGPT tends to overuse “to must” (devoir), ‘to continue’ or the lemma ‘we’ (nous). Moreover, GPT underuses the auxiliary verb ‘to be’ (être), or the modal verbs ‘to will’ (vouloir) or ‘to have to’ (falloir). In addition, when a short text is provided as example to ChatGPT, the machine can generate a short message with a style closed to the original wording. Finally, we reveal that ChatGPT style exposes distinct features compared to real presidential speeches.

auditPapers.title: Patriots and Traitors in Revolutionary Cuba, 1961-1981 By Lillian Guerra
auditPapers.abstract: In Patriots and Traitors in Revolutionary Cuba, 1961-1981, Lillian Guerra extends her long-term project to explain the post-1959 Cuban government’s authoritarian trajectory and to describe the political culture that enabled and emerged from it. auditPapers.title: Determination of baseline groundwater levels for tree conservation in urban historical botanical gardens using applied geophysics
auditPapers.abstract: • Historical botanical gardens are part of cultural heritage. • Root and groundwater interactions are crucial for conserving tree collections. • Their spatial layouts require tailored methodologies for subsurface assessment. • Geophysical techniques digitally map subsurface conditions non-invasively. • 3D visualization of 2D electrical resistivity tomography models. Historical botanical gardens hold a significant place in cultural heritage. They serve as interpretive repositories of past botanical knowledge and practices, showcase plant collections cultivated over centuries, provide space for the emergence of new ecologies, offer numerous human well-being benefits, and supply vital regulating ecosystem services, which are especially important in urban areas. Nowadays, however, plants within urban historical botanical gardens can be at risk due to urban development. Therefore, it is crucial to achieve a comprehensive understanding of these spaces to help implement protective measures and support proper urban planning of the surrounding areas. This study investigates the subsurface of the Botanical Garden of Lisbon (JBL), which is subject to nearby construction works that may alter groundwater flow and depth. We employed a methodology designed for minimal on-site disturbance and high adaptability to the spatial constraints typical of these spaces. Two non-invasive applied geophysical techniques were used: ground-penetrating radar (GPR) and electrical resistivity tomography (ERT). Our main objectives were: (1) to assess groundwater levels in the construction area and establish the piezometric surface, and (2) to determine if the tree-root zones reach the saturated zone, establish a groundwater baseline, and suggest protective measures. The establishment of the piezometric surface and the delimitation of the tree-root zone, extending up to 3.0 m in depth, revealed that tree-root zones can reach groundwater levels. This finding underscores the critical need for vigilant monitoring and management of groundwater levels during excavation activities, as decreased lateral groundwater contributions from the potential excavation site can adversely affect groundwater levels in the plant beds. These findings and methodology can be applied to urban botanical gardens worldwide, as many of these gardens face similar challenges due to urbanization and environmental changes.

auditPapers.title: The Refugee Political in the Age of Imperial Crisis, Decolonization, and Cold War, 1930s–1950s
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract The three decades spanning the 1930s, '40s, and '50s witnessed the birth of the modern global state system, characterized by a protracted and tortuous transition from a world of empires to a world of nation-states. However, as old empires dissolved, new post-imperial states continued older colonial-origin forms of ethno-religious discrimination and ruling-class dominance, or invented novel hierarchies. Hence, this epoch was marked by catastrophic outbursts of racial violence, sectarian war, and genocide. If majoritarian nation-states were the privileged offspring of this transformation, then refugees were the unwanted issue. The national citizen and the refugee were co-created. Against their forced displacement and subalternization, refugees re-politicized their selves. We define this as ‘the refugee political’: refugees constructing themselves as political beings and building wide-ranging alliances – with churches, politicians, and entrepreneurs; with peasants, industrial workers, and feminists. They became ‘subaltern internationalists’, linking the Dachen Islands to the United States, and maritime Southeast Asia to India; connecting central European Jews to Australian women, or impoverished Indians to Soviet and Chinese communists. They created new forms of ‘refugee polis’ – political communities which were simultaneously local and daringly transnational.

auditPapers.title: Citizenship, Expropriation, and Redress: ‘Migrating Objects’ and the Case of Holocaust Victims from Austria
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Forced displacement brings with it the loss of property, belonging, and identity. Objects encode the nexus between citizenship, property, and sense of belonging/emotional attachment. The article explores the connection between citizenship and property and thereby highlights the agency of victims and their refugee’s polis. This case-study focuses on Jewish Austrian citizens who fled from Austria to Shanghai during the Nazi occupation era, expelled by the Nuremberg racial laws. During this racial persecution, they lost their citizenship and subsequently all their assets, with most of their belongings stored at the port of Trieste. Surprisingly, even after the end of the Second World War and Nazi occupation, it proved very difficult for Jews to regain their citizenship and property, for reasons highlighted in this article. The post-war nation-state could not deliver justice to actors whose economic, social, and cultural lives had been shaped through forced migration. Following scandals like the ‘Woman in Gold’ dispute concerning the return of a painting by Klimt in 2006, legal transformation in the fields of monetary compensation and citizenship laws was only brought about by resolutely transnational political-legal activism.

auditPapers.title: La fiesta de los negros: Una historia del antiguo carnaval de Buenos Aires y su legado en la cultura popular By Ezequiel Adamovsky
auditPapers.abstract: Ezequiel Adamovsky’s La fiesta de los negros is a welcome addition to the flourishing literature on race in Argentina. Set in the city of Buenos Aires and drawing extensively on its rich periodical literature and visual archives, the book demonstrates how public festivities surrounding pre-Lenten Carnival in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries served “to process the acute class, gender, and ethno-racial tensions” accompanying the formation of modern Argentina, especially in the wake of mass European immigration. Carnival’s playful irreverence provided a space for Porteños (residents of the capital) of various backgrounds to bridge differences: men dressing as women, the rich as paupers, city-dwellers as rural gauchos, and whites as Indigenous or Black people. With its leveling impulses, the author argues, Carnival slowly eroded social boundaries and helped “forge a sense of belonging” that endured beyond the festivities. La fiesta de los negros focuses on the performances of Blackness that became a central feature of Carnival comparsas (troupes) by the late nineteenth century. Racial masquerade began in the mid-1860s with upper-class comparsas, whose members blackened their faces with burnt cork or makeup and sang songs in an Africanized form of Spanish with allusions to slavery (but whose costumes and musical styles remained European). The “mask of Blackness” was quickly adopted and modified by working-class comparsas that played stylized forms of candombe, an Afro-Argentine music and dance, and dressed in styles that evoked Africa or the slave past. These groups, which exploded in popularity in the 1880s and early 1890s, were typically comprised of either whites or Afro-Porteños, but the author suggests many were interracial. Building on the literature about what scholars have called “blackface” comparsas, but paying closer attention to the meanings of racial impersonation in these working-class troupes, Adamovsky offers a polemical argument: in Carnival’s spirit of unity and leveling, revelers used the “mask of Blackness” heretically (to reject dominant strictures of propriety or masculinity) and in an antiracist way (to affirm Black peoples and cultures, subvert racial hierarchy, or invoke interracial love).

auditPapers.title: Structural assessment of the medieval city wall of Seville (Spain) using low-cost accelerometers
auditPapers.abstract: • Monitoring can be crucial in assessing the vulnerability of heritage buildings. • To design an intervention, it is crucial to establish the structural performance. • Periodical ambient vibration tests and OMA allows heritage risk assessment. • Vibration-based tests enable comprehensive dynamic characterisation of heritage. The remains of fortifications are commonly found embedded in the contemporary urban fabric of historic cities. Due to their typological nature, these heritage assets are usually elements of great size and impact on the urban landscape. Their location within cities exposes them to very specific risks, such as pollution, vibration, biodegradation, and anthropic factors, which must be taken into account for the proper conservation and maintenance of such remains. The case of the medieval wall of Seville (Spain), built on rammed earth, shows specific factors of vulnerability, degradation, and erosion which prompt the need for non-destructive techniques (NDT). In the present research, vibration-based inspection is used and, specifically, when subjected to ambient vibrations. The collection of accelerations, which covered a period of nine months, was conducted in different parts of the structure under study by using mainly high-resolution accelerographs. These data allowed to perform an exhaustive dynamic characterisation of this defensive structure. Among other findings, it was determined that the filling of cracks and voids in the walls increased the fundamental frequency by about 2 %. In addition, no serious damage to the structure was found. Knowledge of the historic buildings' condition is essential in order to determine the most appropriate intervention. To this end, a protocol for the global structural diagnosis of these buildings has been proposed. It is based on the recording of accelerations with low-cost accelerographs. Besides being an inexpensive protocol, it allows a quick decision making, since the dynamic characterization of the structure is performed by means of the fast Fourier transform. Basically, the designed protocol is based on the variation of the fundamental frequency of the structure between two time instants. These values are used for the calculation of a damage index. By means of an exhaustive review of conventional masonry buildings tested in the laboratory, the damage index has been correlated with the state of the structure prior to collapse. Specifically, this threshold, which ranges from DS4 to DS5 according to the criteria of the European Macroseismic Scale 1998 (EMS-98), provides a valuable reference point for the structural assessment of historical box-shaped constructions with conventional masonry load-bearing walls. This simplified procedure for structural diagnosis was applied in its initial phase at the White Tower. It was found that this protocol is able to identify the fundamental frequency of the structure with an error of <0.65 % in comparison to the results obtained through operational modal analysis methods.

auditPapers.title: Digital Media Metaphors: A Critical Introduction. Johan Farkas and Marcus Maloney (eds)
auditPapers.abstract: In the realm of cognitive linguistics, the seminal work, Metaphors We Live By by Lakoff and Johnson (1980), has catalyzed a transformative shift in understanding how metaphors shape human cognition and social interaction. Four decades hence, the digital age has introduced novel complexities, rendering the critical examination of digital media metaphors both timely and imperative. Digital Media Metaphors: A Critical Introduction, edited by Farkas and Maloney (2024), emerges as a pivotal contribution to the ongoing study of how metaphors function in digital media contexts. This volume, a collaborative effort by leading scholars in media studies and digital sociology, dissects the multifaceted role of metaphors in digital technologies, illuminating their power and limitations. As human existence becomes increasingly mediated through digital infrastructures, the metaphors we employ—such as “cloud,” “platform,” “filter bubble,” and “rabbit hole”—are crucial for our understanding of technology and its socio-political ramifications. Digital Media Metaphors is meticulously structured into three thematic parts with an introduction, each addressing a distinct dimension of digital media: infrastructure, content, and users. This tripartite structure facilitates a comprehensive understanding of how metaphors permeate our conceptualization of digital technologies.

auditPapers.title: Technological Unemployment in the British Industrial Revolution: The Destruction of Hand-Spinning
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article analyses the elimination of hand-spinning in Britain during the Industrial Revolution and shows that it produced large-scale technological unemployment. First, it uses new empirical evidence and sources to estimate spinning employment before the innovations of the 1760s and 1770s. The estimates show that spinning employed 8 per cent of the population by about 1770. Next, the article systematically analyses the course, extent and locations of technological unemployment produced by mechanization using more than 200 detailed qualitative sources. Evidence from more than 2,000 observations by contemporary social commentators, county agricultural surveys and the 1834 Poor Law Commission’s Rural and Town Queries shows the breadth and duration of unemployment following mechanization. The destruction of hand-spinning began to impact women and households in the 1780s, and the effects persisted until at least the mid 1830s. This technological shock likely had an unequal effect on family incomes that resulted from variation in household composition and local labour market conditions. The findings demonstrate that unemployment must be incorporated into analysis of the impacts of industrialization on living standards and they highlight the potential long-run costs of job-replacing technology.

auditPapers.title: Beyond the surface: stylometric analysis of GPT-4o’s capacity for literary style imitation
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This study aims to explore the ability of GPT-4o to imitate the literary style of renowned authors. Ernest Hemingway and Mary Shelley were selected due to their contrasting literary styles and their overall impact on world literature. Using three distinct prompting strategies—zero-shot generation, zero-shot imitation, and in-context learning—we generated forty-five stylistic imitations and analyzed them alongside the authors’ original texts. To ensure thematic consistency, we constrained the generated texts to shared narrative themes derived from the authors’ works. We used a distance-based approach to authorship attribution using the 1,000 most frequent words and cosine distance to explore how the large language model’s imitations were positioned in the multidimensional authorship space. Moreover, we exploited a random forest classifier and repeated the authorship attribution task to analyze the authorship distinctiveness of the GPT imitations further. We used a combination of Textual Complexity and Readability, Author Multilevel N-gram Profiles, Word Embeddings, and Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count features. t-SNE visualizations further evaluated the stylistic alignment between original and GPT-generated texts. The findings reveal that while GPT-4o captures some surface-level stylistic elements of the authors, it struggles to fully replicate the depth and uniqueness of their stylometric signatures. Imitations generated via in-context learning showed improved alignment with the original authors but still exhibited significant overlap with generic GPT outputs.

auditPapers.title: Lordship in the Later Middle Ages: A Round Table Discussion
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Over the last few years, a number of articles have featured in Past and Present on the subject of late medieval lordship. Three were accepted within a four-month period between July and October 2023 (Christian D. Liddy, ‘The Making of Towns, the Making of Polities’; Tristan W. Sharp, ‘Seigneurial Predation in the Late Medieval Feud’; Frederik Buylaert, Thijs Lambrecht, Klaas Van Gelder, and Kaat Cappelle, ‘The Political Economy of Seigneurial Lordship in Flanders’). The three pieces approached the subject in quite different ways, and with very different findings; at the same time, they were clearly talking about the same thing, and all were concerned with assessing more closely what lords took from, and had to offer to, local societies, and their social and/or economic impact. This seemed a good opportunity to hold a workshop to place the articles in conversation with each other in order to identify commonalities, reflect on the wider field, and prompt more general questions. The round table took place on 17 June 2024 at King’s College London. The version presented here is a revised and edited transcript, but aiming to retain the feel of the original oral conversation. A brief opening section introduces the articles to give context to the discussion.

auditPapers.title: Lactic acid-based compounds as green alternative solvents for cultural heritage: Application on canvas painting restoration
auditPapers.abstract: • Lactic acid solvents as alternative and biobased green solvents for canvas restoration. • Lactic acid dioxolanes application. • Alternative and user-friendly strategy for historical artifacts cleaning. In the restoration of canvas paintings, solvent mixtures derived from non-renewable sources are commonly employed (e.g. acetone, ethanol, and isooctane), which not only contribute to pollution but also pose potential health-risks to the operators. This research aims to introduce alternative biobased and eco-friendly solvents as possible replacements for common solvents used in artifact restoration. 5-methyl-1,3-dioxolane-4-one (LA-H,H), 2,2,5-trimethyl-1,3-dioxolane-4-one (LA-Me,Me), ethyl lactate (EL), and 2-ethylhexyl pelargonate (ARGO) were selected as biobased solvents candidates. They can be produced from biomass-derived synthons, including lactic acid (LA), which is obtained by carbohydrate fermentation, and pelargonic acid (PA), which is obtained by the oxidative cleavage of oleic acid and high-oleic vegetable oils. To rationalize their solvent properties, their Hansen parameters were used (dispersion δ d , polarity δ p , hydrogen-bonding δ hb ), enabling their placement within the Teas Triangle. Lactic acid-derived solvents, LA-H,H and LA-Me,Me, were prepared in multigram at lab-scale, and characterized using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Their solvent abilities were tested by their application to ad-hoc prepared specimens with different film-forming substances. These tests were performed with both fresh and artificially-aged samples. Their evaporation behavior was studied through thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA) while their ready biodegradability was investigated according to OECD guideline 301F as a key property influencing environmental impact. These solvent mixtures were then employed for the removal of oxidized terpenoid varnish from a 17 th -century canvas painting, demonstrating their potential as green alternatives for restoration practices.

auditPapers.title: From Incarceration to Repatriation: German Prisoners of War in the Soviet Union By Susan Grunewald
auditPapers.abstract: This book traces the path of German prisoners of war (POWs) from their capture by the Soviets to their repatriation. It is written at the intersection of social and political history. It focuses on the state policies toward German POWs and their influence on post-war Europe. POWs from other nationalities are not discussed, nor is the interned German civilian population in the USSR or inmates of Soviet special camps in Germany. The study utilizes an impressively wide array of primary sources from the USSR, GDR, and FRG, primarily diverse departmental documentation from numerous archives. Data from central structures is effectively complemented by references to local materials from the camp in the Russian city of Ulyanovsk. Public moods are explored through newspaper analysis. The author shares findings from hard-to-access Russian archives (such as the Ministry of Foreign Affairs) and recently declassified funds (op. 6 of the repatriation department). At the same time, many documents from the GUPVI, also used by author, are well-known to historians.

auditPapers.title: Emerging Technologies in Smart Libraries for Visually Impaired People: Challenges and Design Considerations
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Emerging technologies are transforming cultural spaces in a variety of ways, presenting opportunities and challenges. Autonomous robots, eXtended Reality, AI, Digital Twins, and Internet of Things are only a few examples of such technologies, with accessibility and inclusivity of people to these technologies to be considered key challenges. In general, the use of emerging technologies in cultural spaces presents exciting opportunities for enhancing visitors’ experience and engaging new participants. However, it is important to also consider the inclusion ability of people with special needs and to ensure that these emerging technologies are used in an accessible-to-all and inclusive way. The aim of this article is to review the state-of-the-art and current trends in approaches that use emerging technologies in the domain of smart libraries designed to include visually impaired people in a common innovative way for the whole community of visitors, discuss open issues and challenges identified in such a cultural environment/case, and propose a novel approach based on specific design considerations of the specific domain.

auditPapers.title: Reckoning and Economic Life in Late Medieval England
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article explores the practice of ‘reckoning’, a means of reciprocal accounting that becomes prominent in late-medieval England. Despite its critical importance to everyday exchange in this period, the practice has not received much attention from historians. The article argues that reckoning should be understood as a kind of economic infrastructure, one that performed some of the same functions as formal markets; and that as a concept, it was critical to the way that contemporaries delineated different forms of economic exchange. I proceed by tracing the emergence of reckoning from a convergence of institutional accounting, increasing technical literacy, and the proliferation of written accounts from the thirteenth century onwards. I go on to argue that as a tool of economic exchange, reckoning was particularly well-suited to the straitened economic conditions of the fifteenth century, in particular the shortage of coin, the retrenchment of formal markets, and the pervasive use of credit. I then examine three case studies in which reckoning went ‘wrong’, in order to explore the ideals of exchange relations on which it drew. In conclusion, I suggest that reckoning can help us to frame some of the broader transformations in economic culture in post-plague England.

auditPapers.title: Black Elders: The Meaning of Age in American Slavery and Freedom By Frederick C. Knight
auditPapers.abstract: In this engaging and timely study, Frederick C. Knight explores the meanings of old age, and the lived experiences of Black elders, in American slavery and freedom. It is, in some senses, an expansive study, taking readers from coastal West and West Central Africa in the age of the Atlantic slave trade, through antebellum slavery to Reconstruction and post-emancipation struggles in the U.S. But it is also a tightly focused one. Chapter one has a wide-ranging treatment of West and West Central Africa, but other chapters tend to prioritize a particular region, with Virginia and North Carolina particularly well represented in the sections on antebellum slavery (chapters two and three); others revolve around or return to select case studies, as with the focus on Philadelphia’s free Black communities when examining post-emancipation developments (chapters four and five). More detail on the analytical case for prioritizing certain regions or particular institutions would have been helpful, but the book is nonetheless effective in establishing how age, and particularly old age, “was a point of power, labor mobilization, ideological struggle, transformation, and contestation in American slavery and emancipation” (5). The book makes important contributions on age and generational power dynamics within West and West Central African polities, and Knight considers how age affected the wider structures of, and experiences in, Atlantic and colonial slavery. There are nuanced observations about the extractive violence of antebellum enslavers and the multi-generational support networks enslaved people crafted to navigate this hostile environment, and Knight provides original insight into the complex politics of emancipation and Reconstruction through the lens of age and generation.

auditPapers.title: Andrew Burstein. Longing for Connection: Entangled Memories and Emotional Loss in Early America.
auditPapers.abstract: Andrew Burstein’s book Longing for Connection: Entangled Memories and Emotional Loss in Early America seeks to understand the emotional lives of people from the founding era of the United States through the Civil War. As Burstein points out, ascertaining the innermost thoughts and feelings of people in the past is not an easy or straightforward task. In the final chapter, he asks, “Do we get these people yet?” and answers his own question, “Yes and no,” arguing that we often fall prey to the temptation of imposing today’s values on a society that was materially and intellectually different from our own (242). Nevertheless, Burstein proposes, one way to approach the challenge is to examine literary influences and cultural references that acted as touchstones for how people in early America translated emotions into words and derived meaning from the world around them. Burstein’s study centers on the core theme of “longing”—striving for understanding in an era that was characterized by optimistic hopes for the future alongside the disruptions of war, political upheavals, and personal tragedies.

auditPapers.title: Strangers Within: the Rise and Fall of the New Christian Trading Elite By Francisco Bethencourt
auditPapers.abstract: Strangers Within is a history of New Christians—Jewish converts to Christianity and their Christianized descendants, who formed a vigorous global economic network from the late fourteenth to the eighteenth centuries. The work’s stated goal is to explain how an ethnic elite of New Christian merchants, most of them of Judeo-Portuguese origin (including New Christians-turned-Jews in the Iberian diaspora), or merely allied with persons of that extraction, came to play “a pivotal role in intercontinental trade” in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and then declined and virtually vanished toward the end of the eighteenth (1). Notably, the author links his explanation to a wide-ranging treatment of questions of “identity, religious allegiance, economic opportunities, political negotiation, and cultural innovation” (ibid.). The point is that New Christians experienced these questions in highly diverse ways, yet both epitomized aspects of early modern history—for example, incipient globalization, rational-capitalistic forms of exchange, as well as skepticism—and were part and parcel of the particular saga of the New Christian ethnic group, whose members, irrespective of their religious allegiances, bore a stubborn stigma by virtue of their Jewish origins. Ambitious and monumental, the book thus brings together, perhaps for the first time in the English language, the economic history of the New Christian group and the group’s social and cultural history. The apparatus is correspondingly extensive, up-to-date, and sterling. The fact that it is missing works in Hebrew is not definitive.

auditPapers.title: The Making of Dissidents: Hungary’s Democratic Opposition and Its Western Friends, 1973-1998 By Victoria Harms
auditPapers.abstract: In October of 1985, representatives of Hungary’s democratic opposition, the so-called dissidents, gathered in a crowded Budapest apartment overlooking the Danube to meet with their Western supporters. This “counter-forum” was scheduled to coincide with an official meeting of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, part of the review process established by the 1975 Helsinki Accords. Among the more than 150 people who participated in the unofficial gathering were Hungarian dissidents like János Kis, Sándor Csoóri, and György Konrád; literary intellectuals like Susan Sontag, Timothy Garton Ash, Hans Magnus Enzensberger; and human rights activists like Aryeh Neier, Gerald Nagler, and Jeri Laber. The Alternative Forum, as it came to be known, captured a paradox of dissident life in Hungary: as Laber put it, “We had been forbidden to meet and we were meeting” (207). Victoria Harms’ revelatory book, The Making of Dissidents: Hungary’s Democratic Opposition and Its Western Friends, 1973-1998, shows how the “golden age” of Hungary’s democratic opposition was made possible by a dense network of personal and institutional connections across Cold War blocs. Her book is not only a major contribution to the transnational history of East Central European dissent, but also to the study of Cold War liberalism on both sides of the Iron Curtain. In addition to spending time in Budapest, New York, and Berlin, the reader travels to Paris, Vienna, and Dubrovnik. To accomplish this impressive range, Harms has combed archives in seven countries and conducted oral histories with dozens of participants in this East-West oppositional network.

auditPapers.title: Sarah Albiez-Wieck. Taxing Difference in Peru and New Spain (16th–19th Century): Negotiating Social Differences and Belonging.
auditPapers.abstract: When did ethnicity emerge as an important social categorization in Spanish America? This is the question that Sarah Albiez-Wieck asked herself when she began the research for her book Taxing the Difference in Peru and New Spain. However, while ethnicity as a social categorization remained important to her study, the author notes that as the work developed, the central questions of the book evolved to focus on fiscal categorizations in the viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru. Thus, the main theme of the book is the characteristics, limits, and negotiations of these fiscal categories among both the categorized and the categorizers. However, we must not forget that fiscal analysis also makes visible social categorizations intimately linked to the fiscal status of the individual. To analyze this issue, the author rightly replaces the concept of ethnicity with a much more pertinent one, calidad. For this purpose, Albiez-Wieck takes as the basis for her study the definition of calidad proposed by David Greeve, which includes elements such as self-construction and ascription, as well as external ascriptions that depended on elements such as ancestry, public reputation, community membership, and legal categorization or religion.

auditPapers.title: The Brancacci Chapel from the Quattrocento to the semantic web: An ontology-assisted case study of cultural data management and site reconstruction
auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: This study proposes an ontological model for cultural heterogeneous data and cultural site reconstructions. It is based on the concept of interpretative unit , which extends the semantics of stratigraphic units also to non-archaeological contexts. Indeed, after a state of the art overview of the development methodology and the description of the most relevant entities, a first test case is proposed. auditPapers.title: Jane Burbank and Frederick Cooper. Post-Imperial Possibilities: Eurasia, Eurafrica, and Afroasia.
auditPapers.abstract: World War I led to the collapse of Europe’s land-based empires as they failed the test of mass mobilization and mass politics. Even the Bolsheviks, who came to power in the former Russian Empire, reconfigured the imperial domain into a socialist federation of nationally defined republics. While the overseas empires persisted, they faced growing anti-imperial movements. The nation-state emerged as the dominant political form. (Though it could rarely be fully realized without mass violence and, ultimately, genocide.) However, many contemporaries envisioned alternative post-imperial futures. In Post-Imperial Possibilities: Eurasia, Eurafrica, and Afroasia, Jane Burbank and Frederick Cooper, prominent scholars of Russian and African history, highlight three such projects and argue that the ideas of “Eurasia, Eurafrica, and Afroasia … addressed the critical political issue of their times—the power of the world’s great empires and the uncertainty of how to escape or supersede them” (14). Their exploration engages with the ideas of solidarity, affinity, and sovereignty beyond the confines of the nation-state.

auditPapers.title: Radoslav Yordanov. Our Comrades in Havana: Cuba, the Soviet Union, and Eastern Europe, 1959–1991.
auditPapers.abstract: In Our Comrades in Havana: Cuba, the Soviet Union, and Eastern Europe, 1959–1991, Radoslav Yordanov takes the reader through four decades of relations between Cuba and the Eastern bloc, focusing on how Havana’s emergence into the socialist world created myriad frictions between itself and the Eastern European regimes that, like Cuba, were heavily dependent on the Soviet Union. In a largely chronological narrative, Our Comrades in Havana uses an impressively multinational range of archives (Albania, Bulgaria, Cuba, Czech Republic, Germany, Dominican Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Russia, Serbia, United Kingdom, and United States) to explore the ups and downs of Cuba’s relations with its Eastern European partners. Yordanov brings these sources into dialogue with recent scholarship on the global Cold War and “East-South” relations between the Soviet Union and postcolonial states to make a compelling case that relations between Havana and its Eastern European comrades swung from one extreme to the other as Cuban visions of internationalism and populism clashed with ideas of peaceful coexistence and scientific socialism.

auditPapers.title: Automatic characterization of the border deterioration in Byzantine seals
auditPapers.journal: Digital Applications in Archaeology and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Byzantine seals were attached to official documents to authenticate the sender, thus enclosing a valuable part of the Byzantine Empire’s history. With the aim to provide computational models to help historians in the seal interpretation, this paper proposes a method to automatically determine the level of deterioration of the seal borders from their photographs, i.e., a non-destructive inspection. The method consists of a segmentation step based on Morphological Geodesic Active Contours, a feature extraction step, and a classification step that groups the seals into four border deterioration categories. Our best results reached 0.80 in accuracy, 0.73 in Cohen’s Kappa statistics score, and 0.80 in the macro F1 score. • Classifying Byzantine seals by their border damage is useful since most are broken. • Byzantine seal characteristics indicating border deterioration level are analyzed. • The first border deterioration-based automated Byzantine seal classification. • A method based on segmentation, feature extraction, and classification is proposed. • Accurate classification results are obtained (accuracy = 0.80).

auditPapers.title: Tyler C. Kirk. After the Gulag: A History of Memory in Russia’s Far North.
auditPapers.abstract: When returnees started emerging from the Gulag in the mid-1950s, they barely spoke of their camp experience. Then, after Khrushchev broke their silence with his Secret Speech, gradually a multitude of stories were revealed by those who were not afraid to speak. The headiness of this anti-Stalin period was short-lived and ended with the 1964 ouster of Khrushchev. At once, the memory of the camps and the victimizations before, during, and after disappeared from the public space. For the next twenty-five years, while returnees navigated their second-class citizenship, they also negotiated the status of being a victim, then a celebrated survivor, then a marginalized, silenced victim once again. Under Gorbachev, however, their fate was to change. This era ushered in an astonishing number of testimonies of the repressed. In After the Gulag: A History of Memory in Russia’s Far North, Tyler C. Kirk chronicles narratives from the province as he examines the development of local memory projects that emerged from the “lost era” (viii) of civil society organizations, such as Memorial. Kirk’s important work is based on memoirs, memoir-letters to Memorial, interviews, local newspapers, and research at sites where the memory of the Gulag was directly connected to the landscape by returnees who had remained in the region.

auditPapers.title: Vernacular Imaginaries of the Southern Seas
auditPapers.abstract: Few people native to the contemporary nation-states that make up the region known in English today as “Southeast Asia” would call themselves “Southeast Asians.”1 The process by which “Southeast Asia” became a distinct region in the international system, separate from the broader East Asian region of which it is a part, as well as a separate disciplinary specialization in academia, has long been understood to be one rooted in external strategic interests dating roughly from the 1940s. Through the upheavals of mid-twentieth-century wars, the region was ascribed a common political and economic character exogenously and militarily. The establishment of the Allied South East Asia Command in 1943 defined it negatively, as a space from which Japan should be expelled: a regionalizing salvo against Japan’s positive identification of a Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere over which Japan should preside. After the defeat of Japan and the creation of an Anglo-American hegemonic compact over the wider East Asian region, it came to be understood variously as a space of concentrated political revolt against Western rule, of underdevelopment, of political instability, and of susceptibility to communism. Eventually, with the establishment of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 1967, it assumed its fullest geopolitical form as an anticommunist space ranged specifically against, and in some ways defined in opposition to, China, despite the long histories of connectivity that have shaped their interactions.2 A measure of its ideological character is that many countries we regard as “Southeast Asian” today—Burma, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos—were incorporated into ASEAN only at the end of the twentieth century, their successful divestiture of communist influence a condition of entry. Capital, particularly American capital, further defined the boundaries of the region as one requiring a particular expertise. In the years after the defeat of Japan, philanthropic foundations from Rockefeller to Carnegie poured funding into articulating the disciplinary boundaries of this space, establishing departments of “Southeast Asian studies” at Yale in 1947 and Cornell in 1950, among others. Meanwhile, the almost contemporaneous transition in Japanese- and Chinese-language descriptions of the region from the older nomenclature (shared in Sinitic script) of Nanyō and Nanyang (南洋) toward direct translations of the English term “Southeast Asia” (Tōnan Ajia and Dongnanya 東南亞, lit. “East-South Asia”), in common use from the mid-1950s, suggests a hegemonic convergence of epistemologies.3 What differentiated the earlier Sinitic names from “Southeast Asia” was, firstly, their maritime orientation and, secondly, their understanding of a region fundamentally connected to others. Where the English term “Southeast Asia” names a portion of the territorial continent of “Asia,” Nanyō or Nanyang—literally “the Southern Ocean”—retained the sense of this space as fundamentally connected by water. Since as early as the period of the Eastern Han (25–220 CE), the Chinese word Nanhai (南海, lit. “South Sea”) has named a range of waters around the southern and eastern Chinese seaboards. Initially, Chinese merchants played a much smaller role in these waters than those Persian and Arab sojourners who boarded seafaring dhows in Basra, braved the Indian Ocean, and used the Malacca Straits as a fulcrum to reach the great emporia of Guangzhou. To Arab geographers of the eleventh century, the region stretching from the coasts of southern India to the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, the Gulf of Thailand, and the seas around Vietnam was known as the “Sea of Malayu”; the evidence points, as Leonard Andaya has shown, to the sea’s naming for a group of people known to both medieval Arabs and Chinese as the orang Malayu.4 Later Arabic speakers, Persian travelers, and Safavid diplomatic missions came to speak of this same space instead as bilād al-jāwā, the lands of the Jāwā people, and as Zīrbādāt, the lands below the winds—the contrapuntal rhythms of the monsoons that shaped movement across these waters. This was likely a phrase that traveled into Persian from Malay (negeri di bawah angin). As Sultan Iskandar Muda of Aceh (r. 1607–36) described himself in a letter to King James I of England in 1612: “I am the lord in power here below the winds [Zīrbādāt] who holds the throne of Aceh and Samudra and all the countries adjacent.”5 Only from the early 1000s did Chinese junks begin to join Arab dhows in these waters in significant numbers.6 Later Song, Ming, and Qing geographers sought to make further distinctions, following the logic of trade routes from China’s southern coast. One route passed through the place named Xiyang (西洋), or Western Ocean. This Western Ocean passage was one of great antiquity dating back to the Tang dynasty, known to Chinese and Indian merchant traders who plied trade in small vessels that cleaved nervously to the coast, edging from Guangzhou to Hainan and thenceforth to the Champa coast and the southern tip of today’s Vietnam. A second route wended eastward through the Dongyang (東洋), or Eastern Sea. This was a more recent passage. Emerging during the Song dynasty and prospering during the Yuan, it brought waves of enterprising Hokkien merchants who cast out from Quanzhou and other sea-facing ports of Fujian province, to Taiwan and the Philippines, and southward to the Celebes Sea and the Moluccas. Ming emperors knew this space as Hainan zhuguo (海南諸國) (various states of the south seas), lands of southern barbarians (nanman 南蠻) that lay “outside civilization” (huawai 化外) and indeed far beyond the four seas (sihai zhi wai 四海之外) that surrounded the Middle Kingdom. The existence of the Selden Map (Fig. 1), a maritime commercial navigation chart dating back to the late Ming era and almost certainly produced in Quanzhou, shows that at least some at the time sought to center these surrounding seas, rather than the “Middle Kingdom” itself.7 During the Qing era, other names emerged, circling cautiously around the encroachment of Europeans into China’s maritime frontiers. The Hakka mariner Xie Qinggao, writing in 1820 on the cusp of the Opium Wars, divided Qing China’s known waters into the Southwest Sea (西南海), comprising the waters of the Malay Peninsula, mainland Southeast Asia, and the Indian coast; the South Sea (南海), now understood to comprise just Sumatra and Java to Celebes; and the Northwest Sea (西北海), some distant place beyond Sumatra from which Westerners had come to nip at China’s maritime frontiers.8 It was a precocious attempt to begin to fit the growing European presence in Asia into the knowledge cartographies of the dynasty, a task that would be carried forward with greater scholarly industry and rigor by the Hunanese jinshi scholar of statecraft, Wei Yuan.9 Then there was the name Nanyang (南洋), which came into more frequent use and eventually replaced Nanhai over the course of the Ming and Qing dynasties. Originally an administrative category alongside its sister name Beiyang (北洋) for the Northern Ocean—including the northeastern coasts of Hebei, Liaoning, and Shandong—it signaled in the most general way the provinces, regions, and seas lying to the south of the Yangtze River, and, crucially, included the terrestrial portions of southern China’s Fujian, Guangdong, and Guangxi provinces, along with the nebulous lands and waters beyond it.10 It was only over the course of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries that the name Nanyang was honed into ever greater specificity, given a second life as the Chinese name for an aspirational quasi-imperial project that emerged in direct competition with Meiji-Taishō Japan, as both gazed southward at new extractive prospects in a “Nanyang” now dominated by European commercial interests. By the middle of the twentieth century, Nanyang—morphing gradually into Dongnanya—had come to correspond almost exactly to the limited Anglophone regional construct we now call Southeast Asia, its older oceanic qualities reduced to a penumbra around a space now understood as primarily terrestrial, its implied historical relationships to China and Japan severed by the guillotines of area studies. The Selden Map, a late Ming watercolor map of East Asia dating roughly to the 1620s, depicting a conception of the region that privileges the sea, and includes China, Korea, Japan, Borneo, the Philippines, the Indonesian archipelago, and the Malay Peninsula. A panel of text on the left of the map near Calicut, its western extremity, gives directions for the sea routes to Aden and the Straits of Hormuz. Photo: © Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford. CC BY-NC 4.0. Other vernacular names recognize the importance of both land and water to the adequate naming of this space. It is no coincidence that the Malay word for “homeland,” tanah-air (lit. “land-water”), discloses an archipelagic or estuarine orientation. The earliest available records for the Javanese name Nusantara (lit. “islands between”) date back to copperplate inscriptions from the fourteenth century, and its most well-known reference is from the sixteenth-century Kawi poem Pararaton (Book of Kings), in which the Javanese imperial chieftain Gajah Mada is said to have used the term “Nusantara” to refer to the furthest fringes of the Majapahit Empire. This usage is affirmed in the oldest surviving manuscript of the Sejarah Melayu, which says of the king of Majapahit, Terlalu besar kerajaannya pada zaman itu, segala seluruh Jawa semuanya dalam hukumnya, segala raja-raja Nusantara pula, setengah takluk kepada baginda. [Great indeed was His Majesty’s kingdom in that era, for all of Java was under His law, and half the kings of Nusantara submitted to Him].11 Nusantara overlapped only partially with Nanyang, its outermost boundaries reaching only into the Sea of Sulawesi and into the archipelagos west of Guinea, as far up the Malay Peninsula as today’s southern Thailand, and the coastal regions of Borneo. Yet it was, like Nanyang, a fundamentally maritime concept, a name that accepted the centrality of water to this region’s connectedness. Nusantara faded with the end of Majapahit, and was resurrected only in the early twentieth century as part of an explicitly nationalist project seeking a name behind which to consolidate against the “Dutch East Indies.” Beginning with the Djuanda Declaration aimed at quelling regional rebellions in the outer islands of Indonesia in 1957, a “Wawasan Nusantara” (Nusantara Vision) began to be promulgated over subsequent decades to inculcate a national and civic vision of a united archipelagic Indonesia that, for some, signaled a resurgent Javanese neo-imperialism over the entire archipelago.12 Yet Nusantara retained its aura of anticolonial indigeneity through the twentieth century, and remains part of a fringe petitioner movement even today that advocates changing the name of Indonesia to one that was not given by foreigners (pemberian asing).13 To expose the politics of naming is to recognize that names like “ASEAN” and “Southeast Asia” might be as much historically constructed political projects as others that have fallen away through history. They are no less real for that constructedness—as Donald K. Emmerson observed, “Some names, like ‘rose,’ acknowledge what exists. Others, like ‘unicorn,’ create what otherwise would not exist. In between lie names that simultaneously describe and invent reality. ‘Southeast Asia’ is one of these.”14 Yet recognizing them as such may help alert us to other visions and alternative worldmaking projects embedded in names that sought to invent other realities, and that have long since fallen by history’s wayside. I offer two examples below that were contemporary with the emerging Anglo-American concept of “Southeast Asia,” but specifically opposed to it. We find one name-project in Chinese, Fengxia (風下, lit. “beneath the winds”), popularized in the political journalism of Hu Yuzhi (1896–1986). Hu was a Chinese communist intellectual exiled in Sumatra between 1942 and 1945, and his gravitation to this name drew directly from his experience and encounter with the Malay world. He had known this region as Nanyang, but in his enthused, world-opening encounters with Indonesian language, geography, and history during his period of exile, he transmuted the Chinese-oriented Nanyang into the Malay Fengxia, to better describe a region that he was coming to understand as “the strategic military center of the British empire” (英帝國的軍事重鎮) and thus the center (中心) of the antiaggression movement of eleven million Chinese compatriots. Fengxia, he said, recognized the fundamentally monsoonal orientation of Nanyang, as well as its dialectical origins as a name distinguishing its peoples from the “white-skinned blue-eyed strangers” who came to the coast of Malacca half a millennium earlier and, when asked where they came from, pointed westward to indicate that they had been blown to these lands by the southwest monsoon. “Therefore,” Hu wrote, “the Malays later called the general countries of Europe ‘the lands above the winds’ [風上之國], and their own lands ‘the lands beneath the winds’ [風下之國].” After centuries of domination by fengshang zhi guo, those who lived in these lands beneath the winds were no longer willing to be enslaved, and it was here, he wrote, that the future of war and peace would be decided. Critically, Fengxia recognized the political significance of ethnic Chinese in this world historical region, while also articulating the essential fluidity of ethnic belonging; in the evolving mental geography he was constructing, Hu came to advocate that the Chinese zuguo (homeland) might not be usefully thought of as “China,” but might evolve to be the place to which one felt linked, politically, economically, or culturally. He came to advocate the creation of a new race in Fengxia, an amalgamation of different racial groups across the region that might be brought together under the name Ma-lai-you (馬來由). A radical vision of region could, in this sense, transmute Chinese into Malays and unite them in a shared anti-imperial project—if one were able to mentally reconstitute those names from ethnoracial containers into, essentially, historical-geographical ones. A second name-project in Indonesian retains the sense of a site of world-historical importance in the battle between imperialist war and socialist peace. Tan Malaka (1897–1949), a Sumatran Marxist intellectual and Comintern representative, began in the late 1920s to imagine a partly geostrategic and partly cultural-linguistic regional concept he named “Aslia.” Aslia, for him, was an amorphous concept produced by a Marxist historical imperative, but also transcended its materialist basis to embrace a metaphysics of belief (kepercayaan). In some of his writings, Aslia is said to comprise a federation of all countries (negara) that are found on the bridge between (pada jambatan antara) Asia and Australia, and in fact should encompass not only Burma, Thailand, Annam, Kalimantan, and what he termed Indonesia sempit (narrow Indonesia) but also about a third of the total area of Australia. In others, he considered Aslia to constitute a continuous unity of race and geography (ilmu bumi dan ilmu bangsa), as well an area of shared belief (kepercayaan) in things that have natures of their own (kodrat), in the existence of a soul (jiwa), and in spirits and ghosts (hantu). He writes that during his travels across this space he was now naming Aslia, he had become convinced of a preexisting oneness imposed by bumi-iklim (earth-climate), kebangsaan (racialism or nationality), economy, and kejiwaan (which he glosses with the English term “psychology,” but is literally “soulness”). Above all, after the end of the Japanese occupation, he spoke of Aslia as the site of a “great conflict [pertentangan hebat] between the socialist and capitalist world.” These variegated elements and characteristics of Aslia, for him, were not in tension with each other but the only possible full realization of what it would take to resist the “ruthless politics” (politik mulus) of European imperial domination.15 Both Fengxia and Aslia were at core socialist utopian imaginaries of a world expunged of colonial rule: a politics of naming that sought to name spaces for political and mental revolution. Their similarities lie in their greatly expanded conceptions of what constituted this East Asian region: Fengxia, in its positing of an intimate relationship to China; Aslia, in its advocacy for unity with portions of the Australian continent. Both propositions became impossibilities in the geostrategic encirclements of the Cold War. Yet they are in a continuous tradition of vernacular names, only a fraction of which I have explored in this article, that have spoken for centuries of the historical continuities of this space and its connections to other regions now demarcated by disciplinary borders, narrow nationalisms, geostrategic interests, and interspecializational hostility. By placing them in dialogue with our more limited Anglophone idea of “Southeast Asia” today as a territorial postwar geopolitical construct, forged in the crucibles of decolonization and Cold War and thought of as a shorthand for ASEAN, I have hoped to show how the latter offers only a partial picture of the richer vernacular imaginaries of these Southern Seas as a historical region of mobility, movement, and an alternative politics. auditPapers.title: British Military Bands, Propaganda, and Diplomacy, 1872–1918
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract During the First World War, British military bands went on tours to Paris (1917) and Italy (1918) to generate support for the Allied war effort. These ‘propaganda tours’ marked the culmination of a trend that emerged in the second half of the nineteenth century when military musicians assumed the role of cultural envoys of the state. With retreat from ‘splendid isolation’ at the turn of the century, the nascent e ntente cordiale witnessed a burgeoning relationship between British and French military bands. While the impetus for these tours came from outside government, the Foreign Office’s cancellation of a tour to Germany in 1907 against King Edward VII’s wishes shows that these activities were considered more than benign gestures of international musical co-operation. After over two years of war, professional propagandists harnessed the mass appeal of military music by organizing concerts designed to reverse dwindling morale and present a unified Allied war effort. Although it is hard to assess their effectiveness, contemporary accounts and similar missions in the interwar period suggest that they met their objectives. By consulting a wide range of materials, from concert reviews to diplomatic correspondence, this article aims to bridge the gaps between political, military, and cultural history by showing the relevance of military music to all three sub-fields.

auditPapers.title: Paul Kreitman. Japan’s Ocean Borderlands: Nature and Sovereignty.
auditPapers.abstract: In this extensively researched and engaging study, Paul Kreitman considers how “the conditions under which particular ideas about how the natural world ought to be governed came to take hold” (20). Focusing mainly, but not exclusively, on uninhabited islands in the Pacific and South China Sea, he tracks the economic activities and territorial thinking that turned these sites into spaces of imperialist and post-imperialist competition and sovereignty-making, as well as the environmental factors that augmented or reduced their value to private and state actors, from Japan and the Euro-American empires to China and Taiwan. Examining both the rapacious extraction that led humans to claim these islands and the ways that wildlife conservation campaigns shaped international relations, he elucidates “the connections, dialectical inversions, and latent continuities between these two ways of claiming” (15). Kreitman begins with the Bonin Islands, showing how long-distance whaling expeditions in the North Pacific produced a “trans-Pacific maritime proletariat,” the gunboat diplomacy and extraterritorial imperialism that protected whalers and their goods along their routes, and the Euro-American beachcombers who exploited these structures to assert leadership of island settlements. After unsuccessful Tokugawa attempts to colonize the Bonins in the 1860s, the Meiji state incorporated them and their inhabitants into Japanese territory by 1882, succeeding because their value as a provisioning hub had not materialized, and the dwindling beachcomber population found themselves devoid of powerful overseas defenders.

auditPapers.title: Adam Bisno. Big Business and the Crisis of German Democracy: Liberalism and the Grand Hotels of Berlin, 1875–1933.
auditPapers.abstract: Detractors of microhistory frequently point to its potential exceptionalism. What is to say that any one case study is representative? The small does not necessarily help us understand the large. Proponents of this methodology, on the other hand, see in its supposed “smallness” its distinct advantage: Scholars come to understand the particular case’s sui generis; in its idiosyncrasies lie richness and explanatory potential. Replete with remarkable detail, from the fraying bedsheets to the separation of bone from gristle in the kitchen, Adam Bisno’s fascinating account in Big Business and the Crisis of German Democracy demonstrates the strengths of microhistory. Berlin’s grand hotels were established in that era of optimism and wealth that followed the founding of the German Empire. Like many capital-intensive projects at that time, funds were raised through joint stock companies, one important way that the up-and-coming middle classes exerted financial power when political power still eluded them. By 1900, Berlin had eight grand hotels, all of them breathtakingly ornate and located in the burgeoning city center, where their guests could enjoy the many consumer diversions.

auditPapers.title: Taylor M. Easum. Chiang Mai between Empire and Modern Thailand: A City in the Colonial Margins.
auditPapers.abstract: After glancing at the title, readers might be tempted to dismiss this book as a parochial history of a provincial city in Northern Thailand. That would be a mistake. Chiang Mai between Empire and Modern Thailand is not so much the history of a city as a history of space, of centers and peripheries, of heritage and modernity. By shifting the perspective from the capital toward the northern borders, Taylor M. Easum helps free the narrative from the confines of the nation-state as the dominant framework of analysis. The author also provides a different glimpse into the dynamics of Western imperialism, internal colonialism, and informal empire. As a study of urbanization, the book interprets Chiang Mai as a palimpsest, focusing on layers of change instead of classifying the city as one type or another. In a field dominated by the colonial and postcolonial era, Easum’s work is refreshing for bridging the modern and premodern histories of Chiang Mai. The book is a necessary reminder that, while the people of this region are inheritors of an ancient culture and heritage, the nation-state of Thailand, with its corresponding borders and identity, is a far more recent invention.

auditPapers.title: Peter Jackson. From Genghis Khan to Tamerlane: The Reawakening of Mongol Asia.
auditPapers.abstract: Traveling through northern Syria in 1909, Gertrude Bell heard a folktale that epitomizes the fearsome reputation of the conqueror Amir Timur (c. 1136–1405)—better known to English audiences as Tamerlane. At Manbij, eighty kilometers east of Aleppo, a Circassian shepherd told Bell how the townspeople, warned by a local holy man, had escaped annihilation at the hands of Timur’s army: They burned their own possessions. When Timur’s forces saw the smoldering ruins, they bypassed the town, thereby sparing its people. In Syrian folk memory, the best one could hope for when Timur’s army rolled into the town was survival; material destruction was inevitable. In this mammoth study, From Genghis Khan to Tamerlane: The Reawakening of Mongol Asia, British historian Peter Jackson offers a broad, perceptive, and deeply learned account of Amir Timur’s career and the developments underpinning it. A speaker of Turkish from a mid-level Mongol tribe, Timur was not part of the “Golden Kin” (altan urugh), descended from Chinggis Khan, which had ruled the united Mongol Empire and its successor khanates since the early thirteenth century. Rather, his father, who served in the royal bodyguard of the Chaghatayid Khanate in Central Asia, was descended from one of Chinggis Khan’s most trusted lieutenants (229). Lacking imperial blood, Timur clawed his way to power as the effective ruler of the Chaghatayid Khanate through a succession of “short-lived alliances, each discarded once it had become a liability or no longer served his purpose” (256). Legitimacy thus remained a concern throughout his reign, and Jackson deftly explores each of the strategies that Timur employed to consolidate and maintain his authority. Foremost among these was relentless campaigning in search of plunder and prestige. From the late 1360s to his death in 1405, Timur’s forces crisscrossed Central Asia and the Middle East, indiscriminately battling Christian, Muslim, and “pagan” opponents and pushing deep into Anatolia, Russia, and northern India. Organized around a core of Turkic and Mongol horsemen, his army deployed technical units, incendiary devices, elephants, and (most effective) trebuchets for sieges (329). His wrath fell heavily on those who resisted. Towers of their skulls were erected outside Isfahan in 1387, Delhi in 1398, Aleppo in 1400, and Smyrna in 1402 (332–34, with additional examples of Timur’s “macabre ingenuity”). Those who escaped death could still suffer deportation, with many being resettled in the empire’s core zone of Transoxiana, where their labor and skills contributed to the construction of Timur’s twin capitals at Samarkand and Kish.

auditPapers.title: Comment by Ruth Mostern
auditPapers.abstract: The landmark 1997 book The Myth of Continents explains that the organization of global landmasses into the familiar group of seven from contemporary maps and textbooks is but one of many schemas by which people have divided the world into constituent regions. Subtitled A Critique of Metageography, the book demonstrates what one can learn about power and ideology by studying how systems of large-scale spatial classification are historically and culturally constrained and discursively impactful.1 The contributors to the “Big Asia: Rethinking a Region” forum are working in the tradition of metageography critique to historicize and complicate the concept of Asia, focusing mainly on an era beginning in the late nineteenth century. As Nile Green points out, that was when an ancient Greek term—one that originally referred only to the eastern coast of the Aegean Sea before its scope spread over the centuries—became widely adopted in European-style school atlases from Tokyo to Istanbul. The case for “Big Asia” as a new metageographic term reflects trends of studying transnational and transimperial spaces in Asian studies; studying networks that foster connections among and between Asian people, commodities, and ideas; and studying climatic and topographical features as environmental historians do.

auditPapers.title: The Idea of “Asia” and Its Alternatives
auditPapers.abstract: It was only from the seventeenth century that the ancient Greek toponym “Asia” began to be adopted across the different regions it conceptually unified through the framework of continental geography. This terminological transfer unfolded along two routes of diffusion via the adaptation of European maps. In 1602, “Asia” was introduced to Ming imperial China—and adapted to Mandarin phonology—as Yaxiya through a world map that the celebrated Jesuit Matteo Ricci translated with local scholars. A few decades later, Ricci’s successor Giulio Aleni drew on European atlases to compile with Chinese partners the Zhifang Waiji (Record of foreign lands) that further transmitted the idea of “Asia” to Japan and Korea in turn.1 By this time, European cartography was also introducing “Asia” to the Ottoman Empire when scholars such as Katib Çelebi used the Atlas Minor of Mercator to produce his 1648 Cihan-nüma (Mirror of the world).2 This was nearly a century before Swedish geographer Philip Johan von Strahlenberg decided in 1730 to demarcate the boundary between “Europe” and “Asia” in the Urals.3

auditPapers.title: Giving Content to Continent Europe and Asia in the Imagination of Russian Muslim Intellectuals
auditPapers.abstract: If nations are “imagined communities,” continents are imagined spaces. As nations are imagined with reference to existing demographic realities, continents are imagined with reference to physical landmasses. However, beyond the landmasses they reference, continents as imagined spaces also symbolize indexes of many suppositions, aspirations, memories, activities, values, and commitments. The indexes that characterize “Asia” and “Europe,” or “Big Asia” as explored in this roundtable, were born in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries out of the demands of modernity that accelerated time, shrunk space, and incentivized matching human activity with delineated spaces on maps. A look at how conceptions of space among imperial Russia’s Muslim communities transformed with the advent of European modernity in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries brings into sharp focus the processes through which these modern continents were constructed. It all started in Europe, for the notions of “Europe” and “Asia” as recognizable units called “continents” were European constructs that people in other parts of the world borrowed subsequently to imagine geographic space. However, existing notions of space and various local concerns underlining each of those peoples’ engagement with European modernity determined the terms of borrowing and, therefore, gave content to continents in their spatial imaginations.1
