auditPapers.title: Ran Segev. Sacred Habitat: Nature and Catholicism in the Early Modern Spanish Atlantic.
auditPapers.abstract: In Sacred Habitat: Nature and Catholicism in the Early Modern Spanish Atlantic, Ran Segev challenges the view that Catholic clerics of the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Spanish Empire were close-minded fanatics hostile to science. In this intellectual history, Segev finds friars, monks, and one nun who were curious about the natural world, intent on systematically understanding it, and creative in advancing interpretations of it. Segev focuses on three fields over four chapters: cosmography, descriptive geography, and zoology. The final chapter on zoology shows the intellectual stakes most clearly with the most convincing evidence. In it, Segev examines how Jesuit José de Acosta and Dominican Gregorio de Garcia squared the existence of previously unknown species from the Americas with their belief in the biblical account of Noah’s ark. Acosta in Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590) argued that the endemic species of animals in the Americas that were saved in the ark later migrated to the New World over a land bridge. The implication was that they became extinct in the Old World, an innovative idea to explain natural processes but one that contradicted Thomas de Aquinas’s assertion that the natural world reflected perfect divine providence (a place for every animal and every animal in its place). Realizing this shortcoming, Garcia in Origen de los Indios (1607) defended fellow Dominican Aquinas by positing instead that angels transported the animals. These creatures later diverged from Old World varieties, Garcia wrote, “due to the disposition of the land, and the particular influences and constellation of the heavens” (147). This conclusion pioneered an explanation for speciation. Here, as with the rest of the book, Segev demonstrates that these clerics were mostly concerned with upholding received theology. Nonetheless, even as orthodox Catholics, they considered some natural evidence and advanced new scientific reasoning.

auditPapers.title: Todd Cleveland. Alluring Opportunities: Tourism, Empire, and African Labor in Colonial Mozambique.
auditPapers.abstract: Todd Cleveland has published an impressive five books as a sole author since 2014. These books explore the labor and social history of Africa in three main fields: diamond mining, sports, and, more recently, tourism. Spaces under former Portuguese colonial rule, often neglected in the historiography, have been the author’s main geographical focus. A History of Tourism in Africa: Exoticization, Exploitation, and Enrichment (2021), designed for students, can usefully be read as an introduction to Alluring Opportunities: Tourism, Empire, and African Labor in Colonial Mozambique. Where the former discussed different forms of tourism in colonial and postindependence Africa, exploring the enduring “allures” of the continent through examples from Egypt, Tunisia, or apartheid South Africa, the latter focuses on Mozambique, the “touristic jewel” of Portugal’s modern empire (3), mostly since the 1940s and up to independence in 1975. One of the main goals of Alluring Opportunities, Cleveland explains in the introduction, is to show how the tourism industry in colonial Mozambique was “codeveloped” by African laborers and foreign visitors (9). Drawing on dozens of interviews with Mozambicans working in the tourism sector, Cleveland contends that despite often enduring racial discrimination and violence in the workplace, many of these laborers benefitted from more stable conditions than in other sectors, gained important skills and prestige, and improved their livelihoods. Tourism, the book argues, created opportunities that allowed these workers paths of upward social mobility in an unequal, racially ordered colonial society. Conversely, as Cleveland’s interviews with tourists show, Mozambique was particularly alluring as a tourism destination for visitors with different socioeconomic profiles, interests, and expectations. It catered to youths looking for a relaxed beach holiday, to men attracted by the relatively more progressive racial dynamics and social mores of Lourenço Marques’ bars, striptease clubs and casinos, to fans of European café culture, bullfighting, and music, as well as to enthusiasts of big game hunting and, later, the photographic safari. Importantly, by the 1960s, Mozambique attracted tourists from across the world, the majority of whom were white and came from South Africa and Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe).

auditPapers.title: Adrian Masters. We, the King: Creating Royal Legislation in the Sixteenth-Century Spanish New World.
auditPapers.abstract: In We, the King: Creating Royal Legislation in the Sixteenth-Century Spanish New World, Adrian Masters provides a fine example of the renewed interest in legal history and the working of the imperial government. While Masters examines the production of laws in the Spanish Empire, he also casts light on the origins of the caste system and the creation of the racial group composed of mestizas and mestizos (those of mixed Indigenous and Spanish descent). Masters converses with significant literature and combines many illuminating examples into a stimulating analysis. He starts out by telling the fascinating protest of the Peruvian mestizos. Originally, the Augustinian friar Rodrigo de Loaysa helped to define this group by suggesting in 1578 that the crown should ban the ordination of mestizos in Peru. The crown approved the petition in the same year. An outcry ensued in Peru. In 1582, mestizo candidates for the priesthood began gathering signatures to rescind the policy; 149 students in Lima, Cuzco, and elsewhere signed off on the petition. Subsequently, the scribe-notary Pedro Rengifo was put in charge, and he claimed hyperbolically, as was common in the empire, that he had the power of attorney to represent ten thousand mestizos of various kingdoms in this matter. Yet not all petitioners were fully aboard to be labeled “mestizos” because of the term’s discriminatory overtones. Students in Arequipa, for instance, rather called themselves montañeses (those from the mountains), akin to the regional and influential group from Burgos in northern Spain. Rengifo also collected documents from bishops, clergymen, and local elites to strengthen the petition. He left Peru and probably arrived in Panama late in May 1584, catching the fleet sailing to Spain, which escaped French and Ottoman-allied pirates near Portugal. After arriving in Seville in September, the Council of the Indies heard him in February of the next year. Then Rengifo was summoned into the palace and “perhaps the bedchamber itself” for a personal audience with King Philip II. Rengifo continued to move the petition along, and finally the king signed off on a new communication in 1588, ordering equal treatment of mestizas and mestizos with Spaniards.

auditPapers.abstract: Sheryllynne Haggerty’s Ordinary People, Extraordinary Times begins with the story of the Europa, which in 1756 was on its way home from Jamaica to Dublin with its hold filled with slave-produced commodities. This unusual changing of hands meant the Europa was sailed to Falmouth to be adjudicated by the Admiralty’s prize court. The ship was searched, and a postal bag was found hidden under one of the guns. The 407 assorted letters, bills, and other communications eventually became part of the Prize Papers of the High Court of the Admiralty and were preserved at the National Archives. Her work complements quantitative demographic research by Barry Higman and Jack P. Greene on Jamaica in the 1750s. Using the Europa’s postal bag as her starting point, she introduces a world of characters into whose lives we might only glimpse, but who would otherwise have remained absent from the historical narrative. The letters give voice to the experiences of merchant’s clerk John Jackson, aspiring carpenter Ewbank Ogle, mother Ann Graham, seamstress Elizabeth Metcalf, mixed-heritage “housekeeper” Mary Rose, and enslaved distillery worker Quaco. From these relatively fleeting archival encounters, Haggerty weaves together a fascinating account of the lives of ordinary people as they stood at the precipice of a global conflict in the guise of the Seven Years’ War, and internal turmoil with the outbreak of Tacky’s Revolt.

auditPapers.title: Juliet B. Wiersema. The History of a Periphery: Spanish Colonial Cartography from Colombia’s Pacific Lowlands.
auditPapers.abstract: Although the historical cartography of the Caribbean Sea coast, which was part of the Viceroyalty of New Granada, is abundant and detailed, largely thanks to the planimetric records of its urban settlements and the various expeditions carried out for decades by engineers in the service of the Spanish crown, the same cannot be said for the Pacific Ocean coast. This region was “terra incognita” (35) in the eyes of the world, disconnected from political and economic centers, administration, and power, despite being home to a significant Afro-descendant population mainly dedicated to gold mining and agriculture. This cartographic void is the starting point for Juliet Wiersema’s exploration of this region’s scarce and sometimes almost illegible maps in her interesting book, The History of a Periphery, which she cleverly calls “The Pacific Lowlands” (5). These maps serve as examples of the peripheral world alluded to in the first part of the title. To achieve her objective, Wiersema selects four maps, all dating from the eighteenth century: the Atrato River and the towns of the Cuna Indians (1759–1778), Chocó, Panama, and Cupica (1777–1808), the Dagua River region (1739–1786), and the Yurumanguí Indians (1742–1780).

auditPapers.title: Brooke Larson. The Lettered Indian: Race, Nation, and Indigenous Education in Twentieth-Century Bolivia.
auditPapers.abstract: The full involvement of Indigenous peoples in national life has been one of the main challenges faced by the governments and societies of the twentieth century in the Americas. Among the various strategies deployed, educational policies were a pivotal tool. And Bolivia, home to a significant Indigenous population, was no exception. The Lettered Indian: Race, Nation, and Indigenous Education in Twentieth-Century Bolivia results from over three decades of research in the Bolivian Andes by the renowned historian Brooke Larson. It offers a critical and insightful study of the pedagogical programs undertaken by the state and its parallel and strategic interpretation of the Andean communities from the early 1900s to the 1970s. Focusing on the rural setting of the highlands of La Paz and the experience of its Aymara inhabitants, the book relies on Larson’s comprehensive archival work in public archives in La Paz and Sucre and private libraries of influential educational figures. It also encompasses US educational policy and diplomatic sources related to Bolivia and the documents and testimonies gathered by scholars—mostly Aymara—of the Taller de Historia Oral Andina (THOA). Notably, the oral history work conducted with key individuals involved in various educational actions analyzed in the book brings a distinct perspective, capturing reflections, memories, and tangible aspects of daily life not always accessible through written and visual sources.

auditPapers.title: Louis A. Pérez Jr. Colonial Reckoning: Race and Revolution in Nineteenth-Century Cuba.
auditPapers.abstract: In Colonial Reckoning: Race and Revolution in Nineteenth-Century Cuba, Louis A. Pérez Jr., one of the most prominent scholars of Cuban history, questions the official narrative of the past, one founded on the premise that throughout the nineteenth century, Cubans of all racial and social backgrounds came together to liberate their land from the yoke of the Spanish Empire and to give birth to a free Cuba. This mythical past, the author argues, informs the present and serves as a marker of Cuban identity. Pérez contends the official history leaves no room for ambiguity—that it erases the complexity of Cubans’ responses to the anti-colonial wars. Pérez shines light on the thousands of Cubans who collaborated with the colonial forces, a topic the traditional historiography has ignored. This shift in emphasis provides a new perspective on Cuba history, disrupting long-established views. To recalibrate the Cuban nineteenth century, the author revisits a well-known past, a story that has been told many times by multiple scholars, including himself: Sugar and coffee production made Cuba the wealthiest Spanish colony, but also the most dependent on an enslaved labor force. By the mid-nineteenth century, the enslaved population had reached over four hundred thousand people, almost half of the island’s inhabitants. The fear of slave revolts made plantation owners loyal to Spain. The elite understood that maintaining colonial ties guaranteed the Spanish army’s protection.

auditPapers.title: Patricia Fortini Brown. The Venetian Bride: Bloodlines and Blood Feuds in Venice and its Empire.
auditPapers.abstract: For more than four decades Patricia Fortini Brown has been one of the leading scholars of early modern Venice. An art historian by trade, she has produced a steady stream of important works that have fundamentally shaped our understanding of the history of Venetian art, from Venetian Narrative Painting in the Age of Carpaccio (1987) to Venice and Antiquity: The Venetian Sense of the Past (1996) to Private Lives in Renaissance Venice: Art, Architecture and the Family (2004). Her interdisciplinary explorations of Venetian art during its early modern highpoint have always overlayed deeply with their cultural and social historical milieus, and with The Venetian Bride, history moves to center stage. The bride at the center of the book is Giulia Bembo, who in 1549, at age eighteen, married Count Girolamo Della Torre. Giulia belonged to one of the most illustrious Venetian patrician families, whose most noteworthy sixteenth-century member was Giulia’s great-uncle, the distinguished Venetian humanist, historian, and cardinal, Pietro Bembo (1470–1547). Her husband came from an important feudal family from the region of Friuli, the often-restive northeastern frontier of the Terraferma, the Venetian mainland state. The marriage was celebrated against the backdrop of the decades-long vendetta between the Della Torre and another powerful Friulian feudal family, the Savorgnan. Indeed, the marriage was a rushed affair because the bridegroom was under a sentence of exile for his role in avenging the murder of his father, and immediately after the ceremony, the couple set sail for the island of Crete, one of the jewels of Venice’s maritime territories, the Stato da mar. With this union, the Della Torre gained kinship ties to a powerful and influential Venetian family that might assist them in their rivalries, and the Bembo gained an alliance with a wealthy Terraferma family with an established noble pedigree.

auditPapers.title: Joanna Story. Charlemagne and Rome: Alcuin and the Epitaph of Pope Hadrian I.
auditPapers.abstract: Charlemagne commissioned an epitaph for Pope Hadrian I, who died in 795, and Alcuin composed it. This forty-line Latin inscription—which usually plays a bit part in studies about Alcuin, early medieval England, Charlemagne, and art and monumental building—takes center stage in Joanna Story’s Charlemagne and Rome: Alcuin and the Epitaph of Pope Hadrian I. In this wide-ranging study, Story compares the epitaph to earlier works to demonstrate ancient and late antique influences, situates it in the context of Carolingian culture, offers insight into Old Saint Peter’s Basilica and how those in northern Europe experienced it through manuscripts, and examines the preservation and later reception of the inscription, which remains visible in Saint Peter’s Basilica. This interdisciplinary investigation utilizes written historical and liturgical sources, art and architecture, manuscripts, inscriptions, coins, and even geology and chemistry. Story argues that the epitaph “forcefully projected, through word, stone, and script, a message of Carolingian confidence and ambition” (4). Charlemagne, as speaker of the epitaph, would be commemorated alongside the pope. The epitaph was skillfully inscribed in Francia, probably around Aachen, on black stone that was likely quarried in Carolingian territory and “complemented the echoes of empire embedded in the poetry and epigraphy” (256).

auditPapers.title: Owen Davies. Troubled by Faith: Insanity and the Supernatural in the Age of the Asylum.
auditPapers.abstract: In Troubled by Faith: Insanity and the Supernatural in the Age of the Asylum, Owen Davies has conscientiously excavated a seam of medical history to investigate the relationship between religion, faith, and insanity in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Britain (and Europe). His research reveals how far the history of psychiatry has traveled since the single-minded focus on the Foucauldian fiction of the “total institution” in the 1980s. By placing religious belief about the supernatural—from the demonic through the orthodox to the spiritualist—at the center of his analysis, Davis shows how much of nineteenth-century psychiatry remained preoccupied by religion, even if these beliefs were often pejoratively explored as “superstition.” Well into the twentieth century, physicians found that religious ideas and fears remained important to a good proportion of their asylum inmates. He suggests how the period, rather than secularizing, became in many ways more seriously “religious,” with newly literate populations able to purchase commercially produced Bibles and prayer books. New forms of Christian worship and belief, such as the Pentecostals, believed ever more fervently in the presence of the Holy Spirit, while new movements—particularly theosophy and spiritualism—often stressed the presence of departed souls in the lives of the living. He is quite right to insist that the arrival of science and technology hardly erased fears of the supernatural. On the contrary, fluids and currents in telegraphy, telephones, and phonographs were often perceived as dangerous precisely because of their invisible and otherworldly capacity to invade and disrupt body and mind.

auditPapers.title: M’hamed Oualdi. A Slave Between Empires: A Transimperial History of North Africa.
auditPapers.abstract: We are sorely lacking in case studies relating to figures from the Muslim Mediterranean world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. General Husayn, who is the subject of M’hamed Oualdi’s A Slave Between Empires: A Transimperial History of North Africa, is a particularly interesting figure, from many points of view, perhaps most notably because of the porosity of the multiple borders that he crossed over the course of his tumultuous life. This is a work that will not only be useful to those interested in the history of the Middle East but also to those interested in global history. The main manuscript is a short 150 pages, which, including the brief glossary, the footnotes of the chapters, a bibliography, and an index, reaches a total of 230 pages. The catchy title of the book plays on the emotional fiber, but it leaves the suspense intact as to its content. The name “Husayn” does not appear in the title, and yet it is him who is in question and who will be the case study. In addition to being very vague, however, the title is misleading, by fixing the category of slave in a static manner, whereas the book shows that Husayn’s trajectory and his status were very dynamic. Thus, this work is also a contribution to the history of transnational elites. Oualdi uses the term “Elite Slave” in the book. But more than the trajectory of the character, at the heart of this case study are questions of property and inheritance, and their management; however, the framing of the book and the attempts by the author in the last paragraphs of the introduction (18–19) to evoke connections to modern migrants in Europe and the revolutions of 2011 fall flat. Husayn, in his Florentine exile, was not an ordinary nineteenth-century migrant.

auditPapers.title: Laura Leon Llerena. Reading the Illegible: Indigenous Writing and the Limits of Colonial Hegemony in the Andes.
auditPapers.abstract: Andean history’s most extraordinary text is a fifty-folio manuscript authored sometime before 1608 in the Peruvian province of Huarochirí and composed almost exclusively in Quechua, the most widely spoken Indigenous language in the Americas. Scholars have grappled with the “singularity” of this anonymous manuscript since its publication in 1939. Nonecclesiastical texts in Quechua are few compared to the corpus in Maya and Nahuatl, and the manuscript’s tales of the mountain deity Pariacaca, the trickster Cuni Raya, and the mummified ancestor Ñam Sapa suggest the many spiritualities targeted by Christian priests. But in Reading the Illegible, Laura Leon Llerena labels the manuscript an “exceptional normal,” in microhistorical terms. This wonderfully thoughtful book reveals a spiritual literacy illegible to non-Andean readers, by which Huarochirí’s peoples used alphabetic writing to explore “what faith [their own ancestors] held” (158). This intervention challenges two historiographies on literacy, conquest, and the sacred in the Americas. The first is the enjoyably recherché debate over the authorship of the manuscript, which ended up in the papers of a priest named Francisco de Ávila (c. 1573–1647). Of late, the prevailing opinion has been that its handwriting is that of a zealous Huarochirano convert mentioned in the text, Don Cristobal Choque Casa, who in 1607 defended Ávila from his flock’s enumeration of their priest’s abuses and neglect. If true, then Choque Casa’s naming of his fellow Huarochiranos’ “idolatries” supports Angel Rama and Walter Mignolo’s arguments that European alphabetic writing advanced spatial control, spiritual colonization, and Indigenous exclusion from the “lettered city.”

auditPapers.title: Andrew W. Kahrl. The Black Tax: 150 Years of Theft, Exploitation, and Dispossession in America.
auditPapers.abstract: In The Black Tax: 150 Years of Theft, Exploitation, and Dispossession in America, Andrew Kahrl, shows how “federated taxation” has been both a marker and a maker of racial inequality in the United States (3). Spanning the century and a half from emancipation through the early twenty-first century’s financial crisis, The Black Tax is a meticulously researched, compellingly argued, and often heartbreaking account of US history that centers “Black people’s struggles against local tax systems that forced them to pay more for less and subjected them to heavy financial penalties and the threat of dispossession” (4). Combining both a structural analysis of the broad political and economic forces that shaped the post-Civil War United States with archival accounts of how individual men and women, Black and white, upheld and resisted those same structures, The Black Tax shows how local tax systems have been used, exploited, and even designed to dispossess Black landowners, enrich white elites, and institutionalize racial inequality and injustice. By correctly insisting on seeing the tax system as built by and for white elites, this important and compelling book refutes the widely held—but historically inaccurate—belief that taxes are simply a way to transfer resources from white taxpayers to implicitly non-white “tax eaters” who feed at the public trough. This “makers and takers” narrative has been central to both the neoliberal project of shrinking the public sphere and the white supremacist project of rolling back the hard-won victories of the Black freedom movements. Kahrl’s work convincingly shows that Black Americans have not only paid their fair share in taxes; they have been overcharged for their share of the American dream.

auditPapers.title: A Scribe's Luxury Manuscript: Text and Image in a Hebrew Medical Tract (Cambridge, University Library, MS Dd.10.68)
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract: The Cambridge Hebrew manuscript stands as an example of a multi-text manuscript. This manuscript's original stage was written by a single scribe who undertook the formidable task of amalgamating content from various sources, carefully curating and sometimes adapting the treatises to align with his specific requirements. Beyond text compilation, the scribe enriching the manuscript with a decorative program that not only adds aesthetic value but also aids in navigation. This program consists of seven illustrative panels, some featuring medical themes, while others depict scenes of classroom instruction, revealing the scribe's intellectual pursuits. Upon closer examination of both the textual content and the illustrations, it becomes evident that this manuscript was crafted for the scribe's personal use. This essay endeavors to illuminate this relatively unexplored manuscript, shedding light on the medical interests prevalent during its time of creation and delving into the significance of its illustrations. By unraveling the scribe's workmanship and analyzing his choices, we can gain valuable insights into the production of luxury secular manuscripts designed for personal utilization.

auditPapers.title: Graphic Narratives and History in the Americas
auditPapers.abstract: Detail from Ghost River: The Fall and Rise of the Conestoga. In recent years, graphic narratives have gained greater recognition within the historical profession. University presses publish series of graphic histories, conferences include regular contributions from historians studying various kinds of sequential graphic narration, and an increasing number of historians are collaborating with artists in the production of graphic histories. In a profession struggling with job precarity, falling budgets, and the attacks of state officials, graphic narratives seem to represent reason for optimism: a medium through which historians might reach broader audiences, increase collaborations across industries, and support our work with students. While it is easy to notice the graphic boom in the historical profession, it is not so easy to fully comprehend its implications. In the Graphic Narratives and History project, we, a comics scholar and two historians, enter into conversation with dozens of scholars working on comics and history in various regional contexts to try and figure out the relationship between history and graphic narratives. As we thought about our approach to the project, we saw our role as that of convenors and facilitators; we wanted to learn from the many comics scholars and historians who have thought about the seam between history and comics for a long time. Our initial idea was to hold a plenary conversation on graphic histories and what academic historians can do with them before embarking on a range of regional conversations that examine questions of history and comics in a particular area of the world. In reality, conversations proved more fluid—regional examples were used in the plenary discussion, and the regional conversations contain insights on graphic narratives as a medium and historians’ relationship to that medium. What we have here, then, is not a polished nor a comprehensive almanac of history and comics, but rather an effort to take stock of what experts on graphic histories in various regions consider to be some of the most relevant questions about the relationship between graphic history and history. This first installment includes our first three conversations: a plenary discussion on comics and history, a conversation on comics and Latin American history, and a conversation on comics and North American history. Some of the questions we ask focus on the methodological end: What kind of history does the graphic narrative do? How do historians research, teach with, and produce graphic narratives, and how can we do it better? And how do scholars studying graphic narratives see the relationship between their work and history? By contrast, some of our other questions focus on the history of graphic narratives as a cultural industry: What can historians learn by paying close attention to the production, distribution, and consumption of comics? How have imperial and national contexts defined the production of graphic narratives? And how do these contexts still shape and constrain our approach and access to various kinds of graphic narratives? No definitive answers await here. Instead, this project compiles a series of conversations where scholars who have studied the problems of graphic narratives and history in various contexts share their expertise, ideas, how-to tips on teaching and research, and advice to historians who are interested in producing graphic histories. auditPapers.title: Teaching the History of the Vietnam Wars
auditPapers.abstract: A visitor encountering a set of historical photographs that were part of the 2023 Vietnamese American Roundtable’s annual commemoration for the end of the Vietnam war in San Jose. Like the organizers of this event, many in the Vietnamese diasporic community in the United States commemorate the war’s end on April 30th as “Black April” (Tháng Tư Đen) in sharp contrast to the celebrations that mark official Vietnamese state commemorations where the anniversary is called Reunification Day (Ngày Thống nhất) or the Day of the Liberation of the South (Ngày Giải phòng miền Nam). Photo courtesy of the Vietnamese American Roundtable. Four high school teachers who were part of a National Endowment for the Humanities Summer Institute in 2022, “Contested Territory: America’s Involvement in Vietnam, 1945-75,” reflect on their teaching of the Vietnam wars and present an ensemble of classroom activities that have helped their students understand war in new ways. Master teachers who work in diverse classrooms across the United States, they offer innovative learning activities on the Vietnam wars that explore the everyday experiences of war; the roles of ideologies in shaping conflict; soundscapes of war; and the use of Geographical Information Systems (GIS) to study the complex geographies of war. Framing essays by the Institute’s co-leaders provide context on new Vietnam war scholarship and the design of inquiry-based practices that foster critical historical thinking. Three years into the official commemoration of the fiftieth anniversary of the first US combat mission in Vietnam, I happened to be teaching a course on the geography of modern Vietnam. On Memorial Day 2012, President Obama had proclaimed a “13-year program to honor and give thanks to a generation of proud Americans who saw our country through one of the most challenging missions we have ever faced.”1 In 2015, Obama’s proclamation was the first reading I assigned to twenty-four first-year students at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and it prompted a lively conversation. Asked to consider whom the document remembered, students praised how it “honored” American servicemen and servicewomen, some of whom were their grandparents. But some noted that it overlooked other Americans, including protesters who, one argued, had also stood up patriotically for democratic ideals. Moreover, many quickly grasped that the proclamation focused exclusively on American actors, mentioning nothing at all about the people of Vietnam. Why were they left out? How did they remember it? What were the war’s local causes and consequences? Evaluating the commemoration for whom it forgot and remembered introduced a critical pedagogy that integrated history with geography. First, it revealed to students fresh out of high school that not even popular, relatively progressive presidents were infallible. Their ready critique of his American-centric point of view recognized that such near-sightedness left out other points of view, especially Vietnamese perspectives. Then, their recognition opened a line of inquiry pointing to the course’s goal: to introduce a large, diverse country with long, complex histories that informed multiple perspectives on what, in Vietnam, is commonly called “the American War.” My course thus featured a bit of bait and switch: Hook students with a war, then argue for understanding it within a geographic context grounded in places and peoples too often left out of the picture. Significantly, the exercise meant it was the students who argued for shifting the gaze. Prepared for the leap from domestic to international perspective, I paired the presidential proclamation with another reading that foregrounded one of many Vietnamese points of view. In his aptly titled essay “The United States Isn’t the Only Country Still Trying to Figure Out the Vietnam War,” political scientist Tuong Vu starts with a different commemoration.2 In Vietnam, April 30, 2015, was celebrated as the fortieth anniversary of the American War’s dramatic conclusion, when People’s Army tanks crashed through the gates of the Presidential Palace in Saigon. “Ever since,” Vu argues, “Hanoi leaders have sought to capitalize on their military victory to legitimize their rule.” Indeed, official memory there, including public school curricula, cultivates a narrative auditPapers.title: Understanding Competing Agendas through a Love Triangle
auditPapers.abstract: Countless commemorations, news reports, and scholarship have underscored the Vietnam wars’ significance in the global history of the twentieth century. However, stories, analyses, and memories appearing in the United States, in Vietnam, and in Vietnamese overseas communities all tell a widely different story. As a result, students who are just learning about Vietnam, Asia, the Cold War, or American foreign policy might feel overwhelmed by the monumental nature of the Vietnam wars. This is where The Quiet American, which the Australian filmmaker Phillip Noyce adapted from Graham Greene’s 1955 novel, becomes a useful tool.1 Starred by familiar faces like Michael Caine and Brendan Fraser, the movie offers an accessible storyline that suggests the multiple scales and dimensions of the wars. The Quiet American intertwines a war story with a murder mystery and a love triangle. The movie opens on a criminal case to elucidate the assassination of an Alden Pyle, an American aid worker. A French inspector in charge interrogates an old British correspondent, Thomas Fowler, through whom the movie uses flashbacks to understand what happened. Covering the war from Saigon in the 1950s, Fowler enjoys this time away from England in the company of a young Vietnamese woman named Phượng. He befriends a young American aid worker, Pyle, and introduces him to Phượng. However, the old man sees the two getting closer together. In the following weeks, Fowler covers battles and political meetings. He keeps seeing the young aid worker in the most unexpected situations. Blinded by his jealousy, Fowler does not realize that Pyle is not the “quiet American” he claims to be. It is only once a terrorist attack hits Saigon that he realizes the American is in fact a secret agent who had planned the bombing to blame the Vietminh and inspire a renewed mobilization against communist expansion in Asia. Fowler eventually agrees to arrange a dinner with Pyle, helping the Vietminh organize an ambush and assassinate the American agent.

auditPapers.title: Kith and Kin
auditPapers.abstract: As a scholar and teacher of the Vietnam War, I have long been dissatisfied with Vietnam War textbooks. Some of the best-known textbooks on the market—such as George C. Herring’s classic America’s Longest War—treat the war primarily as an episode in American history, while paying little or no attention to the Vietnamese dimensions of the conflict. In response, several authors have recently produced textbooks that focus on Vietnamese actors and perspectives. One notable example is Pierre Asselin’s Vietnam’s American War, which teaches the history of the war through the ambitions and decisions of one Vietnamese group: the senior leaders of the Vietnamese Communist Party. To date, however, I have yet to find a textbook that successfully situates the war within the broader frame of modern Vietnamese history while still giving due weight to the US military intervention in the conflict. In lieu of using a textbook in my Vietnam War course at Dartmouth College, I ask my students to read Duong Van Mai Elliott’s The Sacred Willow: Four Generations in the Life of a Vietnamese Family.1 Published in 1999, The Sacred Willow is a brilliantly written family saga that details the lives and experiences of Elliott and her relatives over the course of the twentieth century. But the book is much more than just a compilation of family lore. Elliott carefully locates herself and her family members within the Vietnamese political, social, and cultural contexts in which they lived. Along the way, she provides readers with a wealth of insights about how Vietnamese perceived and experienced the war. At the same time, as someone who is Vietnamese, who was born and raised in Vietnam but studied in the United States, worked with Americans, and eventually became a US citizen, Elliott is unusually well equipped to provide students with a critical perspective on the American involvement in the conflict.

auditPapers.title: Deceptively “Easy”
auditPapers.abstract: The book begins in a hospital in New York City; the first illustration is a tightly cropped image of a woman in labor, the frame drawing attention to her pregnant stomach, medical tubing, and spread legs. In the next panel, her husband stands beside her, but the text and the images spotlight an empty chair. Her mother has “disappeared.” Despite traveling across the country to assist, she “can’t bear to be in the same room” as her daughter1 (1–2). Thi Bui’s graphic memoir The Best We Could Do opens with this explicit childbirth scene, as it sets the stage for an immersive meditation on the fraught relationship between parents and their children, and on the consequences of colonialism and war across generations. The Best We Could Do’s powerful drawings and nonlinear narrative have seeped into my writing on refugee camps and provoked questions about historical method and form.2 It has also become a go-to book in my courses on the US War in Vietnam and US immigration history.

auditPapers.title: History(ies) of Authoritarianism(s) in the Philippines
auditPapers.abstract: “My job is to go places where people die. I pack my bags, talk to the survivors, write my stories, then go home to wait for the next catastrophe. I don’t wait very long.” —Patricia Evangelista, Some People Need Killing, 5. How do we make sense of the history of and return to authoritarianism in the Philippines? This is one of the central questions that scholars and creatives working on the Philippines have engaged since the Marcos dictatorship in the 1970s. In recent years, there has been a renewed focus since the election of Rodrigo Roa Duterte to the presidency in 2016 and the return of the Marcos clan to Malacañang in 2022. There is a political urgency to work on Philippine authoritarianism as most people writing on the topic want to combat the resurgence of authoritarian rule in the Philippines and elsewhere. Four recent works, all dealing with the history and present of authoritarianism in the Philippines, provide insight into both the form and content of the study of dictatorship.

auditPapers.title: Kidada E. Williams. I Saw Death Coming: A History of Terror and Survival in the War against Reconstruction.
auditPapers.abstract: I Saw Death Coming is an incisive and moving analysis of freed people assaulted and murdered by the Ku Klux Klan and other groups across the South in the years following the Civil War, reframing this violence as “the war after the Civil War” (xxi, 222). Kidada E. Williams has crafted a unique contribution to the turn toward understanding the Civil War and Reconstruction at home and in daily life, drawing skillfully from survivors’ testimonies before the United States Congress’s Joint Select Committee to Inquire into the Condition of Affairs in the Late Insurrectionary States (published in 1872), narratives from the Works Progress Administration’s Federal Writers Project (1936–1938), and contemporary literature on trauma and human rights. By shifting our focus from individual office holders and voters to families, and from polling places to homes, Williams exposes the realities of lives caught within the “[f]issures between the letter and the fact of the law,” legislation including the Civil Rights Act of 1866, the Enforcement Acts of 1870–71, and the constitutional amendments for which Reconstruction is best known (54).

auditPapers.title: Sarah Keyes. American Burial Ground: A New History of the Overland Trail.
auditPapers.abstract: In the popular mythology that swirls around the expansion of the United States into the far West, the Overland Trail figures heavily in tales of victory: tenacious white pioneers pushing against tremendous odds to settle the land and claim it for the United States. It was a journey of progress, the story goes, one during which, if we are to believe Frederick Jackson Turner, both the emigrants and the land itself became ever more American with each step along the way. But contrary to cultural and even historical depictions of the movement westward through the romantic haze of white triumphalism, “the Trail was a treacherous, often deadly trek that left a string of burials” (2). Rather than seeing this history as one to celebrate, Sarah Keyes sees the story of the Trail as “a story of death” (9). In her newest book American Burial Ground: A New History of the Overland Trail, Keyes offers “a darker portrait of westward migration than we are used to, remembering, and uncovering the cultural significance of the dead” to the appropriation of the territory by the United States (2). Ironically, emigrant deaths and their graves along the Trail, Keyes argues, literally laid the groundwork for the seizure of these lands from Indigenous peoples. In other words, by remaking the Overland Trail into an American burial ground, “[d]ead emigrants eventually became an answer to another problem [they] hadn’t fully grappled with at the start of their journey: how to definitively claim the West for the United States” (5). Calling the failed emigrants who died on their long journey toward Oregon and California “as successful as those who reached” their destination, Keyes asserts that these dead emigrants became “traces of an expanding nation’s presence across the continent and, ultimately, the seeds of later white settlements” (6).

auditPapers.title: Ayelet Brinn. A Revolution in Type: Gender and the Making of the American Yiddish Press.
auditPapers.abstract: In A Revolution in Type: Gender and the Making of the American Yiddish Press, Ayelet Brinn analyzes the “vital, complex, and often unexpected ways that questions of women and gender” shaped the evolution of American Yiddish press (5). This study of Yiddish dailies in New York from their founding in the 1880s through their decline in circulation and influence in the mid-1920s centers newspaper features like advice columns and human-interest pieces described (and at times disparaged by critics) as “women’s content.” Though the Forverts’s long-running advice column the “Bintel brief” often appears in studies of American Jewish print culture, Yiddish women’s content broadly defined receives less scholarly attention than editorials, news reporting, and literary criticism. Interweaving the history of the rise of the American Yiddish newspaper industry with detailed portraits of editors, journalists, and readers, Brinn challenges the perspective that women’s content and those who produced or consumed it were “peripheral to the development of the Yiddish press” (14).

auditPapers.title: F. Evan Nooe. Aggression and Sufferings: Settler Violence, Native Resistance, and the Coalescence of the Old South.
auditPapers.abstract: In Aggression and Sufferings, F. Evan Nooe seeks to bring the tools of ethnohistory and the insights of Native history to the study of the white South. Specifically, the author wants to explore the question of how white Southerners came to identify as a distinct and coherent entity in the decades before the US Civil War. Nooe acknowledges the crucial and central role that the practice of slavery played in this process, deeply embedded as it was in the social and economic fabric of the white South. However, Nooe notes another dynamic that has received less scholarly attention: the shared experience of settler violence against the peoples of the Native South. Nooe distinguishes his work from that of scholars such as Patrick Griffin and Peter Silver, who argue that anti-Native violence was a formative component of American identity. He argues that perceived federal disinterest in aiding white Southerners’ colonizing ambitions created a rallying effect among them and a defiant attitude toward the rest of the country. When federal aid proved insufficient to match white Southerners’ expectations, states, cities, and volunteer organizations cultivated a siege mentality. They took it upon themselves to aid one another in promulgating settler violence and conquest, and defending newly conquered lands, sometimes in defiance of federal authority. These shared experiences begat a hagiography passed down by families and historical societies for generations, shaping how white Southerners viewed themselves, their ancestors, and their claims to colonized land.

auditPapers.title: Robert A. Schneider. The Return of Resentment: The Rise and Decline and Rise Again of a Political Emotion.
auditPapers.abstract: Early in The Return of Resentment, Robert A. Schneider quotes from a sermon by Samuel Parris, a Puritan who preached in Salem at the time of the witch trials. Parris had failed in a commercial venture in the Caribbean and now watched as farmers in the village succeeded and grew wealthy. His text was Mary and Joseph’s doomed search for lodgings in Bethlehem. He speculated why there was no room at the inn: “The Inne that it may be was full of rich folks” (36). Parris’s resentment was not exactly anger. It registered economic forces beyond his control and signaled a betrayal of the values that had impelled the community’s flight to the New World. The suspicion of harboring such traitors within, Schneider suggests, may have also fed persecution. Schneider’s encompassing and timely book is at once an intellectual history and archaeology of potent forces at work today. Unlike other emotions, resentment thrives from a complex dynamic involving both shared and personal experience. Its French expression, ressentiment—“to feel again”—conveys some of this complexity: Resentment is the memory of a wrong, and with memory comes lasting outrage that time doesn’t always heal. Resentment is relational; it carries a sense of victimization and sometimes humiliation; and it can dwell at length on hopes thwarted or denied. As a collective emotion, Schneider writes, it can also be used to powerful political effect. Unlike most other emotions, he argues persuasively, resentment has a history.

auditPapers.title: Alexandria N. Ruble. Entangled Emancipation: Women’s Rights in Cold War Germany.
auditPapers.abstract: By the late 1950s, the constitutional law of both East and West Germany included a clause that guaranteed equal rights between women and men. At that time, the constitutions of few West European countries explicitly incorporated the principle of gender equality under law. Thus, by the end of their first decade of existence, both Germanys look comparatively progressive on the question of “equal rights” for women. Yet, as Alexandria Ruble shows in her readable, meticulously researched, and evenhanded comparative study, Entangled Emancipation: Women’s Rights in Cold War Germany, this conclusion is simplistic and ahistorical. She does not deny the significance of the equal rights provisions but complicates their meaning by tracing their prehistory in political tensions and debates of the 1940s and 1950s, and by following their after-history in the family law of East and West Germany of the 1960s and 1970s. Her first great contribution to the literature on German women’s rights is to demonstrate convincingly that the process and the content of gendered legal change in each state was related to what was happening in the other German state. As do other feminist scholars, she sees gender relations as a major point of contention in the Cold War rivalry between the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) and German Democratic Republic (GDR). Applying this insight to the case of women’s legal rights, she shows that these rights did not evolve along parallel tracks in East and West but alternately diverged, converged, and crisscrossed as experts, government ministers, legislators, and ordinary citizens looked over their shoulders at debates and decisions in the other Germany—and aimed to prove that their state had more to offer women than did the other.

auditPapers.title: David Parrott. 1652: The Cardinal, the Prince, and the Crisis of the ‘Fronde’.
auditPapers.abstract: French historian Denis Richet wrote that the Fronde was “an infantile disease of absolutism.” He thus placed this episode of civil unrest, which shook the Kingdom of France from 1648 to 1652, within an inexorable chain of events leading up to the reign of Louis XIV. The frondeurs, as its instigators were called, have generally been portrayed as either representatives of retrograde forces concerned first and foremost with defending their privileges against the rise of the state, or as visionaries anticipating the revolutionary chaos of the late eighteenth century. It is also clear that they were doomed to fail in light of the French government’s march toward modernity initiated by Cardinal Richelieu and then continued by Cardinal Mazarin, Anne of Austria’s chief minister when she served as regent for her young son Louis XIV. This failure perhaps explains why historians have shown little interest in the latter stages of the revolt. And yet, according to David Parrott, the year 1652 was a “distinct historical moment with decisive and lasting consequences” that recalls to mind the end of the Roman Republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire. Neither Mazarin nor the great nobles who led the struggle against him were driven by a deep concern for the values that had guided France for centuries or for the future of France and its people, starting with the king and members of his nobility. Rather, much like Augustus and his adversaries, they “systematically hollowed out the values and ideas of the Republic, maintaining only a veneer of outward constitutional forms under which factional and personal interests dominated political decision-making and the allocation of power and resources” (9). The Fronde essentially died out in 1652, giving way to a newfound stability, but the words and actions that characterized those four tumultuous years continued to make their influence felt. And not in a good way, for they were words and actions “from which the recourse to service, loyalty, and obligation was notably absent” (10).

auditPapers.title: Tim Keogh. In Levittown’s Shadow: Poverty in America’s Wealthiest Suburb.
auditPapers.abstract: Levittown is one of the most well-known popular symbols of the postwar American dream—and nightmare. Tim Keogh’s must-read contribution to its prodigious historiography mainly expands on the latter. The title’s double meaning acknowledges Levittown’s prominence. In Levittown’s Shadow: Poverty in America’s Wealthiest Postwar Suburb refers to the people and places dwarfed by the New York community’s fame and serves as an ambitious reorientation of suburban history around what that fame has obscured. In short, it has obscured suburban poverty. Keogh argues that Levittown became the physical manifestation of “suburban exceptionalism,” or the set of discourses, policies, and silences that foreclosed more egalitarian modes of living in the United States between the mid-twentieth century and the present. Under this framing, Keogh tracks how Levittown seemed incompatible with the existence of poverty, making it the model that policymakers, activists, and experts assumed could result in affluence for all Americans. They thus prioritized expanding access to the suburbs to combat social ills. However, once access became the goal, they entrenched the predatory labor, development, and lending practices that accompanied Levittown to Long Island. Keogh grounds this history of poverty with a close examination of local property records, civic and government organizations, and life stories that he traces across multiple chapters.

auditPapers.title: Neil Roos. Ordinary Whites in Apartheid Society: Social Histories of Accommodation.
auditPapers.abstract: As Neil Roos comments in the introductory chapter to Ordinary Whites in Apartheid Society: Social Histories of Accommodation, it is worth asking if historians should “bother” (20) with writing histories of whites in South Africa—about the category of people who benefited the most from apartheid rule and who were the least involved in the anti-apartheid movement. There is significant historical research on poor whites, on Afrikaners, and on white elites, but social histories of white South Africans are—still—best found in photography, novels, and memoirs. Indeed, it is especially striking that Ordinary Whites is grounded in Roos’s own autobiography: It “is set in the world [he] grew up in,” drawing on the stories of people “[he] grew up with” (11), including photographs of Roos’s family and of his parents, Sheila and Dick, and using their biographies as points of entry into the book’s key arguments. Ordinary Whites provides a powerful answer to why social histories of “ordinary” white South Africans is necessary: It is not only the case that “[w]hites form part of the puzzle that constitutes modern South African history” (21), but it also undermines “the idea of a homogenous, one-dimensional, and essentialized whiteness and thus go[es] some way toward unmasking whiteness as an invented idea of superiority” (18). The category of “white” had to be made and constantly reinforced under apartheid, and tracing the experiences of “ordinary” white South Africans is revealing of those efforts to constitute and maintain “whiteness.” As a result, one of the key preoccupations of Ordinary Whites is the state’s management of white, working-class people, from efforts to raise their standard of living, to attempts to “improve” them morally.

auditPapers.title: Freedom in the Here and Now
auditPapers.abstract: The efforts of 20th-century activists to achieve immediate freedom is the concern for Victoria Wolcott and Irvin Hunt. However, each scholar approaches the topic in drastically different ways, reflecting their respective disciplinary differences. In Living in the Future: Utopianism and the Long Civil Rights Movement, Wolcott, a historian of the 20th-century United States, traces the history of utopian communities, including worker education schools, cooperatives, and fellowship houses and churches, and spotlights their pivotal contributions to the long civil rights movement. In Dreaming the Present: Time, Aesthetics, and the Black Cooperative Movement, Hunt, a scholar of English and African American studies, reads Black cooperatives as an artistic practice that facilitated the creation of different temporalities of the present. In Living in the Future, an elegantly composed and meticulously researched book, Wolcott invites us to reconsider utopian practices and ideas within the long civil rights movement. (The long civil rights movement views the struggle for racial equality as extending before the 1950s and past the 1960s. Within this framework, the civil rights movement, spanning from 1954 to 1968, represents a pivotal chapter in this struggle.) Utopian ideals were quite popular from the 1920s through the Second World War, declined in popularity after the war and as the labor movement deteriorated, and resurged in the early 1960s when a fresh wave of visionaries emerged.

auditPapers.title: Philip Gooding. On the Frontiers of the Indian Ocean World: A History of Lake Tanganyika, c.1830–1890.
auditPapers.abstract: One of the most robust analytical debates within East African history and its historiography is the production and articulation of difference—difference between self and other, core and periphery, civilization and barbarism. At the heart of these frictions lays the divide between the salient conceptual metageographies of the region: Africa and the Indian Ocean World. Although intertwined for centuries, artists, intellectuals, and scholars alike have long shown that the regional production of social and cultural difference often relied on imbuing these geographies with meaning. Proximity to the coast and integration into the putative xenophilic and cosmopolitan worlds of the Indian Ocean signaled civilization and culture—ustaarabu and utamaduni, respectively. Alternatively, interior Africa was an archetypal hinterland—a static landscape that, through the trade in ivory, enslaved people, and the spread of Islam, was gradually pulled out of its insularity and into the dynamic and outward-facing coast. Scholars of all stripes have long shown, of course, how contingent, unstable, and violent these categories and characterizations often were. And indeed, the cultural divarication that these geospatial categories produced was often weaker and more porous than those who relied on it for wealth and power often needed it to be. Religious conversion, the appropriation of oceanic-spanning family genealogies, and strategies of consumption could allow for nominative outsiders to slip in and out the Indian Ocean worlds they encountered in coastal East Africa.

auditPapers.title: Elizabeth Dore. How Things Fall Apart: What Happened to the Cuban Revolution.
auditPapers.abstract: How Things Fall Apart: What Happened to the Cuban Revolution invites readers inside a Cuba typically unseen in historical work, relying almost exclusively on extended interviews with seven subjects interviewed between 2004 and 2018. Recently deceased historian Elizabeth Dore argues frankly that the Cuban Revolution has broken its promise to create an egalitarian society. The Cuba of the twenty-first century is one that has left socialism behind and bent to market forces even as propaganda continues to herald Cuban socialism. A warning to historians of Cuba and Latin America, to leftists who saw or continue to see Cuba as a beacon of hope in a landscape of hypercapitalist extraction: this book might break your heart. More happily, it might inspire new historical work on the second half of the twentieth century in Cuba. All seven of the primary interviewees in How Things Fall Apart grew up in the 1980s, coming of age just as the Soviet Union collapsed and sent Cuba into a decade of extreme scarcity. Because Dore and her team interviewed their subjects several times over a period of many years, the reader has rare and valuable access to the evolution of the interview subjects’ understanding of their own lives. Mario, an employee of Cuba’s Ministry of Industry, is initially reluctant to attribute any setbacks in his life—like his failure in art school—to racism. But as he speaks with Dore and her team again and again, he begins to see his life through the prism of anti-Black racism, despite having grown up in an environment that essentially prohibited acknowledgment of it.

auditPapers.title: Alexander Statman. A Global Enlightenment: Western Progress and Chinese Science.
auditPapers.abstract: In 2005, Princeton historian and sinologist Benjamin E. Elman published On Their Own Terms: Science in China, 1550–1900. It contributed to the development of a global history of science by exploring how scholars in China practiced science, during both the Jesuit period (1600–1800) and the era of Protestant influence after the Opium War. He demonstrated that Chinese scientists did indeed integrate key elements of Jesuit science into Chinese modes of knowing and knowledge circulation, and that these were integrated on their terms, such as “the investigation of things” and “the learning of the way,” and by building on Chinese genres like encyclopedias and manuals of popular science. Elman’s book and his other works made visible how Chinese actors changed science during this period, connecting Western science with Chinese progress. Alexander Statman’s book, A Global Enlightenment: Western Progress and Chinese Science, tells the story from the opposite perspective, connecting Chinese science with Western progress.

auditPapers.title: Srirupa Roy. The Political Outsider: Indian Democracy and the Lineages of Populism.
auditPapers.abstract: In recent years, we have witnessed the rise of populism across the world. Whether it is Donald Trump in the United States, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Turkey, Viktor Orbán in Hungary, or Narendra Modi in India, populist leaders everywhere have followed a familiar script. They conjure up a division between a victimized “people” and the elite, and project themselves as political outsiders who alone are able to right the wrongs done to the powerless citizens. There is a burgeoning literature on the subject, analyzing populism and offering explanations. Srirupa Roy’s The Political Outsider acknowledges this literature but finds it inadequate, deeming it presentist and electoralist, and insufficiently attentive to the broader range of politics and history within which populism is embedded. Focusing on populism in India, the book argues that populism is a “project of democratic reform fueled by an imagination of democracy’s repairable lapses” (6). It relies on diagnosing what ails the political system, and its core mission is to cure and restore a flawed and diseased democracy. Populism is remedial rather than revolutionary. Unlike left-wing movements, populists do not try to overturn the unequal sociological and economic order, but only attempt to “cure” the political system of its disease, to restore its health. Such a project of restoration throws up political outsiders whose purported exteriority to the normal system of electoral representation allows them to cleanse it of its distortion and corruption. Roy elaborates this argument by her study of populism in India, which, she suggests, is part of an older and ongoing program of curative democracy that took shape in the long 1970s and gave rise to “outsider politics,” both of which can be witnessed in the present.

auditPapers.title: Scout Blum, designer. Rising Waters: A Game Based on the 1927 Mississippi Flood.
auditPapers.abstract: In the evolving landscape of historical pedagogy, Rising Waters, designed by Scout Blum, emerges as a notable attempt to bridge the gap between interactive learning and historical education through board gaming. At its core, the game seeks to immerse players in the complexities of the Black experience during the 1926–27 Mississippi River floods, a pivotal yet often underrepresented moment in the history of the New South and the Roaring Twenties. Inspired by the “Reacting to the Past” pedagogical framework, which emphasizes role playing and active engagement to teach complex historical dynamics, Rising Waters integrates these methods into its gameplay to foster a deep, empathetic understanding of this catastrophe. However, the complexity of the game’s mechanics and the substantial time required to learn and play it present significant obstacles, potentially limiting its practical application in educational settings. The game distinguishes itself through exceptional artistic design, quality components, and attention to detail. The vivid, colorful illustrations resonate with the Art Deco and modernism of the 1920s, effectively fusing the more mainstream aesthetic of the era with African American artistic traditions and drawing players into the historical context of the floods. Such design choices not only enhance the visual appeal of the game but also serve to create a cohesive thematic experience that supports the game’s educational objectives. Among the 627 pieces included, the game components exhibit remarkable print quality and materials. The game even includes an alternate set of cards with different artwork that can be substituted for the primary deck. The team used the crowd-funding site Kickstarter to enlist the support of 324 people who pledged $19,500 for the initial production costs.

auditPapers.title: Max Weiss. Revolutions Aesthetic: A Cultural History of Ba’thist Syria.
auditPapers.abstract: Max Weiss is a well-respected name among scholars of Middle Eastern history and literature, and this newest publication only further cements his significance to the field. auditPapers.title: Anelise Hanson Shrout. Aiding Ireland: The Great Famine and the Rise of Transnational Philanthropy.
auditPapers.abstract: Media technology today connects potential donors to sufferers of humanitarian crises across the globe. Like most other phenomena, this form of international philanthropy has a rich history. In Aiding Ireland: The Great Famine and the Rise of Transnational Philanthropy, Anelise Hanson Shrout contributes to the Irish famine’s deep historiography by portraying the famine as one of the first truly global humanitarian relief efforts (3). This fine intellectual study provides an alternative explanation for the complex motivations behind disparate groups’ charitable support of starving Irish families. Aiding Ireland contains eight chapters, each devoted to a group of people who sent charitable donations during the famine. The groups’ identities are strikingly dissimilar: US American, English, and Irish; white and Black; middle class and enslaved. Shrout argues that the famine proved to be “the right catastrophe at the right time” that united multiple groups around a common cause. Scholars of philanthropy know well that the charitable impulse has existed as long as human beings and is embedded in all faith traditions. Studies of social movements, moreover, have linked resistance to authority and charitable purpose. Scholarship on the linkage of charities that meet basic needs with social justice advocacy spans abolition, settlement houses, immigrants’ burial societies, the Black church, and civil rights. The pathbreaking argument in this book is not that many different groups supported those in need, nor that social movement organizations fulfill basic needs, but that charity cloaked a variety of political uses to advance other agendas.

auditPapers.title: Grace Sanders Johnson. White Gloves, Black Nation: Women, Citizenship, and Political Wayfaring in Haiti.
auditPapers.abstract: Grace Sanders Johnson’s White Gloves, Black Nation: Women, Citizenship, and Political Wayfaring in Haiti is a much-needed addition to the canon of Haitian history and the history of women’s activism. Spanning some twenty odd years, Sanders Johnson reveals the modes of activism of elite Haitian women and their efforts to secure full citizenship through political rights and ameliorate the conditions of women in the Black Republic. Deeply researched and persuasively argued, the work nuances and elaborates on the practices of the activists and intellectuals in a time of possibilities. The work ebbs between an analysis of the efforts of the Ligue Féminine d’Action Sociale (LFAS) to improve the conditions and secure citizenship rights for all Haitian women, and the inherent tensions of a society that was as classist as it was sexist. It follows the efforts of highly educated, professional, and well-connected women who used their privileges to launch a movement that sought to be representative of all Haitian women and their needs. Sanders Johnson argues that the women of the LFAS’s leadership—those “who got dressed up for tea”—developed a praxis that ultimately garnered “the right to vote” (6–7).

auditPapers.title: On/ In the Ground with Vietnamese Communists
auditPapers.abstract: Undergraduates often arrive in my classes convinced that great men, and a few exceptional women, are the ones who make history. Here, they think of power wielded by presidents, generals, and self-styled geniuses of strategy and diplomacy. (Henry Kissinger’s name invariably bubbles up in class discussions, like it or not.) Perhaps this happens elsewhere? In Singapore, this mindset likely takes root because the country’s record of benevolent authoritarianism underpins the legitimacy and influence of political elites. Equally, male citizens of Singapore perform compulsory military service before entering university and internalize, readily or grudgingly, that rank confers power—it is power—and that those of lower stations must fall in line. This is the lens through which many of my undergraduates initially viewed the Vietnam wars, certain that the conflict was orchestrated chiefly, even exclusively, by politico-military elites. Furthermore, those among my undergraduates who, in their middle or high school years, opted to study history probably absorbed from the national textbook that the Vietnam conflict was essentially a proxy war (though I know teachers take pains to emphasize nuances to this description contained within the same textbook). Hence, a fair number of my undergraduates will cursorily note that the struggle for Vietnam was local in some sense but resolve that the war was more properly an extension of the US-Soviet Cold War from Europe into Asia.1 Some are quick to even conclude that the big powers basically made puppets of the Vietnamese; indeed, they show little concern for the ground-level experiences of ordinary Vietnamese. From that vantage point, the Vietnam wars are a chess game played by powers at great remove from the board, or even a crater-riddled battlefield of tiny, faceless figures glimpsed as if from a high-altitude bomber.

auditPapers.title: Paper Tracings in the Spectacularly Boisterous Archive of Slavery
auditPapers.abstract: Everybody knew what she was called, but nobody anywhere knew her name. Disremembered and unaccounted for, she cannot be lost because no one is looking for her, and even if they were, how can they call her if they don’t know her name. Although she has claim, she is not claimed . . . It was not a story to pass on. Toni Morrison, Beloved . . . not all silences are equal and . . . they cannot be addressed—or redressed—in the same manner. To put it differently, any historical narrative is a particular bundle of silences, the result of a unique process, and the operation required to deconstruct these silences will vary accordingly. Michel-Ralph Trouillot, Silencing the Past In 1831, a will is recorded in South Carolina. The testatrix is Lucy Buchanan, a free Black woman. Like most wills, Buchanan’s included a request that her debts be “punctually paid out of such perishable property” that she might own at the time of her death. She left the remainder of her estate in real and personal property to a local white slaveholder, a man she described as a “friend” and who she named executor of her estate. She asked that he hold this property in guardianship for his son until such time as the son arrived at the age of twenty-one. At that point, the estate would fall to the son and in succession, his “heirs and assigns forever.” Her estate included, she stated, “my son William who is a Slave.” She further stated that she believed this decision represented “the best disposition that according to the laws of this state I can make for his welfare.”1 To date, I have found no other record of Lucy Buchanan or her son—no letters written by either of them or about them, no document created by the state. It is therefore with just the will that Lucy Buchanan and William enter the archive as far as I am aware. Moreover, it is not even clear that the will is a legal declaration. On the line that called for Buchanan’s signature, her name appears in typeset and inserted between her first and last name is the letter “X,” neither of which is unusual. An X-mark signature, typically a mark of handwriting illiteracy or disability made in lieu of an actual signature, is considered legally valid when properly witnessed, and there were witnesses to Buchanan’s will. But what exactly did they witness? Clearly, they did not witness Buchanan making an X signature as the X mark is, like her name, typeset. Was she even present for this non-signed but signed document? These problems notwithstanding, the will provides important insight into Lucy Buchanan’s life, including the violence of slavery that adhered to it. The lack of a signature represents but part of the violence of the system of human bondage that created and operationalized the spectacle of a free Black mother of an enslaved child. Lucy Buchanan’s attempt to extricate herself and her child from this spectacle commands my attention. I linger with her justification for remanding her child—a child enslaved to her—to the care of a white slaveholder. Perhaps the young man to whom she ultimately wills her son is the child’s biological father, but that is pure speculation. I focus on her statement that leaving her child enslaved with this man was the “best disposition” she could “make for his welfare” under the laws of the state in which she lived, South Carolina. It was not what she wanted for her son, only what she thought was best for him under the circumstances.2 It dawns on me that Buchanan used one of the master’s tools—a will—to protect her child the best way she knew how. With this decision, she also telegraphed the violence that attached to her, inserting her testimony into the archive of slavery.3 Entering the archive of slavery is to confront what Foucault calls “the jostling violence of the facts they tell” and Arlette Farge terms “the rustling voices of the population.”4 The archive of slavery is a boisterous place where the violence of slaveholders jostles against the resistance and “rustling voices” of the enslaved, of the kind that characterizes Buchanan’s will and so many documents in which enslaved people cry out despite the curatorial efforts embedded in the archive that aimed to silence them. The “jostling violence” appears in the papers of slaveholding women who talked about Rose, an enslaved woman who led a rebellion in South Carolina during the Civil War. auditPapers.title: Precocious Consumption: The Career of Ming Porcelain in Renaissance Iberia
auditPapers.abstract: Most studies about Ming porcelain in sixteenth-century Europe maintain that these ceramics were extremely rare and expensive, an exotic luxury solely available to the elites and carefully preserved in cabinets of curiosities. This article challenges that view, drawing on a reassessment of sixteenth-century Portuguese and Spanish sources and archaeological evidence. It suggests that mass-produced Chinese blue and white porcelains became more accessible to urban populations in Renaissance Iberia much earlier than previously believed. This early “internalization” of Chinese porcelain in Europe’s material culture contradicts the dominant perspective, which relies heavily on Dutch and English sources from the seventeenth century. Iberian probate inventories and other written records reveal that porcelain prices were not exorbitant and did not rival prices for other Renaissance luxuries like silverware, tapestries, parade armor, jewels, and prized exotica such as Maldives coconuts, rhinoceros horns, or bezoar stones. Five key consumption patterns emerged in Renaissance Iberia: (1) porcelains as prized treasures, when mounted in silver; (2) porcelains as diplomatic or devotional gifts; (3) customized Chinese export porcelains; (4) porcelains as usable collectibles accumulated in large numbers in glass and porcelain chambers; and (5) porcelains as lavish everyday tableware for dining and drinking. Indeed, the initial awe surrounding these ceramics in the early 1500s was short-lived, as they gradually became more common thanks to a rise in imports and a growing familiarity with porcelain consumption cultures in Asia. Despite being the most luxurious ceramic in Europe, Chinese porcelain became relatively prevalent within one or two generations.

auditPapers.title: Challenging Abstraction
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Working with never-published agricultural data collected for Mexico’s pavilion at the 1900 Paris Exposition, this article argues that manuscript and published statistics represent a space to see state making as a multisided, ongoing process. Whereas historians have largely looked at statistics from the perspective of the state, highlighting bureaucrats’ projections of desired realities and political projects, here I show how local enumerators’ investment in statistical undertakings asserted space for conversations and arguments about the nature and composition of the political or economic whole being represented. I present a methodology for working with historical statistics that takes aberrations, anomalies, and unruly data as signposts to be followed rather than errors to be corrected. In doing so, I argue for seeing not only the frustrated yet durable aspirations of statesmen but also the ways those beyond the central state reforged, reinforced, and remade representations of their homes through engagement with and investment in statistical practices.

auditPapers.title: Remembering the Fall of Phnom Penh to the Khmer Rouge
auditPapers.abstract: “We will only execute seven people.” Prince Norodom Sihanouk, former Cambodian head of state, sought to calm fears as the Khmer Rouge closed in on the capital city of Phnom Penh in 1975. Deposed in a coup five years prior, Sihanouk in turn threw his support behind the Khmer Rouge and over the radio issued the group’s death list of seven high-ranking leaders of the US-supported Cambodian government.1 The Khmer Rouge captured the Phnom Penh on April 17, 1975, in a collapse quickly overshadowed in the United States by the fall of Saigon two weeks later. Fifty years later, the following collection of images explores how violence in Southeast Asia extended in time and scope beyond American involvement in Vietnam. One photograph was taken by Samuel Jackson, the director of an English Language Center in Phnom Penh. International governments and organizations carried out evacuations throughout the spring of 1975. In the previously unpublished image (Fig. 6), Jackson captured the end of the American evacuation. He had spent the morning of April 12 arranging for the incineration of identifying student records before evacuating on the last US helicopter out of the city. His photograph shows John Gunther Dean, the US ambassador to Cambodia, as US officials flew out to the USS Okinawa waiting in the Gulf of Thailand. In two weeks’ time, the Okinawa would then go on to host evacuees from Vietnam.
