auditPapers.title: Steve Hindle. The Social Topography of a Rural Community: Scenes of Labouring Life in Seventeenth-Century England.
auditPapers.abstract: Steve Hindle’s The Social Topography of a Rural Community is an unusual contribution to the genre of local studies; rather than thematic or chronological organization, Hindle explores the Warwickshire parish of Chilvers Coton in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries via thirteen residences. The basis for this approach lies in the survival of an unusual census conducted over three days in 1684 when the local lord, Sir Richard Newdigate, tasked jurors with collecting information on the residents of his lands, including a census of all households. Sir Richard devised the plan, but as Hindle demonstrates, this was a survey compiled from below and offers modern scholars a chance to see the parish through its inhabitants’ eyes.

auditPapers.title: Lindsay Schakenbach Regele. Flowers, Guns, and Money: Joel Roberts Poinsett and the Paradoxes of American Patriotism.
auditPapers.abstract: Lindsay Schakenbach Regele’s Flowers, Guns, and Money: Joel Roberts Poinsett and the Paradoxes of American Patriotism is a portrait of a self-interested man with significant power living through an era of dramatic historical change. Joel Roberts Poinsett (1779–1851) was a man of contradictions. He was the first US minister to Mexico who, despite the expansionist times, undermined the United States’ attempts to annex Texas. He was a South Carolinian who opposed protectionist tariffs and yet secretly mobilized military enforcement of federal tax collection in Charleston during Andrew Jackson’s Nullification Crisis. He was a Secretary of War who both introduced Cuban bloodhounds to kill Indigenous people in Florida and supported global exploration missions to obtain knowledge of Indigenous communities around the globe. He condemned US citizens fighting in foreign armies but had himself played a role in Chile’s independence fight. Enslaving many people to work in his several homes and on his wife’s rice fields, he also led the campaign to create the Smithsonian as a site of national enlightenment. He married late and only secretly acknowledged his only known child—a son born “out of wedlock” (58). His most lasting legacy is a Nahua plant marketed as a Christmas flower rechristened with his name: the Poinsettia.

auditPapers.title: Louis Howard Porter. Reds in Blue: UNESCO, World Governance, and the Soviet Internationalist Imagination.
auditPapers.abstract: “Since wars begin in the minds of men,” announced the preamble of the constitution of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), adopted in London in November 1945, “it is in the minds of men that the defenses of peace must be constructed.” The word “peace” made six appearances in the preamble, but not everyone was convinced. In Reds in Blue, Louis Porter explains that the Soviet Union at first shunned the organization, only joining in 1954, after Stalin’s death. How and why did Moscow go from profound suspicion of UNESCO’s “cosmopolitan designs for world governance” (34–35) to participation and engagement? Drawing from a range of international archives and sources, Porter rightly sees here an opportunity to capture the two projects in internationalism as a set of parallel mirrors. The result is an argument that highlights their shared utopian impulses but also a more intimate view of the tensions and contradictions in the practice of internationalism. And though the argument about “homologous utopian aspirations” (12) can only go so far—given the epic scope of the Soviet experiment and its specific challenges of governance—it is a refreshing one. By viewing Soviet internationalism through the UNESCO lens, we get a sense of the public-facing choreography that twentieth-century internationalists have needed to deploy.

auditPapers.title: David L. Cooper. The Czech Manuscripts: Forgery, Translation, and National Myth.
auditPapers.abstract: As The Czech Manuscripts explains, a rare find surfaced in Bohemia in 1817. Soon the Queen’s Court Manuscript (QCM), a fragment comprising about a dozen poems and songs, was dated to the thirteenth or fourteenth century—which made it the oldest known Czech-language document. The following year, another discovery, the Green Mountain Manuscript (GMM), offered a glimpse several centuries deeper into a Czech-language past. Together the QCM and GMM attested to the existence of an unexpectedly rich literary culture with an epic poetic tradition that honored a mythic age when pagan natives had lived in harmony and stood firm against invaders. Adherents of the fledgling Czech movement rejoiced, seeing in the manuscripts a historical counterweight to recent masterpieces of German-language literature for which there were no Czech equals. After all, Czech now figured largely as a language of non-elites, often illiterate. Yet not all was lost. The new evidence of a glorious past helped to inspire many Bohemians to contribute to the “rebirth” of a Czech “nation” defined by ancestral language. Over the following decades, the manuscripts became sacred texts of an increasingly confident Czech national movement.

auditPapers.title: Guillaume Blanc, trans. Helen Morrison. The Invention of Green Colonialism.
auditPapers.abstract: In The Invention of Green Colonialism, Guillaume Blanc investigates place-based conservation injustices in Ethiopia against a broader analysis of the unrelentingly colonial character of conservation work and thought across Africa. The Simien Mountains in Ethiopia might seem a curious place to start a work on “green colonialism”: Ethiopia was notably spared all but a brief occupation during Europe’s colonization of Africa. But Blanc argues that the broader colonial era saw the crafting of a set of narratives about Africa and its nature that endured, expanded, and perpetually renewed themselves after formal decolonization. Their reductive treatment of Africa meant that even Ethiopia was not spared their consequences. Blanc documents the origins of colonial conservation and then traces the broad persistence of the framework, and its particular Ethiopian iterations, across the period of decolonization, through significant changes in Ethiopia’s own political economy, and into an era of “sustainable development.” It is this long arc that gives The Invention of Green Colonialism much of its power for readers new to dimensions of this story, but which might frustrate others. Chapters 1 and 2 are based on existing scholarly literature and retell how Western visions of and assumptions about Africa and its landscapes amounted to the “naturalization” or “dehumanization” of Africa, with “catastrophic consequences” for people (1–2).

auditPapers.title: Katrin Bromber. Sports and Modernity in Late Imperial Ethiopia.
auditPapers.abstract: When most people think about Ethiopia and sport, they think about the country’s storied success in long-distance running. The reasons for this are justified; between 1960 and 2021, the country won fifty-eight Olympic medals in long-distance running events. In Sports and Modernity in Late Imperial Ethiopia, Katrin Bromber tells this story by showing how the body, masculinity, urbanism, and coloniality were important historical and sociological forces that shaped modern Ethiopia throughout the twentieth century. While “modernity” was a global process, and coloniality an integral part of that process, Bromber argues it is necessary to understand the broad range of debates on zemenawīnet—Amharic for “modernity”—regarding Ethiopian politics and scholarship.

auditPapers.title: Ellen Malenas Ledoux. Laboring Mothers: Reproducing Women and Work in the Eighteenth Century.
auditPapers.abstract: Enlightenment ideology created categories for motherhood: those who were “good” mothers cared for and nurtured their children, while “bad” ones were neglectful or poor providers. In Laboring Mothers: Reproducing Women and Work in the Eighteenth Century, Ellen Malenas Ledoux examines texts and images from eighteenth-century England that reflect these categories for marginalized working women. Some women were able to manipulate their public maternal image; Ledoux describes as “privileged” these “white women who had some access to education, and at least a limited ability to self-represent in various media” (3). Sarah Siddons and Mary Robinson were prominent actresses who needed to have public and private personas that were “compelling and attractive” (51), but motherhood could complicate this. Siddons dealt with it by emphasizing her maternal nature, while Robertson, who focused on her sexuality during her stage career, later wrote a memoir that emphasized her care for her daughter. Midwives were also a privileged group who could shape their public image, and unlike other women in Ledoux’s study, motherhood was a career advantage for them. The growing number of male midwives tried to argue that their medical training made them superior to female midwives, but treatises published by women midwives across the century emphasized that being mothers gave them more insight into their clients’ experiences.

auditPapers.title: Ryosuke Yokoe. Alcohol and Liver Cirrhosis in Twentieth-Century Britain.
auditPapers.abstract: The idea that alcohol consumption could damage the liver has been around for a century or more. In Edwardian Britain, a “hobnailed” or “gin drinker’s” liver was widely recognized as a possible consequence of heavy drinking. Cirrhosis, indicated by scarring of the liver that significantly impairs its function, is now understood to be a late stage of liver disease, which begins with the development of a fatty liver, and then often leading to hepatitis, before reaching cirrhosis. Although medical practitioners had long suspected that alcohol played a part in causing cirrhosis, the establishment of a causal link between drinking and cirrhosis was not straightforward. In Alcohol and Liver Cirrhosis in Twentieth-Century Britain, Ryosuke Yokoe explores the crooked path taken by the medical science of cirrhosis from the early 1900s to the 1980s. This journey encompasses not only the ins and outs of scientific debate but also the impact that this had on the political, socioeconomic, and policy response to alcohol. Alcohol consumption fluctuated over the course of the twentieth century, and although Britain never introduced prohibition, alcohol was more or less restricted at different times, and the political space that drink occupied also varied.

auditPapers.title: Sebastián Gil-Riaño. The Remnants of Race Science: UNESCO and Economic Development in the Global South.
auditPapers.abstract: Reframing the race campaigns of the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organizations (UNESCO) from the perspective of the Global South, The Remnants of Race Science reveals the surprising extent to which ideas about racial difference persisted within the organization and, significantly, how these ideas informed postwar development projects in the non-Western world. Although UNESCO’s famous, controversial 1950 Statement on Race rejected strict biological determinism, Sebastián Gil-Riaño provides a rich analysis of other hierarchical views of human diversity that remained. While UNESCO social scientists embraced plasticity and the benefits of race mixing—ideas that reflected the heavy influence of Latin American and Polynesian scholarship, he argues—they nevertheless retained an old, imperialist view of the world’s people as divided between those living in modern, Western civilization and those who remained “primitive” and in need of uplift. Indeed, scientific arguments about human equipotentiality, Gil-Riaño argues, gave new life to the equivalent of old—and overtly racist—colonial civilizing missions by recasting them into the “seemingly nonracial discourse of ‘international development’” (7). Rejection of innate biological hierarchy, in other words, did not dislodge the idea that Indigenous people were “backward” obstacles to modern, productive economies. Rather, it provided new ostensibly colorblind rationales for assimilation.

auditPapers.title: Patois of the Parishes
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This essay examines the birth of French medieval studies in America as a product of the racial anxiety and cultural-linguistic precarity experienced by Creoles. It argues that the idea of the French Middle Ages in North America, the conceptual matrix through which it became thinkable and desirable as a coherent subject of study, was made possible through engagements with minoritized Francophones who were assumed to embody the deep past. Part 1 examines how scholars in France’s Second Empire became invested in patois as a marker of “primitive” French cultural expression thought to have been transmitted over hundreds of years by oral recitation. Part 2 turns to a specific instantiation of French scholars’ pursuit of dialect: collectors of creole stories and grammars in the Caribbean, Indian Ocean, and south Louisiana who analogized creole utterances to the first French vernaculars as they emerged from Latin. Part 3 focuses on the pursuit of creolité as evidence of medievality in south Louisiana, and considers the racial anxiety evident in local deployments of the term creole. It concludes by discussing historical methods informed by creolization and mixed temporalities, and by imagining how these methods might transform medieval studies.

auditPapers.title: Brooke Barbier. King Hancock: The Radical Influence of a Moderate Founding Father.
auditPapers.abstract: King Hancock is not your typical founding father biography. Carefully avoiding the twin traps of hagiography and “myth-busting” that dominate the genre, Brooke Barbier brings careful nuance and deep historical context to a figure known by most Americans only for his larger-than-life signature on the Declaration of Independence. Rather than a paragon or a cautionary tale, John Hancock emerges as a fully fleshed-out human being, replete with virtues and flaws both typical and atypical for his time, and driven not just by high ideals and momentous events but also by the mundane trivialities, petty hardships, and simple pleasures of eighteenth-century life. Although written for a general audience, the book’s engaging prose, rich detail, and compelling narrative will assure it a readership among scholars of the revolutionary era from undergraduates to seasoned experts. With a knack for setting scenes, Barbier deftly takes the reader from Hancock’s origins in sleepy Braintree through his upbringing and adult life in bustling Boston, with stops in metropolitan London, congressional Philadelphia, war-starved Baltimore, and elsewhere. The city of Boston, where Hancock spent most of his life, becomes a character in the biography in its own right, with its wharves, streets, and denizens depicted in a type of contextualized detail that puts the reader in the place of a person on the street. We learn not only the size, furnishings, and architecture of Hancock’s Beacon Hill mansion, for example, but also how it commanded a wide view of Boston Common and the surrounding areas, how the family used it to receive visitors and engage in business and politicking, and how the servants and enslaved people who worked there interacted with neighbors both rich and poor. In describing Hancock’s mercantile empire, Barbier lingers on the area surrounding the merchant’s private wharf, stressing not just the vessels plying their trade but also the taverns, dram-shops, ropewalks, small retailers, and houses of ill repute that were as integral to Hancock’s enterprises as any mercantile firm. This eye for detail is not surprising from an author who also operates historical walking tours, but it is especially refreshing in a genre that too often trades the quotidian experiences that made up the vast majority of people’s lives for the high-flying oratory, intellectual debate, and political maneuverings of a relative instant.

auditPapers.title: Fiscal Innovation Gone Bad: Comprehensive Business Censuses from the Florentine 1427, 1433, and 1458 Catasti
auditPapers.abstract: The first descriptive purpose of this article is to document changes in the industrial composition of Renaissance Florence through business censuses that we have extracted from household-wealth declarations in the 1427, 1433, and 1458 Florentine catasti (tax censuses). These consecutive censuses reveal a decline in the number of businesses in many but not all of the industries in Florence over this thirty-year period. The second purpose of this article is to explain this economic decline. We find, through both quantitative and qualitative evidence, that the innovative tax catasti themselves were to blame: they all too effectively extracted enormous levels of taxes from the wealthy Florentine population in order to fund mercenary wars related to the emergence of Italian Renaissance regional or “territorial” states. The economic decline was due not only to the direct effect of heavy taxes but also to the indirect effect of default contagion among highly leveraged companies doing business with each other on credit. This case study contradicts the rosy portrait in the social science literature of a positive relationship between state formation and economic growth. We show that newly emergent Italian Renaissance regional states did not always produce positive economic gains for the capital cities that constructed them. This raises questions about economic self-interest explanations of that expansion. An important corollary for Florentine political history is our finding that this economic slump contributed structurally to the political rise of Cosimo de’ Medici through drastic contraction and concentration in the domestic banking industry.

auditPapers.title: What Made the Levellers Revolutionary? Reconsidering Leveller Political Economy
auditPapers.abstract: The article addresses the neglect of matters of political economy in Leveller scholarship, which for some time has focused on political and constitutional issues. It foregrounds Leveller approaches to trade and taxation, tithes and enclosure, and the relief of poverty before, during, and after the Leveller zenith of 1647–49. These concerns were as central to Leveller thinking as the issue of the parliamentary franchise, and the Levellers’ attention to such issues helps explain their contemporary appeal. Demanding the elimination of monopolies, tithes, and feudal land tenures, the Levellers projected a vision of flourishing English local and national economies built upon the work of the “laborious and industrious” people. Moreover, their approaches to poor relief were primarily intended not to control the poor but rather to assist them in returning to household independence. The Levellers’ attack on trade restrictions, their preference for taxation that fell predominantly on the wealthy, and their assault upon the tithe income of the state clergy and lay impropriators all struck at the resources of the social elite and at rationales for their predominance. Indeed, the Levellers were social revolutionaries: they both challenged contemporary institutions and practices that they found injurious to the “middling sort” and the “meaner sort” and proposed incompatible alternatives. Their emphasis on the country’s future as a trading and manufacturing nation anticipated the commercial revolution that accompanied the political revolution of 1688–89. Finally, the consistency over time of Leveller argumentation about matters of political economy suggests caution in imposing restrictive Leveller chronologies.

auditPapers.title: More Than Meets the Eye
auditPapers.abstract: I encountered Jonathan Schell’s 1967 New Yorker article “The Village of Ben Suc” as an enthusiastic if somewhat naïve undergraduate conducting research on American counterinsurgency in Vietnam.1 It was absorbing, dramatic, and poignant, and I remember devouring it late one night in a single sitting, then reading it again the following day. At 130 pages, “The Village of Ben Suc” is considerably longer than most of the research articles and book chapters I’m able to assign in my Global Vietnam War course at the University of Leeds. But with reading expectations everywhere wavering due to eroding attention spans if not work ethic, the piece has always been popular with my students, due in large part, I suspect, to Schell’s adept storytelling. Classroom discussions of the text are lively and engaged, and it is routinely listed in my end-of-year course evaluations as one of the readings that students enjoy most. “The Village of Ben Suc” presents a vivid eyewitness account of the 1967 Operation Cedar Falls campaign. This was a massive United States–South Vietnamese military exercise aimed at pacifying the so-called “Iron Triangle,” a rural Communist Party stronghold immediately northwest of Saigon. Schell recounts swooping into the titular village aboard a squadron of sixty helicopter gunships while he was embedded with a company of enthusiastic American soldiers primed for combat with a tenacious and cunning foe. The soldiers, teenagers outside the United States for the first time, find themselves instead deposited into a tranquil and bucolic community that regards them with bemusement, exasperation, or weary resignation. We observe the Americans’ bewilderment and frustration as they attempt the futile task of identifying enemy agents, equipped at best with a few words of broken Vietnamese. When communication proves hopeless, the soldiers instead cite the villagers’ demeanor or clothing in distinguishing friend from foe. A man riding a bicycle and a young couple enjoying a picnic are among the many shot and killed for wearing “the V.C. uniform,” the áo bà ba or “black pajamas” to the Americans, a loose-fitting ensemble ubiquitous in the rural South. “What are you going to do?” a US Army major later concedes to Schell. “We’ve got people in the kitchen at the base wearing those black pajamas” (120).

auditPapers.title: When Elephants Fight, Flirt, or Make Love
auditPapers.abstract: The end of the US wars in Indochina generated much circumspection across the Asia-Pacific region. In the United States, American officials and scholars debated who should be blamed for the American setback in Southeast Asia. In Vietnam, the fall of Saigon brought a close to the American War. In Southeast Asia, governments expressed their concerns that the victorious communists in Indochina and their comrades across the subregion might be inspired to attack or subvert their states.1 Southeast Asian leaders, however, also had broader concerns. With Sino-American ties thawing, Washington adjusting its policies toward Asia, and the Soviets intensifying their activities in the region after 1975, the member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) worried, as they regularly did, about the international politics of the region.2 As Singaporean Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew quipped: “When elephants fight, the grass suffers. Victor Petrov’s Balkan Cyberia joins this line of inquiry with spectacular results. auditPapers.title: Uluğ Kuzuoğlu. Codes of Modernity: Chinese Scripts in the Global Information Age.
auditPapers.abstract: If you learn Mandarin Chinese nowadays, the chances are that you will encounter two writing systems: Chinese characters and its romanization, Pinyin. The former contains tens of thousands of characters, and the latter uses the Roman alphabet. You might wonder about the relationship between the systems, and, bearing the toil of memorizing the characters, even wonder why Pinyin has not already replaced the characters, as they are seemingly much easier to learn and more reflective of the sound of Mandarin. After all, shouldn’t a script conform to what the language sounds like? Indeed, previous scholarship has assumed a hierarchy between language and script, prioritizing the former (3). Particularly in this context, the complexity of Chinese characters was perceived as an obstacle to mass literacy and even “modern scientific progress” (3, 60). This narrative decisively favors Pinyin or other romanizations of Chinese to Chinese characters. Uluğ Kuzuoğlu’s book Codes of Modernity challenges this hierarchy and profoundly complicates the phonocentric narrative by exploring how phonocentrism emerged in the first place. It explores the script reforms in China from the late 19th century to 1986. Instead of treating script reform as secondary to language reforms, Kuzuoğlu argues that script reforms had their own logic that was independent from language reforms, namely, the modern political economy of information (7). Building on James Beniger, Kuzuoğlu points out that in the making of a global information age, information and capital were intimately related (9), and labor efficiency was prioritized and maximized (10). To Kuzuoğlu, this global information age was not even; it was structured through alphabetic technologies as it came from Western historical experiences (12). Chinese script became ill-fitting in this infrastructure, which disassembled the institutionalized practice of knowledge production and de-skilled mental and clerical laborers in China (11). Reformers of Chinese scripts thus sought ways to respond to the challenges provided by this new global infrastructure.

auditPapers.title: Clark Davis. God’s Scrivener: The Madness and Meaning of Jones Very.
auditPapers.abstract: In Transcendentalist circles, the poet Jones Very became briefly infamous in late 1838 for disrupting the refinements of Unitarian literary culture with an astonishing bout of religious enthusiasm. Arriving at Elizabeth Peabody’s door beside himself, he announced that he had come “to baptize you with the Holy Ghost & with fire” and then, sitting in her parlor, he revealed, “I am the Second Coming” (184–85). Just months earlier, Ralph Waldo Emerson had given his startling address at Harvard Divinity School in which he excoriated the dry formality of the New England ministry and extolled the intensity of immediate religious experience. Maybe this youthful enthusiast was exactly the “newborn bard of the Holy Ghost” that Emerson had been prophesying (175). Up to the time of his mystic transformation, Very had a reputation as a promising poet and ambitious literary student; after his Harvard graduation, he was serving effectively as a Greek tutor while also preparing for the Unitarian ministry. However, when he announced to one of his Greek classes that the Holy Spirt was speaking through him and commanded his students to “flee to the mountains, for the end of all things is at hand,” Harvard spared no time in dispatching him for his religious mania (177). His academic career over, he was briefly confined to McLean Asylum, but the implications of his artful ventriloquizing of God’s voice had only begun to be sorted out. In God’s Scrivener: The Madness and Meaning of Jones Very, Clark Davis provides the first major biography of the poet-prophet in over fifty years, placing this episode of dramatic spiritual awakening, which baffled so many of his contemporaries, within the full sweep of his life.

auditPapers.title: Neil A. Knapp. Making Machines of Animals: The International Livestock Exposition.
auditPapers.abstract: Sampson, a four-year-old steer that stood over six feet tall and weighed more than three thousand pounds, attracted crowds at the 1904 World’s Fair in St. Louis. In Making Machines of Animals: The International Livestock Exposition, Neal Knapp demonstrates that Sampson’s extraordinary and prizewinning size was not a genetic oddity. Instead, Sampson and thousands of other steers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century were envisioned by a seemingly odd pairing of land-grant university professors, meatpackers, and farmers. But Sampson’s aesthetic was ideal for a brief moment as the modern slaughter-bound steer emerged with a standard, compact body and less than half the age of Sampson.

auditPapers.title: Emmanuel Kwaku Akyeampong. Independent Africa: The First Generation of Nation Builders.
auditPapers.abstract: In 1957, Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first sub-Saharan African nation to gain independence, and the following year, Guinea, under Sékou Touré, said no to membership in the French community and gained independence from France. Two years later, in 1960, seventeen African nations obtained independence, and the wave of an independence movement continued for the rest of the twentieth century. Independence was marked by high hopes and excitement, but the fanfare and promises ended quickly. By the end of the 1960s, military takeovers occurred in rapid succession on the continent, as many nations tottered on the brink of economic and social collapse. At independence, writes Emmanuel Kwaku Akyeampong in Independent Africa: The First Generation of Nation Builders, one in every four people in sub-Saharan Africa could neither read nor write, life expectancy stood at forty-one years, and disease and poverty were rampant. Two examples illustrate this: At independence, the Republic of Congo had sixteen university graduates, and Tanzania had two trained engineers and three medical doctors. Those numbers were similar in other African nations. Akyeampong’s book is an in-depth analysis of the actions and challenges faced by the first-generation African leaders in their goal to provide solutions to the most urgent problems of their countries. Though the author focuses on four leaders—Nkrumah, Touré, Leopold Senghor, and Julius Nyerere—the study also addressed the actions of others, many of whom were promoters of the ideas of modernization and development theories. Their interactions with Communist nations put them on a collision course with the US. Nkrumah and Touré bore the brunt of America’s negative response to their anti-Western statements and actions. Unlike them, Nyerere was cautious in statements against capitalism, practicing what the author referred to as “soft ideology” (184), and Western nations reciprocated and sent more aid to Tanzania.

They celebrated the first sight of land after leaving the English Channel—usually Madeira or Tenerife. They witnessed flying fish landing on deck; they endured the heat of the tropics; they marveled at the ceremonies crossing the equator. Further south, Cape pigeons followed the ship in strong winds and cold weather, before it finally rounded the Cape of Good Hope and entered the Indian Ocean. He bounds his study in the age of sail, specifically on ships sailing to India (mostly but not exclusively East Indiamen), and specifically on the part of the voyage that took place in the Atlantic, both going and coming.

While this is not the central question of Christopher Ewing’s The Color of Desire: The Queer Politics of Race in the Federal Republic of Germany after 1970, this outstanding book does explain how homonationalism—the alignment of nationalist ideology and LGBTQ rights—gained prominence in Germany. Indeed, we are currently experiencing a retrenchment in the institutional and public support of antiracist policies and queer rights. Ewing cautions us that to consider this turn a “backlash” is a facile explanation that ends up “blaming queer people of color for the brutality leveled against them” (162). Instead, Ewing contends that a tension between “queer fascism” and “queer antiracism” has characterized LGBTQ politics in Germany since the 1970s.

auditPapers.title: Tiya Miles. Wild Girls: How the Outdoors Shaped the Women Who Challenged a Nation.
auditPapers.abstract: In a poem as powerful and resonant today as it was when she first composed it, June Jordan spoke of the power of the outdoors to help reorient our social and political outlooks in dismaying times. Hiking together, as Jordan often did with many of her friends, they were standing in a redwood forest grove in Northern California. According to the poem, Walker called on Jordan to overcome her sense of dismay and political paralysis by focusing on the grove and then on one mighty tree.

auditPapers.title: Mikkel Dack. Everyday Denazification in Postwar Germany: The Fragebogen and Political Screening during the Allied Occupation.
auditPapers.abstract: The Allied occupation of Germany and the early years of the country’s Cold War division have long drawn interest from academic scholarship. auditPapers.title: Mark Santow. Saul Alinsky and the Dilemmas of Race: Community Organizing in the Postwar City.
auditPapers.abstract: In the half century since his death, the community organizer and author Saul Alinsky has become something of a legend. His organizing model was coopted by conservatives in the Tea Party movement and also disparaged by conservatives as radicalism and Marxism. He influenced liberal giants such as Barack Obama, who learned about Alinsky as a neighborhood organizer in Chicago in the 1980s, and Hilary Clinton, who wrote an undergraduate thesis on him. Several popular and academic books have assessed his impact on organizing and the postwar left. Mark Santow’s book Saul Alinsky and the Dilemmas of Race seeks to fill a gap in the literature by analyzing Alinsky’s efforts to integrate the Southside of Chicago from the 1930s through the 1960s and placing them within the broader context of the urban political economy of the postwar era. Santow explains that the book is an attempt to use Alinsky’s strategies and perspectives to better understand the modern struggle for social justice in an era of renewed interested in how race and place shape identity and opportunity. The book is a series of case studies that highlight how incredibly difficult it is to create meaningful change through local organizing and activism, especially regarding race, segregation, and inequity. In my estimation, Alinsky’s attempts to integrate the Southside largely mirror the successes and failures of his other organizing efforts.

auditPapers.title: Wei Yu Wayne Tan. Blind in Early Modern Japan: Disability, Medicine, and Identity.
auditPapers.abstract: An observant visitor to Japan will quickly notice the many accommodations in cities and towns around the country made for visually impaired people. In Tokyo, for example, one routinely encounters braille on elevator panels, audible pedestrian crossing signals, and tactile paving on sidewalks to aid those with vision issues in navigating the city. Such developments are noteworthy given that people with mobility issues still have considerable difficulty accessing even major subway and train stations in Japan due to the lack of elevators and wheelchair lifts. Wei Yu Wayne Tan’s book Blind in Early Modern Japan sheds light on the deep history of blind people in Japan by exploring the social and political conditions that shaped the lives of visually impaired people in the early modern period. Building on the work of musicologist Gerald Groemer, much of this work centers on the “guild of the blind,” an organization that integrated those with vision impairment into the Tokugawa status system. Significantly, this was the only social group for people with a disability that benefited from this form of institutional protection, problematic though it was. Tan goes beyond Groemer’s important body of work by exploring the medical discourse surrounding blindness, as well as the involvement of blind people in other occupations including moneylending, acupuncture, and massage. Consisting of six brief chapters, this clearly written and well-illustrated book offers an important window into conceptions of disability and the lives of people who are disabled.

auditPapers.title: Natasha Erlank. Convening Black Intimacy: Christianity, Gender, and Tradition in Early Twentieth-Century South Africa.
auditPapers.abstract: Natasha Erlank’s Convening Black Intimacy explores how Black South African Christians (largely, but not exclusively, Xhosa from the Eastern Cape) understood, practiced, and articulated their emotional and sexual relationships, roughly in the period between the creation of the Union of South Africa in 1910 and the victory of the National Party in 1948. The book covers a range of issues: conceptions of masculinity as revealed in Xhosa circumcision rituals, the importance of kinship, the fluid and changing boundaries between public and private as conceived in traditional African and in African Christian circles; the role of women, who carried “the privilege and burden of lineage reproduction” (4); issues of polygamy, lobola (the gift/payment of cattle to the parents of the bride), church weddings, and the status that such ceremonies entailed. By its nature, a historical investigation of these matters is sensitive and elusive. The author uses a rich variety of sources: church pronouncements and disciplinary procedures, civil court records, a vigorous African press, in both English and isiXhosa, where articles and the letter pages are replete with diverse opinions on these issues. The book also introduces the importance of intimate letter writing, one of the consequences of Christian education and literacy.

auditPapers.title: Inside the History Lab
auditPapers.abstract: Team Lee, a volunteer group operating in present day Vietnam, is engaged in the work of historical memory. auditPapers.title: Eric C. Nystrom and R. A. R. Edwards. Ordinary Lives: Recovering Deaf Social History Through the American Census.
auditPapers.abstract: In Ordinary Lives: Recovering Deaf Social History Through the American Census, Eric C. Nystrom and R. A. R. Edwards propose a new methodological approach in deaf history. Raising issues with the current state of the field, which tends to center on Deaf cultural institutions (schools, advocacy organizations, and community spaces), they call for more extensive biographical research. In contrast, Ordinary Lives focuses (as the title suggests) on “ordinary deaf people” and the “long-term trends in American history that shaped their lives” (2). Using a combination of social history methods, approaches from digital humanities, and emerging fields like deaf geography, Nystrom and Edwards offer a new approach to the field. Instead of focusing on overarching changes in deaf education and the rise of Deaf culture in American history, Nystrom and Edwards hope to diversify the subjects of deaf history. Deaf thought leaders tended to be white men, and institutional histories often highlight hearing voices above Deaf voices. While scholars like Nora Ellen Groce, Harlan Lane, Richard Pillard, and Mary French have conducted case studies on Deaf-centric spaces, Nystrom and Edwards find fault with these investigations. These studies place “attention on the non-representative, deaf-centric world,” which was largely inaccessible to the majority of deaf Americans (9). Nystrom and Edwards argue that deaf history heretofore has left out audiologically deaf persons (centering hereditarily deaf persons instead) and has forgotten about deaf people who did not attend major schools like the American School for the Deaf or the New York School for the Deaf. The authors also highlight a temporal gap in the field, noting that deaf history has centered either on the rise of educational opportunities in the early nineteenth century or on the solidification and reclamation of Deaf culture in the latter half of the twentieth century. In contrast, Ordinary Lives revolves on the latter half of the nineteenth century, a time period that is critical to deaf history as it demarcates the rise of oralism and eugenics-centered philosophy spurred by Alexander Graham Bell and others (35–56). Nystrom and Edwards propose using “Deaf Social History” to fill this historiographical gap (10).

auditPapers.title: James R. Fichter. Tea: Consumption, Politics, and Revolution, 1773–1776.
auditPapers.abstract: Tea is an obvious candidate for the genre of global commodity history. Linking China, India, and European empires, both directly and through its diverse accoutrements from porcelain to sugar, it evokes emerging early modern capitalism in all its barefaced imperial violence, geopolitical intrigue, and cosmopolitan cultural pretensions. But Tea, James Fichter’s deeply researched second monograph, is not that kind of book. It is, instead, a book about the politics of boycotts, and an account of the revolutionary shift in public authority that took place in parts of British North America during the two-and-a-half years between the famous destruction of the tea in Boston harbor and the United States’ declaration of independence. The ill-fated tea aboard the Dartmouth, the Eleanor, and the Beaver was not the only East India Company tea to reach the mainland colonies in 1773 (that year’s Tea Act having allowed the Company to sell directly to colonial consignees for the first time). Fichter traces the fates of the Polly, triumphantly turned back from Philadelphia by patriot crowds; the William, wrecked off Cape Cod only for its cargo of tea to be rescued and, eventually, consumed by Loyalists and soldiers during the 1776 siege of Boston; and the London, whose tea was seized and landed by the Charleston customs officers and, in the end, sold off for the benefit of revolutionary South Carolina. Their stories show how differently things might have gone in Boston and, thus, how contingent the tea party moment was.

auditPapers.title: Michael H. Kater. After the Nazis: The Story of Culture in West Germany.
auditPapers.abstract: Michael H. Kater’s book After the Nazis: The Story of Culture in West Germany falls into a rare historical genre. It deals with culture as the sum of cultural productions and their creators in the fields of literature, visual arts, music, film, theater, and journalism. Which is very different from the structural version of culture that shapes works like Axel Schildt’s and Detlef Siegfried’s 2009 compendium Deutsche Kulturgeschichte: Die Bundesrepublik von 1945 bis zur Gegenwart (Munich: Carl Hanser Verlag). In Kater’s book, by contrast, culture in the narrow sense is also itself a subject of history; it can have an “apotheosis,” be “in decline,” and “compromise,” (xiv) expressions the author uses to refer to the content of his two preceding books, Weimar: From Enlightenment to Present (2014) and Culture in Nazi Germany (2019). After the Nazis is a big narrative endeavor that aims at understanding culture’s role in the “relative success of the Federal Republic” (xiii). It is hard to argue with the assumption that democracy not only provides the possibility of free cultural expression but also needs enough cultural creations that use their aesthetic possibilities to critically react to oppressive political and social tendencies. After nearly four hundred pages, Kater concludes that West Germany’s culture was indeed “a check” in the checks and balances of the Federal Republic (382).

auditPapers.title: Sarah Percy. Forgotten Warriors: The Long History of Women in Combat.
auditPapers.abstract: Sarah Percy’s new book, Forgotten Warriors, issues a call to arms against a fresh generation of authoritarians and patriarchists who have targeted women’s newly gained rights (at least in Western militaries) to engage in combat. Partly for this reason, the book has already been reviewed widely. Percy, an academic at the University of Queensland, makes her case by appealing to history, although this history is not the stuff of conventional wisdom. Rather, the author takes a revisionist approach to military history, arguing that women in the past had “survived and even thrived as part of a machine of war” (xv), although news of this realty was suppressed and has still not been conceded by many military historians (John Keegan is the author’s main target). Percy does not frame this erasure as a conspiracy, but rather the consequence of long-standing chauvinist patterns of authority, which she describes as “the playbook of patriarchy” (xvi). As Percy notes, the manifest ability of women to succeed in combat has only recently been acknowledged, allowed, and valorized. She admits that historically women have not “fought in the same numbers and in the same ways as men” (xiv), but she attributes this mainly to men preventing them from getting a chance to perform in combat, especially after the 19th century. The takeaway, according to Percy, is that through the longue durée women did succeed in proving their ability in combat, and consistent examples of their presence on the battlefield made female warriors more than exceptions to a general rule. She also condemns political and military establishments for trying—not always successfully—to keep women out of combat, thereby denying them a way to demonstrate “the virtues that we associate with success in society, politics and . . . just about every field of human endeavour” (284–85).

auditPapers.title: Rebekah E. Pite. Sharing Yerba Mate: How South America’s Most Popular Drink Defined a Region.
auditPapers.abstract: Whether consumed as an infusion or in some other form, stimulants are a common feature of human cultures across time and place. While some, like tea and coffee, have been adopted and embraced globally, others have remained largely regional and continue to define regional and national cultures. One example of the latter is yerba mate, a South American stimulant infusion typically consumed using a gourd or cup (mate) and a special straw (bombilla), and often shared and consumed collectively with others. Rebekah E. Pite’s book Sharing Yerba Mate: How South America’s Most Popular Drink Defined a Region is a well-researched, engaging, and important look at yerba mate’s history and geography of cultivation and consumption from the precolonial era to the present. While patterns of consumption and cultivation have evolved over time, yerba mate remains an important marker of culture and identity in parts of South America, even as it has gradually extended its global reach in recent decades. Pite traces mate’s production and consumption from what is now Paraguay to Peru and Chile, and later to Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. Using a variety of written and, perhaps most notably, visual sources, this study weaves this plant and drink into South America’s history in engaging and fascinating ways for regional and nonregional specialists alike.

auditPapers.title: Samuel Moyn. Liberalism Against Itself: Cold War Intellectuals and the Making of Our Times.
auditPapers.abstract: “Cold War liberalism was a catastrophe—for liberalism.” That is how Samuel Moyn opens his latest book, Liberalism Against Itself, pithily summarizing its main message. In the following pages, Moyn gives us a swift overview of Cold War liberalism’s key thinkers, with chapters on Judith Shklar, Isaiah Berlin, and Karl Popper, as well as on lesser lights like Gertrude Himmelfarb and Lionel Trilling. This cast of characters is used to illuminate key aspects of Cold War liberalism, most notably its rejection of any belief in collective emancipation as dangerously proto-totalitarian. Moyn also makes a surprise addition by including a chapter on Hannah Arendt. Arendt herself of course rejected the label “liberal,” but, as Moyn convincingly shows, she might nevertheless be described as a “fellow traveller,” being equally skeptical of the possibility to institutionalize an emancipatory politics. Moyn’s book contributes to a burgeoning literature on Cold War liberalism. But while much of the recent literature has been written by fanboys, Moyn strikes a very different tone. In his account, thinkers like Berlin and Popper remade the liberal tradition for the worse. Their liberalism was drained of any commitment to perfectionism or progressivism, starting instead from a quasi-Augustinian emphasis on the sinfulness of man. (Ironically so, since all protagonists of Moyn’s book were Jewish). Cold War liberals lionized thinkers like Lord Acton and Sigmund Freud, who shared their bleak view on human nature, “yoking liberalism to original sin as well as psychic bestiality” (5). At the same time, they rejected the legacy of theorists committed to the possibility of true human emancipation such as Jean-Jacques Rousseau, G. W. F. Hegel and Karl Marx, and, in Berlin’s case, the entire Enlightenment. Thus, they turned liberalism from a doctrine wedded to hope to one centered on fear.

auditPapers.title: Emma Day. In Her Hands: Women’s Fight against AIDS in the United States.
auditPapers.abstract: Over the last fifteen years, a growing number of historians have described the impact of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the United States and the stories of activists who demanded education, services, and medical research to fight the disease. auditPapers.title: Simon Partner. Koume’s World: The Life and Work of a Samurai Woman Before and After the Meiji Restoration.
auditPapers.abstract: For a good portion of her adult life Kawai Koume (1804–89), a woman born into the lower ranks of the samurai class in central-western Japan, kept a diary. With long gaps in between, the surviving entries cover 18 years between 1837 and 1885. Simon Partner uses this diary as the main primary source for the highly readable and informative book Koume’s World: The Life and Work of a Samurai Woman Before and After the Meiji Restoration. The book proceeds chronologically, beginning with Koume’s upbringing in Wakayama, the castle town of Kishū domain. Her father and grandfather were scholars and advisers to the daimyo, a position that accorded them high prestige but middling to low income. Making ends meet within limited means was a constant challenge, one that fell primarily on women as household managers. In contrast to the image of samurai women as objects of patriarchal domination, Partner points out that Koume had considerable authority in her family not only because of her active role in household governance, but also because she was an only daughter whose husband married into the family as its heir and took the Kawai name—this was a quite common practice among samurai and commoners at the time. Koume’s own father had done the same, and so both Koume and her mother lived their lives in their natal homes rather than marrying “out” and being subject to the wishes of their husbands and in-laws as was the norm in much of Japan. (As a small criticism of an otherwise smooth narrative, Partner repeatedly renders the term for an adopted son-in-law and heir as a “muko [husband] husband,” an odd redundancy when he could simply say “adopted husband” or “husband adoptee,” both far better translations for the commonly used Japanese term for such men, muko yōshi.)

auditPapers.title: Laura K. Muñoz. Desert Dreams: Mexican Arizona and the Politics of Educational Equality.
auditPapers.abstract: Contributing to the rich historiography on schools and schooling as sites of liberation and community affirmation that has emerged in the last twenty years, Laura K. Muñoz’s book Desert Dreams: Mexican Arizona and the Politics of Educational Equality reminds us of the critical nature of placemaking in the shadow of both shifting borders and ideologies. Arizonenses, as Muñoz refers to Mexican American Arizonans, “intellectualized a politics of education—rooted in theory, history and practice—to demand constitutional rights for themselves and their children” (3). In doing so, Arizonenses positioned themselves as facilitating conversations on their own future and that of the newly admitted state. Weaving together newspapers, yearbooks, oral histories, along with federal, state, and territorial records, Muñoz offers a thoughtful history of the intentionality on both sides: Arizonenses quest for education and all its benefits, and the territory’s and later the state’s attempts to halt their progress. Muñoz shows the ways the Arizonenses generational land claims, very much central to their educational or desert dreams, were also tied to dispossession affecting Indigenous communities. Schools and education became the perfect venue for Arizonenses to carve out a place for their community, but this was at times a pathway dependent on their classed, land-owning status, which later became limited by racial scripts that no longer envisioned them as having standing in state politics in the mid-twentieth century. Muñoz shows how Arizonenses sought to affirm contemporary racial views, seeking to embrace or center their citizenship and by extension perceived whiteness to distinguish themselves from African Americans in the area. As Muñoz argues, while Juan Crow and Jim Crow operated to exploit the racial differences of Black and Brown communities to protect the racial hierarchy of the era, “some Mexican Americans promoted these differences to secure their whiteness” (152).

auditPapers.title: Diya Gupta. India in the Second World War: An Emotional History.
auditPapers.abstract: Diya Gupta’s book India in the Second World War has assumed the daunting task of revealing the emotional impact on Indian subjects as they crossed the physical and mental terrain of global war. This is no mean feat, as the conflict’s effects on the socially and culturally diverse “Indian” subject defy any sort of blanket description. The war was felt in vastly different ways depending on one’s perspective, whether a hungry Bengali peasant, a Parsi woman in Bombay, an English educated member of the literati, or a sepoy, those myriad soldiers who fought for the empire. Indeed, the author summons them all in the service of this compelling work. Gupta’s broad approach points to a salient fact: There was no singular Indian experience, no commonly understood national narrative of victory or defeat despite the shared economic depravations the war brought to the subcontinent. In the wake of World War I, B. R. Ambedkar, the Dalit barrister and author of the country’s 1949 constitution, inadvertently argued as much in suggesting that India lacked nationhood since those who held no caste status, such as himself, by no means enjoyed the equality that enabled a population to imagine a common community. As he put it, “a government for the people, but not by the people, is sure to educate some to be Masters and others to be subjects.” Ambedkar saw the end of the British Raj as somewhat moot if it were merely swapped for an elite Brahmin Raj. Even the staid Indian Army, home of the traditionally recruited “martial races” of northern India, was highly stratified in terms of region and language. The Sikh solider, or sepoy, would have no way of communicating with a Gurkha from Nepal. Building an emotional history of wartime India then, as Gupta has done, is especially challenging.

auditPapers.title: Robin Judd. Between Two Worlds: Jewish War Brides After the Holocaust.
auditPapers.abstract: Robin Judd’s book Between Two Worlds: Jewish War Brides After the Holocaust centers the figure of the Jewish war bride, a previously all but neglected subject in modern Jewish- and 20th-century US and European historiography. Judd frames the Jewish war bride in legal, social, gender, and cultural historical contexts and follows these figures through the Holocaust and post-Holocaust landscapes of Central and Eastern Europe, the United Kingdom, and North America, among other places. Jewish war brides and their families, as Judd makes clear, faced unique challenges before and after emigration which, in significant ways, set them apart from the broader war bride population—the civilian women who married male servicemembers (and in rare cases the civilian men who married female servicemembers)—and which Judd uses as an entry point into her rich and multilayered study. Between Two Worlds is elegantly crafted and beautifully written, making it a pleasure to read and suggesting that its reach may well extend beyond purely academic circles. Judd deftly intertwines biographical accounts of her fascinating subjects (including, in the conclusion, the stunning story of her own grandparents) and their often epic struggles with the legal, political, religious, and social situation in allied occupied Europe in the immediate aftermath of the war, making this book at once intensely human and rigorously scholarly, shifting back and forth, as it does, between individual narratives and broader social and political forces. The structure is compelling: The chapters foreground key themes and stages—liberation, encounter, courtship and marriage, immigration, and acculturation—as the narrative moves through time from the war’s immediate aftermath through internment in displaced persons camps; legal, religious, and community struggles over marriage and citizenship applications; immigration stories; and then issues of integration and acculturation in new homelands rife with antisemitic prejudice, racism, and Cold War paranoia.

auditPapers.title: Ashkan Rezvani Naraghi. A Social History of Modern Tehran: Space, Power, and the City.
auditPapers.abstract: Ashkan Rezvani Naraghi’s book, A Social History of Modern Tehran: Space, Power, and the City, takes us on a journey through the transformation of the urban environment of Iran’s capital from the nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century. This book is an incredibly rich mine of information for anyone interested in social history. As a scholar working on political contention and mobilizations, I appreciated Naraghi’s mastery in explaining that the socially embedded knowledge of how and where to protest builds upon existing spatial practices of communal life and how such knowledge has changed across the decades as a reflection of the meaning of “living together”. Intertwining cultural history, human and political geography, economic, gender, and class analysis, A Social History of Modern Tehran is a must-read for any scholar interested in Iran and an extremely beneficial reading for social scientists in general. Written with flair, the volume includes six chapters through which the “ontological shift in the conceptualization and representation of the spatiality of Tehran” during the centuries (1) is examined in depth. Engaging in the analysis of such a shift, chapters 1 and 2 focus on the Constitutional Revolution of 1905–1906 and the period preceding it. The chapters explain how Tehran moved from being a city of fragmented urban communities, divided by profession and other identity markers, who lived in segregated space—the coffeehouses of professional guilds, the zurkhaneh or traditional gyms with their strict hierarchies of belonging, among the others—to become a city with an emerging public and cross-communal space, thanks to the pressure of religion and protest politics, which acted as unifying forces. Mosques, in particular those that were not linked to a specific community but served larger portions of the population (Friday mosques, for instance), transformed into political spaces open to different communities and played an important role in the logistics of the revolution. Naraghi argues that this ignited a process of secularization and gender diversification in how urban spatiality was understood and experienced in Tehran. While women did not live segregated and without contact with communal, outer urban geographies, they existed in separated spaces, the andaruni (the “within”), with sporadic free access to the outer space. The revolution changed this differential access, also thanks to a new urban knowledge that contextually emerged in nineteenth-century Iran.

auditPapers.title: Matthew Bowman. The Abduction of Betty and Barney Hill: Alien Encounters, Civil Rights, and the New Age in America.
auditPapers.abstract: Betty and Barney Hill were an interracial couple from New Hampshire who, in 1961, reported the first ever abduction by extraterrestrial aliens. While accounts of alien abduction proliferated some decades later, the Hills’ account acts as a sort of foundational text in UFO studies, an inflection point in the longer history of belief in UFOs and extraterrestrials whereupon ETs were understood to shift focus from outer space to the inner space of human bodies and psyches. In his book The Abduction of Betty and Barney Hill: Alien Encounters, Civil Rights, and the New Age in America, religious historian Matthew Bowman acknowledges existing scholarship that has examined belief in alien abduction narratives as “an expression of anxiety and unease” (4). Bowman, however, is not fundamentally concerned with explaining or interpreting the belief in aliens or alien abduction. He seeks instead, through a close examination of the Hills themselves, including the social, cultural, and political forces that shaped them, to read their changing narrativization of their experience as a sort of vexing exercise in world building. Ultimately, Bowman’s reading of the Hills’ experience acts as a compelling case study of the history of the broader erosion of trust both in institutions and in the belief that citizens can work with and alongside those in power toward a greater good.

auditPapers.title: Geoffrey M. Hodgson. The Wealth of a Nation: Institutional Foundations of English Capitalism.
auditPapers.abstract: Geoffrey M. Hodgson’s ambitiously titled book has several equally ambitious goals: to explain the rise of capitalism, to offer an account of English economic development from the Norman Conquest to the nineteenth century, to present Hodgson’s brand of legal institutionalism and institutional evolution, and to identify lessons from English economic development. Not least, The Wealth of a Nation wants to tell us why other economists and historians’ explanations are wrong, or at least insufficient. Few would wish to disagree with the premise that explaining the distinctive and unprecedented development of the British economy is an important question. But my suspicion is that few will come to lean heavily on Hodgson’s analysis or method. What might we take from Hodgson’s book? Positively, Hodgson makes a good case that in thinking about capitalism, we should think about financial capital and not just about capital goods, and that in using the word “capital,” we should be careful not to conflate the two. His view that financial development is an important ingredient in economic growth (and that the absence of finance can constrain development) represents one (arguably well-established) position in a debate that has been running for some decades. His description of generalized Darwinism is a digestible summary of an approach to historical and societal development that should allow readers to take a view on its utility. And it is always interesting and thought-provoking to see an attempt to digest centuries of economic, political, and social development into any kind of structure.

auditPapers.title: Susan C. I. Grunewald. From Incarceration to Repatriation: German Prisoners of War in the Soviet Union.
auditPapers.abstract: Susan C. I. Grunewald’s book From Incarceration to Repatriation examines Soviet policy toward German soldiers captured during the Second World War. Of primary interest to the author are the motivations of Soviet leaders as they processed, accommodated, and exploited the large number of prisoners who entered Soviet custody beginning in early 1943. This compact volume is clearly argued and thoroughly documented using archives from Russia, Germany, and the United States. The primary contributions of the work are in three areas: the role of German prisoners in the economy, their importance to Soviet domestic and international politics, and their continuing legacy for Russian political and cultural affairs. Once the Soviet army began capturing large numbers of Germans in 1943, their potential economic contributions were paramount in Soviet officials’ minds. Prisoners of war landed under the jurisdiction of the People’s Commissariat for Internal Affairs (NKVD), which had long experience managing forced labor in the notorious Gulag. It was common after the war, Grunewald points out, to consider the Germans just additional victims of Soviet brutality. While prisoners of war faced privations and restrictions similar to the inmates of the Gulag, however, the Germans often received attention and care not due to Soviet citizens, free or unfree, who faced starvation and political repression during the war and during the lean years that followed. German prisoners certainly suffered, but Soviet authorities labored to keep them alive—and working. Prisoners who became seriously ill or were otherwise incapable of work—whether due to wartime wounds, to the appalling transit arrangements, or the rigors of work and camp life—received priority for repatriation so as to spare the state the expense of their upkeep.

auditPapers.title: Wayne Lee. The Cutting-Off Way: Indigenous Warfare in Eastern North America, 1500–1800.
auditPapers.abstract: Wayne Lee’s The Cutting-Off Way provides a valuable addition to the growing historiography on Indigenous warfare in North America. The scope of the work is impressive. Lee focuses on a region that encompasses what is today the entire United States east of the Mississippi, and he focuses on three hundred years of history. The book represents another milestone in his influential work in early modern Indigenous, North American, and Atlantic military history. The Cutting-Off Way “insists that we take Native Americans and their modes, system, and beliefs about war on their own terms” (2). Lee acknowledges the “need” to “de-exoticize” Indigenous “warfare,” and he uses modern technical military terminology in his analysis (13). The author uses the term “to cut off” because it is descriptive of the “tactical and operational goals of an Indian attack” on enemy targets (3). He argues that Indigenous offensive missions sought to cut off their opponents from stronger forces. Indigenous militaries used the element of surprise, were eager to take prisoners, and sought to retreat when facing stronger defending forces. In early modern North America east of the Mississippi River, Lee maintains, war was an “endemic” feature in Indigenous societies.

auditPapers.title: Cookie Woolner. The Famous Lady Lovers: Black Women and Queer Desire before Stonewall.
auditPapers.abstract: Cookie Woolner’s book The Famous Lady Lovers: Black Women and Queer Desire before Stonewall begins in 1920 with the discovery of a “new sex problem” in the Chicago Whip, a Black newspaper. The problem was that Black women in Northern cities were having sexual relationships with each other and, in some cases, leaving their marriages to do so. Woolner’s engaging new book focuses on the lives of these so-called “problem” women in cities including Chicago, New York, Detroit, and Philadelphia during the 1920s and 1930s. Woolner charts how these women created “modern new identities, social networks, and gathering spaces” in the interwar urban North long before the Stonewall Uprising of 1969 (2). The Great Migration, Woolner shows, enabled Black women’s queer lives by allowing them to leave their families of origin and organize their domestic lives in unconventional ways. They had a lasting impact, she argues, on American culture and sexual norms.

auditPapers.title: H. Yumi Kim. Madness in the Family: Women, Care, and Illness in Japan.
auditPapers.abstract: H. Yumi Kim’s book Madness in the Family: Women, Care, and Illness in Japan is a welcome addition to the history of medicine, society, and the family in modern Japan. Kim’s interest lies in the “centrality of family in the care of those considered mad and in the creation of gendered understandings of madness” (4). The book’s center of gravity lies at the turn of the 20th century, but it looks backward to the Edo period (1600–1868). A brief epilogue sketches 1945 to the present. Across this long era, Kim emphasizes a constant—officials expected families, primarily women, to serve as the main caregivers for those considered mad. The introduction lures readers in with an intriguing story about a young woman in rural Japan plagued by “fox attachment” in the 1890s, a sign of “mental and spiritual affliction” (2). Her relatives sought out various forms of medical care to no avail. During this time, psychiatrists, trained in a new discipline derived from Western models, redefined fox attachment as an indication of mental illness. Government officials did not always agree with them. However, in this case, officials supported the new understanding because it furthered their cause of “civilization and enlightenment” against superstition. In spite of some state concessions to psychiatrists’ demands (for example, a 1919 law mandating a mental hospital in each prefecture), the government expected families to care for ill members except in the most extreme circumstances. Above all, officials wished to avoid building a welfare state.

auditPapers.title: Max Deardorff. A Tale of Two Granadas. Custom, Community, and Citizenship in the Spanish Empire, 1568–1668.
auditPapers.abstract: Building on extensive archival research in Spain, Colombia, and Italy, A Tale of Two Granadas is a fantastic addition to the growing field of governance and citizenship in the multiethnic, composite Spanish Empire during the 16th and 17th centuries. The book explores how Indigenous and mestizo peoples in the New Kingdom of Granada (present-day Colombia) and moriscos (Muslim people who were forced to convert to Christianity) in the peninsular Kingdom of Granada negotiated a place in the political arena within the context of the religious transformations brought by the Council of Trent. The author, Max Deardorff, follows an encompassing comparison in which processes occurring on both sides of the Atlantic influence each other, share protagonists, and ultimately are part of a single, complex drive toward political organization across the Spanish Empire. The key element in the argument is the evolving conflict between two views of integration/segregation of new converts as Christianity expanded among the territories absorbed by the Spanish monarchy in Europe and the Americas. One segment of the political spectrum sought to use concepts of race and blood purity (limpieza de sangre), to exclude former Muslims, mestizos, and Indigenous peoples from power positions and urban governance. Another political posture drove for integration through what Deardorff calls “Christian citizenship,” a set of values and duties associated with community life shaped by church precepts such as marriage, mass attendance, and catechism. Even though the first stance ultimately prevailed, the wide array of case studies analyzed by the author shows how neophytes carved out urban privileges by taking advantage of the church’s role in the political cementation of the Spanish dominions. The result is a highly nuanced discussion that draws the reader deeply into the cultural and political milieu of two little-studied areas of the Spanish Empire.

auditPapers.title: Tobias Becker. Yesterday: A New History of Nostalgia.
auditPapers.abstract: Nostalgia, we all know, comes dressed in sepia. In Yesterday: A New History of Nostalgia, Tobias Becker uncovers it for us in black and white, like a photo negative: not the thing itself—emotion, disease, style, or whatever it may be—but rather a sprawling “nostalgia discourse,” or what is said about nostalgia. This is a book about “how and why the term nostalgia is used” (232), or has been used since the 1960s in the United States, United Kingdom, and, to a lesser extent, Germany and France. These uses have also tended to be negative, but in the pejorative sense of the word, bordering on insult. Few proudly claim to be nostalgic or like to be labeled as such; on the contrary, many are experts at telling others that they are stuck in the past. Herein lies the originality of Becker’s approach: Nostalgia is like modernity’s black hole, the “counterpart or antithesis to progress” (5) that we all need, whether to quietly comfort ourselves in the face of change or imply that we, unlike others, can still change for the better. (No wonder Derrida was interested in it). Its gravitational pull has been hard to ignore since the 1960s, Becker argues, when the teleology of progress came under intense scrutiny. It is not so much the History that is New here, but Nostalgia itself: The thing is in fact older and harks back to the late 17th century, when the term was first coined and defined as a deadly form of homesickness. Nostalgia has always been in dialectical tension with capitalist modernity and for 200 years people succumbed to it when forced to leave their homes (by war, migration, enslavement). But between the 19th and 20th centuries we learned to cope with nostalgic yearning and rearticulate it in time—as a lost past—rather than space. Cope with, and eventually indulge, for as Becker points out, nostalgia became a household word after the Second World War—its success rivaled only by the vitriol of its detractors.

auditPapers.title: Christopher Perreira. Archiving Medical Violence: Consent and the Carceral State.
auditPapers.abstract: In his illuminating book Archiving Medical Violence, Christopher Perreira examines racialized forms of state-sanctioned medical violence in US colonial, imperial, and national contexts. He reads US racial formations through medicine and public health and criminalized bodies and diseases to highlight the fault lines of scientific and national progress in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, arguing that public health and security have borrowed from each other to “inform the production of racialized discourses that give meaning to the figure of the prisoner-patient” (22). Perreira understands medicine and public health as foundational to US settler colonialism, racial capitalism, and cultural politics. He insists that the devaluation and continual (un)making of criminalized, racialized prisoner-patients create the conditions for their necromantic revival and revaluation in triumphalist medicine and public health. The book lies at the intersection of Indigenous, race, ethnic, gender, carceral, and science and technology studies, and cultural theory. Perreira contributes to these fields not just by scrutinizing criminality in a eugenic register (a longstanding approach in historical scholarship) but by tracing how criminality has been defined and activated in medicine and public health and how the meanings of violence in these venues have changed and become normalized over time. Cast in the mold of “the anachronistic (re)turn” in many recent history-informed interdisciplinary studies, Archiving Medical Violence has no qualms about darting back and forth between past and present. Such an approach offers entry points to think about the undercurrents structuring historical racial inequalities, harmful legacies, and contemporary national reckonings (2, 20–21).

auditPapers.title: Jayita Sarkar. Ploughshares and Swords: India’s Nuclear Program in the Global Cold War.
auditPapers.abstract: In this richly research and intricately argued book, Jayita Sarkar shows us how India’s program for the development of nuclear technology had to evolve by seemingly being all things to all people. Its journey toward developing the nuclear bomb—the “sword,” to use Sarkar’s metaphor—had to be completed by making skillful use of the arguments in favor of enabling the pursuit of nuclear research for developmentalist goals—or “ploughshare.” Yet, achieving these aims also involved navigating, and where possible, dismantling the “atomic apartheid” (to use the words of the Indian ambassador V. C. Trivedi, who represented India at the nonproliferation treaty negotiations in Geneva), which precluded countries such as India from accessing technical expertise for the development of nuclear weapons. Sarkar’s book takes us through the stages of India’s negotiations with the United States’ adamant stance that the acquisition of nuclear technology by countries other than itself should be restricted, while making use of the possibilies of the peaceful development of nuclear technology that conditional partnerships with states with nuclear capabilites could offer.

auditPapers.title: Daren E. Ray. Ethnicity, Identity, and Conceptualizing Community in Indian Ocean East Africa.
auditPapers.abstract: Ethnicity looms large over East African history and scholarship. While scholars reinventing the discipline of African history after the fall of European colonialism sought to prove that African ethnicities—rendered as “tribes”—were colonial inventions, the lived legacies of colonial tribalism have ensured the endurance of ethnicity as a category of inquiry. This is particularly true of scholarship on Kenya, where “ethnic politics” continues to define election cycles in the twenty-first century. Yet Daren E. Ray’s book, Ethnicity, Identity, and Conceptualizing Community in Indian Ocean East Africa, takes a novel approach to this familiar topic. Most impressive is Ray’s commitment to a longue durée approach; extending its analysis over at least two millennia, the book is an important corrective to a historiography primarily concerned with the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Interested in a pre-ethnic past, Ray turns to historical linguistics to frame his project around speech communities—specifically those who would come to speak Sabaki languages (including Kiswahili and Chimijikenda)—and the “schemas” that they assembled. Schemas, for Ray, are a dynamic alternative to the more static category of cultures, “shared mental maps” that provide a “reservoir of concepts, ideas, and resources” from which historical actors build categorizations, communities, and political claims (20, 50). By framing his book around Sabaki schemas, Ray seeks not only to conceptualize modern ethnicities as the result of “the incremental elaboration of ancestral strategies” but also to advance a “cis-Oceanic” approach that, by incorporating the hinterland into a broader “littoral” society, challenges coastal exceptionalism (5). Temporally and spatially ambitious in scope, then, a major strength of the book is the interdisciplinary method it necessarily employs.

auditPapers.title: Christopher Michael Blakley. Empire of Brutality: Enslaved People and Animals in the British Atlantic World.
auditPapers.abstract: Empire of Brutality: Enslaved People and Animals in the British Atlantic World examines the “more than human world” of slavery (2). By analyzing the multiplicity of relationships between enslaved people and animals in the British Atlantic in the long 18th century, the book represents a much-needed addition to the existing scholarship. Building on Atlantic histories of slavery and the animal turn in history, Christopher Michael Blakley uses human-animal relations to complicate our understanding of slavery and systems of power. The book explores the so-called dreaded comparison of enslaved peoples to nonhuman animals, and how and why enslavers tried to reduce enslaved peoples socially and ethically to an animal-like position. Throughout the book, Blakley effectively argues that Atlantic slaving did not annihilate African cultures or the minds of African people and render human beings to animal-like subjects. The greatest strength of the book is how Blakley repeatedly acknowledges the agency of enslaved people within the empire of brutality that slavery created, exploring the myriad ways that “enslaved people retained their humanity” (15).
