auditPapers.title: Guo-Quan Seng. Strangers in the Family: Gender, Patriliny, and the Chinese in Colonial Indonesia.
auditPapers.abstract: Guo-Quan Seng’s Strangers in the Family is a meticulously researched history of the formation of a settler Chinese community in Indonesia under Dutch colonial rule (1816–1942). Based on an impressive array of sources, including Dutch government records, the administrative and judicial documents of the Chinese Council of Batavia, and Sino-Malay vernacular press materials, it tackles a key question in the scholarship on Chinese migration and diaspora: How did the Chinese come to be essentialized as a patrilineal race and perpetual outsiders within? The book reflects a paradigm shift in the historiography on Asian mobility in the era of European colonial empires. In a departure from the conventional focus on the labor, capital, and intellect of men, Seng places women and gender at the center of his analysis and uncovers an obscured history of intimacies and estrangements between Asian migrant-to-settlers (his term, more on this later) and Indigenous and local-born women. He shows how profoundly these inter-Asian dynamics—and their regulation by the settler Chinese community—shaped modern ideas about identity and belonging. The result is a compelling challenge to the Eurocentrism of postcolonial studies that remains preoccupied with the European management of race, sex, and desire.

auditPapers.title: Melvin L. Rogers. The Darkened Light of Faith: Race, Democracy, and Freedom in African American Political Thought.
auditPapers.abstract: A renaissance has taken place in recent years regarding Black intellectual history. Thinking through the contributions of Black men and women to the larger streams of American, global, and intellectual history has marked some of the best-known works of history of late. The unique contribution of Black Americans to American political thought has especially seen an explosion, and Melvin L. Rogers’s book The Darkened Light of Faith: Race, Democracy, and Freedom in African American Political Thought is a tour-de-force in this field. For Rogers, reckoning with Black thinkers in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries is not just a question of Black intellectual history. The Darkened Light of Faith is a valiant, and ultimately successful, attempt to recalibrate how we think about American democracy and its fraught relationship with both race and history. Melvin Rogers’s academic monographs, edited collections, and public essays in such forums as Dissent and The Atlantic magazines continually deal with the tensions inherent in American democracy. In The Darkened Light of Faith, Rogers points out how Black thinkers have wrestled with those tensions throughout the history of the United States. “What is it about democracy,” Rogers poses at the beginning of his book, “that justifies our faith, especially African Americans’ faith, in it?” (3). For Rogers, the answer is one that threads the needle between two traditions: the growth of Afro-Pessimism, on the one hand, and the ideal of the “American Creed” popularized by Gunnar Myrdal in his study An American Dilemma: The Negro Problem and American Democracy. It is a push to, in Rogers’s words, “deploy the principle of making and remaking” who and what constitutes the American body politic (5). While white supremacy may be at the heart of the building of American democracy, Rogers’s book reminds us that numerous Black thinkers never accepted that argument without trying to rethink and reimagine what American democracy could, potentially, be.

auditPapers.title: Scott Ingram. Constitutional Inquisitors: The Origins and Practice of Early Federal Prosecutors.
auditPapers.abstract: Given the tremendous power that federal prosecutors have in modern American society, it is remarkable that no historian has explored their origins. In a new book, Constitutional Inquisitors: The Origins and Practice of Early Federal Prosecutors, Scott Ingram argues that the first federal district attorneys were “unintentionally established” as the nation’s premier law enforcement officers (7). According to Ingram, public prosecutors were originally nothing like the investigator-cum-advocates we have today. At the founding, private parties (usually victims) instigated and directed criminal prosecutions. Government attorneys functioned more as clerks, drafting indictments and compiling evidence to aid grand juries in deciding whether prosecution should proceed (though at times they also questioned witnesses and provided legal advice). Most important, public prosecutors did not investigate crimes, and they did not have the authority to direct or decline prosecution. Befitting their minor role, the first federal attorneys were largely an afterthought. The Constitution’s drafters and ratifiers debated the scope of federal criminal jurisdiction but paid little attention to who would enforce it. The only requirement in the Judiciary Act of 1789 was that the president appoint a “meet person learned in the law” to serve as the government’s attorney in each federal judicial district. George Washington tried to appoint well-regarded lawyers who supported the new federal government, but he was more concerned with who would serve as federal judges. Potential candidates were similarly ambivalent; other positions were more prestigious (like judges), or more lucrative (like customs collectors), prompting leading nominees—including future Chief Justice John Marshall—to decline the position.

auditPapers.title: Enrique Rodríguez-Alegría. How to Make a New Spain: The Material Worlds of Colonial Mexico City.
auditPapers.abstract: It is common knowledge that the encounter between Europeans and Indigenous groups in the Americas in the sixteenth century had disastrous consequences for local populations. Indigenous people were killed in great numbers, and colonialism led to a considerable loss of Indigenous languages, customs, and systems of knowledge. Yet despite this unprecedented destruction, a functioning society and new capital city were established soon after the fall of Tenochtitlan, the seat of the Mexica Empire, and we know considerably less about how this happened. It is this gap in our knowledge that Enrique Rodríguez-Alegría wishes to fill with his thought-provoking new monograph, How to Make a New Spain: The Material Worlds of Colonial Mexico City, which focuses on the first eighty years of colonial rule in Mexico (ca. 1521–1600). In this book, instead of centering the obvious conflicts that existed in colonial society, Rodríguez-Alegría shifts our attention to the interethnic alliances that made it possible to establish systems of exchange, build infrastructure, and create domestic livelihoods in the aftermath of the fall of the Mexica Empire. The work follows in the footsteps of scholars like James Lockhart, Matthew Restall, and Barbara Mundy, among others.

auditPapers.title: Rachel Chrastil. Bismarck’s War: The Franco-Prussian War and the Making of Modern Europe.
auditPapers.abstract: As Rachel Chrastil’s engaging new book, Bismarck’s War, demonstrates, the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 vividly combined modern and premodern elements. Like so many conflicts in the ancien regime, its immediate cause was a dynastic dispute—in this case, about the candidacy of a Hohenzollern prince for the Spanish throne. The war ended with a violent urban uprising that Karl Marx and his followers viewed as the model for the class struggles of the future. As they would in the twentieth century’s great wars, railways played a major role in transporting troops; the telegraph was used, albeit with imperfect success by both sides. But the same difficulties of movement and communication that had frustrated strategists for centuries remained; the Prussians won in part because they overcame these difficulties somewhat more successfully than the French. Soldiers fought with the breech-loading rifles that had transformed infantry tactics and even employed a rudimentary form of machine gun. The military use of hot air balloons hinted at the battlefield’s expansion into the air that would revolutionize warfare in the century ahead. At the same time, there were many familiar features from earlier wars, including a massive cavalry charge (perhaps the last in western Europe). As they had so often in the past, heads of state observed the battlefield and personally experienced the thrill of victory and the anguish of defeat. This would never happen again.

auditPapers.title: Wayne Soon. Global Medicine in China: A Diasporic History.
auditPapers.abstract: Meticulously researched and conceptually ambitious, Wayne Soon’s Global Medicine in China: A Diasporic History expands a growing historical revisionism that centers the Chinese diaspora as a proactive agent in transforming China’s modern history. A notable book with which Soon’s study dialogues is Shelly Chan’s Diaspora’s Homeland: Modern China in the Age of Global Migration (2018). Soon illustrates a historical process akin to the one documented by Chan, but Soon’s narrative is nuanced by a distinct viewpoint from the history of military medicine. The book argues that a military medical complex emerged in the 1930s and 1940s, comprising wartime curative and preventive medicine, China’s first blood bank, and military medical education. The architect behind this complex was the Singapore-born physician, Robert Lim, who played an instrumental role in the dissemination, implementation, and modernization of biomedicine in China and Taiwan. The book unveils both the global origins and transpacific consequences of this military medical complex, which culminated in the relocation of the National Defense Medical Center (NDMC) to Taipei, where it has thrived since 1949.

auditPapers.title: Paula S. DeVos. Compound Remedies: Galenic Pharmacy From the Ancient Mediterranean to New Spain.
auditPapers.abstract: This is an ambitious book and the program that it sets out is laudable. It opens with an account of a pharmacy in Mexico City from 1775 (the inventory, translated in an appendix, is a fascinating source for the history of medicine). Paula DeVos then relies on the inventory’s list of simples (singular natural substances), compounds (remedies from multiple substances), and distillations (remedies derived from chemical processing) to launch an exploration of pharmaceutical theory and practice—in terms of materials, techniques, and textual authorities—from the Roman period up through the 18th century. In one sense, the book is a reception history of Galen’s thought; in another sense, Compound Remedies is a global history, examining the medieval Mediterranean and Middle East before shifting focus to the early modern Spanish Empire and the changes (or lack thereof) to the medical landscape wrought by colonial apothecaries. DeVos argues successfully that pharmacy offers a compelling example of both continuity and malleability of thought—indeed, that as a tradition, it was particularly unusual in being constantly “in transit” across regions, cultures, and empires (15). Few monographs have attempted a longue durée study of herbal remedies or of Galenic transformation through to the modern period (Owsei Temkin’s 1973 Galenism appears on page 16 as the still-authoritative work). The great strength of the book is that it frames Mexican apothecaries as simply yet another peak in a long trajectory of the adaptation of pharmaceutical knowledge, calling out historians of science for frequently treating colonial medicine solely in terms of its derivation from, or challenge to, European norms.

auditPapers.title: Thomas Blake Earle. The Liberty to Take Fish: Atlantic Fisheries and Federal Power in Nineteenth-Century America.
auditPapers.abstract: Can the environment play an influential role in statecraft and diplomacy? In a new book examining fisheries as an effective lens for exploring nineteenth-century Anglo-US relations, Thomas Blake Earle answers in the affirmative. The Liberty to Take Fish derives its title from the Treaty of Paris (1783) that forever allowed the United States access to the fisheries on the Grand Banks and along the coasts of Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, and Labrador (5). Earle argues that fisheries, fishermen, and fish were central to the diplomatic tension and turbulence between Britain and the United States from the years following independence until after the Civil War. In the nineteenth-century, the United States was a maritime power comparable to other maritime powers such as the British Empire and the Dutch Republic, and fish were a valuable resource requiring extraction. Long an integral part of US statecraft, Americans saw fishermen and fish as guarantors of US political and commercial independence until a desire for peace with Britain during Reconstruction made the fisheries a lesser priority for the federal government. “The history of fisheries,” Earle contends, “is the history of statecraft” (4).

auditPapers.title: Said Amir Arjomand. Messianism and Sociopolitical Revolution in Medieval Islam.
auditPapers.abstract: Messianism and Sociopolitical Revolution in Medieval Islam is a fascinating and ambitious book. Said Amir Arjomand, who several decades ago produced insightful and historically grounded studies of the Islamic Revolution in Iran and its intellectual roots in Persian political thought and Shi′i notions of religious authority, recently turned to the classical Islamic period and early Islamic political institutions. His goal is “to enrich political theory and the sociology of revolution by a historicized analysis of messianism” (1) from its roots in pre-Islamic developments through the fourteenth century of the Common Era. The study is timely, he suggests, because Islamism, shaped by an apocalyptic and millennial worldview, has replaced the revolutionary model of 1789 and its subsequent refinement in Marxism-Leninism as the dominant revolutionary ideology of our time and “the engine of [contemporary] history” (4). After an introductory chapter that discusses theories of revolution and provides a summary of the book’s narratives and arguments, Arjomand turns to his topic. Recent scholarship on early Islamic history has argued that Islam must be understood not as a sudden break, as the startling eruption of a new historical force, as an earlier generation of Orientalists had assumed; rather, it should be viewed as a continuation of ideas, practices, and trends already present in the Mediterranean and Iranian worlds in Late Antiquity. The caliphate, for example, has been recast as the culmination of late Roman and Iranian caesaropapism. Arjomand worries that this approach has “minimized the distinctiveness of the emerging Islamic civilization and denied the revolutionary break it constituted in world history” (24). On the contrary, he says, we should consider “the rise of Islam as the great apocalyptic revolution of Late Antiquity” (24).

auditPapers.title: Chris Manias. The Age of Mammals: Nature, Development, & Paleontology in the Long Nineteenth Century.
auditPapers.abstract: Dinosaurs play an exaggerated role in the modern psyche, and one can certainly understand why. They are fearsome, mysterious, and charismatic creatures, and they are seemingly ubiquitous. From Saturday morning cartoons to summer blockbusters, dinosaurs have captured the public imagination like few other categories of life. Little surprise that many of the best works in the history of paleontology examine this vibrant interface between dinosaurs and the public, including Caitlyn Wylie’s recent volume on fossil preparators and Elizabeth D. Jones’s work on ancient DNA. In his new book, The Age of Mammals: Nature, Development, & Paleontology in the Long Nineteenth Century, historian Chris Manias writes that while the focus on dinosaurs has borne considerable fruit, it has also resulted in a dearth of scholarship on the equally fascinating role that mammals have played in the history of paleontology. In contrast to our modern obsession with dinosaurs, visitors to metropolitan museums and readers of popular science books were primarily interested in mammals in the 19th century. Like dinosaurs, prehistoric mammals were distant and inaccessible, but, unlike dinosaurs, they were simultaneously proximate and coeval, and thus uniquely instructive. Constructing the history of mammals required diverse bodies of knowledge and expertise, and scientists and scholars from a variety of fields and disciplines worked to excavate deep time in general, and the Age of Mammals in particular. As a measure of geological time, the Age of Mammals spans the Tertiary and Quaternary periods, which corresponds to the past 65 million years or so. As the author astutely notes, this novel timeframe necessarily entails different narrative beats from other chronological frameworks, including the Age of Dinosaurs or the Age of Humans, and it thus offers different lessons.

auditPapers.title: Shira Lurie. The American Liberty Pole: Popular Politics and the Struggle for Democracy in the Early Republic.
auditPapers.abstract: As Shira Lurie notes in the introduction to her excellent first book The American Liberty Pole, the scholarship on the political culture of the early American republic is exceedingly rich. One could argue, seriously, that it might be the most actively developed and thickly engaged subfield of historical inquiry over the last few decades. To add something genuinely new to such a field is an impressive feat, and Lurie has done exactly that. In clear and inviting prose, Lurie picks up the full weight of the scholarly tradition on early American political culture and distills it into a carefully researched narrative history of the liberty pole in the early Republic, with a special focus on the 1790s. Her argument shows us that there was no consensus of national identity and shared meaning at the founding that came apart in moments of crisis later, be they in the nineteenth century or the twenty-first. Rather, Americans have hotly contested their politics and tied their political identifications to the symbolic authority of the nation’s history from the beginning. The story of American political culture is the story of protest, contestation, and changing markers; it was that way from the beginning, and if Lurie is right, the liberty pole as a tool of opposition political symbolism was a founding element in that story. This book leaves little doubt that she is.

auditPapers.title: Muriam Haleh Davis. Markets of Civilization: Islam and Racial Capitalism in Algeria.
auditPapers.abstract: Among its other achievements, colonialism was—and remains—adept at explaining away the effects of the violence and immiseration it inflicted as the natural, racial defects of the populations it subjugated and dispossessed. The “lazy native,” inclined to do no more work than was necessary for survival, and the “imprudent native,” incapable of hedging against the vicissitudes of nature or appreciating the benefits of credit, were stock images of colonial common sense. The belief that something inherent to Islam predetermined Muslims to such recalcitrance in the face of colonial capitalism would prove enduring. In this short but ambitiously wide-ranging book, Markets of Civilization, Muriam Haleh Davis shows how, from the mid-nineteenth century onward, Algeria’s economy was imagined, written about, governed, and planned with reference to a pervasive “racial regime of religion” that saw Algerians’ lives and livelihoods as determined by their being Muslim. Such Muslim-ness had less to do with belief or ritual practice than with a putative orientation to time, labor, and value that was inherited and immutable, dyed into culture, psychology, and physiognomy. The condition of homo islamicus was thus racialized: Racial capitalism in Algeria rested on a conception of religion that, Davis argues, was “a particular expression of racial thought.” According to this durable body of French thought, homo islamicus was all but impervious to the improving and value-creating efforts of commerce, civilization, and capitalism. Homo islamicus, of course, has never actually existed: But actually-existing Muslims would find themselves, for over a century, defined and objectified by a wide range of French technologies of rule—from legislation and welfare provision to the social sciences and psychological warfare—as the binary opposite of an equally imaginary Western homo economicus, whose rational, future-oriented pursuit of progress they were summoned to share while at the same time being denied the means of access to it.

auditPapers.title: Eric Klingelhofer, ed. Excavating the Lost Colony Mystery: The Map, the Search, the Discovery.
auditPapers.abstract: In 2004, a group of scholars from diverse academic backgrounds met in Chapel Hill, North Carolina and organized the First Colony Foundation (FCF), an organization dedicated to researching the history of the sixteenth-century Roanoke colonies, especially the Lost Colony of 1587. Members included historians, archaeologists, curators, preservationists, and other specialists. Over the past two decades, these scholars have conducted fieldwork in North Carolina and documentary research in the United States and England. In Excavating the Lost Colony Mystery: The Map, the Search, the Discovery, edited by Eric Klingelhofer, nine authors, six of whom are members of FCF, summarize their findings to date. As the title suggests, much of the focus is on their methodology and the process of excavating, and they do not claim to have solved the mystery. But they do offer a hypothesis based on new evidence. They argue that after Governor John White left Roanoke, the remaining colonists split into smaller groups to search for food. Some ventured westward across the sound and onto the mainland where they settled, at least temporarily, near the head of the Albemarle Sound on modern day Salmon Creek, a location near the Algonquian town of Mettaquem.

From their speeches, to their community engagement, to their roles in the military, Black women made calls for justice and equality, relying on their lived experiences as sources of knowledge. The work defines public intellectual work in a way that centers Black women for who they are and not by their affiliations, essentially shifting the focus away from the academy by valuing lived experience as something from which we all can learn.

auditPapers.title: Martín Bowen. The Age of Dissent: Revolution and the Power of Communication in Chile, 1780–1833.
auditPapers.abstract: The Age of Dissent: Revolution and the Power of Communication in Chile, 1780–1833, is not just another book on the history of the independence of Chile, nor is it about the “Age of Revolutions,” as might be assumed from its temporal scope (1780–1833). In this insightful, original, and informed study, Martín Bowen focuses on the marked continuity between late colonial and postcolonial Chile rather than the rupture between the new and old regimes. The focus is not on reiterating the well-known idea that colonial social and economic structures persisted well into the republican era nor on assessing how revolutionary the shift from the monarchical to a republican regime was. For Bowen, the “most revolutionary dimension” about the age of revolutions in Chile—and arguably in Spanish America—was “the opening of politics to radical political dissension” (2). To understand the nature of this revolution, the author casts doubt on the assumption that its roots are in the realm of ideas. In turn, he elaborates a sophisticated conceptual framework to demonstrate that the disclosure of politics to a wide range of social actors, such as women, Indigenous people, slaves, and Afro-descendants, was the result of a subtle and gradual transformation in the realm of communication. In this framework, communication is understood as an arena where different actors from the past “elaborated and discussed the worlds they shared” (8) as well as the interactions among them.

auditPapers.title: Joaquín Rivaya-Martínez, ed. Indigenous Borderlands: Native Agency, Resilience, and Power in the Americas.
auditPapers.abstract: The inspiring book Indigenous Borderlands: Native Agency, Resilience, and Power in the Americas is the culmination of a project whose first step was a symposium held at Texas State University in 2018. This academic meeting, which brought together scholars of different nationalities (the United States, Mexico, Argentina, and the United Kingdom), was the seed that allowed the flowering of an ambitious and stimulating work, crossed by revisionist visions anchored in the most recent trends of borderlands studies and the “new” Native American history, which question the traditional view that European colonialism operated without counterweight among the Indigenous societies of this continent. This is a comprehensive work whose case studies cover wide temporal and spatial ranges. The book’s broad geographical and chronological scope covers regions as distant and disparate as New Mexico, the Bolsón de Mapimí in Mexico, the Northern Maya lowlands in Yucatán, Cuba, the Tucumán region in Argentina, the Bolivian lowlands in Tarija and Santa Cruz, Paraguay, and Río de la Plata, embracing chronologies ranging from the last pre-Hispanic phases to the Republican period. The complexity of the topics discussed by the authors has been the main stimulus to promote a multidisciplinary approach, characteristic of ethnohistorical methodology, in which historical analysis is supported by the contribution of related disciplines, such as anthropology and archaeology. In the words of the book’s editor, Joaquín Rivaya-Martínez, “such methodology involves situating the focus on the natives, incorporating indigenous sources and testimonies whenever possible, and trying to comprehend indigenous actions and perspectives through multidisciplinary approaches that often rely on nondocumentary archaeological, linguistic, ethnographic, environmental, or other sources” (22). The result is a work that increases our understanding of Indigenous responses to colonization by amplifying their voices based on evidence not considered in traditional historical research.

auditPapers.title: Nino Vallen. Being the Heart of the World: The Pacific and the Fashioning of the Self in New Spain, 1513–1641.
auditPapers.abstract: Being the Heart of the World is a highly notable book within the growing scholarly attention to the New Spanish Pacific and its central role in the “first globalization.” While the literature on this subject has primarily focused on the economic aspects of the Spanish Pacific, and particularly on the circumstances surrounding the Manila Galleon trade, Nino Vallen’s work, although also addressing trade dilemmas, focuses on how the gradual integration of New Spain with the Pacific between 1513 and 1641 and its conversion into the pivot of an increasingly interconnected world had a significant impact on the narratives developed by Hispanic people about themselves and the changing world around them. This view shows us that the “first globalization” went beyond a simple exchange of goods, people, and ideas between territories, as it also altered societies and identities by creating new ways to understand reality, acquire and maintain privileges, or establish theoretical differences among various power groups.

auditPapers.title: Daniel H. Usner. Native American Women and the Burdens of Southern History.
auditPapers.abstract: Readers are introduced to several “burdens” in Daniel H. Usner’s book Native American Women and the Burdens of Southern History. Among these are the literal burdens that Indigenous women carried as they moved through the Lower Mississippi Valley. Women held their burdens in rivercane baskets they had crafted themselves. Even as the reasons for women’s mobility changed from the colonial period through the early twentieth century—they were traders, migrants, refugees, itinerant laborers, peddlers, craftswomen, travelers, and diplomats—their baskets remained a constant. Traditionally, Usner explains, both Southern observers and Southern historians have pointed to women’s production, use, and sale of rivercane baskets as a sign of their diminished status within Indigenous communities (i.e., drudgery). Similarly, Southerners saw the persistence of Indigenous women’s basketmaking into the twentieth century as evidence of the decline and eventual extinction of Indigenous nations. Usner emphatically disagrees with these interpretations. To him, rivercane baskets represent neither drudgery nor decline but “the role that Indigenous women’s work and knowledge has played in shaping and reshaping relations with non-native southerners across centuries of time” (6).

auditPapers.title: Yunxiang Gao. Arise, Africa! Roar, China! Black and Chinese Citizens of the World in the Twentieth Century.
auditPapers.abstract: Arise, Africa! Roar, China! is an original, intelligent, and deeply researched book. In five rich chapters, it traces the lives and interactions of three well-known 20th-century African American towering figures—the scholar W. E. B. Du Bois, the singer Paul Robeson, and the poet and novelist Langston Hughes (as well as Du Bois and Robeson’s wives, Shirley Graham and Eslanda)—and of two much less known, yet remarkable, Chinese individuals, the journalist and musician Liu Liangmo and the Sino-Afro-Caribbean Sylvia Si-lan Chen (with whom Hughes had a tormented on-and-off sentimental relationship). Five “citizens of the world” (1), as the author Yunxiang Gao rightly defines them, whose travels, loves, dramas, and sometimes political and intellectual inconsistencies are colorfully and precisely reconstructed and narrated. The book possesses at least four significant merits. First, it exemplifies transnational history at its finest. The central theme of the narrative is of course race, serving as the pivotal element around which the story revolves. The five (plus two) protagonists, each in their own way, endeavored to represent and cultivate a global, anti-imperialist alliance among people of color. This pan-racial ambition underpinned their actions and shaped their interactions and collaborations. Si-lan Chen, with her distinctive biography, epitomized and embodied this ideal. During his legendary visit to Beijing University in 1959, for example, Du Bois urged China to recognize its status as “colored” and to understand “what a colored skin in this modern world subjects its owner” (11). In his final years, Du Bois extended his well-known philosophy of Pan-Africanism to encompass a Chinese-centered Pan-Asianism. This represented a significant shift for a man whose pan-racial ambitions had, in the 1930s, led him to uncritically embrace Japan’s regional hegemonic designs, blinding him to Tokyo’s imperial policies and inter-Asian racial hierarchies. Robeson’s enthusiasm for Chinese history and culture led him to diligently study the language. With the assistance of Liu Liangmo, he recorded an album in 1941 featuring Chinese resistance and folk songs, which included “Chee Lai,” the future national anthem of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), later renamed “March of the Volunteers.” Strongly inspired by his experience in segregated Shanghai, where “he felt he belonged with the Chinese as fellow ‘colored people’” (253), Hughes’s radical turn in the 1930s was enthusiastically acclaimed within Chinese leftist intellectual and academic circles. His works were translated in prominent journals, reflecting an effort to draw a new, global color line that connected Black internationalism with Sino–African American collaboration. This effort found an ideal environment during the Cold War, with the PRC emerging as a receptive partner and interlocutor.

auditPapers.title: Pamela Voekel. For God and Liberty: Catholicism and Revolution in the Atlantic World, 1790–1861.
auditPapers.abstract: The genre of the book review may be notable for its use of superlatives, but in this case, it is no exaggeration to say that Pamela Voekel’s deeply researched, highly original study is one of the most important books in the field to appear this decade. She documents the impact of the schism inside the Catholic Church between Jansenist-inflected reform movements and ultramontane reactionaries and shows how it entirely permeated the Spanish American independence era and shaped its legacy political culture. Voekel’s For God and Liberty: Catholicism and Revolution in the Atlantic World, 1790–1861 effectively upends two generations of historiography on the nature of the civil strife that rent asunder the newly independent Latin American states during the 1810s–1830s. Focusing primarily on the experiences of Central America and the four states emerging out of the former Viceroyalty of New Granada—Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panamá—Voekel argues that “[at] the heart of the Age or Revolutions in Spanish America was a Catholic civil war . . . The traditional narrative of the transition from monarchy to independent republicanism as a process of secularization misses completely the warring factions in the church who vied to define humanity’s relation to God and, therefore, the proper order of temporal authority” (1). It’s the sort of forehead-slappingly obvious truth that, after reading the book, one wonders why no one has noticed it before. Generations whose research focused on the formation of the nation-state, or the buildup of economic resentments, or the appeal of Enlightenment political philosophy and constitution-writing have generally ignored or underestimated the ongoing relevance of religion and have tended to see the church as a monolithic entity. Voekel brilliantly resurrects the players and doctrinal positions to show how “[t]his was not a battle between modernizers and traditionalists, but between religious innovators” (251) as the Reform Catholic tradition of people like the abolitionists Abbé Grégoire and various Jansenists prompted an equally intense countermovement among ultramontane factions eager to shore up absolutist monarchies and papal authority.

auditPapers.title: Moe Taylor. North Korea, Tricontinentalism, and the Latin American Revolution, 1959–1970.
auditPapers.abstract: As research on the Cold War in the Global South—especially during the “Global Sixties”—has proliferated recently, the role North Korea played and the relationships Pyongyang had with other parts of the “Third World” have received only sporadic attention. Few works have detailed North Korea’s interactions with Latin America in depth. Moe Taylor’s monograph, North Korea, Tricontinentalism, and the Latin American Revolution, 1959–1970, fills that gap and so deserves the attention of historians of Korea, Latin America, and the Global Sixties. His work brings together source material in multiple languages and places scholars from Korea and Latin America into conversation with each other, further enhancing its value. Through seven chapters, plus an introduction and conclusion, Taylor describes the connections that existed between North Koreans and Latin American revolutionaries in the 1960s. State and nonstate actors on both sides of the Pacific recognized in each other common goals. The vision they shared had more to do with national self-determination in the face of US imperialism than with Marxist class revolution. Taylor emphasizes Latin America’s importance to North Koreans by analyzing the rhetoric of the Kim Il Sung regime and providing evidence of North Korean enthusiasm for assisting Latin America. Sources from Latin America, especially Cuba, suggest that some of the region’s revolutionaries viewed North Korea as a model of self-sufficient development.

auditPapers.title: David Maxwell. Religious Entanglements: Central African Pentecostalism, the Creation of Cultural Knowledge, and the Making of the Luba Katanga.

auditPapers.title: Jaime M. Pensado. Love and Despair: How Catholic Activism Shaped Politics and the Counterculture in Modern Mexico.
auditPapers.abstract: To use a countercultural metaphor, Jaime M. Pensado’s Love and Despair is a wonderfully mind-expanding book. Readers may not agree with all the book’s conclusions; yet they will thank the author for taking them on what can only be called a deeply researched and fascinating historiographical “trip” through Catholic (or Catholic-inflected) 1960s journalism, cinema, sexual politics, campus politics, ecclesial base communities, and urban guerrilla warfare. The book has a somewhat unconventional organization, slipping, within chapters, from wide-angle period discussions—of Tlatelolco and 1971’s halconazo, say—to brief, personalized snapshots of its countercultural protagonists. The juxtaposition of manifesto-length inserts and broader contextual frames gives the book an occasional but entirely appropriate zine-like feel. And, if some protagonists are well known, such as Catholic novelist Vicente Leñero (famed as the Mexican Graham Greene [229]), most are resolutely obscure. Indeed, Pensado offers vivid and memorable portraits of student activists such as Jorge Bermeo; of urban guerrilleros such as Eufemia Almaraz and Héctor Torres (a kind of Mexican Catholic Baader-Meinhof); and of progressive clergymen such as French Dominican Alex Morelli, himself a survivor of the Nazi camps and founder of a cinder-block church in 1960s Ciudad Nezahualcóyotl.

auditPapers.title: Joseph W. Esherick. Accidental Holy Land: The Communist Revolution in Northwest China.
auditPapers.abstract: The traditional approach to the Chinese Communist revolution emphasizes how the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) exploited peasant nationalism, social-economic division, and mass emotion in local societies to mobilize the populations. auditPapers.title: Jason Mayernick. Not Alone: LGB Teachers Organizations from 1970–1985.
auditPapers.abstract: LGBTQ+ teachers have long been the target of identity-based firings and culture wars fear mongering. A poll from 1977 showed that as few as 27 percent of Americans supported the presence of homosexual educators in K–12 schools. Surprisingly, or perhaps because of this prejudice, teachers’ organizations became some of the first labor associations in the nation to secure protections for gay and lesbian individuals. Jason Mayernick’s book Not Alone aptly tells that story. Between the advent of gay liberation and the onset of the AIDS crisis, LGB teachers used the vehicle of unions and professional organizations to secure crucial labor and civil rights. They did so through national behemoths like the National Education Association (NEA) and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), as well as smaller city-based groups. Mayernick did not find evidence of transgender teachers in this early activism, likely due to the intense oppression they faced (hence “LBG”), but invites future research on this topic.

auditPapers.title: Reshaad Durgahee. The Indentured Archipelago: Experiences of Indian Labour in Mauritius and Fiji, 1871–1916.
auditPapers.abstract: Reshaad Durgahee’s book The Indentured Archipelago is an excellent and superbly researched addition to the global historical scholarship on indenture. Indenture is most often studied in the context of the rapidly expanding British Empire in the nineteenth century. Initial scholarly conversations about indenture focused on whether indenture was a “new system of slavery.” In this book, the conversation is reframed from the perspective of historical geography, attending to questions of spatiality, mobility, and agency. auditPapers.title: Lauren Stokes. Fear of the Family: Guest Workers and Family Migration in the Federal Republic of Germany.
auditPapers.abstract: Lauren Stokes’s rigorously researched and elegantly written book, Fear of the Family: Guest Workers and Family Migration in the Federal Republic of Germany, is essential reading for scholars of migration, race, gender, and sexuality both within and beyond modern Europe. Amid the growing literature on West Germany’s guest worker program, Stokes distinguishes herself by emphasizing the understudied topic of family migration, considering all guest worker nationalities rather than one case study, analyzing the intermingling of racialization and the neoliberal welfare state, and emphasizing migrants’ voices and anti-racist activism. Historicizing this topic is crucial: Still today, far-right and even centrist Germans blame West Germany’s lax policy of family reunification (Familiennachzug) for creating a “demographic nightmare.” The book highlights the “fear of the family” on multiple levels—how German policy was rooted in both biologically and culturally grounded fears of being overtaken by migrants, as well as how migrants themselves feared (and fought against) both popular racism and the state’s incursion into their lives. German policymakers frequently sought to frame racially discriminatory policies in terms that appeared beneficial or magnanimous to migrants. In turn, they blamed foreign families for their own problems—particularly blaming parents for the problems of their children—thereby providing “a convenient alibi for state inaction” (127). Stokes tells this complex story through a fine-grained analysis of federal, state, and local regulations, which she supplements with media discourse and migrants’ experiences.

auditPapers.title: John D. Garrigus. A Secret among the Blacks: Slave Resistance before the Haitian Revolution.
auditPapers.abstract: Eighteenth-century Saint-Domingue was a place in great need of healing. On this Caribbean French colony ravaged by famine, drought, unexplained human and animal deaths, poison trials, and the Seven Years’ War, the path to revolution was paved by the responses of those who suffered most. This is the thrust of John D. Garrigus’s book A Secret among the Blacks: Slave Resistance before the Haitian Revolution. The study reaches back thirty years, from 1791, to chronicle the efforts of enslaved and freed men and women to forge bonds of solidarity in the sugar plain surrounding the port city of Cap-Français and the coffee hills of the North Province. Bearing the brunt of an environmental and political crisis of Atlantic proportions, Africans and their descendants drew on their own rituals and medical knowledge to address the collective ills that were exacerbated—and, in some cases, created—by colonialism and slavery. Here is the mystery that Garrigus unravels for the reader: rather than deriving from an articulated “overarching ideology” (174), the slave revolution in Haiti arose organically from the Afro-Atlantic spiritual world of healers, diviners, and their associated communities.

auditPapers.title: Lucia Carminati. Seeking Bread and Fortune in Port Said: Labor Migration and the Making of the Suez Canal, 1859–1906.
auditPapers.abstract: In Seeking Bread and Fortune in Port Said, Lucia Carminati offers an unprecedented glimpse into the lives of the laborers, loiterers, migrants, and transients who passed through the city starting in the middle of the nineteenth century, some held there by choice, imprisonment, or death, and others merely stopping for a few days or weeks before moving on once more to other nodes in the networks of mobility that crisscrossed the Mediterranean. Carminati’s book traces “the successive metamorphoses, from the halcyon days in the early 1860s to the twilight of the 1890s and beyond, of the ‘small nook, remote and neglected’ that Port Said originally was and that, at some point, it reverted to being” (458–9). It does so by paying close attention to a multitude of incidents recorded in various archives, reports, or travelogues, involving coalheavers, prostitutes, unwed couples, and unaccompanied children. These otherwise unremarkable individuals are brought to light vividly as Carminati dwells on the details of their lives that the historical record brings into sharp focus for a moment. Such details were usually made salient by a disruption of the moral, legal, urban, or productive regimen the authorities wished to impose: an incident of public drunkenness, an accusation of theft, forged identity papers, a murder, workers absconding from their posts, or complaints about the rowdy behavior of a café’s patrons. Carminati teases from a host of minor events the texture of life in a city made of and by people on the move: “The migrant labor roaming Egypt and the Mediterranean in the second half of the nineteenth century had disparate and uneven modes of mobility to hand. These, and the attendant formation of an unequal migrant society in Port Said, undergirded the Suez Canal’s genesis and its first half century of operation” (471).

auditPapers.title: Jamie Martin. The Meddlers: Sovereignty, Empire and the Birth of Global Economic Governance.
auditPapers.abstract: Jamie Martin’s book The Meddlers has a straightforward premise: to correct a common misperception. The history of “global economic governance”—initiatives to control and guide political economies justified by international cooperation—tends to be viewed as an outcome of the Second World War. Our collective memory in economic history jumps forward from coercive gunboat diplomacy for debt repayment in the late 19th century, supposedly outlawed by the 1907 Drago Porter Doctrine, to John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White negotiating principles for the Bretton Woods institutions in 1944. Not so, demonstrates Martin in this thoroughly researched and convincing work. Rather, the antecedents of what we today call global economic governance can be found in a range of initiatives from Anglophone and French “meddlers” who concocted schemes to manage debt repayments, international payment transfers, commodity pricing, and what we currently refer to as critical infrastructure. In the wake of the First World War, elite technocrats established a series of organizations, or repurposed earlier imperial and colonial schemes, to act as “political buffers” (83) that could effectively meet the interests of private financial and trading cartels. Such organizations and arrangements ushered in a new institutional order that justified interventions into sovereign states on economic grounds.

Penny also takes issue with Reinhart Koselleck’s threshold period 1760–1860 (the so-called Sattelzeit), identified as pivotal for the emergence of the modern political order of secular nation-states. auditPapers.title: A. Dirk Moses. The Problems of Genocide: Permanent Security and the Language of Transgression.
auditPapers.abstract: Dirk Moses’s book The Problems of Genocide: Permanent Security and the Language of Transgression shows how genocide came to be distinguished from other mass atrocities. The first part of the book recapitulates the language of transgression—how lawyers, rulers, and thinkers conceptualized mass violence between 1500 and the 1930s—before the term genocide officially came into being. A turning point in this history, of course, is Lemkin’s separation of genocidal killing from other forms of atrocities. This first section already announces the main theme of the book: a more expansive framing of genocide—if not a definitive rejection of the term—that considers the multiple ways groups (in totality or in part) can be the targets of murder. The quest for universal principles of prevention and intervention, contends Moses, clashes with the need to account for the unique cultural, political, and historical circumstances of different genocidal events.

A central part of Savala’s proposal is that this solidarity and collaboration has occurred in a space that he calls the “South Pacific World”—a space that has promoted connections between Chileans and Peruvians, where individuals, for different reasons, have distanced themselves from nationalist rationales. Given the central role that war has had in defining the relations between both countries, Chilean and Peruvian readers who have been taught in educational systems that reinforce conflict as a part of national identity will find that Savala’s argument is counterintuitive. That is one of the book’s strengths and one of its challenges—the attempt to disarticulate visions that are profoundly rooted in nationalist discourses found on both sides of the border. Consisting of five chapters, an introduction, and an epilogue, the book starts from the middle of the nineteenth century and covers up until the first decades of the twentieth. It analyzes different instances of solidarity and cooperation among maritime and port workers, Chilean and Peruvian doctors during the cholera epidemic that occurred between 1886 and 1888, and between police from the Callo and Valparaiso ports in their law enforcement efforts.

auditPapers.title: Antal Molnár. Confessionalization on the Frontier: The Balkan Catholics between Roman Reform and Ottoman Reality.
auditPapers.abstract: Since Schilling and Reinhard introduced it in the early 1980s, the confessionalization paradigm has hypothesized a new interpretative framework for investigating how institutional religion intersects with political, socioeconomic, and cultural trends in early modern societies. Although originally focused on Germany, it has since been applied to other case studies within and beyond Europe, including the Ottoman Empire. While innovative and valuable, the paradigm has its limitations, especially as regards the risks of generalization and misinterpretation. In his book Confessionalization on the Frontier: The Balkan Catholics between Roman Reform and Ottoman Reality, Antal Molnár successfully sidesteps these pitfalls of broad and uncritical applications of the concept of confessionalization and demonstrates its heuristic relevance for examining Catholic minorities in the Ottoman Balkans. In so doing, Molnár takes us through an impressive array of non-Ottoman primary sources and provides a detailed historical analysis of key reforms in the Catholic Church as they instantiate in the Balkans. The principal temporal framework of the book is the seventeenth century, when the Balkan missions were implemented, and the spatial is the Ottoman Empire. However, both time and place are presented as porous categories with regular interventions from the past and the outside, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of how political and religious factors gain meaning through specific and practical circumstances.

auditPapers.abstract: Joanne Begiato’s Manliness in Britain, 1760–1900 examines how the male body—depicted and imbued with meaning in a variety of visual, textual, and material forms—helped to construct masculinity over the course of the long nineteenth century in Great Britain. With attention to recent trends in the discipline—labeled by some as a somatic turn—this book urges historians to carefully interrogate cultural constructions of the body, emotions, and “‘lived, embodied experience[s]’” (to borrow from Karen Harvey, as Begiato does) (16) in their explorations of gender. Pushing beyond studies of manliness that center educational institutions, associational life, or leisure pursuits and recreational activities as the most important spaces in which gender formation occurred and admired nineteenth-century masculine attributes were inculcated, this book prioritizes how the ideals of manliness were “made manifest through emotionalized bodies and material culture” (5). In pursuing these interpretive goals, Begiato claims several innovations in her work. First, and perhaps most important, is her attempt to counter a narrative, embraced by many historians of the nineteenth century, that posits that masculine identities were increasingly embodied as Queen Victoria’s reign pushed toward the twentieth century. In rejecting this idea, Begiato asserts that classed and raced bodies were just as important in defining masculinity in the Age of Sensibility as they were in the so-called era of High Imperialism. She also claims several additional interpretive interventions in her work, including a sharply focused analysis on the roles that representations of working-class bodies played in the articulation of masculine ideals and the important place that desire—both heteronormative and queer—occupied in a cultural landscape in which discussions of manliness were ubiquitous. Throughout, Begiato charts not only what it meant to embrace manliness successfully during the long nineteenth century but also what resulted when one failed to achieve the ideals of self-control, bodily mastery, temperance, appropriate emotionality, and hardiness. As such, hers is a work that captures moments of consensus as well as inconsistency and paradox, profitably establishing the messiness inherent in reconstructing gender through a historical lens.

auditPapers.title: Adam Mestyan. Modern Arab Kingship: Remaking the Ottoman Political Order in the Interwar Middle East.
auditPapers.abstract: How are new political orders built on the ruins of destroyed ones? Historians, sociologists, political theorists, and other disciplines have tussled with this question from the moment empires began to die. By focusing on spolia, Mestyan contends that in the creation of post-Ottoman Arab mandates from a European imperial or local Arab standpoint, no party involved could dispense with certain legal, genealogical, religious, and social vestiges of the Ottoman’s unique making. auditPapers.title: Michelle Tusan. The Last Treaty: Lausanne and the End of the First World War in the Middle East.
auditPapers.abstract: During approximately the last 175 years, humanitarian groups have raced around the world trying to help civilian populations ravaged by war and other disasters. That this has become an accepted practice highlights one of the paradoxes of modern humanitarianism: Why does the world allow for the existence of war and other man-made conditions that necessitate humanitarianism in the first place? Perhaps, then, it is not surprising that modern humanitarianism, according to Michelle Tusan in her book The Last Treaty: Lausanne and the End of the First World War in the Middle East, “developed in concert with military and diplomatic concerns” during the largest war the world had yet seen. Analyzing the symbiosis between the “strange bedfellows” of war, peacemaking, and humanitarianism is the core of Tusan’s stimulating monograph (8). Tusan has two additional objectives for this book: First, she argues that historians must acknowledge the “centrality of the Middle East in Allied thinking about the war” and analyze its events as interdependent with the war’s other developments (11). Second, Tusan argues that the oft-repeated contention that the war ended in 1918 is false and misleading. Fighting continued in several places, including in various parts of Anatolia, long beyond 1918. She is not, however, simply arguing for a new end date for the war. Instead, Tusan focuses on the implications of “how the First World War ended,” with continuing violence influencing the way in which peace was negotiated (3, Tusan’s emphasis). To accomplish these tasks, she has employed political and diplomatic sources, as well as utilizing the voices of “refugees, aid-workers, and soldiers” for insight into “why and how those who offered aid did it and in whose name” they did it for (8–9). Reading the sources in this way makes the war in the Middle East seem more like a “strange defeat” for the Allies rather than a victory, as the peace “came at a heavy price for the now former subjects of the Ottoman Empire” (15). Tusan seeks to achieve these goals by interweaving chapters about the conflict, the peace negotiations, and humanitarianism.

The book moves chronologically through the era, starting in 1953, when Stalin’s sudden death initiated a struggle for power among his top lieutenants. The victor, Nikita Khrushchev, immediately began to relax some of Stalin’s policies. In 1956, Khrushchev denounced the purges of 1937 and Stalin’s creation of a “cult of personality” in his famous “Secret Speech.” Hornsby traces the various small “freezes” and “thaws” that followed as the Soviet leadership sought to maintain control of the country—and its satellite states in Eastern Europe—while selectively repudiating elements of Stalinism.

auditPapers.title: Pious Labor: Islam, Artisanship, and Technology in Colonial India, By Amanda Lanzillo
auditPapers.abstract: The historiography of artisanal labor in colonial India reflects a dynamic and evolving field. While traditional Marxist interpretations highlight the detrimental effects of colonialism on indigenous industries, revisionist scholars and recent research offer a more nuanced view, acknowledging the resilience and adaptability of certain sectors and the multifaceted nature of economic change during this period. Yet “De-industrialization versus Modernization” still dominates the academic debates of economic history in South Asian curricula. As a fresh breeze, in Pious Labor: Islam, Artisanship, and Technology in Colonial India, Amanda Lanzillo examines how Muslim artisans in northern India during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries integrated Islamic principles into their crafts amid colonial industrialization. This work is a meticulous exploration of the intersection between Islamic identity, artisanal work, and technological advancements in colonial northern India. Lanzillo argues that Muslim artisans positioned themselves as both technical experts and religiously grounded professionals, producing Urdu technical manuals that framed modern technologies within an Islamic intellectual tradition. This perspective diverges from most of the prior scholarship, which tends to separate religious identity from labor practices, primarily focusing on colonial policies and their effects on labor. Lanzillo’s turn to vernacular Urdu manuals and community histories shows how artisans themselves framed their labor as both economically and morally significant, creating an alternative discourse on labor that countered colonial narratives of progress. This approach challenges the assumption that technological change in colonial India was entirely dictated by British frameworks.

auditPapers.title: Energy Policy and Climate Change in Europe during the Era of Neoliberalism
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article shows how the European Community sought to become a global climate leader during the 1980s and 1990s, only to fail to make progress after Brussels was moved by globalization and by neoliberal ideas to pursue reforms that led the Community to burn more fossil fuels. They bolstered their climate agenda with proposals for a carbon tax, which they envisioned as a model for the world. National politics, however, shaped this agenda and prevented Brussels from implementing its vision in the form imagined by Eurocrats. auditPapers.title: Stylometric Consistency Patterns in Translation of Spoken Chinese to Written English: A Corpus Analysis of the CoVoST Dataset
auditPapers.abstract: This study examines stylometric consistency patterns in professional human translations of spoken Chinese to written English, using the CoVoST corpus. auditPapers.title: Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century, By Douglas Pretsell
auditPapers.abstract: In their effort to bring queer history into mainstream consciousness, public history initiatives have often sought to find touchstones, exemplary figures who can act as historic rallying points. In Germany, one such figure is Karl Heinrich Ulrichs, a Hanoverian lawyer who, in 1867, addressed the Congress of German Jurists in Munich to argue for the rights of people he termed “urnings,” who now would fall under the category of gay men. The centering of “great men,” however, has come at a cost: a simplification of the complex human histories of such characters. Ulrichs has, in some quarters, been regarded as the “first gay man,” and his appearance at the Congress as the “first coming out.” Such characterizations are glib, reducing Ulrichs—and more ephemerally, the “meaning” of Ulrichs—to a handful of chartable moments. In Urning: Queer Identity in the German Nineteenth Century, Douglas Pretsell seeks to do justice to Ulrichs by focusing specifically on the impact of his ideas and theories of what it meant to be an urning, before examining in a broader context how the urning concept populated itself in the German-speaking world. The result is a deeply interesting work that places Ulrichs at the center of an intellectual-identitarian cosmos while at the same time recognizing that, once Ulrichs’s arguments were taken up by a broader public, they exceeded the control and imagination of their originator. Rather than a biography of Ulrichs, Urning is thus a biography of an idea.

auditPapers.title: Gay Student Services v. Texas A&M University: A Social History of the First Amendment in the Struggle for Equality
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract In 1975, students at Texas A&M University created the campus’s first gay and lesbian student organization, Gay Student Services (GSS). When university administrators refused to recognize the group the following year, the student members filed a federal lawsuit claiming that the university had violated their First Amendment rights protecting speech, expression, and association. Nearly a decade later, the students won, and a federal appellate court ordered Texas A&M officials to recognize GSS. The students’ legal strategy differed remarkably from the one employed by the mainstream gay and lesbian rights movement of the era, which relied on a constitutional right to privacy to advance queer equality. In this article, I uncover a largely forgotten and discarded strategy in the national movement for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ) equality. I argue that using the tools of social history to study the Texas A&M students’ legal struggle against the university reveals the ways that constitutional arguments about free speech, expression, and association had more liberating potential than arguments about sexual privacy. Although free speech, expression, and association eventually took a back seat to arguments about privacy in the larger movement, the First Amendment may yet hold a key to preserving the rights of queer people today.

auditPapers.title: Republican Kinship in the Society of Princes: The Dutch States General as Corporate Godparent, 1578–1732
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Throughout the early modern period, the Dutch States General, as if it were a natural person, frequently stood godfather over foreign children. Based on innovative archival research, this article investigates this unknown phenomenon as ‘corporate godparenthood’ and argues that it was an important tool of republican diplomacy in the Protestant society of princes, particularly in the Holy Roman Empire. Corporate godfatherhood allowed the Dutch Republic to partake, and assert its presence, in familial princely spheres to which it did not otherwise have access. The cultural practices of baptism, including the right of the godparents to name a child and baptismal gift-giving, allowed the States to form lasting kinship relations of mutual obligation in an economy of affection. Corporate godfatherhood had important and long-lasting effects: many of the dynasties with whom the States entered into a kinship relation remained allies for several generations, and supplied the States’ army with troops and officers, while the States assumed the role of benefactor, protector, educator, executor, or legal guardian of various of its princely godchildren.

auditPapers.title: The Prestes Column: An Interior History of Modern Brazil, By Jacob Blanc
auditPapers.abstract: Historians of Brazil have embraced region as an important category of analysis since at least the 1970s, a sensible strategy for the world’s fifth largest country, which occupies half a continent. The 1,000-person column engaged in some 150 skirmishes with federal, state, and local forces, marching the equivalent of “Los Angeles to New York and back again three times” from 1924 to 1927 before leaving for exile in Bolivia (1).

auditPapers.title: Identifiable Individuals and Reality: Describing the Past by Formal Propositions
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Data of historical and ideographic sciences, such as cultural heritage studies, geography, geological evolution, biodiversity, but also experimental data of nomothetic natural sciences, are increasingly documented and published in information systems compatible with predicate-logic that refer to things in reality by unique identifiers (or “keys” most likely to be unique in some context). In this article, we argue that only a smaller part of the features in our environment are sufficiently distinct over a useful time-span in order to form such “identifiable individuals”. Ontological categories should each provide specific criteria for the so-called ontological individuation, i.e., about how parts of reality can be subdivided into identifiable individuals that are useful for modelling their behaviour and interactions in reality for answering specific scientific questions, by obeying evidential constraints as a result of applying these criteria in observations. We motivate by several examples that there are always cases in which the individuality of such an instance may be undecidable basically within all such ontological categories and that all ontological categories are more or less effective approximations of reality. We argue that effective knowledge sharing by information systems using formal ontologies is only possible if these limitations of applicability and precision to real world phenomena are well understood and taken into account.

auditPapers.title: Crafting Digital Experiences: Embedding Human-Centred and Participatory Design into Archaeological Practice
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage

Design—used in its broadest definition as a process of conceptual making—is an integral, if often implicit, part of archaeological practices and it is through design that we develop and share our work—from data collection and analysis to interpretation and dissemination—and engage with our stakeholders. Engaging with core design practices offers meaningful opportunities for generating new forms of archaeological knowledge production and sharing, as well as creating digitally mediated experiences that are not guided by our own assumptions about our stakeholders’ needs and can really affect people’s engagement with the past. In this article, I investigate the benefits of embedding Human-Centred and Participatory Design into the archaeology and heritage sectors to create more critically engaged digital encounters with the past.

Additionally, attribute features of parks, such as area, perimeter, and public transportation facilities, equally impact visitors’ landscape perception. This study distinguished the cultural perception and preference characteristics of urban residents in historical gardens and new parks, providing urban managers and urban green space planning and design professionals with more experience in areas such as the preservation and renovation of urban historical landscapes.

auditPapers.title: Hierarchical Weighted LSTM with One-class Classifier for Preventive Protection of Cultural Heritage in Museums
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: Environmental monitoring and assessment of environmental risk levels are of great significance for the preventive protection of cultural relics in museums. Conventional methods focus on univariate statistical analysis, ignoring the interaction among variables and the time-related characteristics in environmental sequences. In addition, the environmental data is mostly unlabeled. Due to the strict requirements of museums on the environment, the monitoring data is mostly in the normal state, and there exists a serious problem of class imbalance. It increases the difficulty of establishing a supervised classification model for evaluating environmental risk levels. To solve the above problems, this article proposes a hierarchical weighted long-short-term memory (HWLSTM) with a one-class classifier for the preventive protection of cultural heritage in museums. Compared with the conventional methods, the proposed HWLSTM pays attention to the interaction among key variables and extracts dynamic features from the multivariate environmental time series. It hierarchically extracts short-term and long-term dynamic features to overcome the long-term dependency caused by long sequences. A dynamic weighting strategy is proposed to highlight the cumulative impact of continuous abnormal states. Furthermore, to address the issue of lacking labeled data, an unsupervised one-class classifier is proposed based on the one-class support vector machine (OCSVM) to achieve environmental monitoring and assessment of risk levels only using unlabeled data. Instead of constructing different models for each task, it provides a unified framework for the preventive protection of cultural relics. In this article, the proposed method is verified with the paper cultural heritage in Shanghai Museum. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

auditPapers.title: Ontology in Dance Domain—A Survey
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: This article presents a literature review on the domain of dance research that exploits ontology artifacts to manage their domain knowledge. Researchers found various approaches to manage this knowledge base, among which the ontology development process is preferred by most people owing to its superficial and easy-to-manage characteristics. However, the heterogenic use of ontology in different dance research aspects demands an organized study to understand its contributions to the domain. Our survey approach toward this objective starts with a systematic literature selection and further grouping them into four categories based on ontology involvement. Finally, we comprehensively analyze the outcomes of our qualitative assessment to present the current research status and their limitations in the candidate domain. This review aspires to be a cornerstone resource, enlightening researchers about the current landscape and future prospects of ontological involvement in dance research.

auditPapers.title: Characterizing Geometric Decoration Styles of the Ilkhanid Period Using Advanced Image Analysis
auditPapers.journal: ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
auditPapers.abstract: This study advances the understanding of architectural heritage by introducing a novel analytical approach for classifying geometric decorations. Focusing on the “shamsa,” a star-shaped geometric motif symbolizing the sun and frequently represented through intersecting lines, the study employs a four-stage process: (1) collecting and processing images of decorative elements; (2) developing and applying an unsupervised clustering algorithm to identify meaningful image groups; (3) creating a comprehensive metadata inventory for each image to support analysis; and (4) interpreting the clustered groups to reveal significant patterns and stylistic insights. Analyzing over 230 images from 34 Ilkhanid buildings using hierarchical clustering produced dendrograms illustrating relationships among the image groups. The metadata inventory validated the clusters by incorporating information on region, function, materials, and geometric patterns. This process identified 12 distinct groups of geometric patterns, demonstrating a range of complexity from simple designs to intricate knot motifs, or “gereh.” Ilkhanid decorations predominantly featured materials such as tile, brick, and plaster, with cyan, brick red, azure, and white being the primary colors. The findings present a comprehensive typology of architectural decorations, surpassing prior studies by analyzing broader features.

auditPapers.title: Non-destructive examination of ancient vitreous materials from Southwest Asia: Synchrotron computed tomography at the BEATS beamline of SESAME
auditPapers.abstract: • Studying ancient vitreous materials is important in different cultural heritage research fields. • Synchrotron X-ray computed tomography (SXCT) allows a non-invasive assessment of unique specimens. • Protocols for SCXT scanning, 3D image reconstruction, and processing are presented. • SCXT provides superior resolution and contrast compared to laboratory micro-CT. • The manufacturing and degradation processes of ancient archaeological glass are revealed. The analysis of archaeological objects poses a set of challenges related to the fragility and uniqueness of the material and requires special non-invasive techniques. The combination of SXCT with synchrotron X-ray fluorescence mapping and X-ray absorption near edge structure allows to examine complementary structural and chemical data of unique examples of the Southwest Asian cultural heritage. The availability of a SXCT facility at the heart of Southwest Asia facilitates and enhances the non-destructive examination and conservation of ancient vitreous materials of the region, proving the relevance of the technique for archaeologists, museums, and cultural heritage specialists.

auditPapers.title: Assessing the structural integrity of the wax-resin lining of The Night Watch using 3D shearography
auditPapers.abstract: Assessing the structural integrity of cultural heritage objects is of great importance for their structural conservation and long-term preservation. This paper focuses on the development of a non-destructive inspection (NDI) approach using 3D shearography to evaluate the structural integrity of wax-resin lined paintings, specifically for The Night Watch (1642), a large-format 17th-century canvas painting by Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669) that is on display in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. The Night Watch has a complex treatment history that has many old repairs of structural defects and damages (holes, tears, etc.) and three wax-resin relinings. In 2021, before a new structural intervention involving retensioning of the canvas support, it was vital to evaluate the structural integrity of the painting, specifically the condition of the treatment carried out in 1975–76 when, among other actions, several long cuts in the area of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq's breeches were repaired and an old canvas insert in the drum was replaced. To assess the structural condition, we applied 3D shearography to quantitatively analyse the in- and out-of-plane surface strains with controlled thermal loading. First, a safe loading procedure was developed by inspecting a representative wax-resin lined test painting where reference delaminations and structural repairs to canvas supports were reliably identified with 3D shearography by raising the temperature with 1-2 °C. As part of Operation Night Watch, in November 2021 an in-situ investigation was carried out in the Rijksmuseum gallery. Two areas of interest in The Night Watch , the restored slashes in the Captain's breeches (0.5 × 1 m) and the canvas insert in the drum (0.2 × 0.5 m), were inspected from the reverse of the painting. Results revealed no critical structural problems associated with the repaired slashes, nor with adhesion of the lining. For the patched canvas in the drum, it showed higher in- and out-of-plane strain variations. Overall, 3D shearography provided valuable non-destructive inspection results for assurances regarding the structural integrity of the 1975 repairs and the adhesion of the lining canvas in The Night Watch .

auditPapers.title: Metodologías de levantamiento gráfico en entornos urbanos subterráneos: las cuevas de Bétera, Valencia
auditPapers.abstract: Entre las diferentes tipologías de vivienda popular que se pueden encontrar en España, encontramos el caso peculiar de las casas cueva. En la Comunidad Valenciana, las encontramos en Paterna, Godella, Rocafort, Moncada, Bétera, Ribarroja y Villamarchante. A mediados del siglo XIX la población de las cuevas llega a números relevantes, y hoy en día constituyen una importante tipología de patrimonio arquitectónico local. El caso de estudio se puede enmarcar en el campo más amplio del Patrimonio Construido Subterráneo (‘Underground Built Heritage’, UBH), teniendo así en cuenta los aspectos, factores y cuestiones que pueden tener influencia a la hora de plantear estrategias y herramientas a utilizar en la fase de toma de datos. El presente articulo presenta las metodologías y los flujos de trabajo utilizados en el levantamiento digital con escáner laser terrestre, tras la comparación con metodologías utilizadas en esta tipología de patrimonio, y la posterior elaboración gráfica de los planos arquitectónicos necesarios, llevado a cabo sobre un caso de estudio, las casas cuevas de Bétera. Explotando plenamente la tecnología ‘Visual Inertial System’ (VIS) integrada en la herramienta utilizada, se alcanzó una cobertura óptima del caso de estudio, manteniendo al mismo tiempo un alto nivel de eficiencia en el proceso de levantamiento del patrimonio. La documentación digital obtenida es sin duda la herramienta fundamental para el conocimiento y la conservación de un patrimonio en estado de semi abandono: solo unas cuevas están en uso hoy en día, y la mayoría de ellas presentan un estado de daño importante. A partir del proceso de levantamiento, se analizan las cuestiones metodológicas peculiares de la tipología del caso de estudio –es decir una arquitectura subterránea en un entorno urbano– que intervienen a la hora de redactar un proyecto de levantamiento, teniendo también en cuenta aspectos relativos a la definición de estándares para el levantamiento. Se proponen además metodologías computacionales que a través la implementación de una definición algorítmica –reutilizable para casos parecidos– nos ayudan a profundizar ulteriormente el nivel de conocimiento del objeto de estudio en una óptica más amplia de automatización de procesos y enriquecimiento informativo de los modelos construidos. Los resultados obtenidos representan un importante testimonio de una relevante tipología de patrimonio arquitectónico local, así como un punto de partida para ulteriores análisis sobre la optimización del proceso de levantamiento en este escenario peculiar.
