auditPapers.title: Economic Change, Silver, and the Plague of 664–687 in England
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Bede and other authors describe a destructive wave of plague sweeping across Britain and Ireland in the period 664–87. In the decades around and after this time, the English kingdoms saw rapid economic changes as urban settlements grew, monasteries were founded, and a large silver currency appeared. Here, it is proposed that these developments were influenced by the effects of the plague. Exact levels of mortality are uncertain, but the survivors may have had the capacity to produce more, and more diverse, goods. Relatively weak seigneurial powers on the part of landlords meant that non-elite cultivators became a more important economic constituency in these circumstances, while elites turned in two directions: to development of small but intensively worked central farms, and to liquidation of large stocks of silver, which enabled them to profit by engaging with a diverse body of partners. This liquidation took the form of a much expanded currency of silver pennies, which provides a case-study of monetization as an important yet comparatively short-term economic change.

auditPapers.title: Decolonizing Vietnam War Syllabi
auditPapers.abstract: The essence of this AHR History Lab forum was to identify a recent work of scholarship that proved to be a game-changer, either for teaching or researching about the Vietnam wars. Without question, the biggest shake-up in the field over the past dozen or so years has been the emergence of a measured, archivally based literature on various aspects of both South and North Vietnam’s conduct and experiences of their mid-twentieth century conflicts. The massive canon of work about the Vietnam wars, which has for too long danced to the beat of one outsized American hand clapping, is now fully cast (or much closer to it). Scholarship about South Vietnam by myself, Philip Catton (Diem’s Final Failure: Prelude to America’s War in Vietnam), Edward Miller (Misalliance: Ngo Dinh Diem, the United States, and the Fate of South Vietnam), Geoff Stewart (Vietnam’s Lost Revolution: Ngo Dinh Diem’s Failure to Build an Independent Nation, 1955-–1963), and Van Nguyen-Marshall (Between War and the State: Civil Society in South Vietnam, 1954-1975), among others, has illuminated the inner workings of the state with which the United States was so fatefully aligned from 1954 to 1975.1 This literature reveals South Vietnam’s autonomy, its infighting, its ideological currents, its deep flaws, and also at times its strength, legitimacy, and even nobility. And works about North Vietnam by Pierre Asselin, Lien-Hang T. Nguyen, Ang Cheng Guan, Tuong Vu, and others have enabled us to assess Hanoi’s war with the United States as a strategic contest between two legitimate—albeit asymmetrically powerful—states. This replaces the conventional view of the conflict as a war waged by a great power against a weak national entity, which has been rendered alternately, and two-dimensionally, as either a patriotic victim of neo-imperialist violence or a diabolical puppet of Sino-Soviet overlords.2 Taken together, this new body of work not only has helped to answer long-standing historiographical questions but, by focusing on the internal complexity of the two Vietnams, has shifted the very terms of scholarly debate away from questions related to the Cold War balance of power and toward issues of Vietnamese decolonization, sovereignty, nationalism, strategy, diplomacy, politics, and civil society. I find myself unable to single out any one of these paradigm-shifting works as more enlightening or influential to my scholarship than the rest, though in sum their influence is profound. Pierre Asselin’s Vietnam’s American War: A History, however, stands out as particularly transformative for teaching students about Vietnam’s war with the United States as a complex, multisided, and multisited conflict that defies pithy characterization.3 The book enables teachers to introduce students to some key elements of the scholarly turn discussed above in a clear, engaging, and digestible package.

auditPapers.title: Analysis of modern strategies for using artificial intelligence technologies in the creation of fantasy content
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This study explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the creation of fantasy narratives, examining the new possibilities AI offers for authors and readers and its impact on the genre’s evolution. The study used literature review, textual analysis, comparative analysis, data analysis, experimental methods, ethical and legal examination, and data processing methods using Natural Language Processing software. Through analysis of films, video games, and qualitative text review, the research found that modern technologies—particularly AI and computer graphics—have greatly enhanced the visualization of fantasy worlds, contributing to the genre’s growing popularity. Interactive AI-driven platforms enable customized experiences, increasing engagement and satisfaction among audiences. A significant finding is that contemporary fantasy works, while retaining traditional elements like the struggle between good and evil, magic, and adventure, are now incorporating modern socio-cultural and political themes. This blend preserves the genre’s appeal to diverse audiences while keeping it relevant in today’s context. Additionally, AI opens new avenues for authors by aiding in overcoming creative blocks, generating fresh ideas, and constructing interactive worlds where readers can shape the plot or create their own characters. This not only accelerates the creative process but also enriches storytelling with more varied narratives. The study concludes that fantasy remains a powerful tool for cultural and social expression and that AI holds great potential for the genre's future growth, promising more innovative and inclusive experiences for audiences.

auditPapers.title: Improving topic modeling for literary studies: a hybrid model combined with Word2Vec visualization in the case of Robinson Crusoe
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Topic modeling techniques, initially developed for the analysis of short texts, often face challenges when applied to literary research due to the complexity of the literary language and length of the text. Algorithms that typically yield clear and distinct topics for concise informative or opinionated texts often produce ambiguous and overlapping results in literary contexts. This article explores the application of one of the most popular topic modeling techniques, latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), in the analysis of fiction and addresses these central questions regarding the effectiveness and interpretation of LDA topics through a case study of Robinson Crusoe. It proposes combining the Word2Vec method with LDA analysis to render topic modeling results more readable by mapping topics words in a three-dimensional space where semantically related words are placed close to each other. Furthermore, this integrated approach undergoes validation using various children’s editions of the novel and other works by the same author to assess its effectiveness. It is found that the combined method is capable of differentiating subtle changes in children’s editions and other novels. This study highlights the promising potential of LDA in literary research and underscores the importance of visualization techniques for nuanced interpretations of LDA topics.

auditPapers.title: Stephen Robertson. Harlem in Disorder: A Spatial History of How Racial Violence Changed in 1935.
auditPapers.abstract: I cannot say that I have encountered a project that has inspired me to think as deeply about the form of a monograph and the many functions it can serve as Stephen Robertson’s Harlem in Disorder: A Spatial History of How Racial Violence Changed in 1935. More than an ebook, this digital project demonstrates the still untapped capacities of the internet to inform how we create knowledge, and how and why we present this knowledge in the ways we do. Additionally, it encourages this reader to think more audaciously about inviting audiences of different levels of preparation, varied curiosities, and diverse physical and cognitive abilities into the oftentimes opaque practices of professional historical production. In this book, Robertson echoes the historiographical refrain that the 1935 riot in Harlem indicates a transformation of the nature, motivations, and practices of “riots” in the United States precipitated by some racial event, in this case rumors that sixteen-year-old Lino Rivera, Puerto Rican and racialized as Black by observers, had been assaulted and killed at the Kress department store after being caught shoplifting. The resultant “disorder,” Robertson is more careful than others to call it, boiled over from persistent economic discrimination by white-owned businesses against Black Harlemites. The participants looted businesses, vandalized white- and Chinese-owned establishments while purposefully sparing Black-owned ones, and physically attacked some white people.

auditPapers.title: Potential and limitations of adhesive identification on museum curated metal objects
auditPapers.abstract: • Potential to identify ancient adhesives on museum-curated metal objects. • Chemical identifications demonstrate exploitation of various adhesive materials. • Wax related conservation treatments may cause limitations in adhesive interpretation. • Iron age objects highlight combined material technologies or réseaux opératoires . In the earlier periods, adhesives were used predominantly for hafting tools and weapons, but their functionality evolved with the advent of ceramic technologies, with use widening to pottery repair and ornamentation. Limited attention has been directed towards their application in metalwork. It is unclear whether the scarcity of adhesives described in association with metal is due to preservation factors, such as corrosion-related issues, or to a research emphasis on other materials associated with metalwork such as coral, amber, and glass. To address this issue, we conducted chemical analyses including gas chromatography – mass spectrometry on 18 adhesive residues present on 15 objects from France and England dated from the mid first millennium BCE to the first century CE. These artefacts include jewellery, vessels, harness fittings and weaponry components. Our findings suggest that a range of adhesives were employed in assembling and applying decoration to diverse types of metal objects. These include birch tar and conifer resins, also bitumen and possibly beeswax, which have not been reported before. However, the application of waxes in past conservation practices introduces challenges that can potentially constrain the interpretation of molecular analyses. Our results have implications for the understanding of the adhesive technologies, and illustrate the potential of identifying adhesives linked to metal ornamentation. They further demonstrate the widening application of long-established adhesive technologies within the framework of increasingly complex craft specialisms.

auditPapers.title: Radiocarbon mortar dating of newly uncovered medieval ceiling paintings at Stavanger Cathedral, Norway
auditPapers.abstract: Radiocarbon dating was carried out on mortar substrates beneath newly uncovered wall paintings on the vaulted ceiling of Stavanger Cathedral, one of only three such examples in Norway and the first uncovered in the last 50 years. Charcoal/wood dates produced a range of calibrated ages, from the early 11th to late 13th century AD. Variation in ages is consistent with wood of different ages (‘old wood’ effect) being used as fuel in lime production or as aggregate in the mortar. Ramped pyrolysis radiocarbon dating was applied to lime lumps extracted from two of the bulk mortars (spatially separated). The 5–6 fractions of CO 2 trapped at different thermal decomposition ranges produced radiocarbon ages that were in excellent internal statistical agreement for each sample and also in excellent statistical agreement between the two samples from different sampling locations. These dates are furthermore in statistical agreement with the youngest of the charcoal/wood samples dated. The results securely date the mortar substrate of the painting's plaster to 1216–1271 cal. AD (99.7 %) and raise the likelihood that the mortar and associated paintings pre-date a fire in Stavanger in 1272, traditionally associated with a phase of rebuilding of the cathedral. As the first in-depth published scientific dating at Stavanger Cathedral and more broadly to medieval wall paintings in Norway, the results highlight the potential of ramped pyrolysis or thermal decomposition mortar dating approaches to understanding not only building archaeologies, but the cultural heritage embedded in these structures.

Therefore, AGNES proved to be an essential and effective addition to traditional search methods. Finally, our study highlighted the fact that clear terminology to describe Vlaardingen Culture sites is presently lacking. As such, the study provided interesting insights into the terminologies employed in development-led archaeology.

auditPapers.title: Heritage Data Governance in Regeneration: Lessons from England’s High Street Heritage Action Zones
auditPapers.journal: Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology
auditPapers.abstract: Heritage data management has become increasingly critical as regeneration initiatives generate vast quantities of digital information, yet systematic approaches to data governance remain inconsistent across the sector. auditPapers.title: On the literary landscapes of vector embeddings
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract From the early use of TF-IDF to the high-dimensional outputs of deep learning, vector space embeddings of text, at a scale ranging from token to document, are at the heart of all machine analysis and generation of text. Specifically, we compare TF-IDF, Doc2vec and several Transformer-based embeddings on a variety of text-specific tasks. Using industry-standard BISAC codes as a proxy for genre, we compare embeddings in their ability to preserve information about genre. We further compare these embeddings in their ability to encode inter- and intra-book similarity. All of these comparisons take place at the book “chunk” (1,024 tokens) level. We find Transformer-based (“neural”) embeddings to be best, in the sense of their ability to respect genre and authorship, although almost all embedding techniques produce sensible constructions of a “literary landscape” as embodied by the Books3 corpus. These experiments suggest the possibility of using deep learning embeddings not only for advances in generative AI, but also a potential tool for book discovery and as an aid to various forms of more traditional comparative textual analysis.

auditPapers.title: Towards efficient and accessible geoparsing of U.K. local media: A benchmark dataset and LLM-based approach
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract Location mentions in local news are crucial for examining issues like spatial inequalities, news deserts and the impact of media ownership on news diversity. To address these challenges, we identify key considerations for successful geoparsing and review spatially oriented local media studies, finding over-reliance on limited geospatial vocabularies, limited toponym disambiguation and inadequate validation of methods. These findings underscore the need for adaptable and robust solutions, and recent advancements in fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) for geoparsing offer a promising direction by simplifying technical implementation and excelling at understanding contextual nuances. However, their application to U.K. local media – marked by fine-grained geographies and colloquial place names – remains underexplored due to the absence of benchmark datasets. This gap hinders researchers’ ability to evaluate and refine geoparsing methods for this domain. To address this, we introduce the Local Media UK Geoparsing (LMUK-Geo) dataset, a hand-annotated corpus of U.K. local news articles designed to support the development and evaluation of geoparsing pipelines. We also propose an LLM-driven approach for toponym disambiguation that replaces fine-tuning with accessible prompt engineering. Using LMUK-Geo, we benchmark our approach against a fine-tuned method. Both perform well on the novel dataset: the fine-tuned model excels in minimising coordinate-error distances, while the prompt-based method offers a scalable alternative for district-level classification, particularly when relying on predictions agreed upon by multiple models. Our contributions establish a foundation for geoparsing local media, advancing methodological frameworks and practical tools to enable systematic and comparative research.

auditPapers.title: Microbial biodeterioration of historic wood based on classical and omics methods with model studies
auditPapers.abstract: • Moulds, bacteria and algae responsible for biodeterioration of wood artifacts were identified. • Microbial consortia have higher biodeterioration potential than single cultures. • Dark conditions favoured the growth of microorganisms on the wood. • Light or dark determined the microorganisms metabolism on wood. A variety of methods, including culture methods, MALDI-TOF MS, and high-throughput sequencing, were used to identify microorganisms. Model studies were then conducted on oak wood samples under light and dark conditions, using single isolates from the tested samples and a mixed culture of isolated bacterial, mould, and algal strains. Changes in the samples were investigated by metabolomics analysis using UHPLC-MS/MS. Colour change was assessed in the CIELAB system. We also measured water absorptivity, pH levels, and degradation of cellulose and lignin. The most frequently isolated microorganisms were bacteria from the phyla Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria , particularly Actinomycetes, Cytophagales, Sphingomonadales, Burkholderia, Bacillus, Staphylococcus ; fungi from the phyla Ascomycota and Basidiomycota , with genera including Cladosporium, Penicillium, Aspergillus Cladophialophora, and Pleurotheciella ; green algae belonging to the phylum Chlorophyta , including the genera Chloroidium, Stichococcus, and Diplosphaerea . Model tests confirmed that these microorganisms are capable of altering the properties of wood, resulting in colour and pH changes, increased water absorption. Wood biodeterioration was found primarily to depend on the types of microorganisms present and on the light or dark conditions, which influenced the profiles of the metabolic pathways and the direction of the degradation process. Dark conditions favoured the growth of microorganisms on the wood and significantly increased water absorptivity, also contributed to yellowing, as confirmed by the production of β-carotene. Light conditions stimulated the activation of metabolic pathways related to photosynthesis, primary metabolism, and the TCA cycle. Although they did not favour the growth of microorganisms, light conditions triggered adaptive mechanisms, as evidenced by the production of more diverse and higher quantities of lipids in the microbial biofilms.

auditPapers.title: Advancements in adaptive thermal comfort models: Application to the case study of Le Corbusierʼs Maison Jeanneret
auditPapers.abstract: • Historic buildings face discomfort and energy issues due to high permeability. • Adaptive models suit historic buildings by integrating adaptive mechanisms. • A 1-year study in Le Corbusier's Maison Jeanneret analysed adaptation. • Models consistently predict sensations, but discrepancies exist in neutrality. • Neutral temperatures ranged from 21.5 °C to 23.0 °C, close to PMVʼs 22.3 °C. Historic buildings often face discomfort and energy consumption challenges due to their high permeability to external conditions. While Fangerʼs heat balance and adaptive models are widely employed for thermal comfort assessment, recent advancements have introduced adaptive heat balance models aimed at integrating adaptive mechanisms from real environments. While promising for predictive accuracy, the choice of a model can impact both building comfort and energy consumption. However, there is a lack of systematic, long-term application of these models in real case studies, revealing potential differences among models. Thus, through a 1-year campaign in Le Corbusier's Maison Jeanneret, this study aims to: (i) critically assess the evolution of adaptive heat balance models, (ii) quantify differences in comfort prediction, and (iii) analyse the inclusion of adaptive capacities. auditPapers.title: Epistemic capture through specialization in post-World War II parliamentary debate
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract This article investigates how parliamentary debate in the Dutch House of Representatives (“Tweede Kamer”) (1945–1995) narrowed as MPs turned into domain specialists. We call this narrowing epistemic capture: a few experts progressively bound what can be said. To detect epistemic capture, we deploy a three-layer computational pipeline. Latent-Dirichlet topic modeling converts 8.2 million sentences into 250 semantic themes; Pointwise Mutual Information networks connect themes within six-month windows; Louvain clustering traces the birth, drift and endurance of topical communities. Capture appears on every scale. Macro-level: network modularity almost doubles after 1960 while density falls, marking compartmentalized debate. Meso-level: cabinet turnovers act as “reset switches”: topic-neighborhood similarity drops in the half-year after a new coalition forms, then anneals along partisan lines. Micro-level: enduring communities – foreign policy, agriculture and education – lock topics and MPs together for decades, yet resistance to capture is visible in distinct contentious topics. These multiscale patterns show how 20th-century Dutch parliamentary debate saw a rise of technical specialism that significantly constrained the breadth of political debate. Methodologically, the study demonstrates the value of structural (network) distant reading over purely lexical counts and offers a transferable workflow for measuring how democratic discourse undergoes structural transformations.

The ED-XRF and micro-Raman results do not exclude the possibility that parts of the painting were executed by del Sarto. The IFF method also uncovered several “ pentimenti ”, including a small (human?) figure, which opened intriguing comparisons with other works by Andrea del Sarto.

auditPapers.title: Metronome: tracing variation in poetic meters via local sequence alignment
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract All poetic forms come from somewhere. Prosodic templates can be copied for generations, altered by individuals, imported from foreign traditions, or fundamentally changed under the pressures of language evolution. Yet, these relationships are notoriously difficult to trace across languages and times. This article introduces an unsupervised method for detecting structural similarities in poems using local sequence alignment. The method relies on encoding poetic texts as strings of prosodic features using a four-letter alphabet; these sequences are then aligned to derive a distance measure based on weighted symbol (mis)matches. Local alignment allows poems to be clustered according to emergent properties of their underlying prosodic patterns. We release an implementation of the algorithm as a Python package with an open license.

auditPapers.title: Love’s Next Meeting: The Forgotten History of Homosexuality and the Left in American Culture By Aaron S. Lecklider
auditPapers.abstract: Thirty years after red and lavender scares washed over American politics, John D’Emilio revealed that the historical connection between homosexuality and communism was not just a figment of the imagination of early Cold War politicians. These same leftists were themselves soon purged when the organization they created, the Mattachine Society—like so many American unions, industries, and groups—banished actual and suspected communists from its ranks. In Love’s Next Meeting, Aaron Lecklider finally provides a full-scale, nuanced, and sophisticated account of the relationship between the American Left and homosexuality in the years between the Bolshevik Revolution and the 1950s. This book is anchored in the Popular Front era, when leftist activism and influence in the U.S. was at its height and there was not yet an organized gay movement. Lecklider notes accurately that much scholarship in queer history “discounts the Old Left due to its perceived homophobia;” his book replaces that stereotype with vivid, complicated portraits of leftists who “brought sexual dissidence and the Left into conversation” (6). Confronting the task of reconstructing people and communities who were deliberately cautious about leaving written traces, historians have often turned to records kept by state agents. Often, the repression itself becomes a key focus of our narratives. Lecklider, by contrast, keeps his attention squarely on the lives and especially the ideas of queer leftists in these decades, as well as their fellow travelers, sympathizers, and critics.

auditPapers.abstract: The increasing use of GIS (Geographic Information Systems) and computational methods in archaeological research runs into various methodological and interpretative roadblocks when used for non-ideal or incomplete datasets. This paper makes use of sampled legacy data on the Indian Lower Palaeolithic obtained by the authors from the Archaeological Survey of India’s annual publication called Indian Archaeology – A Review. It has a three-fold focus: a) How a simple GIS process such as geo-coding can run into various obstacles when the dataset in question is not ideal, i.e. inconsistent in detail and format; b) How preferential archaeological sampling in a region can be better understood through an appreciation of the social, political and economic realities of the time; and c) Additionally, a temporal perspective on the sequence of site surveys, the nature of their reporting and the changing geographic locations of reported sites over two post-Independence decades revealed nuanced information on the changing historical narratives of Indian prehistory within global context. This is a pilot study of the use of geocoding services to enhance and analyse an imperfect and challenging legacy dataset. This study also demonstrates that geocoded sites are not necessarily accurate, but rather indicate the most likely option. The distant structure (ie. top down) and application of GIS make it intrinsically divorced from local reality. Including vernacular sensitivity in GIS, thus making it better suited to work with non-western datasets, would make it far more accurate and useful.

auditPapers.title: INDIAN EDITION: Slandering the Sacred: Blasphemy Law and the Shaping of Indian Secularism By J. Barton Scott. U.S. EDITION: Slandering the Sacred: Blasphemy Law and Religious Affect in Colonial India By J. Barton Scott
auditPapers.abstract: NOTE: Page references throughout are to the Indian edition. Writing about Colonial India, Christopher Pinney has used the term iatrogenic to describe state interventions that were intended as cures or solutions to anti-colonial speech, but made the original problem worse. In this astonishingly wide-ranging (thematically, chronologically, theoretically) book Scott repeatedly draws our attention to the iatrogenic nature of blasphemy law in India from the mid-1920s onwards; intended to regulate religious conflict, the laws in fact fueled it. Scott argues that this was because it gave social actors the vocabulary and the tools to employ law’s attention to their aggrieved sentiments. As he memorably puts it, “polemicists learned to speak law’s language, alleging that their ‘religious feelings’ had been outraged, and thus performatively constituting those feelings in the very act of transmitting them to others… Law contained the script for communal violence. It educated its subjects in outrage” (18). The central concern of the book is thus to illustrate the cultural production of law (taking blasphemy law as an exemplar) as well as the entanglements of law and religion as “technologies for the governance of emotion.” (27) Part I of the book focuses on the making of a specific law (section 295A of the Indian Penal Code, hereafter IPC) in the 1920s; Part II on the IPC’s draftsman, Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800-1859), his “private self-government” and its implications for a public law governing millions; Part III sketches in great detail the animating ideology and activities of the Arya Samaj from the 1870s through the 1920s, in order to better understand the context of the law’s application and utilization by non-state actors.

auditPapers.title: “They Do Not Have Physiognomies of Their Own”: Tracking Racialization of Maritime Professions in the Eighteenth-Century Portuguese Empire
auditPapers.abstract: Abstract During the second half of the long eighteenth century, various nations and empires began keeping records of sailors arriving and departing certain ports. In Portugal, all sailors were required to register at the Junta do Comércio (the board of trade), a measure enacted in the wake of a ban on the importation of enslaved people into the kingdom in 1761; an exemption was later made for enslaved sailors or crew members. This article draws on a data set of 344 sailors registered in logs of the Junta’s Lisbon office, dating from 1767, when the board was formed, to 1788, when it was absorbed into the royal court. Our analysis shows how the Junta’s logbooks became a contested space in which enslaved and free sailors of color attempted to define their own occupations, racial identities, and legal status in terms that frequently conflicted with the increasingly homogenized racialization of the state. We link the patterns of increased racialization of sailor records in Portugal to wider Atlantic developments in Brazil, France, Britain, and elsewhere to show how, during a period of immense political, economic, and social change in the long eighteenth century, racial categories were created, expanded, and disseminated across empires. The racialized vocabulary and mechanisms of anti-Blackness were developed, tested, and implemented via maritime networks during an age of capitalist and imperialist growth.

auditPapers.title: Bystander Society: Conformity and Complicity in Nazi Germany and the Holocaust . By Mary Fulbrook
auditPapers.abstract: This is an important book on a highly relevant topic. Author Mary Fulbrook makes a daring attempt to offer new insights to an already extensively explored field: the question of (ordinary) Germans’ complicity in the Nazi crimes of World War II and the Holocaust. While Fulbrook’s essential research question is not original, it remains crucial. What conditions and factors allowed the radical regime under Hitler to “kidnap” German society to go along with committing heinous crimes? To be clear, Fulbrook does not bother querying the degree of knowledge among ordinary Germans about the crimes committed in the name of their country. The perhaps stubborn postwar myth—upheld by many Germans post-1945—according to which most knew nothing or very little has long been debunked. But to ask what Germans knew, Fulbrook says, is to pose the wrong question. Instead, she urges the reader to investigate what Germans made of what they knew. The book thus concentrates not on the doings of German perpetrators and their collaborators but instead sets a clear focus on the silent majority of Germans, what Fulbrook refers to as a bystander society. Her argument is sobering. Conformity alone was sufficient for the regime to go unchecked (181). Popular perceptions and (in)actions were not shaped by a morally weak society but by the calculation of the relative risks versus the potential benefits of different forms of action (though the discussion of a balance sheet is quite one-sided and the discussion on how Germans benefitted from Hitler’s regime comes too short). Despite possible inner misgivings, most Germans went along with the system, played their allotted roles and in effect, helped the radicalization of the regime (341). These bystanders, according to Fulbrook, became over time and to varying degrees “complicit—whether through looking away, condoning violence or more actively sustaining the system.” (375).
